# Nava-vraja-mahima. Vol. Six

## Dedication

Although I have written Nava-vraja-mahima for the pleasure of all Vaisnavas who either physically or mentally reside in Vrndavana, I dedicate this book to those whose hearts are devoted to Radha-Syamasundara and New Vraja-dhama. It is my hope that they will pass their time in this way:

*iha vatsan samacarayad*  
*iha nah svami jagau vamsim*  
*iti sasram gadato me*  
*yamuna-tire dinam yayat*

**“Here our Lord herded the calves, and here He played the flute. I pray that I may pass my days shedding tears as I speak these words on the Yamuna’s shore.” (Sri Raghupati Upadhyaya)**

## Chapter 24 - Ujani to Bhandira-vata

Obeisances to the sacred Yamuna River! Saints describe her as a moat of black mascara encircling Bhauma Vrndavana. In New Vraja-dhama I see her as the stem of the golden lotus of the holy dhama.

This chapter and the next describe Krsna’s pastimes along or near that holy river. I feel inspired, then, to begin by offering some words of praise to Yamuna-devi, the purest of all transcendental rivers.

I pray that the river who offers lotuses to Vraja, who embraces the Lord with her waters, and who dances to the sound of His names, will manifest the whitecaps of her own glories upon these pages.

Since only the Supreme Lord knows all the truths about His associates, I begin by citing Lord Caitanya’s praise of the Yamuna, words He spoke in ecstasy just after accepting sannyasa.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu happily said,

*cid-ananda-bhanoh sada nanda-sunoh para-prema-patri drava-brahma-gatri*  
*aghanam lavitri jagat-ksema-dhatri pavitri-kriyan no vapur mitra-putri*

**“O river Yamuna! You are the blissful spiritual water that gives love to the son of Nanda Maharaja. You are the same as the water of the spiritual world, for you can vanquish all our offences —**

**“And the sinful reactions incurred in life. You are the creator of all auspicious things tor the world. ? daughter of the sun god \[Mitra-putrl\], kindly purity us by your pious activities.”**

By describing Yamuna-devi as both the spiritual water that gives love to Krsna and as the daughter of the sun god, Caitanya Mahaprabhu tells us that Yamuna-devi is both a gopi and a goddess.

But who is the goddess, and who is the gopi? Kalindi, Krsna’s queen in Dvaraka, is the goddess. And Visakha, one of Radha’s favourite friends, is the gopi. Now let us hear more about these truths.

It is said that the demigoddess Dhara was a partial expansion of Mother Yas'oda. In the same way, the goddess Kalindi, who married Krsna in Dvaraka, is a partial expansion of Visakha, Radha’s friend.

The main rivers of Goloka Vrndavana are the Manasa-gariga and the Yamuna. Prema-varada-marijari is the personified form of the Ganga, and Visakha-devi is the personified form of the Yamuna.

Indeed, Visakha-devi’s loving desire to serve Krsna manifested itself in a second body as the Yamuna River, which also accompanied Krsna to this world in order to give Him bliss.

It was Nanda Maharaja’s younger brother Sannanda who convinced the Vraja-vasis to move from Mahavana to Vrndavana. At that time he narrated the history of how the Yamuna descended from Goloka.

In the presence of the elders of Nanda’s kingdom, Sri Sannanda told how Krsna had ordered Vrndavana, Govardhana Hill, and the Yamuna to appear on earth to facilitate His pastimes.

As Yamuna-devi happily prepared to leave Goloka to serve the Lord, the Ganga and another spiritual river, the Viraja, eager to see the Supreme Lord’s pastimes on earth, merged into Yamuna’s waters.

Thus, because water from the spiritual sources of both the Ganges and the great Causal Ocean, Viraja, are present within the Yamuna, she is celebrated in this world as the most purifying of all rivers.

From Goloka, the river Yamuna passed through countless universes until she found the opening in the covering of this universe made by Vamanadeva’s toe, through which the Ganga was already flowing.

Taking permission from her sister Ganga-devi, Yamuna also entered this universe, descending with Ganga onto Dhruvaloka, from there to Brahmaloka, and then to the demigods’ planets, one after another.

On the peak of Mount Sumeru, Yamuna-devi flowed south to Mount Kalinda and thus became known as the Kalindi, while Ganga flowed north to Mount Himavat and became known as the Himavati.

Kalindi flowed to earth, breaking the rocks on the slopes of Mount Kalinda and purifying everything she touched, until she arrived at Khandava forest near the place where Indraprastha would be built.

At that time, the sun god’s daughter Yamuna — who was an expansion of Visakha and whose tears formed a celestial river that merged with the spiritual Yamuna — was staying in the Khandava forest.

Within the depths of the river, Surya had constructed a mansion for his daughter, who performed austerities without compromise. Her sole intention was to attain the Supreme Lord Visnu as her husband.

After Krsna had moved from Vraja to Dvaraka, He would come to this forest with Arjuna. At that time He came to know of Kalindi’s desire, accepted Her proposal, and married her in His capital.

From Khandava forest Yamuna-devi continued to flow south to Vraja-mandala, through Vrndavana, Mathura, and then to Mahavana, where she would be born as the daughter of Pavana-gopa.

Although she was reluctant to leave Krsna’s holy land, the Yamuna River had to continue her course to the sea. But before doing so she embraced Vrndavana by again flowing westward.

Then, bowing three times to Vraja-mandala and flowing parallel to the Ganga, Yamuna-devi turned east through Prayaga, where she continued to flow to the sea along the same riverbed as her sister.

After reaching the ocean, the two rivers parted ways: Ganga-devi flowed down to the lower planets and Patalaloka, while Yamuna made her way up through the universe and finally returned to Goloka.

This narration traces the descent and course of the Yamuna within this world and shows how her spiritual waters arc the liquid form of Lord Krsna’s intimate associates, Queen Kalindi and Visakha-devi.

No river is as sacred as the Yamuna. Srila Prabhupada writes,

**“As far as sanctity is concerned, the river Yamuna is more directly connected with Lord Krsna than the Ganges.**

**“The Lord sanctified the river Yamuna from the beginning of His transcendental pastimes in the world. While His father Vasudeva was crossing the Yamuna with baby Lord Krsna —**

**“\[Looking\] for a safe place at Gokula on the other bank of the river from Mathura, the Lord fell down in the river, and by the dust of His lotus feet the river at once became sanctified.”**

It is said that Jiva Gosvami once travelled to the court of the emperor in Agra to participate in a lengthy, heated debate with other scholars over which river was greater, the Yamuna or the Ganga.

Citing evidence given by Srila Rupa Gosvami, Sri Jiva glorified the Ganges as water that had washed Krsna’s lotus feet, but explained that as Krsna’s own consort the Yamuna was more glorious still.

Pleased with Jiva Gosvami, Emperor Akbar wanted to offer him a gift, and so Sri Jiva requested some paper he had noticed in his court. At that time paper was still a rare commodity reserved for aristocracy.

All glories to Yamuna-devi! She is known to the people of the world as the daughter of the sun god but is worshipped in Vrndavana as the beloved girlfriend of Radha and Krsna, Visakha-devi.

The divine Yamuna never leaves Vraja. Just as Krsna manifests His Vasudeva form when He goes outside of Vraja, the Yamuna manifests her partial expansion Kalindi when she flows to other places.

Let us now return to our glorification of Yamuna-devi by elaborating upon the aforementioned verse Caitanya Mahaprabhu spoke in a trance of ecstasy, mistaking the river Ganges for the sacred Yamuna.

Because the Yamuna originates from Goloka Vrndavana, where all water is nectar (toyam armrtam), Caitanya Mahaprabhu praises her waters as completely spiritual (drava-brahma-gatri).

It is interesting to note the Lord’s use of the compound *drava-brahma-gatri*, which means that all of Yamuna’s limbs, or parts (gatri), are molten or liquefied (drava) spiritual substance (brahma).

In connection with the birth of Marici, scripture says*,*

*raso yah paramadharah sac-cid-ananda-laksanah*  
*brahmety-upanisad-gitah sa eva yamuna svayam*  
*pavanayasya jagatah sarid bhutva sasara ha*

**“The flood of eternal, blissful spiritual nectar, which the Upanisads call brahma, has become a flowing river named Yamuna, who purifies the three worlds with her transcendental waters.”**

Visakha is an expansion of Sri Radha, Krsna’s pleasure potency, and so Lord Caitanya has specifically described the Yamuna’s spiritual identity (cit) as a manifestation of bliss (ananda).

In his translation of the phrase cit-ananda-bhanoh (“of the direct manifestation of spiritual energy and bliss”), Srila Prabhupada does not specifically mention bhanoh, which means “of the sun.”

The verse itself mentions mitra-putri, “the daughter of the sun god,” which refers to the goddess Yamuna. But, as daughters of the devas, demigoddesses are not “direct manifestations of spiritual energy.”

Thus, a meaning of bhanoh that avoids redundancy and maintains contextual integrity is “the original sun, Krsna.” The verse then refers to the spiritual Yamuna, who is Visakha-devi.

We may ask why the spiritual nature and personified forms of the Yamuna are not visible to us. The answer is that such things cannot he perceived by the materially conditioned mind and senses.

The mind and senses of an advanced Vaisnava are anointed with the same spiritual potency of which the Yamuna is comprised, so such a devotee can see her eternal transcendental form, free from doubt.

Spiritually realised souls of such calibre can see Krsna and His associates sport in the dark waters of the Yamuna, whose banks are lined with desire trees, cintamani staircases, and blooming groves.

**\* \* \* \***

In the verse under discussion, Caitanya Mahaprabhu goes on to praise Yamuna-devi by saying, *aghanam lavitri*: “You can vanquish all our offences and the sinful reactions incurred in life.”

It is well known that sacred waters free one from sin. Srila Prabhupada’s translation indicates another thing we can he freed from — offence. This topic will later he discussed in depth.

Now let us hear one explanation how Yamuna, in her form as a goddess, acquired special powers to purify, powers that are eternally and supremely present in the Yamuna’s spiritual form from Goloka.

Soft-hearted Yamuna was acutely suffering to see the distress of conditioned souls. She pondered what she could do to alleviate the cause of their distress — sin — and the distress itself—reactions to sin.

Once, on her birthday, Yamuna invited her brother Yamaraja to an opulent feast she had prepared with many savoury and sweet dishes. The feast was so pleasing to Yamaraja that he offered her a boon.

Seizing the opportunity, Yamuna turned to the all-powerful controller of death and said, “Dear brother! Please grant me the boon that whoever bathes in my waters with faith on this day —

“Will be freed from the tendency to sin, from sinful reaction, and, rising above the threefold miseries, freed from the cycle of birth and death.” Clapping his hands with satisfaction, Yama said, “So be it!”

Since that time, when observing rhe festival of Bhratr-dvitiya, or Yama-dvitiya — in which girls honour their brothers — people bathe in the Yamuna, knowing her waters to he especially potent on that day.

Scriptures confirm that the benefit derived from bathing in the Yamuna on any day is one hundred times greater than that gained from bathing in the Ganga, not to speak of other holy rivers.

Lord Varaha told Bhumi, “Within Vraja, the Yamuna, with its many secret bathing places, is undoubtedly one hundred times more sacred than the Ganga, and the person who bathes there becomes glorious.”

The way a sinner is purified and transformed into a righteous man by bathing in the river Yamuna can be compared to the way in which iron is transformed into gold by a philosophers’ stone.

Whether one is a faithless materialist, an uneducated ritualist, a respectful jnani or yogi, or a faithful devotee, a hath in the Yamuna transforms the bather by lifting the burden of past karma.

Still, the benefit one derives from the Yamuna is proportional to one’s faith, and so the bather’s benefit may range from diminished sinful reactions to liberation from the sins of billions of births.

Yamuna-devi always tastes the bliss of pure devotion. Thus her purpose in freeing people from suffering is not to facilitate material enjoyment hut to make devotional service to Krsna easier for them.

Despite the austerity involved, great devotees, including Srila Prabhupada, would bathe daily in the Yamuna, even during the winter, for this is an austerity that should never he abandoned.

If for some reason one is unable take a hath, merely sprinkling a few drops of water on one’s head or even touching the Yamuna will give the result of being freed from sin: one will become a saintly devotee.

Indeed, the mere sight of Yamuna’s charming waves enables the most sinful person to cross over the ocean of sin, and smelling the slightest fragrance of her waters stops the cycle of repeated birth and death.

Thus hy bathing in, touching, seeing, or smelling the Yamuna, or even hy thinking of performing any of these activities, Yamuna-devi frees us from suffering and opens for us the gateway to auspiciousness.

Srila Prabhupada writes that the Yamuna also vanquishes all our offences, which may include, amongst others, offences to the holy name or offences to the Deity.

When Rupa Gosvami writes that the Yamuna “burns away the greatest sins” (durmadoru-??pa), the word “greatest,” in terms of severity of effect, can be taken to mean offences to the holy name.

Those of us unfortunate enough to have committed offences to the holy names, especially offences to the Vaisnavas, should immerse ourselves in Yamuna’s watery embrace and pray for her shelter.

Narada Muni once told Maharaja Yudhisthira,

**“O Yudhisthira! One becomes virtuous if he takes a bath in the Yamuna, drinks the pure water, and sings her glories. Even her darsana gives auspicious results.**

**“A person who enters the Yamuna River and drinks its waters purifies seven generations of ancestors, and one who dies in the waters of the Yamuna \[or upon its banks\] goes to the supreme destination.”**

After praising the power of the Yamuna to purify conditioned souls of all reactions to past sins, Caitanya Mahaprabhu refers to her as *jagat-ksema-dhatri*, “the creator of all auspicious things for the world.”

Auspicious things (ksema) mean those things that guide us back home, back to Godhead — any goal other than Goloka is inauspicious. Those things that guide us back home can be direct or indirect.

Welfare work and religious piety are auspicious only indirectly; their immediate goal is not Goloka. But, guided by the Vedic system, they purify the heart and lead to direct auspiciousness — bhakti.

It is commonly known that Yamuna’s mercy easily fulfils one’s desires. Less intelligent men therefore serve her to get the results of making offerings to the ancestors and of executing horse sacrifices.

No doubt such people are elevated to heaven temporarily, but their real benefit is the unknown piety (ajnata-sukrti) they accrue, piety that matures until they are at last eligible to associate with Vaisnavas.

Materially auspicious acts pale in the light of real auspiciousness— pure devotional service — which is Yamuna-devi’s gift to the universe, especially to those who worship her in Vraja-mandala.

Bathing in the Yamuna is equal to visiting all other holy places. It is included in the acts of bhakti called pada-sevanam, which Srila Prabhupada says, “...help one advance in spiritual life very quickly.”

By serving Yamuna-devi, we not only purify our hearts but also acquire sufficient spiritual strength to control our senses so that the saintly qualities of a true sadhu can awaken in us.

In the words of Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura,

*yasyasty aho kajjvala- jata-jata samantatah sa parikheva krsna*  
*namaj-janan majjanato visuddhan karoti ya krsna-hrdas tathapi*

**“They who offer respectful obeisances to the Yamuna, or bathe in her water, which is like a moat of black mascara encircling Vrndavana, transform into pure devotees carrying Krsna in their hearts.”**

Srila Rupa Gosvami declares that Yamuna-devi’s greatest kindness to devotees is to submerge them in “...a great flood of confidential pure devotional service to Sri Nandanandana.”

In other words, she gives love of God to those who actually desire to eternally reside near her banks in Goloka Vrndavana, serving Sri Krsna in the same way His eternal Vraja-vasi companions do.

Love for Krsna is true auspiciousness, for no one can enter Goloka without it. Devotees like Narottama Dasa Thakura pray to die in the Yamuna and thus be guaranteed their desired destination.

He sings, “As I leave my body, I shall place it in the Yamuna and while floating along chant, 'Jaya Radha-Govinda!’”

The word dhatri, from Lord Caitanya’s verse, is generally translated as “nurse,” a word that beautifully describes Yamuna-devi’s role as one who nurses devotees with all-auspicious pure devotional service.

Flowing throughout the three worlds, she attracts conditioned souls to Vrndavana, where she then awakens their attraction to Radha and Krsna and in due course gives them transcendental love (pr?m?).

Love for Krsna is rarely attained, and then only by divine grace. It appears first as a ray of sun on the horizon of the heart, softening it with divine emotions and awakening spiritual ecstasy within.

Because Yamuna-devi is the liquefied form of divine ecstasy in its most intimate feature as amorous love, she can transform anyone into a lover of Krsna by infusing him or her with these qualities.

As we shall now see, Yamuna-devi is authorised not only to freely distribute love for the son of Mother Yasoda to aspiring devotees but also to bestow love upon the Lord Himself.

**\* \* \* \***

Caitanya Mahaprabhu concludes His prayer with the words, *sada nanda-suno!} para-pr???-patri*: “O beautiful Yamuna River! You give love to the son of Nanda Maharaja.”

We know that Visakha-devi gives love to Krsna indirectly by helping Srimati Radharani love and serve Him as only Radharani can, but Visakha also gives Him love directly through her own loving service.

As Yamuna-devi, Visakha loves Krsna in her own ecstatic mood, but in ways uniquely suited to a river. It is for this reason that Visakha assumes that form: to serve Krsna in ways even a gopi cannot.

Similarly, the three presiding deities of the universe — Visnu, Brahma, and Siva — become hills in Vraja just to love and serve Krsna and the Vraja-vasis in ways otherwise unavailable to those Lords.

Yamuna pleases Krsna by giving love for Him to His devotees, by pleasing Krsna’s senses with her unique features, by facilitating His pastimes in various ways, and by her embrace.

We have already heard how Yamuna-devi bestows love of Krsna, an important way of showing her love for Him. In that way she expands His circle of companions and serves Him through those devotees.

Through her personal features, Yamuna pleases Krsna’s senses, causing her heart’s longing to flood her banks in ecstasy. Sukadeva Gosvami tells of Krsna’s reaction upon seeing Yamuna’s beauty.

Describing the Vraja-vasis’ move from Gokula, the sage says, “O King Pariksit! When Rama and Krsna saw Vrndavana, Govardhana, and the hanks of the river Yamuna, They both enjoyed great pleasure.”

Could it he that due to constant absorption in Him, the Yamuna has adopted Krsna’s silky blackish sheen — eschewing Visakha’s golden complexion—to certify that it is most suited to sports of love?

With the playful motions of her rolling waves, Yamuna worships Krsna’s lotus feet with offerings of flowers, while swans and other waterfowl sing arati songs of Krsna’s names, glories, and pastimes.

Intoxicated hy living within the Yamuna, jewelled fish regularly jump out of the water to catch a glimpse of the divine couple, or to invite Radha and Krsna to enter the nectar kingdom of Yamuna’s embrace.

Krsna’s pastimes take place all over Vraja; thus Yamuna-devi distributes herself in untold tributaries to serve Him at Govardhana, Varsana, Nandagrama, and along the breadth of Vrndavana forest.

The nature of love for Krsna is that it makes devotees’ greed for it increase. Yamuna is no exception. She flows to where Krsna enacts His pastimes just so that she can taste the mellows of loving devotion.

Her offerings of love include the ancient trees upon her hanks, from which cowherd boys often jump into the water, and beneath which they enjoy their lunch, rest when tired, and lovingly serve Krsna.

Yamuna’s nectarean water is an elixir for both the gopas and their thirsty cows, her riverside orchards a source of delectable fruits, and her gardens eager donors of flower ornaments for Krsna and His friends.

Each grove along her shore is a jewel that Yamuna-devi adds to Krsna’s treasure trove of loving pastimes. Her jewelled bathing ghatas are open invitations for Krsna to enjoy water sports with the gopis.

Krsna and His beloveds enter the river to swim, splash, and refresh themselves while Yamuna-devi submerges them, not in water, hut in the powerful currents of romantic love.

And at night, illuminated hy silvery moonshine, Yamuna’s beaches appear like powdered camphor or diamond dust, the perfect dancing stage for Krsna and His sublimely talented companions.

The Yamuna is like a guru to the trees, gardens, groves, birds, and creatures upon her hanks and in her waters. She teaches them how to give love and pleasure to Krsna, both individually and collectively.

Yamuna-devi’s intense love for Krsna is peculiarly evident when, at the sound of His flute, her jewelled staircases melt and her waters become semi-solid, making the fish and waterfowl immobile.

Krsna, like His devotees, thrives on love, and because Yamuna is a storehouse of devotion to Him, He spends day and night wandering by her shores, thereby earning the name Yamuna-tira-vana-cari.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda says Yamuna-devi is the life of Krsna because He dances the rasa dance on her banks. Krsna is likewise the life of Yamuna-devi because she tastes His water sports amongst her waves.

These are but a few of the countless ways in which Yamuna-devi gives service, love, and pleasure to the Supreme Lord Sri Krsna and His eternal companions, thereby earning the Lord’s love for herself.

After offering His words of praise to Yamuna-devi, Caitanya Mahaprabhu adds, “O daughter of the sun god! Kindly purify us by your pious activities.”

May that celestial river who carried water from Goloka to earth to serve Sri Krsna and liberate conditioned souls, who is blackish in Bhauma Vrndavana and golden in New Vraja-dhama, be kind to us.

May that transcendental river upon whose shores cows graze peacefully, devotees worship, and desire trees stand waiting to give the gift of divine love, fulfil our hearts’ deepest spiritual desires.

May Yamuna’s charming waters — worshipped hy Vaisnavas, demigods, and perfected souls alike — wash away the troubles of this world and bestow loving devotion upon godly souls.

**\* \* \* \***

One day, the king of Ayodhya, Maharaja Mandhata, visited his son-in-law Saubhari Muni, who lived in Vrndavana by the of the Yamuna atop a hillock currently known by the name Sunrakh.

The king asked how he could win an empire in this life and attain a form like Krsna’s after leaving his body. In reply, Saubhari Muni taught him the fivefold process of worshipping rhe Yamuna.

May Sri Yamuna, whom sages worshipped in ancient times by chanting her kavaca, stava, and sahasramama, and by conducting her Patala and paddhati, be now equally satisfied by our chanting Hare Krsna.

May she who is known as the daughter of the sun god and the girlfriend of Radha, whose appearance is reminiscent of the pastime described in the following song, remember this humble request.

Narottama Dasa describes evening by the Yamuna,

*vrndavana ramya-sthana divya-cintamani-dhama ratana-mandira manohara*  
*avrta kalindi-nire raja-hamsa keli kore tahe sobhe kanaka-kamala*

**“Beautiful Vrndavana is filled with cintamani gems and jewelled palaces and temples. Regal swans play in the waters of the Yamuna, and in those waters a splendid golden lotus flower grows.”**

He then reveals a beautiful Yamuna pastime of Radha and Krsna,

*tara madhye hema-pitha asta-dale bestita*  
*asta-dale pradhana nayika tara madhye ratnasane ba ‘si achen dui-jane syama-sange sundari radhik*

**“In the middle of that lotus is a golden plinth surrounded by eight petals upon which the eight principal gopis sit. In the centre on a jewelled throne sit Syamasundara and beautiful Srimati Radharani.”**

Radha and Krsna exchange sweet talks between Themselves,

*o-rupa-labanya-rasi amiya pariche khasi' hasya-parihasa-sambhasane*  
*narottama-dasa kaya nitya-lila sukha-maya sadai sphuruka mora mane*

**“The great beauty of the divine couple and Their charming joking and laughter appear to he constantly showering nectar everywhere, a nectar Narottama Dasa prays will always manifest within his heart.”**

I first heard this song sung by one of our ISKCON sannyasis while I was still a brahmacari in Montreal, before I had ever been to India. It was my first impression of the Yamuna, one I treasure to this day.

Dear readers! Now that you have heard the glories of Yamuna-devi, let us continue our parikrama of the Lord’s pastime places on both hanks of the south end of the Yamuna River.

After viewing the pastime places on the southern petal of New Vraja- dhama, I followed the parikrama path down the hill into Khelanavana, one of the more remote and thus rarely visited areas of the dhama.

At Ujani in Vraja, the extraordinary cross-currents and whirlpools in the Yamuna testify to a time when Krsna completely reversed the river’s flow from north to south with His flute-song.

This incident took place at a time when Krsna was experimenting with different melodies, trying to find one that would bring the defiant gopis under His control. Why were they so unsubmissive?

After He had killed Dhenukasura, the gopis' attraction to Krsna intensified daily, like a volcano preparing to erupt. Krsna heard about their passion, watched it from a distance, and also hankered for them.

Despite Their acute desire to be together, Radha and Krsna were unable to meet. Day or night, at work or at play, They suffered in separation whether alone or with Their relatives, friends, or servants.

Their only relief came when, having succumbed to fainting spells due to the intolerable pain of separation, each one dreamt of the other; that is, until Their anxious friends revived Them.

Autumn came and went, with both the gopis and Krsna hiding their mutual love from one another, from their parents, and even from their respective girlfriends and boyfriends.

Upon the arrival of winter, the gopis who had been married as girls were to move from the homes of their parents to the homes of their husbands in order to take up the duties of chaste wives.

But the girls’ minds were fixed on Krsna. To them, the prospect of this move was worse than walking through a wall of fire. Their misery showed on their faces, and their parents had no idea what to do.

Their mothers-in-law were angry and the villagers critical, and so the gopis’ parents, whose daughters refused to leave home, turned to Yogamaya for a solution to this perplexing problem.

The young gopis thought: “Separated from Krsna, my father’s home has become like a prison for a king. If I go to my mother-in-law’s house, it will be like living in a prison meant for criminals.”

With sweet words, Yogamaya pacified the young girls, their parents, and their in-laws. She promised to protect the gopis personally. Then she took them from their weeping parents to their frowning in-laws.

The gopis had to tolerate the scolding of their mothers-in-law, but Yogamaya created duplicates of the girls so that they never had to have intimate contact with their husbands: they remained unsullied.

This new situation only increased their attraction to Krsna, however, and out of fear of transgressing the rules of dharma incumbent on new brides, the gopis hid even from their own desires.

For instance, Radha thought, “How can I give up the person who is My life? Thoughts of His sweet form and qualities are My sustenance, hut how can I transgress the strictures of dharma?”

Krsna’s thoughts were similar: “Now Radha — My life and soul — is the property of another, and yet My ruthless mind casts dharma aside. Day and night it seeks out Her form and qualities.”

Krsna was bold enough to disclose His intentions to Radha and the gopis through furtive glances, but the gopis turned their backs on His glances and kept their love hidden under the cloak of indifference.

Still, Krsna’s glances did not go in vain. They poured fuel on the fire of separation that consumed the gopis, whose flaming hearts felt His glances to be both a soothing balm and a burning poison.

After being pierced by Krsna’s glances, the gopis would say things like, “O Krsna! In beauty Your glance excels the whorl of the finest, most perfectly formed lotus within an autumnal pond.

“O Lord of love, Surata-natha! O bestower of benedictions, Varada! You are killing the maidservants who have given themselves to You freely, without any price. Isn’t this murder?”

Krsna continued to incite the gopis, looking back over His shoulder at them as He left for the forest in the morning, or giving them sidelong glances when He returned home in the afternoon.

But all this was to no avail! His glances gave them great bliss and caused their love for Him to grow, but the gopis could not respond to His advances, nor could they submit to His control.

Secretly they thought, “Let me love Krsna, even though it is immoral!” But publicly the gopis rejected Krsna, their rebuffs feeling to Him like blows from a stick. His only shelter was the flute.

At first Krsna played tunes on His flute while herding cows. He would astonish His friends with His virtuosity on the pretext of pleasing Balarama, but actually He was trying to entice the gopis.

Krsna thought, “I will play a tune that will bewilder and attract the gopis — especially Radha. I just need to find the notes to which those girls are most susceptible, to which their senses will be attracted.”

One day Krsna played a tune that stunned the cows, who gave up eating grass in favour of relishing the flute-song with their ears and tasting the sweetness of Krsna’s face with their eyes.

The next day, Krsna tried another tune and the forest animals and birds were stunned. Like the cows, they all stood still where they were, as if they had been confined within invisible cages.

On the third day, Krsna’s tune singled out the deer, which flocked to Him en masse. Mesmerised by His attractive appearance, they worshipped handsome Krsna with love-filled eyes.

Krsna’s attempts to capture the gopis with these melodies did not escape their attention, nor did they overlook the good fortune of these creatures, whom the gopis accepted as superior lovers of Krsna.

Concealing their real intent, the gopis once told Krsna’s mother, “O pious Mother Yasoda! Your son, who is expert in the art of herding cows, has invented various novel styles of flute-playing.”

On the following day, Krsna played another tune. This one attracted the demigoddesses, who were so bewildered by the sound that in front of their husbands their clothes loosened and their ornaments fell off.

On the fifth day, Krsna played a melody so powerful that all animate things became unconscious and inanimate things came to life. The gopis were still unaffected, but the Yamuna River was deeply moved.

When Yamuna heard the flute-song she stopped flowing, completely bewildered. Her waves swelled, and her waters trembled. Changing course (ujana), she flowed towards Krsna.

Overcoming her natural current, the Yamuna instead flowed to Krsna and, with her waves, offered lotus flowers at His feet. The part of the Yamuna where this miracle occurred is now called Ujani.

Did Krsna find the right melody to attract the gopis? He did eventually, but not before playing other melodies that mesmerised the clouds overhead and Vrndavana’s mountains, such as Govardhana.

Until Krsna finally found the proper tune He was in a precarious condition, as were the gopis. Actually, the gopis’ condition was worse: their in-laws often thought that their sons had married madwomen.

The most unhinged of all the gopis was Sri Radha, who contemplated how She could become a bamboo flute. Radha thought,

**“The flute is fortunate because, as a male, it does not have to be shy like us gopis.**

**“Thus it rests in Krsna’s hands and transforms the nectar of Krsna’s lips into beautiful music that causes the rivers to swell and the bamboo along the rivers’ banks to shed tears in the form of honey.**

**“I pray for the body of a bamboo flute! I reject this body of a supposedly respectable woman. No other type of body can relish what the flute does as Krsna plays it with eagerness and affection.**

**“The day I become a flute, My consciousness will surely ebb. No doubt I will forget My identity. But Krsna will remember Me as the gopi who became a piece of wood from suffering in separation from Him.”**

**\* \* \* \***

The stretch of forest along the Yamuna from Ujani to Gopi-ghata is called Khelanavana or Khela-tirtha, for here Krsna and Balarama are often lost in play (khelana) with Their friends.

Khela-tirtha natural bounty of fruits and flowers and its abundant playgrounds, most notably the Yamuna and Aksaya-vata, make it a favourite of the cowherd boys, who fill the air with sounds of joy.

The boys play all sorts of games here — imitating the dancing of peacocks, mounting each other’s shoulders, and having mock fights with sticks — completely immersing themselves in whatever they do.

Srila Prabhupada says that when Krsna and the gopas were in Bhauma Vrndavana they would be so absorbed that they would forget to eat. Mother Yasoda would have to call them to take their meals.

While Caitanya Mahaprabhu was visiting Vrndavana, He came to Khela-tirtha from Sesasayi. From there He crossed the river to Bhadravana and made His way to Gokula-mahavana.

The forest animals would follow Caitanya Mahaprabhu as He visited the places where Krsna and Balarama used to play with Their friends and the pastures in which Their cows would graze peacefully.

Walking along the bank of the Yamuna, the Lord would be lost in the mood of Gopala-Krsna. In ecstasy, He would call out, “O friend Sridama, where are you? O Subala! Have you left Me?”

In this way the Lord would remember the gopas' friendly competitions in Khela-tirtha. When His mind was no longer fixed on Krsna’s pastimes of childhood and boyhood, He continued on His way.

Khelanavana was not only a playground for cowherd boys. Krsna often met Radha and the gopis here. Naturally, they saturated the forest and the riverside groves with the mellow of amorous love.

Khelanavana is rich with the jewels of Krsna’s amorous sports, so much so that its fruits and flowers bear the taste of romantic love. To taste or smell them inspires one with devotion like that of the gopis.

Rupa Gosvami writes, “On the shore of the Yamuna River is the sacred place known as Khela-tirtha, where Lord Krsna eternally enjoys pastimes with His dearmost, Srimati Radharani.”

In his Lalita-madhava, the acarya also tells how Krsna left Vrndavana for Mathura and Srimati Radharani practically went mad. Ultimately unable to cope with Her lover’s departure, She fainted.

After a long time Radha returned to consciousness. Still bewildered, She told Her anxious friends, “Lalita! Listen! I just had the most frightening dream. It was so vivid I thought I was awake.

“In this dream a wicked messenger of King Kamsa came to Vrndavana and with a chariot took Krsna...” Unable to utter the rest, Radha shook Her beautiful head, joined Her palms, and concluded:

“I pray there will always be peace and prosperity in Vrndavana. Now, in order to become free from the ill effects of this nightmare, I will bathe in the Yamuna River and then go to see Krsna.”

Taking Radha’s hand in hers, Visakha said, “Let us go to Khela-tirtha, where Krsna eternally enjoys pastimes.” The two girls then walked to a riverside ghata, put on bathing clothes, and entered the water.

In the ecstasy of love, Radha mistook the large waves of the river for Krsna and said, “O Visakha! Look! Look! There is your friend Krsna hiding amongst the blue lotus flowers and playfully waving His arms.”

Rupa Gosvami describes how, as Radha swam to where She imagined Krsna to he, the deep swirling waters of the Yamuna engulfed Her, and it appeared to onlookers that She and Visakha had drowned.

But the two girls did not drown. Visakha took Radha to the sun planet, where they both lived until the time came for them to enter Krsna’s Dvaraka pastimes as Satyabhama and Kalindi.

To commemorate the divine couple’s pastimes, a temple with Radha- Krsna Deities is situated near Balarama-kunda, which is dedicated to Krsna’s and Balarama’s sports with Their friends in Khelanavana.

Although there are no records to indicate that it is connected with Khelanavana, there is another pastime of Radha and Krsna often told here to illustrate Srimati Radharani’s supreme fidelity to Krsna.

In time Krsna finally discovered the flute melody that could enchant the cowherd girls of Vrndavana and bring them under His control. Thus He began to meet regularly with Srimati Radharani.

But Krsna’s frequent absence from His friends and His nightly escapes from Nandagrama were just as frequently discussed amongst Vraja’s gossips as were Radha’s infidelities to Her new husband.

Nanda’s and Yasoda’s parental love made them deaf to any suggestion that Krsna could possibly he engaged in unsavoury pursuits, hut Jatila and Kotila were obsessed with thoughts of Radha’s infidelity.

Spreading the rumour of Krsna’s clandestine meetings with Radha was the work of His pastime potency, which always strives to enrich Radha’s and Krsna’s sports with obstacles They must overcome.

Without obstacles to cross over, the pleasure and freshness of Radha’s and Krsna’s eventual meetings would be less tasty. Whoever plays the role of giving impediments, then, is a very special servant of the Lord.

These are the ways of vraja-lila, both here and in Goloka: the results of the gossip surrounding Krsna’s dealings with the young brides of Vrndavana make Radha the victim of Her in-laws’ harsh criticism.

Jatila never has solid evidence to support her allegations of Radha’s infidelity, but her mind is ill-disposed towards her daughter-in-law; indeed, she calls Her Kula-kalankini, “the disgrace of Her family.”

Sri Radha suffers greatly from this verbal and emotional abuse, as do the other gopis. But the scrutiny does nothing to decrease Her desire for Krsna, although it does make it harder to rendezvous with Him.

One consequence of Jatila’s harsh criticism is that — funny as it may sound — she and her foolish daughter Kotila often think themselves to be the most qualified and chaste women in all of Vrndavana.

All-knowing Lord Krsna, wise to Radha’s suffering and Jatila’s delusion, once decided to silence all criticism of Radha’s character, and at the same time to put Jatila and Kotila in their place.

Krsna approached Yogamaya with a plan He had hatched and requested her assistance. The white-haired brahmani, overjoyed at being enlisted in a new pastime, at once blessed the clever plot.

**\* \* \* \***

One morning, Yasoda and Yogamaya went to wake Krsna as usual, but He barely stirred in response to their calls and caresses. Instead, He pulled the blanket over His head and moaned, “I feel sick!”

Those three words struck Mother Yasoda’s heart like three bolts of lightning. It was her concern for Krsna, and nothing else, that kept her from collapsing unconscious onto her son’s soft bed.

Paurnamasi felt Krsna’s forehead and took His pulse and announced that He had a fever. Mother Yasoda turned to her maidservant and with a voice full of anxiety said, “Call the royal physician at once.”

Soon Krsna’s bedroom was crowded with friends, parents, and well-wishers. Not only the royal physician but also every other doctor from the villages around Nandagrama had come to take care of Krsna.

Each and every doctor’s diagnosis was the same — high fever. Yet none of them could pinpoint the cause. Thus unable to prescribe medicine or suggest a cure, they could only voice their dismay.

Still, they tried an array of pills and tinctures and treated Krsna with cold compresses all over His body, but nothing would bring His fever down nor stop Him from repeatedly moaning like a distressed calf.

Yasoda was in tears, Nandaraja’s face was lined with worry, and boys like Madhu were frozen silent by helplessness. Even the birds crowding the windowsill, birds that usually sang for Krsna, were still.

After consulting amongst themselves, the doctors declared, “Unless this fever can be brought down — regardless of whether it was caused by poison, spells, or disease — we fear that Krsna will not survive.”

In the silence of the moments following the doctors’ prognosis, Paurnamasi, more concerned for Krsna’s dear ones than for Krsna Himself, spoke up, “I know mantras that will cure Krsna.”

As if pulled back from a precipice, the Vraja-vasis crowded around Yogamaya to hear her cure. She said, “Even if Krsna is suffering from a sorcerer’s curse, my austerities will save Him.

“However..she said, pausing for effect, “the presiding deity of my mantras is the sun god. My incantations will only be effective with his blessings and the blessings of his daughter, the Yamuna River.”

Nanda Maharaja said, “Surely the deity of the sun will bless you.” Paurnamasi replied, “His blessings will come through water that I must sanctify with mantras and then rub over Krsna’s body.

“I will know that Surya has blessed me if a perfectly chaste married woman brings Yamuna water to me in a special pitcher.” Turning to Nandaraja, she said, “Bring me the most chaste woman in Vraja!”

Since the news that Krsna was deathly ill had already drawn most of Vrndavana’s residents to the palace courtyard, Nanda Maharaja did not have far to go in search of chaste women.

But who was the most chaste? And was she really the only person who could help Krsna? Nandaraja thought, “My son’s life is at stake. I must strictly follow the orders of Mother Paurnamasi.”

But every woman in Vrndavana was chaste. Who could say which was the purest of the pure? Yasoda consulted the elder ladies; every one had her own opinion, each one arguably as valid as all the others.

No one could agree on who was the purest woman in Vrndavana. When Yogamaya finally came out of the palace she was given a very long list of chaste women all willing to bring Yamuna water for Krsna.

Paurnamasi looked around to see that the women of Abhimanyu’s clan, including Radha, were all present. Pleased to find that they were there, she instructed Nandimukhi to bring the special pitcher.

With typical aplomb, Paurnamasi announced: “The son of Nanda is deathly ill! But the waters of the Yamuna, if carried by a spotlessly pure wife and empowered by my mantras, will surely cure Him.

“While Yasoda and her physicians attend to Krsna, let all pure women accompany me to the bank of the Yamuna.” Her proclamation complete, Paurnamasi set out on the path that led to the Yamuna.

Many gopis and some gopas followed the brahmani Meanwhile Krsna’s close friends stayed behind and paced fretfully up and down or tended to Krsna, who was burning up with fever.

Madhumangala's mantras would have undoubtedly cured Krsna, but he was so distressed that his mind was a complete blank, much like Kama, who had forgotten his mantras when he needed them most.

Meanwhile, Paurnamasi and gopis young and old arrived at the bank of the Yamuna. Nandimukhi was already waiting there with the special pitcher — a golden pot with one hundred holes.

Paurnamasi lifted the pot in the air and said, “You are all chaste wives. But only the purest one amongst you can carry this pot without spilling a drop. Through that person, Surya will bless my mantras.”

To demonstrate the pitcher, Yogamaya dipped it into the river. When she lifted it up, water poured out of its sides in a hundred tiny streams. She held out the pot and asked, “Who will carry it?”

Paurnamasi’s query was met with nervous silence. This test would not just show that they were faithful wives, it would certify which one of them was the purest woman in Vrndavana. Who would that be?

“Whoever it is,” thought Vraja’s many ladies, “each and every one of us — but one — will not only meet with disgrace, we will also become soaking wet in our attempts to carry this pitcher.”

To avoid being ridiculed by the others, each lady volunteered someone else, and those thus nominated deferred the honour to other ladies they insisted were more pure than themselves.

This was supposed to be a sombre event, but Yogamaya could hardly contain her laughter. And sure enough, just as she and Krsna had planned, when Jatila and Kotila were nominated, they accepted.

Of all the women of Vraja, only these two were vain enough and foolish enough to think that they were the most pure. Considering the special pitcher too heavy for her, Jatila told her daughter to lift it.

As Kotila dipped the pitcher into the Yamuna, Sri Radha’s gopi friends glanced at one another. Their eyes sparkling with glee, they all thought, “What a fool! Now she will learn a welbdeserved lesson.”

And sure enough, the pitcher spouted water from the moment it was lifted. But Kotila was so sure of herself that she thought the leaks would stop once the pitcher was on her head. They didn’t.

Standing before the assembled gopis, Kotila held the pitcher proudly on her head as the water poured out in a hundred different directions. Very soon the pot was empty and she was soaked.

Vrndavana’s cowherd women could not restrain their laughter. Humiliated, Kotila handed the pitcher to her mother and said, “Mother! No doubt you are the purest of the two of us.”

Despite the obvious folly of the situation, Jatila could not resist the opportunity to authenticate her supreme chastity, and so with help from her daughter she too dipped the pitcher into the Yamuna.

As expected, Jatila’s effort brought the same result. Both women stood side by side, soaking wet and humiliated by their foolishness, a living demonstration of the adage “like mother, like daughter.”

Yogamaya petitioned the women of Vrndavana: “O wise gopis! Consult amongst yourselves and quickly tell me who is the purest, lest Maharaja Nanda’s son perish as a result of your humility.”

At this Lalita stepped forward and declared, “Respected elder! There is no need for consultation, for we all know that King Vrsabhanu’s daughter Srimati Radharani is the most chaste of all.”

The reaction to this proposal was mixed. The village gossip-mongers shook their heads and hissed like venomous snakes, but those favourable to Radha nodded their heads and spoke words of approval.

As usual, being easily influenced, Jatila was torn between the two camps, not knowing whether to speak for or against her daughter-in law. But Paurnamasi did not care to wait for Jatila’s opinion.

**\* \* \* \***

Seizing the moment, Paurnamasi handed Radha the special pitcher and said, “You are a highborn princess of spotless character. Won’t You carry water for the welfare of Queen Yasoda’s son?”

For a moment the two women looked into each other’s eyes. Then, humbled by respect for her, Radha shyly lowered Her face to look at Paurnamasi’s feet and replied, “Whatever you order, I will do.”

Radha dipped the special pitcher into the Yamuna and lifted it out of the water. As the Vraja-vasis looked on in wonder, She raised it onto Her head. Not a single drop escaped from the hundred holes.

For one magnificent moment Sri Radha stood amidst the incredulous Vraja-vasis, Her head held high, the golden pitcher glistening in the bright sun. She then followed Paurnamasi back to Nandagrama.

Of all the women in Vraja, Radha was the most chaste. The other gopis were faithful to their husbands, but Radha was faithful to Krsna, the ultimate husband and the maintainer of every living entity.

Radha transgressed conventional morality to serve Krsna, Her eternal husband, in full pursuance of His order, sarva-dharman parityajya: “Abandon all varieties of religion and just surrender unto Me”

She bad risked everything to serve Krsna, and true to His promise Krsna personally protected Her from all sinful reaction. Moreover, He arranged this pastime just to exalt Her above all others.

Just as Krsna had made the water of the Yamuna solid by the sound of His flute, He now kept the water in the pitcher by the power of His will. It sparkled through the pitcher’s holes, but it would not flow.

Although the ladies’ initial reaction to Lalita’s proposal had been mixed, when Radha carried the pitcher without spilling a drop, they were all of one mind: “The daughter of Kirtida is the most chaste.”

The doubters who were fond of spreading rumours that Radha was secretly meeting Krsna all felt ashamed of themselves. In their minds they begged Radharani’s forgiveness for their wickedness.

Radha’s friends crowded around Her and clapped their hands as they sang songs in praise of Krsna, their faces beaming with pride. After so much hardship, Radha’s name and reputation had been restored.

As the procession of gopis returned to Nandagrama, their voices rose up to Krsna’s quarters, drawing anxious Yasoda to the window. Vraja’s queen looked down, tears of happiness falling from her face.

The sight of beautiful Srimati Radharani carrying a golden vessel full of water was a medicinal balm to Mother Yasoda’s bloodshot eyes, as well as a reassuring message to her heart: “Your son will live!”

The gopis followed Radha into the palace. Usually, they would he too shy to enter Krsna’s bedroom, but their Radha was the only one who could carry the pitcher, and so they all piled in behind Yogamaya.

Paurnamasi didn’t waste a moment. She stood Radha at the head of the bed, sat beside Krsna, and chanted mantras over the water as she gently spread it all over Krsna’s burning limbs.

As soon as Radha had entered, Yasoda comforted her son by saying, “O Krsna! Now that Vraja’s holy mother and the chaste daughter of King Vrsabhanu are here, You will be cured. Have no fear!”

At the mention of Srimati Radharani, Krsna opened His eyes. And before Yogamaya had even touched Him, His fever, which was actually the fever of separation from Sri Radha, began to subside.

As Paurnamasi administered the water, now surcharged with mantras, Krsna’s parents and friends eagerly watched for signs of recovery, and the elderly brahmani repeatedly assured them:

“By the purity of Princess Radha, the blessings of the sun god are with us. Without doubt, that eye of the world has empowered my mantras, which will cure this boy within just a short time.”

As always, the guru of the Vraja-vasis had spoken the truth — Krsna’s fever quickly subsided. Stealing glances at Sri Radha, who now stood shyly in a corner, Krsna sat up and told His mother, “I am hungry.”

These words elicited cheers of “Jaya!” from one and all. The gopas all embraced Krsna, while euphoric Yasoda turned to Rohini and said, “Mother! Quickly take Radha and Her friends to the kitchen.

“Prepare a feast to aid the recovery of my hungry son.” What a feast it was! The countless dishes were all touched by Sri Radha’s hands, which made them taste like nectar, as they usually did.

Krsna had fully recovered by the time the feast began, but during the meal — unlike during other meals — everyone present continually praised Paurnamasi-devi and Srimati Radharani.

Outside the palace, news of Krsna’s recovery and of Radha’s supreme chastity spread like wildfire throughout the villages of Vraja. People were saying, “The sun god has personally attested to Radha’s purity.”

For some time thereafter no one dared question Radha’s comings and goings. Her meetings with Krsna were easier to arrange and not as tainted by anxiety — until Paurnamasi again exerted her power.

By Yogamaya’s influence, the Vraja-vasis gradually forgot the incident of the special pitcher. Jatila and some villagers again became suspicious of Radha’s frequent sojourns into the forest.

Once again obstacles were placed in the way of the divine couple’s affections, obstacles that merely increased Their desire for each other and made Their inevitable rendezvous all the more precious.

**\* \* \* \***

Walking along the bank of the Yamuna, one comes to a deep bend in the river. This is sacred Rama-ghata, from which numerous channel-deep furrows lead through the forest and into the fields beyond.

At Rama-ghata, divinely intoxicated Balarama taught the Yamuna a lesson in surrender. With His plough He changed her course by creating a multitude of irrigation ditches to supply water to Vrndavana.

After Krsna and the Yadus had defeated Banasura and Lord Siva in battle, Lord Balarama felt homesick and suggested to Krsna that They return home and give happiness to the sorrowful Vraja-vasis.

Krsna said, “If You can convince Vasudeva and Devaki to let Me go, I can satisfy the innermost desire of My heart. Please speak to them.” Hearing this, Balarama approached His father and Devaki.

Although they gave permission for Balarama to visit Vraja, they would not let Krsna go. Somewhat angry, Balarama said, “What’s the difference between Krsna and Me? We are both sons of Nanda and Yasoda.”

Lord Balarama felt slighted by His parents, Vasudeva and Devaki, but He informed Krsna of their decision and told His brother that He would be leaving for Vrndavana as soon as possible.

Krsna lamented the circumstances that kept Him from those He loved most. He took Balarama aside and said, “I have sent messages to the Vraja-vasis through Uddhava, but You must also console them.

“If You cannot completely satisfy them with words, then promise them that I will come back soon. And if You see that they are still troubled, then by My power I will appear to them directly.”

Looking around to be sure that no one was listening, Krsna added, “There are some gopis in Vraja who will not be pacified by My words. I have told You the names of the gopis attached to You.

“These were the same girls with whom We played Holi together one night. But because that demon Sankhacuda interrupted our sports, You could not fulfil their hearts’ desire. Now You must do so.”

Balarama tried to interrupt, but Krsna held His hand: “Don’t be concerned that the elders will come to know. My Yogamaya will arrange everything. Please give mercy to the gopis who love You.”

Nodding in agreement, Balarama asked, “But what of the gopis who love You? What will I say to them?” At this, Krsna’s eyes, which were already full of tears, spilled over and His voice choked up.

Unable to continue, Krsna sighed deeply. He threw His hands up as a sign of helplessness and retired to the privacy of His room. Later, more composed, He called Uddhava and dictated a letter to the gopis.

Uddhava reassured Krsna that Balarama was the best person to pacify Srimati Radharani and the gopis. Thereafter, he left Krsna and delivered the letter to Lord Balarama along with Krsna’s instructions.

Lord Balarama, very eager to see Vrndavana, placed the letter in His belt, made all necessary arrangements, and departed from Dvaraka at an auspicious time, travelling so fast that He could not be seen.

We have already heard about the reception the Vraja-vasis offered to Balarama and the messages from Krsna He relayed to the different groups of associates — friends, parents, and gopis.

Balarama saw that although the Vraja-vasis were internally pained by separation from Krsna, in order to please Him they still tended their cows, carried out their duties, and maintained their bodies.

As the days passed, Balarama enjoyed the same activities He had many years before, but He too felt unhappy within; life in Vraja without Krsna was useless, like eyes deprived of sight.

Wherever Balarama looked, everything He saw reminded Him of Krsna. In sorrow, He gave up herding the cows and simply stared at them instead, shedding tears and repeating Krsna’s names for solace.

On the third day after His arrival in Vrndavana, Lord Balarama met in a secluded place with the gopis, who in the ecstasy of madness greeted the Lord with uncovered heads and laughter.

Ever since Krsna left, the gopis had been waiting for Him to fulfil His promise to return. When only Balarama had arrived, they expressed their grief by punctuating their words with awkward laughter.

Now the gopis welcomed Balarama and were open with Him because, unlike Uddhava, He had also been born in Vraja. Having grown up with Krsna, He understood their relationship with the Lord.

Suddenly, the gopis confronted Balarama with a barrage of questions. One asked, “Krsna must be enjoying Himself in Dvaraka with all those cultured women, but does He ever remember the Vraja-vasis?”

Another reflected, “Does He remember His friends, His father, His mother, or even His house?” A third added, “Why should we enquire about Him? He may not even remember our service.”

Yet another gopi added, “We rejected our families and homes to love Him, and even after His rejecting us, our hearts continue to go to Him. I am sure the city women are as bewildered as we are.”

Throwing her hands in the air, another gopi said, “Is there no woman on earth who can tame this lotus-eyed person who has perfected the art of sweet-talking women into becoming His slaves?”

Another gopi sighed in exasperation and then declared, “Why speak about Him? Let’s talk about something else. If He can spend His time happily without us, we can spend our time happily without Him.”

The gopis’ ecstatic outpouring stunned Balarama, and for a moment the Lord just stood there bewildered, tears streaming from His reddened lotus eyes. Then He remembered Krsna’s letter.

Lord Balarama addressed the gopis as mothers. He assured them that Krsna was indeed thinking of them and that He was only staying in Dvaraka to kill the remaining demons, who were inimical to Him.

Balarama reiterated, “Krsna will return!” Just as the gopis’ lives were intolerable without Him, His life was nothing hut pain without them. That Krsna had sent Balarama to reassure them was evidence of this.

Taking the letter from His belt, Balarama said, “May this message give you happiness!” Then He read, “‘Through Uddhava and now through My brother, I have promised to return. I cannot make them liars.

‘“Please, therefore, accept My words to be true. And also know this: I am living with you because I am simultaneously present in both Dvaraka and Vraja. The evidence is that both places are perfect.

“‘I am as eager to see you as you are to see Me. As soon as I kill the remaining enemies of My devotees, in seven or eight days, I will return to Vrndavana. ? gopis, do not doubt Me.

As Uddhava had predicted, Balarama’s conciliatory words and Krsna’s letter pacified the gopis, who felt that Lord Krsna had appeared before them in the form of His message.

On another day the same gopis approached Lord Balarama with a message of their own. The message was from the gopis who were attached to Lord Balarama. They requested the Lord to marry them.

Having already been instructed by Krsna in this matter, Balarama agreed, but with two provisions: that the village elders give their blessings, and that Krsna be personally present at the wedding.

When Nanda and his brothers heard about this proposal from Yasoda and the other gopis, they approved. They also agreed that the actual marriage celebrations would only he held upon Krsna’s return.

But the gopis could not wait that long, so hy Yogamaya’s arrange - ment they met nightly with Lord Balarama in the remote forests of Vrndavana, just as other gopis had years ago met with Krsna.

Some argue that Lord Balarama consorted with the exact same girls as Krsna had. They don’t accept that Krsna’s gopi lovers and Balarama’s gopi lovers were two different groups of cowherd girls.

Acaryas such as Jiva Gosvami and Vrndavana Dasa Thakura, however, give evidence to show that the gopis dedicated to Krsna could not have been the same as those dedicated to Lord Balarama.

Sri Jiva, for example, in his analysis of rhe words that Krsna’s gopis speak to Lord Balarama in Srimad-Bhagavatam, shows repeatedly that the gopis’ attachment to Krsna is exclusive.

Since Krsna had stolen the hearts of the gopis, how could they give them again to Balarama? If a thief steals a priceless heirloom, how can the victim give that heirloom to someone else?

Those who challenge this conclusion say that Krsna and Balarama are both the Supreme Personality of Godhead and thus there would be no fault in Them sharing the same gopi lovers.

Jiva Gosvami uncovers the defect in this logic: For the Lords to share the same women would indeed be improper, a fact that would be even more obvious if They had been sharing Krsna’s wives in Dvaraka.

The acarya concludes that “only fools think that these \[Krsna’s\] gopis could develop attachment to Balarama” and that these foolish arguments “spoil the respect of the most honourable of women.”

**\* \* \* \***

On a full-moon night, Balarama and His *gopis* met not far from the Bhandira forest in a beautiful riverside garden caressed by breezes carrying the aroma of flowers mixed with spray from the Yamuna.

Although He was the Supreme Lord and fully self-satisfied, Lord Balarama appeared to behave like a mortal, eagerly enjoying Himself with the adoring young daughters of Vraja’s herdsmen.

Well aware of Balarama’s identity, the demigod Varuna desired to serve the Lord’s pastimes, and so he called for his daughter Varuni, the presiding deity of honey-wine, and said, “O daughter!

“You are the favourite of Lord Ananta, who is now present in this forest in the dress of a cowherd. Go! Add to the Lord’s pleasure.” Submissive Varuni appeared from the hollow of a kadamba tree.

The sweet aroma of that beverage spread throughout the forest, luring Lord Balarama and the cowherd girls to the tree from which Varuni was flowing like a fountain of golden liquid joy.

Balarama and the gopis drank honey-wine until they were tipsy. Their red eyes rolled, their nonsensical words slurred together, and they staggered as they walked arm-in-arm through Vraja’s pleasure groves.

It may have seemed that Sri Balarama was intoxicated, but His consciousness was fully transcendental. His complete dominion over His potencies remained intact, His absolute divinity unaltered.

While consorting with thousands of beautiful gopis, passionate desire never touched Lord Balarama, and neither He nor His consorts fell into ignorance as they enjoyed the tasty Varuni wine.

Lord Balarama felt too tired to walk to the nearby Yamuna, and so He called to the river: “Come here in person, ? exalted one, and bring your waters. We are in need of refreshment.”

Bewildered by her feminine nature (stri-svabhavena), and considering Balarama to be intoxicated, Yamuna-devi foolishly ignored the Lord’s request and kept flowing along her own course.

Angered by this impudence, Lord Balarama wielded His plough and plunged it into Yamuna’s bank. He dragged the river behind Him here and there, thus draining a large lake in the middle of the river.

In doing this, Lord Balarama altered the natural course of the Yamuna and created a major tributary that brought the river — along with its many fishes, birds, and animals — to the interior of Khelanavana.

The sound of the birds was like the crying of the river. When Yamuna- devi saw her waters were in danger of being diverted all over Vraja, she appeared before Lord Balarama in her personified form.

Seeing the Lord’s eyes still red and rolling with anger, Yamuna-devi said, “O elder brother of Krsna! O unconquerable one! Please he merciful. Excuse me for my offence and he pleased with me.

“O carrier of the plough! Your strength has humbled me. I place my head at Your feet. Please let go of Your anger and kindly tell me how I should now flow to my ultimate destination, the sea.”

Lord Balarama could see that Yamuna was now repentant and submissive, and so He said, “O auspicious one! I have drawn a course through which you should flow to provide water for this land.

“Follow My order. You may then continue your journey to the sea. As long as this world exists, learned men will retell this pastime of ours and the glories of this forest of Khelanavana. Be at peace!”

After this, Yamuna-devi disappeared. Lord Balarama entered the river with His consorts, sporting as the king of elephants sports in the water with his many wives—happy and carefree.

Dark blue garments, a lotus for one ear, an earring for the other, and a lotus-flower garland were all part of an offering Varuna sent for the goddess of fortune to give to Balarama when He came out of the river.

Beautifully dressed and ornamented, Lord Balarama continued to enjoy Himself with the gopis in ways that pleased their hearts and made their years of waiting for their beloved hero worthwhile.

Balarama and the gopis met every night, pleasing each other with memorable expressions of their mutual love. In this way His two- month visit seemed to pass by in just a moment.

Thereafter, Balarama, eager to see His brother, again abandoned the dress of a cowherd. He donned His royal robes and left Vrndavana with great difficulty, reiterating Krsna’s promise to soon return.

In describing this pastime, Sukadeva Gosvami glorifies Rama-ghata to Pariksit Maharaja as follows,

“Even today, o King, one can see how the Yamuna flows through the many channels created when it was dragged by the unlimitedly powerful Lord Balarama. Thus she demonstrates His prowess.”

East of Sri Rama-ghata in Vraja is a meadow surrounding a banyan tree. Here Lord Balarama enjoyed the rasa dance with the gopis. Even today a purified soul can hear the gopis glorifying their Lord in song.

Lord Nityananda, on His visit to Vrndavana, came to the rasa-lila playground of Rama-ghata and loudly called for varuni and the Yamuna, absorbed in the mood of Lord Balarama.

The Lord stayed here for some time, playing with cowherd boys, eating fruits when He felt hungry, and trying to conceal His identity from the locals, who thought, “This sannyasi must be Lord Balarama.”

A eucalyptus tree here provided twigs for Lord Nityananda to clean His teeth, and in a small grove the Lord revealed to one of His pure devotees His form as Krsna’s elder brother holding a plough.

Kalindi once appeared before Lord Nityananda as He bathed in the Yamuna. She begged His pardon for her past offences and asked to be blessed by the nectar ?f krsna-pr?m? the Lord was there to distribute.

Nityananda would sleep on the ground beneath the trees. In His sleep He once called out, “When the master of Navadvipa reveals Himself to liberate the jivas, then I will go to see Him with My own eyes.”

In 1977, on my second visit to Vrndavana-dhama, I curiously accompanied a group of devotees on a long bus ride to what was promised to be “a very special pastime place,” Sri Rama-ghata.

In addition to the pastime places mentioned above, we also saw a powerful black Deity of Lord Balarama that had been discovered in a nearby lake, although it was originally installed by Vajra long ago.

All glories to Sri Baladeva, who is called Sankarsana because while visiting Vraja He would sometimes draw Krsna from Dvaraka and present Him before a particular gopi in a secluded place.

All glories to Sri Balarama, who fulfilled the desires of the gopis attached to Him and displayed His own rasa-lila — distinguished by its mood of awe and reverence — by Yamuna’s shore.

All glories to the carrier of the plough, who — during the months of Caitra and Vaisakha — gave pleasure to the inhabitants of Vraja by constantly describing to them the pastimes of Sri Krsna.

Downstream from Lord Balarama’s rasa-sthali, next to Khela-tirtha, is beautiful Viharavana, thick with flowering trees, bushes, and vines, and rich with floral scents that incite spiritual romance.

At the centre of this forest are Banke-bihari’s temple and Vihara-kunda, the banks of which Krsna once sat upon, playing a mystical flute melody uniquely composed to attract Srimati Radharani.

No friend is as reliable as the venu. As a fisherman casts his net and hauls in a school of fish, Krsna’s flute-song captured Radharani and Her cowherd girlfriends and dragged them to Viharavana.

What’s more, the vibration of the flute also relieved Srimati Radharani of Her typical contrary nature, delivering Her into Krsna’s presence in a very rare state of complete submission.

Radha’s mood pleased Krsna so much that He responded by pleasing Her with sweet words and gentle behaviour. In doing so, He satisfied not only Radha’s heart but the hearts of the other gopis as well.

Because this forest witnessed such exchanges of divine pleasure (vihara), pleasure that can still be felt by pilgrims who come here in a submissive state of mind, it has come to be known as Viharavana.

Nonetheless, a nearby forest garden called Nivaranavana is testament to the fact that Radha and Krsna do not always attain the pleasure of meeting so easily—They often meet with many obstacles (nivarana).

**\* \* \* \***

Assuming that Viharavana had a special potency that made it easier for Him to charm Radha, Krsna returned there and again played the same mystic melody that had attracted Her before.

This time Radha arrived with only Rupa-manjari and a few maidservants. After Radha and Krsna had greeted each other with kind words and blossoms from the trees, They sat down in a grove.

The spring forest felt honoured to host Krsna and His consort, and so it displayed all its sweetness and opulence in a humble effort to serve the divine couple, the embodiments of natural beauty.

The flowers’ fragrance rode upon gentle breezes, the humming of bees filled the grove, and the songs of the cuckoos were the lead singers in a sylvan orchestra that sang an anthem with the words “Jaya Syama!”

Radha’s and Krsna’s combined auras lit up the grove with an emerald glow as a sign of Their gratitude for the forest’s service, filling the eyes of Their maidservants and the forest creatures with bliss.

Just as Krsna thought He had found the formula for making Radha submissive, something went awry. Krsna’s effulgence, like a mirror, showed Radha Her reflection—She thought another gopi was there.

Radha was unable to recognise Herself because of loving envy. She was convinced that another girl now sat between Her and Krsna. Furious at Krsna’s apparent infidelity, She turned Her back on Him.

Radha’s sudden and inexplicable change bewildered Krsna. This special flavour of loving ecstasy made Him see His own reflection in the mirror of Radha’s effulgence — it was another boy!

Krsna was shocked! He never expected Radha to allow another dark-skinned youth to come between Them. Offended to the core, He turned His back on pouting Srimati Radharani.

Seated on the same cot, Their hacks to each other, Radha thought, “How dare He embrace another gopi in My presence,” while Krsna thought, “I can’t believe Radha has accepted another boy.”

Luckily, Rupa-manjari quickly realised what had happened. Alert to serve Them, she would soon have an opportunity to help Radha and Krsna understand the mistake They both had made.

But first divine pride (garva) conspired with causeless anger (ahaituka-mana), preventing either one of Them from being the first to speak up and humbly admit Their own impetuousness.

This is the nature of love in Vraja! When Radha and Krsna are separated, all They can think about is meeting. And when They finally meet, They end up sitting side by side in angry silence.

Still, even though Radha and Krsna refused to speak, Their natural eagerness for each other conflicted with Their pride and Their bodies became like battlegrounds exploding with ecstatic emotions.

Fortunately, Rupa-manjari was there. She knew what was on Radha’s and Krsna’s minds, and so she decided to intervene. She said aloud, “Don’t wink at me Mukunda. I can’t change Radha’s mind.”

Incensed, Krsna replied, “I didn’t wink at you.” “You did so,” Rupa retorted. “I did not!” Krsna snapped back. Unwilling to tolerate hearing Her maidservant reprimanded, Radha interrupted.

“Winking at Rupa is useless. I’m not talking to You anyway.” “She’s lying!” Krsna said, now looking at Radha, “I never winked.” Now Radha looked at Him, “Lying? Rupa doesn’t even know how to lie.”

“Anyway, I’m not talking to You,” Radha added. To which Krsna replied, “And I’m not talking to You either.” “You’re talking now!” Radha countered. “I was talking to Rupa,” Krsna snapped back.

Unable to contain themselves, the manjaris laughed out loud. Their laughing was like a spark that ignited the dry tinder of Radha’s and Krsna’s mutual desire to talk. Soon the forest was filled with laughter.

Their pride now swept away by the loving ecstasy of laughter, Radha and Krsna faced each other and humorously wagged Their forefingers: “You spoke first!” “No! It was You!” Sri Riipa writes —

*Parasparam apasyatoh pranaya-maninor vam kada dhrtotkalikayor api svam abhiraksator agraham*  
*dvayoh smitam udancaye nudasi kim mukundamuna drg-anta-natanena mam uparamety alikoktibhih*

**“O lovers who rarely see each other but always long to meet! When will I make You smile by pretending to complain, ‘Mukunda! Why do You tempt me with the dancing corners of Your eyes? Stop it!’”**

Because Srimati Radharani here checked (nivarana) Krsna’s romantic advances, this forest has been revered as Nivaranavana, and the stairs on the Yamuna’s bank have come to be known as Nivarana-ghata.

Nama'sankirtana in Nivaranavana removes all obstacles to spiritual advancement. Just as Radha and Krsna laughed at Their mistake, we will laugh at the ridiculous illusion that is material affection.

Further on from Rama-ghata on the bank of the Yamuna is Kacchapa-tirtha, a cluster of ancient trees also known as Kacchapavana. Here the playful gopas imitated turtles (kacchapa).

Once, the cowherd boys brought their cows to drink by the Yamuna and they saw, on a sandbank that sloped into the river, a sizeable bale of turtles basking in the blistering rays of the midday sun.

While the cows drank peacefully downstream, the boys first observed the turtles passively and then tossed a few small pebbles at them, sending the creatures to the safety of Yamuna’s water.

The boys found the stiff necks and mechanical movements of the turtles so entertaining that they jumped onto the sand flats where the turtles had been and scampered around on all fours.

“Look at me!” shouted one boy as he humorously crawled along the sand and then dove headlong into the water. Standing still as if sunning himself, neck jutting out, another boy shouted, “Look at me!”

Imitating the movements and behaviour of the turtles, the boys scuttered along the sand, splashed in the water, and called out to each other, saying, “Look! Look!” The air filled with their laughter.

One boy saw Krsna watching from the riverbank and said, “Friends! Krsna, who long ago appeared as the king of turtles, Kurma, and held the Mandara mountain on His back, is too good for our game.”

Krsna called back, “If I assume the form of a turtle, then both the demigods and demons will come to churn the Yamuna. Do you really want to invite that lot to come and interrupt our play?”

The boys called back, “We don’t care. We’re not afraid of demons. You always protect us!” Yet for all of their bravado, after a brief conversation the gopas hurried up the bank to where Krsna was.

“Anyway!” said one boy. “We’re tired of playing turtle! It’s time for lunch.” With unanimous approval the cowherd boys abandoned their game in Kacchapa-tirtha and sat down for a picnic.

Further downstream in Vraja one comes to tranquil Gunjavana, a cluster of trees thick with gunja vines, themselves heavy with bright red berries that are also scattered abundantly over the ground.

The flowers of the gunja vine are pink. But when the ripened berries are separated from their pods, they turn bright red with a jet black spot, making them appear almost like ladybugs.

Their bright red colour is reminiscent of Srimati Radharani’s passionate feelings for Krsna. Gaudiya Vaisnavas string the berries into necklaces and worship them as symbolic of Her.

A sannyasi named Sankarananda Sarasvati once returned to Purifrom Vrndavana and presented Caitanya Mahaprabhu with a stone from Govardhana Hill and a garland of gunja beads.

Lord Caitanya would place the gunja garland around His neck and lovingly touch the sacred stone to His head, eyes, nose, or heart, declaring, “This stone is directly the body of Lord Krsna.”

Three years later the Lord gave both items to Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami. He personally instructed Dasa Gosvami how to worship the Govardhana-sila and told him that the gunja necklace was Sri Radha.

Dasa Gosvami thought, “By offering me the Govardhana-sila, the Lord has offered me a place near Govardhana Hill, and by offering me the gunja garland, He has given me shelter at Sri Radha’s lotus feet.”

As the following examples show, Krsna also accepted gunja necklaces as ornaments that symbolise Sri Radha and Her love for Him; indeed, He constantly wears a gunja-mala to remind Him of His beloved.

Visakha-devi once offered Krsna a gunja garland and said, “May virtuous Radha, who chants the name Krsna, and whose heart passionately loves You, hang around Your neck like this necklace.”

Paurnamasi-devi once observed that sometimes Srimati Radharani’s heart would overflow with ecstasy when She saw a gunja necklace. At such times Radha would shed tears and cry out loud.

To express Their mutual fondness for each other with gunja ornaments, Radha and Krsna would come to Gunjavana and make crowns, necklaces, and bracelets solely from gunja beads.

The divine couple would then decorate each other with these items. Covered head to toe in gunja ornaments, They looked like the presiding Deities of the gunja plant or the Deities of Gunjavana.

Flowers, peacock feathers, minerals, and gunja berries arc amongst the natural opulences of Vrndavana the divine couple favour, more so than the gold and jewel ornaments in the treasury of Laksmi-devi.

All glories to Gunjavana! Krsna sings the praises of Vrndavana’s gunja berries thus:

**“Now that autumn has come, the Yamuna has become thin, widening the sandy beaches on the river shore.**

**“The forest of Vrndavana is filled with extended peacock tails, billions of gunja berries, and buzzing bees that fly within the boundaries of creepers bearing many clusters of fragrant flowers.”**

**\* \* \* \***

From Gunjavana I continued towards the famous yan tree known as Bhandiraka, or Aksaya-vata. In honour of this tree, the forest that surrounds it is known as Bhandiravana.

In Vraja there are two forests called Bhandiravana — one where Pralambasura was killed, and another where Radha and Krsna were married. There are also two Bhandiravanas in New Vraja-dhama.
