Lord Balarama’s killing of Pralambasura happened to coincide with the arrival of summer. As a result of this pastime, King Indra awarded Balarama the names Baladeva and Pralambaghna.

The people of India do not normally welcome the intense heat of summer, but while Krsna was in Vrndavana, summer displayed the qualities of spring, also known as Madhava, one of Krsna’s names.

The breezes that swept across the rivers and lakes of Vraja, carrying with them aromatic lotus pollen, not only cooled the air for the Vraja-vasis but also kept the grasses fresh and tender for the cows.

When Krsna and Balarama herded the cows in Bhandiravana, boys and cows alike enjoyed the beautiful atmosphere of this forest, which was lush with grass for grazing and fruit trees for refreshment.

While herding their cows, the boys decorated themselves with peacock feathers, leaves, flowers, and buds. Unable to contain their youthful exuberance, they often danced and sometimes wrestled.

Especially playful, Krsna and Balarama sometimes challenged each other, sometimes sang together, and sometimes fed each other fruit, occasionally calling out the names of Their many cows.

The two brothers were most attractive. Colourful flower-laden turbans rested at jaunty angles atop Their heads, ropes for tying cows hung on Their shoulders, and forest garlands swayed on Their necks.

Balarama’s cloud-white complexion was swathed in deep blue cloth, reflecting His constant absorption in His younger brother, whose own body was like a puppet made of kajjala wrapped in gold.

The boys arrived at the Bhandira-vata tree with great flurry and fanfare. They decorated the branches of that great banyan with their colourful lunch packs, sticks, turbans, and upper cloths.

The morning’s entertainment began with Subala, Arjuna, Krsna, and Balarama staging a dance performance, accompanied by other boys, who sang and kept time with their hands, horns, and bamboo sticks.

Sometimes all four boys would dance at once, sometimes just two or three of them, and sometimes one would dance by himself. When it was Krsna’s turn to dance alone, His skill was mesmerising.

Balarama was so inspired that He could not restrain Himself. He jumped onstage to join Krsna as if possessed, while the boys clapped approvingly and praised Them who are a mystery to even the Vedas.

Balarama and Krsna appeared like the moon moving behind black clouds, and Their movements reflected the sunlight, which made it appear that lightning was flashing around the moon and the clouds.

The dancing stopped after some time, and the cowherd boys offered their own jewellery in admiration. But Krsna said, “The only payment We request is that you accept Our challenge to wrestle.”

These words elicited a roar of excitement from the gopas. But before i hey could even rise to their feet, Krsna and Balarama were amongst them, singling out contestants and giving joy by Their touch.

Soon the entire area beneath Bhandiraka had become a giant wrestling arena in which boys were pairing off, grappling with opponents, and charging at one another like young bulls.

The gopas’ groans, shouts, and grunts drowned out the sound of the wind and lapping waves. They punched each other, slapped their arms together, and struck one another’s chests with full force.

As Sridama sat astride Krsna, hitting his friend with his fists, did the Lord feel pain or pleasure? Sridama’s blows felt more like an offering of flowers due to the nature of their affectionate relationship.

Krsna revels in any loving service rendered hy His devotees, be it through praying, wrestling, or flirting. About Bhismadeva fighting with Krsna, for example, Srila Prabhupada writes:

**“Thus his throwing of sharp arrows at the...body of the Lord is as good as the worship of another devotee who throws soft roses upon Him... .The Lord enjoyed the wounds created hy His great devotee.”**

Eventually the boys grew tired of fighting. To regain their energy they crowded onto the swings that hung from the branches of Bhandiraka and challenged one another to see who could go highest.

Krsna and Balarama sat on one swing, four boys stood on another, and six on yet another, all flying through the air as if to challenge the soaring of the many parrots that chattered as they watched the fun.

Suddenly Krsna leapt off His swing, ran to a nearby amalaki tree, collected an armful of fallen fruit, and began pelting the boys, who swung back and forth like moving targets in a shooting gallery.

Unable to withstand Krsna’s attack, or to resist the challenge now before them, the boys all leapt to the ground, ran to nearby fruit trees, and also threw fruit at anyone or anything that moved.

The sounds of the mele? attracted the cows, who had been grazing nearby, but when they came too close they too were bombarded with fruit, and so they retreated to a more distant and peaceful pasture.

With the trees surrounding Bhandiraka now picked clean of fruit, a new game began: Krsna and Balarama pretended that They were two kings and the gopas divided into two groups of subjects.

The cowherd boys established Their borders and ruled Their kingdoms. But a territorial dispute soon brought a declaration of war, a march to battle, a fight, defeat, and a peace accord.

Eventually the boys tired of politics and warfare, deciding instead to amuse themselves with other games, such as imitating animals, playing ball, telling riddles, and running races of varied description.

About this day Sri Suka says,

**“In this way Krsna and Balarama played all sorts of welhknown games as They wandered among the rivers, hills, valleys, bushes, trees, and lakes of Vrndavana.”**

While Krsna and Balarama played, demigods like Siva and Narada disguised themselves to play as cowherd boys, to cheer the two brothers on, and to directly taste the ecstasy of Their pastimes.

Why were the demigods in disguise? They wanted to avoid interrupting Krsna’s play. Had they come in their original forms, the gopas would have stopped to offer respect to the celestials.

Meanwhile, in Mathura, Kamsa was becoming increasingly depressed over the death of his associates, the latest being Dhenuka and his gang of donkeys, who had all been wiped out by Krsna and Balarama.

Amidst Kamsa’s lamentations, his servant Pralamba approached, offered his respects, and asked, “O King! Why do you lament?” Kamsa answered, “Because all my friends are dead. Who else is left?”

Pralamba vainly replied, “If you give me the opportunity, I will solve your problem within an hour.” Kamsa was silent. He simply shook his head. “O Lord,” Pralamba said hopefully, “just order me!”

Kamsa laughed at his foolish servant, who was like a moth compared to the likes of Aghasura. The King said sarcastically, “Go ahead. Follow the path into the blazing fire. Do as you wish.”

Thus insulted by Kamsa, foolish Pralamba thought to prove himself to his master. The reactions to his evil deeds drove him to Vrndavana, where he saw Krsna and Balarama playing with Their friends.

In a previous life, Pralamba had been a Vaisnava named Vijaya, the son of Huhu, a Gandharva. Vijaya had once trespassed into Kuvera’s private garden to collect flowers for an offering to Lord Visnu.

Vijaya was unaware that Kuvera had pronounced a curse that anyone taking flowers from his garden would be transformed into a demon. As soon as Vijaya picked a flower, he took on the form of Pralamba.

Having no recourse, Vijaya took shelter of Kuvera, who reassured him: “O devotee of the Lord! Do not lament. At the end of Dvapara- yuga, you will be liberated by Lord Balarama in Bhandiravana forest.”

**\* \* \* \***

Fordeful of his past life and steeped in ignorance, Pralamba went to Nandagrama, where he overheard an elder gopi tell her son Bhadra that he could not go herding cows with Krsna that day.

During Bhadra’s bath, Pralamba stole the gopa’s clothing, ornaments, and walking stick. Assuming the form of Bhadra-gopa, Pralamba followed the path that led to Bhandiravana, and to his death.

When Pralamba arrived, the cowherd boys thought that he was Bhadra and eagerly accepted him into their fold. They treated him like a brother and laughed with him as they enjoyed their games.

Playing as a gopa, Pralamba constantly kept an eye on Krsna and Balarama, waiting for an opportune moment when the two heroes might display some sign of weakness or inattention.

As he watched, Pralamba could discern that Krsna’s unlimited prowess made Him invincible. He decided that at the next available opportunity he would kidnap Balarama instead.

But Pralamba had not escaped Krsna’s vigilant, all-knowing eye. To trap the demon in the pit of his own evil deeds, Krsna greeted him affectionately, “O Bhadra! You’re late! You’ve missed the fun.

“Never mind!” continued the Lord, eager to deceive the demon. “Today you will be My sidekick and Sridama will be on the side of Balarama, who is the perfect sparring partner for you.”

To get the boys’ attention, Krsna called out, “Ho! Ho! Brothers! Stop your dancing. We’re going to play a new game.” “Which game are we going to play?” the boys asked as they gathered around.

Krsna replied, “We’ll divide into two groups to play harina. Balarama will head up His group and Bhadra will lead Mine. Whoever loses will have to carry the winner to the starting point on his back.”

The two groups paired off. Keeping their feet together, they raced to the finish line by hopping like deer (harina).The winners and losers declared victory or defeat with cries of “I won!” or “He lost!”

Sri Krsna defeated Sridama, which meant that Sridama would have to carry his dear friend. Pralamba would have to carry Balarama, just as the other losing boys had to carry their triumphant opponents.

Lining up at the trunk of the Bhandiraka in a joyful mood, the losers began to carry their adversaries, running to the finish line and then hack to the tree, all the while calling out, “Jaya!”

But Pralamba did not turn around at the finish line. He just kept running, faster and faster. Balarama, unsure where this gopa was going, exhibited tremendous weight to slow down His eager carrier.

Unable to tolerate Balarama’s great mass, the demon reverted to his original hideous form. Together, the two resembled the moon riding upon a bank of billowing black clouds, both flying off to Mathura.

The demon’s body was expansive. His blazing eyes, copper-coloured hair, and long fangs were so fearsome that even Balarama felt some apprehension being lifted into the sky by this horrid-looking creature.

Earlier, the ecstasy of Lord Balarama’s absorption in play had covered His omniscience. He had neither recognised the demon, nor did He know how to react now that He was seeing Pralamba’s true form.

Baladeva gazed at His brother for guidance. Krsna, with the movement of His brow, revived Balarama’s godly powers. His glance seemed to say, “Why are You acting like a human now.”

Thus reminded of His transcendental identity, Lord Balarama hastily invoked His unlimited strength and struck the demon on the head with His fist, just as lightning strikes a mountain.

That one blow had all the force of the universe behind it, so it was not incredible that Pralambasura’s head cracked open. The demon at once lost his life, and his body fell to the earth, bleeding profusely.

As the demigods showered flowers, the soul of Pralamba — previously the Gandharva saint Vijaya — went to Vaikunthaloka. Balarama, eager to escape the ghastly scene, ran to embrace His brother Krsna.

The cowherd boys surrounded Balarama to congratulate Him. Celestial voices glorified the Lord’s display of incomparable strength and bestowed upon Him the name Baladeva, “God of Power.”

The cowherd boys embraced Balarama with so much love it was as if He had just come back from the dead. They praised Him, offered Him profuse blessings, and repeatedly said, “Well done, friend. Well done!”

Because the area around Pralambasura’s body was covered in blood, the cowherd boys left it in disgust and returned to the trunk of Bhandiraka, whose branches straddled both sides of the Yamuna.

Lord Balarama is the origin of Maha-visnu. He is therefore known as the reservoir of all living entities. Pralambasura was the personification of covered Buddhism, known as Mayavada.

Pralamba’s attempt to steal Balarama represents the Mayavadi phi' losophers’ efforts to disprove the personal identity of the Supreme Brahman, Krsna, and the eternality of pure devotion to Him.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda says that just as Pralamba disguised himself to enter amongst the cowherd boys, Mayavadi philosophy sometimes enters the Vaisnava community in the guise of service to Krsna.

Hearing about Pralambasura’s death at the hands of Lord Balarama will infuse us with the spiritual strength to identify and root out Mayavadi ideology when it infiltrates our ranks under false pretence.

Upon returning to their base camp at Bhandiraka, the gopas found that during their play the cows had strayed deep into the forest. They were nowhere to be seen, and so the boys despaired.

Sukadeva Gosvami says that the boys’ great anxiety was due to having lost their families’ means of livelihood (ajivya), anxiety further fuelled hy hearing the cows crying in distress.

Krsna looked in the direction of the lowing and noticed that the birds in the trees, suddenly startled, were flying away in fear. “Where have our cows gone?” Krsna wondered aloud with apprehension.

“Balarama has removed all inauspiciousness from this forest, so what could be amiss? Still, we are unable to see any of our fathers’ cows! We must search them out and make our way home.”

With no one to herd them, the cows had wandered off in search of fresh grass and entered deep into a swampy forest of cane and bul-rushes (*munja*), from which they could find no way out.

The cowhed boys trusted Krsna’s words of reassurance, hut they could not help hut wonder whether another one of Kamsa’s demons might he responsible for the disappearance of their cows.

Veritable cow experts, Krsna and the gopas found the path their cows had taken hy searching for fresh hoof prints and patches of grazed or clumps of partially eaten grass. They followed the trail.

Krsna walked ahead and climbed a high hank from which He could see the cows and he seen by them. He waved His yellow cloth and loudly called out, and the cows all responded with unhappy lowing.

To reassure the cows, Krsna — also known as Gopala, protector of cows—called out their names in a voice saturated with affection. And the cows replied, calling out to the Lord with love.

Their cows now in sight, the gopas ran into the Munjatavi forest to rescue them. Just then, a servant of Kamsa who had witnessed Pralamba’s death took the opportunity to avenge his friend.

While the boys were reassuring their cows with the soft, soothing sound of mantras, Kamsa’s servant invoked a ring of fire, shooting flames towards the sky and showering sparks everywhere.

The fearsome flames were fanned hy fierce winds and fed by dry cane, creating an unbearable heat that made the cows huddle together in fear. The cowherd boys bravely surrounded Krsna to protect Him.

But the fire was quickly closing in. Now terrified, the gopas appealed to Krsna and Balarama,

“O Krsna! Krsna! Most powerful one! O Rama! You whose prowess never fails! Please save Your devotees, who are about to be burned by this forest fire and have come to take shelter of You!”

The cowherd boys’ first and only thought had been for Krsna’s safety, but thinking that He would be inclined to save His devotees, they now called on His help as if thinking of their own safety.

The pitiful words of the cowherd boys had their effect. In an angry mood, Krsna thought, “Upon seeing this inferno, My friends, who are dearer to Me than life, are frightened. Hence I will devour this fire.”

Just as He opened His mouth, however, Krsna caught Himself, think' ing, “The boys should not see Me swallow fire. If they do, the shock may he so great that some might die on the spot.

“What’s more, mother once chastised Me for eating a little dirt. When the boys tell her what they’ve seen, she will surely take Me to task. Better that no one sees what I am about to do.”

Above the roar of the approaching flames, Krsna shouted, “Friends! Just close your eyes and don’t be afraid.” “You must be joking!” the boys yelled back. “How can we escape this fire by closing our eyes?”

Krsna replied, “Don’t be afraid! I have a special plan to protect you.” The gopas looked at each other. Did they really have a choice? Who else hut Krsna could save them from dangers like this?

One boy said, “Listen friends! Probably Krsna is a master in chant' ing mantras to disperse fire, but these mantras are ineffectual in the presence of others, so He wants us to close our eyes.”

This was enough to convince the gopas. As soon as they had closed their eyes, Krsna opened His mouth and swallowed the entire fire and restored the forest, its trees, and animals to their previous state.

Krsna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Even though the forest fire resembled the flames with which Ananta annihilates planets at the time of dissolution, Krsna swallowed it entirely.

With the same sort of unlimited yogic power by which He swallowed the fire, Krsna transported the boys and cows out of Munjatavi forest to the base of the Bhandira and said, “You can open your eyes now!”

After a silent moment the boys opened their eyes. Immediately they started to chatter, incredulous, “What happened!” “Were we dreaming?” “Where is the forest fire?” “How did we get here?”

As the boys tried to make sense of the ordeal, the demigods showered flowers and recited prayers. This, along with what had just happened, made the gopas think that Krsna must he a powerful demigod.

The gopas witnessed Krsna exert His divine power, hut the sweetness of their spontaneous fraternal love was unaffected. They explained away His superhuman feat hy accepting Him to be a demigod.

Next they thought, “We are Krsna’s friends. We are on the same level as He. If He is a demigod, then we must he demigods too.” This realisation filled the cowherd boys with boundless bliss.

The cows were also happy that the forest fire had been extinguished. Overwhelmed with joy and affection for Krsna, they licked His body as He caressed their heads and rubbed their ears with His soft hands.

An exciting day of pastimes at Bhandira-vata and nearby Munjatavi was thus drawing to a close as the gopas blew their horns and flutes and prepared to return home to a well-earned supper.

Both as they walked home and in response to their parents’ questions about their day, the gopas glorified Krsna incessantly, for sankirtana was their life. Sukadeva says:

**“It was now late in the afternoon —**

**“And Krsna, accompanied hy Balarama, turned the cows back towards home. Playing His flute in a special way, He returned to the cowherd village in the company of His friends, who chanted His glories.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Before moving on to Gopi-ghata, I paused to recall a favourite pastime, which also takes place beneath the boughs of the Bhandiraka — Krsna’s wrestling match with Radha and the gopis.

One day, while the cowherd boys were elsewhere, Krsna came to the Bhandira-vata alone. After embracing the tree and speaking kind words to it, He settled down on an exposed root shaped like a throne.

Krsna placed the flute to His lips and played an enchanting melody that disturbed the natural operations of material nature. It was especially composed to attract Sri Radha’s heart — and it did.

Radharani heard the sound of the flute. Her mind, like the waters of the Yamuna, rose up in high waves of ecstasy. Along with Her girlfriends and assistants, She hurried to answer Krsna’s call.

At Bhandira, Radha stopped to take in the sight of Krsna nestled in the roots of the tree, His eyes shut in absorption. He was surrounded by thousands of parrots drinking the nectar of the flute.

Green parrots are usually noisy, especially when gathered together in such numbers, but these birds sat side by side in silence. They covered all the branches of the great tree, leaving only the roots exposed.

To avoid interrupting Krsna’s playing or the parrots’ reverie, Radha spoke softly to Lalita: “O friend! In this forest all the birds have risen onto the beautiful branches of the trees to see Krsna.

“With closed eyes they are simply listening in silence to the sweet vibrations of His flute, and they are not attracted by any other sound. Surely these birds are on the same level as great sages.”

Even though Krsna did not hear Srimati Radharani’s voice, He felt Her presence. Thus He opened His eyes, stopped playing, placed the flute in His lap, and gave the girls a welcoming smile.

The parrots, sensing the concert was finished, also opened their eyes. Rotating their heads in unison from Krsna to Radha, they flew off, the wind created by their wings billowing the gopis’ clothes.

Radha, followed by Her friends, approached Krsna like a deer might gracefully approach a stag. She inquisitively surveyed the gopas’ well-worn playground and the clear evidence of their sports.

Swings hung from some branches, bars for chin-ups from another. A vine rope was tied to a branch that extended over the Yamuna. Much higher up, upon some crossing branches, there was a tree house.

Just in front of Krsna was a square slab of clay — clearly a wrestling arena — marked by waist-high stone pyramids at its four corners that were connected by shallow trenches filled with white pebbles.

Radharani stood before Him, pointed at the square, and in Her cuckoo-soft voice asked, “How do You play with Your friends at this spot?” Politely rising to His feet, Krsna answered:

“This is a wrestling arena. We dress as wrestlers and engage each other in hand-to-hand combat.” Intrigued, Srimati Radharani raised Her eyebrows and asked, “Do You sometimes win?”

Krsna seemed surprised, perhaps hurt, by the question. He replied, “Devi! No one knows how to wrestle like I do! I always win, except for the times I pretend to lose to Your brother. He’s quite a poor sport!”

Sri Radha took a breath and smiled, “My brother Sridama tells Me just the opposite. He says that he always wins and that You never take it well.” Krsna pursed His lips and replied, “He would say that.”

Lalita took a step forward from the ranks of the gopis and said, “Syama! Won’t You show us Your wrestler’s dress and wrestling holds? We would love to see the moves You use to defeat the others.”

Pleasantly surprised by the direction in which things were going, Krsna wondered if Radha’s and Lalita’s questions might be part of a plan the gopis had hatched, one He thought He would likely welcome.

Shaking His head, Krsna replied, “That’s impossible. Wrestlers dress only for a live match. We don’t model, even for royalty.” Looking at Radharani and then back at Krsna, Lalita said:

“What if someone were to challenge You to a match? Would You accept?” “Sakhi! I am the son of a king!” Krsna boasted. “How can I refuse a dare to fight, to gamble, or to protect a woman’s honour?”

Now it was Lalita’s turn to interrupt: “Then You should accept my challenge: Fight with my friend Radha, the goddess of victory, Jaya Sri.” This nearly made Krsna faint from ecstasy.

Krsna pinched Himself. He was thinking, “Is this a dream? No! I’m awake. My pious life spent protecting cows has yielded this juicy fruit, the sweet request from the gopis to wrestle with them. Incredible!”

Krsna furrowed His brow as if deep in contemplation and finally said, “How can I, a prince, wrestle with a weak, untrained woman, especially a delicate princess like Radha? No! It would not be right.”

Radha turned away, unable to keep from smiling. Visakha then took her cue: “But how can You, ? noble one, refuse a challenge? If the people of Vraja hear of it, Your father will hide his head in shame.”

Nodding His head, Krsna replied, “I see! I see! King Cupid, the enemy of pure brahmacaris like Myself, has sent you ladies to test the strength of My continence. So be it, then! So be it!

“Never let it be said that the son of Nanda fled from a challenge, even against insurmountable odds.” Walking around Radha, who had covered Her smiling face, Krsna concluded, “Then get ready!”

Giggling and chatting, the gopis ushered Radha into a nearby grove to change, while Krsna selected His most colourful cloth from a storehouse, all the while lauding the apparent planetary alignment.

Shortly thereafter, the gopis emerged from the grove and Krsna walked out from behind Bhandiraka, each amazed at the charm of the others’ wrestling attire and hair, which was tied neatly in top-knots.

Krsna’s golden cloth, knotted in front and back, left His legs exposed below the knee, a bright orange belt circled His waist like a sash, and His only ornaments were blue wristbands and His sapphire sheen.

The gopis had tied their lower cloths in the manner of ksatriyas. Their upper cloths criss-crossed at the front and tied in the back to cover their brightly coloured colis. They too wore bright cloth belts.

Being host to the match, Krsna invited the gopis into the arena and smeared ghee on the ground in worship of the earth. He positioned the girls on one side while He stood at the other and said:

“Dear friends! Before we begin, let Me describe the rules of encounter that our wrestling school (akhara) follows. There are four schools of wrestling: Bhimaseni, Hanumanthi, Jambuvanthi, and Jarasandhi.

“We gopas concentrate on technical superiority over strength or locks that cause pain to our opponents. Hanuman is our hero, and so we follow the Hanumanthi school delineated in the Malla Purana.

“Because you are of the weaker sex, we will not engage in the combat wrestling I do with My friends, instead favouring ‘pastime wrestling’ (mallakrida), recommended for play and amusement.”

The gopis nodded in agreement. Krsna continued, “In killing demons and sometimes in play, I have been known to use knee strikes to the chest, punches to the head, hair-pulling, and strangleholds.”

At this, the *gopis’* eyes grew wide. Mild-mannered Citra leaned over to Lalita and whispered, “What kind of game have you gotten us into?” But Krsna was too absorbed in His speech to hear her.

“My wrestling style,” He said, “is similar to that used by the Vanara king Vali in his defeat of Ravana.” Tungavidya whispered to the girls, “Now He is comparing us to Ravana. Oh dear!”

Krsna’s introduction was finished. Joining His palms, He directed the *gopis* to offer prayers to the patron deity of His wrestling school, Hanuman. Then He threw down the gauntlet.

“You being women, it is only fair that you fight Me all at once, rather than one at a time. I have already defeated My friends — superior wrestlers to you — in the same way. But enough talk! Let’s fight.”

Krsna stepped into the arena, slapped His palms on His crossed arms, reached down to rub some earth between His hands, bent His knees, placed His hands in readiness, and bellowed, “Jaya Hanuman!”

**\* \* \* \***

Krsna’s intensity startled the gopis. Each girl tried to push another girl forward. Finally, with Radha at the front flanked by Lalita and Visakha, the gopi army advanced from their side of the arena

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami has described this transcendental scene, the ensuing pastime, and the underlying purpose of it all,

*malli-krtya nijah sakhih priyatama garvena sambhavita —*  
*Malli-bhuya mad-isvari rasamayi mallatvam utkanthaya*  
*yasmin samyag upeyusa bakabhida radha niyuddham muda kurvana madanasya tosam atanod bhandirakam tam bhaje*

**“I sing the glory of Bhandiraka, where charming Radha, eager to please Cupid, dressed Herself and Her friends in wrestling costumes to challenge the enemy of Baka, Krsna, also dressed as a wrestler.”**

The acarya goes on to explain that Srimati Radharani’s purpose in challenging Krsna to wrestle was to give pleasure to the god of love, which can be taken to mean either Cupid or Krsna.

Radha exists only to serve Krsna, and so this unfolding plan that started with talks of wrestling and ended in physical contact in hand-todiand combat was, no doubt, primarily for Krsna’s pleasure.

It is well known that Krsna’s confidential friends like Sridama delight the Lord with their enthusiasm for wrestling on the platform of fra' ternal love, but Krsna craves other tastes in such battles.

To taste real animosity, for example, and the physical exertion of a battle to the death characteristic of pure heroism, Krsna arranges to wrestle with professionals like Canura and his followers.

But even after relishing both mock fighting and real fighting, Lord Krsna’s insatiable heart still hankers for a taste rarely attained in battle: the fully satisfying mellow of amorous love.

And how else could Krsna taste amorous love in the midst of combat but by wrestling with the gopis? Knowing Krsna’s heart and hearing from Her brother, Radha was inspired to serve Him in this way.

Krsna charged towards the gopis and grappled with each one in a separate wrestling hold, a novel experience for both Him and them, incomparable even to their loving embraces in the groves.

Their mutual touch, close physical proximity, and shouts of exertion enlivened Krsna and the cowherd girls in unique ways, distinct even from the ways their limbs touch in the rasa dance.

Sometimes Krsna appeared to be wrestling with all the gopis at once. Then suddenly He would slip out of their grasp and confront only Srimati Radharani at the centre of the arena.

At such times the other gopis would encircle Them, encouraging Radha with cheers of “Victory!" and “Get Him!” Once, Radha seemed to have Krsna’s shoulders pinned to the ground, but He disappeared.

Without warning, Krsna reappeared and caught each and every gopi from behind and wrestled them all to the ground, even as they protested this illegal tactic by calling out, “Foul play! Not fair!”

Then the gopis again freed themselves from Krsna’s grasp, only to turn the tables on Him. Two gopis held His legs, two held His arms, one straddled His chest, while another held Him in a headlock.

The sight of Krsna’s soft, bluish body entangled with the gopis' golden limbs resembled blue and yellow lotuses tossed about together on the Yamuna by strong waves and high winds after a big storm.

But, unlike gold and yellow lotuses, which do not belong together, Krsna’s and the gopis’ limbs looked quite compatible when entwined, so much so that the entire scene bewildered Cupid by its novelty.

Krsna’s most formidable foe proved to be Sri Radha. In this battle amorous affection weighed in more heavily than either martial skill or bodily strength, and so in Radha, Krsna had met His match.

Even after gopis like Indulekha and Rangadevi had been successfully subdued, Radha stayed in top form, repeatedly slipping from Krsna’s grasp then attacking Him from another angle with some new hold.

Finally, all the fatigued but blissful gopis surrounded the wrestling arena to watch the divine couple face off in a fight to the finish. This amorous tussle reminded the girls of the rasa dance.

Radha and Krsna were wrestling, not dancing, but to the gopis, who voiced their pleasure hy yelling, “Sadhu! Sadhu!” the skill, bliss, and exertion in both events appeared to be the same.

It was not long before the gopis had given up favouring either of the two combatants. Their interest was in the contest itself, and not one of them believed there could be a loser in such a tournament of love.

Still, Krsna’s touch appeared to give Radha energy, while Her touch weakened Him. With every passing moment Krsna displayed the ecstasy of fatigue. The gopis could see that Radha had the upper hand.

This turn of events revived the competitive spirit in the gopis. Now they were chanting “Jaya Radhe! Jaya Radhe!” in unison and slapping the ground with their palms or kicking it with their heels.

Up to this point, the forest creatures that had been watching this incredible pastime were too enchanted to support either side. But Radha’s advantage inspired them to join in the gopis cheering.

In no time at all the entire forest of Bhandiravana was resounding with calls of “Jaya Radhe!” Only one person — tears of ecstasy decorating his cheeks — remained neutral.

That person was Cupid, blissfully perched on a branch of Bhandiraka and too absorbed in the loving exchange to make any distinction between Radha and Krsna, let alone favour one over the other.

Cupid had been party to countless acts of love, but what he now saw was new even for him. Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami writes that Cupid watched the wrestling with great satisfaction.

Srimati Radharani wanted to please Krsna by serving Him the nectar of the amorous mellow through the chalice of a wrestling match, and Krsna drank and drank that elixir until He could drink no more.

Krsna made it known that He was fully satisfied by groaning, "I give up!” thereby bringing this pastime to an end and broadcasting Radha’s name, Jaya Sri, the goddess of victory, far and wide.

Moreover, by conceding defeat, Krsna also polished the touchstone of His own pastime potency, which perpetually displays novel sports, thus confirming that He is factually Ananta, the unlimited.

And lastly, because Cupid is completely distracted by watching the unlimited loving pastimes of Radha and Krsna, those who faithfully hear those pastimes will attain freedom from Cupid’s power.

## Chapter 25 - Gopi-ghata to Sanorakha

The Bhandiraka tree—where Krsna wrestles with gopas and gopis, swallows the forest fire, and has Balarama dispose of Pralamba — is a jewel in the crown of pastime places that decorate Yamuna’s shore.

Further downstream is another such crown jewel — no less glorious — where, desiring Krsna as their husband, the unmarried young girls of Vrndavana worshipped goddess Katyayani and received her blessings.

Three sites are connected with this pastime: Tapovana, where the gopis performed austerities; Gopi-ghata, where they bathed in the Yamuna; and Cira-ghata, where Krsna stole their clothes.

This group of gopis is not to be confused with Sri Radha and Her associates. They are young unmarried friends of Dhanya, who Cakravarti Thakura says are also eternally liberated (nitya-siddhas).

A similar pastime in the Garga-samhita suggests that these girls once desired to be wives of Lord Rama. The appendix “Were the Kanya- kumaris the Reborn Sages of Dandaka Forest?” refutes this claim.

These girls took birth in Vraja, where Krsna is always seen and spoken of. Their spontaneous attraction to Him having been aroused in childhood, they harboured the desire to marry Him ever since.

These kanya-kumaris had forgotten their eternal identities as Krsna’s beloveds. They thought they needed to perform some ritualistic worship to fulfil their desire, but they didn’t know how.

They would pray to various deities, such as Siva, Durga, and Surya, but without success. In disappointment, the girls would wander aimlessly throughout Vraja, their bodies pale and thin.

All the girls of this age and disposition shared the same desire, but they dared not reveal their hearts to one another or to their families. Because of their secrecy, they were like simmering kettles of love.

Simmering kettles eventually come to a boil, so naturally this secret common to the young gopis eventually came out as they were having emotional, confidential talks on the shore of the river Yamuna.

In the past, some of the girls had been inimical to one another, but their shared love for Krsna now swept all that away. Their love bound them by affection, and they now cried in one another’s arms.

Vrnda took pity upon the kanya-kumaris, seeing that they were determined but lacking direction. Desiring to serve their cause, she appeared before these young gopis disguised as a female ascetic.

After the girls had offered their obeisances, Vrnda told them what was in their hearts without having asked, just to impress upon them her wisdom. The goddess of Vraja said, “O young girls!

“I am a resident of this forest. I know of your attraction to Krsna. If you want to achieve your goal, then you must follow a vow for one month and repeat a mantra I myself have perfected. Are you willing?”

The kanya-kumaris were more than willing. Vrnda taught them the intricacies of the worship, pronounced the mantra in their ears one by one, blessed the girls with success, and then disappeared.

With an authorised process for approaching Krsna, the gopis’ love blossomed, just as flowers open at the first hint of dawn. Symptoms of excessive attachment to Krsna appeared in their bodies and minds.

When the young gopis returned home and each of them spoke of their plan to get a good husband, their parents were naturally supportive, for they too wanted their daughters to be married.

The girls did not reveal that they wanted Krsna as their husband, but when the girls’ mothers heard the details of the vow, they tried to discourage their daughters from taking up such severe austerities.

The elder gopis affectionately said, “You are too young and delicate to endure such hardships. You will not be able to maintain the determination needed to complete this vow. Please do not take it up.”

But these dispiriting words only served to increase the girls’ resolve. The girls’ mothers then asked, “Which deity will you worship, which acarya will guide you, and which mantra will you chant?”

And each girl replied, “I will worship Katyayani-devi to satisfy my desire. My acarya will be my mind, and it will reveal to me the best of secret mantras at just the right time.”

The elder ladies spoke dismissively of these proposals, discouraging the vraja-kumaris. But on the day before winter began, Vrnda’s words stirred the love in their hearts, inspiring in them an intense resolve.

At the girls’ renewed determination to collect havisyanna and other items for the Katyayani vow, their mothers’ relented, giving blessings and support to their daughters, despite their lingering concern.

The vow that Vrnda-devi had set out for the month of Agrahayana was demanding: The vraja-kumaris were not allowed to chew betel, massage their bodies with oil, or apply oil to their hair.

They had to rise while it was still dark, leave their homes four dandas before sunrise, walk to the Yamuna, bathe in the river, worship Katyayani, chant their mantras, and then return home.

They could eat only once a day, and then only unspiced havisyanna. But Vrnda assured them that if they followed this schedule to the end of the month, then they would accomplish the purpose of their vow.

The gopis’ eyes were often red from lack of sleep. After bathing each morning in the cold river, they shivered until warmed by the sun. And because they ate only once a day, they became emaciated.

At first glance the gopis might have appeared pale and drawn, but their ecstasy was visible in the radiance of their complexions, the sparkle in their eyes, and the trembling of their voices.

On the first day of the month, the girls rose, washed their mouths, eyes, and faces, and after performing acamana, they declared their resolute determination (sankalpa) to complete their vow.

Leaving their homes long before sunrise, the vraja-kumaris met together on the outskirts of the forest, greeted and embraced one another with love, and shared their thoughts about Krsna.

They walked arm in arm down the forest path to the Yamuna, spreading light and life in all directions as they sweetly sang of the qualities of Krsna, accompanying themselves with vinas and karatalas.

During their sankirtana, the cowherd girls sang a song disclosing the true goal of their vow to those forest creatures in Vrndavana fortunate enough to hear. The vraja-kumaris sang:

“O friend! The form of all auspiciousness, wearing a garland, along with all good qualities, will marry you. When Nanda Maharaja comes to know of this, he will spread the joyful news.

“Overjoyed at this news, your mother and father will distribute wealth to everyone; meanwhile, clever Krsna will fuel your love with jokes He sends through friends, jokes that make you sublimely angry.

“The wedding day set by the matchmaker, Krsna will arrive at your home, riding a brightly decorated bullock cart, dressed in His best finery, including a yellow vest, priceless ornaments, and crown.

“O friend! When you hear the sound of Krsna arriving outside the house, your heart will be agitated. And when He knocks on your door, won’t you faint in bliss? I am certain you will.

“The women of the house will greet Krsna with songs, offer Him arati, and shower Him with flowers. Then they will worship Nanda, and after much joking bring you to Krsna along with a valuable dowry.

“As you stand before Krsna, you will tremble in ecstasy, and as your father pours water to join your hand with Krsna’s, no one but the Lord will know the great happiness in your heart.”

By the time the gopis arrived at the Yamuna, the first rays of the sun were dancing on the river’s waves. At Gopi-ghata, the girls discarded their warm shawls and donned cotton bathing dresses.

The morning air was so chilly that steam rose from the Yamuna, but ignoring the cold, the gopis offered their obeisances and entered the water to carefully observe the rites Vrnda had prescribed for them.

Their ritualistic bath finished, the kanya-kumaris scurried up the ghdta, elated at having braved the cold water, and offered a first oblation into the sacrificial fire of their love for Krsna.

They shivered uncontrollably as they dried themselves, tied up their hair, and dressed in fresh clothes. All the while they repeated Krsna’s names through lips trembling in the cold wintry air.

The sun god took pity on the gopis and warmed their cold bodies with his rays as they selected a secluded part of the forest with clean sandy beaches in which they could perform their worship.

The part of Vrndavana forest where the gopis regularly came to bathe, worship, and offer prayers to Katyayani, is named Tapovana because of the severe austerities (tapa) the gopis performed there.

**\* \* \* \***

As they were placing their puja items on the sand, one girl asked, “Since this is the first day, we should decide whether we will worship Katyayani individually or all together. What do you think?”

The answer another gopi gave met with unanimous approval: “I am sure that if we worship the goddess together she will he more pleased. And that will he more beneficial for us. Let’s do it together.”

Some of the more artistic girls fashioned an extremely attractive deity of Katyayani-devi from pure clay, sand, and earth, then enhanced the goddess’s already lifelike features with berries, leaves, and grass.

Other gopis versed in mantras offered flowers to the deity. After all the girls had purified themselves hy sipping sanctified water, they sat in meditation and invoked the goddess’s presence with this mantra:

*Iha gaccha gaccha devi, sannidhanam ihacara*  
*krsnasya sannidhanam nah, prapayasva namo namah*

**“Devi! Please enter this deity to hel us come close to Krsna. Obeisances to you, again and again.”**

The gopis then began their formal worship by offering Katyayani a seat, water for washing her feet, mouthwash, pleasant scents, a new sari, flowers, a ghee lamp, and so on, each with an appropriate prayer.

As they offered bathing water in a golden vessel, for example, the gopis prayed, “We offer you this finely scented bathing water. Please arrange for us to bathe in the nectar of Krsna’s company.”

As they offered things like milk, butter, bananas, and coconuts, along with different kinds of sweets and cakes, they prayed, “Please eat this and give us remnants from the mouth of youthful Krsna.”

Finally, after offering food and performing arati, each gopi chanted the mantra given to her by Vrnda-devi,

**“O goddess Katyayani, o great potency of the Lord, ? possessor of great mystic power and mighty controller of all, please make the son of Nanda Maharaja my husband. I offer my obeisances unto you.”**

The gopis chanted this mantra out loud and silently as well. Their minds fully absorbed in the transcendental sound vibration, they were in direct communion with goddess Katyayani herself.

The gopis prayed, “Please make Krsna our husband!” Katyayani then spoke to each of them within their minds: “I will inspire your parents to get you married. Don’t ask for my direct involvement.”

But the gopis adamantly replied, “Devi! Krsna cannot marry until He is initiated. We can’t wait that long for Him to be our husband.” “Then what are you asking of me?” Katyayani demanded.

Each gopi replied, “Do not involve our parents. Neglect the rituals of marriage and arrange for us to marry Krsna in the way of the Gandharvas — by mutual consent, without parental sanction.”

To test the strength of the young gopis’ will, goddess Katyayani protested, “How can I fulfil your desire to have a conjugal relationship with Krsna without your parents’ knowledge?”

But the gopis persisted, “You have unlimited power. You can make the impossible possible. You can bewilder our parents in such a way that they won’t even know of our marriage to Krsna.”

Such a mindset, along with the willingness to endure hardships expected only of accomplished yogis, and the gopis’ relentless desire to serve Krsna’s senses as His wives, amazed Katyayani-devi.

Their prayers finished, the gopis offered their obeisances and respectfully consigned the deity of Katyayani to the Yamuna. Then they returned home, singing the glories of their beloved Krsna.

The vraja-kumaris performed their daily ritual throughout the entire month, their tongues and minds completely absorbed in Krsna, their love for Him waxing along with the winter moon.

The night before their vows were complete, Katyayani appeared to the girls in a dream and said, “O auspicious girls! I am very pleased by your pure offerings and regulated worship. All good fortune unto you!

“Your prayers have made me glorious. Very soon you will attain Krsna’s company according to your individual desires.” With these words echoing in their hearts, the gopis awoke, full of excitement.

They sang all the way to the Yamuna, their minds absorbed in thoughts of how they would get Krsna. By the time they had met one another, their left sides were quivering — an auspicious omen.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that on this full-moon day the vraja-kumdris had invited Radha and other gopis to bathe in the river with them and participate in the final day of their worship.

After completing their vow, the gopis again removed their clothes and entered the water naked to take the ceremonial bath (avabhrtha-snana ) that customarily follows the completion of a sacrifice.

The girls were in a playful mood. They felt that something wonderful was about to happen, so they frolicked for some time, unaware that Krsna was nearby watching and waiting to satisfy their desire.

Sukadeva Gosvami describes Krsna’s secret arrival at the gopis’ bathing place:

**“Lord Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead and master of all masters of mystic yoga was aware of what the gopis were doing, and thus He went there surrounded by His young companions to award the gopis the perfection of their endeavour.”**

Krsna had been with the cowherd boys tending the cows, but when He remembered the vraja-kumaris their love drew Him away from His friends, and so He went to Tapovana on some pretext or another.

The companions Sukadeva mentions were toddlers, two or three years old. They were too young to distinguish between male and female. Indeed, they too were naked, except for tigers’ claws and waist bells.

The names of the children were Dama, Sudama, Vasudama, and Kirikini. They are external manifestations of Krsna’s mind, intelligence, consciousness, and sense of identity, respectively.

Since these children were expansions of Krsna Himself, the Lord cannot be criticised for going to see the bathing gopis in someone else’s company. He was accompanied only by His own subtle energies.

The girls had left their clothes hanging over bushes or folded on clean patches of earth. They were some distance out into the water, so they did not see Krsna when He approached with His four tiny friends.

Krsna stopped in the shadows, bundled His hair up under His turban, hiked up His dhoti, removed His ankle bells, and silenced the boys’ silly chatter with a stern glare and reproachful gestures.

Like a thief, Krsna crouched down behind bushes and trees as He quickly collected the gopis’ clothes. Slinging them over His shoulder, He climbed into a kadamba tree to eavesdrop on the girls’ chatter.

Unable to restrain themselves any longer, the young boys started to laugh. Krsna could sec that His exposure was imminent, so He too laughed aloud, still concealed in His perch by leaves and branches.

The gojns were startled by the sound of voices. They looked anxiously here and there, arguing over who could he laughing. When they saw that their clothes had vanished, they became fearful.

Krsna pushed the branches aside to reveal His effulgent beauty, crowned by His radiant smiling face. Now fully visible to the gopis, He continued to laugh and joke with His bubbly little friends.

The gopis at once submerged themselves so that only their heads were above water. Too shy to look at Krsna, they glanced down at their own reflections, which danced on watery ripples.

With the girls’ clothes resting there on the branch next to Him, Krsna now teased the vraja-kumaris, who had just come to realise that the fruit of their vow was ripening before their very eyes.

The goal for which the gopis had abandoned creature comforts, risen early, bathed in the cold, and dutifully chanted mantras had suddenly materialised. They thought, “Goddess Katyayani is truly all-powerful.”

**\* \* \* \***

Indeed, Katyayani had brought Krsna to the gopis. But if the gopis wanted Krsna as their husband, they would have to go one step beyond simply keeping their vow. They would have to surrender.

To satisfy Krsna they would have to set aside shame, religion — even moral conduct. By so doing, the sprouts of their love would fully blossom, manifesting the aroma of great ecstasy.

Krsna came to Cira-ghata to reciprocate the gopis’ love, bringing it to perfection. With sweet words He wanted to draw the girls out from the waters of reluctance to fully embrace the shelter of His lotus feet.

Krsna said, “Young girls! Do you know who has left these clothes on this branch? I saw the tree from a distance and was attracted hy what appeared to be colourful fruits and flowers, so I climbed up.”

The gopis answered in unison, “They are our clothes.” Krsna chuckled and said, “How could they be yours? They are on such a high branch.” The gopis replied, “Because You put them there.”

Feigning indignation, Krsna said, “Are you calling Me, the son of Nanda Maharaja, a thief?” The gopis tried to pacify Him, “Don’t he angry. Just tell us if they are men’s clothes or women’s clothes.”

Krsna looked through the garments and replied, “They arc colourful enough to he women’s clothes. But you are not the only women in Vraja. They could be the clothes of some other women.”

The gopis rolled their eyes and said, “Maybe! But who amongst them, other than us, comes to this forest — ” Krsna interrupted, “Other girls like you, who like to wander in lonely places and splash in the water.”

That was too much for the gopis: “Nonsense! We are not here to play water games but to worship Mother Durga.” Krsna teased, “And are there no other young women worshipping Durga here?”

Wasn’t it enough to shiver in the cold water, did the gopis also have to he ridiculed? “No! There are no other women!” Krsna clapped His hands in disbelief, “What about goddesses who come here at night?”

Some girls slapped the water in frustration, “Why would they leave their clothing here and then fly away?” Krsna replied, “To return later, worship, bathe, and then dress in these clothes. Obviously!”

The gopis had had enough. The clothes were theirs. “You are wrong! Only we worship Durga here. No one else! Perhaps while we were bathing, a forest goddess placed our clothes there for safekeeping!”

Krsna nodded, “If these clothes actually are yours, then come here individually, identify your garments, and take them from Me after paying the price of a necklace for the insults I have had to bear.”

The gopis shook their heads and said, “We cannot go there.” Laughing, Krsna replied, “Obviously you have become weak from your austerities. Don’t delay any longer. Just trust Me.”

But the gopis knew of Krsna’s reputation. They replied, “That’s just it. We know You, and You’re a liar.” Offended, Krsna snapped, “I have never told a lie in My life. These boys can attest to that.”

It was no use arguing with a liar over his trustworthiness, and so the gopis pleaded, “Please throw down our clothes. Or just have the boys bring them to us.” Krsna fumbled with the clothes and answered:

“How can I tell who owns which dress? You will have to come and identify them yourselves.” By this time, the gopis had a clear picture of Krsna’s plan but needed somehow to be saved from their shyness.

By His humour and His skill in the art of gentle persuasion, Krsna had to free the girls from the strict moral codes that now prevented them from achieving what they had prayed for all month.

And Krsna would do just that. Not with mere words, but with a lifeline woven from the fibre of their mutual love, cast to each and every gopi through the medium of enchanting, humorous talks.

The gopis’ verbal comebacks were their hold on that lifeline, Krsna’s continued arguments His means of reeling them into the lifeboat— the branch upon which He sat ready to accept them as wives.

The gopis were still not yet ready to surrender. “Do not embarrass us,” they said. “We are respectable women. We cannot come near You.” Krsna was adamant: “Come one at a time or all at once, as you like.”

He then added, “The head is considered the foremost part of the body. You are not too shy to show Me your heads. Why make such a fuss about the rest of your limbs, including your slender waists.”

Krsna’s joking words were having their effect: the gopis’ resistance was crumbling. They no longer scowled at Him, but were now starting to laugh and joke amongst themselves, even in their embarrassment.

The gopis thought, “We should make Krsna happy and not be so self-conscious.” But when they looked around at one another, they realised they could not hide their lingering embarrassment.

But then again, here was Krsna, joking freely with them as if they were His wives, something they had dreamt of for years and prayed for all month. How could they not reciprocate His jokes and smiles?

One gopi told another, “Friend! Krsna is calling you!” “You go first,” her friend replied. “Let’s see if He plays any tricks.” The girls joked with one another like this but continued to shiver in the cold water.

Krsna said, “I am quite tired from having stayed up all night. If you don’t come here and get your clothes, I will tie them together to make a hammock and a pillow on this branch, and go to sleep.”

One gopi said, “Your cows have strayed into a cave. We can hear them crying. Go rescue them.” Unmoved, Krsna replied, “Why don’t you give up these water sports and return to your household chores?”

Another vraja-kumaris countered, “Our parents have ordered us to follow this vow, and so we are not meant to go home for a month.” Leaning against a leafy branch, Krsna yawned, “Very good!

“I too have developed a surprising mood of detachment. I will accept the vow of living up here in the clouds (nabho-vrata). But whenever you invite Me, I’ll happily fast in the water with you.”

The cowherd girls were shivering, but not just from the cold. Anxiety, joy, and anticipation also made them tremble. Meanwhile, they tried to pacify Krsna with diplomacy, but to no avail.

Krsna turned each of their arguments against them. The girls said, “O son of Nanda! Proposing that we behave immorally is not worthy of one born in a cultured family and honoured throughout the land.”

“Foolish women! How can a king’s son do wrong? Besides, if I am so immoral, how can I also be loved and respected everywhere? You’re not making any sense.” “O Syamasundara!” the gopis replied.

“We are Your maidservants and must do whatever You say. But give us back our clothing. You know what the religious principles are, and if You don’t give us our clothes we will have to tell the king. Please!”

With this statement the gopis still attempted to pacify Krsna by proclaiming themselves maidservants sold out to His order in exchange for the price of seeing His incomparable dark-hued beauty.

But that tactic had already failed, so next the cowherd girls tried to weaken Krsna by inspiring in Him the fear of sinful reaction. After all, for a man to see women naked would be irreligious.

It did not take long, however, for the gopis to realise that trying to instil fear of irreligion in Krsna was futile, so they resorted to threats — they would file a complaint with the king.

His arms crossed defiantly, Krsna said, “Go ahead. Tell the king of Mathura. What can he do to Me?” Pausing for effect, Krsna could see that He had called their bluff. They were defeated.

“You are truthful women,” Krsna continued. “You have admitted that you are My maidservants. Shouldn’t you therefore act according to My request? Come and get your clothes or go home without them.”

The gopis smiled at each other. Their lips clearly revealed the amorous love Krsna had drawn out of their hearts, a love that was now spreading its influence all over their limbs and faces.

With their faces turned down, the gopis looked at Krsna, openly smiling, thus revealing their willingness to leave the Yamuna. To rally support for their cause, the gopis whispered amongst themselves:

“O friends! Krsna has defeated all our arguments. Our fate seems inevitable. We must yield to Krsna’s demands. Let us close our eyes, cast aside all shame, and get out of the water.”

Hoping that the darkness behind their eyelids would cover their naked bodies, the girls shut their eyes, covered themselves with their knee length hair, and slowly walked out of the water.

**\* \* \* \***

Sri Krsna asks us to abandon all sorts of religious formularies (sarva-dharman parityajya) that obstruct exclusive surreiv der to Him. And He means not just some, not almost all, but all — every last one.

The gopis had followed Krsna’s order by getting out of the water, but they knew the true intent of His order was not yet fulfilled: He wanted to see the beauty of their bodies, which their hair obscured.

As the supreme, self-satisfied person, Krsna had no interest in seeing young girls naked. His interest was in teaching the world — through these gopis — that real religion means completely selfless service.

Draupadi had once been in danger of being disrobed in the Kuru assembly. When no one would protect her honour, she turned to Krsna as her last resort and called out “Hey, Govinda!”

But Draupadi continued to struggle against her oppressors — first with two hands, then with one — so Krsna did not respond. Only when she threw up both arms in desparation did He finally come to her aid.

The gopis who stood naked before Krsna were symbols of full surrender, as was Draupadi in her desparate appeal to the Lord. But the gopis and Draupadi came to full surrender by different paths.

Draupadi was brought to completely depend upon Krsna hy force of circumstances: she could not match the strength of Duhsasana. But Krsna personally led the gopis from partial to full surrender.

The display of the vraja-kumaris' loving affection greatly satisfied Krsna. As He placed their colourful garments over His shoulders He caught a trace of their bodily fragrance and thought:

“Out of love for Me, the gopis have done something remarkably difficult for any woman to do. But there is something still more difficult. I wonder if they can do it. Let me now test their love.”

The gopis' long hair concealed their beauty, but Krsna convinced them that loose, dishevelled hair was inauspicious, so they tied up their hair. Still, they continued to cover themselves with their hands.

Krsna smiled to Himself. The young gopis had done as they were told, but by keeping themselves covered they were not completely yielding to His desire to see the full beauty of their forms.

Certainly the gopis were willing to do whatever Krsna wanted, but they were waiting for Him to explicitly make His desire known. Krsna said, “You girls bathed naked while executing your vow.

“That is certainly an offence against the demigods. To counteract your sin you should offer obeisances while placing your joined palms above your heads. Then you should take back your garments.”

The gopis accepted Krsna at His word. They had not endured a month of austerity just to have it undone at the last moment by a playful act. But where were the demigods to accept their apology?

And though the gopis had finally realised Krsna as their husband and were willing to do His bidding, they also thought it improper for the four young boys to see them completely uncovered.

To divert the boys’ attention, one of them said, “Look! Someone is coming!” When the boys turned around to see who it was, the gopis bashfully gazed at Krsna, who is the husband of everyone.

Taking Krsna — whom Garga Muni had said was as good as Narayana— as the representative of all rhe demigods, the gopis joined their palms above their heads and offered their obeisances to Him.

Srila Prabhupada comments,

**“Thus they \[the gopis\] became the greatest lovers of Krsna, and His most obedient servitors. Nothing can compare to the Krsna consciousness of the gopis.”**

Krsna climbed down from the tree with the pile of clothes on His shoulders and, flanked by His young friends, handed each gopi her clothes, now scented by the touch of His hands.

After dressing and ornamenting themselves, the gopis, who had finally achieved the result of their vows, could not leave. They stood around Krsna like bees swarming around a honey-filled lotus.

We can learn the following lesson from the vraja-kumaris: Even though Krsna cheated them, robbed them of their modesty, and slyly manipulated them, they never resented Him.

To the contrary, the gopis followed Krsna’s instructions with love. They were overjoyed at the chance to serve and associate with Him. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura summarises the state of their hearts:

**“When one is considered dear, whatever that dear one docs is experienced with pleasure, even if it gives pain.”**

In Krsna Book, Srila Prabhupada confirms this truth by quoting Lord Caitanya.

In the final of His Siksastaka, the Lord prays,

**“My dear Lord Krsna, You may embrace Me or trample Me under Your feet, or You may make Me broken-hearted by never being present before Me.**

**“Whatever You like, You can do, because You have complete freedom to act. But in spite of all Your dealings, You arc My Lord eternally, and I have no other worshipable object.”**

The young gopis’ satisfaction at being with Krsna was written clearly upon their beautiful faces. Still, they were not sure that Krsna was pleased or that He had actually accepted them.

Krsna clarified His feelings by saying, “O saintly girls! I understand that your real motive in this austerity has been to worship Me. I approve of your intent, and indeed it must come to pass.”

By Krsna’s mercy, the meaning of His words and the full extent of His transcendental power were both evident to the gopis. They realised that Krsna was not just like Narayana, He actually was Narayana.

With that realisation fresh in their minds, they attentively and faithfully heard His next instruction,

“The desire of those who fix their minds on Me does not lead to material desire for sense gratification, just as barleycorns burned by the sun and then cooked can no longer grow into new sprouts.”

To reassure the gopis that He had accepted them as His wives and that they would meet Him again to share intimate pastimes as lovers and beloved, Krsna added, “Go now, girls, and return to Vraja.

“Your desire is fulfilled, for in My company you will enjoy the coming nights. After all, this was the purpose of your vow to worship goddess Katyayani ? pure-hearted ones.”

The gopis were perfected souls, but had acted like practising devotees by observing the Katyayani-vrata, and in so doing fulfilled their own desires while bringing great pleasure to the Lord of their hearts.

Krsna had accepted the gopis according to the Gandharva rite, for only a husband can see his wife naked. But as He pointed out, further loving exchanges would take place at a later time.

In the following year, on the full-moon night of Karttika, the kanya-kumaris , their love ablaze with anticipation, would revel in the intimacy of amorous love with Krsna, along with other gopis of Vraja.

For now, however, they would have to go home. Krsna had returned their clothes but, true to His ways, He had kept their stolen hearts with Him, and they were more than happy that He had.

The gopis left Cira-ghata and returned to their parents, meditating on Krsna’s lotus feet. On the last day of the Katyayani-vrata— just as Vrnda promised — they had attained Krsna as their husband.

The kanya-kumaris’ bodies, words, and actions were saturated with the bliss of having attained Krsna, the rarest treasure, achievable only through spotless love for that cowherd hero of Vrndavana.

Dasa Gosvami says,

**“Entering the waters of the Yamuna to prepare for the incomparable worship of goddess Katyayani, the girls of Vraja left their garments on the shore. Smiling and clever Krsna —**

**“Stole those garments, climbed a kadamba tree, embarrassed the girls with joking words, and eventually returned the garments. I take shelter of Cira-ghata, where the Lord enjoyed these pastimes.”**

**\* \* \* \***

In Syaraha village in Bhauma Vrndavana, Cira-ghata, an ancient kadamba tree, and a temple of Katyayani mark the kanya-kumaris place of worship. A Radha-Krsna temple stands nearby in Tapovana.

North of Cira-ghata are Nanda-ghata and Bhaya, where the servants of Varuna kidnapped Nanda Maharaja. The residents of Vrndavana, upon seeing this, called out to Krsna in fear (bhaya).

Nanda Maharaja always strictly observed Ekadasi. On one particular Dvadasi he came to the Yamuna in order to break his fast by bathing. There he entered the river at what is now called Nanda-ghata.

As Nanda Maharaja stood in the water and meditated on Lord Narayana, his worshipable Deity since birth, he entered into a trance and completely lost awareness of his surroundings.

Just at that moment a demonic servant of Varuna arrested Nandaraja for bathing during a technically inauspicious period of the night. The errant constable then whisked the king off to his master’s abode.

Varuna’s servant was at fault both because he failed to recognise Nandaraja as the Lord’s father and because he did not know that the importance of breaking Ekadasi supersedes other considerations.

Varuna had established his residence in a large cave accessible from the bottom of the Yamuna River. His servant was thus able to quickly bring Nanda Maharaja before the lord of waters.

Varuna recognised Nandaraja immediately; the king was adorned with tulasi beads, tulasi garland, and still absorbed in samadhi. Lull of fear, Varuna respectfully placed Maharaja Nanda on a celestial bed.

Varuna knew that Krsna would not tolerate His father’s abduction; indeed, Krsna would come to Nanda’s aid at once. Hurrying to the entrance of his abode, Varuna waited there to greet his master.

Meanwhile, Nanda Maharaja’s friends and attendants discovered their king had disappeared. Full of fear, they searched the river in all directions, but the pious king of Vrndavana could not be found.

The cowherd men then loudly called out for Krsna, who was sleeping on a bed of flowers some distance away. Hearing their call, Krsna rose to His feet and quickly ran to the riverbank, Balarama by His side.

Speculation that Nanda Maharaja had drowned brought all the Vraja-vasis running, but the two brothers arrived there first and heard from panicked guards about Nanda Maharaja’s disappearance.

Krsna said to Balarama, “O brother! Take care of mother and the others until I return with Our father.” He then tied His dhoti tight, plunged into the Yamuna, and swam to the giant cave at the bottom.

Yasoda and the gopis soon arrived at Yamuna’s shore. Seeing Balarama alone, they asked, “Where is Your younger brother?” To pacify the women, Balarama replied, “O mothers! Do not worry.

“Your powerful son has gone to rescue His father. He will soon return and make you happy.” But Mother Yasoda and the elder women of Vrndavana would not be so easily appeased.

Rohini first scolded and then gave Balarama a slap for having allowed Krsna to go alone to rescue Nanda; meanwhile, four women tried to stop Yasoda, wild with fear, from running into the river after her son.

The Vraja-vasis were in a state, having lost their equilibrium. They spoke feverishly, “Are we really awake, or is this a bad dream? Or are we delirious? Maybe we have fainted. O Krsna! Where are You?”

Of all the Vraja-vasis, the young gopis fared the worst. Unable to see, hear, or say anything, their minds flew after Krsna. Their bodies shook uncontrollably until they finally fell down, unconscious.

Radha’s faint temporarily relieved Her agony, but when some gopis revived Her by saying, “Krsna is coming,” Her suffering began anew and She stared vacantly into the waves of the Yamuna.

Meanwhile, Krsna approached the entrance to Varuna’s kingdom. His anger was clearly visible in His countenance, which resembled that of Lord Nrsimha as He burst out of the pillar to kill Hiranyakasipu.

His black complexion had turned red, His kindly glance now burned with anger, His normally soft demeanour was fierce, and His voice sounded like the rumbling of the Samvartaka clouds.

“Where is that Varuna!” Krsna thought. He had already invoked His powers to punish the upstart, but when He saw the demigod and his followers offering obeisances at a distance, He was somewhat pacified.

Despite His anger at the disrespect that had been shown to His father, Krsna felt some affection for Varuna; still, in a stern voice He demanded, “Where is My worshipable father, the abode of all piety?”

Varuna offered prayers in praise of Krsna’s supremacy, also lauding his own good fortune at being able to see the Lord in person. But Krsna impatiently demanded, “Why do you embarrass Me like this?

“Where is My father?” “He’s here, my Lord,” Varuna replied nervously. He guided Krsna to the place where Nandaraja was still in devotional trance. Varuna then said, “Please take Your father.”

Even from within his trance, Nanda Maharaja could smell the fragrance of Krsna’s body. To the amazement of all present, he suddenly regained external consciousness, his meditation complete.

At the sight of his son, Nanda Maharaja’s eyes filled with tears. He embraced Krsna and asked in astonishment, “Where are we?” Krsna replied, “You were confined here in King Varuna’s palace.”

Nanda Maharaja looked around in wonder at the opulent and expansive underwater kingdom. In even greater wonder he took note of the reverence with which Varuna served his son.

Wary that His father not be caught up in Varuna’s mood of reverential worship, Krsna stood up to leave, but the demigod then appealed to his worshipable Lord in a piteous voice.

With joined palms, Varuna said, “Your father, who is sitting here, was brought to me by a foolish, ignorant servant of mine who did not understand his proper duty. Therefore, please forgive us.”

Varuna could understand that his assistant had committed an offence to the Supreme Lord and to a peerless Vaisnava, an offence for which he too would have to suffer if Krsna did not forgive him.

Varuna said, “O Krsna! You are compassionate. I have offended both You and Your father. Please punish me, or give me mercy. If You do not, unthinkable reactions will be forever on my head.”

Krsna abandoned His anger and forgave Varuna, reassuring him that his devotion would grow unimpeded. Varuna also lavished such a bounty of gifts upon the Lord that two servants had to carry them.

At the mouth of the underwater cave, Varuna offered his obeisances and, causing the waters of the Yamuna to part, sent the servants carrying gifts to accompany Krsna and Nanda back to Vraja.

Varuna was filled with bliss, for he was sure that his darsana of the Lord had made his life successful. After his guests had left, Varuna returned to his palace, dancing and singing the holy names of Krsna.

Meanwhile, the Vraja-vasis were almost lifeless, lying like so many fallen leaves on the riverbank. But as Krsna and Nanda emerged from the river, the Vraja-vasis sprung to life, only to faint again in bliss.

Only Balarama was conscious enough to receive Nanda and Krsna. Beginning with His mother, Krsna went about reviving the Vraja- vasis with His touch, while Nanda held Balarama in a firm embrace.

It is said that when the demigods saw Krsna and Nanda Maharaja come out of the water they showered them with flowers and chanted “Jaya! Jaya!” Thus the place adjacent to Bhaya is called Jayeta.

After all the cows and Vraja-vasis had regained consciousness, they surrounded Nanda Maharaja and Krsna, making a tumult by lowing, clapping, talking excitedly, and uttering sacred mantras.

Balarama sat Nanda Maharaja and Krsna in an elevated place, and as the others sat around them, rapt in wonder, the king of Vrndavana recounted everything, just as it had happened.Nanda Maharaja then completed his Ekadasi vow: he fed the brahmanas, offered them gifts, and received their blessings. Finally he returned home, walking with his two sons on either side of him.

I offer my obeisances to Nanda-ghata and to Bhaya, where the servant of Varuna kidnapped Lord Krsna’s father. Remembering this pastime with full faith brings relief from every kind of fear.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda says that the kidnapping of Nanda Maharaja is symbolic of practising devotees’ trying to enhance their devotion by taking intoxicants, which surely results in even more bad habits.

Pure devotees never take intoxicants. By remembering how Krsna delivered His father from the watery kingdom of Varuna, practising devotees will never succumb to such unbecoming temptations.

It is said that Jiva Gosvami sometimes lived in the area of Nanda-ghata, at times in a cave, at other times in the jungle. He is supposed to have composed his famous Sat-sandarbhas at this place.

The scholar Vallabhacarya once visited Vrndavana and suggested some changes to a manuscript Rupa Gosvami was writing at the time. Sri Jiva was sitting nearby and overheard the conversation.

Although the suggested changes were unnecessary, Rupa Gosvami humbly accepted them. Sri Jiva, however, dismayed that his spiritual master’s perfect compositions might be compromised, could not.

Later, Vallabha went to the Yamuna. Jiva Gosvami approached him and a debate ensued in which Jiva refuted the brahmanas proposed changes and proved that Rupa Gosvami’s composition was faultless.

After returning from the river, Vallabhacarya told Rupa Gosvami about the debate and voiced his great appreciation for Jiva Gosvami’s intellectual acumen and his knowledge of the scriptures.

But after Vallabhacarya had left, rather than praise Jiva, Rupa Gosvami chastised him for seeking distinction through being the victor in a debate. This was not conduct becoming a Vaisnava.

Rupa Gosvami said,

**“You can neither stay with me nor live in Vraja. Go wherever you like, but you must leave.”**

Broken-hearted, Jiva Gosvami went to Nanda-ghata and lamented his offence.

It is said that the acarya lived in a large alligator hole and would only eat raw wheat flour mixed with water. Because of this poor diet he became seriously ill. The local villagers feared for his life.

One day Sanatana Gosvami found Sri Jiva in this sorry state. Upon returning to Vrndavana, Sanatana told Rupa that by banning Jiva he had violated a sadhu’s prime duty: being merciful to all (jiva-daya).

Rupa Gosvami then brought Srila Jiva Gosvami back to Vrndavana, personally nursed him back to health, and entrusted him with the intimate service of editing his books, like Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu.

Vajra established a village here by the name of Bhaya-grama, which is called Bhegrama today. Jiva Gosvami’s cave is still there, and at Nanda-ghata there is a temple of Nanda, Yasoda, and Radha-Krsna.

**\* \* \* \***

Downstream from Bhaya is the forest of Vatsavana, which contains many places, such as Unai, connected to the pastimes of Krsna’s killing Vatsasura and Aghasura and the bewilderment of Brahma.

The physical locations of the pastime places along this part of the parikrama path do not follow the chronological order in which the pastimes took place, and so the narrations also will be out of order.

First let us hear about the killing of the calf (vatsa) demon, Vatsasura, and the bewilderment of Brahma, both of which took place in peaceful Vatsavana. Then we’ll hear about the killing of Aghasura.

Towards the end of boyhood, Krsna and Balarama gave up drinking Their mothers’ milk and taking their mothers’ help to get dressed. They began dressing Themselves, though not always as neatly.

The boys took a keen interest in milking the cows and practised tying ropes and carrying empty milk pails. Whenever Nanda Maharaja went out to tend the cows, They would go with him.

As the adults looked on in bliss, Krsna and Balarama would separate a few cows from the herd, run ahead, and try to herd those cows Themselves, just as They had seen Their elders do.

But when the boys began to miss lunch because of being with Their father, Yasoda put her foot down. She told Nanda, “What kind of unprecedented practice is this, taking children into the forest?”

Thereafter, Mother Yasoda and Rohini-devi refused Nanda Maharaja’s requests to take the boys out. As a consequence, the brothers became morose; They felt cheated of Their source of happiness.

After consulting with his brothers and negotiating with the elder gopis, Nanda arranged that Krsna and His friends could herd calves in nearby pastures, where meals could be delivered to them.

Then, on an auspicious day, as brahmanas chanted mantras, the gopas entrusted the care of the calves to their little sons, who wore handsome turbans and held sticks, ropes, flutes, and buffalo horns.

The cowherds offered special shoes to their boys, but Krsna would not accept them, so Balarama and the other boys followed His lead. In this way They blessed the earth with Their sacred footprints.

As the boys were set to leave on that first day, their mothers dressed and decorated them opulently, performed arati to them, took protective vows, and offered them blessing after blessing.

The cows, children, and especially Krsna were the Vraja-vasis’ wealth. From their homes they protected that wealth by their thoughts, just as turtles nurture their eggs from far away by meditation.

After venturing out some distance, the boys allowed their calves to roam freely and graze on fresh grass. Meanwhile, they imitated bulls fighting, played ball games, and tossed fallen fruits around the forest.

Krsna and Balarama imitated the sounds of forest animals, which made those animals come to Them. But when the boys imitated the lion’s roar, all the animals fled, so They stopped.
