At noon, maidservants sent by the boys’ mothers arrived with baskets of food. Krsna called His friends with His flute, and the gopas sat in lines, making eager noises as the women served them.

After lunch the boys rested a little, played again, gathered their calves, and returned home to a splendid reception from their parents. The boys felt the satisfaction of having fulfilled their religious duties.

In this way days passed, bringing Krsna and His friends the happiness of boyish play and taking away the lives of demons, lives which were futilely dedicated to disturbing the blissful atmosphere of Vraja.

Through spies, Kamsa had come to know of Krsna’s arrival in Vrndavana. Kamsa suspected that somehow this young cowherd was the son of Vasudeva that the goddess Durga had said would kill him.

Kamsa thought, “The mere sound of this boy’s name brings fear to my heart. One way or another, He must be killed.” Kamsa called for one of his spies and asked him, “What is this boy most attracted to?”

The spy answered, “He has great affection for the calves He herds daily.” A plan at once hatched in Kamsa’s mind. He called for the powerful Vatsasura, who was known to have defeated great demigods.

Vatsasura arrived, and Kamsa said, “Dear friend! Go to the pastures of Nanda, where one boy in particular, Krsna, plays and tends His calves. Disguising yourself as a calf, destroy Him and His kin.”

Fool that he was, Vatsasura thought this to he a golden opportunity to gain King Kamsa’s favour, and so he went to Vatsavana and joined Krsna’s herd by the riverbank in a clearing called Vatsa-kridana.

Vatsasura looked like a calf, but he could not hide his demonic nature; the other calves and Krsna — eyeing him from a distance — could sense his impiety. Krsna called Balarama over and asked:

“O Dauji! Did You see that calf by the river? He did not come from Vraja with our herd.” Balarama had not seen it, but upon examining the creature at Krsna’s request He said, “It seems to be ferocious.”

Krsna added, “Surely, it’s a demon.” Balarama responded, “Just see the cruel glances it casts at the calves and at us! How evil!” Krsna whispered so as not to he heard, “If You permit, I will kill it.”

Balarama shook His head and said, “People will criticise us for killing a calf.” Krsna argued, “When the creature is dead, it will be clear to everyone that it was a demon all along. There will be no complaints.”

Lord Balarama smiled. In the spirit of a new adventure, He warned, “Be careful! I can tell that so-called calf is very devious. No doubt You will have to carefully approach it under some pretence.”

Smiling, Krsna called the calves with His flute and began to walk amongst them, scratching their heads, throats, and bellies, and giving them joy by His radiant smile and gentle words.

Vatsasura saw this as his chance — he too nuzzled up to Krsna to be scratched. The Lord affectionately placed His hands on the demon’s body, hut then suddenly grabbed it by the forefeet and tail.

Krsna held Vatsasura tightly and then whirled the demon around and around at such high speed that the creature’s soul was ejected from its body. The Lord then threw its body into the boughs of a kapittha tree.

As Krsna had foretold, Vatsasura’s body resumed its original, horrid form, seeing which the cowherd boys congratulated Krsna by saying, “Well done!” and “Thank You!” The demigods also showered flowers.

After this incident the boys sat down to enjoy a picnic by the river-side, chatting gleefully about how Krsna had killed the demon, and occasionally glancing up at its dead body in the distant tree.

Before they returned home, however, Krsna warned His friends, “If you tell our parents about this demon, they will put an end to our blissful pastimes with the calves. Don’t mention it to anyone!”

Who was Vatsasura that he had such good fortune to die by Krsna’s hands and thus be liberated? In his previous life, Vatsasura was a demon of the name Pramila who had set out to defeat the demigods.

Pramila achieved his goal and was passing by Vasistha Muni’s asrama when he noticed the sage’s kamadhenu cow, Nandini. Pramila was obsessed with the idea of possessing opulence.

Pramila transformed himself into a brahmana, approached the sage, and begged him for the magical cow. Vasistha could see through the demon’s disguise, but he let the cow speak on its own behalf.

Nandini said, “You are the demon Muru’s son. You have assumed the form of a brahmana just to steal my master’s cows. For this offence, O wicked-hearted one, you should now become a calf.”

Pramila was transformed at once into a calf, and he begged — as the accursed are wont to do — that Nandini relieve him of the reaction to his sinful deeds. Taking pity on him, Nandini added:

“O demon! Suffer the reaction to your deeds. But let your contact with the great sage Vasistha not go in vain. At the end of Dvapara-yuga, when mingling with some calves, you will attain liberation.”

This explains why — just as Vatsasura’s lifeless body landed in the kapittha tree — the boys saw the soul of the demon, appearing like a brilliant light, hover above Krsna and then enter into His body.

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura says that the calf-demon Vatsasura is a symbol of the infantile offences living entities commit due to their identification with the temporary material body.

Souls who surrender to Lord Krsna, however, are freed by His grace from the results of such offences, as He personally promises: “I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions. Do not fear.”

**\* \* \* \***

Kamsa fainted when he received news that Vatsasura had been slain. The king's evil ministers revived him and, like moths drawn to a flame, advised him to send another demon — Baka — to kill Krsna.

After Krsna killed Bakasura near Nandagrama, Kamsa sent Aghasura, who, like Vatsasura, was also killed some distance from Vatsavana. The demigods rejoiced upon seeing Aghasura vanquished.

Brahma, the leader of the demigods, also saw Krsna kill Aghasura. Yet the creator still doubted that this little boy could be his master, the Supreme Narayana. Brahma decided he would test Him.

Brahma’s origin, the lotus of creation, was material. Deluded by the same potency that covers all conditioned souls, he thought his mystic powers could conquer Krsna, whom he considered inferior.

After killing Aghasura, Krsna gathered His friends and calves for a blissful procession back to Chatikara town. On the way, they shared jokes, games, songs, and untold loving exchanges.

Even after being swallowed by Agha, the cowherd boys’ possessions— including the delectable lunch packs that they had tied to sticks and slung over their shoulders — stayed pure and intact.

Passing by the Yamuna at Vatsavana, Krsna noticed a level, sandy beach that looked like an ideal picnic spot. “O friends,” He said, “isn’t this pristine shoal an ideal place to share a meal?”

After their trying ordeal with Aghasura, the boys hardly needed to be convinced to sit down and eat. They cheered Krsna’s proposal, calling out, “We must truly be one soul! As You are hungry, so are we.”

The boys quickly sat down in concentric circles, with Krsna in the centre, and placed their lunches in front of them on rocks or leaves. Each boy thought Krsna was sitting beside and looking just at him.

This incident confirms the truth that the Lord’s hands, feet, faces, and eyes are everywhere, as He Himself states in the Bhagavad-gita, sarvatah pani-padam tat sarvato ’ksi-siro-mukham.

Flute, horn, and stick tucked into His belt, Krsna held a lump of yogurt mixed with rice in His left hand. Just to amuse His friends, He held pieces of lemon and amla pickle in between His fingers.

From Parikhama — not far, as demigods fly—the celestials watched in awe as He who accepts oblations of ghee purified by mantras took, directly from His friends’ hands, food they had already tasted.

As He joked, scolded, and praised His friends, Krsna exchanged half-eaten food with those sons of cowherds. Brahma thought, “I can’t accept this. I must test (pariksa) this cowherd boy’s power.”

In the midst of this festive atmosphere, the calves, drawn by fresh grasses, strayed deep into the forest. As soon as the boys noticed, they called out Krsna’s name in fear and jumped up to find their herds.

Just by calling out Krsna’s name, the boys’ fear abated. Krsna wanted the gopas to continue enjoying their lunch, so He stood up and said, “Don’t stop eating. I will find the calves and bring them back.”

Without waiting for an answer, morsels of food still in His hand, Krsna followed the tracks made by the calves across pastures and creeks and into the jungle until the tracks disappeared.

“How did the calves go so far in such a short time?” He wondered. Krsna was determined to find the herd. He searched the nearby mountains, caves, valleys, and forest groves, but found nothing.

Apparently confused, Krsna returned to the spot where He had left the gopas eating lunch. He arrived to find everything as it was before, except for one thing — all the cowherd boys were gone.

Walking sticks lay about and ropes for tying calves still hung in the trees. Partially eaten prasada still sat on plates strewn about the ground, but the cowherd boys were nowhere to be seen.

Watching from Parikhama, Brahma had hatched a plan to test Krsna’s power by using his own mystic potencies. At Balahara He had stolen (hara) both the calves and the cowherd boys (bala).

All-knowing Krsna was aware of the theft as it was taking place. But wanting to trick Brahma, He continued to look for the boys and calves, pretending — with appropriate drama — to be bewildered.

Krsna’s performance was convincing. Brahma — sure he had gained the upper hand — thought Krsna was confused. Then Brahma disappeared to watch Krsna attempt to retrieve His friends and cows.

The creator thought, “Let’s see if Krsna can display some wonderful pastime, or find the calves Himself. Maybe He will pray to me. Or perhaps He will simply remain completely baffled.”

But it was Lord Brahma, a firefly before the sun, who would he baffled. The creator thought that he had stolen the calves and boys, but he had only stolen illusory representations of them.

When Brahma decided to steal the boys and calves, Yogamaya hid them. Mahamaya then produced replicas for Brahma to steal, just as Ravana had unwittingly stolen an illusory replica of the real Sita.

Once Brahma had gone, Krsna showed His superior prowess, as described by Sri Suka,

*tatah krsno mudam kartum tan-matrnam ca kasya ca*  
*ubhayayitam atmanam cakre visva-krd isvarah*

**“Thereafter, just to create pleasure both for Brahma and for the mothers of the calves and cowherd boys, Krsna, the creator of the entire cosmic manifestation, expanded Himself as calves and boys."**

By His own spiritual potency Krsna perfectly manifested all the unique personality traits, mannerisms, dress, ornaments, and cowherd paraphernalia of each gopa. Even Krsna marvelled at His own skill.

Similarly, the calves were identical to their prototypes in size, colouring, age, and disposition. Krsna was sure that neither the calves’ nor the boys’ mothers would be able to tell the difference.

Then, as if nothing out of the ordinary had occurred, these new gopas, followed by their new calves, sang and danced their way back to Vrndavana to the captivating sound of Krsna’s flute.

Upon arriving in Vrndavana, Krsna in the form of the calves ran to the shelter of the calves’ mothers, and in the form of the gopas ran to their mothers and fathers in their respective homes.

The expansions of Krsna, in forms like Subala and Sridama, pleased their parents as usual by bathing, eating, and dressing, hut for the first time they did not say anything about their day with Krsna.

The cows greeted their offspring hy licking the calves’ bodies and feeding them with continual streams of milk, showing that their affection for the calves was even greater now than it had been before.

Similarly, the children’s mothers, who had always secretly harboured greater affection for Krsna than the affection they had for their own sons, now felt a new intense affection for their boys.

The elderly cowherd women used to pine: “Will I ever be like Queen Yasoda and have Krsna as my child?’’ Now Krsna, having taken the forms of the gopis’ sons, had kindly fulfilled their desire.

The gopis’ affection for their sons had always been based on their love for Krsna, for they saw their sons in relation to Him. In caring for their sons, they would think, “He is a friend of Krsna.”

Jiva Gosvami tells us that during the year Krsna stood in for the gopas, the elder gopis’ love for Krsna was twice that of Yasoda’s. In this way the Lord rewarded His devotees with the greatest bliss.

Moreover, the affection that Krsna displayed for these women was not the same as the affection their sons showed to them, it was greater. We may wonder why that was so.

If Krsna duplicated each boy’s qualities, why did He not display the exact same love as they did? The answer is that even though Krsna is the supreme controller, He does not control love; love controls Him.

The mothers’ love for Krsna was so powerful, so irrepressible, that He could not control the display of His love for them, and so He fully reciprocated with them as if He were actually their son.

Krsna’s subordination to love is the cause of Vraja’s sweetness. It is a special ornament of His personality, not a fault. Sridhara Svami thus comments, “This irregularity was impossible for Krsna to suppress.”

For one whole year, Krsna, having become the calves and cowherd boys, continued His pastimes as before, tending the calves, playing in the forest, and giving love to the residents of Vrndavana.

Just before the year was up, Krsna, Balarama, and the boys were herding calves near Giriraja. The cows and gopas nearby showed such excessive love for their offspring that Balarama became suspicious.

Lord Balarama quickly concluded that all the calves and gopas must he Krsna. But because He could not understand the reason that Krsna had assumed these roles, He asked His brother to explain.

Krsna’s Yogamaya was conducting this pastime, thus even Lord Balarama could not understand it fully. But once He did, He was upset that He had been deprived of His real friends’ company.

For the next few days, Balarama would not go out with Krsna; on the day Brahma returned, He was absent just as He had been a year before, when He had stayed home to celebrate His birthday.

**\* \* \* \***

After a moment of Brahma’s time had passed — a year by human calculation — he returned, only to find Krsna playing with the boys and calves just as He had been a year before.

Brahma went to where he had hidden the calves and boys and confirmed that they were still sleeping. He then returned and again saw the very same boys and calves, just as they had been before.

The creator was thoroughly bewildered. He thought, “A second group of calves and boys are playing with Krsna as usual. Have they been doing so all this time? Who are they and where did they come from?”

Just west of Balahara, where he had originally stolen Krsna’s friends and calves, Lord Brahma tried to understand which of the two groups of calves and gopas was real and which was an illusion.

Unable to comprehend what was happening, Brahma entered trance and invoked his power of omniscience, hut even then his confusion was not cleared. With every moment his humiliation grew.

For an inferior person to test one who is superior in every way is surely an offence. What then becomes of one who tries to test He who is supreme in every way, the Personality of Godhead?

If even Lord Balarama could not pierce the veil of Krsna’s yogamaya, what hope was there for someone like Brahma, who from time to time falls under the influence of the material mode of passion?

Brahma’s attempt to test Krsna resulted in his own bewilderment. Sukadeva Gosvami sums up what is called the brahma-vimohana-lila:

**“Thus because Brahma wanted to mystify the all-pervading Krsna, who can never he mystified, hut who, on the contrary, mystifies the entire universe, he himself \[Brahma\] was put into bewilderment hy his own mystic power.”**

As Brahma reflected on his predicament, the calves and boys playing nearby said, “Brahma! You are a goat! You wanted to bewilder us, hut you do not know who we are. Just see the truth. Look!”

By Krsna’s grace, Brahma was given the spiritual vision to see the calves and boys with four arms, rain-cloud complexions, yellow garments, and the ornaments, marks, and symbols of Lord Visnu.

Those Visnu forms appeared to be all-compassionate, with brilliant smiles and sidelong glances that induced all creatures — from Brahma to lowly blades of grass — to glorify Them through sankirtana.

The personified forms of mystic opulences, the elements of creation, time, and the modes of nature worshipped those Visnu-forms, which were unlimited and full of knowledge and bliss.

As he beheld this all-expansive wonder and opulence, Brahma simultaneously saw the calves and boys, whom he now understood to be Krsna’s expansions. He was stunned, overcome with bliss.

Brahma now realised that the cowherd boy whom he had challenged was indeed the Supreme Brahman. He thought, “He is that” (ei sei). Thus the place where Brahma stood at that moment is known as Sei.

Seeing that Brahma had reached the limit of his ability to comprehend His opulence, Krsna withdrew the curtain of yogamaya and His expansions, the calves and gopas. Brahma stood there alone.

As he returned to external consciousness, Brahma first perceived the sweetness of Vraja, the trees of which were heavily laden with fruit and flowers, and the atmosphere of which was free of material taint.

Srimad-Bhagavatam beautifully portrays Brahma’s vision of Vrndavana,

*yatra naisarga-durvairah sahasan nr-mrgadayah*  
*mitranivajitavasa-druta-rut-tarsakadikam*

**“Vrndavana is the transcendental abode of the Lord, where there is no hunger, anger, or thirst. Though naturally inimical, both human beings and fierce animals live there together in divine friendship.”**

Now Brahma saw Krsna just as he had seen Him a year ago: with stick, flute, and buffalo horn tucked under His belt, His hand full of yogurt mixed with rice, searching high and low for His lost calves.

Krsna had resumed the role of a lone, innocent cowherd boy. This time, however, Brahma was not misled by his own foolishness. Repentant and embarrassed, he got down from his swan carrier.

The demigods usually do not touch the earth, hut Brahma gave up his prestige and repeatedly fell to the ground like a golden rod before the Supreme Lord, bathing Krsna’s lotus feet with profuse tears.

Lord Brahma, whose four heads face the four directions, repeatedly rose and fell before the Lord in order to touch Krsna’s feet with his heads, all the while displaying various symptoms of ecstatic love.

Brahma offered respects, but he felt his effort to be imperfect because while placing one head on Krsna’s feet the other three faced up; still he remained blissful because with those six eyes he could see Krsna.

The place where Brahma bowed his four heads (catur-mukha) before child Krsna is known as Caumuha. Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami glorifies this place:

**“Afraid that he had committed a grave offence —**

**“By stealing the cowherd boys and calves, Brahma fell down on the ground, and, with tears in his eyes, spoke many wonderful and unprecedented prayers glorifying gently smiling Krsna —**

**“Who is both the giver of liberation and the wonderful cowherd son of Vraja’s king. Let us glorify this sacred place, Sesabhiru-caturmukha, where frightened Brahma offered prayers to the Lord.”**

Lord Brahma’s devotional prayers arc particularly famous. Srila Prabhupada said that they were amongst the most difficult parts of Srimad-Bhagavatam to translate and comment upon.

In concluding his prayers, Brahma expressed his admiration for the Vraja-vasis he had so carelessly kidnapped, declaring in essence that they arc the most treasured source of happiness for Krsna.

Brahma prayed to be blessed by the dust of the Vraja-vasis’ lotus feet. He begged to be born as a blade of grass in Vrndavana, or even as a stone on the footpath that leads to Nandagrama.

Srila Prabhupada paraphrases these thoughts of Brahma:

**“But if I am not so fortunate as to take birth within the forest of Vrndavana, I beg to be allowed to take birth outside the immediate area of Vraja —**

**“So that when the devotees go out they will walk over me. Even that would be a great fortune for me. I am just aspiring for a birth in which I will be smeared by the dust of the devotees’ feet —**

**“Because I can see that everyone here is simply full of Krsna consciousness. No one here knows anything but the lotus feet of Krsna, or Mukunda, for which the Vedas themselves are searching.”**

Brahma said,

*tad bhuri-bhagyam iha janma kim apy atavyam yad gokule 'pi katamanghri-rajo-'bhisekam*  
*yaj-jivitam tu nikhilam bhagavan mukundas tv adyapi yat-pada-rajah sruti-mrgyam eva*

**“My greatest possible good fortune would be to take any birth what-ever in this forest of Gokula and have my head bathed hy the dust falling from the lotus feet of any of its residents.**

**“Their entire life and soul is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Mukunda, the dust of whose lotus feet is still being searched for in the Vedic mantras.”**

Krsna remained silent thoughout Brahma’s prayers. At first, to impress upon Brahma the severity of his offence, Krsna was very grave. But as Brahma went on, Krsna could not help but smile.

Krsna smiled out of juvenile amazement at the way Brahma was speaking: all four of the creator’s mouths spoke the same words simultaneously, appearing like puppets’ mouths pulled by strings.

Child Krsna found this very amusing. At the conclusion of his prayers, Brahma begged permission to bring back the calves and the cowherd boys, permission happily granted by the Lord.

Krsna’s expansions had brought bliss to the Vraja-vasis, but not to Krsna. How could He be as satisfied in their company — that is to say, in His own company — as He is in the company of His friends?

Lord Brahma closed his eyes for a moment as he used his mystic powers to free Krsna’s calves and friends, making sure that they would remain unaware that a whole year had passed.

Humbled by his misbehaviour, ashamed at his offences, yet blissful from having seen both Krsna’s opulence and sweetness, Brahma bowed down once again and then departed for his own planet.

Krsna found the calves in a forest not far from Unai and brought them hack to the riverbank where the cowherd boys were sitting and waiting for Him to return, just as they had been one year ago.

Although a year had gone by as this pastime played out, the cowherd boys thought that only a few moments had passed, during which time Krsna had brought the calves back from a nearby forest.

Krsna arrived, smiling at His friends as they called out, “Gopala! Please come sit down. We couldn’t eat a bite while You were gone. You know that we do cannot anything without You.”

Resuming their comical meal-time sports, the cowherd boys finished eating. Then—the afternoon shadows getting longer— they returned to Vrndavana, passing by the dead body of Aghasura on their way.

Once again Krsna played sweet melodies on His flute, occasionally calling one calf or another by name. His friends chanted His glories, exuberant to be returning to the pastures of Nandagrama.

Krsna was especially blissful; after a year of separation He was once again in the company of His calves and friends. As they entered the village, the boys called out, “Today Krsna killed a giant serpent.”

As the boys herded the calves along the lanes of Nandagrama to their homes, they all sang of the giant snake Aghasura, who had swallowed them whole but was killed by Krsna, deliverer of His devotees.

The next morning Krsna met with Balarama in a secluded place and pacified His anger by showing Him loving affection. Together again, They gathered Their friends to take out the calves.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda likens the bewilderment of Brahma to the sort of illusion that stems from hearing only the flowery words of the Vedas, words that can cause one to doubt the supremacy of Krsna.

If we absorb our minds in speculative books that debate useless controversies and inconclusive philosophies, we gradually lose the realisations about Krsna we attained through devotional service.

Several places are connected to Krsna’s brahma-vimohana-lila. Before going on, let us hear about them in the sequence of the pastime. From Parikhama, Brahma first spotted Krsna and the gopas playing at Unai.

Parikhama is so called because it was there Brahma decided to test (pariksa) Krsna. Balahara is the place where the cowherd boys (bala) were stolen (hard) while Krsna was searching for the calves.

Unai - so known as Janai and Basai — was where, after one year of earthly time had elapsed, Lord Brahma found the same cowherd boys he had stolen at Balahara still playing with their friend Krsna.

Unai or Janai is so named because it was there that Krsna made known (jnana) to Brahma the truth of the boys and calves by revealing His inconceivable potencies and forms.

And at Sei, where Brahma also saw Krsna in the cows and calves, the creator finally understood that Krsna is indeed the Supreme Lord. Over and over Brahma repeated, ei sei, ei sei: “He is that! He is that!”

In Sei one can visit Sei-kunda and the temple of Vatsa-bihari. Near that temple is a pippala tree whose trunk resembles — and is therefore duly worshipped as — the four-headed creator, Lord Brahma.

In a grove outside the village is a temple with a deity of Brahma. The present deity is a replacement for the original, which was sadly stolen. Also nearby is a temple of Gopala, to whom Brahma offered prayers.

At Caumuha, Lord Brahma prayed to Gopala for forgiveness. Caumuha, or Caumunha, the final pastime place connected to Krsna’s brahma- vimohana-lila, is named after the four-faced (catur-mukha) creator.

**\* \* \* \***

Near Caumuha arc pastime places connected with the killing of Aghasura. This pastime, which happened before the bewilderment of Brahma, was reported to the Vraja-vasis a year after it took place.

The demon Aghasura met his death in Aghavana, the demigods glorified Krsna’s victory further north at Jayeta, and afterwards the cowherd boys ate their lunch together at Jonai.

Aghavana is also known as Sapauli, or Sarpasthali, as Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami refers to it:

**“Seeing His friends, for whom He is more dear than life, enter the sinful Aghasura’s belly, which burned —**

**“With a great fire of virulent poison, Krsna also entered the demon, killed him, and rescued His friends. I pray that Sarpasthali, the place where Krsna enjoyed these pastimes, protects me.”**

It all started on the day child Krsna had planned to have breakfast, not at home as usual, but in the forest. He rose early that day and woke His friends by blowing His buffalo horn.

In no time at all the boys swarmed into Nandaraja’s palace compound at Chatikara, buzzing with excitement, brandishing their flutes, horns, and sticks, and showing off their breakfasts to one another.

Krsna received His mother’s blessings for the early outing, affectionately greeted His friends, and proceeded with them to the crossroads where He was to wait for His brother Balarama.

But instead of Balarama, a message arrived: “O brother! My maternal uncle has come to see Me on My birthday. He is rooted in My room like a tree. Please fulfil Your desires without Me today.”

The boys were sorry to hear this news, hut their childish glee made up for Balarama’s absence. They quickly rose to their feet, collected the calves from their pens, and plunged enthusiastically into the forest.

Already lavishly dressed hy their mothers, the boys decorated themselves and Krsna with flowers, leaves, buds, feathers, fruits, and coloured minerals, until they all looked like forest elves.

It is said that the cowherd boys numbered in the millions, and that their calves outnumbered them, yet each of their interactions with Krsna was direct and personal, as if there were only a few of them.

We can just imagine the joyous din caused by so many boys blowing horns, flutes, and pipes, and laughing, shouting, and singing, mixed with the lowing of calves and, above all else, Krsna’s flute-song.

Srila Prabhupada would fondly quote this verse when describing the cowherd boys:

**“In this way, all the cowherd boys used to play with Krsna, who is the source of the Brahman effulgence for jnanis —**

**“Desiring to merge into that effulgence, who is the Supreme Personality of Godhead for devotees who have accepted eternal servitorship, and who for ordinary persons is but an ordinary child.**

**“The cowherd boys, having accumulated the results of pious activities for many lives, were able to associate in this way with the Supreme Personality of Godhead. How can one explain their great fortune?”**

When the boys arrived in Aghavana they hung their sacks of food on the trees and set the calves free to graze. Now the boys could go about their unlimited games, which were all meant to please Krsna.

As the cowherd boys were absorbed in play, moving from one part of the forest to another, they came upon an open clearing in which a giant python lay on the pathway with its mouth wide open.

It was Agha — the younger brother of Putana and Baka and another one of Kamsa’s cohorts — who was greatly distressed at the loss of his siblings and eager to take revenge on the mystic child Krsna.

Finding no way to overcome his remorse, Agha had taken to hibernating, as snakes do. After Vatsasura’s death, Kamsa had to personally wake Agha and incite him to do the needful — kill Krsna.

Kamsa said, “With your ability to devour everything, O Agha, you are my only hope. You must kill this upstart Krsna, who has wiped out not only your family but also many of my near and dear friends.”

Keeping Kamsa’s order on his head, and inspired by the Supersoul to meet his destiny, Agha entered the forest where the cowherd boys were so lost in play that they had neglected their breakfast.

Aghasura’s plan was sinister. He thought, “By killing my brother and sister, Krsna has brought an end to my dynasty. I shall kill Him and His friends, and when their parents hear of it, they will die of shock.”

Agha assumed the form of a gigantic snake, whose open jaws touched the clouds. Lying in the path of the approaching boys, Agha, the personification of sin, was fearful even to the demigods.

Just on the edge of the clearing the boys stopped in their tracks and fell silent, awestruck by what they saw. Was it the statue of a snake created for their play, or perhaps a mountain cave?

Some gopas correctly identified Agha as a giant snake and started to run away, but the others chided them: “Silly boys! Snakes don’t grow so big. This must be a plaything created for us by the Lord.”

The more astute gopas replied, “Judging by the awful smell coming from its mouth, it does not seem to be a statue but a living thing just waiting to swallow us all. Let’s leave this place now.”

One cowherd boy tried to calm the others: “Why worry! Even if it is a real snake trying to gobble us up, Krsna is here. He will kill it just as He has killed other demons. Why should we worry?”

After his speech the gopa smiled and looked with great love at Krsna, who was standing some distance away. The cowherd boys accepted the argument and called out, “Friends! Let’s see what’s in its mouth.”

Some boys still had serious doubts, but curiosity and faith in Krsna silenced their fear. Creating a variety of noises to display their courage — or perhaps to scare away the snake — they ran ahead.

The gopas ran into the snake’s mouth, and the innocent calves, tails raised, galloped in after them. At this, Krsna anxiously called out, “Stop! Don’t go inside. That is a living snake, not a cave!”

But it was too late. The cowherd boys and calves had disappeared into Aghasura’s gaping mouth, where they instantly fainted from the poisonous vapours. Krsna watched, awed by His own potencies.

For a moment, Krsna appeared to be confused. But, as the Supreme Lord, He is never actually confused; rather, He was deliberating on why His friends had entered the jaws of death. It was intriguing.

He thought, “Surely My friends are free from any karma that would oblige them to accept such a death. Neither would the Supersoul prompt them to act in any way that would cause Me grief.

“I can only conclude that this is the work of My pastime potency, Yogamaya, who is orchestrating this apparently tragic event in order to sec Me perform some extraordinarily wonderful feat.”

Krsna’s astonishment at how even He was a puppet in the hands of Yogamaya dissipated the sorrow He felt at the fate of His friends. Confident of His power, He nonchalantly strode into Agha’s mouth.

Like the demigods, demons such as Kamsa had the mystic power to see Krsna disappear into Aghasura’s mouth. And so, as the celestials cried out, “Alas! Alas!” the demons rejoiced, yelling, “Bravo! Bravo!”

Aghasura felt that his end was nigh hut, unable to abandon his demonic nature, he tried to close his mouth and swallow Krsna, His friends, and their calves. Yet try as he might, Agha’s mouth was stuck.

As soon as Krsna heard the distressed cries of the demigods, He began to expand His body within the demon’s throat. In response, Aghasura expanded his body to avoid suffocation, but to no avail.

Krsna manifested His gigantic universal form, suffocating Agha and forcing the snake’s life air out through a hole in the top of his head — all this while the calves and gopas lay unconscious within the demon.

While in His original form as a cowherd, Krsna would never kill a demon in front of His friends and disturb the flow of their spontaneous love for Him hy a careless display of supernatural power.

But now, with no one watching, Krsna allowed His divine potencies to fully manifest. He expanded His body in all directions until Aghasura split open like a fetid and overripe melon.

Seeing His friends and calves lying helter-skelter within the demon, Krsna revived them with a stream of nectar that poured from His compassionate, love-laden glance. They slowly rose to their feet.

The gopas and calves emerged from the demon like a bubbling stream trickles from a mountain cave, shouting praise like “I knew He would save us!” and “Krsna is the saviour of His devotees!”

Krsna’s pastime potency decorated Him with a garland of fresh forest flowers. As the Lord and His companions stood in plain view of the demigods, the effulgent soul of Aghasura entered Krsna’s body.

**\* \* \* \***

From the commentaries of Sridhara Svami, Sanatana Gosvami, and Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, we learn the following about Sukadeva Gosvami’s narration of Aghasura’s liberation.

By entering the body of Aghasura, Krsna purified the demon, raising it to the stature of pure goodness and awarding it a spiritual form that resembled the Lord’s own. This is called sarupya-mukti.

To instil faith that He awards liberation to the demons He kills, Krsna allowed the onlookers to see the effulgence of Agha’s spiritual body, which is usually invisible, as it merged into His own form.

Aghasura’s death was like that of Sisupala’s and Dantavakra’s, who both attained spiritual forms, their souls entering the Lord in the presence of others. This is the mature conclusion of the acaryas.

The demigods rejoiced at seeing the miracles of Krsna’s killing and liberating Agha and reviving His companions. They showered flowers, beat drums, and glorified (Jaya) Krsna at a place called Jayeta.

Everyone from Gandharvas in heaven to brahmanas on earth praised Krsna in their own ways. From far above Jayeta, Brahma heard the booming cries of “Jaya! Jaya!” and came to see what was going on.

Incredulous that the devas could praise a little boy as the Supreme Lord, Brahma went to Parikhama to see the procession of calves and boys with his own eyes. It was there that he decided to test Krsna.

And because Brahma then stole the calves and boys, the pastime of Krsna’s killing Aghasura did not become known until one year later, when Krsna and His friends entered boyhood (pauganda).

For an entire year Yogamaya kept the body of Aghasura looking as if he had just been killed so that when Brahma returned the gopas, the boys saw Aghasura in the same way they had remembered him.

Thereafter, Aghasura’s body dried up and turned into a large skeleton draped by skin. The carcass became a place of interest for the Vraja-vasis and a playground for the cowherd boys for many years to come.

After being saved from Aghasura, the cowherd boys met at Jonai and refreshed themselves with a snack before proceeding to Unai, where they would eat their full meal under Brahma’s watchful eye.

The boys sang Krsna’s glories all the way back along Chatikara road. At Sayano, the first place they passed, the villagers praised Krsna’s cleverness (seyana) when they heard the miracle He had performed.

The Vraja-vasis were wonderstruck at how little Krsna could have killed such an enormous snake. Despite Krsna’s success, Yasoda trembled in fear, overcome with worry for her son’s safety.

Yasoda thought, “Within a lew days Vatsasura, Bakasura, and Aghasura all attacked my son. Only by the mercy of Lord Narayana did Krsna escape harm. Therefore, how can we live peacefully?”

Distraught, Yasoda called together the senior gopas and gopis and, as her son slept soundly in another room, poured out her heart to her friends and well-wishers, “What shall I do? Where shall I go?

“We left the dangers of Mahavana because Vrndavana was supposed to be as safe as Vaikuntha. Yet day after day a different demon comes to harm my son and your children. What kind of peace is this?

“Where will we go if we leave Vrndavana? Even if I forbid my sons to leave the house, They are so restless that They will find some means to escape. Who knows what dangers lie in wait for Them?”

Unable to continue, Yasoda began to weep, but wise Nanda Maharaja consoled her by reminding her, and everyone else, of Garga Muni’s words. Nanda said, “The words of brahmanas are always true.

“That great sage told us that we people of Gokula will overcome all difficulties by Krsna’s grace because anyone attached to Him — who is like Narayana in qualities — will never be defeated by demons.”

Nanda Maharaja continued to placate his wife: “Considering the wise words of Garga Muni, we can rest assured that real auspicious' ness will be invoked by giving charity. That is what we should do.”

The next day Mother Yasoda invited many brahmanas and, in the name of Krsna and Balarama, gave away her own ornaments, along with a vast number of cows, in charity. Such is her love.

Narada Muni once disclosed that Aghasura, in his previous birth, was the handsome son of Sankhacuda who, while walking through the Malaya Hills, saw Astavakra Muni and ridiculed the great sage.

Astavakra Muni replied, “O wicked one! May you become a snake — the ugliest snake on earth.” Agha was transformed on the spot into a horrible python that immediately begged the sage for mercy.

Feeling compassion for the wretch, the sage replied, “In the future Sri Krsna will enter your stomach and by His touch will not only free you from the body of a snake but from material entanglement as well.”

Thakura Bhaktivinoda says that Aghasura is a personification of intolerance and cruelty. For a Vaisnava, these inauspicious qualities mean one’s failure to show compassion for conditioned souls.

If we do not show compassion to others by giving them Krsna, then our own Krsna consciousness will be hampered, for it is the order of both Lord Krsna and Caitanya Mahaprabhu that we do so.

Krsna’s pastimes on earth are in themselves displays of His causeless mercy and evidence that He cares for us. Why else would He deliver sinful creatures like Aghasura who wanted to kill Him?

Isn’t the fact that Krsna made such a demon His associate in Goloka enough to give us faith that He will also deliver sincere devotees who serve Him by spreading His mercy through the sankirtana mission?

Sukadeva Gosvami concludes this pastime by echoing these thoughts in the following beautiful words:

**“If even only once or even by force one brings the form of the Supreme Lord into one’s mind —**

**“One can attain the supreme salvation by the mercy of Krsna, as did Aghasura. What then is to be said of those whose hearts the Supreme Personality of Godhead enters when He appears as an incarnation —**

**“Or those who always think of the lotus feet of the Lord \[Krsna\], who is the source of transcendental bliss for all living entities and by whom all illusion is completely removed?”**

**\* \* \* \***

Walking along the trough of New Vraja-dhama — in which, a little further north, fourteen springs form the source of the Yamuna — I left the places connected to Agha and Brahma and came to Sakaroya.

This little garden in Bhauma Vrndavana was originally called Sakrasthana, in connection with Indra (Sakra), who went there after sending devastating rain to inundate Vraja and its inhabitants.

Indra saw Krsna easily frustrate his greatest efforts by nonchalantly holding up Govardhana Hill like an umbrella to protect the Vraja- vasis. The king of heaven therefore came here in great fear.

Indra had already suffered humiliation in his own heavenly court because of his failure, and now he had to face his master, Narayana, whom he did not recognise in His original form as a cowherd boy.

Seeing that the floodwaters from his Samvartaka clouds had receded, and that the Yamuna was now calm, King Indra understood that the time had come for him to approach Krsna and apologise.

From some distance away, Indra could see, by his mystic power, Krsna circumambulating Govardhana Hill and surveying the damage Indra’s lightning bolts had caused during the seven-day tempest.

In Sakrasthana the king of heaven performed acamana with water from the Yamuna, removed his shoes, and flew with the heavenly Surabhi cow to Kadambavana, where Krsna was walking alone.

In New Vraja-dhama, east of Yamunotri — where natural springs feed the Yamuna — is Atasu and Devi Atasu. The name Atasu is a corrupted form of Astavakra, the name of the sage.

Demigods and sages from all parts of the universe are constantly visiting Vraja: those who are devotees do bhajana, jnanis and yogis practise meditation, and ascetics perform severe austerities.

Only pure devotees factually know Vrndavana, but these other spiritual practitioners also make advancement, not so much by their endeavours but by the touch of Vrndavana’s sacred dust.

In this way, yogis like Durvasa and impersonalists like Astavakra are gradually transformed into devotees of the Lord. Atasu is the place where Astavakra resides and where he gradually became a pcrsonalist.

Adjoining Astavakra’s asrama is Devi Atasu. Here, Maharaja Vajra established a deity of Yasoda’s daughter, Krsna’s twin sister, Ekanamsa-devi, who also resides in the Vindhya mountains.

Ekanamsa was born to Yasoda and then brought to Kamsa’s prison by Vasudeva. There the demon tried to kill her just as he had killed Vasudeva’s and Devaki’s other children. But this time he failed.

Slipping out of Kamsa’s grasp, Ekanamsa-devi, who is Krsna’s internal potency, warned the demon that the boy who would kill him had already taken birth elsewhere. Then she disappeared.

Before appearing in several other places, where her varied forms were worshipped with a variety of names, Ekanamsa came to Devi Atasu to relish the atmosphere of Vraja and witness her brother’s pastimes.

From where the Yamuna first becomes visible in New Vraja-dhama, it meanders in a golden stream along the western petal of the dhama, the focal point for many of Syamasundara’s delightful pastimes.

These pastimes and the holy places associated with them arc the subjects of the next chapter, but I will end this chapter by describing the first two of those places, Narayana-pura and Sanorakha.

At Narayana-pura the gopis asked Krsna to show them the four-armed Narayana form that the gopas bragged they had once seen while Krsna was riding upon the shoulders of His friend Sridama.

The cowherd boys saw Krsna’s four-handed form at a place called Garuda-Govinda near Chatikara. Upon returning home, they recounted the entire episode, as they did all of Krsna’s amazing feats.

Due to their great love for Krsna, the senior Vraja-vasis revelled in hearing their sons glorify Vraja’s prince, even though they did not always believe what they heard — like Krsna displaying four arms.

Everyone accepted that Krsna was special, but when they heard that Sridama had carried Krsna in the air, or something similar, the Vraja- vasis were inclined to accept it as products of the boys’ imaginations.

Indeed, Krsna Himself often reassured His anxious mother that she need not worry about the demons His friends were always talking about because most of those stories came from their fertile brains.

Nevertheless, news of four-armed Krsna intrigued the cowherd girls. After all, hadn’t the infallible Garga Muni said that Krsna was like Narayana? But, then again, was He that much like Narayana?

Both the gopis and gopas had seen Krsna use mystic powers to make Himself appear as if He had two additional arms, a divine crown, and a Kastubha gem. He had done it at Paitha and Hara-Narayana.

But the gopis thought those arms were just illusions. They were not real! Still, the gopas’ persuasive arguments, especially those of Sridama, intrigued the girls and prompted them to test Krsna.

We may remember that it was not far from Narayana-pura that Brahma became an offender by testing Krsna. But the gopis’ testing Krsna did not offend the Lord; to the contrary, it pleased Him greatly.

Brahma was offensive because, even though inferior to Krsna, he thought that he had the right to challenge Him. But the gopis’ stature is equal to the Lord’s by dint of their loving devotion to Him.

Pure love brings Krsna under His devotees’ control. And in the context of loving mellows, such love makes Krsna equal or subordinate to His lovers. And so it was with Krsna and the gopis.

The cowherd girls committed no offence in testing Krsna; in fact, their desire was born of love, not ego like Brahma’s. They pleased the Lord as much by challenging Him as they did by dancing.

As Krsna and the gopis were walking through the gardens of the Yamuna, the topic of Krsna’s divinity came up; as usual, Krsna defended His Godhood, and, also as usual, the gopis made light of it.

Krsna argued it was nearby that Garuda — the great carrier of Lord Visnu who is factually an authority on the Lord — had realised Krsna’s supremacy and seen Him in His four-armed expansion.

“But where is Your chief witness now?” the gopis challenged. “Besides,” one gopi added, “we don’t want the testimony of others. We want to see for ourselves that You are Lord Narayana.”

Another gopi said, “If You are Lord Narayana, then what possible obstacle could there be to Your revealing Yourself to us?” Krsna then realised that only one thing would convince these sceptical girls.

Shrugging His shoulders, He replied, “There is no obstacle. Just see!” Krsna snapped His fingers and displayed a beautiful four-armed form that had His own features combined with Narayana’s.

That stunning form joined Lord Narayana’s majestic four arms and divine ornaments to Krsna’s smiling face and effervescent sweetness. It was not an embodiment of opulence to he revered.

In that form the gopi could see both Krsna and Narayana simultaneously, but to make sure that the two were the same person, they gathered around Krsna for a closer examination.

Satisfied that this was not some magical creation, they all declared in unison, “We are convinced.” Hearing this, Krsna resumed His cowherd form, which gives more pleasure to His devotees.

And although the gopis were especially respectful to Lord Narayana, they did not lose their spontaneous attachment for Krsna; they continued to think of Him as a cowherd, just like them.

Narayana-pura thus became one more place in which Krsna revealed His supreme divinity to His eternal companions. Their inconceivable love somehow reconciles Krsna’s being both God and a human being.

Sanorakha lies on the bank of the Yamuna. Here the great Saubhari Muni performed austerities in the water and lived upon a small hill on the shore, where his deity is still worshipped today.

Once while Saubhari Rsi was underwater in trance, Garuda caught a large fish to eat. Feeling compassion for the fish, Saubhari wrongly cursed the carrier of Lord Visnu to die if he ever returned.

Garuda could have easily counteracted the curse, but out of deference to the sage he did not come again to the Yamuna, which explains why Kaliya, who was also hunted by Garuda, came there to live.

But cursing an associate of the Lord carries a reaction, and so Saubhari, while meditating underwater, once saw a pair of fish mating. Sexual desire then overwhelmed him, and he fell down.

The sage rejuvenated his aged body and married the fifty daughters of King Mandhata. The Muni then enjoyed household life until the reaction to his offence had slackened and he regained his senses.

Sitting in a secluded place, Saubhari Muni once contemplated the cause of his downfall. He resolved to give up material enjoyment and return to the path of detachment and spiritual practice. He thought:

“A person desiring liberation from material bondage must give up the association of persons interested in sex life and should not employ his senses externally \[in seeing, hearing, talking, walking, and so on\].

“One should always stay in a secluded place, completely fixing his mind at the lotus feet of the unlimited Lord, and if one wants any association at all, he should associate with those similarly engaged.”

Followed by his devoted wives, Saubhari Muni accepted the Vanaprastha order and again returned to Sanorakha, where in time he and his wives — by his power — attained ultimate perfection.

Sanorakha is a place to contemplate many topics: the trap of misplaced compassion, the consequences of Vaisnava aparadha, and the power pure devotion has to deliver us, even at the end of life.

I have often gone to Sanorakha in Bhauma Vrndavana and prayed to the deity of Saubhari Muni on the hilltop there, recalling his life story while looking out over the fields where Yamuna once flowed.

From Sanorakha Hill one can see all the way to Vrndavana town — Madana-mohana temple and Kesi-ghata. In New Vraja-dhama, one can see the length of the Yamuna from Kaliya- to Bhramara-ghata.

In this chapter I have tried to glorify some of the places of Krsna’s pastimes along the Yamuna, between Sanorakha and Ujani, in order to purify my heart of the countless unwanted things that linger there.

The stream of Krsna’s Vraja pastimes is like the blackish waters of the Yamuna: the players in those pastimes are its waves, their loving ecstasies its lotuses, and the ears of those who hear them, its aquatics.

Dear reader! Please immerse yourself in Sri Krsna’s nectarean sports as they are eternally enacted in Goloka and Bhauma Vrndavana, and are so mercifully accessible to us in places like New Vraja-dhama.

If you were to ask, “Why would Krsna want to sport anywhere but the best place, His eternal home, Goloka?” I would tell you that He is eager to please His devotees and to taste the nectar of His pastimes.

Like a wealthy man who always distributes his wealth profusely just as he goes on accumulating more, Krsna always strives to increase loving exchanges with His devotees and with His eternal associates.

As the supreme enjoyer, Krsna continues to enjoy on earth, both in the place He once appeared in person and anywhere His Deity is worshipped. In this way He increases the fields of His enjoyment.

And so, again I beg you: Please come and visit the holy places of New Vraja-dhama where, by Their darsana, Radha and Syama bestow blessings upon pilgrims and enjoy other transcendental pastimes.

## Chapter 26 - Varaha-ghata to Kesi-ghata

The year we purchased the Krsna Valley land, I drove my mother out to see the new property in my motor home. We entered what would soon he our farm project along a dirt track at what is now Ujani.

At the time we had no access along the present main road, and temple construction had not yet begun. To avoid potential conflicts with the locals, I dressed in civilian clothes, as did all the devotees.

We parked the motor home near Sakaroya. As lunch was being cooked, my mother and I walked along a small creek that meandered down the valley as far as Papadavana, then an impenetrable wood.

From there we hiked up the hill, thick with high summer grass, to where the temple now stands. I described to her how we planned to construct a place of worship on that spot, overlooking the valley.

“It is very beautiful,” she said. I had not thought of our farm in those terms. As they say, “beauty is in the eye of the beholder.” It took a while before I began to see New Vraja-dhama as “beautiful.”

The transformation in the eyes of this beholder took place as devotees began to serve New Vraja-dhama with agriculture, cow protection, land development, and eventually temple construction.

Once Radha and Syama had come to stand on the window ledge of my office at Bhaktivedanta Manor, my eyes filled up with Their beauty, which I increasingly saw reflected in Their future home.

The beauty of the dhama was even more evident when Radha and Syamasundara entered Their temple to accept the services of those devotees who had made New Vraja-dhama their home and their life.

My ever-increasing attachment to Their Lordships and to Their place of residence has gradually opened my eyes to the natural beauty of New Vraja-dhama. Now I also say, “It is very beautiful.”

My eyes feast on the multicoloured blossoms of spring flowers, the gracefully undulating fields or summer wheat, the golden splendour of autumn leaves, and the pristine white of winter snow.

How beautifully the sun rises over Kamaravana, sending shimmering rays through my window. As the full moon rides across the sky, it reflects its silvery mystical brightness on snow-covered Seva-kunja.

The unparalleled stillness of New Vraja-dhama sings of the visible beauty of the divine couple as well as the invisible wonder of Their pastimes, both daily and seasonal, which fill our hearts with love.

Where wide-open spaces overgrown with weeds once stood, fruit orchards and vegetable gardens now flourish; where tracts of muddy land once languished, gardens tended by devotees serve the Lord.

But for me the crowning beauty of New Vraja-dhama, like light reflecting off a diamond, first came when Radha and Syama inspired me to assign Vraja’s pastime places to different parts of the property.

Now shrines commemorating Krsna’s pastimes dot the landscape and remind us of eternal Vrndavana. Pavilions and gardens enhance the beauty of these places, bringing a new dimension to the dhama.

The devotees’ words and thoughts, as they speak about or remember Radha’s and Krsna’s eternal pastimes, further embellish these places, invoking the presence of the divine couple’s pleasure playground.

Amongst these pastime places is the Yamuna River, which was created by constructing two dams in the path of our spring-fed creek. Now we have a physical manifestation visible to the eyes.

Inspired devotees sponsored the creation of this prominent pastime place for the pleasure of Radha and Syama, and still others gave funds for the pavilions, steps, and gardens that now decorate its banks.

I once dreamt I was hovering above our Yamuna: both sides of the river were rich with handsome bathing ghatas and beautiful pavilions where devotees bathed, prayed, and engaged in spiritual activities.

At the time of writing this book, landmarks at Kaliya-ghata, Bhramara-ghata, and Brahmanda-ghata have been installed. We plan to add many more places for the pleasure of the divine couple.

The “Golden Yamuna,” as I call it, is a tranquil waterway in two main segments: the upper from Sakaroya to Raja-ghata, the lower from Raval to Cintaharana-ghata. Its course continues past Visrama-ghata.

Tinted yellow by the colour of New Vraja-dhama’s soil, our Yamuna reminds me of Sri Radha’s complexion, just as the blackish colour of the Yamuna in Bhauma Vrndavana reminds devotees of Sri Krsna’s.

Many fish peacefully ply the river’s waters, at times jumping in the air, sometimes nibbling the long grasses that grow along its banks, sometimes playing amongst the reeds that stand in the shallows.

Naturally there is no fishing in New Vraja-dhama, so large schools swim freely in the Yamuna. But they are fair game for the many herons and storks that shadow the waterways, chasing their prey in comical ways.

Sparrows and terns skim its surface, deer and fox drink on its banks, and from June through August the frogs’ nocturnal sankirtana rings through every corner of New Vraja-dhama, sometimes all too loudly.

Many groves of trees, especially weeping willows, thrive along the banks by drinking the Yamuna’s water, their reflections looking like watery expansions mirrored on the river’s surface.

Leaves and flowers from the trees’ overhanging branches fall onto the water, as if offering puspanjali to their worshipable deity, and bees and other insects provide a chorus that seems to sing her praises.

During the summer months flower pollen dusts the surface of the Yamuna, adding sweetness and aroma to her waters, intensifying her golden hue, and lending a soft velvety texture to her surface.

Like many devotees, I often walk along t he eastern bank, which runs alongside the temple road. When looking for seclusion, I cross to the western bank and do sankirtana in places like Mana-sarovara.

I meditate on the Yamuna as the stem of the golden lotus of New Vraja-dhama, although it also appears like a golden necklace upon the forest of the dhama, or like a welcome banner to arriving pilgrims.

A river is the lifeline of any tract of land —as is the Yamuna in New Vraja-dhama — but because Krsna enjoys pastimes on her shores and in her waters, the Yamuna River is a spiritual lifeline as well.

And yet, it is Krsna that is the life of all that lives (bhutanam asmi cetana). Srila Prabhupada says, “He is the life of the river Yamuna (yamuna-jivana), because He used to enjoy jumping over \[it\].”

May the golden Yamuna of New Vraja-dhama remind us of our divine life, Sri Krsna, whose own life is Sri Radha, and may our devotion flow effortlessly to the lotus feet of that divine couple.

**\* \* \* \***

After Sanorakha, the first pastime place on the Yamuna is Varaha-ghata, where Krsna revealed His form as the great boar to the curious cowherd girls. Gautama Muni also had his asrama there.

In Bhauma Vrndavana, this place is on the parikrama path as it turns onto the cowherd-boy trail that runs along the old bed of the Yamuna, a short walk from iskcon’s Krsna-Balarama temple.

When I first visited Varaha-ghata, it was a charming, secluded temple in the shade of a great banyan tree. It had a beautiful Deity of Lord Varaha that, unfortunately, was later stolen and sold as an antique.

People in this age have become so materialistic that they will exchange even Krsna for money. This practice, widespread in India, has led to the disappearance of many important Deities.

Recently, a part of the Varaha-ghata temple collapsed. Without the original Deity, which was installed by Vajra, its once charming atmosphere has become even more hidden to ordinary vision.

Let us offer our obeisances to Sri Krsna, the blackish cowherd boy who charmed the gopis with His sweetness and displayed His majestic opulence and unlimited strength as a great red boar — Varaha.

One day the cowherd boys were tending their cows in Ramana-reti when a messenger arrived and told Krsna that Radharani and Her gopi friends had come to the Yamuna to collect water for cooking.

Krsna left His friends, saying that He was searching for stray cows. He found the gopis by the bank of the Yamuna, casually dipping their pitchers in the water as if waiting for something, or for someone.

As Krsna approached, the gopis pretended not to notice Him, so He made His presence known. The gopis, as if surprised, said, “O son of Maharaja Nanda! What are You doing in this part of Vraja?”

“My cows are grazing nearby,” Krsna replied, “and I am searching for some strays.” “As You can see,” one gopi said, “there are no strays here.” Lifting their pitchers onto their heads, the gopis rose to leave.

Krsna marvelled at the aristocratic poise with which each girl kept one hand on the pitcher on her head and the other on her graceful hips. “You carry those pitchers so elegantly,” He said.

Radha turned back to look at Him as She replied, “Unlike You, we are accustomed to such service.” Krsna recoiled at Her unnecessary sarcasm and replied, “You are not the only ones who carry pitchers.”

Now all the gopis turned towards Krsna and said in unison, “Syama! When have You ever lifted a water pot onto Your head?” Krsna placed both hands on His hips and nodded His head as He replied:

“Water pot! A water pot is nothing. I have lifted this whole planet on My head.” This answer drew so much laughter from the girls that their pitchers shook and water splashed on them from above.

In a sweetly patronising tone, Radha asked, “When have You lifted this planet on Your head?” ‘‘Long ago,” Krsna shot back, “when I appeared as a boar to raise the earth out of the ocean.”

After a moment’s silence, a gopi asked, “How can we believe such an outlandish statement?” Krsna replied, “The sage Garga has said so himself—in the past I appeared with a red complexion.”

Another gopi remarked, “Just because You had a red complexion doesn’t mean that You were the red-haired Varaha incarnation of Lord Narayana. But if You show us, then we might believe You.”

Krsna could understand that the gopis were curious to see a display of His divine strength, and so just to please them He agreed: “All right. If seeing is believing, then behold My Varaha-rupa!”

Before the gopis’ eyes, Krsna disappeared. In His place stood a small boar, just thumb-high. The girls stepped closer to get a better look. Just as they were about to ridicule its size, the boar began to grow.

Within moments the boar had expanded so much His body scattered the clouds. Crown and ornaments flashing, He proclaimed His might with thunderous roars that made the gopis cover their delicate ears.

The gigantic Lord’s four white tusks glittered like the brahmajyoti, and His lotus-petal eyes glowed red with anger. Gradually turning around and around, Lord Varaha roared several times.

Standing up on His rear legs, the mighty boar displayed His divine body, thick with red quivering hair, brilliant with arrow-sharp hooves, and fragrant with a garland of forest flowers.

The Lord bent down and rammed His tusks into the ground. As He lifted His head, the astounded cowherd girls could see the earth suspended on the tips of the Lord’s curved tusks.

They could clearly see the globe with its continents, oceans, and mountain ranges easily resting on the tusks of the Lord; indeed, it appeared as if the earth were floating in the air merely by His touch.

Then, as angelic voices from the sky chanted Vedic mantras and demigods recited prayers like the Purusa-Sukta, Varaha-deva extended His right hoof and invoked His Sudarsana cakra.

The gopis were not only speechless to behold this spectacle but also confused as to where they were. They stood on the same ground as Varaha, but they also felt as if they were on the globe on His tusks.

One of the girls managed to whisper, “Is He really our Krsna?” To answer, Varaha changed the colour of His body from red to cloud- blue — the gopis understood that He was indeed their Krsna.

For moments that might as well have been ages, the gopis watched the earth rotate on the Lord’s tusks. Then, as suddenly as the boar had appeared, He disappeared, leaving them standing there in silence.

The damsels of Vraja looked around to see where Krsna was, but He too was gone. Was this some kind of illusion or magic trick? Had He really been there, or had their minds deceived them?

Without speaking, they came to where Varaha had stood. There they saw His giant hoofprints in the soil and, beside them, the familiar footprints of Krsna with their characteristic markings.

What they saw was no illusion. Krsna had actually shown them His form as a boar and how He had held the earth on His head. But why had He gone? Why had He not stayed to receive the gopis’ acclaim?

They thought, “He probably left thinking that we would doubt what we had seen and make fun of Him.” But the gopis had no doubts; they accepted that in a previous birth Krsna had been a giant boar.

But, as incredible as it might sound, they were infinitely more interested in what Krsna was now — the cowherd prince of Vraja. Resigned to the fact that He would not return, the gopis also left.

On the way back to Vasati the gopis saw Krsna and His friends herding cows. As the girls covered their faces, they saw a smile cross Krsna’s lips, which they acknowledged with submissive glances.

From that time on, the landing at the Yamuna where Krsna displayed His boar incarnation has been known as Varaha-ghata. Also at this place, as already mentioned, Gautama Rsi practised austerities.

Gautama Rsi was present when Sukadeva spoke Srimad-Bhagavatam, so he and Krsna were contemporaries; still, it is not clear whether Gautama was residing at Varaha-ghata while Krsna lived in Vraja.

Srila Prabhupada told us that his family’s genealogical line comes from disciples of Gautama Muni, who is recognised as one of the seven great sages of the universe and the father of Krpacarya.

We may note with interest that both Srila Prabhupada (at Krsna- Balarama Mandira) and Gautama Muni (at Varaha-ghata) chose Ramana-reti as their place of residence in Bhauma Vrndavana.

The forest between Varaha-ghata and the next pastime place, Go-ghata, is called Gocaranavana because it was here that Krsna and His friends blissfully herded (carana) their cows (go) along the riverside.

Go-ghata, also known as Gopala-ghata, is a clearing sheltered by a few trees. It is linked to the chastisement of the serpent with one hundred one hoods, Kaliya, a pastime that took place at nearby Kaliya-ghata.

After Krsna had banished Kaliya from Vrndavana and returned to shore, Nanda Maharaja, at the advice of brahmanas, gave away many cows in charity to ensure the continued protection of His divine son.

The king of Vraja was an eyewitness to his small son’s victory over the serpent king; nonetheless, Nanda could only think that the special mercy of Lord Narayana was responsible for Kaliya’s defeat.

Krsna is the origin of Lord Narayana and all other incarnations, but Nanda Maharaja and his subjects, blinded by their selfless love, could think of the Lord only as their favourite cowherd boy.

Consequently, as Nanda Maharaja and the Vraja-vasis watched Krsna struggling in Kaliya’s coils, they thought, “Our child is now in the grip of death. Only divine intervention can save Him.”

**\* \* \* \***

The Vraja-vasis had known that a portion of the Yamuna River was poisoned by the presence of the great serpent Kaliya, who had been living there out of fear of his mortal enemy Garuda.

The elder gopas had repeatedly reminded the boys not to herd their cows in that area. Not only the water but also the grass there was poisonous; anyone who had contact with either one would die.

But these warnings only increased Krsna’s curiosity to see the Kaliya Lake; in fact, they strengthened His resolve to ban the demon from the precincts of Vrndavana. Krsna had no patience for demons.

The day Krsna selected to dispose of Kaliya happened to be Balarama’s birthday, so Balarama stayed home that day to attend the festivities, just as He did on the day Aghasura was killed.

The boys first went to a small forest where the cows quickly ate all the available fresh grass. From there Krsna led the boys and cows to the area of the Yamuna where Kaliya lived with his family.

Kaliya Lake was deep, wide, and tranquil, yet the demon’s poison had so contaminated the water that the vapour rising from the lake killed birds flying overhead and the spray of its waves killed all vegetation.

Even crocodiles avoided the lake. Only poisonous snakes lived in the holes on its hanks, making the lake unapproachable to animals, Vraja- vasis, and demigods, who had been known to bathe there in the past.

It is said that the lake must have been separated from the main current of the Yamuna, since there is no mention of people downstream, like Mathura-vasis, suffering from the polluted waters.

As Krsna approached the lake with His retinue, He reflected upon how Kaliya had destroyed the beautiful forests by the lakeside and transformed the area into a dangerous, uninhabitable place.

Seeing the barren trees and deathly still waters, Krsna resolved, “I must destroy this serpent so that the residents of Vrndavana can again make use of this lake and worship its sacred waters.”

As Krsna was thinking in this way, the boys and cows, apparently overwhelmed by the summer heat but actually influenced by Yogamaya, forgot their parents’ warnings and drank from the river.

At first sip the gopas and cows at once fell unconscious. Krsna was horrified, the colour drained from His face. “Look what’s happened!” He lamented. “Alas, My impulsive nature has caused this catastrophe.

“These cows and boys are like My very life. What will I say to their distraught parents?” Krsna’s heart burned with compassion to see His fallen friends. Self-reproach ruled over Him.

His mind filled with regret, Krsna kept repeating, “Why did I come here?” Profoundly aggrieved, He cried for some time, and the hot tears that fell from His eyes revived the boys lying nearest to Him.

Then, one by one, Krsna revived the rest of His friends and cows with life-giving glances. After each boy sat up or rose to his feet he lovingly embraced Krsna, while the cows repeatedly licked His body.

The gopas rejoiced, “Krsna rescued us from the poison of the Yamuna just as He did from the poison of Aghasura. He must know the science of Sanjivani, by which He repeatedly brings us back to life.”

The cowherd boys exchanged affectionate glances and smiles with Krsna. He was relieved to see their jovial mood return, because it meant that the effects of the poison had been completely neutralised.

But Krsna’s peaceful demeanour did not last for long. The thought that Kaliya had nearly killed His friends and cows made Krsna furious. He was determined to exterminate the snake.

Nearby stood a kadamba tree in full bloom. Long ago Garuda had sprinkled nectar on it, and now the tree was healthy and thriving, despite the noxious effects of Kaliya’s poison.

To move His friends out of harm’s way and to ensure that they did not try to stop Him from combating Kaliya, Krsna said, “Look at this kadamba tree, hale and hearty even under these adverse conditions.

“Garuda once drank nectar while sitting on this tree. Some nectar spilled into a hole on a high branch. I will climb up to taste it. You take the cows away from the river, lest they drink the water again.”

As the cowherd boys led the cows away to a safe place, Krsna scampered up the kadamba and out onto a thick branch that stretched far out over the brackish waters of the lake.

Preparing Himself for a fight, Krsna tucked His hair under His turban and tightened His belt. Then He waved His clenched fists in the air and shouted “Don’t be afraid!” to His friends — and dove in.

Krsna’s impact with the water caused high waves to flood the shore on both sides of the lake, disturbing Kaliya and his serpent cohorts, who hissed vehemently and unleashed their virulent poison.

Krsna swam about like a baby elephant. His arms churned the water, creating a deafening sound like tidal waves crashing. Roused by the noise and unable to tolerate the intrusion, Kaliya rushed to the spot.

But Kaliya was startled to see Krsna. “Who is this attractive boy with delicate features, sweetly smiling and swimming about fearlessly in these poisonous waters?” he thought, feeling oddly drawn to the Lord.

“Who is this creating such a disturbance in my kingdom, and where did He come from?” But despite being attracted to Krsna, Kaliya’s demonic nature got the best of him — he bit Krsna on the chest.

But not surprisingly, His bite had no effect on the Lord. Kaliya then angrily enveloped Krsna in his mighty coils and attempted to crush his attacker just as he had crushed many others in the past.

Yasoda’s ropes of love could not bind Krsna without His consent, so how could Kaliya’s coils of envy do Him any harm? Still, out of concern, Yogamaya covered Lord Krsna with an invisible shield.

Krsna practically lounged in the coils of Kaliya, just as Lord Visnu reclines on the bed of Ananta. But from the gopas' perspective on shore, their Gopala was being crushed to death.

Seeing the cherished object of their love trapped in the coils of a demon, the boys and cows ran forward to help Krsna. But Yogamaya froze the Lord’s devotees to the spot, so all they could do was cry.

The boys saw the whole world coming to an end. They held their palms to their foreheads and cried, “We can no longer live!” They collapsed as they displayed all eight kinds of transcendental ecstasy.

Some cowherd men working in fields nearby heard the commotion and came running. When they saw Krsna — to whom they had dedicated their lives — in certain peril, they too fell to the ground.

Fear had dried the cows’ tears, and so they could not cry; they could only look at Krsna with love and repeatedly low in pained voices, as if to say, “What can we do? Only You can save Yourself. Please do it!”

The demigods, watching from above, had been following these events with great concern. They could understand that unless they took matters into their own hands, no one would alert the Vraja-vasis.

To inform Vrndavana’s residents of Krsna’s peril, the celestials created dreadful omens in the sky, on the land, and in the bodies of the elder gopas and gopis. Everyone could sense impending danger.

The Vraja-vasis were all assembled at the court of Maharaja Nanda to join in the festival celebrating Lord Balarama’s birthday, but upon seeing the bad omens, their festive mood was disturbed.

Mother Yasoda gave up her usual shyness and accosted the king. “Krsna should have returned long ago,” she said. “The gods are sending signs of a disaster, and you sit here preparing for a feast!”

Frightened by Mother Yasoda’s words and worried that perhaps Krsna had met with His death, the women, children, and elder gopas all rushed out of the palace intent on finding their beloved, Krsna.

All-knowing Balarama could recognise Krsna’s pastime; He alone was undisturbed. He thought, “What could an insignificant worm like Kaliya possibly do to invincible Krsna, He of unlimited power?”

Balarama saw the panicked Vraja-vasis and feared they might drown themselves in the Yamuna at the sight of Krsna in Kaliya’s coils; still, He smiled to reassure them that nothing inauspicious could happen.

As they followed Krsna’s unique footprints, marked by symbols like the thunderbolt and lotus flower, the thought of Balarama’s gentle cheerful smile soothed the frazzled nerves of the Vraja-vasis.

**\* \* \* \***

Accompanying Vraja’s townsfolk, Balarama laughed as He thought, “Krsna is now playing with Kaliya, a common snake, but He never plays with Me in My form as Sesanaga? How is that?”

From a distance the Vraja-vasis spotted Krsna lying motionless within the coils of the giant serpent, the gopas lying scattered on the ground, and the cows on the riverbank, crying out loud for their Gopala.

In shock and anguish the elder gopas and gopis came closer, unable to bear the sight of the snake yet unwilling to take their eyes from their beloved Krsna. Not realising that the boys had fainted, they asked:

“What happened? Did Kaliya drag Krsna into the water, or did Krsna jump in by Himself? Was it His idea or someone else’s?” When they failed to answer, the Vraja-vasis realised the boys were unconscious.

Just at that time the young gopis arrived, last in the procession to the Yamuna. Seeing Krsna’s condition and remembering His soft words and smiling glances, they thought the world to be an empty void.

At first the cowherd girls just gazed at Krsna with love, but once freed from the shock of the moment, they filled the air with their shrill wailing and muddied the ground with their tears.

The sound of the young gopis’ misery was amplified by the loud cries of the elder women, who were wiping perspiration from Mother Yasoda’s face as they tried to keep her from running into the water.

Yasoda-devi acted as if deranged; she flailed her arms wildly and dug her feet into the ground as cows sometimes do. Only the elder gopis’ songs about her son kept Krsna’s mother from losing her will to live.

This alarming show of motherly distress so distracted Balarama that He hardly noticed Nanda Maharaja and the cowherd men climbing down the riverbank and preparing to wade into the water.

Nandaraja stretched his arms out towards Krsna and cried, “O my son! What have You done? Please come back at once.” Balarama ran after His father, physically restraining Nanda and the gopas, saying:

“O father! O Vraja-vasis! Listen to Me. Please calm down. You may think that our Krsna is in danger, but I can tell you this: Garga Muni assured us that not a hair on Krsna’s head can he harmed.

“You do not know the strength of My younger brother. Not even the demigods know His strength. But I know. And I can assure you that He will dispose of this insignificant water snake any minute.”

The Vraja-vasis were momentarily pacified by Balarama’s words, yet He knew that their love for Krsna would soon have them running into the water again. “Krsna’s influence is amazing!” He thought.

Meanwhile, from His perch in Kaliya’s coils, Krsna could see all these displays of ecstatic love for Him. His heart went out to the gopas and gopis, to whom He was more dear than life itself.

Finally, Krsna saw that the Vraja-vasis’ distress was too much for them to bear. The cowherd men were trying to enter the poisonous water yet again. At that moment, Krsna knew it was time to act.

After being in Kaliya’s grasp for one muhurta, Krsna told the snake, “Kaliya! You have shown Me the limit of your strength. Now watch Me, a little cowherd boy, show you a tiny sample of real power.”

Krsna then expanded His body to such extent that Kaliya was forced to loosen his grip. First he freed Krsna’s lotus face, and Krsna quickly beamed a loving smile to His parents and friends.

As soon as Yasoda saw Krsna’s smiling face, she cried out, “O my son! My darling son!” Then Krsna freed His arms and waved at the Vraja-vasis. They responded with a roar of “Jaya!” that shook the heavens.

Krsna put His lotus hands on Kaliya’s coils and wiggled free from the serpent’s grip. After waving again to the Vraja-vasis, He ran along the length of Kaliya’s body and jumped on top of one of his many hoods.
