The demigods, overjoyed at this happy reversal, beat celestial drums to herald what they were sure would he Krsna’s imminent victory. The rhythms revived the gopas and gopis who were still unconscious.

Hearing the joyous vibrations, the boys who had just awoken raised themselves up on their arms and saw smiling Balarama standing over them. Their spirits lifted, despite the horrible scene before their eyes.

Kaliya resembled a tall black palm tree rising out of the lake. From his rhythmically swaying heads his hundred mouths spat poisonous foam and his two hundred fearsome eyes shot fiery sparks.

His hoods flapped like the wings of a flock of eagles, his nostrils spewed steaming vapour like craters on countless volcanoes, and his tail snapped like a whip, spraying water at the clouds.

The jewels on Kaliya’s hoods resembled lightning in the sky. Unable to tolerate Krsna casually walking on his body, Kaliya attacked his tiny adversary, who looked like a puppet made of musk.

But no matter how swiftly Kaliya moved to strike Krsna, the Lord dodged out of the way with ease. Krsna’s nonchalant, defiant smile infuriated the already envious serpent, weakening his judgement.

Krsna leapt from hood to hood, making sure He gave Kaliya a good kick with every step. The Lord resembled an eagle circling its prey, looking for a chance to swoop down for the inevitable kill.

Krsna moved so quickly that He not only evaded Kaliya’s jaws but also repeatedly caused the serpent to bite his own flesh. Thus Kaliya was dizzy trying to keep up with Krsna and faint from his own poison.

To reassure the Vraja-vasis that Krsna now had the upper hand, Balarama shouted, “Look at Krsna! He is death personified for Kaliya! Just to please you, He has made kusa grass mats out of Kaliya’s hoods.

“Look at our Krsna, adjusting His ornaments and tightening His belt as He prepares to entertain us with a dance recital. Now do you have faith in My words? What is there to worry about?”

Krsna heard Balarama’s speech and laughed aloud, affirming His brother’s statements. The rays of light reflected off His teeth removed all fear from His devotees’ hearts and filled them with wonder.

Jumping on top of Kaliya’s main hood, Krsna kicked it repeatedly, weakening the serpent’s other hoods as well. Like an expert snake charmer, the Lord quickly brought the creature under His control.

Krsna sent a glance to the Vraja-vasis, as if to say, “Now watch this!” Then the original master of fine arts danced on Kaliya’s hoods, the soles of His feet reddened by the glow of the serpent’s jewels.

Kaliya would raise one head behind Krsna, who would gracefully slap that hood with His palm and then jump on it to continue His dance, uttering sounds like thai thai, in imitation of percussion instruments.

The Lord was pleased to perform on such a novel stage to such a captive audience. Youthful Krsna was especially keen to attract and impress the young gopis, who had already given Him their hearts.

Krsna’s eyes met the gopis’, promising them, “Some time in the future we will dance together, as I am dancing now.” The girls shyly lowered their eyes, hopeful that Krsna would indeed fulfil this silent pledge.

Krsna’s dance recital did not go unnoticed in heaven either. The demigods’ musicians and singers soon arrived to accompany Krsna on their instruments, sing songs, shower flowers, and offer prayers.

Yet, despite his obvious defeat, Kaliya was too stubborn to surrender to Krsna, and so the Lord, eager to rectify this most envious creature, trampled the snake’s heads, one after the other.

If one head would not bow before Krsna as He danced, the Lord would stomp on that head with His lotus feet, causing the snake to vomit blood and suffer misery after misery.

In appreciation of Krsna’s efforts to subdue Kaliya, the demigods praised the Lord with mantras and showered Him with flowers. To reciprocate their devotion, Krsna kicked Kaliya’s hoods all the more.

Krsna danced with such dexterity that He embarrassed the celestial musicians, who could not keep pace with His rhythms; instead they danced to their own music as they sang the Lord’s praises.

**\* \* \* \***

Kaliya was covered in his own vomit and humiliated before his family members. Finally his demonic spirit broke. With the purifying touch of Krsna’s lotus feet, the seed of devotion sprouted in him.

How had Kaliya received the seed of devotion? By hearing of Krsna’s glories from his wives. Still, that seed was stunted by Kaliya’s offences, which were neutralised when Krsna danced on his heads.

The devotion awakened in Kaliya made him realise that his present opponent was stronger than even Garuda. He thought, “Perhaps this is the Supreme Lord of whom my wives have often spoken.

“He has taken the position of my guru and put His feet on my head. By His display of extraordinary power He has made me realise my insignificance. Now I will take shelter of Him, the Supreme Lord.”

Kaliya’s wives had given up on their husband. They were hoping that the Lord’s kicks would do him in. But when they saw a glimmer of devotion in Kaliya, they instead thought to save him.

“Our husband has become a Vaisnava hy the touch of the Supreme Lord!” they thought. Keeping their children before them, the wives of Kaliya, the Naga-patnis, bowed before the Lord with joined palms.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura remarks that Kaliya grasped Krsna in his coils on an island in the middle of the lake, which was also where his wives offered their obeisances to the Lord.

The beautiful and extensive prayers of Kaliya’s wives highlight how merciful Krsna’s punishment is to the wicked: He relieves them of sin and gives them the highest gift — pure devotion to Himself.

Kaliya’s wives praised the Lord in prayers such as this: “What You have done here is actually mercy for us, since the punishment You give to the wicked certainly drives away all their contamination.

“Indeed, because this conditioned soul, our husband, is so sinful that he has assumed the body of a serpent, Your anger towards him is obviously to be understood as Your unconditional mercy.”

At the conclusion of their prayers, the Naga-patnis begged the Lord to give their husband back to them. Krsna, who is mercifully disposed to His devotees, then stepped off of Kaliya’s hoods and set him free.

Since the entire creation is situated in Krsna’s abdomen, Kaliya had felt as if he were being crushed by the weight of the world; freed of that burden, his life returned to him, and he surrendered to Krsna.

Krsna accepted Kaliya’s prayers but ordered him to immediately leave Vrndavana along with his family and return to Ramanaka Island, which had been his home before he was banished by Garuda.

The marks of Krsna’s footprints branded on his hoods, Kaliya no longer had to fear Visnu’s avian servant. The Yamuna would he free of Kaliya’s poison, and the surrounding forest would soon be revived.

Kaliya felt remorseful for his past sins and greatly obliged to Krsna for freeing him of his offences to Garuda and to the Vraja-vasis. In clear consciousness, the snake king now desired to worship the Lord.

Kaliya prayed, “O Lord! By marking my heads with Your footprints You have shown me mercy even great devotees have not attained, and that, after I burned Your body with poison from my fangs.

“Allow me, therefore, to offer You cooling sandalwood pulp.” Anxious to return to His associates, Krsna hesitated to accept this proposal. The Lord said, “But that will take too much time.”

Kaliya was insistent, “Please sit down my Lord!” Then, along with his wives, Kaliya smeared aromatic sandalwood pulp all over Krsna’s body, fulfilling his heart’s desire and attaining the Lord’s mercy.

Before leaving the Yamuna, the Naga-patnis offered Krsna all kinds of jewels, including the eternal Kaustubha, which had fallen into the water at the time Krsna was ensnared in Kaliya’s coils.

Smiling affectionately and very pleased, Krsna placed His hand on Kaliya’s heads and removed all the pains in the snake’s body. Kaliya bowed low and said, “O one who rides on Garuda!

“If by chance Garuda is not present to carry You somewhere, then just remember me, the servant of Your servants. Even if I am a million yojanas away, I will come to You in the wink of an eye.” Then he left.

It is said that the Yamuna and Kaliya Lake regained their original purity — “free of poison and full of nectarean water” — the moment Kaliya left.Such is the result of Krsna’s human-like pastimes.

Freshly garlanded, ornamented, and dressed by Kaliya’s wives, Krsna then returned to shore, walking upon the heads of snakes Kaliya had ordered to act as stepping stones for the Lord.

Seeing Krsna approach, some Vraja-vasis hummed in bliss like a swarm of bees, some spoke in broken words, some laughed gleefully, and some cried tears of joy, but everyone relished bliss.

Krsna’s arrival prompted the Vraja-vasis, young and old, to do away with decorum. They crowded around the Lord and showered Him with affection according to their individual relationships.

First Yasoda repeatedly exclaimed, “My son is saved!” Then Nanda Maharaja pushed his way past the elder gopis and embraced Krsna, touching all His limbs just to make sure his son was in one piece.

Balarama laughed while He embraced His younger brother with gusto, lifting Krsna off the ground. Next came the relieved cowherd boys, while the gopis cast Krsna bashful glances from a distance.

The cows were also excited hy Krsna’s arrival. Even the trees and creepers, which had wilted in grief, now blossomed in joy, offering Krsna leaves, buds, and flowers in happiness.

The brahmanas and their wives showered blessings upon the Lord and advised Nanda Maharaja to generously distribute charity to ensure that his mischievous son would always be protected.

Krsna enacts the pastime of subduing the serpent Kaliya in different ways at different times, but some basic details always remain the same: Krsna chastises the demon and dances on his hoods.

Sanatana Gosvami explains that in Goloka, Krsna extends His hands to the gopis from atop Kaliya’s hoods and, unseen by those on shore, the Lord and His beloveds relish rasa-dancing on Kaliya’s heads.

Always willing to please Krsna in any way they can, the gopis join Krsna — in spite of the fact that they are terrified of serpents — and dance on Kaliya’s hoods simply because He wants them to.

Sanatana Gosvami also tells us that, after accepting Kaliya’s repentance and the prayers of the snake’s wives, Krsna seizes the Naga-patnis’ shawls and uses them to make a bridle for the serpent.

Holding the bridle in His left hand and playing the flute with His right, Krsna makes Kaliya go here and there at will, sometimes prodding the serpent with His flute to entertain the gopis.

When the Naga-patnis offer Krsna jewels, garments, garlands, and flowers, He decorates Himself and the gopis with these treasures and then returns the girls to the river’s shore, unseen.

Another variation is found in a Puranic reference cited by Cakravarti Thakura in which Krsna, in a different day of Brahma, rides to the wrestling match in Mathura on Kaliya, not Akrura’s chariot.

These are just a few variations on Krsna’s wondrous, never-ending, ever fresh pastimes, in which Kaliya symbolises malice to other living entities, malice that poisons the waters of pure devotion.

Such malevolence has no place in Vrndavana or in devotees, so Krsna mercifully banishes such snake-like qualities from the dhama, just as He does from the hearts of His devotees.

To be purified of vice and blessed with the treasure of Krsna’s feet, Vaisnavas pray to and bathe at Kaliya-ghata, a practice praised by Krsna in this way:

**“If one bathes in this place of My pastimes and offers the water of this lake to the demigods and other worshipable personalities, or if one observes a fast and duly worships and remembers Me, he becomes free from all sinful reactions.”**

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami worships Kaliya-ghata in this prayer,

*priyapriya-prana-vayasya-varge dhrtaparadham kila kaliyam tam*  
*yatrardayat pada-talena nrtyan harir bhaje tam kila kaliyam hradam*

**“When the Kaliya serpent offended His friends, for whom He is dearer than life, Krsna punished the snake, dancing on him and kicking him with the soles of His lotus feet. I worship Kaliya-hrada.”**

According to Bhakti-ratnakara, bathing at Kaliya-ghata not only frees one from sinful reaction but also grants one success in business — *kaliya-tirtha-sthane bahu-karya-siddhi haya*.

In Bhauma Vrndavana, the original kadamba tree from which Krsna jumped into the water still stands along the old bed of the Yamuna, alongside the Deity of Kaliya-mardana installed hy Vajra.

In a small courtyard behind that tree is Prabodhananda Sarasvati’s samadhi and bhajana-kutira, where that saint composed numerous books in glorification of Radha and Krsna. All glories to him!

**\* \* \* \***

The area surrounding Kaliya-ghata is called Kaliyadamana- vana. Next to it is Radhabagh, or Radhavana, the luxuriant riverside forest that extends from there all the way to Vamsivata.

The hill Dvadasaditya-tila rises up from Yamuna’s banks just above Surya-ghata and Praskandana-tirtha, both of which are related to events that followed Krsna’s banishing Kaliya from Vrndavana.

Long ago the sun god — knowing that the Supreme Lord would take birth in His original form to enact pastimes in the land of Vraja — came to Krsna’s eternal abode in pursuit of divine grace.

Surya is an expansion of Narayana — hence, an expansion of Sri Krsna — but that effulgent deity considers himself Krsna’s servant. Surya’s prescribed duty is to provide light and heat to the universe.

Just as Maha-visnu creates universes and yet stays far from Lord Krsna and personal service to Him, Surya-narayana is generally unable to serve Krsna directly or see Him face to face.

Surya-narayana took up residence at what is now known as Surya' ghata and performed austerities by the bank of the Yamuna with the aim of directly seeing and serving Krsna on some future date.

The sun god bathed in the Yamuna regularly, chanted a mantra of Krsna’s names, and prayed to the dust and creepers of Vrndavana. In time he received assurance that his desire would be fulfilled.

Surya’s opportunity to serve the Lord came when Krsna had freed Himself from Kaliya’s grasp, returned to shore to give pleasure to His companions, and basked in the warmth of their pure love for Him.

Despite the unlimited affection Krsna’s family, friends, and loved ones heaped upon Him, He continued to shiver in the cool afternoon shadows because He had been in the water for such a long time.

Anxious, Mother Yasoda wrapped Krsna in soft blankets and vigorously rubbed His body, but even that did not generate enough heat to stop the uncontrollable shaking of His limbs.

On the advice of the elder gopas, Krsna was taken to the top of Dvadasaditya-tila to get closer to the rays of the setting sun, but it was too late in the day for that dwindling sunshine to warm His body.

Radha could not tolerate seeing Krsna suffer from the cold. She had already seen Him in the coils of death as He duelled with that hideous monster, which was just about as much distress as She could take.

It was too much to think that He might get sick as well. She walked a short distance to a large bakula tree, joined Her palms, and secretly begged the sun god to intervene on Krsna’s behalf.

She said, “O eye of the world! O unlimitedly powerful one! If I have performed pious acts, observed vows, and worshipped cows, on the strength of those acts please warm the son of Nanda Maharaja.”

Radha’s request was just what Surya had been waiting for. In the company of his brothers, like Aryama and Indra, and invisible to all hut Radha and a few Vraja-vasis, he appeared before the Lord.

Krsna acknowledged the presence of the demigods with a smile and welcomed the soothing rays from Surya’s body, which felt like pleasing shafts of sunlight on the most pleasant of all spring days.

Gradually Krsna’s body warmed, His shivering stopped, and drops of perspiration appeared on His limbs. He removed His mother’s shawls, but large beads of sweat were now rolling from His body to His feet.

From His feet, Krsna’s perspiration flowed down the hill in a rivulet to form a small pond called Praskandana-kunda, which even in His time was a holy tirtha, a tirtha later visited by Lord Caitanya.

Unfortunately, in Bhauma Vrndavana, Praskandana-kunda is now lost to our vision. It is a gupta-tirtha, a holy place whose location is known but whose features are hidden (gupta).

Another category of holy places is called lupta, or lost. Such lupta- tirthas have been completely obscured by the ravages of time; neither written records nor oral tradition exist to locate them.

At the time of Lord Caitanya, Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda were lupta-tirthas — not only covered by time but also forgotten by the locals — until the Lord personally rediscovered them.

When Krsna was personally present, Praskandana-tirtha was famous for its gardens of wild roses; indeed, it was known as the foremost rose forest of Vrndavana and was naturally a most aromatic place.

Even today many gardeners have their flower gardens in the area of Praskandana-tirtha, where they grow the famous aromatic roses of Vrndavana for stringing into garlands for temple Deities.

At the time of Krsna’s clash with Kaliya, Srimati Radharani and Krsna had not yet met, hut Their simmering attachment to each other was certain to bring about Their first meeting.

To reward the sun god — fulfilling his desire to witness Krsna’s pastimes — Krsna arranged that His auspicious first meeting with Radha take place in the rose gardens of secluded Praskandana-tirtha.

Radharani had been unable to restrain the force of Her attachment to Krsna. Despite being a young bride, She finally expressed Her feelings to Him in a letter She consigned to Lalita and Visakha.

Dedicated to the cause of their friend, the two girls found Krsna with Madhumangala at a distance from the herd. Lalita placed the letter in Madhu! hand and said, “Varsana’s princess has sent this to Krsna.”

“Krsna,” Madhumangala teased, “what is the value of a letter? Better to have received some sweets.” But Krsna was eager to know what Radharani had written to Him. “Read it anyway,” He said.

Madhumangala unrolled the letter. His eyes opened wide in surprise as he softly read, “O dearly beautiful one, the artistic loveliness of Your picture is now impressed within My mind.

“Since You are now living within My mind, wherever I wish to run because I am agitated by impressions of You, I find that You, O My friend, are blocking My way.”

After having Madhu reread the letter, Krsna thought to Himself, “Saintly housewives of Radha’s calibre never transgress strict moral codes. This letter must he a sign of a great love.”

Krsna was excited by this turn of events hut feigned indignation before the gopis: “Friend! Why should I, who am averse to even hearing about women, he polluted hy the conduct of such a loose girl!”

He paced back and forth as He concluded, “I will complain to the elders of the village about this.” Taking Krsna’s cue, Madhumangala added sternly, “O king of brahmacaris. Listen!

“While You reprimand these brazen gopis, I will go to the queen of Gokula and relate everything that has happened here, beginning with Radha’s shameful irreligious conduct. How unforgiveable!”

Krsna stopped pacing beside Madhu and said to Visakha, “Actually, Radha has never seen Me, nor have I seen Her. This letter must be intended for some other boy who has captured Her heart.”

The two girls couldn’t believe their ears. What was Krsna saying? They could not tell that Krsna was equally in love with Srimati Radharani but was just testing the strength of Her love.

On behalf of Radha, Visakha replied, “By the same power with which You lifted Govardhana Hill, You have stolen the heart of a saintly gopi, a gopi who now appeals to You and to no one else.”

Turning to Lalita, Krsna abruptly said, “Lalita! I have heard too much of this kind of talk. Please stop.” But Lalita wouldn’t stop, “You are the happiness of Vraja. How can You make this poor girl suffer?”

“My brahmana colleague Madhumangala does not tolerate any deviation from the path of piety,” Krsna persisted, “and Sridama is so busy searching for My faults that he does not even sleep at night.

“Moreover, cruel Kamsa rules this country with an iron fist. O bewildered girl! Under such circumstances how could I have made a pious girl burn in the flames of anguish? It is not possible."

**\* \* \* \***

Lalita was dumbfounded. After all the sweet smiles and crooked glances Krsna had sent Radha’s way, how could He he so indifferent now? Turning away, she indignantly spoke into the distance:

“Our hearts are so polluted by miserable conditions that we are certainly going to Pluto’s kingdom. Nevertheless, Krsna does not give up His beautiful loving smiling, which is full of cheating tricks.

“O Srimati Radharani, You are very intelligent. How could You have developed such great loving affection for this deceitful debauchee from the neighbourhood of the cowherds?”

After saying this, Lalita-devi began to cry. Visakha tried to dismantle Krsna’s resistance by garlanding Him with Radharani’s gunja necklace, but He refused to wear it and gave it back.

Visakha was disappointed by Krsna’s rebuff but still found value in the rejected gunja necklace, for it carried the scent of Krsna’s touch. She carefully wrapped it in a cloth to give to Sri Radha.

Speaking through her tears, Lalita said, “Fate has revealed to us the spotless celibacy of this snake who loves millions of gopis. We must warn Radha, who has fallen in love with this despicable boy.”

“Friend, you are right,” replied Visakha. Turning on their heels and shooting a final volley of fiery arrow-like glances at Krsna, the girls disappeared into the shadows of Vrndavana forest.

Once Madhu was sure the two giris had gone, he said, “Radha adores You. Why didn’t You reciprocate Her love? Why did You say things that will build a staircase leading to the top of a mountain of regret?”

Pausing a moment, Krsna rubbed His hands together and replied, “Friend! You are right. It was cruel of Me to mock Her.” Reflecting on His misbehaviour, Krsna concluded He had gone too far.

His voice full of remorse, Krsna murmured, “Upon hearing of My cruelty, moon-faced Radharani may establish some kind of tolerance in Her aggrieved heart. But then again, She might turn against Me.

“Or, fearful of the lusty desires invoked hy Cupid’s bow, She might even give up Her life. Alas! I have foolishly uprooted the soft creeper of Her desire just when it was ready to hear fruit.”

Madhu slapped his thighs, “What will we do now?” Krsna raised His forefinger in the jnana-mudra and replied, “There is only one thing to do: answer beautiful Radharani’s letter with a letter of My own.”

Tears of joy welled up in Madhu’s eyes as he asked, “What will You write a letter on?” Krsna replied, “Upon rose petals. If I have turned Her away, their scent may help bring Her back to Me.”

Madhumangala clapped in approval and said, “Then why don’t we go to nearby Praskandana-tirtha? It is decorated with a great forest of roses. They will be very happy to serve Your purpose.”

Meanwhile, Lalita went to take counsel from Paurnamasi, and Visakha explained to Radha how Krsna had completely dismissed Her letter. Tears flowed down Radha’s cheeks with no sign of stopping.

Visakha-devi tried to pacify Radharani by placing the gunja necklace around Her neck, but the fragrance of Krsna on the necklace just revived Her disappointment at being rejected hy Him.

Her words broken by sorrow, Radha said, “Desiring the happiness of His association and embraces, My dear friend, I disregarded even My superiors and relaxed My shyness and gravity before them.

“Furthermore, although you are My best friend, more dear to Me than My own life, I have given You so much trouble. Indeed, I even put aside the vow of dedication to My husband —

“A vow kept by the most elevated women. Oh, alas! Although He is now neglecting Me, I am so sinful that I am still living. Therefore I must condemn My so-called patience.”

Visakha tried to comfort Radha in many ways, but the princess of Varsana had already decided that death would he better than life without Krsna. She thought, “Krsna does not care for My body.

“Of what use is it then? Better that I drown it in the waters of Kaliya Lake.” She then said to Her friend, “Visakha! Tell My superiors that I have gone to Dvadasaditya-tirtha to worship the sun god.”

Happy at this apparent change in Radha’s attitude, Visakha said, “That was Jatila’s order.” They headed towards the Yamuna, each with a different plan in mind. As She walked, Radha thought:

“Even though Krsna has rejected Me, the hostile and insatiable hope to attain Him burns in Me still. O mind! The deep water of the Yamuna, the sister of the king of death, is My only shelter.”

As they approached Praskandana-tirtha, Visakha tried to cheer Radha by pointing out auspicious signs. When they reached the blooming forest of roses so dear to the sun god, Visakha said:

“Smell those beautiful roses! Let’s pluck some to make rose water.” Just then Madhu and Krsna arrived nearby, planning to press rose petals into oil to use as writing material for a love letter to Radha.

As they approached the garden, however, Radha’s golden aura and the sound of the gopis' anklets caught Krsna’s attention. “The goddess of beauty must have come here to enjoy pastimes,” He said.

Astute Madhu at once understood the situation. He whispered, “Ah! The deer now places Her foot in the trap.” Krsna spoke in Madhu’s ear, “Let’s hide behind this tree and listen to what they say.”

From behind a large bakula tree, the boys watched and listened as Srimati Radharani approached and, unable to hide Her true feelings any longer, began to cry inconsolably on Visakha’s shoulder.

Between sobs, Radha said, “Do not forget Me in the future.” At this, Visakha also started to weep, but replied, “Friend! You are known for Your gravity, patience, and virtue. Why are You so disturbed?”

“This rogue has robbed Me of My virtue,” Srimati Radharani replied. “His chest is a dam that stops the river of My patience. His face is a moon that withers the lotus flowers of My pious deeds.

“His arms are the pillars in the arena of a sacrifice intended to drive away My perpetual shyness. And on top of everything, O friend, the crooked snake of His glance devours My very being.”

As if in a daze, Krsna whispered, His disembodied voice floating out from behind the kadamba, “Beloved! Stunned by Your sweetness, Krsna has also lost His virtue.” Madhu covered Krsna’s mouth.

Radha raised Her hands to the sky and prayed, “O Krsna! O killer of Putana! I was engaged in My own playful activities in My home, and because of My childish innocence I did not know right from wrong.

“Therefore, is it good for You to have forced us into being so much attracted to You and then to have neglected us? Now You are indifferent to us. Do You think that is right?”

Krsna sighed at this expression of love. Meanwhile, Radharani turned to Visakha, removed Her gunja necklace, and said with finality, “Friend! Please accept My favourite necklace and wear it well.”

Visakha caught Radha’s hand and forcibly replaced the necklace, saying, “Why are You trying to incinerate me in the wildfire of Your words?” Bursting into tears, she cried, “I wish Lalita were here.”

Radha was no longer Herself. She sank deeper and deeper into a quagmire She thought would eternally separate Her from Krsna. The intolerable pain in Her heart forced Her, like a puppet, to say:

“My dear friend! If Krsna is unkind to Me, there will be no need for you to cry, for it will not be due to any fault of yours. I shall then have to die, but afterwards please do one thing for Me —

“To observe My funeral ceremony, place My body with its arms embracing a tamala tree, like creepers, so that I may remain forever in Vrndavana undisturbed. That is My last request.”

Krsna was about to run to Radha’s aid, but Madhu held Him back, gesturing that they should wait. Anxious, Krsna whispered in Madhu’s ear, “Friend, just see how great Her love is!”

**\* \* \* \***

Srimati Radharani continued, “After I have finished worshipping the sun god, please do one thing for Me. When I have gone, please pick a flower for each time I have bathed here — ”

Radha took a few steps towards Surya-ghata, hut then reconsidered: “But if I die,” She continued, “I will never again see Krsna, whose face is like the moon, and who enchants the three worlds.”

Turning on Her heels and facing Visakha, whose eyes had become red from crying, Radha’s heart suddenly filled with longing for Krsna. Innocently, She said, “Friend, will you kindly show Me His picture?”

Visakha replied, “I have no writing tools here. How can I draw You a picture?” Radha’s innocence then turned to anxiety. She sat on the ground and declared, “Then I will make Him appear by meditation.”

Seeing Radha — eyes closed, sitting in the pose of a yogini— Krsna could no longer restrain Himself. He said, “This is the sweetest nectar I have ever heard, let’s go,” and He stepped out of His hiding place.

Visakha’s joy at the sight of Krsna was unbounded. Her face glowing with bliss, she said to Radharani, “Friend! I think You should open Your eyes and taste the fruit of Your meditation.”

Peering through the slits of Her eyelids, Radha was struck dumb with wonder. Visakha tried to reassure Radha that She was not dreaming: “The hoy who has devastated Your heart with irrepressible love —

“The sight of whom has caused Your delicate body to burn in flames of passion, who wears a new peacock-feather crown, and whose playful ways made Him the master of Your life, stands before You.”

Thinking that She had entered a trance, Radharani murmured, “How sweet this dream is!” Visakha rubbed Radha’s shoulders to rouse Her, saying, “Unbeliever! This is no dream. He is real.”

Srimati Radharani opened Her eyes wider and gazed at Krsna before Her. She whispered to Herself, “O My broken heart! Good fortune has truly smiled upon you and made you whole again.”

As Radha rose to Her feet, Krsna addressed Visakha-devi, “Rascal! I have been looking everywhere for you. A girl who resembles you in every way bewildered Me and robbed Me of My gunja necklace.

Both Visakha and Madhumangala realised that Krsna was looking for an excuse to flirt with Radharani- Madhu suggested, “I see Your necklace on Radha. You can just take if back from Her.”

But Krsna shook His head and replied, “I can see that She has the necklace, but I cannot accept your advice. Even in a dream, not to mention while awake, I would never touch a girl as beautiful as Her.”

Radha turned away and looked at the ground. She took Krsna’s statement as another rebuff. Radha thought, “Perhaps He is joking; still, I think His unwillingness to touch Me shows His true feelings.”

Visakha could see Radha’s disappointment. Knowing that Krsna’s inner purpose was to be closer to Radha, Visakha dismissed His supposed reluctance with a laugh and chided Him:

“O great ocean into which the rivers of many beautiful girls flow! You decorate Your body with gunja necklaces, so why he surprised when these ornaments become mementos to those whom You attract?”

Revived by Visakha’s bold words and Krsna’s proximity, Radha lightly ran Her fingers across the gunja necklace on Her neck, immersing Krsna’s mind in Her graceful and affectionate ways.

Amazed by Her love for Him, which like a gentle breeze continued to unfold the petals of Radharani’s unparalleled beauty, Krsna joyfully thought, “When Radha smiles, waves of joy overtake Her checks —

“And Her arched eyebrows dance like the bow of Cupid. Her glance is so enchanting that it is like a dancing bumblebee, moving unsteadily due to intoxication. That bee has bitten the whorl of My heart.”

Krsna took a step closer to Radha. He was about to take Her hand when a terrible voice pierced the air: “Granddaughter Visakha! Where arc you?” It was Jatila stumbling out from the rose bushes.

“Why is He here?” Jatila thought, eyeing Krsna. “Visakha,” she said aloud, “why did you forget the incense, sandalwood paste, and fragrances meant for Radha’s worship of the sun god?”

Visakha gave some false reply while Krsna, looking as innocent as He could, thought, “Just as the cakora bird was about to drink the sweet rays of moonlight, a mass of dark clouds covered the moon.”

Joining His palms, Krsna said aloud, “O wife of My mother’s maternal uncle, I offer respects to you.” Jatila replied, “If You want my blessings, then better You not look at young giris with such crooked eyes.”

Madhumangala interrupted, “O lady! My dear friend’s glance is ever innocent and gentle, never crooked. Your feeble eyes see others in a questionable light. Bless yourself to no longer squint.”

As usual, Madhu’s words enraged Jatila, who hissed at Krsna, “Oh, You girl-chasing snake! Why have You come here?” Krsna replied, “For the same reason as your daughter — the beauty of these roses.”

The two girls extracted the following message from Krsna’s answer: “Who could fail to be attracted by Radha’s rose-like beauty or hy the fragrance of Her love, which both permeate this garden?”

Jatila would have none of Krsna’s sweet talks. “Charming hoy,” she growled, “please leave at once.” But Krsna was not intimidated: “Talkative old lady! Why he so agitated? I will go when I wish.”

Jatila scowled at Krsna with a furrowed brow and grumbled, “Here, filled with charm and sweetness, is my young daughter-in-law; there, with crooked eyes, You stand by Her side. Of course I’m agitated.”

Then, pouncing on Visakha, the old lady continued, “Why are you two here anyway?” Visakha tried hard to dream up a clever excuse, “On our way to worship Surya we saw a deer and followed it here.”

Just then a deer came into the clearing, eyes darting here and there, then hastily retreated into the bushes. Shaking her head, Jatila said, “Whimsical girls, give up your infatuation with this deer.

“You have come here to worship the sun god, but the afternoon is rapidly coming to an end.” Visakha cast a glance at Radha that said, “It seems we must now leave this place. Such is fate.”

Radha looked at the sun’s reflection in Krsna’s toenails and thought, “O heart, be steady. Be still. I have yet to drink the nectar of Krsna’s words. I have yet to glance at His face from the corners of My eyes.

“O My friend! After such a long time I finally had the chance to enjoy pastimes with Krsna. But alas, wicked fate has used this old lady as an instrument to stand in My way. How cruel! How very cruel!”

Jatila grasped Srimati Radharani by the arm and demanded, “With the sun setting we must hurry to the sun god’s temple. Come daughter! Spend not a moment longer with this prince of rakes.”

Radha hid sadly behind Her veil, too shy to steal one last glance at Krsna’s face. Along with Jatila and Visakha, Radha disappeared along the path that leads up to Dvadasaditya-tila.

Rupa Gosvami recorded this first meeting of Radha and Krsna at Praskandana-tirtha in his Sri Vidagdha-madhava, which is rich with descriptive soliloquies, divine humour, and clever double meanings.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu, on His visit to Vrndavana, first went to Praskandana and from there to Dvadasaditya-tila, which Sanatana Gosvami had meticulously prepared for the Lord’s arrival.

For those who aspire for material enjoyment, a bath at the foot of the hill by Surya-kunda, where a deity of the sun god was once visible, gives entrance into the sun planet to serve its fiery Lord.

Or if one bathes at Surya-kunda on a Sunday that falls on a sankranti, as the sun travels from one zodiac sign to another, one will attain speedy fulfilment of all one’s desires.

Pure Vaisnavas, however, offer respects to Surya-ghata, Dvadasaditya-tila, and Praskandana-tirtha because these sacred places free them from sinful reactions and qualify them for pure devotion.

Dasa Gosvami praises two of these places:

**“Once, accompanied by the gopas, gopis, and Surabhi cows, the supremely opulent, noble, and magnanimous Krsna felt very uncomfortable in the winter cold.**

**“Twelve suns then appeared at that place, and with great devotion warmed the Lord with their intense shining. I eternally take shelter of this sacred place, which bears the name Dvadasasurya-tirtha.”**

**“When the twelve suns shone from every direction, perspiration fell from Sri Krsna’s transcendental body, and from this perspiration came a charming, splendid, clear lake —**

**“Bearing the sweet fragrance of the Lord’s delicate, supremely handsome, and supremely opulent transcendental limbs. Bowing down, I worship this lake, known as Praskandana-sarovara.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Further along the Yamuna River past Surya-ghata are Yugala-ghata and Vihara-ghata, two pastime places that are connected to the bathing and resting pastimes of the divine couple.

The word yugala (“pair”) refers to the divine couple, Radha and Krsna, who — during Their daytime meetings near the Yamuna — come to Yugala-ghata to ease Their fatigue and the heat of the day.

With no one hut a few maidservants to assist Them, Srimati Radharani and Sri Krsna don bathing clothes and enter the lotus-filled water of the Yamuna River with youthful enthusiasm.

In the water, Radha s and Krsna’s bodies appear like two blossoming lotuses — one gold, one blue — Their honey-like qualities attracting swarms of bees and lending Their sweetness to the river.

The Yamuna River is naturally sacred and pure, but when she embraces the bodies of Radha and Krsna her waters attain a superlative quality that can only be compared to itself.

What is that nectarean quality the Yamuna acquires from Radha and Krsna? It is a mixture of many ingredients, starting with the natural aroma of Krsna’s own form — musk, aguru, and camphor.

Added to that aroma are unguents, sandalwood paste, and minerals that scent, cool, and adorn Krsna, along with the dust of Vraja that collects on His limbs, especially His feet, all dissolved in the water.

Perhaps the most outstanding ingredients are the moonshine of Krsna’s smile, the thunderous rumbling of His words, the darkness of His bodily complexion, and the whiteness of His gleaming smile.

These eleven items mix with the river’s blackish water to create the unimaginable honey-nectar that flows from Krsna, the emperor of blue lotuses, as He plays within the waters of the Yamuna.

But the liquid honey from the Krsna-lotus pales in comparison to that even more wonderfully sweet liquid from the Radha-lotus, which Krsna Himself savours hy always trying to play downstream from Her.

The nectar that flows from Radha’s form comes from Her natural fragrance, which resembles a blend of camphor, kunkuma, and roses, further enriched hy the musk and aguru in Her tilaka and unguents.

Added to these are the sandalwood pulp the gopis daub on Her limbs, the aloe perfume they spray on Her hair, and the black ointment (kajjala) they carefully apply to Her eyelids.

These eight substances, when further combined with Her golden complexion, cuckoo-like voice, and radiant smile, constitute the sweet nectar that flows from Sri Radha, the empress of golden lotuses.

There are two additional items, hut they do not dissolve in the Yamuna: the painted makara fish on Radharani’s cheeks and the dolphins on Her breasts. They both prefer to swim.

The influence of the amorous mellow and the exuberance of Radha’s and Krsna’s water sports combine the two elixirs. Finally, the powdered flower pollen of eternal youth is mixed with this potion.

After all of this, Yamuna-devi’s water is so sweet that bees collect it; in fact, its nectar is more concentrated and more wonderful than the nectar found in any of the flowers of Vrndavana.

Vaisnavas who hear about this divine, concentrated sweetness— which laps upon the steps of Yugala-ghata— naturally want to know how they can taste it, even in their conditioned states.

No doubt it is difficult for even great sages and demigods to appreciate the special attributes of Yamuna-devi’s waters, which are so enriched by the water sports of the divine couple.

But by hearing Radha’s and Krsna’s Yamuna pastimes narrated by great souls like Kaviraja Gosvami, the transcendental vibration can transmit, through the ears, the taste of the enriched river water.

King Prthu confirms this in principle,

*sa uttamasloka mahan-mukha-cyuto bhavat-padambhoja-sudha kananilah*  
*smrtim punar vismrta-tattva- vartmanam kuyoginam no vitaraty alam varaih*

**“My dear Lord! You are glorified by the selected verses uttered by great personalities. Such glorification of Your lotus feet is just like saffron particles. When the transcendental vibration —**

**“From the mouths of great devotees carries the aroma of the saffron dust of Your lotus feet, the forgetful living entity gradually remembers his eternal relationship with You.**

**“Devotees thus gradually come to the right conclusion about the value of life. My Lord, I therefore do not need any other benediction but the opportunity to hear from the mouth of Your pure devotee.”**

After bathing at Yugala-ghata, Radha and Krsna came out of the water and put on dry clothes. Then They happily went to a nearby grove at Vihara-ghata, where They enjoyed various pleasures (vihara).

Radha and Krsna decorate each other with fragrant flowers and flower ornaments brought hy Their assistants, until They appear to merge into the richly blossoming grove that surrounds Them.

After this amusement, the divine couple enjoy eating fresh fruits the gopis collect, along with sweets that Srimati Radharani prepared at home and brought to the forest for Krsna.

Their picnic complete, Radha and Krsna lay down upon a soft bed — a mattress stuffed with flower petals — while some of the younger cowherd girls massage Their lotus feet and others fan Them.

As Radha and Krsna drift off to sleep and continue Their pastimes in Their dreams, birds sing soft songs, bees hum gently, and aromatic breezes rustle the leaves on the trees.

The divine couple rest, and the gopis quietly withdraw to another grove nearby to eat Radha’s and Krsna’s remnants and to relax before the next chapter in the day’s pastimes begins.

In Bhauma Vrndavana above Yugala-ghata rests the temple of Yugala-bihari, where Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura and his followers once stayed during their visit to Vrndavana.

**\* \* \* \***

In New Vraja-dhama, the shoreline between Vihara-ghata and neighbouring Andhera-ghata is thick with weeping willows that form a small sub-forest and whose pliant branches caress Yamuna’s waters.

This part of Radhavana forest marks where Krsna would engage Radharani and Her friends in playing hide-and-seek, a game popular with young cowherd boys and girls alike.

It is the nature of children to entertain themselves with playful diversions. Actually, this propensity originates in Krsna, who is the original pleasure-seeking person (anandamaya-purusa).

One achieves the perfection of childish play when, after becoming qualified for Lord Krsna’s company, he or she can play with the Supreme Lord in the manner of cowherd boys or girls.

Srila Prabhupada writes,

**“Other devotees play with Krsna as friends on equal terms.... All day and all night they think of Krsna. At night, when they are sleeping they think, ‘Oh! In the morning —**

**“‘I shall go and play with Krsna.’ And in the morning they go to Krsna’s house and stand by while Krsna is decorated by His mother before going out to play with His friends in the fields.”**

In Krsna’s manifest pastimes the gopas and gopis played a variety of games from childhood through youth, some of which arc still current today, although in different forms and with different names.

For example, while the cows peacefully graze nearby, the boys play one game called gulli-danda, similar to today’s cricket. The Mahabharata mentions Bhima’s special proficiency in the sport.

The young gopis played games more suited to girls, like ball and tag. Sometimes the boys and girls played together; Holi, for instance, involved gopas and gopis. It has remained popular through the ages.

Krsna joined the gopis in games like ball, hide-and-seek — even wrestling — games in which He could relish the flavour of amorous affection on the pretext of enjoying these natural diversions.

Conditioned souls enjoy not only the pleasure of sport itself but also the “team spirit,” or the bond that develops amongst the players. That mundane bond is a reflection of pure spiritual mellow.

The pastimes of Krsna’s liberated companions are, first and foremost, diverse ways of exchanging love with Krsna. The enjoyment that comes from the game itself is only secondary.

As Srila Prabhupada said, when the cowherd boys think, “Tomorrow I shall play with Krsna!” their primary motive is to share their love with their dearest friend. The play itself is incidental.

At Andhera-ghata, on the plea of playing hide-and-seek, Krsna fulfils His desire to taste the endless facets of the gopis’ love. That love inspires Him to reciprocate with them in special ways.

Once, as Radha and Krsna walked along a riverside path, taking in the natural beauty of Vrndavana with Their transcendental senses, They came to the dense thicket near Andhera-ghata.

Krsna turned to Radha, and the gopis behind Her, and said, “Why don’t we play hide-and-seek?” Always eager to please Krsna, the gopis replied, “Let’s play. There’s no better place to do it than here.”

With a note of sarcasm, Lalita-devi added, “But only if You don’t cheat. No peeking while others hide!” Krsna was about to protest Lalita’s unfair remark, but then He had a better idea.

“If you’re so worried about Me cheating,” Krsna said, “then why don’t you cover My eyes with your hands?” Lalita nodded in approval and replied, “Good idea! We’ll draw straws to see who gets the honour.”

But setting the rules of the game was not easy. Krsna wanted the seeker to tag the hiders, while the gopis — wary of Krsna’s gusto — insisted that being seen would suffice. In the end Krsna got His way.

Because the cowherd girls agreed to His rules for the game, Krsna volunteered to be the first seeker. The girls, however, insisted that they should draw straws, but again Krsna got His way.

A large tree served as the base. It was agreed that if Krsna promised not to peek, which He did, no one need cover His eyes. And because of the large number of gopis, He would count to fifty before searching.

When Krsna first leaned against the tree to count, a few girls, having conferred amongst themselves, remained there to see if He would peek. Sure enough, He did. “You cheated!” they cried out.

Lalita then stood behind Krsna to cover His eyes — as first proposed — her fingers tightly shut as He counted and the gopis ran in all directions to hide behind trees, bushes, pavilions, and the like.

When Krsna reached fifty, He called out, “Here I come!” First He looked to Lalita for hints, but she gave none. Then He searched for signs of where the gopis—especially Radha — had gone to hide.

Sometimes when playing this game Krsna finds Radha by following Her distinctive footprints, or perhaps a monkey might betray Radha and reveal Her hiding place. But sometimes Krsna just can’t find Her.

At these times, when Krsna has searched high and low without finding Her, Radha gets so excited that Her effulgence glows brighter and gives Her away. Sometimes, though rarely, a gopi betrays Her.

In the process of looking for Radha, Krsna invariably finds other gopis. Some of them He tags, while others outrun Him to the base. But on this occasion He found neither Radha nor any of the other gopis.

“Where did they vanish to?” He wondered. He looked at Lalita but — as expected — received no hints, only a smug grin. Krsna searched for footprints. He found not a one. He even interrogated His flute.

It was risky to venture too far from base, but Krsna had no choice, so He headed for a marble pavilion near the ghata. Suddenly, the forest exploded with shrieking gopis making mad dashes for the base.

One after another came cries of “Safe!” Krsna, thoroughly humiliated, failed to catch even a single gopi; He had gone searching too far afield. But where had they been hiding?

A sore loser, Krsna first accused the gopis of using mystic powers to become invisible. “Ridiculous!” they cried. Then He accused Lalita of chanting mantras over His eyes to muddle His vision.

That second excuse made the gopis clutch their sides and laugh hysterically. With no alternative, still flushed with embarrassment, Krsna was the seeker again. This time Citra covered His eyes.

In this way, Krsna and the gopis amused themselves at Andhera-ghata by taking turns covering their eyes so that they could not see (andha) where the others had hidden, and then finding them.

By the arrangement of Yogamaya, Krsna found Radha on the second try and regained His pride. Once Radha had become the seeker, Krsna cheated by becoming invisible and sneaking back to base.

In another game, all the gopis became seekers and searched after one hider— Krsna. In this version of the game, whenever a gopi found Krsna she would quietly join Him in His hiding place.

In this way one by one the gopis would swarm around Krsna like bees around their hive. The last gopi to find the hive would be the next hider, but Krsna always volunteered to hide again.

This reverse form of hide-and-seek was Krsna’s favourite, for it gave Him the chance to relish being very close to the gopis, giving pleasure to them and to Cupid in a way not unlike this description:

“My dear friends! Just see how Sri Krsna is enjoying the season of spring! With the gopis embracing each of His limbs, He is like amorous love personified \[*srngarah sakhi murtiman*\].

“With His transcendental pastimes, He enlivens all the gopis and the entire creation. With His soft bluish-black arms and legs, which resemble blue lotus flowers, He has created a festival for Cupid.”

**\* \* \* \***

As the Yamuna River widens and gently curves to the south, the sub-forest around Andhera-ghata gives way to a clearing, home to a famous tamarind tree known as Imli-tala, also called Tentuli-tala.

This tree has been extant in Bhauma Vrndavana from the time of Sri Krsna. Caitanya Mahaprabhu would sit on a platform beneath it, chant the Hare Krsna mantra, and enjoy the divine atmosphere.

Worship of Imli-tala was inaugurated hy the pujaris of Madana-mohana, but after the Deities were moved to Karauli, the worship was neglected until it was restored hy Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura.

Up until a few years ago the original tree — fifty centuries old — was present, but then it passed away because of neglect. A new tamarind tree has been planted in what remains of the original tree’s trunk.

A yearly festival is held at Imli-tala on the full-moon day of Karttika to commemorate Lord Caitanya’s arrival in Vraja. A picture of Mahaprahhu is brought there in procession from a nearby temple.

Because it is situated along the Parikrama path of Vrndavana town, I often used to visit the Imli-tala tree, pray to it, and remember the pastime Krsna enacted there. I now do the same in New Vraja-dhama.

One moonlit night, while the rasa dance was in full swing at Seva- kunja, Srimati Radharani felt neglected. It seemed to Her that Krsna was delighting too much in the company of the other gopis.

Rather than dancing with Radha at the centre of the rasa circle, Krsna was watching and applauding the performances of individual dancers. Slighted, Radha left the rasa dance and Seva-kunja.

Almost at once Krsna noticed that His beloved was gone. Because She is the primary medium through which He realises the essence of His desires, His happiness in the company of the other gopis waned.

Krsna then disappeared from the rasa dance as well. The other girls were bewildered and distraught, without a clue as to what they had done to lose Krsna’s company or where to go to find Him.

Krsna walked through the moonlit forest and searched the places dear to Radha—Jhulanavana, Vihara-ghata, Srngara-vata — but could find neither Her nor Her confidential companions. Krsna despaired.

What a sad end to a wonderful festival! Not knowing what else to do, Krsna sat beneath the large tamarind tree by the Yamuna and listened to the lapping waves. Perhaps they would advise Him.

Krsna heard Radha’s names in the river’s current and the rustling leaves, the singing birds and chirping crickets. But the owner of that name remained far away — too far for Krsna to tolerate.

Radha’s sudden disappearance stirred intense feelings of separation in Krsna. As time passed and the length of Her absence increased, the ecstasies of separation became too much for Krsna to bear.

Ecstatic love made Krsna faint and fall to the ground, like a doll knocked over by a restless child. He appeared unconscious, but internally His feelings of separation continued to rage.

The forest creatures surrounded Krsna, disturbed at seeing Him in such a state. They tried to wake Him in their own ways — and they succeeded. He sprang to life again, but His torment still blazed.

He still heard Radha’s name in the sounds of the night. The forest shadows reminded Him of Her form. He repeated Her name again and again, and that sound gave Him some solace.

By repeatedly chanting “Radha! Radha!” Krsna inspired the animals around Him to chant. Soon all of Radhavana echoed with the sound of Srimati Radharani’s divine name.

Eventually Krsna’s intense call for His beloved reached Radha’s ears and drew Her toward Imli-tala. Meanwhile, those names awakened within Krsna the sense of being Radha (radha-bhava).

Repeating Radha’s names with great yearning transformed Krsna’s sense of identity from one of being the prince of Vraja to that of being its princess. In short, He thought He was Radha.

And along with this new sense of identity came Srimati Radharani’s beautiful golden complexion; Krsna’s body, normally cloud-blue, became like molten gold. He became Gaura-Krsna.

By identifying Himself with Radha, Krsna now felt separated from Krsna instead of from Radha. This feeling of separation further reinforced both His new sense of identity and His new bodily hue.

In this state Krsna spoke to some gopis He imagined to be there, “My dear friends! Please listen to Me. What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where can I go to get Krsna? Please... tell Me how I can find Him.”

Krsna’s golden complexion lit up the area. Soon Radharani and Her close friends stepped out of the forest into the clearing by Imli-tala and stopped in their tracks, taken aback by what they saw.

“Who is that?” whispered Visakha. “It looks like Krsna!” replied Lalita. “It is Krsna!” said Radha. The girls watched various ecstasies dance on the stage of Krsna’s limbs as He sang Radha’s name.

Sri Radha and Her friends, completely amazed, watched this unprecedented golden-complexioned Krsna, who now exuded a presence and a mood exactly like Srimati Radharani’s own.

Radha’s real presence, however, quickly exerted its own divine influence on Krsna, subduing His feelings of being Radha and bringing Him back to an awareness of His factual identity.

To the extent that He became more aware of His own self, Krsna’s feelings of separation from Sri Radha increased more and more. At last He opened His eyes, hoping to find a way to mitigate His pain.

The sight of Radha and the gopis standing before Him was as soothing to Krsna’s tearful eyes and troubled heart as was His golden complexion a source of joy for Sri Radha and Her friends.

But Krsna had still not noticed His new bodily hue. Then Srimati Radharani pointed it out: “Pray, tell! Why arc You sitting here, and how have You acquired this new colour?”

Krsna looked down at His arms and the rest of His body without a trace of surprise. Then He flashed His signature smile at Radha; that smile doesn’t change whatever His complexion happens to be.

Krsna said, “When You disappeared from the rasa dance I was so distraught at having offended You that I wandered all around Vrndavana. Unable to find You anywhere, I came here.

“Thinking of You and calling out Your divine name made Me feel as if I were You, and so Your mood has become Mine and Your golden bodily complexion has now covered My usual cloud-blue lustre.

“Identifying Myself with You, I felt and voiced the sentiments that arise in You when You are separated from Me. That consciousness further intensified My new sense of identity and outward appearance.

“Why do I look like this? It’s simple. I am adorned with Your mood and complexion.” Radha stepped forward to have a closer look at Krsna’s golden form. She said, “I have never seen You like this before.

“Is there some special significance behind this form? When do You display it and why?” Krsna had Sri Radha and the gopis sit down before Him and then He answered Her questions at length.

Krsna’s complexion gradually regained its usual sapphire lustre as He told them how in Kali-yuga He would appear as the yuga-avatara, Sri Krsna Caitanya, to start a global movement of nama-sankirtana.

Exuberant, Krsna explained that whoever chanted His names with faith would also be blessed with the Vraja-vasis’ special feelings of love in separation, the only means by which to meet Him face to face.

Intrigued by this revelation, Radha asked, “Who in the age of Kali will he qualified to receive the innermost moods of Our hearts?” Krsna clapped His hands and replied, “Practically no one!”

The gopis looked at one another. Krsna was becoming increasingly excited hy what He had said. “Kali-yuga means that hardly anyone is qualified. Hardly any time or place is suitable. But it doesn’t matter!”

Doesn’t matter? The gopis’ eyes opened wide in disbelief. What does that mean? How docs the supreme religion — love for Krsna — become indiscriminately available to anyone, anywhere, at any time?

Even more amused by the gopis’ reaction, Krsna raised His arms in the air and said, “O gopis! You pretend not to know! But in fact you are the supreme donors of the love that courses in your hearts.

“Your adhirudha-mahabhava is the pinnacle of loving compassion. Its own desire is to endow others with its tastes, tastes that make those in whom it resides helpless puppets in the hands of a puppet master.

“O Radha! You know better than anyone the effect Your unmatched ecstasy has on its enjoyer. One so blessed bestows it indiscriminately, regardless of time, place, or the recipient’s qualification.

“And so when You ask, ‘Who is qualified to receive vraja-bhakti?’ I say — impelled by Your own mood — it doesn’t matter! Let anyone who chants Our names — Hare, Krsna, and Rama — have love for Us.”

Swept up in the current of Krsna’s inconceivable magnanimity, overcome by the very ecstasy of which Krsna spoke, Radha threw Her arms around Krsna, crying out, “You are so wonderful!”

Wanting to give Herself to Krsna — who is so willing to give Himself to anyone and everyone — Srimati Radharani tightly embraced Him. And He, in the same loving mood, held Her close to His heart.

When Lalita-devi and the others saw the divine couple embrace it appeared that sometimes They were two separate forms — Radha and Krsna — and sometimes one united form — Gauranga.

Like driftwood tossed by waves, the gopis, caught up in the ecstasy of the divine couple’s union in the form of Gauranga, spontaneously hurst into nama-sankirtana beneath the Imli-tala tree.

Perhaps that nama-sankirtana could have lasted an entire night of Brahma, but then what would have become of the other gopis still sorrowfully searching for Radha and Krsna in Seva-kunja?

Taking pity on those girls, who shared the same loving sentiments as those of Radha and Krsna, Yogamaya transported the divine couple and Their friends from Imli-tala back to Seva-kunja.

To avoid interrupting Radha’s and Krsna’s ecstatic mood, Yogamaya made the gopis forget that the rasa dance had stopped. The festival of sankirtana simply continued, infused with the wonders of divine love.

Many centuries later Lord Caitanya sat beneath Imli-tala. As He looked out over the Yamuna flowing nearby, He remembered Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes and Their vow to distribute love of God.

He had blessed the people of Bengal, Orissa, and South India, but the Mayavadis of Varanasi had thus far escaped His loving embrace. Now He had redoubled determination to save them as well.

Thus on His return to Varanasi, Lord Caitanya debated with Prakasananda Sarasvati. Consequently, the Mayavadis of Varanasi took part in nama-sankirtana, and through it received pure devotion.

At Imli-tala in New Vraja-dhama I couldn’t help but remember Lord Caitanya’s causeless mercy, by which I was chanting Krsna’s names, residing in the dhama, and aspiring to love Radha and Syama.

The Lord is determined to distribute vraja-prema, thus it is only a matter of time before His will touches us all. I am far from being a Vaisnava myself, but by the Lord’s measure I am eligible.

Thus I continued to walk through the holy places of New Vraja-dhama, recalling the pastimes of the divine couple with the conviction that someday divine love might also appear in me.

Kaviraja Gosvamis reassuring words came into my mind:

**“In distributing love of Godhead, Lord Caitanya and His associates did not consider who was a fit candidate and who was not —**

**“Nor where such distribution should or should not take place. They made no conditions. Wherever they got the opportunity, the members of the Panca-tattva distributed love of Godhead.”**

**\* \* \* \***

The next pastime place along the Yamuna is Srngara-vata, the banyan tree (vata) beneath which Sri Krsna once decorated (srngara) Radha and where the cowherd boys once decorated Him.

Lord Nityananda also used to live here, absorbed in remembrance of Krsna’s pastimes as He waited for the time to join Caitanya Mahaprabhu in Navadvipa, so it is also known as Nityananda-vata.

Unlike many pastime places in Vraja, Srngara-vata is frequented hy gopas and gopis alike — albeit at different times — and both groups render the same service there: dressing and ornamenting.

Although the specific meaning of srngara is “amorous love,” the word also indicates the activities related to amorous love, like dressing and ornamenting. As we sing, sri-vigraharadhana-nitya-nana-srngara.

In his Sri Gurvastaka, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura says that one of the duties of the spiritual master is to engage his disciples in dressing and ornamenting the Deity form of the Lord.

Srila Prabhupada elaborates on the term Srngara:

**“It is not that one should worship Krsna once a week or once a month. Rather, one should worship Krsna twenty-four hours a day (nitya). The Deity —**

**“Should have a new dress once or twice or four times a day — as many times as possible. This is called Srngara. Krsna is the most opulent enjoyer, and we should supply Him things by which He can enjoy.”**

Krsna Himself set the example at Srngara-vata in a grove called Srngara-santi, where the Lord carefully dressed and ornamented Srimati Radharani in preparation for the rasa dance.

The gopis generally offer Radha these kinds of services at least eight times a day. When Krsna has an opportunity to help, or to do anything Himself, He considers it an extra-special privilege.

Whenever Krsna does get a chance to dress or ornament Radha, He does it so expertly and with such love that the gopis eagerly watch His every move in order to improve their own service to Her.

Once I went alone to Srngara-vata in Bhauma Vrndavana, where one of the resident brahmanas showed me the throne upon which Srimati Radharani sat as Sri Krsna dressed Her.

The brahmana explained that prior to a scheduled rasa dance, Radha and Krsna had met here and enjoyed many confidential pastimes. They lost track of time, until reminded hy Vrnda that They were late.

Radharani was cross with Krsna both because They had not paid attention to the time and because She looked unkempt. These two things made it obvious that They had just enjoyed loving pastimes.

Krsna reassured Her, “Devi! If You let Me make You up, it won’t take more than a minute.” Radha suspected that Her friends would be more efficient, hut She wasn’t angry enough to say no.

Nodding Her head, Radha said, “All right. But do it nicely, not just quickly.” Having received Her blessings, Krsna had the gopis bring the items needed for Radha’s Srngara. Then He set to work.

As devotees, we each have a worshipful Deity whom we love to serve in so many ways, so Krsna too has His worshipful Deity — Srimati Radharani — and dressing Her is the life of His life.

Full of devotion, highly adept, and constantly glorifying Her features and qualities, Krsna adorned Radha such that the gopis at attendance were singing His praises, calling Him the “emperor of pujaris.”

As Srila Prabhupada writes,

**“Krsna is the most opulent enjoyer, and we should supply Him things by which He can enjoy.”**

In Srngara-vata, adorning Srimati Radharani was Krsna’s enjoyment.

“I am done!” Krsna declared. After Radha had examined Herself in a mirror and showed Her approval with a smile, they all hurried to where the other gopis were waiting in Nikunjavana.

On another occasion, the gopas rested under the Srngara-vata and let their cows drink the crystal clear waters of the Yamuna and graze on the succulent grasses that grew along the riverside.

Lazing in the shade, the boys opened their lunch packs. Later they played games, until Subala suggested that they all decorate Krsna and Balarama just as they had seen brahmanas decorate village deities.

The cowherd boys all agreed, for just as Radha and Krsna are the gopis' worshipable Deities, Krsna and Balarama are theirs. Following orders from the leading boys, the others collected items for srngara.

The cowherd boys seated Krsna and Balarama on a marble platform beneath the tree. With twigs, flowers, leaves, and vines they expertly fashioned a throne with an elaborate canopy.

Some gopas then bathed Krsna’s and Balarama’s feet, others wiped Their bodies with damp cloths as Madhu chanted the Purusa-sukta, and still other boys sang songs glorifying the two brothers.

As soon as Krsna and Balarama had been dried with cotton towels, servants surrounded Them with trays holding flower ornaments, garlands, coloured minerals, and fresh silk cloths.

Supervised by Subala and Sridama, the boys quickly and efficiently dressed the two brothers and decorated Their faces and limbs with beautiful and intricate images of fish, birds, and flowering vines.

Just as the gopis are always prepared to accommodate any need or desire of Radha and Krsna, the cowherd boys always have every conceivable item on hand for serving Krsna and Balarama.

And as expert as the gopis are in conducting services like beautifying, entertaining, and praising the divine couple, the gopas are just as expert in similar services to the two divine brothers.

Since the object of worship common to the gopas and gopis is Krsna, shouldn’t we be able to tell by His dress, ornamentation, and adornment which group is more expert at srngara?

No doubt both boys and girls vie to outdo each other, but in Vraja their transcendental competition never produces envy, only admiration for the others’ service. That is the Vaikuntha way.

In the hours after midday Krsna is generally at Radha-kunda with Srimati Radharani and the gopis, who decorate Him in their own unique way as the eternal woodland Cupid of Vrndavana.

When Krsna returns to His waiting friends the boys whisper to each other and joke, “Krsna looks a lot different now than when He left us. How dashing He looks! I wonder who dressed Him this way?”

And in the afternoon, as the boys prepare to herd the cows back to Nandagrama, they also dress Krsna in their own distinctive style. He then looks like the infallible killer of demons and king of cowherds.

As Krsna comes into the village the gopis see Him from the rooftops and remark, “Look at Vanamali! He looks different than He did when we dressed Him. Now He’s like an actor or a dancer. How wonderful!”

This transcendental competition of srngara is eternally a source of bliss for those who are being dressed, for those who do the dressing, and for those who are fortunate enough to observe the final result.

Srngara-vata is a place where we may come to meditate on the expertise of Krsna, the gopas, and the gopis in dressing their respective Deities, and to refine that devotional art ourselves.

Lord Nityananda lived at Srngara-vata and played like a little boy along the bank of the Yamuna. When local children came to swim, He would join them in their childish games.

Absorbed in the mood of Lord Balarama, Lord Nityananda would enact pastimes He had displayed millennia ago with the cowherd boys. Yet He yearned — with all His heart — for Krsna’s company.

Sometimes He would sit beneath the banyan tree and loudly chant the Hare Krsna mantra. Sometimes He would decorate Himself with flowers, garlands, and ornaments as if He were a landowner or a king.

Sometimes His body would fill with ecstasy and His eyes would overflow with tears. He would roll in the dust and cry out, “O My brother! O Kanai! Where are You? Where are You?”

Lord Nityananda was aware that Caitanya Mahaprabhu had appeared in Navadvipa, but because Lord Caitanya had not yet revealed His sankirtana movement, Lord Nityananda continued to wait in Vraja.

Finally, after twenty years of touring and residing in holy places, Nityananda Prabhu could no longer stay away from His Lord. At the age of thirty-two He left sacred Srngara-vata for Navadvipa.

**\* \* \* \***

Govinda-ghata lies north of Srngara-vata. It is linked with two rasa-lila pastimes: one in which Krsna returned to the gopis, as told in Srimad-Bhagavatam, the other in which Krsna searched for Radha.

These are two separate pastimes. Later, at nearby Vamsivata, I will elaborate on the first, the well-known episode from the Bhagavatam. Now let us hear about the second pastime, Krsna’s search for Radha.

The gardens surrounding Radha-kunda are Radha’s and Krsna’s favourite pastime places. The shores of the Yamuna — with their groves, gardens, and beaches — are Their second favourite place.

The divine couple may meet by the Yamuna River at any time during the day, but They are almost always found there at night, enjoying the untold diversions afforded hy the rasa dance.

Like other eternal pastimes, the rasa dance is regularly performed, but in a variety of ways, in various parts of Vraja, with different groups of gopis. But it is never performed without Srimati Radharani.

The first rasa dance, enacted on the full-moon night of Karttika, was very special in that it included a variety of gopis who by their spiritual practices had just attained perfection (sadhana-siddhas).

In order to establish in the hearts of the gopis the depth of unity required for the rasa dance, Krsna disappeared from their midst, thus binding them together with the common bond of separation.

But in the dance presently under discussion, it was Radha who left in the middle of the festival, thus obliging Krsna to abandon the other gopis, find Radha, determine Her reason for leaving, and pacify Her.

Srimati Radharani is Krsna’s pleasure potency; thus, His enjoyment of amorous pastimes depends upon Her. She further enriches Krsna’s enjoyment by expanding Herself as Her own gopi friends.

In the rasa dance under discussion, Krsna became so absorbed in exchanging love with other gopis that Srimati Radharani felt neglected. Offended by His conduct, She disappeared.

The gopis are like tinkling bells on the metaphorical Radha-anklet that graces Krsna’s dancing feet. When that anklet disappeared, its bells fell silent. Krsna’s dance was then bereft of life.

The musicians played, the singers sang, and the gopis danced; still, melancholy descended on Vraja and deprived the festival of pleasure, just as the contents of a pot leak out from a hole in its base.

Music failed to stir the heart, lyrics were hut empty words, dance steps were clumsy strides to nowhere in particular, and the prevailing atmosphere was like a thick fog of gloom without a trace of joy.

The gopis and Krsna looked around bewildered, as if they had been transported to some faraway land. Was this the Vrndavana of endless effervescent bliss, or a lower planet filled with suffering and sorrow?

The gopis and Krsna silently stared at one another and all at once they realised that Radharani was no longer there. With a rueful look in His eyes, Sri Krsna told the girls, “Wait here.”

Krsna searched Yamuna’s groves and pleasure gardens, but Radha was nowhere to be found. He looked for signs of Her footprints — there were none. He called after Her — there was no reply.

The Lord thought, “Radha is displeased with Me, and I won’t be able to find Her unless She wants Me to.” With no other recourse, Krsna sat down at Govinda-ghata and began to chant Radha’s name.

“Radha and Her name are one,” He thought. “If I repeat Her name with a penitent, loving heart, She will know it. If She does not, then this night, which began with so much promise, may be My last.”

Seated like a yogi, Krsna continuously recited Srimati Radharani’s name, a sound that soothed His pain like a cooling breeze, made His limbs tremble, and caused His hair to stand on end.

In the two syllables ra-dha Krsna felt Sri Radha’s presence, beauty, qualities, and moods. As He continued to chant, that feeling transformed within His mind into a vision of Her form (sphurti).

In His heart Krsna saw Radharani, just as She had been earlier in the rasa dance. Kneeling before Her, He prayed, “Devi! You are the essence of My existence and the energy of My very being.

“Krsna without Radha — like the sun without sunshine, water without liquidity, perfume without aroma — is meaningless; thus I pray that You return and again give meaning to My life.

“I reciprocated the love of the other gopis because I vowed to do so. But You must know that My love for them is like a sesame seed compared to the Mount Meru of My love for You. ? Radha!

“Punish Me as You like, but please do it in person. This is My one request.” His prayer complete, Krsna opened His eyes and continued chanting Radha’s name in the hope that She would soon appear.

Do scriptures not say that Krsna is famous in the world because He is connected to Radha, and that She is famous in the world because She is connected to Him? Would that connection now show itself?

It would. Just then Radha stepped out of the forest like a lone timid doe and gazed at Krsna with eyes full of hurt and disappointment, a look that made Him want to run and comfort Her. He didn’t though.

He had to be careful not to make Her disappear again. Krsna slowly rose to His feet, meeting Her gaze with His own, full of humility and remorse. And then He fixed His eyes on Her lotus feet.

For some time They stood there not speaking, hut saying so much, at a distance from each other, but very much together. Then, like a buck bashfully courting a doe, Krsna stepped towards beautiful Radha.

It took time for Krsna to pacify Radha’s heart, to make Her willing once again to take part in the rasa dance. To do so He had to win Her over in so many ways, and so this place is called Govinda-ghata.

Krsna pleased (inda) Radha’s mind and senses (go), and so He is called Govinda. And this place, its atmosphere saturated with His attempts to please Her, is also called Govinda-sthali.

To find out the many things Krsna said and did to convince Srimati Radharani that He had never meant to neglect Her, we have only the strength of nama-sankirtana to depend upon.

While visiting Govinda-ghata, we may meditate on this scene: Radha and Krsna looking at each other from a distance, neither sure of what the other is about to do, hut both eager to he reunited.

Humility and love are not just compatible, they are inseparable — as one increases, so does the other. The scene of the divine couple’s reconciliation abounds with both of these sublime moods.

To Govinda, who pleased Radha at Govinda-ghata and returned Her to the rasa dance, let us offer our obeisances,

*namo brahmanya-devaya go brahmana-hitaya ca*  
*jagad-dhitay a krsnaya govindaya namo namah*

**“I offer repeated obeisances to Lord Krsna, also known as Govinda, the reservoir of pleasure for all senses, who is the well-wisher of the cows and the brahmanas, as well as the living entities in general.”**

**\* \* \* \***

In New Vraja-dhama, the Yamuna’s hank projects into the water where the river widens between Cira-ghata and Bhramara-ghata, as if to give special emphasis to the pastimes Krsna enjoys there.

This Cira-ghata, also known as Cayana-ghata, is often confused with the Cira-ghata we have already discussed upriver in Tapovana where the Vraja-kumaris worshipped goddess Katyayani.

I have heard devotees both dismiss the Cira-ghata next to Govinda-ghata as something dreamt up by opportunistic pandas and mistakenly assert that it is the place where Krsna stole the Vraja-kumaris’ clothes.

Both speculations, however, are incorrect. This Cira-ghata is where Krsna stole the clothes of other gopis — including Sri Radha — when they went bathing after an exhilarating rasa dance nearby.

The pastime at the Cira-ghata in Tapovana took place in winter. It was meant to bless the unmarried gopis who had undergone the Katyayani vow in the hopes of getting Krsna as their husband.

The pastime at this Cira-ghata in Radhavana happened after a rasa dance. Neither the time of year nor the classes of gopis involved are known, hut it is clear the two places played host to different pastimes.

Narahari Cakravarti refers to the two different places and to the two different pastimes I have just mentioned, and Kaviraja Gosvami describes Lord Caitanya’s visit to Cira-ghata in Radhavana:

While residing at Akrura-ghata, Caitanya Mahaprabhu would visit Cira-ghata and other nearby places along the Yamuna before continuing to Imli-tala for His daily absorption in nama-sankirtana.

Before He chastised His servant for accepting the local people’s false claim that the light on a fisherman’s boat was Krsna in Kaliya-ghata, Mahaprabhu bathed at Cira-ghata and then rested at Terntull-tala.

Certainly neither Caitanya Mahaprabhu nor Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami would have referred to a Cira-ghata near Imli-tala if there had been any doubt it was an authorised pastime place.

In summary, just as there are various Krsna-kundas in Vraja that denote different pastimes, there are two different Cira-ghatas where two different pastimes ocurred. Let us hear of the one near Imli-tala.

Once Radha and Krsna and the gopis displayed such artistic skill in dancing that the demigods showered flowers on them. Meanwhile, the demigods’ wives fainted at the sight of Krsna’s handsomeness.

The scene was so extraordinary that the stars stopped twinkling and the moon froze in its orbit; indeed, all the constellations realigned themselves to better see Krsna and the gopis in their rasa dance.

Yogamaya served Krsna by extending the time of the dance to the length of Brahma’s night, but as with everything in this world, the dance had to come to an end, its performers finally exhausted.
