The gopis seated Krsna on their shawls, surrounded Him, and praised Him with songs of their own composition, songs that filled Krsna’s mind with the sweetness of their affectionate messages.

Krsna then led the gopis into the refreshing waters of the Yamuna, whose happy waves welcomed them as if clapping. Bees collecting pollen from lotuses also glorified them with their humming.

Krsna and the gopis resembled a bouquet of lotuses tossed into the river by demigods from heaven — many long-stemmed golden lotuses surrounding one fully blossomed blue indivara water lily.

The gopis held hands and surrounded Krsna, keeping Him in the centre. Then they splashed Him from all directions, forcing Him to swim underwater to safety outside the gopis’ circle.

Krsna resurfaced and splashed the gopis nearest to Him, who shrieked with false fear and swam to the shelter of a large cluster of lotuses. Other girls swam behind Krsna and threw lotus buds at His back.

Humiliated by the attack from behind, Krsna chased His adversaries into deep water, where they were unable to take the offensive. Singling out Radha, He took Her hostage in the middle of the river.

The gopis were unable to help their friend, so they headed for shore. This lured Krsna back into the shallows, where, armed with lotus stems, the gopis accosted Him and freed Srimati Radharani.

Before Krsna could recover from the lotus barrage the gopis waded upstream and around a bend — out of sight — leaving Him suddenly alone with nothing but the sound of the Yamuna’s lapping waves.

But Krsna had His own plan. He got out of the water and scooped up the gopis’ clothes and ornaments. Scampering up a large kadamba tree, He hid the girls’ belongings out of sight in an upper branch.

Returning to the water, Krsna cleverly waded upstream to where the gopis lay in wait for Him with more splashing games and lotus flower fights, some of which He won, some of which He lost.

After flavouring the Yamuna with their amorous pastimes — as well as the kunkuma powder from their limbs, kajjala from their eyes, and perfume from their bodies — Krsna and the gopis returned to shore.

As the girls came out of the water they saw that their clothes had disappeared. They exclaimed, “Thieves have taken our clothes and ornaments!” Krsna shook His head. “This is tragic!” He exclaimed.

One cowherd girl wondered aloud, “But how did they manage to come and go without us noticing them?” “They must have waited until we were upstream and out of sight,” Krsna replied.

During this conversation, the gopis were standing in their wet bathing clothes trying to cover themselves in front of Krsna. They were terrified at the thought of returning to their homes in this state.

Krsna pretended to help the girls figure out how they could return to their villages without scandal, but He was actually enjoying the gopis’ bashful attempts to conceal their beauty from Him.

The Lord knew that these older girls were transcendentally envious of the intimate exchange He had had with the vraja-kumaris, so He arranged for them to endure a similar embarrassment.

Even though it was not at once apparent that Krsna was the culprit, the gopis consulted amongst themselves and quickly came to the conclusion that only He could have taken their clothes.

An animated debate then took place in which the gopis threatened, then implored, and finally cajoled Krsna to return their clothes. Krsna made demands similar to those He had made to the kumaris.

These gopis, however, were not novices in dealing with Krsna; they could not be so easily tricked into submitting to Him. And yet, like all the girls of Vraja, they also considered themselves His maidservants.

According to their desire, then, the gopis enjoyed Krsna’s novel arguments, naughty demands, the bliss of surrendering to Him, and, of course, the relief of finally getting their clothes back.

After dressing and ornamenting themselves, Krsna and the beautiful damsels of Vrndavana enjoyed drinking Varuni on the moonlit bank of the Yamuna, filling the forest with their joking and laughter.

Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes are a never-ending downpour of nectar. I pray that these pastimes flood my mind and heart with their sweetness, leaving no room for other thoughts or memories.

In New Vraja-dhama, Bhramara-ghata juts out into the Yamuna. At the time of writing this book, it is one of the more developed pastime places, with its pavilion, gardens, and paved walkways.

From its vantage point, this small peninsula provides a striking view of pastime places on both sides of the river as well as the serene, breathtaking beauty of New Vraja-dhama’s main waterway itself.

In Bhauma Vrndavana, Radha and Krsna once met here alone in the shade of a wise desire tree. Free to express Themselves without reservation, They submitted to an outpouring of honey-laden words.

Although no one was present to hear what They were saying, the sweet smell of the divine couple’s breath attracted a swarm of bees that had been searching the area for flower pollen.

The bees (bhramara) sensed a source of some extraordinary sweetness nearby and, driven by their natures, flew from all directions to where Radha and Krsna were seated, now known as Bhramara-ghata.

As the divine couple came into their vision, the bees thought, “Here are two personified flowers — one golden and one blue — unlimitedly oozing honey for the purpose of enjoying Their own sweetness.

“But no! Everything about Them is pure nectar — Their limbs, words, breath, beauty, and aura. They must he more than personified flowers. They must be the presiding Deities of all flowers.”

Radha and Krsna heard the bees’ humming, but They weren’t prepared for the swarm that descended upon Them just as a rain cloud suddenly engulfs twin mountain peaks.

The bees went wild over the abundance of nectar emanating from the divine couple. In that intoxicated state they collided with each other, flew into Radha and Krsna, and then off into the surrounding foliage.

Since Krsna is the essence of sweetness, and Radha is the taste of that sweet essence, the bees had attained the ultimate perfection the most learned bees amongst them had spoken of in their hives.

Once having found Radha and Krsna, they thought, “There is no sweeter taste than this.” Indeed, to Krsna’s amusement and Sri Radha’s dismay, the bees did not want to leave.

By waving Her hands, Radha was feeding the bees Her bodily aroma, and by raising Her voice, She mesmerised them with Her breath. The bees, then, became more attracted than ever. And Krsna just laughed.

Burying Her face in Krsna’s shoulder, frightened Radha implored, “Please do something! Please!” But there was no danger; none of the bees would have stung Them. Krsna finally managed to calm Radha.

He placed His flute to His lips, invested a special melody with all of His divine sweetness, and sent that nectarean flute-song meandering downstream along the course of the Yamuna.

Contained within that melody was a sweetness so extraordinary that the bees were confused. In a stupor, they thought, “What kind of superlative taste is this that redefines the very meaning of nectar?”

The flute-song may not have been as visually enticing as Radha and Krsna, but the excessive sweetness of its sound was enough to distract the greedy bees and lure them off into the distance.

As quickly as the bees appeared, they disappeared. In just moments, their humming could no longer be heard. Krsna placed His flute in His lap, looked at Radha with smiling eyes, and said:

“Dearest! In Vrndavana, not just the bees but all living entities live on nectar. Please restrain Your unlimitedly sweet beauty before the entire forest inundates Us and forces Us to leave this lovely spot.”

**\* \* \* \***

In Bhauma Vrndavana, the edifice at Kesi-ghata is one of the most stunning monuments on the banks of the Yamuna, built to commemorate Krsna’s killing of the horse demon, Kesi.

The king of Bharatapura and his queens built the structure. Because the Yamuna River flows along Kesi-ghata, a beautiful arati is offered here to Yamuna-devi every evening at sunset.

The temple behind the ghata is called Yugala-kisora. On different occasions, both the temple and the ghata were offered to iskcon for purchase, but a successful transaction was never made.

Like everyone who has done parikrama of Vrndavana town, I have walked along the beautiful ghata, circumambulated the presiding siva-lingas, and touched the kadamba tree near which Krsna killed Kesi.

Govinda Maharaja and I bathed at Kesi-ghata many years ago when the Yamuna was flooding. While we were in the water a large snake passed between us and quickly disappeared before we could react.

A local, sitting at the top of the stairs, said, “pani-wala,” referring to the water snake. Ever since that time, whenever we take a sacred bath together—anywhere—Maharaja and I search the area for pani-walas.

Kesi was the last of the demons that Krsna killed in Vrndavana. His death was a harbinger of Akrura’s arrival in Nandagrama and the Lord’s sorrowful departure for Mathura.

After the death of Arista, Kamsa was so demoralised that for an entire year he made no further attempts on Krsna’s life; rather, along with his surviving friends, he seethed with fear and anger.

During that year Krsna enjoyed the camaraderie of His companions undisturbed, especially relishing amorous pastimes with Srimati Radharani and the gopis in the sweet ripeness of youth.

Krsna’s pleasure was so sublime that He thought He was living in Goloka. He forgot all about the mission for which He and Balarama had descended — ridding the earth of demons.

But one night, Krsna dreamt that He was in Mathura. In the dream He dragged Kamsa from a dais and killed Him. The next morning the Lord awoke to the reality that He was living in the material world.

As He lay in bed, Krsna thought, “Today Kesi is coming to Vrndavana to kill Me. After disposing of him — because Kamsa is afraid to come here — I will have to go to Mathura and kill him too.”

The thought of leaving Vrndavana, His parents, and His loved ones disheartened Krsna, so much so that He lay in bed for a long time lamenting the fate that had transformed His joy into sorrow.

It was Kesi’s arrival in Vraja that finally got Krsna out of bed. But before we hear how Krsna fought and killed the demon, allow me to relate some of the incidents that led up to Kesi’s demise.

Narada Muni had watched a year go by in which the demons of the world committed their atrocities unopposed. He decided to incite Krsna’s wrath upon King Kamsa and the king’s cronies in Mathura.

Narada told Kamsa that Krsna and Balarama were the sons of Vasudeva. He also revealed that the brothers were secretly being protected in Nanda’s house, and that They had killed Kamsa’s friends.

Kamsa once again imprisoned Vasudeva and Devaki and concocted an elaborate plan to dispose of the brothers once and for all. Calling on his friend Kesi, Kamsa ordered, “Go kill Rama and Krsna.”

“How will I recognise Them?” Kesi asked. Kamsa answered, “The boy who wears a peacock feather crown, yellow garments, and holds a flute is Krsna. His older brother, dressed in blue, is Balarama.”

Unaware that he was about to meet his death, Kesi ran off towards Vrndavana. Meanwhile, Kamsa called on thugs like Mustika to organise a wrestling tournament with Kuvalayapida as its guardian.

Suspecting that Kesi would fail in his mission — as had so many others— Kamsa then called on Akrura to go to Vrndavana and extend an invitation to Krsna and Balarama to fight his wrestlers.

Kamsa hoped that his giant elephant, his trained wrestlers, or — if need be — his powerful armies would succeed where all others had failed. “And who can face my power!” he concluded.

Kamsa addressed Akrura with great diplomacy: “Please go to Nanda’s village, where the two sons of Anakadundubhi \[Vasudeva\] are living, and without delay bring Them here on this chariot.”

The king pointed at a brand new chariot that had been built for him, which Akrura readily accepted as befitting Krsna, since it was both opulently decorated with gems and as yet unused by Kamsa.

Meanwhile, as Krsna lay in bed lamenting the thought of leaving Vraja, Madhumangala approached Him with a proposal: “O friend! It looks as if You are not prepared to go to the pastures.

“Don’t while away our valuable breakfast time. Why not lend me Your dhoti, peacock feather, and flute? Disguised as You, I am sure to receive many candies, sweets, and laddus in the village.”

Krsna readily complied with His friend’s request. He even helped Madhu with his disguise and watched through the window as His chubby lookalike begged Nandagrama’s residents for sweets.

At that time, running at the speed of mind, tearing up the soil with his hooves, and scattering the clouds with his mane and tail, Kesi arrived in Vrndavana, creating havoc for its residents.

His loud neighing echoing throughout Nandagrama, Kesi so frightened the cows and bulls that they all panicked and ran from their barns to the safety of Vrndavana forest.

Kesi, in the form of an enormous black horse, terrorised the village of Nandagrama in search of the boy who fit Kamsa’s description of Krsna. Suddenly, he looked up one street and saw such a boy.

Of course that boy was Madhumangala going door to door decked out as Krsna. Without wasting a moment, Kesi charged forward, thinking to make short work of the chubby little cowherd boy.

Moments before, the Vraja-vasis had left their homes at the sound of Kesi’s thunderous hooves and their cows’ fearful lowing. Concerned for the welfare of their herds, they approached Kesi with caution.

Krsna jumped out of bed and rushed to the palace gates, where His mother stopped Him. “My son!” she said. “Where are You going?” Krsna replied, “Mother! I saw an enormous horse.”

Firmly holding her son’s arm, Mother Yasoda said, “It is enormous, but it is also clearly ill-intentioned.” Krsna smiled back at her, “Most probably because it doesn’t have a rider. That’s why I am here.”

But Mother Yasoda was not about to let Krsna break in a giant horse. Pulling on His arm, she said, “Go back into the house.” But Krsna protested, “Don’t you think I know how to bring it under control?”

At that point Mother Yasoda lost her patience and turned to her husband, “O King! You are the master of this house. Take charge of this boy and send someone else to rope that wild horse.”

Suddenly Krsna remembered Madhumangala, who was now somewhere in the village, dressed like Him. Krsna thought, “What if the demon mistakes Madhu for Me and attacks him?”

Quickly slipping out of Yasoda’s grasp, Krsna ran in the direction of Kesi — whose head and tail could be seen above the rooftops of Nandagrama — to the street where Madhu was begging door to door.

There Krsna saw the giant horse rear on its hind legs and charge in the direction of His friend, who had been so absorbed in the success of his little venture that he was oblivious to Kesi’s arrival in Vraja.

But when Madhumangala saw a giant fire-breathing horse bearing down on him with ill intent, he turned and ran for dear life, dropping his morning’s collection of sweets along the way.

Krsna had arrived just in time to save His friend from danger. He charged Kesi at lightning speed. As He passed Madhu, He said, “O friend! Not to worry! I shall slay this enemy of the brahmanas”

“O impetuous prince!” Madhu replied. “Be careful. That doesn’t look like an ordinary horse.” Krsna pushed Madhumangala out of harm’s way and said, “That beast? It is just a pony.”

As Kesi charged forward he saw two Krsnas where before there had been only one. Confused, he stopped. But the real Krsna waved His arm at the demon, beckoning Kesi to come to Him.

“Such impudence,” thought Kesi. Comparing the two boys, he concluded that the real Krsna was the slimmer one. To impress his foe with his incredible speed, Kesi galloped off to the Yamuna’s shore.

**\* \* \* \***

Kesi enlarged his body, roared with the strength of a million lions, and tried to swallow the demigods, who had assembled in the clouds above the river. Seeing the devas in danger, Krsna roared back.

The Lord ran to meet Kesi. Once there He tightened the yellow sash around His waist, making clear His intention to fight. This filled the demon with rage and plunged the Vraja-vasis into anxiety.

The two combatants charged, appearing like two ocean waves set to crash together, but at the last moment Krsna grabbed Kesi by the legs and tossed him into the sky, like a wave tossing foam into the air.

Bruised and humiliated, the demon again charged Krsna. He tried to kick the Lord with his hind legs and slash Him with his razor-sharp tail. Krsna deftly stepped aside, however, smiling all the while.

The Lord then grabbed Kesi’s extended legs, twirled him repeatedly around, and without moving from the spot, tossed the demon a hundred bow-lengths, just as Garuda would discard a snake.

It is said that the two opponents fought fiercely for six hours, until Krsna decided to end the demon’s life and relieve His devotees and the demigods of their anxiety. But the fight was not over yet.

Kesi attacked again, roaring in anger with his mouth wide open. Krsna merely laughed, showed His right thumb, and playfully teased the demon, saying, “Do you want something to eat? Here, eat this.”

Krsna then thrust His left arm into Kesi s open mouth, just as a snake shoots into a hole to devour a mouse. The demon tried to bite off Krsna’s arm, but his teeth fell out like the petals of a dead flower.

The Lord’s arm, which felt to Kesi like red-hot iron, then expanded within the demon’s body, blocking his airway, making him choke, and causing his limbs to convulse uncontrollably.

The demon’s stomach burst, his eyes bulged from their sockets, and his soul left his body. As Krsna pulled His arm from Kesi’s mouth, the demigods showered flowers, beat drums, and chanted “Jaya!”

Jiva Gosvami says that Kesi’s dead body resembled two things: Jarasandha’s dead body and a karkati fruit. The acarya also says that the demon attained the liberation of merging into the Lord.

The Garga-samhita gives this account of Kesi’s liberation: When the demon expired, an effulgent being wearing a crown and earrings emerged from the body and with joined palms bowed before the Lord.

That effulgent being said, “O Lord! My name is Kumuda. I was the parasol-bearer of Indra. After killing Vrtra, Indra performed a horse sacrifice to be freed from the sin of killing a brahmana.

“Out of curiosity, I stole the horse and rode it here and there until the Maruts caught me. When they brought me back to heaven, Indra cursed me: ‘Wretch! Become a demon in a horse’s form on earth.’”

“By the touch of Your hand,” Kumuda went on, “I have now been freed from that curse; still, I pray that I may become Your unalloyed devotee, with my heart always fixed upon Your lotus feet.”

As Kumuda circumambulated the Lord, a celestial airplane appeared. After offering his obeisances again, Kumuda mounted the divine conveyance and flew to Vaikuntha, lighting up the sky as he went.

Kesi’s body lay motionless on the ground. The Vraja-vasis joyously surrounded Krsna and praised Him with love-soaked voices. But Krsna shed tears at the thought His Vraja pastimes were about to end.

After everyone was satisfied that no harm had come to Krsna, and after they had showed their love for Him in various ways, they all went to the nearby Yamuna to purify themselves with a bath.

Sanatana Gosvami tells that Kesi also appears in Goloka, and that Krsna subdues him there. When Kesi attacks eternal Vrndavana, Krsna mounts the horse like a cowboy and breaks him in.

After Kesi is completely tamed, Krsna has His boyfriends mount the creature and ride with Him. He then entertains them by making Kesi jump over things, run on the earth, and fly in the sky.

Thereafter, Kesi is kept tied up in a corral in Nandagrama to serve as a source of entertainment for Krsna and His friends. Kesi, who remains tame, is available whenever the boys want to take a ride.

The place on earth where Krsna killed Kesi and then bathed in the Yamuna is known as Kesi-tirtha. Since everyone was very tired after witnessing the battle, they went to nearby Cira-ghata to rest.

Jiva Gosvami says the original name of this Cira-ghata is Cena-ghata, from cena (“the happiness of resting”) in the Mathura dialect. Over time the name changed and is known today as Cira-ghata.

While everyone else rested, Krsna walked along the Yamuna. At that time Narada Muni met Him in a secluded place, offered prayers, and beseeched the Lord to relieve the sufferings of Mathura’s residents.

But Krsna didn’t want to hear anything about leaving Vrndavana. “Why are you making this request of Me?” He asked. Narada was ready with his answer, “O Lord! You arc within me as the Supersoul.

“You have inspired me to say this. As the creator and maintainer of this world, You have appeared to protect Your devotees and to destroy demons like that horse, Kesi, lying dead nearby.”

Narada had already witnessed Krsna’s pastimes in a previous day of Brahma, and so He listed some of the Lord’s activities in Dvaraka to show that Krsna’s move from Vraja was His own inevitable will.

Having fulfilled his responsibility to make that unpleasant proposal, and having reminded Krsna that Vasudeva and Devaki were again suffering at King Kamsa’s hands, Narada Muni disappeared.

Krsna returned to Cira-ghata, where the Vraja-vasis were waiting for Him. Although He tried to appear happy, He was really full of sorrow. He thought, “I can now count the minutes I have left with them.”

Just as Krsna thought this, Madhumangala slipped out from the shadows, holding Krsna’s cloth, flute, and feather in his hands. Again dressed in his own brahmana, attire, he whispered, “Friend!

“Wearing Your clothes is favourable for begging, but it also invites too many dangers. I think You should take them back.” With that, Madhumangala embraced Krsna and chatted away as usual.

Much of the day was already gone, but Krsna insisted on rounding up the cows that had fled into the forest. After pacifying them, He took the cows, along with His friends, to the pastures of Vrndavana.

At the end of the day, as He had done so many times before, Krsna drove the cows through the villages of Vraja to Nandagrama, but this time He knew that it was the last time He would do so.

While Krsna and His blissful friends approached Nanda Maharaja’s palace by one road, Akrura was approaching by another, charged with a mission that would change the Vraja-vasis and Vrndavana forever.

As Krsna solemnly walked along the same dusty paths the gopis had washed with tears of joy at the sight of Him, His only solace was, “I will come back. I must leave, but I will come back.”

Thakura Bhaktivinoda tells us that Kesi represents the horse-like pride of practising devotees who, thinking themselves superior to other devotees, create disturbances in the community of Vaisnavas.

This superiority complex leads one to disrespect even Krsna, and thus one falls down, so it must be avoided at all costs through sincere humility, lest one’s devotion face the same fate as Kesi — death.

It is said that Kesi-tirtha is a hundred times more sacred than the river Ganges and that offering food there to the forefathers (pinda) gives the same result as offering pinda at sacred Gaya.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami teaches us to pray at Kesi-ghata:

**“With his mad neighing, Kesi made the three worlds tremble, and with the wild rolling of his eyes he set the entire universe on fire.**

**“Lord Krsna killed this demon as easily as one splits a blade of grass and then washed the blood from His hands at a place now known as Kesi-tirtha. I worship that sacred place again and again.”**

## Chapter 27 - Dhira-samira to Bhatrola

In New Vraja-dhama, the shore between Kesi-ghata and Vamsivata glistens with gardens and groves that represent Dhira-samira, or Dhira-samira-ghata, where Radha and Krsna perfected Their youth.

In Bhauma Vrndavana the gardens and groves of Dhira-samira have disappeared. The Yamuna has changed course, so it no longer flows nearby. But the breezes (samira) still blow softly (dhira) there.

Jayadeva Gosvami has etched the significance of this part of the Yamuna and of Krsna’s amorous sports there into the hearts of devotees by singing, *dhira-samire yamuna-tire vasati vane Vanamali*:

**“Decorated with a forest garland, Krsna eagerly awaits You in a grove on the windswept bank of the Yamuna.”**

In this song, a gopi speaks to angry Radha about Krsna waiting for Her at Dhlra-samira.

Radharani feigns reluctance, but She is actually eager to hear about Her beloved. With an arched eyebrow She seems to ask, “What is He doing?” Radha’s friend then tells Her of Krsna’s plight.

“Dressed in a way that would excite Cupid himself, Krsna has crossed all obstacles to meet You hy the shore of the Yamuna, where a soft breeze carries the scent of sandalwood from the Malaya Hills.

“As He calls Your name with His flute, Krsna rejoices in the thought that the breeze-blown pollen has touched Your delicate limbs, and when a leaf falls to ground, He wonders whether it is Your footfall.

“Over and over again He checks to see if the decorations in the grove are just right. Then He walks out into the courtyard and looks down the path for You. Not seeing You, He sighs in sorrow.

“O Radha! Using the cloak of night, go to meet Him, but please leave Your telltale ankle bells behind.” Still playing hard to get, Radha frowns at the idea, but She has already welcomed it within Her heart.

Her friend continues, “You glow like shining lightning, but of what use is such overwhelming beauty if it cannot rule over a monsoon cloud decorated by a formation of flying swans.

“O Radha! If You think Yourself not up to playing a reconciliatory role, then listen to this: The very sight of Krsna will effortlessly remove all obstacles and draw You two together in a joyous meeting.”

The gopi then takes Radha’s hand and says, “Don’t think that time stands still. As the night grows older Krsna’s patience wanes and His pride grows. How then will You two reconcile Your differences?”

Jayadeva Gosvami concludes this song by advising his readers, “O saints! Krsna is joyful and gentle. Give your heart to Radha, Krsna, and Their pastimes together — all three will appear in your minds.”

Devotees inclined to follow Jayadeva Gosvami’s request are advised to chant the Hare Krsna maha-mantra at Dhira-samira and peacefully recall the loving exchanges Radha and Krsna had there.

Cakravarti Thakura has revealed one such pastime for our benefit,

*yada sa vamsivata-gah sva-vamsim vamsivado 'vadayad asu tarhi*  
*dhirah samiro 'pi babhuva yatra sthalam ca tad-dhira-samira-nama*

**“Once, as Sri Krsna was walking away from Vamsivata, not far away a gentle breeze sprang up from His flute-playing. Since that time learned souls have called that area Dhira-sarmra.”**

Vamsivata is a banyan tree (vata) beside the Yamuna, beneath which Krsna once played His flute (vamsi) to call the gopis to the rasa dance on the full-moon night of the autumn season (Sarat-purnima).

This pastime is described in the five chapters of Srimad-Bhagavatam called rasa-pancadhyaya. Over millennia the pastime has been retold and commented upon by countless pure-hearted souls.

Dear readers! This pastime is an ocean of nectar in which swim the fish of profound philosophical points, and upon which toss countless waves of love. I hesitate to tell it, lest I extend this book even more.

My intention is to elaborate on this pastime in a separate book, should the Lord provide me with the opportunity. In this chapter I will now recount it only briefly. May Radha and Syama be pleased.

In one sense, the pastime at Vamsivata begins during Krsna’s sixth year, at the end of the first month of winter (Margasirsa), when at Cira-ghata He stole the Vraja-kumaris' clothes.

At that time Krsna made a promise to the young girls that He would enjoy with them in the future. He intended to fulfil His promise with a rasa dance festival on the full-moon night of Karttika.

But, due to a string of dramatic events, the fated night of His seventh year did not pass as planned: On the dark-moon day of Karttika, Krsna preached the doctrine of karma-mimamsa to His father.

On the first day of the waxing moon Govardhana-puja took place. The second day was the feast of Bhratr-dvitiya hy the Yamuna. Then for seven days, up to the ninth day, Krsna held up Govardhana Hill.

On the tenth day of the waxing moon, the cowherd men discussed the incident. On the eleventh, King Indra bathed Krsna. And on the twelfth day, Nanda Maharaja was kidnapped by Varuna’s servant.

On the full-moon day, Krsna showed the spiritual world to the cowherd men of Vraja at Akrura-ghata. And with that the month of Karttika came to an end, as did the romantic autumn season.

Srila Prabhupada writes,

**“It appears from the statements of Srimad- Bhagavatam that Krsna had to wait another year for such a moon before enjoying the rasa dance with the gopis."**

It wasn’t until the age of eight — almost two years later — that Krsna was able to fulfil His promise to the Vraja-kumaris, which happened on the full-moon night of Karttika as He had planned.

The serene beauty of autumn, the picturesque charm of Vrndavana, and the blossoming love of the vraja-gopis — specifically Sri Radha — inspired Krsna’s eventual meeting with the cowherd girls.

One day, as Krsna was wandering about the forest, He found a tamala leaf with the following message from Radha written on it: “Always thinking of Your transcendental beauty, I burn in Cupid’s fire.

“When I hear the sweet strains of Your flute, Your black effulgence appears to engulf Me. I am then lost to You in every way; still, I find that You are far distant from Me. Alas, I have not attained You.”

This was proof that Radha desired to meet Him, as He did Her. To fulfil Their mutual longing now Krsna had to remove all obstacles, such as Radha’s fear of transgressing religious traditions.

If Krsna could persuade Radharani to let Her love roam free and unfettered, then the other gopis would follow, Her being their natural leader. Krsna’s well-practised flute-songs would bring Him all success.

He sat in Nandagrama eagerly waiting for night to fall. As the reddish full moon rose over the horizon Krsna summoned four confidential gopas and posted them as guards at His bedroom doors.

Then, tucking His flute into His belt, He climbed down from the balcony. Protected by deep forest, He hurried unseen towards the bank of the Yamuna and the banyan tree to be known as Vamsivata.

Krsna’s flute first called Radha, for without Her the rasa dance would be useless. Then it called the other gopis. It is said that the melody Krsna played to call Radha had never before been heard on earth.

Heard by Her alone, its message was: “O Radha, with face as sweet as the moon! ? creeper of amorous love. For a long time Your qualities have been piercing My heart. Please be merciful to Me.”

When Krsna understood that Radha was on Her way, He called the other gopis with one message for them all. Excepting some of those who had previously been sages in Dandaka forest, all the gopis came.

The appendix “The Different Practitioners Who Became Gopis In Krsna’s Pastimes” explains how sadhana-siddhas such as the Dandaka sages came to join Krsna in the rasa dance at one time or another.

Due to lingering impurities, this last group of gopis could not overcome familial opposition; instead they entered a trance in which they met Krsna and became qualified to join Him in the future.

According to Cakravarti Thakura, Pariksit noticed doubts appear on the faces of some audience members as Sukadeva spoke about Krsna and the gopis. To remove those doubts he asked, “O sage, the gopis —

“Knew Krsna only as their lover, not as the Supreme Absolute Truth. So how could these girls, their minds caught up in the waves of the modes of nature, free themselves from material attachment?”

Sukadeva Gosvami answered that Lord Krsna accepts and reciprocates love, the essence of relationship of any sort. That love is offered according to the individual devotee’s mood of service.

The sage also pointed out that if Sisupala could attain liberation simply by thinking of Krsna in anger, why should anyone doubt that the gopis could do the same by serving Krsna in amorous love?

The gopis proved their love for Krsna by giving up everything to serve Him as paramours, and although the form of their love may have resembled something mundane, it was their eternal perfection.

No one should doubt Lord Krsna’s ability to bestow such causeless mercy; He is the unborn master of all masters of mystic power. And it is He, after all, who is liberating the whole world.

The gopis followed the path the music of the flute laid out for them and quickly arrived at Vamsivata, which was attractive with forest groves, singing birds, fragrant breezes, and moonshine.

Beneath the banyan tree, upon earth rich with sparkling gems, Krsna looked every bit the transcendental Cupid for whom the gopis had hankered their entire lives. Now they were meeting Him face to face.

**\* \* \* \***

The gopis could not get enough of seeing Krsna. He too greedily gazed at them until His eyes fell upon Srimati Radharani, who stood out amongst the others like a land-lotus amongst daisies.

Reassured that Radha, the cynosure of His pastimes, was present, Krsna welcomed all His lovers,

*svagatam vo maha-bhagah priyam kim karavani vah*  
*vrajasyanamayam kaccid brutagamana-karanam*

**“O most fortunate ladies,” Sri Krsna said. “Welcome. What may I do to please you? Is everything well in Vrndavana? Please tell Me the reason for your coming here.”**

These words of welcome suggested to the gopis that they would not get Krsna so easily, and the advice He gave them confirmed that He would test them: He told them not to abandon religious principles.

Krsna argued that the gopis did not need to enter an adulterous relationship with Him to show their love. They could worship Him at home as faithful wives. That would bring the same result.

He then went on to advise them just as He would advise the brahmanas' wives in Bhatrola. But unlike them, the gopis would not heed Krsna’s advice. To do so would deny them His physical touch.

Krsna’s words of wisdom to the gopis, words that caused those innocent girls only frustration and anxiety, were this: “Transcendental love for Me arises by the devotional processes of—

“Hearing about Me, seeing My Deity form, meditating on Me, and faithfully chanting My glories. The same result is not achieved by mere physical proximity. So please go back to your homes."

Krsna’s purpose in showing indifference and initially hesitating to accept the gopis’ offering of themselves as lovers was to increase their longing for Him and to prompt them to express their love for Him.

At first the gopis contemplated giving up their lives, falling at Krsna’s feet, or becoming angry with Him. But then they patiently explained that their being married was only a material consideration.

From the time of their births they had thought of Krsna, the soul of all living entities, as their true husband and the only object of their affection. To whom else did they owe their chastity but to Him?

The words of the gopis were just like nectar for Krsna’s ears. Finally yielding to their desire, He said, “Usually you show stubbornness towards Me. Tonight it was My turn to be stubborn.”

Then, to show His unlimited mystic potency, Krsna reached out His arms and embraced all the gopis. By that single act He immediately dispelled their sorrow and turned another page in their pastimes.

To get a hint of Krsna’s power, just consider that there were millions of gopis, each with unique desires and characteristics. Krsna dealt with each one individually, and they were all completely satisfied.

We should understand the descriptions of Krsna placing His arms around the gopis, embracing them, and playfully touching them as ways to generally depict the interactions in their loving exchanges.

But actually, even though they numbered in the millions, each gopi perceived that she was alone with Krsna having unique intimate exchanges as couples do according to their individual personalities.

At the same time, Krsna inconceivably brought all of His exchanges with the gopis together into one cohesive pastime, the rasa-lila, just as many drops of water together form a rolling ocean wave.

All glories to Sri Krsna! As they strolled along the banks of the Yamuna in pairs, beautifying the gardens with their presence, Krsna and the gopis sang praises of each other’s beauty, qualities, and love.

At Dhira-samira Krsna intensified His exchanges with the gopis by sitting with them in the camphor-white sand and arousing desire in them by His touches, jokes, and glances. In this way they enjoyed.

One may question how the relatively small area of Dhira-samira could accommodate so many couples in privacy. The answer is that Yogamaya arranged that Vrndavana expand proportionately.

Cakravarti Thakura explains that Yogamaya achieves this feat through her power to make the impossible possible, the aghatana-ghatana-sakti. Afterwards she returns things to their original state.

Krsna’s kindness made each gopi think herself to be the most fortunate girl in the world. That pride checked the primary purpose for which Krsna arranged the rasa dance — to sport with Radha.

Krsna thought, “Because I am enjoying with so many women, Radha has been reduced to the same level as the others. I shall now put them in their place and reveal Radha’s unparalleled superiority.”

Radha, alongside Krsna, is at the centre of the rasa dance. All the other gopis take supporting roles. Krsna thought, “If the gopis think of themselves as Radha’s equals they will only quarrel, not dance.”

Krsna decided He must humble them. Only then would the gopis be able to taste the bliss of rasa. He would show them His mercy by removing both Himself and Radha from their company.

Speaking to the gopis, Krsna said, “Considering that you have all become so tired, you need time to rest. I am going to visit nearby places and will be back soon.” Then He disappeared with Radha.

Regarding Krsna’s leaving the rasa dance, Srila Prabhupada says:

**“The Supreme Personality of Godhead is always full with six kinds of opulences, and this is an instance of the opulence of renunciation.**

**“This renunciation confirms Krsna’s total non-attachment. He is always self-sufficient and is not dependent on anything. This is the platform on which His transcendental pastimes are enacted.”**

The first part of the rasa festival — Krsna’s meeting with the gopis — concludes with His leaving, which also introduces the second part: the gopis’ search for Him throughout Vrndavana forest.

This second part has five phases: the gopis’ madness in separation, their enquiring from the trees and the deer, their imitating Krsna’s pastimes, and Krsna’s enjoyment with and abandonment of Radha.

The increasingly unbearable pain that Vraja’s maidens felt after Krsna’s departure drove them to divine madness (pramada), but they were completely absorbed in thoughts of Krsna.

The gopis’ minds were absorbed in remembering Krsna’s movements, words, and deeds. They acted out those thoughts in a way that would have misled an ordinary person to think they had gone insane.

In truth the gopis were the greatest transcendentalists, as shown by their subsequent symptoms of complete madness (unmada). Now they were so absorbed in Krsna that they identified themselves with Him.

Due to intense absorption in Krsna’s activities, they imitated Him, eventually losing all distinction between themselves and the object of their love. Declaring, “I am Krsna,” their golden bodies turned black.

In time the gopis’ madness subsided somewhat. In that state of semimadness they wandered around Vrndavana searching for Krsna. All seeing Krsna was filled with wonder at everything they said and did.

First they asked the banyan tree at Vamsivata if it knew where Krsna was. Receiving no reply, the gopis questioned other trees, and then the tulasi, the creepers, the earth, and finally some deer.

Having enquired from every possible witness in the forest for a hint of Krsna’s whereabouts, the gopis felt despondent in their failure and soon re-entered the ecstasy of complete madness.

All the gopis thought, “Unless my friends and I get some relief from this pain we shall die!” They then acted out Krsna’s many pastimes, which allowed them to taste some fleeting pleasure.

In these dramas one gopi was Krsna while another was Putana, or Trnavarta, Sakatasura, Kaliya, or Vatsasura. We may wonder how the gopis could have assumed the roles of demons.

Could they ever be antagonistic to Krsna, even in make-believe? No! Such acts would be inconsistent with their devotional mood. It was Yogamaya who assumed the forms of gopis to play the roles of demons.

Thereafter the gopis enacted Krsna’s less ferocious pastimes with the Vraja-vasis. They acted out how He played the flute, played games, devoured a forest fire, was bound by His mother, and lifted Giriraja.

In identifying with the Lord (tad-atma), child Prahlada had also imitated Krsna’s pastimes, but he was not impelled by such advanced stages of ecstasy as those the gopis were now exhibiting.

As the joy of enacting Krsna’s pastimes reduced the intensity of the gopis’ madness, they wandered from forest to forest in search of Him, again enquiring from everything they saw, animate or inanimate.

**\* \* \* \***

At one point the gopis noticed a low-lying creeper in blossom suspiciously out of season. As one gopi spoke to it, she noticed Krsna’s footprints marked with the distinctive flag and lotus.

The excited girls then followed those footprints for some distance until they saw another set of lighter and smaller footprints to the left of Krsna’s, footprints that had markings similar to His.

Based on the position of the two pairs of footprints, the gopis guessed what had happened, again becoming somewhat envious of the lucky girl Krsna had chosen to steal away with Him.

Radha’s friends, such as Lalita, recognised the footprints but avoided enunciating Radharani’s name, saying,

*anayaradhito nunam bhagavan harir isvarah*  
*?an no vihdya govindah prito yam anayad rahah*

**“Certainly this particular gopi has perfectly worshipped the allpowerful Lord, Govinda, since He was so pleased with Her that He abandoned the rest of us and brought Her to a secluded place.”**

Srimati Radharani’s close friends, along with the gopis favourable to Her, were happy that Krsna had given Radha an opportunity to be with Him alone. But other groups of gopis reacted differently.

Gopis neutral to Radha pretended that She did not exist, but Radha’s competitors, such as Candravali, were antagonistic; thus various conversations went on as the girls followed the footprints.

In narrating the conversations of the gopis in his “Krsna Book,” Srila Prabhupada often repeats Srimati Radharani’s name, leaving no doubt that the word aradhita is an indirect reference to Her.

Critics accuse the Gaudiyas of artificially exalting Radha. They say Her name is never mentioned in Srimad-Bhagavatam. In the Caitanya-caritamrta, Srila Prabhupada directly refutes this claim:

**“Sometimes the critics of Srimad-Bhagavatam find it difficult to find Radharani’s holy name in that book, but the secret is disclosed here in the word aradhita, from which the name Radha has come.”**

All Gaudiya Vaisnava acaryas share Srila Prabhupada’s conclusion. Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami, for example, makes the following statement before he quotes the anayaradhitah verse:

**“Her worship \[aradhana\] consists of fulfilling the desires of Lord Krsna. Therefore the Puranas call Her Radhika.”These pieces of evidence substantiate that Radha was Krsna’s “dearmost consort.”**

The gopis saw Krsna’s affection for Radha in their analysis of the footprints, which to them revealed how He carried Her, arranged Her hair, and after collecting flowers, lovingly decorated Her with them.

We may question why Krsna needs to enjoy with Sri Radha. Isn’t He self-satisfied (atmarama)? The answer is that She is His pleasure potency; that is, His pleasure increases in Her presence.

We may also wonder whether Krsna’s dependence on Radha implies that He is incomplete. Absolutely not! Even when separated from Him, She remains one of His many energies, His internal potency.

In short, even though Krsna is self-satisfied, He is eager to enjoy with Radha, and even though She gives Him pleasure, His perfection is not compromised. These are basic truths of the Lord’s amorous pastimes.

The footprints led to a remote grove. But the entrance to that grove was guarded by a swarm of bees, and try as they might the gopis could not get past the bees to reunite with the divine couple.

Inside the grove, Radha and Krsna had been enjoying various trainscendental amorous diversions enhanced hy the sounds of singing cuckoos, humming bees, and rustling leaves.

Vrnda had personally decorated the grove. Both she and Yogamaya had anticipated the events of the entire pastime, including the place Radha and Krsna would choose as Their ultimate sanctuary.

The divine couple were both startled by the sound of the gopis trying to gain entrance to the grove. Krsna urged Radharani to leave by another entrance, but She was too exhausted to move.

Despite Krsna’s persistent requests, Radha would only repeat, “If You want Me to go elsewhere, then please carry Me.” Finally, Krsna affectionately reprimanded Her, hut this made Radha morose.

Trapped between the approaching gopis and Radha’s reticence, Krsna thought, “If the gopis catch Me with Radha they may quarrel again. Then the purpose of My having disappeared with Her will be lost.

“But if I leave Radha the gopis will witness Her ecstatic feelings of separation and thus recognise Her superiority, both in terms of Her devotion for Me and the pastimes We have enjoyed together.”

By the effect of His pastime potency, Krsna was unaware that in asking Him to carry Her, Radha was not being domineering. Her only concerns were for Him and the gopis coming into the grove.

She thought that Krsna must be very tired after Their pastimes and should be resting in the grove. Moreover, She thought that the other gopis who had been in so much distress also deserved to be with Him.

But as the sound of the gopis’ voices drew nearer He jokingly said to Her, “Climb on My shoulder.” Then He suddenly disappeared, as unexpectedly as if Rahu had devoured the full moon.

Radha was in shock. Her smile vanished, Her eyes went dim, Her face faded, and like a withered golden lotus She tumbled to the ground, reaching out desperately for Krsna with Her hands.

As reality began to dawn on Her, Radha cried out, “O master! My lover! O dearmost, where are You? Where are You? Please, o mighty-armed one, o friend, show Yourself to Me, Your poor servant!”

Finally Radha realised that Krsna had actually gone and She fainted. The gopis, who were now entering the grove, did not see Her there on the ground, but Her brilliant effulgence drew them to where She lay.

The signs of intense pain on Radha’s unconscious face and Her distressed voice murmuring “Where are You?” brought out the gopis’ empathy for Her. They made every effort to revive and comfort Her.

The beauty of spiritual relationships can be seen in this attitude of the gopis. In the mutual pain of separation from Krsna even competitors’ feelings of rivalry transform into mutual affection.

Cakravarti Thakura quotes an unknown author, *ata eva hi vislese snehas tasam prakasate*: “Separation \[from a mutual beloved\] awakens the spontaneous display of heartfelt affection \[in lovers\].”

Despite their best efforts the gopis could not bring Radha back to life. Her condition put the girls into such distress that Her close friends fainted and the hearts of even Her most vehement opponents melted.

Finally, the fragrance of Krsna still lingering on the gopis’ bodies reached Radha’s nose and caused Her to stir. Gradually She sat up, and Her friends, like puppets tied to their master, also arose.

The gopis comforted Srimati Radharani, sat Her on the bed, and asked what had given Her so much distress. Full of remorse, Radharani told them everything that had happened.

Sri Radha berated Herself, expressed some enmity towards Krsna, and displayed humility towards the other gopis. The girls were astonished by the force and blend of Her divine emotions.

Lest Radha’s sorrow drown all of them in an ocean of misery, a wise gopi shone a ray of hope into Her heart by suggesting they search for Krsna. “He might be out of sight,” she said, “but He must be nearby.”

Radharani took the hand of a friend for support, rose to Her feet, and joined the others. Following Krsna’s distinctive footprints, they gathered flowers to make a garland as they searched.

But, even though it was a full-moon night, the dense tree cover created such darkness that the cowherd girls could barely see one another, to say nothing of Krsna’s footprints. One girl suggested:

“The forest Krsna has retreated to is so dark that even moonlight cannot enter. How can we follow Him if we can’t even see His footprints? Better we return to the Yamuna and let Him come to us.”

The other gopis agreed: “No one can see Krsna unless He wants to be seen. But if we chant His names and qualities, His heart will be moved. Then He will reveal Himself to us, without a doubt.”

They unanimously concluded that this was the best course of action and returned to the bank of the Yamuna near Govinda-ghata. Deeply absorbed in Krsna, they sang of Him in a unified concert of voices.

The gopis ’ plan of action confirms a well-known philosophical truth proclaimed by scriptures: The Supreme Lord reveals Himself to His worshippers in His own time, by His own sweet will.

For example, sruti says, yam evaisa vrnute tena labhyas tasyaisa atma vivrnute tanum svam: “To that person whom the Supreme Soul chooses...to that person the Lord reveals His personal form.”

This concludes the second part of the rasa festival, the gopis’ searching for Krsna. The third part begins with the gopis’ singing beautiful prayers about Krsna, such as *jayati te ’dhikam*.

**\* \* \* \***

Seated by the bank of the Yamuna, the gopis sprinkled the all-auspicious waters of songs glorifying Krsna upon the blazing fire of separation from Him. This was their only means of extinguishing it.

The nineteen beautiful songs of the Gopi-gita reveal the ecstasies of individual gopis, or groups of gopis, as they glorify Krsna with the common message — explicit or implied —“Please return to us!”

Sukadeva Gosvami says that the gopis could not see Krsna as they sang, but commentators also conclude that He was hiding nearby and listening to the gopis’ songs, the most perfect prema-sankirtana.

Krsna Himself says that He leaves Vaikuntha just to hear His devotees’ sankirtana. How then could He remain hidden as the gopis filled one of Vraja’s forests with their words of love and longing?

How could Krsna resist His ears’ craving to relish the supreme nectar to which they are entitled? Even if He tried to resist, surely His ears would drag Him to the place where Radha and the gopis were singing.

Some commentators, such as Kavi-karnapura and Cakravarti Thakura, use parallel conversations between Krsna and the gopis to reveal the varieties of the girls’ mentalities and trains of thought.

In these conversations Krsna did not speak to the gopis face to face; rather He increased His ecstasy by speaking with them in their minds, inducing a secondary kirtana in counterpoint to the Gopi-gita.

Imagine these two levels of sankirtana to he a vina recital in which the gopis’ songs are the melody played by the main strings of the vina and the conversation with Krsna, the sound of the drone strings.

Together they create an irresistible vibration that captures our minds and hearts, plunges us into the waters of devotional separation, saturates our very being, and gives us a taste of that essential nectar.

These verses are not only full of devotion but also beautifully composed. I reproduce Sukadeva’s verses here for the pleasure of my readers, including the acaryas commentaries on only the final verse.

The poetic meter and alliteration in the verses is exquisite: in each line the first and seventh syllables begin with the same consonant, as do the second syllables in all four lines. The gopis sang—

*Jayati te ’dhikam janmana vrajah srayata indira sasvad atra hi*  
*dayita drsyatam diksu tavakas tvayi dhrtasavas tvam vicinvate*

**“O beloved! Your birth in Vraja has made it exceedingly glorious.**

**“Thus Indira, the goddess of fortune, always resides here. It is only for Your sake that we, Your servants, maintain our lives. We have been searching everywhere for You, so please show Yourself.”**

*Sarad-udasaye sadhu-jata-sat-sarasijodara-sri-musa drsa*  
*surata-natha te ’sulka-dasika vara-da nighnato neha kim vadhah*

**“O Lord of love! In beauty Your glance excels the whorl of the finest —**

**“Most perfectly formed lotus within an autumnal pond. O bestower of benedictions, You are killing the maidservants who have given themselves to You freely, without any price. Isn’t this murder?”**

*Visa-jalapyayad vyala-raksasad varsa-marutad vaidyutanalat*  
*vrsa- mayatmajad visvato bhayad rsabha te vayam raksita muhuh*

**“O greatest personality! You have... saved us from all kinds of danger —**

**“From poisoned water, from the terrible man-eater Agha, from the great rains, the wind demon, the fiery thunderbolt of Indra, from the bull demon, and from the son of Maya Danava.”**

*Na khalu gopika-nandano bhavan akhila-dehinam antaratma' drk*  
*vikhanasarthito visva-guptaye sakha udeyivan satvatam kule*

**“You are not the son of the gopi Yasoda, o friend, but rather-**

**“The indwelling witness in the hearts of all embodied souls. Because Lord Brahma prayed for You to come and protect the universe, You have now appeared in the Satvata dynasty.”**

*Viracitabhayam vrsni-dhurya te caranam iyusam samsrter bhuyat*  
*kara- saroruham kanta kama-dam sirasi dhehi nah sri-kara-graham*

**“O best of the Vrsnis, Your lotus-like hand, which holds the hand —**

**“Of the goddess of fortune, grants fearlessness to those who approach Your feet out of fear of material existence. O lover, please place that wish-fulfilling lotus hand on our heads.”**

*Vraja-janarti-han vira yositam nija-jana-smaya-dhvamsana-smita*  
*bhaja sakhe bhavat-kinkarih sma no jalaruhananam caru darsaya*

**“O You who destroy the suffering of Vraja’s people!**

**“O hero of all women! Your smile shatters the false pride of Your devotees. Please, dear friend! Accept us as Your maidservants and show us Your beautiful lotus face. \|That will be Your service to us.\]”**

*Pranata-dehinam papa-karsanam trna-caranugam sri-niketanam*  
*phani-phanarpitam te padambujam krnu kucesu nah kmdhi hrc-chayam*

**“Your feet destroy the sins of those who surrender to them.**

**“Those lotus feet follow the cows and are the abode of the goddess of fortune. Since You once put those feet on the hoods of Kaliya, please place them upon our breasts and remove the lust in our hearts.”**

*Madhuraya gird valgu-vakyaya budha-manojnaya puskareksana*  
*vidhi- karir ima vira muhyatir adhara-sidhunapyayayasva nah*

**“O lotus-eyed one! Your sweet voice and charming words —**

**“Which attract the minds of the intelligent, are bewildering us more and more. ? dear hero! Please revive Your maidservants with the nectar of Your lips. \[Or, again bewilder us hy its taste.)”**

*Tava kathamrtam tapta-jivanam kavibhir iditam kalmasapaham*  
*sravana- mangalam Srimad atatam bhuvi grnanti ye bhuri-da janah*

**“The nectar of Your words and the descriptions of Your activities —**

**“Are the life and soul of those suffering in this material world. These narrations, transmitted by learned sages, eradicate one’s sinful reactions and bestow good fortune upon whoever hears them.**

**“These narrations are broadcast all over the world and are filled with unlimited spiritual power. Certainly those who spread the message of Godhead are most munificent. \[None are equal to them.\]”**

*Prahasitam priya-prema-viksanam viharanam ca te dhyana-mangalam*  
*rahasi samvido yd hrdi sprsah kuhaka no manah ksobhayanti hi*

**“Your smiles, Your sweet loving glances —**

**“The intimate pastimes and confidential talks we enjoyed with You — all these are auspicious to meditate upon, and they touch our hearts. But at the same time, o deceiver, they very much agitate our minds.”**

*Calasi yad vrajac carayan pasun nalina-sundaram natha te padam*  
*sila-trnankuraih sidatiti nah kalilatam manah kanta gacchati*

**“Dear master! O dear lover! \[Why pain us even at Your own expense.\]**

**“When You leave the village to herd cows, our minds arc disturbed by the thought that Your feet, more beautiful than a lotus, will be pricked by the spiked husks of grain and the rough grass and plants.”**

*Dina-pariksaye nila-kuntalair vanaruhananam bibhrad avrtam*  
*ghana-rajasvalam darsayan muhur manasi nah smaram vira yacchasi*

**“\[Even when we meet, You are not willing to make us happy.\]**

**“At the end of the day, You repeatedly show us Your lotus face, covered with dark blue locks of hair and thickly powdered with dust. Thus, o hero, You arouse lusty desires in our minds.”**

*Pranata-kdma-dam padmajarcitam dharani-mandanam dhyeyam apadi*  
*carana-pankajam santamam ca te ramana nah stanesv arpayadhi-han*

**“Your lotus feet, worshipped by Lord Brahma —**

**“Fulfil the desires of all who bow down to them. They are the ornament of the earth, they give the highest satisfaction, and in times of danger they are the appropriate objects of meditation.**

**“O lover, o destroyer of anxiety, please put those lotus feet upon our breasts. \[By so doing You will not become tired; rather, You will feel pleasure and Your heart’s desire will be fulfilled.\]”**

*Surata-vardhanam soka-nasanam svarita-venuna susthu cumbitam*  
*itara-raga-vismaranam nrnam vitara vira nas te ’dharamrtam*

**“O hero, kindly distribute to us the nectar of Your lips-—**

**“Which enhances amorous pleasure and vanquishes grief. That nectar is thoroughly relished by Your vibrating flute and makes people forget any other attachment. \[In this way you resemble Dhanvantari.\]”**

*Atati yad bhavan ahni kananam truti yugayate tvam apasyatam*  
*kutila- kuntalam sri-mukham ca te jada udiksatam paksma-krd drsam*

**“When You go off to the forest during the day —**

**“A tiny fraction of a second becomes like a millennium for us because we cannot see You. And even when we can eagerly look upon Your beautiful face, so lovely with its adornment of curly locks —**

**“Our pleasure is hindered by our eyelids, which were fashioned by the foolish creator. \[Thus misfortune alone is the cause of our grief, which You alone can rectify — if You are so willing.\]”**

*Pati-sutanvaya-bhratr-bandhavan ativilanghya te nty acyutagatah*  
*gati-vidas tavodgita-mohitah kitava yositah kas tyajen nisi*

**“Dear Acyuta! You know very well why we have come here.**

**“Who but a cheater like You would abandon women come to see Him at night, enchanted by His flute-song? Just to see You, we have rejected our husbands, children, ancestors, brothers, and others.”**

*Rahasi samvidam hrc-chayodayam prahasitananam prema-viksanam*  
*brhad-urah sriyo viksya dhama te muhur ati-sprha muhyate manah*

**“Our minds are repeatedly bewildered —**

**“As we think of the intimate conversations we had with You in secret, feel the rise of lust in our hearts, and remember Your smiling face, Your loving glances, and Your broad chest, the resting place —**

**“Of the goddess of fortune. Thus we experience the most severe hankering for You. \[With these five elements of illusion, like the arrows of Cupid, You have ignited a fire in our hearts.\]”**

*Vraja-vanaukasam vyaktir anga te vrjina-hantry alam visva-mangalam*  
*tyaja manak ca nas tvat-sprhatmanam sva-jana-hra-rujam yan nisudanam*

**“O beloved! Your all-auspicious appearance —**

**“Vanquishes the distress of those living in Vraja’s forests. Our minds long for Your company. Please give to us just a bit of that medicine, which counteracts the disease in Your devotees’ hearts.”**

*Yat te sujata-caranamburuham stanesu bhitah sanaih priya dadhimahi karkasesu*  
*tenatavim atasi tad vyathate na kim svit kurpadibhir bhramati dhir bhavad-ayusam nah*

**“Dearly beloved!**

**“Your lotus feet are so soft that we place them gently on our breasts, fearing that Your feet will be hurt. Our life rests only in You. Our minds, therefore, are filled with anxiety that Your tender feet —**

**“Might be wounded by pebbles as You roam about on the forest path. \[Alas! Alas! What a rash thing to have done, and all in the name of following the dharma of cowherds. How unfair!\]”**

In response to this last appeal of the gopis Krsna said within their minds, “What is your fear?” The gopis replied, “The hardness of our breasts.” Perplexed, Krsna said, “Then why hold My feet on them?”

The cowherd girls answered, “Because when we do, we see that You enjoy it. But we also worry that Your tender lotus feet might feel pain, and so we hold them there very carefully.”

One might not expect such a concern to be voiced during the intimacy of amorous love, but such is the effect of the gopis' extraordinary love for Krsna, the goal of which is only to please Him.

The gopis said, “We could pray to the creator in solitude to soften our breasts, but in our absence You would not be able to enjoy. Thus we must endure sorrow in Your presence as much as in Your absence.”

The gopis' acute concern over the comfort of Krsna’s feet is difficult to understand for persons who have not a whit of their type of love for Him. But, for the gopis, such loving concern is all they know.

They scolded Krsna, “We know that You are independent in Your ways. But what benefit do You gain or what purpose do You fulfil hy wandering barefoot from forest to forest? We just don’t understand.”

To test the steadiness of the gopis’ love, Krsna sometimes speaks curtly, as He did then: “I walk barefoot because I want to. I do what comes to mind. Of what business to you are My walking habits?”

Whether He speaks kindly or harshly, the gopis’ love for Krsna never wavers. But their words to Him, always expressions of the highest love, can be just as pointed as Krsna’s most critical remarks.

They said, “No doubt Your feet must be pained. Do You endure that pain just to make us suffer? Perhaps the pain feels like happiness to You because You derive happiness from knowing that we suffer.

“Tell us! How have You become so hard-hearted? Have You adopted the hardness of our breasts by contact with them? And what about Your feet? Have they become hardened in the same way?

“It must be Your hard-heartedness that will not allow You to admit that Your feet feel no pain, either because they too are hard, or because by their touch, stones, grass, and thorns become soft.

“O prince of cowherd men! Is there some other secret You are hiding from us, knowing which would ease our pain? Is mother earth holding out her soft tongue beneath Your every step?

“Or, dare we ask, are You so in love with us that pain cannot touch Your lovelorn mind? In trying to understand the cause of Your behaviour, which causes us so much sorrow, we are quite bewildered.”

Eager to hear from the gopis’ own lips about their love for Him, Krsna pretended to doubt them. He proposed, “The suffering you speak of must be a pretence, for if it were real you would no longer he alive.”

Indifferent to Krsna’s accusation and determined to prove the depth of their love for Him, the cowherd girls emphatically responded, “Our lives are only in You. Indeed You are our very life.

“So long as You live, we will also live — and suffer. We arc consigned to this fate by the creator, who like You apparently takes pleasure in making young girls cry. This is why we continue to live.’’

Thinking of their lives as so many flowers to he offered at Krsna’s lotus feet, the gopis conclude, “Though full of suffering, may our lives be of use to You as You enjoy playing in Vrndavana.”

As the gopis spoke of their sorrow and their eagerness to sec Krsna they succumbed to their emotions and wept so forcefully that their tears swept mascara down their cheeks and onto their chests.

His cars filled with the gopis’ beautiful songs, Krsna saw that for Him to hide even a moment longer would be too painful for them. He decided it was time for Him to reappear and continue the rasa dance.

**\* \* \* \***

The rasa festival’s fourth part is the reunion, in which prominent gopis react to Krsna’s reappearance. He then leads the girls to the Yamuna and puts them at ease with His glances and His touch.

The gopis question Krsna about the nature of different kinds of lovers: Is He callous? Is He indifferent to their love? Krsna reassures His beloveds by revealing the depth of His affection for them.

As already mentioned, Krsna reappeared at Govinda-ghata. The gopis saw Him step out of His hiding place from within a dense thicket, flashing His effulgence and beaming a wide smile.

We should note that Krsna’s smiling was not a sign of disinterest in the gopis’ suffering, which had truly pained His heart; rather He smiled to please them and put an end to their unhappiness.

Out of humility Krsna had wrapped His golden upper cloth around His neck. Ashamed for having abandoned those who love Him most, He stood before the gopis with a bashful look about Him.

Bhadra was the first to see Him. She called out, “Krsna! Krsna!” and then fell silent. Hearing His name, the others opened their eyes and saw Krsna standing before them in a very special form.

Sukadeva Gosvami calls this form “the one who bewilders Cupid” (*manmatha-manmathah*). In other words, Krsna fully displayed His enchanting sweetness to make the gopis forget their intense sorrow.

He succeeded. Just as rivers rush to the ocean, the dazzling beauties of Vrndavana spontaneously gathered around Him, and their leaders welcomed Him according to their different natures.

Candravali held Krsna’s hand, Syama put His arm on her shoulder, Padma accepted His chewed betel, Saibya placed His feet on her breasts, and Radha, biting Her lips in anger, frowned at Him.

Seeing that Krsna was hardly aware of anyone but Sri Radha, Lalita simply drank in His sweetness with Her eyes, and Visakha took the image of Him into her heart and continually embraced Him there.

The Agamas say that there were three billion gopis at the rasa dance, amongst whom sixteen thousand were prominent, one thousand more prominent, and the eight just mentioned the most prominent.

Of these eight, Candravali and Radharani are the best. And of these two, Radharani is accepted — by scriptures, saints, and the gopis themselves — as the foremost consort of Sri Krsna.

After the gopis had finally abandoned their distress, Krsna appeared especially effulgent and beautiful. As the master of everyone's senses He was now fully satisfied to see the gopis happy once again.

Krsna held the gopis hands and selected a place by the Yamuna He considered best suited for the rasa dance. The gopis quickly set out seats for Him with their kunkuma-stained veils, and Krsna sat down.

Each and every gopi made her own seat for Krsna. To reciprocate their service, Krsna expanded Himself, unseen by them, into as many forms as there were seats and sat on all of them at once.

The gopis worshipped Krsna with smiles, glances, betel nuts, and other services, but they harboured a slight anger towards Him for having treated them so callously. Did He really love them?

To find out, the gopis asked Krsna general questions about the dealings between lovers. In this way they tried indirectly to get to the bottom of why He had treated them as He had.

The gopis asked, “Please tell us about the following types of lovers: those who reciprocate affection, those who show affection to everyone, and those who do not show affection to anyone.”

Krsna’s analysis of these three categories of lovers served to disassociate Him from those who do not reciprocate the love of their affectionate admirers. He then concluded:

“But the reason I do not immediately reciprocate the affection of living beings even when they worship Me, ? gopis, is that I want to intensify their loving devotion.

“They then become like a poor man who has gained some wealth and then lost it, and who thus becomes so anxious about it that he can think of nothing else \[Therefore I am a merciful lover\].”

At times Krsna docs not reciprocate with practising devotees in an attempt to awaken their love, just as He sometimes does not return the love of those who already love Him just to intensify their love.

All that made perfect sense, hut Krsna knew that the gopis wanted to know more. Just to know what He thought was not enough, they also wanted to know what He felt. And Krsna wanted them to know —

So He opened His heart to them,

*na paraye ’ham niravadya-samyujam sva-sadhu-krtyam vibudhayusapi vah*  
*ya mabhajan durjara-geha-srnkhaldh samvrscya tad vah pratiyatu sadhuna*

**“I am not able to repay My debt for your spotless service, even within a lifetime of Brahma. Your connection with Me is beyond reproach. You have worshipped Me, cutting off all domestic tics —**

**“Which are difficult to break. Therefore please let your own glorious deeds he your compensation.”**

Of all the verses spoken by Lord Krsna directly, this one is especially magnificent.

In the moment of silence that followed Krsna’s heartfelt declaration of love, the gopis quietly considered the events of the night, especially His leaving them. Yes! He did love them!

The gopis were ashamed. As the Supreme Lord He knew all about their love for Him. He had disappeared only to proclaim to the world that their love is so great that even He becomes indebted to them.

Instead of trusting Him and His oft-proclaimed love for them, the gopis had doubted His intentions and censured Him with riddles, even as He was trying to exalt them as His greatest devotees.

“Krsna was consistent in His affections, and yet we wavered and doubted Him,” they thought. Looking around at one another, the gopis agreed: “We have indeed been conquered hy Krsna’s love.”

Krsna achieved His purpose: the gopis had yielded to His will and accepted Srimati Radharani’s superiority. Now the rasa dance could proceed with feelings of full harmony abounding.

**\* \* \* \***

The fifth and final part of this pastime begins with the rasa dance, followed by amorous diversions, bathing in the Yamuna, strolling in the forest, Krsna’s sending the gopis home, and the phala-stuti.

It is said that when the activities of dancing, singing, embracing, and kissing are combined together they generate rasa. The aggregate of these activities, then, is called the "rasa dance” or rasa-krida.

Cakravarti Thakura reminds us of the one characteristic of the rasa dance that elevates it above all of Krsna’s other pastimes: empowered with supreme independence, it fully controls its participants.

This means that the rasa dance alone, not Krsna, is the cause of the rasa dance. In other words, Krsna, like the gopis, is a subordinate participant, and His movements are directed by the dance itself.

Our acaryas all agree that this particular rasa dance was comprised of a large circle of gopis with Radha and Krsna at its centre, but their opinions vary as to how Krsna appeared beside the gopis.

Those opinions deal with two ideas regarding how Krsna danced between the gopis: how He manifested Himself, and in how many forms. Ultimately they all agree that the differences are immaterial.

How did Krsna appear between the gopis? Srila Prabhupada writes that Krsna “...expanded Himself into many forms.” Cakravarti Thakura says that one Krsna moved rapidly amongst the gopis.

By calling Krsna Yogesvara (“the master of all artistic skills”), Sri Suka accommodates both possibilities, especially because, by Yogamaya’s influence, each gopi thought Krsna was by her side alone.

And bow many forms did Krsna assume? Srila Prabhupada says that Lord Krsna placed “His bands on the shoulders of the gopis on both sides of Him.”This could mean one of two things:

One Krsna danced with each pair of gopis, or Krsna was alone with each gopi. Visvanatha also gives these two scenarios, but says that if the former were true, Yogamaya made the girls think it was latter.

From the gopis’ point of view, then, Krsna was with each of them exclusively, a trifling feat for He who is the master of mystic powers wholly inconceivable to the conditioned souls of this world.

Pointing to the vast expanse of beach along the Yamuna, Krsna said to the three hundred million gopis, “Although you are many, can you make a circle upon this beautiful pebble-free dancing stage?”

Fearing that they would again be separated from Him, the gopis replied, “If we stand in a circle, we will be too far from You. And we will lose our enthusiasm for this dance festival You have arranged.”

“Don’t worry!” Krsna pacified His beloveds. “As I stand at the centre of the circle with Radha, I will also stand beside each of you.” Their doubts removed, the gopis joined hands and formed a circle.

When Krsna first called the gopis into the forest, in their haste many of them came to Him improperly dressed. In the ensuing pastimes of meeting and separation their clothes became further dishevelled.

To give Krsna the greatest pleasure, Yogamaya invisibly dressed and ornamented each gopi with fresh clothes, garlands, and ornaments befitting the unchallenged apex of Sri Krsna’s pastimes.

Krsna noticed the gopis’ fresh appearance and felt His attraction to them increase dramatically, but even He could not understand what had happened. Such is Yogamaya’s expertise.

As news of the rasa dance spread throughout the universe the demigods and their wives crowded the skies over Vrndavana to see Krsna’s celebrated festival of love with their own eyes.

Because the demigods were in the mood of servitorship — and were for the most part not above the modes of material nature — their ability to see the rasa dance was limited: they could see only Krsna dancing.

But their wives, drawn to serve Krsna in the amorous mood, could see not only His dancing but also His intimate exchanges with the gopis. The demigods’ wives were thus more privileged than their husbands.

At the beginning of the rasa dance, the gopis showed that they accepted Srimati Radharani as their superior by encouraging Her to stand beside Sri Krsna at the centre of their circle.

It is also said that Radha and Krsna first observed the dancing of the gopis from a throne as They were served in various ways by Their friends. Only later did They join the dance Themselves.

As the gopi instrumentalists began to play, celestial accompanists like the Gandharvas and Apsaras joined in with their own instruments and also sang fitting songs in a variety of festive melodies.

Some of the instruments the gopis played to accompany their singing were crafted by Vrnda-devi’s own hands: a tambour for Radharani, vina for Lalita, sarangi for Sudevi, and a santoor for Indulekha.

Radha watched as the great wheel of gopis began to rotate and the individual participants began to dance, repeatedly tightening the circle whenever they moved too far from Krsna.

To fulfil His promise, both to the gopis and to Himself, Sri Krsna entered amongst the girls and placed His arms on their shoulders, all the while striking enthralling poses with His lower body.

Krsna would place His arms on the right shoulder of one gopi and the left shoulder of another. Embracing the neck of one, He would then swing to the shoulder of a third gopi, and so on around the circle.

The gopis felt bliss at Sri Krsna’s touch, gazed at His beautiful form, and sang His praises as their ornaments and braids jingled and swayed in time with the movements of their limbs.

Their long-cherished desires to freely enjoy with Krsna in the way of paramours was finally realised, and so they celebrated the auspicious occasion by offering absolutely everything they had.

From the swaying of their earrings to the flowers falling from their hair, from the tinkling of their anklets to their shining toenails, the gopis clearly showed the bliss that overwhelmed their hearts.

Along with their singing, dancing, and bodily poses, the gopis displayed various hand gestures (mudras), with which they expressed the drama of the music and the prevailing mood of their hearts.

Kavi-karnapura lists twelve hand gestures used by the gopis, such as the flag (pataka), the swan’s head (hamsa-mastaka), the lotus bud (padma-kosa), and the half-moon (ardha-candra).

One noteworthy aspect of the rasa dance familiar to Srila Prabhupada’s followers is a dance step performed with the rhythmic words thaiya thaiya tatha tatha thaiya thaiya thaiya.

Raising their arms in the air and swaying from left to right as they moved forward one step at a time, the gopis went around the circumference of the circle, doing what we know as the “Swami step.”

Visakha-devi thoroughly impressed Krsna with her melodious tunes. When Lalita repeated Visakha’s melodies even more wonderfully, Krsna, full of admiration for both girls, called out, “Sadhu! sadhu!”

Tired from dancing, Radha, Her braid and ornaments loose, leant on Krsna’s shoulder with Her right arm and struck a pose of superiority over Her lover, a gesture that drew applause from the others.

The Lord placed His fragrant arm on Syamala-devi’s shoulder, and she kissed it. Saibya put Her cheek next to His and gratefully received the chewed betel from Krsna’s lotus mouth.

Fatigued from exerting herself, Padma placed Krsna’s soothing hand on her breast, as other gopis shared loving exchanges with the consort of Laksmi, whom they had now attained as their intimate lover.

In this way the gopis, the most beautiful women in creation, and Krsna, the perfection of masculine good looks, tasted the pinnacle of delight by fulfilling their desires in one another’s company.

**\* \* \* \***

Krsna is the Supreme Narayana, the origin of everything. His embracing, caressing, and glancing at His internal potencies, the gopis, are vividly explained by Sukadeva Gosvami.

To stress the perfect innocence of Krsna’s conduct with the gopis, that great sage compares Krsna to a child playing with its own reflection (yatharbhakah sva-pratibimba-vibhramah).

The importance of understanding this concept cannot he overstated, lest we mistake Krsna for a lusty young boy enjoying Himself with many impressionable young girls infatuated with His beauty.

Krsna is the Supreme Lord, and the gopis are all expansions of His own body in the form of His pleasure potency. His interactions with them are therefore likened to a boy playing with His own shadow.

As Krsna and the gopis danced, the sublime sound of their tinkling anklets and ornaments caught the ears of the demigods, who then gave up their inferior habit of drinking heavenly nectar.

The sight of dark-hued Krsna moving amongst the fair-complexioned gopis resembled a dark cloud passing through moonlight, or a sapphire bead spinning on a golden loop. It was the epitome of visual contrast.
