The pairs of Krsnas and gopis in the one large circle soon formed many concentric circles, and those circles transformed into many smaller circles that all moved around Radha and Krsna in the centre.

After some time Krsna could tell that the gopis were exhausted, so He stopped the circles from revolving and led each gopi away into her own grove. Suddenly the rasa dance arena was empty and silent.

Krsna, who self-controlled sages worship as the self-satisfied Supreme Lord, thus realised the topmost perfection of the amorous mellow by fully enjoying the company of the gopis, just as they enjoyed His.

If they had not been by dancing, the gopis were now completely exhausted by enjoying with Krsna. But He kindly dispelled their fatigue by wiping their lotus faces with His nectar-giving hand.

The gopis perspired from their exertions in the rasa dance and the ensuing pastimes, creating rivulets that flowed into the Yamuna and enriched its waters with the liquid form of their love.

Eventually Krsna and the gopis left their groves and came together again. Followed by swarms of bees singing Krsna’s glories, they all entered the refreshing waters of the Yamuna to enjoy various sports.

Splashed from all sides by frolicking gopis, and showered from above by flower-throwing devas, Krsna looked like an elephant playing with his consorts, and in so doing He broke the dykes of Vedic morality.

After they had played in the water to their hearts’ content, Krsna and the gopis returned to shore. Assisted hy maidservants, they dried their bodies and dressed in fresh clothes.

Until the first light of dawn, they continued their amorous diversions in one form or another: strolling through moonlit gardens, drinking honey-wine, and enjoying a picnic on the Yamuna’s soft, sandy beach.

That rasa dance on the full-moon night of Karttika was the subject of Sukadeva Gosvami’s narration, but every night thereafter — until Krsna left Vrndavana — played host to a similar festival.

As Pariksit Maharaja heard about Krsna’s transgression of Vedic morality, he noticed troubled looks on the faces of some non-devotees in the assembly, looks that may be reflected in doubts we too harbour.

These sages still carried material desires in their hearts, thus they could not comprehend the completely transcendental nature of Krsna’s amorous exchanges with the fully-liberated gopis.

Krsna’s libertine conduct with the wives of other men inspired in the karmis and jnanis present two doubts: Was Krsna actually the Supreme Lord? And if He was, how could He act as He did?

The very purpose of Krsna’s appearance in this world was to establish and protect religious principles. How, and for what reason, could He transgress the very laws He Himself teaches, institutes, and upholds?

“O brdhmana!” Pariksit Maharaja said. “The Supreme Personality of Godhead has descended to earth along with His plenary portion to destroy irreligion and reestablish religious principles.

“Indeed, as the Lord of the universe He is the original speaker, follower, and guardian of moral laws. How, then, could He have violated them hy touching other men’s wives?”

The Emperor’s question was clear enough, hut still he added another: “What purpose did the self-satisfied Lord of the Yadus, Yadu-pati, have in mind when He acted so contemptibly?”

One may rightly argue that no act is irreligious for the Supreme Lord, but the question still remains: Why would He perform acts that set a had example for those who are subject to religious principles?

To say that the Lord does so to fulfil His own desires is also not a satisfactory explanation; He is self-satisfied. That is to say, by His nature all the Lord’s desires are already fulfilled (apta-kamah).

And to say that these pastimes are a special feature of Krsna’s appearance begs yet another question: How can Krsna act in such a way and still lead the Yadus, the purest followers of Vedic principles?

Moreover, that Sukadeva Gosvami, a celibate spiritual leader, would narrate such pastimes raises doubts about his integrity. Why would he repeat things that could cause a disturbance for so many hearers?

Smiling, the son of Vyasadeva happily addressed these important questions, which have repeatedly arisen throughout the centuries as Krsna’s rasa-lila pastimes are recited to new audiences.

In reply to Pariksit’s first question, “How could Krsna engage in immoral acts?”, Sri Suka explained that if demigods do not suffer reactions to their occasional sins, how could the Supreme Lord?

There is a distinction to be made between ordinary humans and powerful controllers (isvaras), who are unaffected by acts that for us are immoral, just as fire is unpolluted by anything put into it.

To the argument that great souls should not commit immoral acts because common men will follow in their footsteps, Sukadeva says that we must discriminate between “following” and “imitating.”

Following means to act in ways that have been prescribed for us as suitable, whereas imitating means to blindly ape our superiors’ conduct, which can only lead to our ruination.

The only way to distinguish the boundary between following and imitating is through proper guidance. For instance, an intelligent person would never drink an ocean of poison, as Siva once did.

Krsna’s own statement, “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow,” naturally begs the question: When does this rule apply in our practical lives and when does it not?

The answer is that only those actions of powerful controllers consistent with the conduct prescribed for us by the scriptures should be followed. Those that contradict scripture should not.

Krsna, for example, ordered Arjuna to kill Asvatthama. Sastra enjoins that a brahmana, even if sinful, should never be killed. But Sastra also says that a person armed to kill another should be killed.

Asvatthama was a brahmana, even though acting as a ksatriya. And when captured, he was not armed to kill. Thus Arjuna was right in not killing him. Krsna ordered that he be killed to test Arjuna.

Sukadeva Gosvami summarises His first answer:

**“If the demigods cannot be blamed for transgressing religious principles, then what to say of their creator, Sri Krsna. Moreover —**

**“Yogis attain freedom from the effects of material acts by the power of yoga, devotees by the power of bhakti. How, then, could Krsna, who is the goal of yoga and bhakti, be bound by reactions?”**

If we expand the scope of this answer, applying it to Lord Krsna’s feature as the all-pervasive Supersoul, then we gain further evidence of His innocence in His dealings with the gopis.

As the Supersoul, Krsna embraces the gopis and constantly observes their minds and bodies from within their hearts; what fault can there be, then, in His exchanging loving affairs with them externally?

In answer to the king’s second question, “What was Krsna’s purpose in acting this way?” Sri Suka says,

*anugrahaya bhaktanam manusam deham asthitah*  
*bhajate tadrsih krida yah srutva tat-paro bhavet*

**“When the Lord assumes a human-like body to show mercy to His devotees, He engages in such pastimes as will attract those who hear about them to become dedicated to Him.”**

Persons who hear Krsna’s human-like pastimes become attracted to Him. Discriminating persons who hear the quintessence of those pastimes — the rasa-lila — are attracted to Krsna further still.

The amorous sports of the rasa dance possess an extraordinary potency to attract and purify the hearts of those conditioned souls fortunate enough to have attained human birth.

After answering his disciple’s questions, Sukadeva Gosvami looked around at the faces of his audience to reassure himself that they too were satisfied, which they apparently were.

In concluding his narration of the rasa dance, the sage then explained how it was that the gopis could be away from their husbands every night without the men becoming angry at Krsna.

When the gopis left their homes, Yogamaya created duplicates of their bodies. Each gopa thought his wife had remained by his side. Therefore they had no reason to suspect Krsna.

It is also interesting to note that these replica gopis, due to being products of the spiritual energy, had no intimate contact with their husbands. When the gopis returned home the replicas disappeared.

By human calculation, the saradiya rasa-lila lasted only one night, but by the inconceivable power of Krsna’s pastime potency a thousand ages, or a night of Lord Brahma, had miraculously elapsed.

Brahma saw all of Vaikuntha in Vraja, and Yas'oda saw the universe in her son’s mouth. In the same way, the gopis felt a thousand ages pass in one night as they satisfied their desire to enjoy with Krsna.

**\* \* \* \***

The sounds of early morning awoke Krsna and the gopis from their rest. As they came out of their groves, they saw that the sun had indeed begun to paint the eastern horizon red.

As the presiding Deity of consciousness, Lord Krsna overcame the gopis’ reluctance to return home by infusing their hearts with fear of their husbands and older relatives.

To console the gopis, Krsna embraced them, offered them respect, and instilled hope in them with the words: “Just as we have met tonight, we will meet every night. You need not be morose.”

Krsna reinforced His words with meaningful glances as He added, “To ensure that we can continue to meet without obstruction, you must keep our love a secret. Agreed?” The gopis nodded.

Then, taking one another’s hands in the same way that they had done earlier that night, the gopis returned to their homes in Vrndavana by the same paths they had taken to meet Krsna.

Gradually the gills were separated from one another by forks in the paths that led to their individual villages until finally they returned to the confines of their houses, unseen by anyone.

At home the gopis performed their household duties, but within their minds they were absorbed in the singing, dancing, and music of the rasa dance and their own pastimes with Krsna.

To their family members it appeared as though they were happily engaged in household chores, but internally the gopis were still with Krsna. Yogamaya concealed any discrepancy in their conduct.

Radha and a few of Her friends had lingered for some time after all the other gopis had gone. Then they came to bid Krsna a final farewell, at which time they soaked His clothes with their tears.

After all the gopis had departed, Krsna — with a heavy heart but nonetheless satisfied that He had finally launched His love affair with the gopis — returned to His bedroom in Nandagrama.

The saradiya-rasa dance began at Vamsivata and ended in Nidhuvana, but it continues eternally in the hearts of those devotees who covet the treasure of the gopis’ pure service to Krsna.

Sukadeva concludes,

*vikriditam vraja-vadhubhir idam ca visnoh sraddhanvito nusrnuyad atha varnayed yah*  
*bhaktim param bhagavatipratilabhya kamam hrd-rogam asv apahinoty acirena dhirah*

**“One who faithfully hears or describes the Lord’s playful affairs with the gopis of Vraja will attain pure devotion to Krsna. Thus he will quickly become sober and conquer lust, the disease of the heart.”**

Cakravarti Thakura’s commentary on this verse proclaims that whoever hears and chants about Krsna’s rasa-lila, the crest jewel of all pastimes, will receive the crest jewel of all boons, love for Krsna.

For someone such as myself, unqualified as I am, to write about pastimes fit for swan-like devotees is surely audacious. Nonetheless, Sukadeva Gosvami and Cakravarti Thakura validate my attempt.

These great acaryas assert that even those whose hearts are tainted by lust may describe this autumnal rasa dance, or subsequent rasa- lilas, provided that they have full faith in the subject.

With such faith, absorption in Krsna’s loving pastimes with the gopis will generate prema within the heart. That prema will then drive away all lust, making one fully qualified.

It may seem logical to conclude that one must first become free of lust before one can receive the gift of divine love, but in his commentary Cakravarti Thakura declares that the process works in reverse.

By hearing, describing, or writing about the rasa dance, prema makes its appearance even in a sullied heart. Pure love drives material lust from the heart, which then shines with even greater brilliance.

This is the power of love for Krsna, which sober devotees may avail themselves of if they have strong faith in the extraordinary power of the rasa-lila and the autonomous power of prema.

Conversely, says the acarya, love for Krsna will elude devotees until they become sober and acquire such faith. May we all be blessed with faith in the potency of hearing about Krsna’s rasa-lila!

May that sublime rasa-lila, said to be the loving smile of the Lord’s confidential companions, who are praised for having conquered Krsna by their pure love, grace the lips of all faithful devotees.

I conclude the pastimes at Vamsivata by describing Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s visit there on His tour of Vrndavana. Hearing this pastime dispels all doubts regarding the Lord’s identity.

On the way to Vamsivata the brahmana Krsna Dasa first took Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu to a quiet grove of asoka trees north of Brahma-kunda where Radha and Krsna used to meet.

From there they went to Vamsivata, where Krsna Dasa described how, on the full-moon night of Karttika, Krsna called the gopis with His flute and, after leaving them for a time, enjoyed the rasa dance.

As Krsna Dasa narrated the details of the rasa dance he saw Caitanya Mahaprabhu take on a sapphire lustre, enter amongst a throng of exuberant gopis, and dance with them.

The gopis and Mahaprabhu were beautifully dressed, garlanded, and ornamented. The sound of their voices, their clapping, and their tinkling ornaments echoed throughout the forest.

Whichever aspect of the pastime Krsna Dasa described, He was able to directly perceive, including the night-time glow of blossoming flowers and the gentle caresses of aromatic autumnal breezes.

Enthralled by the wonders of the rasa dance — and by the gopis’ lover, who crushed the pride of Cupid — Krsna Dasa observed the pastimes of Vamsivata fully manifest there before Him.

And although the brahmana was enlightened with the vision of the rasa dance in which Lord Caitanya played the role of Krsna, after a while that revelation disappeared as quickly as it came.

So as not to inhibit Krsna Dasa from guiding the Lord on parikrama, Yogamaya covered his memory, allowing him to resume his role as a guide and show Lord Caitanya Krsna’s pastime places in Vrndavana.

**\* \* \* \***

Not far from Vamsivata lies the peaceful forest of Gahvaravana and a pastime place relatively new to Vrndavana: the residence of Jagannatha, Baladeva, and Subhadra called 'Jagannatha-ghata.

The pastime places of Vraja are almost exclusively connected with Lord Krsna and Lord Caitanya, but Jagannatha-ghata is a generally accepted pastime place that came into being somewhat recently.

How is a new pastime place established in Vraja? When activities of the Lord or of the Lord’s devotees are recognised by advanced Vaisnavas to be authentic and worth commemorating.

One obvious example: Srila Prabhupada’s rooms at Krsna-Balarama Mandira, the place of His Divine Grace’s departure. They are of historic significance to iskcon, to the dhama, and to the world.

Another example: the tamala tree in the central courtyard of the Krsna-Balarama temple, a tree Srila Prabhupada confirmed to he a nocturnal meeting place of Radha and Krsna.

Jagannatha-ghata is a similar pastime place of Purusottama-ksetra’s Lord, who decided that He wanted to reside in Vrndavana and consequently made His own arrangements to go there.

A devout Vaisnava named Haridasa used to live and worship at Vamsivata. One night Jagannatha appeared to Haridasa in a dream and told His devotee He would like to live in Vrndavana.

Lord Jagannatha informed Haridasa that since it was the time of nava-kalevaram, the changing of His body in Puri, Haridasa should go there and bring His old body to be worshipped in Vraja.

Haridasa followed the instruction of the Lord and set off for Puri. As soon as he arrived, Haridasa informed the temple priests of his dream and of Lord Jagannatha’s order, but the priests would not cooperate.

They rightly replied, “We cannot change our scriptural traditions every time the Lord appears in a dream.” But they added, “If you want to pursue the issue further you can approach the king.”

The king of Puri is the chief manager of the temple. He agreed with the pujaris. Just for the sake of a dream He was unwilling to interrupt Jagannatha’s well-established tradition of going into samadhi.

Haridasa was in a quandary. The Lord had given Him an order, but the servants of that same Lord would not accept the order he had received. Only Lord Jagannatha could resolve the dilemma.

Haridasa sat on the beach, fasted, and prayed for the Lord’s intercession. That night Lord Jagannatha appeared to the king in a dream and angrily rebuked him for denying the saint’s request.

“Why have you neglected My order? Call for Haridasa at once and make arrangements for Me to go to My home, Vrndavana.” The king awoke with a start and personally went to find Haridasa.

He found the saint on the beach, begged forgiveness for his offence, and told him of his own dream. The king then went to the temple priests and made all arrangements for the Lord’s travel to Vraja.

Thus, instead of being placed into samadhi in the sacred Jagannatha Garden behind the temple, Jagannatha, Baladeva, and Subhadra were placed on a royal chariot pulled by horses.

Accompanied hy soldiers, priests, and the paraphernalia with which they had been worshipped in Puri, the Deities were taken to Vrndavana and installed hy Yamuna’s shore at Jagannatha-ghata.

There they stay, surrounded hy a high wall with a large gate facing the parikrama path that is easily recognisable as one of the landmarks devotees see every time they circumambulate Vrndavana town.

Lord Jagannatha, feeling so much separation from Vrndavana, decided to return home to enjoy a lovely grove by the Yamuna, its charming rural atmosphere so much absent in Jagannatha Puri.

The Ratha-yatra festival in Puri is symbolic because after a short time Jagannatha returns to His opulent temple, hut the Ratha-yatra of Haridasa actually brought Jagannatha to Vraja permanently.

Every year after the Budapest Ratha-yatra Lord Jagannatha and His brother and sister come to New Vraja-dhama. They are first received at Jagannatha-ghata with kirtana, arati, and an offering of food.

Then the divine siblings come to Radha’s and Syamasundara’s temple, where They remain for the day, before again returning to Budapest. In this way Jagannatha visits New Vraja-dhama and enjoys bliss.

Not far from Jagannatha-ghata is Pani-ghata, which is related to Pani-grama on the opposite bank of the Yamuna and to the pastime that forms the basis of the second part of the Gopala-tapani Upanisad.

Later in this work I will describe that entire pastime and its theology in detail. For now, let us hear a brief summary, which begins with Krsna advising the gopis to please Durvasa Muni with their cooking.

Once, the gopis asked Krsna for the blessing that they would never he separated from Him, and He advised them to visit the asrama of the powerful Durvasa on the other side of the Yamuna.

But because it was the rain season, the gopis were in a quandary. How could they cross to the other side of a river swollen from heavy rains? Not even ferry boats would brave the turbulent waters.

Krsna told the girls to take shelter of His strict vow of brahmac-arya— if they appealed to the Yamuna on the strength of that vow, her waters would part and grant them passage to the other side.

This instruction flew in the face of the gopis’ personal experience. But as simple-hearted girls faithful to their beloved, they followed it. Led hy Sri Radha they came to Pani-ghata to cross the Yamuna.

The gopis respectfully touched the river and addressed the Yamuna, “Dear Devi! On the strength of Krsna’s vow of brahmacarya, please allow us to cross to your other shore without difficulty.”

No sooner had Radha pronounced these words than the Yamuna’s waters slowly parted to make way for the girls. They beheld a wide path lined with lotus petals leading to the opposite side of the river.

At first the gopis were reluctant to walk between the two towering walls of water. But they remembered Krsna’s words of assurance, held one another’s hands, and bravely took the passage offered to them.

Because the waters of the Yamuna parted here, this place is called Pani-ghata. Those who share the gopis’ faith can make the ocean of material existence part and show them the way to Krsna.

The next pastime place is Adibadri-ghata, where Krsna revealed Himself to the gopis as the divine brahmacari Badari-narayana. After such events, how could they doubt His vows of celibacy?

Srila Vyasadeva is said to have written the tenth canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam at this very place because it afforded him greater inspiration for Krsna's Vraja pastimes than the Himalayas.

In Bhauma Vrndavana a small pavilion marks Vyasa’s sitting place at the bend in the parikrama path leading back to Vrndavana town. In New Vraja-dhama it is at the southeastern corner of the Yamuna.

I have often sat at this place praying to the great poet-philosopher and compiler of transcendental knowledge for both the wisdom to understand his teachings and the inspiration to elaborate upon them.

No doubt, residing in this forest — in which badara trees still grow and which some call Adibadrivana — is a greater source of inspiration for expressing the sweet mellows of Vraja than are the Himalayas.

But I have often wondered how Vyasadeva actually wrote at Adibadri- ghata. Did he reside here? Did he mystically transport himself here just when writing? Or did he simply meditate on being here?

According to Srimad-Bhagavatam, an asrama called Samyaprasa on the western bank of the Sarasvati is the place where Vyasadeva wrote that most confidential Vedic text. It mentions no other place

We do know, however, that Srila Vyasadeva had the mystical ability to both transport himself anywhere at will and also to observe any place in all phases of time — past, present, and future.

Thus my personal conclusion, based on the available evidence, is that while residing in the Himalayas, Vyasa transported Himself to Adibadri-ghata, either physically or mentally, to write the Tenth Canto.

Let us offer our respectful obeisances to Srila Vyasadeva, who gave humanity the greatest gift: the recorded conversation between his divine son, Sukadeva Gosvami, and the emperor, Maharaja Pariksit.

**\* \* \* \***

Papadavana stretches from Adibadri-ghata to Bhatrola. At its centre is Raja-ghata, a landing from which boats once ferried people to the other side of the river when the Yamuna still flowed here.

Krsna was fond of disguising Himself as a boatman here, and Radharani and Her friends were fond of crossing the river with milk products destined for relatives living in Raval and Gokula.

Varying accounts describe how the boatman and His passengers agreed on a fare, what happened once they were afloat, and how Krsna’s disguise was finally exposed, to everyone’s delight.

In one version the gopis arrived at the boat dock and all but one boat was engaged. That boat looked old and rickety, but having no choice, the girls offered the boatman one anna to take them across.

“The price you are offering for My boat is an offence,” the boatman protested. After much bargaining, the gopis — only because they had no alternative — settled on six annas and were on their way.

Halfway across the Yamuna, however, the boatman stopped rowing and declared that He had not eaten and was thus too tired to go any further. Unless He ate something soon, they would float downstream.

Sri Radha was upset by the inconvenience, hut after some prodding by Her friends, She agreed to feed the boatman. The result: He quickly consumed their entire stock of yogurt and ghee.

As the gentle current of the Yamuna carried them downstream towards Mathura, the boatman lay down to take a nap on one of the scats, His feet dangling overboard into the water.

Having already paid an exorbitant price to cross the river, Sri Radha was furious at being further exploited. Just as Radha was about to have the boatman tossed overboard, one gopi exclaimed:

“What’s that sticking out of His belt?” The gopis’ eyes flew to the sash around the boatman’s waist and saw their arch-enemy, the flute. “It’s Him!” they called out in unison. “It’s Krsna!”

Having discovered the real identity of the boatman, Radha and the gopis enjoyed a love quarrel with Krsna, after which they considered themselves suitably compensated for the exorbitant fare.

Another version of the pastime has the boatman insisting that He must wash the feet of one of the gopis in addition to the high fare. When asked which gopis feet He prefers, He consults His boat.

The boatman says, “My boat tells Me that the gopi by the name of Radha should be honoured before She sets foot in it.” And although Radha is reluctant, the situation dictates that She do the needful.

After washing Srimati Radharani’s fect, Krsna sprinkles the water on Himself, His boat, and the Yamuna. Then He invites the gopis to come aboard with their pots of yogurt, milk, and ghee.

As in the first version, hungry Krsna requests the girls to share their milk products with Him, which they reluctantly do. When He is so full He can no longer row, He lays down in the boat.

In this version, however, Krsna reveals His identity to avoid a thrashing from the angry gopis. He then immerses Srimati Radharani and Her friends in the transcendental bliss of novel pastimes.

In both versions, the furious Radharani and Her companions threaten to report the lazy boatman to the king (raja) for appropriate punishment. The landing is therefore called Raj a-ghata.

A stately banyan tree stands at Raja-ghata. Caitanya Mahaprabhu would rest beneath this tree on His way to and from Akrura-ghata and Kesi-tirtha, as well as other places near Vrndavana town.

This spot is therefore reminiscent of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, more than many others in the Vrndavana area. Devotees often sit there during their parikrama of the town to meditate on His pastimes.

This spot is one of the few sections along the parikrama path of Vrndavana town that is still undeveloped, making it easier to picture the dhama as it was centuries ago when Lord Caitanya visited.

Who knows what thoughts passed through the transcendental mind of the Supreme Lord as He sat beneath this noble tree, from which Radha’s and Krsna’s boating pastime blossomed.

Let us offer our respectful obeisances to that golden-formed Lord, who has come to teach us absorption in His own pastimes as the prince of Vraja. May He make us all His worthy students.

The next pastime place is Brahma-hrada, also known as Akrura-tirtha, where Krsna revealed the wonders of the brahmajyoti, Vaikuntha, and Goloka Vrndavana to the cowherd men.

After he was released from the demigod Varuna’s underwater kingdom, Nanda Maharaja wondered at the extraordinary respect Varuna and his followers had shown to Krsna.

Nanda Maharaja briefly related the incident to the Vraja-vasis just after coming out of the water. But some time later he disclosed his thoughts again, this time in detail, just to friends and relatives.

The cowherd king said, “The great respect and submission the chief of the demigods showed to my little son has left me in doubt. Who is Krsna? I suspect that He may be the Supreme Lord.”

During a brief silence the cowherd men looked at Nanda Maharaja and then at one another. They knew that their king was spotless in character and as exalted as a demigod. His word was truth.

One gopa said, “O king! Previously you told us that Garga Muni predieted Krsna would be just like Narayana. Now you have concluded that Krsna is Narayana. This is truly wonderful.”

The cowherd men reflected on Nanda Maharaja’s words and said, “Krsna may be God, but He is also our kin, the son of our brother and our sister. He should satisfy the requests of His family.”

One cowherd said, “He should give us liberation.” Another said, “He should make us residents of Vaikuntha.” And yet another gopa said, “He should reveal to us His own transcendental abode.”

All of the gopas were eager to get Krsna’s help in their pursuit of spiritual perfection, and yet their awareness of His divinity did not weaken the intimacy of their spontaneous relationships with Him.

Krsna was well aware of His kinsmen’s desires. Always subordinate to their spontaneous love, He agreed to give all of them a vision of the brahmajyoti, the Vaikuntha planets, and Goloka Vrndavana.

The Vraja-vasis were already relishing the highest stage of perfection — krsna-prema; still, playing the roles of conditioned souls, they were curious whether they would be liberated at the end of life.

As the cowherd men talked, they repeatedly wondered aloud, api nah sva-gatim suksmam upadhasyad adhisvarah: “Will the Supreme Lord bestow upon us His transcendental abode?'’

Krsna wanted to reassure His kin that they were not only eligible to go back to Godhead but also that they were residing in a place equal to Goloka — far beyond the bliss of Brahman or even Vaikuntha.

Krsna thought, “The perfections of Brahman and Vaikuntha pale before the rich sweetness of the cowherd men’s love, but because they have never seen these lesser attainments they are curious about them.

“My powers may be unlimited, but I still feel deficient in the presence of My father. I cannot love Him like he loves Me. But if I reveal Gokula to him, he may realise his own greatness and good fortune.”

Considering all this, Krsna said, “So be it!” Just as He had invited the cowherd men to see Ganga-devi at Manasa-ganga, He invited them to see Vaikuntha at Akrura-ghata, also known as Brahma-hrada.

**\* \* \* \***

In the wee hours of the full-moon day of Karttika, Krsna led His father, the gopas, and the brahmanas from Nandagrama to Brahma-hrada. Gopas from other parts of Vraja met them there.

The Vraja-vasis who had all assembled there entered the waters of the Yamuna at Akrura-ghata along with Krsna. Then, as the older men chanted their diksa mantras, Krsna returned to shore.

The Vraja-vasis stayed in the waters of the lake called Brahma-hrada and perceived the all-pervasive brahmajyoti. Deprived of the taste of prema, however, they were unhappy with that vision.

In the state of Brahman the gopas could taste neither the bliss of Krsna’s company nor the sublime pain of being separated from Him. They could only lament the loss of their Krsna consciousness.

By His inconceivable power Krsna then freed the gopas from sayujya-mukti, a state that strikes horror in the hearts of practising devotees hut could only momentarily bewilder His eternal associates.

Krsna’s purpose in revealing impersonal liberation to the Vraja-vasis was to teach us that the difficult-to-attain destination of jnanis is hell for devotees who have tasted the nectar of pure devotional service.

Srila Prabhupada often quotes the verse beginning *kaivalyam narakayate* (“impersonal liberation is hellish”) to emphasise the difference between the taste of jnana and that of bhakti.

Krsna called the Vraja-vasis out of the waters of Brahma-hrada and the lifelessness of the brahmajyoti. He then displayed to them the grandeur of Vaikuntha with its countless spiritual planets.

For the gopas, seeing Vaikuntha after feeling sayujy-mukti was like waking up from a had dream, yet they still had their doubts. They asked, “Is it possible to hear, touch, or smell anything in Vaikuntha?”

Of course it is! But in Vaikuntha they could not perceive anything in relation to their beloved cowherd hero. There was no Krsna in Vaikuntha! In that sense it was no better than Brahman.

True, Vaikuntha is above the modes of material nature, opulent beyond conception, the residence of Lord Narayana, but for the gopas every minute spent there was a torturous millennium.

As the gopas were thinking in that way the residents of Vaikuntha offered them obeisances. The cowherd men felt embarrassed and confused that they were objects of respect for the Lord’s associates.

But the Vaikuntha-vasis said, “O residents of the forest! Do not protest! The Supreme Lord, whom the Vedas glorify, is your family member. He lives in your midst. How fortunate you are!”

The Vraja-vasis looked to sec the Supreme Lord — whom the Vaikuntha-vasis had just pointed to — but with His four arms, weapons, crown, and ornaments He hardly resembled their Krsna.

Having realised that the happiness of Vaikuntha did not include seeing the face of Krsna and relishing His abundant sweetness, the Vraja-vasis no longer had any desire to stay there.

Krsna saw the plight of His kinsmen and took pity on them. He removed their suffering and revived their happiness by withdrawing the vision of Vaikuntha and manifesting Goloka Vrndavana instead.

At the same place where Akrura would later see Vaikuntha, the cowherd men were given direct access to Goloka Vrndavana — Krsna’s abode of love — of which He is the presiding Deity.

Krsna could have revealed the brahmajyoti and Vaikuntha to the Vraja-vasis from anywhere in Vrndavana, but He chose to exalt the riverside ghata Brahma-hrada by displaying this pastime there.

Sukadeva Gosvami describes the scene,

*nandadayas tu tam drstva paramananda-nivrtah*  
*krsnam ca tatra cchandobhih stuyamanam suvismitah*

**“Nanda Maharaja and the other cowherd men —**

**“Felt the greatest bliss when they saw that transcendental abode. They were especially amazed to see Krsna Himself there, surrounded by the personified Vedas, who were offering Him prayers.”**

The cowherd men saw that Goloka Vrndavana was exactly the same as their Vrndavana on earth. After having spent time in the abyss of the brahmajyoti they rejoiced to again see their beloved Krsna.

As the cowherd men looked on, the personified Vedas glorified Krsna with sacred hymns, while gopas and gopis who resembled the cowherd men and their kin served Krsna in villages identical to their own.

The Vraja-vasis saw the striking similarity between their way of life and life in Goloka, which brought them to the natural conclusion that their way of life on earth was equal to the topmost perfection.

Jiva Gosvami also attests that the Vraja-vasis saw cowherd men and women in Goloka. And he explains why in Srimad-Bhagavatam Sukadeva Gosvami mentions only the personified Vedas:

When the Vraja-vasis saw the houses in Goloka, they recognised them to be their own. They thought, “If those houses, barns, gardens, and pastures are ours, then we must be residents of Goloka.

The Vraja-vasis realised that they were residents of Goloka Vrndavana who had appeared on earth in a place and under circumstances that were just like those In the spiritual world.

Despite that revelation, the Vraja-vasis were convinced by Yogamaya to see themselves as conditioned souls forced to wander this world as the result of their karma but who had met Krsna by good fortune.

Aside from the similarities between Vrndavana on earth and in Goloka, there were startling differences between Krsna’s conduct in the two places. In Goloka, Krsna displayed divine restraint.

The Vraja-vasis’ thought, “There is Krsna, but for some reason He does not embrace us, and somehow we feel reluctant to approach Him. He seems self-sufficient, not in need of anything at all.

“If Mother Yasoda cannot feed Him, then what will be the value of her life? And if we can not embrace Him, joke with Him, eat dinner with Him, or teach Him to herd cows, why should we bother to live?”

In short, just as the Vraja-vasis had little affection for Krsna’s Narayana form in Vaikuntha, they felt estranged by the reverential worship of the Vedas and the reserve Krsna showed as a result.

Even though the Vraja-vasls were astonished hy the wonderful visions of Vaikuntha and Goloka, they concluded that the best place to love and to be loved by Krsna is in earthly Vrndavana.

In this way Krsna was able to show the Vraja-vasis that they were already liberated; otherwise, how could they see themselves as superior to eternally liberated souls in Goloka Vrndavana?

Srila Rupa Gosvami summarises this exquisite pastime and confers upon us the blessings of sweetly-smiling Krsna at Brahma-hrada with the following prayer,

**“May you be protected by Mukunda —**

**“Who in order to teach the cowherd men that there is no place as sweet as earthly Vrndavana, effortlessly showed them Krsnaloka in the spiritual world and then brought them back to earthly Gokula.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Some time after Krsna brought the Vraja-vasis to Brahma-hrada and revealed that they were His eternal associates He gave a similar vision to Akrura, for whom this place is also named Akrura-ghata.

Prior to Akrura’s visit to this place it was known as Brahma-hrada, the lake (hrada) where the planet of the Absolute Truth (Brahma) was revealed. Today the place is known by both names.

The day Akrura arrived in Vraja was a dark one. Darker still was the next, the day he took Krsna and Balarama to Mathura on his chariot. That day the Vraja-vasls’ lives were forever changed for the worse.

As Akrura attempted to move the chariot forward the young gopis became aggressive, so much so that had Krsna not intervened they might have pulled Akrura to the ground and beaten him to death.

Anticipating that the Vraja-vasis would block the main road to Mathura, stop the chariot, and possibly kidnap Krsna and Balarama and bring Them back home, Akrura decided to take a detour.

Akrura successfully navigated around the villages of Vrndavana without obstruction, but the circuitous route tired the horses, so he decided to let them graze and drink by the Yamuna.

Akrura and the two boys arrived by a grove of trees, climbed down from the chariot, and quenched their thirst by drinking from the Yamuna. Akrura said, “Please feed and water the horses.

“I will take my midday bath and worship the most opulent Lord Ananta with mantras. You two boys stay safely on the chariot.” Krsna replied, “Return quickly, otherwise We will miss you too much.”

Krsna spoke kind words to His uncle and maintained composure in front of His brother, but secretly He lamented in separation from the Vraja-vasis, especially the gopis. Would He ever see them again?

Akrura was a devotee of the thousand-hooded Anantadeva, master of the universes and abode of auspicious attributes. He worshipped the Lord strictly according to scriptural injunctions.

Leaving the two smiling brothers in the chariot, Akrura entered the river. As he chanted his diksa mantras he saw Krsna and Balarama conversing together in the water, leaving Akrura astonished.

He thought, “The two sons of Vasudeva must have left the chariot and come into the water.” But when he went back to shore he saw the two boys sitting on the chariot just as he had left Them.

“What did I see in the river?” Akrura pondered. “Was it an illusion?” Returning to Brahma-hrada, He again entered the water and chanted his mantras. This time he saw the Lord of serpents, Ananta.

Many classes of celestials with bowed heads praised the Lord, whose snow-white body was garbed in blue robes and whose many swaying hoods were adorned with golden helmets sparkling with jewels.

Akrura could see that Lord Ananta was Lord Balarama. He thought, “My worshipable Deity, the Lord of Vaikuntha, has descended \[as Lord Balarama \| in the home of Vasudeva in Mathura.”

Surrounding Lord Ananta, Akrura saw the vast expanse and opulent realm of Vaikuntha. Upon Ananta’s coils lay Lord Narayana, comfortably basking in His own transcendental glory and beauty.

Just as Akrura saw Ananta as the partial expansion of Balarama, he saw Narayana as the partial expansion of Krsna. A host of attendants, demigods, devotees, and potencies praised the two Lords.

As Akrura beheld this wonderful sight his hair stood on end and tears flowed from his eyes. In that ecstatic state Akrura steadied himself and attentively offered prayers with a choked voice.

In response to Akrura’s devotion, which was tinged with the mood and purpose of his diksa mantra, Krsna showed His uncle Vaikuntha and the expansions He and Balarama assume in that realm.

Actually, the company of the Vraja-vasis had already enabled Akrura to see something even more astonishing: Vrndavana-dhama, along with Krsna and Balarama, the original forms of His worshipful Lords.

But since he no longer had the company of the Vraja-vasis — actually, since he had incurred their wrath — Akrura was no longer able to perceive Vrndavana or its cowherd prince.

But how can we say that Akrura could no longer see Krsna? It was Lord Narayana that he saw in the Yamuna, but didn’t Akrura see Krsna and Balarama still seated on the chariot?

If we carefully study the sequence of Akrura’s visions in the Yamuna we will indeed conclude that after getting down from the chariot Akrura no longer saw the Krsna of Vraja but the Krsna of Mathura.

Akrura’s first vision in the Yamuna was that of Krsna and Balarama. After returning to the chariot and seeing the brothers seated there, his second vision was that of Lords Narayana and Ananta.

After leaving Akrura-ghata, although the divine brothers looked the same, Akrura was really carrying Mathura’s Vasudeva and Sankarsana, the expansions of Vrndavana’s Krsna and Balarama.

This conclusion is in keeping with Rupa Gosvami’s statement in this famous verse,

*krsno ’nyo yadu sambhuto yah purnah so ’styatah parah*  
*vrndavanam parityajya sa kvacit naiva gacchati*

**“The Krsna known as Yadu-kumara is Vasudeva Krsna, who is different from Nanda Maharaja’s son. Yadu-kumara displays pastimes in Dvaraka and Mathura, hut Krsna never leaves Vrndavana.”**

It is interesting to note that the Harivamsa Purana and Garga-samhita both give versions of Akrura’s vision that differ dramatically from the version of Srimad-Bhagavatam already presented.

In Harivamsa Akrura first sees Krsna and Balarama seated on Anantadeva in the Yamuna. When Akrura returns to the Yamuna for the second time he sees Them just as the Bhagavatam describes.

In the Garga-samhita Akrura first sees Krsna and Balarama talking in the Yamuna, just as Srimad-Bhagavatam relates. But when he returns to the Yamuna what he sees is different from any other version.

Akrura sees Ananta lying on the river with Vrndavana forest resting on His coils — the Yamuna, Govardhana Hill, indeed all of Goloka Vrndavana is there being worshipped by all the worlds.

In that Vrndavana forest Akrura also sees Krsna — more glorious than a host of Cupids — standing with Radha at the centre of mulitple concentric circles of gopis blissfully enjoying the rasa dance.

Why do these two versions differ from that of Srimad-Bhagavatam? It is likely that the different versions describe the pastime as it took place during Krsna’s appearances in different days of Brahma.

Still, all three scriptures agree on this point: Vasudeva and Sankarsana go with Akrura to Mathura while the cowherd boys Krsna and Balarama invisibly stay in Vraja.

Akrura is famous for having perfected his Krsna consciousness through the process of prayer (vandana), such as the prayers he offered upon arriving in Vraja or seeing Vaikuntha in the Yamuna.

At Akrura-ghata he fixed his mind on the lotus feet of Lord Narayana and elaborately praised Him as the source of the material elements and their ultimate combination, the material creation.

Akrura then depicted the Supreme Personality of Godhead as the direct and indirect goal of all kinds of spiritualists, who ultimately reach Him just as flowing rivers ultimately reach the sea.

Akrura went on to recount the Lord’s different forms: the Supersoul, the universal form, and His prominent incarnations ending with Kalki. Finally, he prayed for protection from the illusory energy.

After highlighting his very lowly and deluded condition, Akrura begged, “Being thus fallen, I am approaching Your fect for shelter, O Lord, because although the impure can never attain Your feet —

“I think it is nevertheless possible by Your mercy. Only when one’s material life has ceased, ? lotus-navelled Lord, can one develop consciousness of You by serving Your pure devotees.”

Cakravarti Thakura explains the above verse through an enlightening parallel dialogue between Akrura and Krsna. Akrura began, “What I have said about myself is true, but I surrender to You.

“Although this surrender is impossible to attain as long as one is impure, by Your mercy it is surely possible.” Krsna enquired, “When will you get My mercy?” And Akrura replied, “O lotus-navelled one!

“When a person worships Your pure devotees, consciousness of You develops.” Krsna further enquired, “When will that happen?” “When a person is finished with His material life,” Akrura answered.

But Krsna continued to press his uncle, “And when is one’s material life finished?” Without hesitation, Akrura concluded by declaring, “When one receives Your causeless mercy, o Lord.”

In summary, when we become the object of a pure devotee’s causeless mercy our material existence gradually comes to an end. We can then cultivate Krsna conciousness by serving the pure devotees.

**\* \* \* \***

On His visit to Vrndavana, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu spent more time at Akrura-ghata than at any other place, seeming to favour, amongst other things, the purity and tranquility of the area.

The Lord first circumambulated Vrndavana, from Madhuvana to Gokula, and then took up residence in Mathura. But because so many people were coming to sec Him, He left the city in search of solitude.

Walking upstream along the river Yamuna, Caitanya Mahaprabhu and His companions came to Akrura-ghata, called Akrura-tirtha at the time, where they lived peacefully in a solitary place.

During the day Lord Caitanya would go to places like Kaliya-hrada, Praskandana, and Kesi-tirtha to bathe and chant Krsna’s names. In the evening He would return to Akrura-ghata to have His meal.

As mentioned, sometimes the Lord would go to Tentuli-tala, now known as Imli-tala, and chant japa beneath the old tamarind tree. At those times He would return to Akrura-ghata at noon for lunch.

But Akrura-ghata was a well-known pilrimage spot, and there was a village nearby. Soon masses of people came to see Lord Caitanya and they disturbed His peaceful chanting of the holy names.

One day a humorous event took place. People came to Akrura-tirtha with the news of a miracle: Krsna had again appeared in Vrndavana. At night He could be seen dancing upon the hoods of Kaliya.

The people excitedly said, “Everyone has seen Lord Krsna Himself. There is no doubt about it.” Hearing this, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu laughed and replied, “Everything is correct.”

And it was correct, but not in the way the people thought. Krsna had appeared in Vrndavana, but not at Kaliya-hrada dancing on Kaliya’s hoods. He was a sannyasi, chanting Hare Krsna at Akrura-tirtha.

This excitement went on for three successive nights. Even the Lord’s assistant Balabhadra Bhattacarya was convinced, until news arrived that there was no Krsna and no Kaliya in Kaliya-hrada.

Some respectable gentlemen revealed that a fisherman had lit a torch in his boat at night, and foolish people seeing this from a distance thought the fisherman’s moving light was Krsna dancing on Kaliya.

The myth of Kaliya-Krsna now dispelled, the villagers near Akrura- ghata made their suspicion known: Caitanya Mahaprabhu was actually Krsna who had returned to Vrndavana.

The Lord tried to hide His divinity, but the villagers said, “No one considers You an ordinary human being. You are like Krsna in every respect, in both bodily features and characteristics.

“By Your bodily features we can see that You are none other than the son of Nanda Maharaja, although the golden lustre of Your body has covered Your original complexion.”

These simple villagers pleased Caitanya Mahaprabhu. By His causeless mercy He made them ecstatic with love of God, engaging them and the pilgrims who visited Him in chanting Krsna’s names.

Sometimes Lord Caitanya would go to Mathura and have lunch at the home of one brahmana or another. Sometimes brahmanas would come to Akrura-ghata with their salagrama-silas and cook for Him there.

One day, as Caitanya Mahaprabhu sat at the bathing ghata, He thought, “At this bathing place Akrura saw Vaikuntha, the spiritual world, and all the inhabitants of Vraja saw Goloka Vrndavana.”

Remembering how Akrura had seen Krsna and Balarama in the water, Lord Caitanya jumped into the Yamuna and stayed beneath the river’s waves until His anxious associates pulled Him out.

This incident greatly alarmed Balabhadra Bhattacarya, who was concerned for Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s safety. He therefore convinced the Lord to leave Vrndavana and go to Prayaga for the Magha-mela.

Although Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu had no desire to leave Vrndavana He felt so indebted to Balabhadra Bhattacarya that He at once agreed, saying, “Wherever you take Me, I will go.”

The next morning Caitanya Mahaprabhu rose and took His last bath at Akrura-ghata. Knowing that He was about to leave Vrndavana, the Lord was highly emotional with ecstatic love.

From Akrura-ghata they took a boat across the river to Mahavana. With a heavy heart, His mind filled with ecstatic love, Caitanya Mahaprabhu walked until He passed the boundary of Vraja-mandala.

Let us take inspiration from Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s perfect example of living and worshipping in Vrndavana. Let us visit pastime places, chant Krsna’s names, and bathe in sacred waters.

Similarly, devotees eager to cultivate Krsna consciousness will take advantage of bathing in the holy places of New Vraja-dhama, especially those along the shores of the Yamuna, like Akrura-ghata.

The Varaha Purana contains an historical account that illustrates the direct and indirect benefits of bathing at Akrura-ghata. This narration is a worthy conclusion to our praise of this holy place.

There was once an affluent devotee of Krsna named Sudhana. He made his livelihood by trading in grains. He was always conscientious to maintain his family and he was exceedingly honest.

He worshipped his own Deity of Krsna strictly according to regulative principles. He would observe Ekadasi with a full fast, staying awake all night as he sang the Lord’s glories and danced in ecstasy.

Once Sudhana decided to observe EkadasI at Akrura-tirtha. There he stayed up the entire night chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra and remembering the Lord’s pastimes. Half the night passed in this way.

At midnight a horrible Brahma-raksasa with a huge black body and fierce fangs caught hold of Sudhana. “O merchant!” he growled, “Tonight I will satisfy my hunger by eating you.”

Sudhana was fearless. In that mood he answered the creature, “Please let me complete my vow of staying awake all night. After I do so I shall offer my chubby body to you for your satisfaction.”

The hungry demon, taken aback by this proposal, replied, “Foolish man! Do you expect me to believe that if I let you go you will voluntarily return to me? No man would do such a thing.”

But Sudhana was unfazed. He explained his devotion to truth and glorified He who is the origin of the world, the wealth of the brahmanas, and the protector of men, women, kings, and the world.

“If I did not return,” said Sudhana, “my offence would be equal to that of raping a woman, neglecting to feed a guest, performing sacrifice out of greed, killing a brahmana, or drinking liquor.

“I have never committed a sin in this life. Thus you can be assured that after glorifying the Lord throughout the night I will come to you. You may then do with me as you like. I tell you the truth.”

Highly impressed, the Brahma-raksasa released Sudhana, who then continued to glorify the Lord at Akrura-tirtha until dawn, at which time he bathed in the Yamuna, where he saw Lord Narayana’s form.

As soon as Sudhana came out of the water and prepared himself to meet the Brahma-raksasa, Lord Krsna appeared to him as an ordinary man and asked Sudhana what his plans were for the day.

When Sudhana explained that he had given his word to offer himself to a man-eater, the Lord in disguise tried to dissuade His devotee. But truthful Sudhana was determined to keep his promise.

Sudhana then met the Brahma-raksasa and said, “I have come. You can now eat me as we have agreed.” But the Raksasa, whose heart was softened by his victim’s attachment to dharma, said:

“Dear Sir! You are truthful and righteous. Therefore I will spare your life in exchange for the merit you accrued last night by dancing and singing for the pleasure of the Lord at Akrura-ghata.”

Sudhana was reluctant to part with his devotional piety. He asked the Raksasa to explain how he had attained such a body. The demon laughed and replied, “In my last life I was your neighbor Agnidatta.

“I was a Vedic brahmana, but I would steal bricks from others’ homes to build my own house. At death I was punished with this body. Please help me and share with me a measure of your devotion.”

Being a devotee, Sudhana was very merciful, and so he said, “I give you the benefit of one step of my dancing at Akrura-ghata.” At once the Raksasa shed his horrid form and attained liberation.

At that time Lord Narayana appeared before Sudhana and embraced him. The Lord said, “Stay no longer in this world. Along with your family, come to My own abode and serve Me there.”

The Varaha Purana goes on to say that not only Sudhana but also all bis family members mounted a glistening Vaikuntha airplane and in their selfsame bodies were transported to the Lord’s abode.

The power of Akrura-ghata, Sudbana’s devotion to truth and bis great faith in the power of observing Ekadasi, and the performance of nama-sankirtana at that holy place all made this miracle possible.

For those with less faith than Sudhana, a bath at Akrura-ghata can still liberate one’s ancestors or grant pious credit equal to the credit received by performing a horse sacrifice. All glories to Akrura-tirtha!

In Bhauma Vrndavana, Vaisnavas can have darsana of the deity of Akrura, with Krsna to his right and Balarama to his left. In New Vraja-dhama we meditate upon the two brothers and Their uncle.

**\* \* \* \***

The final place of pastimes along this stretch of the Yamuna is the village of Bhatrola, where Krsna once blessed the wives of brahmanas to show that He values devotion over ritualistic religious observance.

Dasa Gosvami praises the holy places Bhojana-sthali and Bhatrola:

**“The beautiful, wealthy, and learned wives of the sacrificial brahmanas voluntarily, happily, and devotedly fed Krsna, Balarama —**

**“And all Their affectionate friends many varieties of the four kinds of food, each dish surpassing the taste of nectar. We bow down to offer our respects to the place where Krsna enjoyed this pastime.”**

Bhatrola is the village of the sacrificial brahmanas, from where rice (bhakto.) and other edibles were delivered by the brahmanis to Bhojana-sthali, the place (sthali) where the gopas ate (bhojana).

One summer day — some months after Krsna had stolen the clothes of the unmarried gopis — Krsna, Balarama, the cowherd boys, and their cows were meandering down the riverbank towards Mathura.

Krsna knew that ritualistic brahmanas were performing sacrifices nearby, and that the wives of those brahmanas were pure devotees worthy of His mercy, so He directed the cows towards Bhatrola.

The boys followed the cows as they headed towards the river, and Krsna indirectly signalled His awareness of those brahmanas’ petty mindedness by glorifying the magnanimity of the trees.

It was the middle of summer, but by walking in the shelter of the trees, whose shade brought welcome relief from the intense heat, Lord Krsna felt inspired to speak to His friends:

“O Stokakrsna, Amsu, Sridama, Subala, and Arjuna! ? Vrsabha, Ojasvi, Devaprastha, and Varuthapa! Just see these fortunate trees, who tolerate the elements even as they give us shelter from them.”

The gopas listed here, from Stokakrsna to Ojasvi, surrounded Krsna and protected Him on all sides. Devaprastha held an umbrella over Krsna’s head, and Varuthapa swept the path in front of Him.

“Like great saintly souls, these trees live to benefit others. Whatever we beg from them — leaves, flowers, fruit, bark, or wood — they give without hesitation. Thus no one goes away from them disappointed.”

To emphasise that one should use one’s life to serve others, Krsna spoke this famous verse,

*etavaj janma-saphalyam dehinam iha dehisu*  
*pranair arthair dhiya vaca sreya-acaranarm sada*

**“It is the duty of every living being to perform welfare activities for the benefit of others with his life, wealth, intelligence, and words.”**

To give emphasis to His words, Krsna caught the eyes of His friends.

Krsna implies in this verse that there may be many humans and non-humans in this world who act as benefactors to others, but the trees of Vrndavana are special due to their elevated spiritual status.

To facilitate His meeting the brahmanas’ wives, Krsna directed His friends away from the fruit orchards, where they could have satisfied their hunger, to the river, where they and the cows could drink.

During the time Krsna spent in Vraja, rivers like the Yamuna as well as lakes and even ponds were full of clear, cool, auspicious water fit for cows and humans to drink. How things have changed!

While the cows drank to their hearts’ content, Krsna sat upon the exposed root of a tree. He looked radiant as He devised a plan to test the loving affection of the brahmanas’ wives.

On that day, the lunch Yasoda usually sent did not arrive. Judging from their own hunger, the boys knew that Krsna and Balarama must also be hungry, but they had left the fruit orchards far behind.

The boys approached the two brothers, who had detected the smell of musk in the air, and said, “The Vedas say that hunger is man’s worst enemy. Today, conquer that enemy by vanquishing our hunger.”

“Friends!” Krsna said with a smile, “I empathise with your plight. Go straight on this path towards Mathura. On the way you will come to a village of brahmanas, filled with many sacrificial arenas.

“Learned in the Vedas, these brahmanas are just now performing the Angirasa sacrifice to enter heaven. Explain to them that My brother and I have sent you, and in Our names ask them for food.”

Krsna knew that these brahmanas, though austere and religious, lacked devotion. They would surely ignore the boys’ request, and such arrogance made the brahmanas ineligible to receive Krsna’s mercy.

Their wives, however, though simple housewives, were devoted to Krsna, and He was eager to bestow His mercy upon them. Indeed, the Lord was going out of His way to do just that.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura tells us that some commentators say Krsna was intent on reciprocating with one brahmani in particular who was on the verge of attaining the tenth stage of love for Him.

Krsna and Balarama waited in a large riverside grove, and the boys set out on their mission, Krsna’s words of warning fresh in their minds: “Remember My friends! Beggars must always be tolerant.”

The softhearted gopas accepted Krsna’s order. They were tired but they joyfully made their way to the main sacrificial arena, where they enjoyed seeing the fire and smoke and smelling the burning ghee.

The singing of the Sama Veda resounding in their ears, thoughts of the delectable food they would offer to Krsna dancing in their minds, the cowherd boys’ mouths watered in anticipation.

The boys humbly approached the preoccupied brahmanas with joined palms and offered them prostrated obeisances just as they had been taught at home and had seen their parents do.

The brahmanas were falsely proud of their social status. They saw the boys as mere cowherds so they could not recognise them as Krsna’s representatives; in fact, the brahmanas didn’t even greet the boys.

Recalling Krsna’s warning, the cowherd boys, whose radiance eclipsed that of the ritualistic priests, said, “O earthly gods! We are friends of Krsna and Balarama and request you to kindly hear us.

“Today we have come a great distance from Nanda’s house, herding our cows and play-fighting with one another. We have not brought any food from home. Now, like Balarama and Krsna, we are hungry.

One boy said, “We come here as your guests. Since you are compassionate, charitable, and just like our fathers, we request that you give us some food to take to Balarama and Krsna.”

Krsna had told the boys to mention Balarama first, because the caste-conscious brahmanas would be more likely to give to His elder brother, a ksatriya, than to Him, a vaisya. The brahmanas replied:

“Krsna and Balarama are not brahmanas. We cannot offer Them food until after the brahmanas have eaten.” The boys then spoke the ultimate essence of truth, “But Krsna and Balarama are hungry.”

Blinded by ritualistic injunctions, the brahmanas saw Krsna and Balarama as ordinary boys. They could not understand that by giving food to the gopas they would fulfil every detail of their sacrifice.

The Supreme Lord—the ingredient, the fire, the mantra, the offering, and the goal of all sacrifice—had personally approached them; still, unable to recognise Him, they had refused His order.

The boys insisted, "Please tell us whether you will give us food or not.” But the brahmanas ignored Krsna’s emissaries and foolishly continued to pour ghee into the fire to appease the Supreme.

“These boys are asking for food at an improper time,” the brahmanas whispered to one another. “The best way to get rid of them and make sure they don’t return is to ignore them. That is what we will do.”

But the boys were not so easily dismissed. They were on a mission for Krsna and Balarama and were determined not to leave empty- handed. They said, “There is nothing wrong with giving us food now.

“Scriptural injunctions set this time as an auspicious moment to give food. So please do so.” But the brahmanas— indignant that children would tell them what to do —ignored the cowherd boys’ request.

The brahmanas consulted amongst themselves, “This is how Kali-yuga enters. These greedy boys are asking us for unoffered food. And they want it for boys who some say are gods, but gods are never hungry.”

Having said this, the brahmanas neither directly refused the boys’ request nor gave them food, even though as householders it was their religious duty to give charity, especially to hungry children.

As Sukadeva narrated this pastime, Maharaja Pariksit became more and more angry to hear of the brahmanas' irreligious behaviour. Seeing the king’s reaction, the sage said, “O subduer of enemies!

“O righteous king. Had you been present \[when the brahmanas ignored the gopas' request\], even though they were the best of brahmanas, you would have punished them like enemies.”

The reasons these learned brahmanas ignored the boys’ request included hard-heartedness from performing animal sacrifices, a lack of piety, and, above all, the absence of Krsna’s mercy.

Finally the cowherd boys concluded that they had failed to carry out their mission. Disappointment written on their faces, feet dragging, they returned to where Krsna and Balarama were waiting.

**\* \* \* \***

The boys were reluctant to report their failure directly to Krsna, so they addressed Balarama: “O Rama! Just imagine what happened to us. Although we requested food in Your names, we were ignored.

“We have never met such insensitive, low-class brahmanas. They completely ignored us. But, even worse, they didn’t give us food even though, right in front of us, they were cooking for their sacrifice.”

Turning to Krsna, their heads hung low in shame, the gopas said, “Dear friend! We failed to bring hack anything for You. And all we could consume was our pride and the smoke from the sacrificial fire.”

Intending to teach all those who are forced to beg—by instructing His own dear friends—Krsna shrugged off the cowherd boys’ dejection with a laugh and said, sweetly smiling:

“Beloved friends! Why should you show anger towards ignorant brahmanas or find fault with them? No doubt they were too busy to listen to your pleas. The nature of begging is that one is often refused.

“Still, you should never become despondent. Instead, let us develop an alternate strategy for achieving our purpose.” The gopas stirred uneasily. Did Krsna want them to return to the brahmanas?

“Your plan is beyond us,” one of the boys complained. Krsna replied, “Go to the brahmanas’ wives instead and ask them for food.” The boys let out a collective groan. Some even held their heads in disbelief.

“We will get the same treatment from them as we did from their husbands,” they protested. Krsna raised both His palms to calm the boys and assured them, “The brahmanas’ wives are different.”

But the boys were not so easily convinced: “In what way are they different? They are married to misers. Why should they be anything but misers themselves?” Krsna patiently explained:

“Because, like you, they also love Me.” Taken aback by this answer, the boys enquired, “How is that?” Krsna said, “Just imagine! These women did not drink for two days, nor eat for three, just to see Me.”

Eyebrows raised, the gopas looked at one another: “Is that true?” “Absolutely!” Krsna reassured them. The boys clapped their hands: “Wonderful! Then they must be different from their husbands.”

A spark of hope now twinkled in the gopas’ eyes: “Then we will go and ask them for food—” Krsna interrupted with a warning: “Tell the brahmanas’ wives that Balarama and I are here.

“But don’t tell them that We are hungry because that news will put them into too much distress.” The boys shrugged their shoulders, “Why would they give us food unless we tell them You are hungry?”

“When the ladies see that you are hungry,” Krsna replied, “they will also give you food for Us.” Still smarting from the brahmanas’ rebukes, the boys asked, “But won’t their husbands stop them?”

Krsna had confidence in the brahmanas’ devotion to Him. “No! These women’s minds always live in Me. Only their bodies live in their homes. Surely they will disregard their husbands’ objections.”

With fresh determination to fulfil Krsna’s desire, the gopas left Krsna’s garden of creepers. All competing with one another to get there first, the boys went directly to where the brahmanas were.

Seated on golden chairs, decorated with ornaments, the wives of the brahmanas, due to their intense feelings of separation from Krsna, radiated complete detachment from sense gratification.

As soon as the boys saw the ladies they thought, “They arc surely devoted to our Krsna.” And at first sight of the boys the ladies thought, “Who else could these gopas be but Krsna’s friends?”

We may wonder how the brahmanas’ wives had developed such attachment for Krsna. A combination of factors was responsible: Bards had passed through their village praising the Lord—

They had occasionally heard the sweet notes of His flute, and while buying flowers from gardeners of Vrndavana, they had heard descriptions of His form, qualities, and heroic deeds.

By hearing of Krsna, then, the brahmanas’ wives developed love for Him. But because their husbands had thwarted their every attempt to see Him, their purified hearts had been crushed again and again.

The brahmanas noticed the boys’ flutes, sticks, and peacock feather crowns and concluded that Krsna Himself had arrived. They at once rose from their seats and offered their blessings to the boys.

After bowing before the ladies, the boys said, “O gentle wives of learned brahmanas! We are close friends of Krsna and we offer our obeisances at your lotus feet. Please hear our appeal.”

Simply hearing the name Krsna caused ecstatic bliss to erupt in the brahmanis: some fainted, others were bewildered, and yet others wandered around saying, “What mystical mantra is this?”

The cowherd boys tried to calm the women and command their attention, but when all else had failed, they cried out, “Krsna is hungry and you should give food to Him and His friends.”

As the words “Krsna is hungry” entered the women’s ears they snapped to attention. Their bliss barely contained, they surrounded the cowherd boys to hear more. The boys made the following appeal:

“O wives of the brahmanas! Today we had no breakfast. We are extremely hungry from playing all day. Krsna, the reigning Cupid of Vrndavana, the object of your worship, has sent us to beg for food.

“He is waiting nearby with His elder brother Balarama, who is as powerful as Indra. Surely you must have heard about Krsna from the lips of devotees. As a baby He mercifully made Putana His nurse.

“As a child He smashed Trnavarta to earth, killed the giant Agha, and banished Kaliya from the Yamuna. Need we say more of He whose glories are like an ocean of all sublime things in creation?”

The brahmanas’ wives felt as if Krsna had suddenly appeared before them. The thought that they might soon meet Him face to face melted their hearts and captured their minds.

Ecstatic symptoms like tears, goose humps, and shivering decorated their bodies. They were unable to respond, but the women still went to their kitchens and gathered a variety of freshly cooked food.

The boys had not indicated any type of food in particular, and so the brahmanis brought everything they had in their kitchens. Stacking pots on their heads, they followed the gopas out of their homes.

The boys and the brahmanis marched past crowds of people who were milling about the sacrificial arena. As they made their way into the forest, the ladies exchanged excited glances and restrained smiles.

Every so often the women would eagerly ask, “How much further?” The playful gopas ran ahead to show the way to Krsna, encouraging the brahmanis and guiding them with gentle voices.

The weight of their love, combined with the weight of the food they carried, made the women move too slowly for their anxious minds. They would occasionally run forward only to slow down again.

The intensity of the ladies’ love nudged them to the threshold of madness. They scanned the forest for signs of Krsna, taking the drooping vines, for example, to he offering obeisances to Him.

Krsna responded to the brahmanis’ ecstatic zeal. He greeted them first with His unmistakable bodily fragrance, then with His blackish effulgence, and after that with His deep, sonorous voice.

Finally Krsna was there before the women in person. They paused for a moment to convince themselves that it was actually Krsna they were seeing and not a mirage created by their eager minds.

The brahmanis saw Krsna strolling along the riverbank through a forest of asoka trees. His left arm rested on Subala’s shoulders as He calmly chatted with other friends in the company of Lord Balarama.

To the women of Bhatrola, Lord Krsna looked just as they had conceived Him to be. His complexion was cloud-blue, His garments bright gold, and His bearing that of a dramatic actor.

He wore a colourful turban decorated with peacock feathers, flower blossoms, and buds. A water lily was tucked over His ear, and a flower garland swayed as He walked, grazing His feet with His every step.

Curly locks framed His forehead and hung over His cheeks, which were painted, just like His chest, with colourful designs made of minerals. His lotus face smiled as He looked directly at the ladies.

In His right hand Krsna twirled a lotus that broadcast two messages: “Ladies! I have taken your lotus hearts and I am twirling them about,” and, “By your love you have made My heart twirl in happiness.”

The brahmanas had heard about and meditated upon Krsna for a long time; indeed, He had become the ornament of their ears (karna-pura). They were always absorbed in hearing about Him.

Their amorous feelings had become so strong that they could not hear their husbands’ protests when they left to meet Krsna, just as the gopis had ignored their husbands when called by the flute.

Now, as they observed Krsna from a distance just as He observed them, the brahmanis thought, “Today, at long last, the object of our meditation has appeared before our eyes. Our lives are successful.”

**\* \* \* \***

Still holding pots of food on their heads or in their arms, the women of Bhatrola welcomed Sri Krsna into their hearts and revealed their individual feelings of paramour love for Him.

Having waited so long to meet Krsna, the brahmanis acted boldly, making Krsna lay down upon the flower bed of their hearts, where they held Him in their loving embrace for a long time.

By Krsna’s magical presence within them they were relieved of the pain they had felt in the long years of separation. The bliss of reunion could be seen in the ecstasy that shone upon their beautiful faces.

Upon opening their doe-like eyes, the ladies also saw that Krsna was standing before them. They were enchanted that He was simultaneously in two places: in their hearts and in the Asoka forest.

The ladies moved closer to Krsna, eager to he near Him. They were still holding the pots and plates of food, and so Krsna began to laugh and put them at ease by greeting them with kind words.

Krsna said, “Welcome, o fortunate ladies! Please set your pots on the ground and sit down. I can sec that you have great love for Me because, unlike your husbands, you have brought food for Me.”

Krsna’s voice resembled the rumbling of clouds, which soothed their minds. His words resembled drops of nectar raining from the sky. They thought, “Just hearing Him is the pinnacle of perfection.”

The brahmanis sat around Krsna just as the gopis would do in the future. Krsna also spoke to them with words similar to those He would use in his autumn-evening discourse with the gopis. He said:

“Your coming here befits your love. I know that you have overcome many obstacles, which has left Me in your debt. The only thing I can ask is that you rest here for a while and spend time with Me.”

As He spoke in this way, Krsna was aware that the brahmanas’ wives desired to serve Him in amorous ways. But Krsna decided that satisfying them would not nourish their mellow of devotion.

Without nourishing rasa, incompatible feelings would mix and render their pastimes less than satisfying. Thus, to inspire them to return to their villages, Krsna addressed the women in a formal tone.

The Lord said, “It is natural you are attached to Me in the manner of great souls: I reside within every heart as the Supersoul, dearer to the individual soul than the body, the husband, sons, daughters, or family.

“As the indwelling guide of everyone, I always hold you close to Me from within; rather than remaining here, therefore, you should return to your husbands and help them complete their sacrifice.”

Despite Krsna’s speaking very softly and sweetly, the brahmanis took His words to be like poison arrows. How could He send them away just a few moments after welcoming them and asking them to sit?

Tears flowed from the women’s eyes as they replied: “How can we give You up, the Supersoul standing before our very eyes?” “By obedience to My order,” Krsna said, “which is to help your husbands.”

But the women of Bhatrola were not so easily dismissed after having been called by Krsna; in fact, they responded with the exact same words the gopis would later use to deny Krsna’s instructions.

The wives said, *maivam vibho ’rhati bhavan gaditum nr-samsam*: “O almighty one, please do not speak such cruel words.” And what of Krsna’s promises to reciprocate His devotees’ surrender?

Citing Krsna’s own statements—ye yatha man prapadyante and mam eva ye prapadyante—the brahmanis insisted that Krsna allow them to remain in the forest as His maidservants.

Krsna replied, “How can members of the brahminical aristocracy like yourselves surrender to a mere cowherd like Me?” The women shook their heads as if trying to shake Krsna’s words from their ears.

Lord Krsna’s rejection made the Rahu planet of the brahmanis' pain devour the full moon of their joy. With cheerless faces they abandoned all shyness and appealed to Him in choked voices:

“We have already surrendered our lives and souls to You by leaving behind our families and homes. Isn’t it clear to You by now that we no longer identify with the brdhmana community?”

But Krsna persisted, “I am a cowherd boy. Only cowherd girls are suited to be My maidservants or lovers.” Realising that Krsna was fixed in His determination, the ladies exclaimed, “So be it!

“If You would be embarrassed to have brahmana women as maid servants, then we will just stay in Vrndavana forest, satisfied by insignificant contact with You from a distance.

“We know that the stature of being Your girlfriend or maidservant is rare and difficult to attain, so we will be satisfied to collect the tulasi leaves fallen from Your feet and bind them in our hair. That’s all!”

Almost swayed by their humility, Krsna asked, “But what about your family members?” The women laughed, “Our husbands and relatives have already rejected us. They will never take us back.

“They have been suspicious of us ever since our youth, when You first stole our hearts. It was at that time we heard stories of Your form and sweetness from the garland makers and betel nut sellers of Vraja.”

Ready to reject their families, desperate for Krsna’s shelter, the wives touched their heads to Krsna’s feet—which they washed with their tears — and begged Him to remove all obstacles to their love.

Torn between the brahmanis’ devotion and the best course of action for the occasion, Lord Krsna finally concluded, “Pure love for Me means to be dedicated to My happiness and to nothing else.

“Don’t be stubborn. Please return home.’’ The brahmanis lowered their heads and made one last attempt to capture Krsna: “Until today we had never been outside our homes, or even exposed to the sun.

“Having entered deep into the forest to be with You—the infamous rake of Vrndavana’s forests—our family ciders and husbands won’t even allow us to return to the village, to say nothing of our homes.”

But Krsna was adamant, “How could they reject you when we have had no intimate contact? Besides, the demigods whom your husbands worship through sacrifice are My devoted servants.

“Those demigods will advise your husbands that I am the faultless Supreme Lord and that your attachment to Me cannot be impious; rather it is the sign of the topmost devotion. Don’t he afraid.”

Finally accepting Krsna’s order, the wives enquired, “But will our desire for an amorous relationship ever be fulfilled?” Lord Krsna reiterated His earlier argument: “I have already explained—

“People would criticise our intimacy, and that would hinder the fulfilment of your love for Me. But if you long for Me in separation, with your minds absorbed in Me, You will attain Me very soon.”

Lord Krsna then gave them the same instruction he would later give to the gopis,

*sravanad darsanad dhyanan mayi bhavo 'nukirtanat*  
*na tathd sanmharsena pratiydta tato grhan*

**“It is by hearing about Me, seeing My Deity form, meditating upon Me, and chanting My names and glories that love for Me develops, not by physical proximity. Therefore please go back to your homes.”**

The brahmanis sensed Krsna’s resolve and understood that it was no longer appropriate for them to be close to Him. They took the food they had brought and placed it on leaves and plates.
