Then, one last time, they filled their eyes with Krsna’s astonishing blackish form. Accepting the blessings He offered them from the corners of His eyes, the wives respectfully hut sorrowfully departed.

Krsna would also instruct the gopis to return to their husbands, but unlike the brahmanis, they would refuse and enjoy with Him in the rasa dance. But the brahmanis would attain Krsna just the same.

The difference between Krsna’s reciprocation with the two groups of women was due only to social convention. The brahmanis would simply have to wait until their next birth to he with Krsna physically.

But the growth of their love for Him would nor at all be obstructed by time. One lesson we can learn from this pastime is that we can attain perfection solely by serving the Lord in separation.

This conclusion is consistent with Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s teachings: by confidently serving Krsna in the mood of separation, surely we will attain His company at a time of His choosing.

Sukadeva Gosvami speaks of one exception amongst the wives: There was one lady whose especially bad-tempered husband locked her in the house to keep her from going with the others to see Krsna.

Disregarding her crazy husband, the brahmani absorbed herself in loving thoughts of Krsna, who then appeared before Her and said, “Give up everything and come live with Me in Vrndavana.”

By the power of Krsna’s mercy (krpa'-Sakti), that brahmani gave up her material body and was awarded a spiritual form. Unlike her friends, she was immediately able to enjoy Krsna’s company.

But we should not think that Krsna neglected to bestow special mercy upon the other women of Bhatrola. Indeed, Cakravarti Thakura confirms that after leaving the Lord they too were blessed.

They did not have to leave their bodies. Their material bodies were transformed into spiritual forms suitable for amorous love with Krsna. They had no more physical contact with their husbands.

In His inimitable way Krsna awarded the brahmanas’ wives perfections beyond their expectations. Meanwhile, their mantra'chanting husbands offered oblations for paltry, temporary gains.

**\* \* \* \***

As the wives of the brdhmanas arrived at Bhatrola, they were greeted by a miracle. Not only their pots but also their houses had been transformed: they were now made of precious gems set in gold.

Their husbands were prepared to banish them with harsh words, but when the brdhmanas saw that their village was now a veritable jewel-mine, they restrained themselves and reconsidered:

“We have heard that infant Krsna once filled a fruit vendor’s basket with jewels, and now we see that in exchange for food delivered by our wives we have been blessed with unfathomable opulence.”

Realising that this must be the work of the Supreme Lord, who had appeared in Vraja as a gopa, the brdhmanas greeted their wives with kind words and humbly acknowledged the ladies’ spiritual superiority.

The men had already come to regret their conduct, which caused the inauspicious death of one brahmani. And now the transformation of their homes confirmed that their wives were rightly situated.

In the presence of their pure-devotee wives, the brahmanas felt remorse. At last they condemned themselves for their blind ritualism and lack of devotion to the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

Each man saw the futility of his physical birth, brahminical initiation, and initiation into the performance of sacrifices: “To hell with our threefold birth, our vow of celibacy, and our extensive learning!

“To hell with our aristocratic background and our expertise in the rituals of sacrifice! These are all condemned because we were inimical to the transcendental Personality of Godhead.”

The brahmanas witnessed first-hand how their wives, who were ignorant of Vedic rituals, came to understand the goal of the Vedas — to develop love for Krsna — just by hearing about Him from devotees.

The brahmanas had never seen ecstatic love like that of their wives, by which homes, families, and social convention were all discarded for Krsna’s pleasure as easily as one tosses away pieces of straw.

But what touched the brahmanas most was the passing away of one of the women. They could only compare her departure to that of a yogi who attains perfection after lifetimes of severe austerities.

They said, “In order to see her beloved Lord, this lady surmounted all obstacles to attain a position rarely attained by the greatest yogis. Who can understand the nature of love for Krsna?”

Finally remorse awakened in the brahmanas’ hard hearts. They lamented their misconduct — indeed their offences — to their wives, to the gopas, and to the Supreme Lords, Krsna and Balarama.

Beholding the effulgence of their wives and sensing their own comparative worthlessness, the brahmanas cast aside their pride and sat upon the ground, thunderstruck. How had all this happened?

Their wives had become liberated souls, more exalted than their scriptures and acaryas. Reflecting upon this cheered the brahmanas and made them see the need to make amends for their offences.

With remorse, the brahmanas looked down the path their wives had trod — towards Krsna— and prayed, “Let us offer our obeisances unto Lord Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

“His intelligence is never bewildered, whereas we, with minds confused by His power of illusion (yan-maya-mohita-dhiyo), are simply wandering about on the paths of fruitive work.

“We were bewildered by Lord Krsna’s illusory potency and thus could not understand His influence as the original Personality of Godhead. Now we hope He will kindly forgive our offence.”

Krsna forgave the brahmanas but remained indifferent to them. Because, after all was said and done, they retained their material consciousness and identified themselves with their bodies.

One would expect that after committing such blunders they would have rushed into the forest and at least apologised to the cowherd boys and to Krsna, even if they could not fully surrender to the Lord.

But they couldn’t even apologise. Why? They were afraid that if Kamsa came to know that they had somehow favoured Krsna, that tyrannical king would punish them. Such is material conditioning.

The brahmanas’ wives had no concern for King Kamsa’s punishment, but the brahmanas, influenced by a fear bom of bodily identification, refused to go see Lord Krsna and beg His forgiveness.

In truth, the brahmanas' misfortune was that their wives did not feel compassion for them and try to inspire them with devotion. Thus they were unable to get any spiritual benefit from Krsna’s presence.

In stark contrast, the wives of Kaliya were merciful to their husband. As a result he was able to derive benefit from contact with Krsna. In short, without the blessings of the devotees, one cannot see the Lord.

Bhaktivinoda Thakura elaborately comments upon this pastime, stressing that if one follows Vedic injunctions without faith in and knowledge of their purpose, he or she is sure to be misled.

Attachment to rituals and fruitive activities leads to materialism. Speculative attempts at self-realisation lead to impersonalism. And self-centred meditation leads to bewilderment by mystic powers.

All three pursuits generate pride from a selfish approach to the Vedas, which is an obstacle to accepting the Vedas’ goal, even when that goal personally comes knocking on one’s door as did Krsna.

Proud of their caste, their learning, and their families, the brahmanas of Bhatrola considered that performing sacrifices was the highest pursuit; therefore, they did not give Krsna any food.

By contrast, the brahmanas’ wives had faith in and attachment to Krsna, and although they were not learned they recognised the call of the Supreme, answered that call, and thus attained perfection.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda draws the following conclusion from this pastime,

*etena darsitarh. tattvam jivdndm sarnadarsanam*  
*srnkrsna- pritbsampattau jatPbuddhir na kdranam*

**“By this incident the equality of all living entities is ascertained. There is no consideration of caste in pleasing Krsna, rather caste consciousness is an obstacle in the development of love.”**

As a postscript, the Thakura explains that the brdhmanas' attempts to suppress their wives show what happens when those with undeveloped faith try to lord it over those who are more advanced.

While the brdhmanas continued to offer prayers into the ether, Krsna and His friends busied themselves by relishing the feast brought by the brahmanis, which was flavoured by the ladies’ love for Krsna.

Krsna made His friends sit in rows. He then served them with His own hands, beginning with those boys who had gone to beg at Bhatrola. Krsna asked each one whether the food was to his liking.

Krsna Himself then sat in the midst of His friends and took great pleasure in the feast, for He always enjoys eating foods that have been cooked with love, skillfully prepared, and artistically presented.

As usual Madhumangala became intoxicated from eating. Speaking over the din of the feast, he said, “Dear friends! Please listen to me so that you may more fully appreciate what you are eating.

“Food cooked in exchange for payment is third-class. Superior to that is food one eats at home. But food obtained by begging from affectionate well-wishers is superior to either; it is first-class.

“O Krsna! This food surpasses even first-class food. Therefore my suggestion is that you call these brahmanis back and lock them up in a hut in the forest where they can cook for us on demand.”

Krsna and Balarama laughed at Madhu’s outrageous proposal. And the other boys laughed along with them, feasting their eyes on the two brothers as they rocked back and forth with laughter.

May the vision of Krsna and Balarama smiling as They enhance the cowherd boys’ enjoyment of the feast brought by the wives of the brdhmanas remove your sorrows and protect you always.

Devotees who visit Bhauma Vrndavana can see the beautiful smiling face of the Deity of Krsna, Bhatrola-bihari, who is worshipped in a citadel-like temple at as yet remote Bhojana-sthali.

## Chapter 28 - Kuruksetra, Sukratal, and Naimisaranya

From Bhatrola I walked a little distance north along the road, surveying the familiar landscape of New Vraja-dhama, with its rolling hills, tranquil waterway, scattered woods, and peacefully grazing cows.

How many times had I walked this way, marvelling at the unique spiritual atmosphere of the dhama and revelling in the sights, sounds, and aromas that always remind me of eternal Vraja?

The sound of my own footsteps punctuated the stillness of a sunny afternoon as I recalled the words I have several times used to convince sincere souls to dedicate their lives to New Vraja-dhama.

These words were originally inspired by a passage in scripture that glorifies Mathura-mandala. It touched my soul the moment I read it, and, in my own words, I have repeated it countless times.

“O friend! For so long you have been tossed about in the ocean of birth and death, constantly bitten by aquatics in the form of threefold miseries. Isn’t it time to exchange suffering for true bliss? Listen!

“Live in New Vraja-dhama! Live in New Vraja-dhama, where Krsna, the creator of everything, has appeared as Syama. With Sri Radha at His side, He has manifested around Him the wonders of Vrndavana.

“O friend! Radha’s and Syama’s abode, also called New Vraja-dhama, is a seaworthy boat personally captained by the divine couple. In this boat we can safely cross to the far shore of this material ocean.

“Do not let Maya trick you! Know for a fact that calamity always follows prosperity, that the goddess of fortune is fickle, and that our bodies are destined to die. Take shelter of Krsna’s divine abode.

“If after having attained this human body — which is meant not for sense gratification but for liberation — we do not see Radha and Syamasundara in Their land, then we have truly wasted our lives.

“We may have eyes, but if we don’t see the promise offered by New Vraja-dhama, if we continue to suffer the reactions of our own fruitive activities, then we might as well he blind.

“Give up all illusion, misfortune, and foolishness. Serve the two transcendental youths who have appeared with Their eternal home to offer us a life of harmony through service to Their lotus feet.”

As I recalled these glories of the dhama, I came abreast of a large field — gently sloping towards the Yamuna — that marks Kuruksetra, with Raval and Durvasa Muni’s asrama clearly visible across the river.

Beside Kuruksetra is a forest with two places that commemorate the recitation of Srimad-Bhagavatam: Sukratal, where Sukadeva Gosvami spoke to King Pariksit, and Naimisa, where Suta addressed the sages.

Before crossing the Yamuna and visiting the five forests on Balarama’s side of the dhama, I offered my respects to these holy places and reflected on but a portion of their unlimited glories.

Amongst all holy places outside the precincts of Vraja, these three are special because of the roles they play in the Gaudiya Vaisnava tradition; thus they have been assigned places in New Vraja-dhama.

Actually, scripture reveals that not just these three but all holy places in the universe have their original forms in Vrndavana. Lord Varaha says, “Sixty billion sacred places reside in My Mathura.”

And the Skanda Purana proclaims, “O King! In the course of time it may be possible to count the grains of dust on the earth, but it will not be possible to count the number of holy places in Mathura.”

Stopping at the juncture of Kuruksetra and Sukratal, I offered my respects to these three places and briefly recalled their glories as a kind of sequel to the Vrndavana pastime places I had already visited.

The field of Kuruksetra comprises land five yojanas in radius between the Sarasvati and Drsadvati rivers, bound in the north by the Punjab, the south by Khandava, the west by the desert, and the east by Parin.

Kuruksetra was the main holy place (tirtha-sthana) in Satya-yuga, just as Puskara was in Treta-yuga, Naimisaranya in Dvapara-yuga, and Navadvipa in Kali-yuga, the age in which we now live.

Tradition has it that Lord Brahma created the earth in all its diverse features as he sat in the centre of Brahma-sarovara, a lake in Kuruksetra that has its subtle origin on Brahma’s abode in Svarga.

The Taittiriya-aranyaka Upanisad contains the earliest reference to Kuruksetra, which is also called Brahmavarta, Samanta-pancaka, Brahmaksetra, Bhrguksetra, and Aryavarta.

It was also at this place, known then as Bhrguksetra or Bhrguksetra, that Bali Maharaja willingly gave the entire universe to V?m?n?-deva when the Lord begged the king to give Him three steps of land.

Parasurama killed twenty-one generations of ksatriyas and collected their blood here in five lakes called Samanta-pancaka. This is also the place where he performed penance to atone for killing so many kings.

This tract of land became known as Kuruksetra after King Kuru, forefather of the Pandavas and Kauravas, settled there on the bank of the Sarasvati River in order to practise austerities.

Maharaja Kuru is said to have tilled the area of Kuruksetra with a golden plough, an act which yielded eight religious virtues: truth, yoga, kindness, purity, charity, forgiveness, austerity, and celibacy.

The Lord so much appreciated the king’s labour and the purpose behind it that He gave the king two blessings: that land would always be known after him, and anyone who died there would be liberated.

During King Kuril’s reign in Dvapara-yuga, Kuruksetra’s sanctity and prosperity made it popular with all classes of men, and it flourished as one of the most desirable places in all of Jambudvipa.

Pulastya Muni described some of the glories of Kuruksetra when he said,

**“O King! Go to Kuruksetra, which fulfils all desires. By seeing that place, all living entities are liberated from their sins.**

**“Whoever merely says, ‘I will go to Kuruksetra!’ is freed of his sins. If the dust of Kuruksetra raised by the wind touches a great sinner, freed from his sins, he attains the highest abode.”**

In Dvapara-yuga, Kuruksetra was not only spiritually potent but also beautiful, as it featured groves, lotus-filled lakes, and fertile pastures. People would say, “One who lives in Kuruksetra lives in heaven.”

During Krsna’s time two important events occurred at Kuruksetra: the dynastic pilgrimage on the occasion of a solar eclipse and the great eighteen day war between the Pandavas and the Kurus.

While Krsna and Balarama were residing in Dvaraka, brahmanas told Them that a total eclipse of the sun was imminent, so the Yadus joined other pious families at Kuruksetra to purify themselves.

Along with the prominent royal families of the land, the Vraja-vasis came to Kuruksetra. But in truth their only purpose was to meet Krsna and convince Him to come back home to Vrndavana.

After fulfilling religious duties such as fasting, bathing in Brahma- sarovara, and distributing charity to the brahmanas, the pilgrims spent a number of days happily exchanging affection with one other.

Krsna was the cynosure of the pilgrimage and the loving exchanges the pilgrims enjoyed there. This was especially true for the Vraja-vasis, but even more so for the gopis and Srimati Radharani.

Mother Yasoda and Nanda Maharaja, overjoyed at seeing their darling son Krsna again, treated Him just as any parents would treat their child — like a little boy, paying no attention to His actual age.

After Krsna had pacified His parents, relatives, and Vraja-vasis friends, He sought out the gopis in a secluded place and reassured them of His unfailing love for them and His intent to return to them.

At first the gopis were sulky at having been abandoned by their lover so long ago, but their happiness to be reunited with Krsna could not be ignored. Although they were happy to see Him, they wanted more.

They wanted Krsna to return with them to Vrndavana, where they all hoped to enjoy one another’s fully blossomed beauty, qualities, and love, something that was simply not possible in Kuruksetra.

The milkmaids of Vraja induced Srimati Radharani to act as their spokeswoman. If anyone could convince Krsna, it would be Her. Speaking to Lalita in earshot of Krsna, Sri Radha said:

**“My dear friend! Now I have met My very old and dear friend Krsna on this field of Kuruksetra. I am the same Radharani, and now We arc meeting together. It is very pleasant —**

**“But still I would like to go to the bank of the Yamuna beneath the trees of the forest there. I wish to hear the vibration of His sweet flute playing the fifth note within that forest of Vrndavana.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Krsna was aware of the gopis’ desire; in fact, He shared their desire. Wasn’t it He who had encouraged the Vraja-vasis to come to Kuruksetra so that He would have an excuse to return with them?

When Nanda and Yasoda heard that Krsna would be going to Kuruksetra, they also wanted to go but were unable to determine how to protect their homes, cows, and other belongings in their absence.

As the Vraja-vasis were deliberating on this topic, a letter arrived from Krsna: “Father! I have not yet killed all My enemies, and so I haven’t been able to return to you and My other loved ones in Vraja.

“This is causing Me too much pain. But the upcoming meeting at sacred Kuruksetra for the solar eclipse presents an opportunity. Everyone is going, and thus we could easily meet there.”

Krsna’s invitation brought joy to the all the Vraja-vasis, except for the young cowherd men, whom the Lord told to stay back and look after the cows with the assurance that He would come to them soon.

Krsna had also sent a secret letter to thego/Ts in which He told them that although they were seeing Him daily in His sphurti feature, they could meet Him at Kuruksetra in person. What could be better?

And since the gopas— which included the gopis’ husbands — would stay behind to guard their homes, there would be little hindrance to Krsna’s meeting with the gopis given a suitable time and place.

The Vraja-vasis wasted no time. The very next morning they were on the road, heading north to Kuruksetra. And even though they would usually have been singing about Krsna, at that time they were unable.

The Vraja-vasis’ anticipation at meeting Krsna was so intense that their teeth clattered and their voices choked. Their words came out garbled and their minds were confused. How could they possibly sing?

Indeed, as a result of constantly serving Krsna in their minds, the Vraja-vasis were so absorbed that they forgot to eat or sleep. By the time they arrived at Kuruksetra, they were all emaciated.

As the Vraja-vasis’ approached Kuruksetra, even from a distance they could smell the aroma of Krsna’s transcendental body. Knowing that they would soon arrive, Krsna saw Himself more and more as a gopa.

To ensure that His enemies did not see Him interacting with His kinsmen, Krsna had Uddhava keep the Vraja-vasis some distance away in a secluded place where He could meet with them privately.

After meeting the Vraja-vasis—the gopis last of all — the hidden purpose for their visit became clear. Krsna then had to answer to His mother and father, and ultimately Srimati Radharani.

Addressing Radha, Krsna said, “O Beloved. Your desire is My desire. But there are still a few demons to he killed. After having done so, I will certainly return to You on the bank of the Yamuna.”

Krsna’s intention was pure; still, He failed to divulge the challenge He faced in fulfilling His promise: to leave Dvaraka He would have to get the blessings of Vasudeva and Devaki. That would be difficult.

In the weeks that followed, Krsna spent His days holding court and meeting with kings and sages, but in the afternoons He and Balarama would bask in the spontaneous love of the Vraja-vasis.

The brothers played amongst the Vraja-vasis’ canopy-covered carts like young children, much to the surprise of anyone who saw Them. Their parents felt great satisfaction, thinking of Them as children.

After nightfall, when everyone else was asleep, Krsna would meet with the gopis in a distant forest, dance with them, and then please each of them according to their individual desires.

After three months had gone by, many pilgrims had returned to their homes, but the Vraja-vasis continued to serve Krsna. And Krsna also pleased the Vraja-vasis by taking them to nearby holy places.

He also arranged for cows to be brought to the Vraja-vasis’ encampment because His kinsmen could not be happy if they neglected their dharma. Nor could they live without milk.

The brahmanas' camps resounded with mantras and the crackling of sacrificial fires, the kings’ camps featured the sounds of their armies, but the Vraja-vasis’ camp was filled with the lowing of cows.

Finally Vasudeva, inspired by Yogamaya, said to Krsna, “Nanda’s heart and my heart are one. I know that he wants You to return to Vraja; therefore, You may do what satisfies him.”

Krsna was happy to hear this but still asked for time to make a decision. He at once went to consult Balarama, Uddhava, and Rohini, who best understood His feelings and the sensitivity of the situation.

Their talks were cut short, however, when Vasudeva and Devaki went to see Nanda Maharaja. After an exchange of sweet words, Vasudeva said, “O brother! We arc like one soul in two bodies.

“You love Krsna more than I do; thus, you have a greater right to Him. Your happiness will be so profound when He returns to Vraja that my own sadness at His separation will transform into joy.

“Our conclusion is that Krsna and Balarama should now spend time with you. In this way all of Vrndavana will be illuminated by bliss. Nonetheless, it is true that your son still has a few enemies.

“For His own protection, and that of His subjects, He should first rid the world of these rascals. Then He will feel secure in coming to live with you. And in this way your and my happiness will be permanent.”

Nanda and Yasoda, speechless at Vasudeva’s selflessness, could only think, “What a great soul he is!” They were so absorbed in discussing this fact between themselves that they forgot Vasudeva was there.

Taking advantage of His parents’ ecstasy, Krsna slipped away to deliver the incomparably good news to the cowherd girls of Vraja — He had been granted permission to return to Vrndavana.

After so many years of waiting, it was now only a matter of days before they could be together just as they had been in the days of their youth. The gopis left at once to prepare for His visit.

Like a blanket of morning mist is gradually dissipated in the rising sun’s rays, the Vraja-vasis and Yadus, full of love for Krsna, dispersed from Kuruksetra and headed for their respective capitals.

After all the affectionate farewell embraces, Maharaja Nanda, by now well on his way, realised that despite Vasudeva’s comforting words, he was still going back to Vrndavana without Krsna.

The gopis also awoke from their reverie. Even if Krsna were coming to Vrndavana tomorrow, every moment until then would seem as long as an age. Once again the gopis felt that Krsna was lost forever.

Riding in their carts along the bank of the Yamuna, the gopis recalled Krsna’s farewell words the night before. It was a night they had wanted never to end, but time, their enemy, made sure that it did.

Krsna had said, “The reason I cannot return with you is that a few of My enemies still live. I must eliminate them. You have waited this long. Please wait a few more days for good fortune to shine on us.”

“O Krsna!” Sri Radha replied. “Do we have a choice? We must do as You say. But we will bear witness to the truth of Your words only if we live long enough.” In tears, Krsna embraced Radha and the gopis.

Srimati Radharani sat in Her own cart like a statue, staring into the clouds of dust behind Her, knowing that Krsna was travelling in the opposite direction — to Dvaraka. Tears rolled down Her cheeks.

Lalita-devi placed a comforting arm around Her friend’s shoulders and said,

**“O Radharani! O beautiful friend! Do not lament! It is well known that sacred Kuruksetra fulfils all desires.**

**“The great King Kuril tilled this land and made it fertile with His piety. Now Krsna has planted the seed of His promise there, a seed that will sprout and bear fruit by the time we arrive in Vraja.**

**“Rest assured that He for whom we came to Kuruksetra, giving up our home and lands, will soon be tapping on Your window, begging You to join Him in a grove by the shore of the river Yamuna.”**

**\* \* \* \***

The Vraja-vasis’ great hope for Krsna’s return, and the pain of being separated from Him once again, are two transcendental moods that permeate Kuruksetra and outshine all other influences there.

The influence of this mood upon Krsna and Balarama is so spiritually significant that it has long been the central theme of the annual Ratha-yatra festival celebrated in Puri, and by ISKCON worldwide.

As we engage in pure nama-sanikirtana, we try to enter this mood of meeting and separation by contemplating the transformations it caused in Krsna, Balarama, and Their sister Subhadra.

Krsna’s Kuruksetra pilgrimage must have occurred before Maharaja Yudhisthira’s Rajasuya sacrifice because at that time the dealings between the Kurus and Pandavas were still warm and friendly.

It was at the Rajasuya-yajna that Duryodhana’s enmity towards the Pandavas was irrevocably fixed. The gambling match followed soon after. At that time Draupadi was insulted and the Pandavas exiled.

At the completion of the thirteen-year exile, after negotiations between the two camps had broken down, the Kurus and Pandavas again met at Kuruksetra — not for pilgrimage but for war.

The most significant event of the war was Krsna’s sermon to Arjuna, a discourse given at Jyotisar beneath a banyan tree whose descendent thrives today by the essence (sura) of truth (jyoti), the Bhagavad-gita.

I have a fond memory of my visit to Jyotisar in India. I sat by a statue of Krsna and Arjuna and recited all eighteen chapters of the Bhagavad-gita as I meditated on the scene just before the battle.

On New Vraja-dhama’s Kuruksetra plain I hope to one day erect a grand chariot with Krsna standing upon it, instructing Arjuna in the science of surrendering to Him in pure devotion.

I purchased my first copy of the Bhagavad-gita in the McGill University bookshop. Fortunately for me, I chose Srila Prabhupada’s Bhagavad-gita As It Is from the various other editions on the shelf.

When I first started to read the Bhagavad-gita seriously, I was in a rebellious mood. I thought, “Why should I read someone’s commentary? Let me understand Krsna’s words for myself.”

Needless to say, I couldn’t make head or tail of the text. But when I took a humble approach and read Srila Prabhupada’s purports, the true message of the Bhagavad-gita came shining through.

True revelation came at the moment I understood that Krsna was God. I believed that God existed, but it never occurred to me that He was a person, not to mention a person named Krsna. Now I knew.

Since the days I camped out on Big Pine Key and first read the Gita, I have re-read, studied, memorised, and taught the Bhagavad-gita with an appetite and a fondness that continue to increase to this day.

Srlla Prabhupada’s purports act as a powerful lens through which to see Krsna’s teachings as He gave them, in a literary framework that transmits eternal truths to modern man — purity through simplicity.

Myriad are the praises I can shower upon the Bhagavad-gita, our shelter in times of need, a textbook for preachers, Krsna’s solutions for the ills of mankind, the essence of the Absolute Truth.

I cannot count how many times I have quoted from Krsna’s advice to Arjuna. But I can definitively say not a day goes by that I do not recall and take solace from Krsna’s reassuring words:

**“Always think of Me, become My devotee, worship Me, and offer your homage unto Me. Thus you will come to Me without fail. I promise you this because you are My very dear friend.”**

Two phrases here provide boundless inspiration for me: “...you will come to Me without fail” (*mam evaisyasi satyarii te*) and “I promise you this because you are My very dear friend” (*pratijane pnyo ’si me*).

From the core of my heart I know these reassuring words to be unfailingly true, for they accompany an instruction the Lord makes a point of twice repeating, word for word, in the Bhagavad-gita.

I have cited but one of seven hundred verses of the Bhagavad-gita, the glories of which have been endlessly sung both by those who truly understand and by those who cannot fathom its contents.

Sahkaracarya, for example, obscured the actual meaning of the Gita’s verses by writing a commentary with which Vaisnavas are at odds. But he also praised the Gita in prayers that Vaisnavas appreciate.

The most poignant verse of Sankara’s “Glories of the Gita” is its conclusion,

*ekarri sastram devakoputra-gitam eko devo devaki-putra eva*  
*eko mantras tasya namani yani karmapy ekam tasya devasya seva*

**“In this age when people are very eager to have one scripture, one God, one mantra, and one occupation, let that scripture be the Bhagavad-gita and the one God for the world Sri Krsna —**

**“Let the mantra after which everyone is seeking be the Hare Krsna maha-mantra and the common religious occupation of all souls the service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna.”**

After Krsna had completed His teachings to Arjuna, the war began. There are several locations connected to the events of that exciting eighteen-day battle that still exist today. Let us hear about a few.

One such place is Bhisma-kunda, also called Bana-ganga, where the great grandsire fell on the tenth day of battle. To quench Bhisma’s thirst, Arjuna shot an arrow into the earth and invoked the Ganges.

At a second Bana-ganga, Arjuna again pierced the earth, this time creating a lake from Ganges water for his horses as he battled the Kauravas in his effort to kill Jayadratha before sunset.

Another place connected with this pastime is a secluded wood in Samanta-pancaka. The father of the Kuru warrior Jayadratha was performing penance there as the war raged some distance away.

Arjuna decapitated Jayadratha with an arrow that carried Jayadratha’s head onto the lap of his meditating father, who reflexively threw his son’s disembodied head to the ground in disgust.

Unknown to his father, Jayadratha had received a boon from Lord Siva that the head of whomever made Jayadratha’s head touch the ground would at once shatter into one hundred pieces — and it did.

Karnavadha is a trough where Kama’s chariot wheel got stuck in the ground. That great Kuru hero was then killed (vadha) by one of Arjuna’s infallible arrows as he was trying to free his chariot.

At Cakravyuha, Drona arranged his army in the disc (cakra) formation (vyfiha). Abhimanyu broke the formation but once inside, besieged by many of the Kuru generals, he lost his life.

A wooded area called Sthanesvara was the encampment (sthana) of Krsna (isvara), where He and Arjuna set up their tents. The two friends would eat and rest here in the evenings after fighting stopped.

As already mentioned, Brahma-sarovara has existed since Lord Brahma created the universe, but King Kuru excavated and beautified the area for the comfort of pilgrims.

From here Krsna observed the solar eclipse along with the other pilgrims. It continues to be the choice of the pious for such observances. A bath here is equal to one thousand horse sacrifices.

Nearby is another, smaller kunda, Sannihita-sarovara. There pilgrims offer oblations for departed souls. More significantly, this was the secluded area where Krsna met with the Vraja-vasis.

There are many other pastime places throughout Kuruksetra and the nearby area, too many to mention here. We offer respect to them all by bowing down to Jyotisar, the essence of all such places.

May we all be blessed with exclusive surrender to the Supreme Lord, Sri Krsna, of which He speaks at the end of the Gita. Such surrender qualifies us to hear and apply the teachings of Srimad-Bhagavatam.

**\* \* \* \***

I conclude this praise of Kuruksetra and the Bhagavad-gita with an example that illustrates exclusive surrender to and dependence upon Krsna. My hero, Arjuna, exemplifies surrender of this sort.

Srila Prabhupada tells this story: When it was clear that war was inevitable, both the Pandavas and Kurus solicited the kings of the world to join their side in what we would now call a “world war.”

Krsna had returned to Dvaraka by that time, and due to His being a great warrior as well as the general of His own army, the Narayani Sena, both the Pandavas and the Kurus were eager for His support.

Krsna was related to the combatants on both sides, so both generals had reason to believe that Krsna would accept their request. Arjuna and Duryodhana thus set off for Dvaraka with this in mind.

Duryodhana reasoned that it he arrived first, Krsna would fulfil his desire, and Arjuna would then have to return to Indraprastha empty-handed. As fate would have it, Duryodhana did reach Dvaraka first.

When Duryodhana arrived, he was told that Krsna was sleeping. Eager to achieve his goal, Duryodhana stood by the head of Krsna’s bed so that he could make his request as soon as the Lord awoke.

Just then Arjuna arrived and, out of natural humility, stood by the toot of Krsna’s bed. In time, the Lord opened His eyes, looking first at Arjuna at His feet and then Duryodhana near His head.

Both heroes made their request, and Krsna replied, “Since you arc both dear to Me, I must satisfy you both. The only way I can do that is to offer My army to one of you. To the other I offer Myself.

“But you should know that because we are all family, the one who chooses Me will have Me only as an advisor, not a warrior. I cannot raise a weapon against My own kin — be he Pandava or Kaurava.”

Duryodhana began to speak, but Krsna cut him off: “Brother! I saw Arjuna first. He should make his request now.” Duryodhana objected, saying that he had arrived first, but Krsna insisted.

Turning to Arjuna, Krsna asked, “Friend! I can stand by your side unarmed on the battlefield, or you can have My army, the most powerful army in the land. Which do you prefer?”

Arjuna’s answer was spontaneous and immediate. What did he have to consider? “O friend!” He said. “If all the warriors in the universe were on one side and You were on the other, I would choose You.”

Duryodhana could hardly believe his ears. He thought, “Arjuna may be a great bowman, but he has made a strategic blunder that will cost him the war and the throne. Soon I will be crowned emperor.”

Hearing Arjuna’s reply, Krsna had to restrain His tears as He told Duryodhana, “King! My army is at your disposal. Every last one of My soldiers will meet you at the time and place of your choice.”

Overjoyed, Duryodhana could scarcely contain himself. He thanked Krsna profusely and left the palace at once, eager to return to Hastinapura and share the news with his brothers and Kama.

Once Duryodhana had left the room, Krsna beckoned Arjuna to sit beside Him on the bed. Taking Arjuna’s hand, the Lord said, “Kaunteya! Blinded by affection you have made a strategic error.

“Yudhisthira will certainly not be happy to hear what his forces have lost and what the Kauravas have gained.” Arjuna smiled as he placed his hand on Krsna’s. Looking into his friend’s eyes, he said:

“Krsna, after so many years, must You still test me and my brothers? My king may sometimes reprimand me, but when I return to our camp with You at my side, he will do nothing but praise my decision.

“O Lord! Whether we win or lose is up to You. Any victory without You is worthless. But a defeat with You by my side — though impossible— would be worth more than control of the universe.

“We will fight to put Yudhisthira on the throne of Hastinapura because it is Your desire. But the Pandavas would never fight a war in which You are our opponent, or a war of which You disapprove.”

Krsna relished teasing His friend. His eyes twinkling with mirth, Krsna replied, “Arjuna! Didn’t you hear? I will not raise a weapon. If I wanted, I could annihilate the entire Kaurava army with My cakra.

“But they are related to Me, and so I will fight against neither them nor their soldiers.” Arjuna nodded, “I heard You! Of course. But You need not fight. With You beside me, I can defeat their army myself.”

Arjuna paused for a moment. With a voice quivering with emotion, he asked, “Don’t You know that night and day I only think of You, that every particle of my existence wants only to he with You?

“Friend! Don’t You know? Whether awake or asleep or eating or fighting with the enemy, I think only of You. My life is for You. Every moment I am away from You I stay alive only in hope of seeing You!

“Don’t You know — ” Krsna placed His hand over Arjuna’s mouth. Krsna’s voice choked up with affection for His friend, and so He whispered, “I know!” For a moment Krsna could not talk.

Then He added, “I do know! And so I belong to you! Whatever you ask of Me is yours.” Krsna then stopped speaking, sensing that something was on Arjuna’s mind but that he was hesitating to speak.

Krsna said, “Friend! Tell Me what is on your mind. Don’t keep thoughts from Me.” Arjuna began slowly, “What is in my mind should not be spoken. But because I cannot control my heart, I will say it.

“The upcoming war will be my ultimate service to You! I will be but an instrument in re-establishing dharma. During this great sacrifice, in which many will perish in the fire of war, I will be the main priest.

“That is Your will. My thought—” Arjuna again hesitated, until Krsna reassured Him with a smile. “My thought is that during this sacrifice I may lose sight of You, the yajna-purusa.”

Finally revealing his desire, Arjuna leaned forward and said, “O Krsna! You are the Supreme Personality of Godhead, but I request that You personally act as My charioteer throughout this great war.

“Your unmatched skill in steering horses in the thick of battle is well known. If You drive my chariot, Yudhisthira’s victory will be assured. In addition, I will have the great fortune to see You constantly.

“Will You?” As Arjuna asked these words, Krsna recalled the times He had carried His father’s shoes on His head, braided His mother’s black hair, and massaged Balarama’s feet as His older brother rested.

He remembered how He had strung garlands for Sri Radha and painted red lac on Her feet. He counted every opportunity He had ever had to serve His devotees amongst His most cherished memories.

The hairs on Krsna’s body stood on end as He embraced His dear friend Arjuna and said, “Yes! Yes! Of course, My friend! Please let Me drive your chariot. Serving you will be the perfection of My life.”

Arjuna eagerly returned Krsna’s embrace, and the two friends wept tears of joy while in each other’s arms. Later, relaxing together, Krsna and Arjuna laughed as they made plans for the upcoming battle.

As the two armies finally assembled on the battlefield, news spread that Krsna was driving Arjuna’s chariot. Reactions amongst the ranks were mixed. The role of chariot driver was reserved for sudras.

Ignorant persons were confused, irreligious persons critical. But devotees like Bhisma wiped away tears of ecstasy as they searched the phalanxes of soldiers to catch a glimpse of Arjuna’s charioteer.

Whatever their opinion, during the next eighteen days the soldiers referred to Krsna as Partha-sarathi. To this day, sincere devotees remember and glorify Krsna’s eagerness to serve His servant Arjuna.

To remind us of Krsna’s affection for His devotee, Srila Prabhupada installed Deities of Radha-Partha-sarathi in iskcon’s New Delhi temple, which has since become the most famous temple in the city.

Dear readers! Just worship the dust of Sri Arjuna’s lotus feet, our hero and inspiration and the very emblem of surrender. May he bless us to be fully dependent on the divine orders of our Srila Prabhupada.

May the infinitely kind Lord who yoked and watered Arjuna’s horses, and, always carefully protecting His devotee, drove Arjuna’s chariot throughout the day, be kind upon us, for we are His aspiring servants.

May the chariot driver of Arjuna — who took up a chariot wheel to kill Bhismadeva and in the process of protecting His friend even dropped His garments without a care — sprinkle His mercy upon us.

The combatants chose to do battle at holy Kuruksetra because by dying there the fallen achieved liberation. But the fallen soldiers who saw Krsna were more fortunate, they achieved their original forms.

We have hardly tasted a drop in the ocean of Kuruksetra’s glories. Let us offer our respectful obeisances to Jyotisar, to the speaker and the hearer of Bhagavad-gita, and to the great commentators on the Gita.

With straw between our teeth, let us offer respectful obeisances to the crown jewel of commentators, whose Bhagavad-gita As It is has made Krsna’s teachings and Arjuna’s surrender known all over the world.

Although there have been hundreds of editions and commentaries on the Bhagavad-gita, only Srila Prabhupada’s has inspired wave after wave of conditioned souls to surrender to Krsna in pure devotion.

I offer my respects to those Vaisnavas who have accepted Bhagavad-gita As It Is as their road map to Vrndavana and who have dedicated themselves to helping others use that map on their spiritual journeys.

**\* \* \* \***

Next to Kuruksetra, in the northern part of the adjoining forest is Sukratal, where Sukadeva sat beneath a banyan tree in the midst of eighty thousand sages and spoke the —Bhagavatam to King Pariksit.

Although Srimad-Bhagavatam says that Sukratal is by the bank of the Ganges, Srila Prabhupada supports Jiva Gosvami’s assertion that the great sage actually spoke to Pariksit on the hank of the Yamuna.

In New Vraja-dhama, Sukratal is situated on the hank of the Yamuna, an ideal place to read or recite Srimad-Bhagavatam, or to recall how Vyasadeva’s son delivered his transcendental narration to Pariksit.

The specific place where Sukadeva Gosvami sat and spoke to Maharaja Pariksit is called Suka-tirtha. The events that lead up to that exchange are well documented in the Srimad-Bhagavatam itself.

When the Pandavas decided to retire from their kingdom, Yudhisthira Maharaja handed over the post of world emperor to the highly qualified grandson of Arjuna, Maharaja Pariksit.

Pariksit Maharaja was hunting in the forest when he came upon the hermitage of the sage Samika. The sage, absorbed in spiritual trance, was unaware of the external world, including the king’s arrival.

Tired and thirsty, the king requested the sage for water, but Samika Rsi appeared to neglect the monarch’s simple appeal, so Pariksit Maharaja took offence at this, considering it an affront to the throne.

Driven by divine fate, the king impulsively draped a dead snake around the sage’s neck, like a garland. After committing this offence, which he would later regret, the king returned to his palace.

News that the king had humiliated the Rsi quickly reached the Rsi’s young son, Srngi, who had been nearby playing with friends. In anger, the child cursed Pariksit Maharaja with the following words:

**“On the seventh day from today a snake-bird will bite the most wretched one of that dynasty \[Maharaja Pariksit\] because of his having broken the laws of etiquette by insulting my father.”**

After pronouncing the curse, the boy at once realised that he had meted out undue punishment for a slight offence. Regretting his misdeed, Srngi ran to his father to tearfully tell him of his foolishness.

The sound of his young son crying brought Samika Rsi back to external consciousness. The sage, who could immediately understand the situation, lamented that Srngi had shamed the brahmana caste.

Brahmanas are famous for showing both tolerance and forgiveness. But Srngi had shown the absence of such good qualities, a defect that signalled the impending downfall of brahminical culture.

Meanwhile, Pariksit Maharaja was regretting that he had mistreated a saintly person. As he wondered what type of reaction would befall him, a disciple of Samika Rsi arrived with a message from the sage.

The king graciously accepted the news that in seven days the serpent Taksaka would bite him. He saw it as an opportunity to become indifferent to the burdens of family, wealth, and governmental duties.

Bequeathing the kingdom to his son Janamejaya, Pariksit came to a hill, now known as Sukratal, by the bank of a branch of the Ganges. The king decided to stay there and fast until his imminent death.

Pariksit Maharaja was, even at that time, universally renowned as a great devotee; Krsna had personally saved the king when Asvatthama unleashed the brahmastra at Pariksit, then still in his mother’s womb.

As word spread that he had retired from royal duties to prepare for death, sages from all over the universe converged on Sukratal along with their disciples, hoping to witness the king’s ascent to Goloka.

As these saints—joined by demigods and kings — arrived to bless Pariksit Maharaja in his final days, the pious king offered them sweet words of greeting and humbly prostrated himself before them.

Once his guests had taken their seats, Pariksit Maharaja said, “O gentle souls! I have accepted Lord Krsna as my life, thus I surrender to you and humbly request that you continue to sing His glories.”

In full approval of the king’s determination, the sages said, “O King! We shall remain here to assist you in whatever way we can until you attain your desired destination, the eternal abode of Lord Krsna.”

Humbled by his illustrious guests, the king asked them two questions,

*tatas ca vah prcchyam imam viprcche visrabhya vipra iti krtyatayam*  
*sarvatmaim mriyamanais ca krtyam suddham ca tatramrsatabhiyuktah*

**“O trustworthy brahmanas What is my immediate duty? Please, after proper deliberation, tell me of the unalloyed duty of everyone in all circumstances, and specifically of those who are just about to die.”**

Of these two questions, the second — regarding the duty of those about to die — was especially relevant to the king. Actually, he knew the answer: devotional service to Krsna. But would everyone agree?

Pariksit Maharaja and some of his guests, such as Vyasadeva and Narada Muni, were pure devotees. But other guests were yogis or brahmavadis, who could have suggested some other form of sadhana.

To avoid controversy, Pariksit Maharaja wanted to make his own conviction clear and to receive the approval of the sages, whatever their individual opinions on the process of self-realisation might be.

But before disagreements could be aired or a consensus reached, Sukadeva Gosvami appeared, trailed by a gang of rowdy children who ridiculed him for his nakedness and apparent status as an outcaste.

The sages, however, at once recognised Sukadeva Gosvami’s peerless spiritual stature by his bodily symptoms. With the exception of Vyasa, Narada, and a few others, they all stood up to honour Sukadeva.

The son of Vyasadeva was only sixteen years old at the time. He had delicately formed limbs and facial features and a complexion that resembled Krsna’s, all signs of beauty and auspiciousness.

Sukadeva tried to conceal his transcendental attributes, but the other sages could easily recognise them. They unanimously agreed that the young saint was the best person to answer the emperor’s questions.

Sri Suka respected their conclusion by accepting a seat of honour. He addressed Pariksit's questions and affirmed his conviction that to hear about, glorify, and remember Krsna is everyone’s prime duty.

By citing his own example as a self-realised soul who, even though liberated, became attracted to glorifying Krsna, Sukadeva GosvamI pacified those sages who might have disagreed with his conclusion.

And what had attracted Sukadeva to Krsna? Srimad-Bhagavatam, the very essence of Krsna’s glories, recorded by Suka’s great father, Vyasadeva, as the ultimate conclusion of all the Vedas.

Sukadeva GosvamI therefore proposed that for the next seven days he recite Srimad-Bhagavatam. By hearing that great work the king would fulfil his final duties and prepare himself for his next destination.

Forsaking food, drink, and sleep, living by the invigorating nectar of Sukadeva’s words about Krsna, Pariksit Maharaja was held spellbound by the description of Krsna’s creation, incarnations, and devotees.

Towards the end of the third day Sukadeva Gosvami began narrating topics of Krsna’s appearance and pastimes, topics that fulfilled the king’s inner desire to hear about the person he had long searched for.

In the womb of his mother Pariksit Maharaja had seen Krsna in a tiny form, the size of a thumb, wielding His club to protect the embryonic Pariksit from the destructive glare of Asvatthama’s brahmastra.

Living under Yudhisthira Maharaja’s protection, Pariksit — first as a child and then as a youth — had constantly heard stories of Krsna’s sublime adventures in Vrndavana, Mathura, and Dvaraka.

In his grandfathers’ courts, conversations revolved around governing the world. But in the private quarters of those same monarchs, especially Arjuna’s, all conversations dealt only with Krsna.

Now Pariksit Maharaja was hearing from Sukadeva Gosvami about that very same all-attractive Krsna. Although the king’s days were numbered, he could think of no better way to spend them.

At the end of the seventh day, as Sukadeva Gosvami’s narration came to a close, he reminded the king that he should not fear death, for it would affect only his temporary body, not his eternal self, the soul.

The sage then asked his disciple if he had any more questions. The king asked that Suka bless him to be able to withdraw his mind and senses from maya, and to absorb them in Krsna at the time of death.

After Pariksit had duly worshipped Sukadeva Gosvami, the sage departed. The king then sat down completely still on the bank of the Ganges so that he could meditate on his worshipable Lord Krsna.

As the time of the king’s demise approached, the snake-bird Taksaka was on his way to Sukratal in the guise of a brahmana. On the path he met Kasyapa, who knew the science of counteracting snakebites.

Kasyapa Muni hoped to neutralise the snakebite meant to kill Maharaja Pariksit. To test Kasyapa, Taksaka bared his fangs and bit a nearby tree, which hurst into flames and quickly burned to ashes.

Undaunted, Kasyapa Muni chanted his mantras and returned the tree to its original state. Taksaka could understand that in the presence of Kasyapa he would be unable to carry out his mission.

But Taksaka could sense that Kasyapa’s motive for reviving Maharaja Pariksit was the promise of great wealth, so, as a resident of the lower heavenly planets, Taksaka offered the muni a fortune to desist.

The place where Kasyapa showed his prowess is known as Beraheri, and the place where he accepted Taksaka’s bribe is called Modna. After bribing the muni, Taksaka walked unimpeded to Suka-tirtha.

Scripture gives varying accounts of how Taksaka was able to bite the king. Srimad-Bhagavatam says that he disguised himself as a brahmana so that the soldiers would allow him to approach Maharaja Pariksit.

According to other texts and oral tradition, however, Taksaka was unable to pass by the king’s armed guards so he transformed himself into a caterpillar and hid in a basket of fruit placed before the king.

Nonetheless, in both versions Taksaka assumed his original form as a snake-bird and attacked the great king at the appointed time, reducing Pariksit Maharaja’s body to ashes with his powerful poison.

Everyone present at that time lamented the king’s death; still, as the demigods showered flowers and beat drums, they felt joyful knowing that Maharaja Pariksit had attained the supreme destination.

The area that surrounds Sukratal is steeped in the sweetness of the pure devotion Srimad-Bhagavatam propounds, especially in the Bhagavatam' s unique portrayal of Lord Krsna’s sublime pastimes.

The followers of Caitanya Mahaprabhu cherish Srimad-Bhagavatam as “the spotless Purana,” the scripture that reveals the confidential realisations of the topmost swan-like devotees (paramahamsas).

The Bhagavatam teaches not only the means of freeing oneself from the bonds of reactive work but also the essence of transcendental knowledge, the means to attain life’s fifth goal — loving devotion.

We may think that perfections such as Pariksit's fearlessness in the face of the invincible snake of time or His going back home, back Godhead are only available to exceptional souls like him.

But that conclusion is not correct. Suta Gosvami says, “Anyone who seriously tries to understand Srimad-Bhagavatam, who properly hears and chants it with devotion, becomes completely liberated.’

For that reason Srila Prabhupada asks us to regularly hear and discuss Srimad-Bhagavatam together and to apply its teachings in our lives, especially its instruction to chant the Hare Krsna maha-mantra.

Truly, this is the ultimate conclusion of Srimad-Bhagavatam, the final verse of which reads,

*nama-sankirtanam yasya sarva-papa pranasanarn*  
*pranamo duhliha-samanas tam namami harim param*

**“I offer my respectful obeisances unto Lord Hari, the congregational chanting of whose holy names destroys all sinful reactions, and the offering of obeisances unto whom relieves all material suffering.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Just next to Sukratal in New Vraja-dhama is Naimisaranya forest, best known amongst devotees as the place where Suta GosvamI recited Srimad-Bhagavatam after he had heard it from Sri Suka.

It is worth noting that, up until middle of last century, the area of New Vraja-dhama that commemorates Naimisaranya had long been the site of community meetings for Somogyvamos village.

The shady area under two ancient oak trees where the villagers used to meet now represents the place at which Suta Gosvami recited Srimad-Bhagavatam to sixty-thousand sages headed by Saunaka Rsi.

In New Vraja-dhama, because Sukratal and Naimisaranya are both in one forest, and because both places mark those spots where Srimad-Bhagavatam was recited, I named that forest Bhagavatavana.

Unlike Sukratal, Naimisaranya was a holy place long before Krsna appeared; in fact, ancient scriptures like the Ramayana refer to Naimisaranya, saying that it dates back to the time of creation.

Situated on the bank of the Gomati River in the state of Uttar Pradesh, Naimisaranya is a large forest with a radius of one hundred and thirty kilometres. Like Vraja, it has an established parikrama.

Many holy places grace the sacred forest of Naimisaranya. The most important place for Gaudiya Vaisnavas is the area surrounding Suta-gadi, where Suta Gosvami sat to recite Srimad-Bhagavatam.

There are various accounts of the history of Naimisa forest. In one version, sages requested Lord Visnu to show them a place of pilgrim-age that would free them from the influence of Kali-yuga.

In response to their plea, Lord Visnu released His Sudarsana cakra and assured the sages that the spot where the cakra landed would be the sacred place of pilgrimage the sages were seeking.

The cakra circled the universe, entered Naimisaranya forest, and plunged into the earth, threatening to slice the world in half. Hoping to avert such a calamity, the sages took shelter of Mother Durga.

That universal mother appeared as a lady named Lalita-devi and stopped the cakra from spinning. Even today the impression of the cakra’s axle bears witness to this pastime of millennia gone by.

Another account from the Varaha Parana also reveals how Naimisaranya got its name. Once a devotee of the Supreme Lord who was living in the forest was attacked by a horde of demons.

Having no other shelter, the devotee prayed to Lord Narayana, who immediately dispatched His Sudarsana cakra, killing the ferocious man-eating demons in the wink of an eye (nimisa).

Srlla Prabhupada also gives a derivation of the name Naimisaranya in one of his word-for-word translations of the beginning of Srimad-Bhagavatam from the phrase naimise nimisa-ksetre.

Naimise means “in the forest known as Naimisaranya,” animisa-ksetre refers to “the spot which is especially a favourite of Visnu,” and ammisa is a name for Lord Visnu, “who does not close His eyelids.”

Therefore, Naimisaranya is the place (ksetre) especially dear to Lord Visnu (aninusa), who does not close His eyelids. These arc some of the ways in which the sacred Naimisaranya forest received its name.

The pastimes connected with Naimisaranya are numerous, many of them dating from antiquity. For example, Lord Brahma once planned for a wheel (cakra) that would enclose the entire universe.

The hub of the cakra was to he fixed at Naimisaranya, hut the wheel shattered and its rim created a lake in the forest. That lake is still called cakra-tirtha today, and its waters relieve one of all sin.

Naimisaranya is especially attractive to those who perform sacrifices because the sacred atmosphere of the place subdues demons just as it purifies pious souls and the devotional activities they perform there.

Maharaja Dasaratha thrice visited Naimisaranya to purify himself for a horse sacrifice. Lord Rama, following in His father’s footsteps, came here to perform a sacrifice for the empowerment to kill Ravana.

The well-known story of the sage Dadhici also took place in Naimisaranya. Dadhici donated his invincible body to the demigods so that they could transform it into a weapon to kill the demon Vrtra.

The powerful demon Vrtrasura once drove the demigods from their kingdom, leaving them bereft of their weapons and their opulence. Helpless and confused, the demigods petitioned Lord Visnu.

The Lord told them that Dadhici Muni’s body had become invincible by chanting the Narayana-kavaca and that, if the demigods requested, the sage would donate his body in service to them.

The Lord said, “When Dadhici awards you his body, Visvakarma will prepare a thunderbolt from his bones. This thunderbolt will certainly kill Vrtrasura because it will be invested with My power.”

As predicted by the Lord, Dadhici generously agreed to the demigods’ request. He entered a deep trance and gave up his body without hesitation, just as a rich man throws away a torn piece of clothing.

From the bones of Dadhici, Visvakarma created a thunderbolt surcharged with the power of both the sage and the Supreme Lord. With that weapon King Indra gained victory over the demon Vrtra.

Those who bathe in Dadhici-kunda, where Dadhici performed austerities, awaken in themselves that sage’s spirit of selfless service to others and his exemplary detachment from the material body.

A self-manifest deity of ten-cubit-tall Hanuman carrying Lord Rama and Laksmana on each shoulder stands at Dadhici-kunda to this day. The deity is said to date back to the Ramayana war.

One night during the battle for Lanka, one of Ravana’s brothers cast a spell over Rama and Laksmana, kidnapped Them as They slept, and took the two brothers to his kingdom at the bottom of the sea.

Hanuman followed the demon’s path and rescued the two Lords of his life. He brought Them back to safety, returning to dry ground at Naimisaranya, from where the three heroes returned to Lanka.

At Naimisaranya pilgrims can place sweets directly in Hanuman’s mouth and receive his blessings to perfect their mood of service to the Lord, which is the prerequisite for success in any spiritual mellow.

Another important place is Vyasa-gadi, where Vyasadeva dictated the Mahabharata to Ganesa. Ganesa accepted the task on the condition that the sage dictate at such a pace that Ganesa’s pen need not stop.

Vedavyasa agreed, but he had his own stipulation: Ganesa would not record the verses mechanically. He would write them down only after he had fully understood what Vyasa dictated to him. Ganesa agreed.

When Vyasadeva needed time to reflect on his composition, or just to answer the call of nature, he would waylay Ganesa with a very difficult verse. These verses are known as Vyasa-ghattas.

Pilgrims can glean deep spiritual insight into books such as the Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam by reading them at Vyasa-gadi, where the great Vyasadeva still gives guidance to the sincere.

Certainly, the most significant pastime that took place at Naimisaranya was Suta Gosvami’s recitation of Srimad-Bhagavatam, an event precipitated by Balarama’s earlier visit to that holy forest.

Resigned to the fact that war between the Pandavas and Kauravas was inevitable, Lord Balarama, who was loath to take sides in a family feud, left Dvaraka on the pretext of going on pilgrimage.

The Lord travelled to various holy places where He worshipped deities and bathed in sacred waters, finally arriving at Naimisaranya to find great sages performing an extended fire sacrifice.

Although the sages at once recognised the Lord and respectfully greeted and worshipped Him, their elected speaker, Romaharsana Suta, remained seated on the vyasasana and showed Him no respect.

**\* \* \* \***

That a representative of Vyasa would fail to show proper respect to Him—the Supreme Lord — angered Lord Balarama, who then used the tip of a single blade of grass to kill Romaharsana Suta.

The sages were surrendered to the Lord’s will; still, they reminded Lord Balarama that even though He was above the Vedic injunctions, by killing a brahmana He had set a dangerous precedent.

The sages requested Lord Balarama to set an example for others by atoning for His apparent sin. They suggested that He go on a yearlong pilgrimage, a pilgrimage the Lord was already undertaking.

To further oblige the sages, Lord Balarama put Suta Gosvami forward as Romaharsana’s replacement, fulfilling the Vedic injunction, *dtmd vai putra utpanna*: “... one’s own self takes birth again as one’s son.”

In addition, at the request of the sages, Lord Balarama also killed a demon named Balvala, who would regularly contaminate the sacrificial arena with all kinds of impure substances.

The sages then worshipped the Lord, offered Him clothing and ornaments as gifts, and blessed Him with a garland of lotuses that would never fade. In that garland resided the goddess of fortune.

Taking leave of the sages, Lord Balarama then left Naimisaranya and began His year-long tour by going first to the Kausiki River, then to the source of the Sarayu and following the Sarayu to Prayaga.

Meanwhile, the sages at Naimisaranya recognised Suta Gosvami as their spiritual guide by offering him the same seat of honour that his father Romaharsana Suta had occupied before Lord Balarama’s visit.

The sages had assembled at Naimisaranya to conduct a thousand-year sacrifice with the aim of pleasing the Supreme Lord and His devotees, but certain omens signalled that their success would be limited.

The fire did not burn without smoke, and the disturbances the demon Balvala created had left some participants feeling insecure. In that state they were unable to properly concentrate on their mantras.

Doubting whether they were actually on the right path, the sages humbly petitioned Suta Gosvami, hoping that he would reveal the best means to fulfil their goal — to benefit the people of the world.

They said, “Please, therefore, being blessed with many years, explain to us, in an easily understandable way, what you have ascertained to be the absolute and ultimate good for the people in general.”

The sages went on to ask Suta Gosvami five more questions. The answers to these six questions form the framework of Suta’s recitation of Srimad-Bhagavatam, as he had heard it from Sukadeva Gosvami.

Devotees sometimes wonder how the chronology of the different narrations we now read as Srimad-Bhagavatam correlates with the original version of the Bhagavatam penned by Vyasadeva.

The Supreme Lord revealed the four seed verses of Srimad-Bhagavatam to Brahma, who gave them to Narada. Narada delivered them to Vyasa, who compiled a shorter and then a longer version.

Within the eighteen thousand verses of the expanded version of the Bhagavatam we read now, at least three narrations exist; Sukadeva’s to Pariksit, Suta’s to the sages, and Sankarsana’s to Sanat-kumara.

To understand the chronology of Srimad-Bhagavatam it is helpful to distinguish between the transcendental nature of the Bhagavatam’s contents and the written form those contents presently take.

Srimad-Bhagavatam is an historical record of the universe in relation to the appearances and disappearances of the incarnations of the Supreme Lord, who is the ultimate source of the universe itself.

As such, the Bhagavatam is unlimited in length, in scope, and in the accounts it presents. That unlimited nature can be easily understood by considering that it describes the unlimited pastimes of Sri Krsna.

The incarnations of Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, are said to appear and disappear in countless universes like the waves in an ocean. How could they be exhaustively presented in written form?

Moreover, the pastimes of even a single incarnation — such as Varaha— often occur in different ways at different times, making it literally impossible to comprehensively record all of Krsna’s activities.

Considering all this, it is easy to see why there are unlimited versions of the Bhagavatam, which Srila Prabhupada says has millions of verses in the higher planets. On earth we have a condensed version.

Suta Gosvami chose to begin Srimad-Bhagavatam by describing the incidents after the Kuruksetra war, while Sukadeva began with the process of creation followed by the Lord’s instructions to Brahma.

Lord Sankarsana, however, whose narration comes down to us from Sanat-kumara through Maitreya Muni, began his recitation with the secondary creation and the appearance of Lord Varaha.

In describing Krsna’s endless glories, then, the sages may choose completely different portions of those glories, or present the same portions but give different versions. These are all Srimad-Bhagavatam.

Nonetheless, are there requirements by which a particular narration is considered an authentic presentation of Srimad-Bhagavatam? Yes. It must contain the ten essential ingredients of a Maha-purana.

Sukadeva Gosvami lists these ten requirements:

**“In the Srimad-Bhagavatam there are ten divisions of statements regarding the following: the creation of the universe, subcreation —**

**“Planetary systems, protection by the Lord, the creative impetus, the change of Manus, the science of God, returning home, back to Godhead, liberation, and the summum bonum.”**

Any pure devotional glorification of the Supreme Lord Krsna that contains these ten characteristics, even though it may differ from others, constitutes an authentic narration of Srimad-Bhagavatam.

It is said that the written versions of Srimad-Bhagavatam vary from planet to planet. Srila Prabhupada says that the text for the demigods is nearly one million verses, or fifty times the length of ours.

As this example demonstrates, both the length and the content of Srimad-Bhagavatam may vary according to the qualification of the audiences found throughout the universe’s diverse planetary systems.

Now that we have heard something about the unlimited nature of Srimad-Bhagavatam itself, let us hear something about the physical printed text presently available to us here on earth.

Of the many possible versions of Srimad-Bhagavatam spoken by great persons since time immemorial, Srila Vyasadeva chose to commemorate in writing the version spoken by Suta Gosvami.

That version contains the subjects Vyasadeva had spoken directly to Sukadeva Gosvami, plus Suta Gosvami’s introduction to the First Canto and his summary and epilogue, the Twelfth Canto.

In his infinite wisdom, Vedavyasa gave us the essence of Srimad-Bhagavatam , based on what would best serve souls struggling to surmount the spiritually debilitating influence of Kali-yuga.

Suta Gosvami confirms that Srila Vyasadeva’s rendition of Srimad-Bhagavatam gives us its very essence,

*tad idam grahayam asa sutam atmavatam varam*  
*sarva-vedctihasanam saram saram samuddhrtam*

**“Sri Vyasadeva delivered it \[Srimad-Bhagavatam\] to his son, who is the most respected amongst the self-realised, after extracting the cream of all Vedic literatures and histories of the universe.”**

What makes Vyasa’s edition of the Srimad-Bhagavatam especially sweet? Half of it, ninety chapters, describes Krsna’s earthly pastimes, and half of those chapters are narrations of His life in Vrndavana.

Without doubt, Vyasa’s edition of Srimad-Bhagavatam emphasises vraja-bhahti. Krsna facilitated this emphasis Himself by appearing as Caitanya Mahaprabhu and teaching us how to become Vraja-vasis.

Lord Caitanya personally certified Srimad-Bhagavatam as the spotless (amala) scripture. In the words of the text itself, it is able to deliver the topmost perfection to persons who are fully pure at heart.

**\* \* \* \***

We should note with interest that Vyasadeva did not put Srimad-Bhagavatam into written form immediately upon realising its content, although he possessed the spiritual maturity required to do so.

Once Vyasadeva had attained spiritual perfection (prema), his spiritual master, Narada Muni, directed him to enter spiritual trance, wherein he saw the Supreme Person and His personified potencies.

In that state, Vyasa felt compassion for the conditioned souls, who, by embracing the external potency of the Lord, identify themselves with matter and are thus bereft of the shelter of Krsna’s internal potency.

According to the order of his guru, and inspired by the misfortune of the fallen souls and the compassion born of love of God, Vedavyasa compiled Srimad-Bhagavatam, also called the satvata-samhita.

Here the word “compiled” means that Vyasadeva recorded and elaborated upon the transcendental sound vibration of Srimad-Bhagavatam, which had been sheltered within his pure mind.

As just mentioned, Vyasa did not put Srimad-Bhagavatam into written form right away. Why? In the beginning of the text Vyasa hints that he wanted the contents to become even sweeter — but how?

Wasn’t the Bhagavatam already perfect? As Suta Gosvami says,

*yasyam vai sruyamanayam krsne parama-puruse*  
*bhaktir utpadyate pumsah soka-moha-bhayapaha*

**“Simply by giving aural reception —**

**“To this Vedic literature, the feeling for loving devotional service to Lord Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, sprouts up at once to extinguish the fire of lamentation, illusion, and fearfulness.”**

Yes, it was perfect. But Srimad-Bhagavatam becomes even more attractive when it comes from the lips of realised souls; thus, after revising it to his full satisfaction, Vyasadeva taught it to his son Suka.

Sukadeva Gosvami was already realised in spiritual existence, hut when he heard his father Vyasadeva reciting Srimad-Bhagavatam, he recognised it to be the path to ultimate perfection.

People wonder why self-realised, self-satisfied souls would he attracted to Krsna’s glories. Sri Suta replies,

*atmaramas ca munayo mrgrantha apy urukrame*  
*kurvanty ahaitukim bhaktim ittham-bhuta-guno harih*

**“All different varieties of atmaramas \[those who take pleasure in atma, or spirit self\], especially those established on the path of self-realisation, though freed from all kinds of material bondage —**

**“Desire to render unalloyed devotional service unto the Personality of Godhead. This means that the Lord possesses transcendental qualities and therefore can attract everyone, including liberated souls.”**

After having thoroughly studied Srimad-Bhagavatam, Sukadeva Gosvami taught it to Maharaja Pariksit. Suta Gosvami was amongst the assembly of innumerable sages who heard it at that time.

When the sages of Naimisaranya asked Suta Gosvami to enlighten them, he mercifully repeated Srimad-Bhagavatam, adding his own narration of Maharaja Pariksit's life and some of Krsna’s pastimes.

It was Suta Gosvami’s narration of the Bhagavatam that Srila Vyasadeva decided to record in written form. How did that compilation become sweeter by being recorded and expanded upon?

Vyasadeva humbly replies that even though his original narration was already attractive to even liberated souls, when the likes of Sukadeva and Suta repeated Srimad-Bhagavatam, they made it even sweeter.

Srila Vyasadeva consequently guides and encourages us with these words:

**“O expert and thoughtful men, relish Srimad-Bhagavatam, the mature fruit of the desire tree of Vedic literatures.**

**“It emanated from the lips of Sri Sukadeva Gosvami. Therefore this fruit has become even more tasteful, although its nectarean juice was already relishable for all, including liberated souls.”**

Srila Prabhupada uses a classic example to illustrate how Srimad-Bhagavatam becomes sweeter: when the beak of a bird, like a parrot, taps a ripe fruit, that fruit’s already sweet taste is enhanced.

In this example Sukadeva and Suta are parrots and Srimad-Bhagavatam is the fruit, the sweetness of which does not increase by mechanical repetition, however faultless. How then does it increase?

Srila Prabhupada provides the answer. He says that the two sages sweeten Vyasadeva’s narration by their “... ability to present the work in a manner that would appeal to all classes of men.”

Srila Prabhupada’s words bring two thoughts to mind: the first is that Vyasadeva compiled the Bhagavatam while he was in seclusion in the Himalayas, whereas Suka and Suta recited it before large audiences.

In other words, Vyasadeva’s compilation and transmission of Srimad-Bhagavatam was kirtana, but the two sages’ recitation to wider audiences was sweeter and more powerful — it was sankirtana.

Narada explains the principle that underlies this idea: “Compared to that person who is attached to chanting japa, he who performs loud chanting of the holy name of Hari is one hundred times better.

“This is because the person who chants japa purifies himself, whereas the person who chants the holy name loudly in sankirtana purifies himself and everyone else who hear the holy vibration.”

The second point Srila Prabhupada’s statement brings to mind is that Sukadeva Gosvami, and possibly Suta Gosvami, had realised the purport of Srimad-Bhagavatam more fully than had its author.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu, quoting Lord Siva, gave evidence of this while speaking to Sanatana Gosvami by saying,

*aham vedmi suko vetti vyaso vetti na vetti va*  
*bhaktya bhagavatam grahyam na buddhya na ca tihaya*

**“Lord Siva said, ‘I may know; Sukadeva Gosvami, the son of Vyasadeva, may know; and Krsna-dvaipayana Vyasa may know or may not know Srimad-Bhagavatam.**

**“‘On the whole, Srimad-Bhagavatam, the spotless Parana, can be learned only through devotional service, not by material intelligence, speculative methods, or imaginary commentaries.’”**

Evidence of Sukadeva Gosvami’s more elevated spiritual stature is also seen when he arrives in the assembly of sages and is at once offered the vyasasana, even in the presence of his father, Vyasadeva.

And in Srimad-Bhagavatam itself, Suta Gosvami compares Sukadeva Gosvami to the moon and the other sages, including Vedavyasa, as lesser heavenly bodies like stars and planets.

What part does the speaker’s spiritual advancement play in a narration of Srimad-Bhagavatam? The greater the speaker’s realisation, the greater effect that narration has on the audience.

We know that we derive spiritual benefit from hearing our own japa or sankirtana in proportion to our knowledge of and faith in the sublime philosophical truths related to Krsna’s holy name.

Similarly, the spiritual benefit an audience derives from hearing the sankirtana of a particular Vaisnava is in direct proportion to that Vaisnava’s knowledge of and faith in the truths of the holy name.

For this reason Srila Prabhupada repeatedly warned his followers that they should not hear the sankirtana of Mayavadis, sahajiyas, or professional musicians, no matter how attractive it may sound.

His Divine Grace would often quote the following verse to highlight the detrimental effects of such so-called sankirtana:

**“Just as milk touched by the lips of a serpent has a poisonous effect —**

**“Talks of Krsna (hari-katha) or nama-sankirtana when heard from the lips of non-devotees, is poisonous. Both those who speak it and those who hear it will suffer from the effects of poison.”**

While this quote describes the poisonous effects of hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam from one inimical to Krsna, it also asserts, in principle, that to hear Bhagavatam from a Vaisnava is like drinking nectar.

To the degree that one is envious of Krsna, to that degree his chanting is deleterious; to the degree that one loves Krsna, to that degree his chanting of the Lord’s names is wholesome and beneficial.

Krsna confirmed as much when, prior to worshipping Govardhana, He explained that a person gets the result of an activity in proportion to knowledge that he has of that activity’s purpose and result.

It is then reasonable to conclude that, amongst other reasons, Vyasadeva was present during Sukadeva’s recitation to receive further enlightenment on the same scripture he had taught his son.

And while Srimad-Bhagavatam does not list the names of those sages at Suta Gosvami’s recital, if Vyasa was not directly present, through his mystic powers he must have witnessed everything that was said.

By repeating Vyasa’s original composition, the two sages added the sweetness of their realisation and spiritual empowerment to the sound vibration of Srimad-Bhagavatam, thereby improving it.
