The potency of transcendental sound vibration (sabda) is not only in the words themselves but also in the consciousness of those who speak it. It is Krsna consciousness that brings the words to life.

To the degree that such transcendental life, or realisation, permeates the words of Srimad-Bhagavatam, to that degree the sound can awaken Krsna consciousness in the hearts of those who hear it.

In describing the effect that Sukadeva Gosvami had on Srimad-Bhagavatam by reciting it, Srila Prabhupada says,

**“The subject matter is so presented through the lips of Srila Sukadeva Gosvami that any sincere listener that hears submissively can at once relish transcendental tastes \[rasas\] which are distinct from the perverted tastes of the material world \[rasa-abhasa\].”**

In summary, Srila Vyasadeva did not fix Srimad-Bhagavatam in its written form until after it had been spoken by Sri Sukadeva and Suta Gosvami, ensuring that their recitations would enhance his own.

The recitations of the two Gosvamis were sankirtana on a grand scale, the sweetness and spirit of which Vyasadeva was able to capture as a member of the audience and then transmit in writing to his readers.

Moreover, because of the superior devotion of the two Gosvamis, his own comprehension of Srimad-Bhagavatam would be enhanced, and that increased realisation would also be passed on to his readers.

Considering that the contributions of Sukadeva Gosvami and Suta Gosvami were so significant to his Srimad-?hagavatam, Vyasadeva gave them recognition by recording their recitations for posterity.

Srila Vyasadeva, by hearing from and then glorifying the two Gosvamis in his book, gave us, who are truly the most in need of spiritual instruction, the best possible version of Srimad-Bhagavatam.

And Srila Prabhupada’s transparent translation and fully realised commentaries make the Bhaktivedanta Book Trust’s edition of the Srimad-Bhagavatam all the more potent. Jaya Srila Prabhupada!

Still, Srila Prabhupada taught that even though Srimad-Bhagavatam is available to us in written form, we must study it under the guidance of a self-realised soul while taking shelter of Lord Caitanya.

The word Bhagavata applies both to the book and to the agent of Krsna’s mercy who lives by and transmits to us the teachings of the book, according to the method presented by Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

To fully enter the transcendental sound vibration of Srimad-Bhagavatam, we must adhere to these transcendental principles, lest in the spiritual sense we cheat ourselves of its inestimable value.

I conclude this description of Naimisaranya forest with a prayer by Sanatana Gosvami,

*mad-eka-bandho mat-sangin mad-guro man-maha-dhana*  
*man-nistaraka mad-bhagya mad-ananda namo ’stu te*

**“\[O Srimad-Bhagavatam!\] My only friend, my constant companion, my spiritual master, my great wealth! My saviour, my good fortune, my source of ecstasy, I bow down to You.”**

In Dvapara-yuga, Naimisaranya was considered the foremost of all tirthas. We have now heard some of its glories, most significant of which are those in relation to the narration of Srimad-Bhagavatam.

May the forest of Naimisaranya, that king of holy places, bless us with increased devotion to Radha and Krsna and to the treasure trove of Their glories that comes to us in written form, Srimad-Bhagavatam.

## Chapter 29 - Kinarai to Devanagara

Let us now hear about the pastime places in New Vraja dhama’s western petal, of which Krsna’s elder brother, Lord Balarama— the source of all strength, spiritual and material — is the presiding Deity.

Only by the grace of Lord Balarama and Lord Nityananda have I been able to glorify Radha-Syamasundara’s chosen abode. I must therefore offer my prostrated obeisances to Them again and again.

From Kuruksetra I walked back to Raja-ghata and came to the open field that slopes down to the Yamuna and up again on the western shore, which marks where the Vraja^vasls crossed into Vrndavana.

In Krsna’s fourth year, sometime after He pulled down the two arjuna trees, the elders of Gokula decided that Mahavana was a place too dangerous to safely raise Krsna and the other children of their clan.

It appeared that the Vraja-vasis’ love for Krsna was the inspiration for this move, but underlying that was a deeper cause: Krsna’s desire to enjoy His boyhood in the playgrounds of Vrndavana forest.

Mahavana may have been well-suited to the joys of childhood, but because it had been inhabited for a very long time, its forests lacked the abundance of trees Krsna desired for His boyhood pastimes.

One day, while Krsna and Balarama played in the forest alone, Krsna said, “Dear brother! Because out kinsmen and their cows have resided in this forest for so many years, its natural opulences are depleted.

“Grass is scarce, the trees do not bear fruit, and the lakes are exceedingly shallow. I think that it’s time our people relocate to a better home, like nearby Vrndavana, which is lush and uninhabited.”

But Balarama objected, “We are just little children. Why would the leaders of Gokula village listen to Us?” Nodding in agreement, Krsna replied, “Because they will come to see the danger in staying here.”

As Krsna said this, wolves emerged from the pores of His body. Although these creatures were dark-coloured like Krsna and bore the divine insignia of Srivatsa, the villagers were frightened of them.

Indeed the wolves chased after calves, harassed the cows, howled throughout the night, and inspired such terror in the Vraja-vasis that the women and children were afraid to leave their homes.

The Vraja-vasis had many children of their own, but Krsna’s welfare was their primary concern. With His safety in mind they prevailed upon Nanda Maharaja to relocate their entire village to Vrndavana.

At a meeting in Maharaja Nanda’s assembly hall, Nanda’s elder brother Upananda said, “Between Nandisvara and Mahavana is a place named Vrndavana. It is a very suitable place for us to live.

“It is lush with grass, plants, and creepers for our cows and other animals. It has nice gardens, tall mountains, and it contains all the resources we need to make the gopas, gopis, and the animals happy.”

After some discussion all the Vraja-vasis agreed that moving to Vrndavana was a good idea. They immediately began to prepare their personal belongings and livestock for crossing the Yamuna.

With their possessions loaded on bullock carts beside the women, children, and elders, the Vraja-vasis set out for Vrndavana carrying bows and swords for protection, driving their large herds before them.

Nanda Maharaja’s people proceeded along the main road that ran parallel to the Yamuna, passing by Raval, where King Vrsabhanu also had made preparations to relocate his clan to Vrndavana.

The procession of cows, carts, and people with their lowing, rattling and shouting sounds, looked and sounded like a moving village in which everyone floated on the blissful waves of love for Krsna.

Proudly dressed in new clothes, the women sang the following song with this refrain, nanda-mahipati-jata nanda yasoda-mata: “O son of King Nanda! ? son of Mother Yasoda! May You be happy.”

Then they sang of Krsna’s childhood pastimes, *janma-maha-maha-digdha ramita-samasta-snigdha*: “Anointed at Your birthday celebration, You showed such love to Your delighted relatives!”

*Sparsardita-visa-yosa apancitapara-dosa*: “O child who, with a touch, killed the poisonous witch Putana! You forgave all her grievous sins and accepted her as Your nurse. All glories to You! Glories to You!”

*Sakata-vigkattana-sesa gokula-punya-visesa*: “O child who broke the cart and thus destroyed the demon Sakata! O most pious child in the transcendental abode of Gokula! O Krsna! O Krsna!”

*Krta-namabhir abhirarna santata-rdmdrdma*: “O child who has an unlimited number of attractive names like Gopala, Hari, and Krsna! O child who continually plays with His elder brother Balarama!”

*Ringa-bhrtangana-ranga angi-krta-sakhi-sanga*: “O child who runs and plays in the courtyard of His father Maharaja Nanda’s house! O child who is inseparable from His playful childhood friends!”

*Langhita-maruta-cakra nandita-gokula-sakra*: “O child who killed the terrible whirlwind demon Trnavarta! ? child who continuously delights the magnanimous heart of Gokula’s glorious King Nanda.”

*Vatsa-vimocana-moda vraja-jana-sarma-yaso-da*: “O child who takes pleasure in releasing the calves from their pens! O child who brings boundless happiness and fame to us, the fortunate people of Vraja!”

*Sarvananda-caurya tasmin darsita-saurya*: “O child who delights everyone with His adorable pastimes as a thief of butter and yogurt! O child who displays great prowess and heroism in this way!”

*Ayi damodaradila akhila-sukha-prada-sila*: “O child whose pastime as Damodara delivered Kuvera’s two sons, cursed to stand as twin arjuna trees! O child whose pastimes bring everyone transcendental bliss!”

*Nanda-mahipati-jata nanda yasoda-mata*: “O son of Maharaja Nanda! O son of Mother Yasoda! May You be happy. O son of Maharaja Nanda! O son of Mother Yasoda! May You be happy.”

Yasoda and Rohini sat with their divine sons, who moved around restlessly in the royal cart. Other women walked beside them, eager to see Krsna’s smiling face and to hear His charming childish prattle.

“Mother!” Krsna asked. “Where are we going?” “To live in a beautiful forest called Vrndavana,” Yasoda replied. “And when will we return to our house again?” asked Krsna. Yasoda smiled as she told her son:

“Our houses are with us in these carts. See, here are the cooking pots, and there is the furniture. We are taking everything from Gokula with us.” At that, Krsna gave His mother a quizzical look.

He then pointed over the side of the cart and said, “You are right. I can see that the trees are also coming with us.” At this all the cowherd women laughed, and Rohini-Devi happily corrected Him:

“No, the trees are not coming with us. They just appear to be moving because we are moving.” Capricious Krsna ran to the other end of the cart and asked, “Where is this Vrndavana we are going to?”

“It is on the other side of the Yamuna,” Rohini-Devi replied. This piqued Balarama’s curiosity. He asked, “The Yamuna River is far behind us in Gokula. Is there another Yamuna where we are going?”

As the women around the cart clapped their hands in delight, Mother Rohini replied, “O my son! The river Yamuna in Gokula and the river Yamuna in Vrndavana are both one unbroken stream.”

Balarama was astonished to hear this, but Krsna voiced a doubt: “O mother! Are you sure that you are not just imagining the movement of the Yamuna, like I imagined the movement of the trees?”

The two mothers and their female entourage giggled at this amusing comment. Pleased with Himself for being so witty, Krsna went on asking questions: “O Mother! What wonders await us in Vrndavana?”

Rohini replied, “My little boy! You will soon see for Yourself. There are many places to play and many things to play with.” Krsna erupted with glee at this good news and playfully jumped into Balarama’s lap.

On the way to the point where they would cross the Yamuna, the two boys played with each other, asked more questions of Their mothers, and giggled at the humorous way the toothless elders conversed.

After a long day of travel the caravan of carts and cows finally arrived at the ford in the Yamuna, but the sun was setting, so Maharaja Nanda ordered the men to set up camp for the night.

The men busied themselves with milking the cows, the women cooked supper, the children explored their new surroundings, and the servants set up the tents while carefully protecting the camp.

At nightfall, campfires lit up the Yamuna’s sandy shore as the Vraja-vasis strolled about their camp, sat and chatted, or prepared to take rest. But whatever they did, all they could talk about was Krsna.

Finally everyone but the guards went to sleep. Even while dreaming, the Vraja-vasis’ minds were absorbed in Krsna. They would either talk with Him or chant His irresistible names throughout the night.

In the morning everyone rose, bathed, ate, and readied their carts. When all was prepared, they lined their carts and cows along the sandy hank of the Yamuna, like an army marching to the front lines.

Krsna and Balarama were restless. Jumping from Their mothers’ carts, They climbed into the taller cart of Their father, from where They could see the beauty of the Yamuna and the forest on the far shore.

Nandaraja exclaimed, “Just see how beautiful Vrndavana forest is. Its fragrant flowers and singing birds and its endless bouquet of colours invite us like a welcome-banner to accept its merciful shelter.”

Jiva Gosvami says that after the cows had crossed the river, the gopas constructed a floating bridge from reeds and bamboo to transport their carts, families, and possessions to the other side of the Yamuna.

According to Kavi'karnapura, the Vraja-vasis had beautifully decorated boats in which they transported their women and belongings. He says that Nanda Maharaja’s vessel was especially opulent.

Both acaryas relate that upon reaching the far shore, Krsna and Balarama jumped onto dry land, called out to Their friends, and at once began to explore Their new home, eternal Vrndavana.

Because Krsna’s first interest was playing (krida) with His boyfriends (vatsa), the place where the Vraja-vasis disembarked from their boats and gathered their carts and animals together is called Vatsa-krida.

From there Krsna and Balarama rode on Their relatives’ shoulders, which provided good vantage points from which They could see and excitedly point out the best features of Their new playground.

With the beating of drums, Nandaraja called his people into a large level field and directed them to form their carts into a semicircle enclosed by a line of trees. He then named their new home Chatikara.

Vrndavana forest had been praised by visiting saints and demigods alike since time immemorial, but when Krsna finally arrived there, it shone with splendour, as if it had just awakened from a deep sleep.

**\* \* \* \***

From where I stood at the crossing, the path along the western bank of the golden Yamuna in New Vraja-dhama leads north towards Gokula, ending opposite Visrama-ghata, and south towards Ujani.

I chose to go south as far as Varahara and then west to the very tip of the western petal of New Vraja-dhama, where I would again turn south, following the road on the riverside all the way to Raval.

Along that route I would visit all the major pastime places in the western part of New Vraja-dhama, complete my circumambulation of the dhama, and thus conclude my parikrama at Visrama-ghata.

Two pastime places to the north relate to Krsna’s childhood: Kinarai, where the boys played by Yamuna’s shore (kinara); and Jayapura, the place (pura) where Krsna’s friends were victorious (jaya) over Him.

As He approached boyhood, day by day Krsna became more eager to go deeper into the forest and avoid the restrictions His elders were putting on His play. One day He and Balarama hatched a plan.

While Mother Yasoda was busy cooking Nanda Maharaja’s meal, and the servants watching over Krsna and Balarama were momentarily inattentive, the brothers sneaked off to Kinarai with Their friends.

Before long the servants realised they had been tricked. They went in search of the brothers, loudly calling Their names in the forest. But it was soon clear that the boys were evading them, so they turned back.

They informed the boys’ mothers of their mistake, saying, “Your sons tricked us and ran off to where the river is quite deep.” Hearing this, Yasoda asked Rohini to collect the boys so she could finish cooking.

Mother Rohini found the boys by the riverside, but Krsna had them so engrossed in play that even Rohini’s own son ignored her pleas to come back for His meal. She returned to Gokula empty-handed.

Rohini-Devi said, “Your son fears no one but you. And the others, including my own son Balarama, are fully under His control. If you want Krsna to come back, you will have to go get Him yourself.”

By the time Mother Yasoda found Krsna, the boys had moved from Kinarai to Jayapura, where Krsna had been soundly defeated in some childish game and obliged by His friends to reward them with sweets.

But Krsna did not take losing well. He wanted to play one last game and — winner take all — finally come out victorious over His friends. But just as they had begun, Mother Yasoda arrived and called out:

“My dear lotus-eyed Krsna! Come here and drink the milk of my breast. My dear darling, You must be very tired because of hunger and the fatigue of playing so long. There is no need to play any more.”

But Krsna was so determined to win this game that He ignored her. Mother Yasoda then called Balarama, who was more obedient than His brother. As she figured He would, Balarama came to Her side.

Yasoda saw no other way to rein in her son than to trick Him. She told Him, falsely, that it was His birthday and implored that He do His sacred duty. “Be pure and give cows to the brahmanas,” she said.

Krsna had been raised under the protection of the brahmanas, so this call to dharma brought the impulsiveness of His play to an end. Conceding defeat to His friends, He went home with His mother.

In each of her hands Mother Yasoda held the hands of her sons, gently escorting Them back to Gokula and assuring the two brothers that after They had eaten dinner They could go back out and play.

And to the other boys that followed behind, Yasoda sweetly said, “From now on, do not keep playing with my son when it is time to eat. When we call, you must stop and return to your homes.”

When hearing Krsna’s childhood pastimes, we revere the greatness of His parents,

*srutirn apare smrtim itare bharatam anye bhajantu bhava-bhitah*  
*aham iha nandam vande yasyalinde param brahma*

**“Those who are afraid of material existence worship the Vedic literature. Some worship smrti, the corollaries to the Vedic literature, and others worship the Mahabharata.**

**“As far as I am concerned, I worship Krsna’s father, Maharaja Nanda, in whose courtyard the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the Absolute Truth, is playing.”**

As I walked along the road by the river, I recalled how in 1993 I would ride along the same path on our horse Citra, sometimes shadowing the elusive herd of deer living in the shelter of New Vraja-dhama.

Then, the bottom of the valley was an impenetrable forest. The bridle path was the only access to the property from the western side of the creek, which I would circle at Sakaroya and ride up the temple hill.

The first pastime place south of the dam in our Yamuna is Pani-grama, the residence of Durvasa. At this place the gopis, after crossing the river at Pani-ghata, fed the muni with food brought from home.

Some authorities say that Pani-grama is Durvasa Muni’s birthplace, others say that his residence (asrama) is there, and still others say it is the place at which Durvasa once met the gopis near his hermitage.

But it is generally accepted that the Vraja gopis brought food to Durvasa Muni on Dvadasi, and that on another DvadasT the sage went to Madhuvana forest and visited Maharaja Ambarisa.

Srimad-Bhagavatam says that at that time Durvasa picked a quarrel with Ambarisa Maharaja. For offending the pure Vaisnava king, the muni was chastened by the Supreme Lord and His infallible disc.

When the gopis had lavishly fed Durvasa, they asked him how they would cross the Yamuna. The sage said, “Request Yamuna-Devi to let you pass on the strength of my vow to drink only durva grass juice.”

Gopala-tapani Upanisad tells us that Srimati Radharani respectfully asked the sage — who had just eaten a feast in front of the gopis — how he could truly be living solely on the juice of durva grass.

She also asked him how they could have crossed the river to get to his asrama on the strength of Krsna’s brahmacarya, as Krsna had told them to do, when the gopis had direct evidence to the contrary.

These questions are answered in detail in chapter thirty-five. In brief, Durvasa explained that because neither he nor Krsna had any desire to enjoy materially, their vows were unaffected by their deeds.

On the waterfront near Pani-grama is the dhrama of another great sage: Parasara Muni. A little further upstream we find the home of a fisherman and his beautiful daughter Satyavati, the mother of Vyasa.

Parasara Muni was the learned grandson of the sage Vasistha. Having assimilated the Vedas while in the womb of his mother, Parasara is well respected as an authority on the Rg Veda and its corollaries.

In addition to Puranic compositions, such as the Parasara-smrti, his codes of religion, he wrote a treatise on astrology as well as a treatise on botany that serves as a primer to students of Ayurveda.

He also composed the Visriu Purana. Srila Prabhupada often cited the definition of Bhagavan given there,

*aisvaryasya samagrasya viryasya yasasah sriyah*  
*jnana-vairagyayos caiva sannam bhaga itingana*

**“Bhagavan, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is thus defined by Parasara Muni as one who is full in six opulences — who has full strength, fame, wealth, knowledge, beauty, and renunciation.”**

Parasara Muni once desired to cross to the other side of the river Yamuna, so he went to the nearby landing where the fisherman had engaged his daughter Satyavati in ferrying people across.

Satyavati was extremely beautiful, but because she was the daughter of a fisherman she also smelled of fish. During the boat ride, in jest Parasara nicknamed her Matsyagandha (“fishy smell”).

The joke hurt Satyavati’s feelings, so Parasara Muni used his mystic powers to not only remove the fishy odour from her body but also to give it a floral aroma that could be smelled for one yojana all around.

Indeed, Satyavati was so fragrant that Parasara was attracted to her, so much so that he wanted to unite with her. But she objected: nei ther were they married, nor was a boat a fit place for amorous acts.

The sage then manifested an attractive island in the centre of the Yamuna and promised her that she would remain a virgin, even after hearing him a son. At this, Satyavati submitted to his superior will.

The child horn to Satyavati was Vedavyasa, also known as Krsna-dvaipayana Vyasa due to his dark (krsna) complexion, and to his having been conceived and born (ayana) on an island (dvipa).

But Parasara did not stay in one place for long, and Vyasadeva quickly grew up and left for the Himalayas, so Satyavati returned to her father and her service ferrying people across the Yamuna River.

Some time later, Maharaja Santanu, who was then practising austerities at Satoha, also came to the boat landing to cross the river. While being ferried to the other shore, he and Satyavati fell in love.

The great king approached Satyavati’s father for his daughter’s hand in marriage, but the fisherman would not give her unless Maharaja Santanu agreed that only Satyavati’s son would inherit the throne.

Santanu already had one highly competent son, Bhisma; thus the king could not agree to the fisherman’s demand. Crestfallen, Maharaja Santanu returned home, his mind filled with thoughts of Satyavati.

But when Bhisma discovered the cause of his father’s lamention, he went to the fisherman and voluntarily renounced the throne for life, after which he brought Satyavati home to Santanu Maharaja.

A little further upstream is the asrama of the learned sage Dattatreya, who is a combined incarnation of the three presiding deities of the universe, and who embodies the Lord’s potency of knowledge.

Dattatreya was the son of Atri Muni and brother of Durvasa. He taught the philosophy of the spirit soul to persons of renown, such as Prahlada and Yadu. Such were the residents of this area in Vraja.

**\* \* \* \***

Not far inland from the Yamuna is Mana-sarovara, also known as Hrdaya-sarovara. It is famous as one of Vrndavana’s crown jewels, both for its sylvan beauty and for the pastimes Krsna enacts there.

Having visited Mana-sarovara in Bhauma Vrndavana on many occasions, I can testify that it is to this day one of the most scenic and secluded places in which to meditate on the divine couple’s pastimes.

It is said that in the past the Yamuna River flowed on the eastern side of Mana-sarovara, hut further upstream she took two courses so that her waters surrounded Mana-sarovara on both sides.

Later, Yamuna-Devi's eastern branch dried up, leaving only her west' ern branch. And so it is today that the Yamuna separates Mana-sarovara from Vrndavana forest and the town of Vrndavana.

Often Mana-sarovara is mistaken for Manah-sarovara, a lake in the Himalayas that was born from Brahma’s mind (manah). The Manah-sarovara in Vraja was created by Radha’s tears of proud anger (manah).

Once, on the occasion of a rasa dance on a sandy shoal of the Yamuna, Srimati Radharani felt slighted when She noticed that Krsna was treating Her just as He was treating the other gopis.

Offended, Sri Radha left the rasa dance, crossed the Yamuna by Herself, and wandered in this area until She came to a thick grove of pilu trees surrounded by pairs of kadamba and tamala trees.

Seated on a flat stone, with nothing but the sounds of crickets, bees, and birds to keep Her company and offer their sympathies, Sri Radha shed tear after tear until a small pond had formed around Her.

Radha considered Krsna’s neglect to be His loss. What other gopi could sing, dance, love, and serve Him as She could? By treating Her as equal to the others, then, He only cheated Himself of happiness.

In other words, Srimati Radharani cried for Krsna’s loss, not for Her own. She cannot conceive of happiness independent of His; indeed, the very reason Sri Radha exists is to give Sri Krsna pleasure.

If She were no longer needed as the supreme instrument of His enjoyment, if He considered Her hut one of many, then why should She continue to live? She might as well die! But then She thought:

“If I died, and then Krsna came to His senses, how could He ever he happy again?” Weighed down by such melancholy thoughts, the result of Her anger at Krsna for denying Himself happiness, Radha wept.

Sri Radha sobbed through Her tears, “What a cheater! A man who spends His life stealing the butter, yogurt, clothes, hearts, and lives of others ultimately ends up cheating Himself in the process.”

The gopis had already expressed a similar opinion of Krsna’s cheating mentality on the full-moon night of Karttika. It seemed as though He had not taken their words seriously. But did He ever?

The gopis had said,

*pati-sutanvaya-bhratr-bandhavan ativilanghya te ‘nty acyutagatah*  
*gati-vidas tavodgita-mohitah kitava yositah kas tyajen nisi*

**“Dear Acyuta! You know very well why we have come here.**

**“Who hut a cheater like You would abandon women who come to see Him at night, enchanted by the song of His flute? Just to see You, we have rejected husbands, children, ancestors, brothers, and relatives.”**

Vraja’s young brides had answered Krsna’s call expecting Him to fulfil His many promises to accept them as His own; instead, at the height of their ecstasy, and without warning, He had disappeared.

“What a cheater!” thought Radha. Not only had He cheated the millions of gopis but He had also cheated Himself out of their company—just to prove that He was not under their control.

What young man would deprive Himself of the company of beautiful women who were falling over themselves to serve Him? “What a cheater!” She whispered. “Cheating everyone, including Himself!”

The ecstatic loving anger Radha displayed through Her thoughts, words, and behaviour is called maria. That maria also manifested itself in liquid form as Her tears flowed together to create Mana sarovara.

Moments after Radha had disappeared, Krsna’s bliss subsided and Her absence was all of a sudden glaringly obvious. Alarmed, He left the rasa dance and walked along the Yamuna’s banks in search of Her.

Radha’s distinctive footprints led Krsna to the Yamuna. Crossing it, He trod through Bilvavana until He came to a pilu grove. There sat Radha. Her sobs had plunged the forest into transcendental despair.

The atmosphere surrounding the grove had already brought Krsna to tears, but when He saw Sri Radha seated on a rock — which was now an island in a lake made from Her tears — His heart melted.

A painting worshipped in the temple at Mana-sarovara in Bhauma Vrndavana portrays the scene that followed, in which Krsna made every effort to placate Srimati Radharani’s heartbreaking tantrum.

In that painting, Krsna has placed His flute at Sri Radha’s lotus feet. Like a repentant thief, or a cheater begging His victim for forgiveness, Krsna’s head hangs low before Her in submission.

Though pretending to be indifferent, Radha was actually feeling satisfaction now that Krsna was finally enjoying the unsurpassed pleasure to which He is entitled, the happiness only She can provide.

And though Radha displayed fury in order to reprimand her beloved, Her desire was to shower Him with the priceless gifts of Her love. Thus Their separation eventually ended in the happiness of union.

Mana-sarovara, then, is not only the emblem of Radha’s supreme love for Krsna but also the place where She shows Him that love. The solitude this lake provides is rare amongst pastime places in Vraja.

Because Sri Radha’s unparalleled anger (mana) brought forth a lake (sarovara) of tears, the water of which bestows upon those who bathe there a love similar to Her own, this place is known as Mana-sarovara.

Krsna once gently told Radha, “O beautiful one! This lake born of Your tears is just like My heart (hrdaya)” To which Radha replied, “O Syama! No doubt it resembles Your heart, but it is My heart.”

Therefore Mana-sarovara, being the heart of both Radha and Krsna, is also called Hrdaya-sarovara. Thoughtful devotees who perform nama-sankirtana there can feel the divine couple’s heartbeat.

Beneath a silky silence punctuated by the chirping of parrots and the calls of cranes is an undeniable spiritual atmosphere, attractive and caring, enjoying and loving, ever fresh and eternal.

Dear devotees! To be cleansed of all sins and blessed with loving devotion, make your hearts one with Mana-sarovara, submerge your bodies and minds in its water, and chant the divine couple’s names.

By doing so, Lord Siva qualified himself to attain a form like that of a gopi. And in that form he became the eternal guardian of the rasa dance. The following pastime corroborates this truth.

**\* \* \* \***

Lord Siva and Asuri Muni once heard that Krsna would enjoy a rasa dance. The two sages came to the bank of the Yamuna with the hope of seeing and participating in the Lord’s most confidential pastime.

As Lord Siva and Asuri Muni approached the entrance to a beautiful grove of trees, vines, and archways, from which emanated honeyed sounds, they were blocked from entering by gains wielding sticks.

The sages said with desperation, “We have come a great distance to see Lord Krsna.” Unimpressed, the girls continued to block the entrance as they offered the two great souls this advice:

“We, like the many other women you see holding sticks, are appointed to guard the rasa dance, in which Krsna is the only male and everyone else is female. Therefore you two may not enter.”

Lord Siva and Asuri Muni were disappointed at being turned away. Seeing their sincere devotion, the leader of the guards said, “If you wish to see Krsna in His pleasure dance, then accept a gopi’s body.”

The two men looked at each other and wondered aloud, “How can we be transformed into milkmaids of Vraja? Is such a thing possible?” Speaking in a confidential tone, the chief guard said, “O sages!

“If you bathe in Mana-sarovara with the pure desire to serve Krsna as we do, you will certainly become gopis. Once you do, we can give you permission to enter the rasa dance, not otherwise.”

Encouraged by these words, the two saints made their way to Mana-sarovara. After offering many prayers, they bathed in the lake and, as promised, their bodies were transformed into the bodies of two gopis.

But, although Siva and Asuri Muni now looked like gopis, they were still not gopis at heart. Thus, as we shall soon hear, they were able to see Lord Krsna but not participate with Him in the rasa dance.

Without the shelter, training, and full blessings of the cowherd girls of Vraja, no one can attain the spiritual identity of a Vrajagopi. And without such attainment, no one can enter Krsna’s amorous pastimes.

This is especially true for those sahajiyas who dress their material bodies to resemble gopis, thinking that such an external show will give them access to the confidential realms of transcendental love.

In this case, Lord Siva and Asuri Muni did not artificially cover their male bodies with feminine garments. Their spiritual purity enabled them to access the transformational powers of Mana-sarovara.

And even then they gained only restricted access to Krsna’s pastimes. Thus, when the two gopi-sages returned to the area of the rasa dance, they received a warm welcome to the realm of the ultimate mellow.

Beyond the gates of the rasa-mandala, they saw a wonderful land paved with jewels, shaded by desire trees, illumined by the spring moonlight, and ornamented with golden arches, ghatas, and palaces.

The air was rich with birdsong and the fragrance of spring flowers. The sounds of musical instruments and singing voices blended with tapping feet to create a pulsation that made their hearts beat in time.

Then, from afar they saw Radha and Krsna seated on a bejewelled throne surrounded by gopis. The two saints bowed down and, with hearts full of bliss, offered sincere prayers to the divine couple.

Krsna listened to the prayers of His devotees. Pleased at being called *sri-rddhika-hrdaya-kantha-vibhusanas tvam*, “the ornament Radhika wears around Her neck and heart,” the Lord offered them a boon:

“Since you are both beyond material desires, controlled in mind and body, equipoised to all, and favourably disposed towards Me and My beloved, please ask from Me any benediction your hearts desire.”

As pure devotees satisfied with Krsna’s happiness, the two celestials wanted only eternal devotion to the Lord. Knowing their minds, Krsna smiled sweetly and said, “Your desires will come true.”

Both Lord Siva and Asuri Muni were then given residence at Vamsivata, where they too became gopi guards and were assigned posts from which to see the rasa dance and taste transcendental bliss.

Fixed in their celestial identities, however, the sages were not permitted to enter the pastimes and ecstasies of the rasa dance as participants, even in their female forms. But they could observe.

Even today near Vamsivata Lord Siva, in the form of a siva-linga, is worshipped as Gopisvara. In honour of this pastime and keeping with his desire, occasionally that form of Lord Siva is dressed as a gopi.

The cowherd maidens of Vraja have full access to Krsna’s rasa-lila pastimes; still, in the ecstasy of their spiritual perfection, at times they worship Gopisvara for the fulfilment of their own desires.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami confirms that the gopis would sometimes worship Lord Siva as their master (isvara) at Vamsivata:

**“Desiring to quickly attain the treasure of Lord Krsna’s embraces —**

**“The splendid and affectionate gopis devotedly and happily worshipped Lord Siva on the bank of the Yamuna. I daily worship Gopisvara-tirtha, where the gopis performed their worship.”**

Moreover, Dasa Gosvami’s prayer is also instructive for practising devotees who aspire for the perfection of the gopis’ love for Krsna— they too can benefit from worshipping Gopisvara Mahadeva.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura prays,

*vrndavanavani-pate jaya soma soma-maule sanaka-sananda-sanatana-naradedya*  
*gopisvara vraja-vilasi-yuganghri-padme prema prayaccha nirupadhi namo namas te*

**“O gatekeeper of Vrndavana! ? Soma! O you whose forehead is decorated with the moon, and who is worshipped by the sages headed by Sanaka, Sanatana, Sanandana, and Narada, all glories to you!**

**“O Gopisvara! Desiring that you bestow upon me prema for the lotus feet of Radha-Madhava, who perform joyous pastimes in Vrndavana dhama, I offer obeisances unto you time and time again.”**

We may wonder, “Would Srila Prabhupada approve of us praying to Lord Siva?” His Divine Grace writes,

**“The gopis also worshipped Lord Siva in Vrndavana, and the lord is still staying there as Gopisvara.**

**“The gopis, however, prayed that Lord Siva bless them by giving them Lord Krsna as their husband. There is no harm in worshipping the demigods, provided that one’s aim is to return back to Godhead.”**

I repeatedly offer my humble obeisances to Mana-sarovara. Like Radha-kunda, Kusuma-sarovara, and Brahma-kunda, it has the power to transform into a gopi anyone who bathes there with pure motives.

**\* \* \* \***

Mana-sarovara is on the edge of the eighth forest of Vraja, a forest even the most senior demigods worship to attain love for Sri Krsna. It is known by three names: Bilvavana, Belvana, and Srlvana.

This forest is known by these names because it is full of rose-apple trees — called both bilva and bel—and because the goddess of fortune, Sri, still undergoes austerities here to attain love like that of the gopis.

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu visited this forest and while resting here recalled how Krsna and the cowherd boys would come to enjoy the bountiful bel fruits that fell from trees at the slightest touch.

Once, however, during winter, when bel were not in season, the boys assembled in Bilvavana and insisted that Krsna provide them with ripe fruits that they could eat and also use to make into a drink.

Always up for a challenge and ever ready to please His friends, Krsna played a beautiful melody on His flute that caused the trees to flower, sprout, and grow the hard-shelled bel fruits, all within minutes.

The gopas were overjoyed that their desire had been fulfilled, and happier still with the wizardry of their friend. Shaking one another’s hands, they said, “You see! I told you. Krsna can do anything.’’

Even today the residents of Vraja, accompanied by temple priests, come to Bilvavana on each Thursday during December to commemorate Krsna’s pomicultural miracle at Krsna-kunda.

Bel fruits are a favourite of the cowherd boys. The round, hard-shelled fruits make ideal balls for playing catch. They also make a delightful splattering sound if the catcher misses them.

The gopas would either eat the fruits whole or mix the strained pulp with water and sugar to make a refreshing drink. In this way Krsna and His friends enjoyed the opulences of this sublime forest.

Visiting Bilvavana is equivalent to travelling to the major holy places, and one who passes through here on parikrama of Krsna’s holy land is glorified even on Brahmaloka. Such is the greatness of Bilvavana!

Perhaps the most significant pastime to take place in Bilvavana, one referred to by prominent acaryas and referenced in many scriptures, is Laksmi-devi’s performance of austerities to enter the rasa dance.

Uddhava, the wives of Kaliya, and even Krsna Himself are just a few of the authorised persons who have referred to Laksmi-devi’s unsuccessful attempt to win the same favour Krsna shows the gopis.

While staying with Venkata Bhatta in Ranga-ksetra, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu joked with Venkata about the austerities Laksmi-devi performed to become a gopi, and the reasons for her failure.

This topic is relevant to us because it highlights the difference between the boons offered to those who follow Lord Caitanya and to those who follow acaryas of other sampradayas, such as Ramanuja.

The goddess of fortune is the wife of Lord Narayana, a partial manifestation of Sri Radha, and the head of one of the four disciplic successions. Certainly she knows that Krsna is the Supreme Person.

She is eager to hear of Krsna’s unique glories, such as His flute playing and His loving exchanges In the rasa dance. Indeed, she has been intently meditating on them from beginningless time.

As a consequence of her devotional absorption, goddess Laksmi once wanted to enter Krsna’s rasa dance and personally taste the special mellows of paramour love known only to the cowherd girls of Vraja.

Krsna and Narayana are the same person, but Krsna’s pastimes as a paramour to many gopis sets Him above Lord Narayana. Laksmi could no longer resist the power of such transcendental attraction.

Laksmi-devi decided to undertake austerities in the land where Lord Krsna eternally resides — Sri Vrndavana-dhama. She thought that Krsna’s divine abode would surely empower her and fulfil her desires.

Laksmi-devi came to beautiful Bilvavana, casting off her jewellery and celestial finery. Fasting from all food and drink and consuming only the dhama’s invigorating air, she chanted Krsna’s names.

Srila Prabhupada comments that the goddess of fortune performed penance not only to become the object of Lord Krsna’s love but also “...for the association of the gopis, who are pure devotees.’’

From this we can conclude that those attracted to the pastimes of the rasa dance desire the company of the gopis— the shelter of the amorous mellow — as much as they desire the company of Krsna.

Goddess Laksmi had heard about the different episodes of the rasa dance and wanted to relish the ecstasy of union with and separation from Krsna, just as the gopis taste during those pastimes.

Yet even after her body had become emaciated from hundreds of years of austerities and her mind was absorbed in thoughts of Krsna, admittance to His blissful company and pastimes still eluded her.

The wives of Kaliya described Laksmi-devi’s penances: “Even the goddess of fortune, for this end, performed austerities for centuries, giving up all other desires and observing austere vows.”

Uddhava comments on Laksmi’s meditations: “Sri herself, along with Brahma and the other demigods, masters of yogic perfection, can worship the lotus feet of Krsna only within her mind.”

Laksmi’s asceticism was in such stark contrast to her usual opulent Vaikuntha lifestyle that Krsna sympathised with her. He was eager to instruct her in the manner of devotion that leads to vraja-bhakti.

He therefore appeared before the goddess one day in His charming two-handed form and asked her why she was petitioning Him by enduring such intense hardships in a secluded place.

Laksmi-devi said, “Dear Lord! By always hearing of Your paramour pastimes, I have developed a desire to enter the rasa dance just as the cowherd girls of Vrndavana do every night. Please bless me!”

Krsna replied, “O goddess! You are the wife of Lord Narayana and the most virtuous woman in creation. Why have you abandoned the happiness of Vaikuntha to mix with a cowherd boy like Me?”\*

“Please do not try to deceive me,” Laksmi answered. “You and my husband are the same person, so my chastity is intact. Nonetheless, I long for the unique sweetness of Your amorous sports.

“Please allow me to taste the transcendental bliss that comes from touching You in the festival of a *rasa* dance. I am Your wife. Your duty as my husband is to protect me from the demands of my senses.”

Krsna smiled as He replied, “That I cannot do.” Shocked at this response, Laksmi-devi asked, “What have I done wrong to be rejected by my eternal consort? How have I become so unfortunate?”

Krsna shook His head reassuringly and replied, “You are faultless. And I am deeply touched by your determination. But your reverential mood is incompatible with the selfless devotion of Vraja.

“In Vrndavana My devotees are unaware that I am the Supreme Lord. They see Me not as God but as the object of their love in the mellows of servitude, friendship, parenthood, or amorous affection.

“Here no one knows that I am God. My mother accepts Me as her son and binds Me to a grinding mortar. Subala thinks that I am his intimate friend and in our games playfully climbs upon My shoulders.

“How could you enter the *rasa* dance with the body and identity of the goddess of fortune and show Me the respect due to Lord Narayana while the *gopis* are thinking of Me as their *gopa* lover?

“My unbounded sweetness is the special feature of Vrndavana that attracts the Vraja-vasis’ hearts to Me. Its power depends upon their being completely free from awareness of My majesty.”

Krsna concluded His explanation to the goddess, “Therefore, O Devi! As much as I am indebted to you for your service and austerities, I cannot fulfil your desire. Please ask Me for something else.”

Laksmi-devi was contemplative. She did not want anything else. She thought of an argument: “The personified *Vedas* worshipped You to become *gopis* and You fulfilled their desire. Why not fulfil mine?”

Krsna relished seeing Laksmi’s enthusiasm and determination to succeed. He said, “You are correct! The personified *Vedas* did worship Me in the ecstasy of the *gopis,* but they too were at first unsuccessful.

“They also wanted to enter into the *rasa* dance by simply absorbing themselves in the mood of the *gopis.* I told them, as I am telling you, such effort is insufficient and will not bear the fruit you desire.”

Leaning forward, Laksmi enquired, “Then how did they achieve success?” “Later they took birth as *gopis* in Vrndavana,” Krsna said, “and were spontaneously absorbed in the *gopis’* love for Me.

“They forgot their identities as personified *Vedas* and My identity as the Supreme Lord. They were allowed to enter the *rasa* dance because they thought themselves to be milkmaids, and Me their paramour.”

Krsna leaned forward, just inches from Laksmi’s face, and said, “O Devi! You want to enjoy Me as a cowherd boy and at the same time retain your body as the goddess of fortune. That is not possible!

“You want to circumvent the process of following the *gopis,* but you cannot succeed like that. If you want to enter the *rasa* dance, you must give up your present identity and pray to take birth in Vraja.”

**\* \* \* \***

At this Krsna stopped speaking and disappeared, leaving Laksmi-devi to reflect on His final instruction: “If you want to enter the *rasa* dance, give up your identity and pray to take birth in Vraja.”

Yes! Now Laksmi-devi was even more determined then ever. She would continue her austerities in Bilvavana, but she had a new goal: like the personified *Vedas,* she wanted to reborn as a Vraja *gopi.*

To this day, invisible to all, goddess Sri continues her austerities in Bilvavana in Bhauma Vrndavana. And, visible to all, a deity of her is worshipped there. Thus Bilvavana is also celebrated as Srivana.

This pastime is often cited to extol the *gopis*’ unique standing as objects of Krsna’s favour above all others, a standing that even the goddess of fortune — not to mention lesser women — has yet to equal.

During his visit to Vrndavana, Uddhava realised the *gopis*’ privileged position and declared, “When Sri Krsna was dancing with the *gopis* in the *rasa-lila,* the *gopis* were embraced by the arms of the Lord.

“This transcendental favour was never bestowed upon the goddess of fortune or other consorts in the spiritual world. Indeed, never was such a thing even imagined by the most beautiful girls —

“In the heavenly planets, whose bodily lustre and aroma resemble the lotus flower. And what to speak of worldly women who are very beautiful according to material estimation?”

The wives of Kaliya also marvelled how, on one side of the Yamuna, Krsna had embraced the *gopis* in His arms, while on the opposite bank He declined to embrace Laksmi-devi, despite her austerities.

As we analyse the gopis’ transcendental supremacy over Laksmi-devi, we must he careful not to criticise her, to doubt her purity, or to minimise her position as an intimate associate of the Supreme Lord.

Srila Prabhupada warns us that we should not fault LaksmI for wanting to associate with Krsna as His paramour. Krsna is her husband, Narayana, but in a different, more “sportive” form.

We may also doubt why Laksmi-devi was unaware that she had to become a *gopi* to associate with Krsna. The answer is that without the mercy of Krsna and the gopis, that secret remains inaccessible to all.

Brahma once told Bhrgu Muni,

*sasti'varsa'sahasrani maya taptam tapah pura*  
*nanda-gopa-vraja-strinam pada-renupalabdhaye*

**“To understand the dust of the** ***gopis’*** **lotus feet I underwent austerities —**

**“For sixty thousand years. Still, I could not understand it. To say nothing of me, even Lord Siva, Lord Sesa, and the goddess of fortune, LaksmI, could not understand it.”**

We should never doubt Laksmiji.

Finally, Jiva Gosvami clarifies one of Krsna’s statements that may lead one to underrate Laksmi’s — and even the *gopis’* — amorous love for the Lord, the most exalted of the five kinds of relationships.

Lord Krsna once told His cousin in Dvaraka, “My dear Uddhava, neither Lord Brahma, Lord Siva, Lord Sankarsana, the goddess of fortune, nor indeed My own self are as dear to Me as you are.”

We may misunderstand this statement of the Lord to mean that Uddhava’s mellow of servitorship is superior to Laksmi-devi or the *gopis’* paramour love. This conclusion is certainly erroneous.

Jiva Gosvami asserts that these words of praise for Uddhava are meant to extol devotional service and the devotees in a general way. They do not mean that Uddhava is superior to goddesss Laksmi.

Amorous love is the most confidential way to serve the Supreme Lord. And the pastime at Srivana confirms that the amorous love of the *gopis* is more intimate than the love of Laksmi-devi.

Indeed, Uddhava aspires for a position like that of the *gopis.* And he adopted a unique austerity to achieve that end. He took birth in Vraja as the creepers that grow underfoot at Kusuma-sarovara.

Uddhava reasoned that the *gopis* who pick flowers at this lake would regularly walk upon him, blessing him with the dust of their lotus feet, which in time would result in the fulfilment of his desire.

After concluding that he would have to abandon his identity as Krsna’s cousin, Uddhava prayed,

**“The** ***gopis*** **of Vraja have given up the association of their husbands, sons, and other family members —**

**“Who are very difficult to give up, and they have forsaken the path of chastity to take shelter of the lotus feet of Mukunda, Krsna, which one should search for by Vedic knowledge.**

**“Oh, let me be fortunate enough to be one of the bushes, creepers, or herbs in Vrndavana** ***\[gulma-lata-osadhinam\],*** **because the** ***gopis*** **trample them and bless them with the dust of their feet.”**

We may also justifiably wonder why the goddess of fortune, Laksmi- devi, did not try to become a queen of Krsna in Dvaraka, a position more easily attained than that of a *gopi* in Vrndavana.

The answer is that even the queens of Dvaraka, including Rukmini-devi, cannot enjoy the elevated mellows of love relished by the *gopis.* To this day, then, Laksmi-devi remains in trance at Srivana.

In the corner of Bilvavana is Dagauli, or Dag, named after the stick *(dag)* that Krsna once lost there while herding Nanda’s cows. That stick has yet to be found, though many devotees have searched for it.

In addition to their cowherd dress, turbans, feathers, flutes, and bugles, the *gopas* carry colourful sticks. They use these sticks to control the cows by tapping the ground or the cows’ backs.

Krsna’s flute is His most celebrated companion, but like His brother Balarama, who sports a red stick, Krsna always goes cowherding with one of the many sticks his father has fashioned for Him.

The famous Krsna Deity of Udupi in Karnataka — once worshipped by Rukmini-devi in Dvaraka and later discovered by Madhvacarya— has such a stick in one hand and a lump of food in the other.

The boys use these sticks for more than just herding cows. The staffs serve as batons for twirling and tossing. Amongst the *gopas,* Krsna and Balarama are most adept at this requisite cowherd skill.

To know just how adept the brothers are at this sport, and what it entails, let us recall how Caitanya Mahaprabhu and His associates included twirling batons as a part of their Janmastami celebrations.

On Nandotsava, Caitanya Mahaprabhu and His devotees would dress up as cowherd boys and go to a festival site with pots of milk and yogurt hung from rods on their shoulders.

One devotee dressed as Nanda Maharaja, another as Mother Yasoda. As the devotees chanted Hare Krsna, they would also dance and throw milk, yogurt, and water mixed with turmeric on each other.

While all this fun was going on, Advaita Acarya asked the Lord to prove that He was not just imitating a *gopa,* saying, “I shall know that You are a cowherd boy only if You can wheel this rod about.”

Cheered on by His associates, Caitanya Mahaprabhu accepted Advaita’s challenge and began to twirl a staff, repeatedly throwing it high into the air and then catching it when it came back down.

Lord Caitanya’s skill at twirling, throwing, and catching the stick became apparent when He caught it not only in front of Him but also at each side, behind His back, and even between His legs.

After some time a large crowd surrounded the Lord, laughing and clapping at His feats. And when He whirled the staff around in a circle like a firebrand, the audience was thoroughly astonished.

Lord Nityananda, fully immersed in the mood of a cowherd boy, and not to be outdone, took a stick of His own and began to whirl it about, matching and sometimes even surpassing Lord Caitanya.

Krsna and Balarama have similar contests with Their friends while herding the cows in Bilvavana. They try to see who can twirl a stick the longest, throw it the highest, catch it behind his back, and so on.

Fighting with these staffs is another essential sport amongst the cowherd boys’ colourful pastimes. The *gopas* often duel in pairs or in groups, with each side always eager to defeat the other.

But, as with all games, the cowherd boys soon become tired and hungry. On one occasion they were so engrossed in feasting on *bd* fruit that when it was time to leave, Krsna left His staff behind.

It was one of His favourite sticks. Unfortunately, when the boys returned the next day it was nowhere to be found. Since that day no one has seen the staff, although many have offered prayers to it.

Because that stick enjoyed the bliss of Krsna’s touch and served to amuse Him, it is worshipable for us. Along with the lost stick, we worship another kind of stick, one that is readily available to us.

Kaviraja Gosvami explains,

**“My path is very difficult. I am blind, and my feet are slipping again and again. Therefore, may the saints help me by granting me the stick of their mercy as my support.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Next to Bilvavana is Bhandiravana, Vrndavana’s eleventh forest. It is a favourite pastime place not only for the *gopas* and *gopis* but also for yogis, who take advantage of its —serene spiritual atmosphere.

A person who fasts and bathes in this forest without knowledge of devotion will attain Indraloka in his next life. But pure devotees who just see this forest will not have to enter a mother’s womb again.

Narada Muni, on a visit to Vrndavana, once rested in this forest and was astonished to hear two parrots debating the truths of the *Vedanta-sutra.* Such are the forest creatures living at Bhandiravana.

Rati-manjari once drew a picture of Krsna and brought it to Srimati Radharani, who was seated on a flower throne surrounded by Her friends deep in the heart of beautiful Bhandiravana.

Radha and the *gopis* were extremely pleased with the picture because it was a perfect likeness of their beloved. Krsna soon arrived, and Radha had Rati show Him the picture, which He praised as well.

On another occasion, Radha and Krsna were enjoying the pleasing atmosphere of Bhandiravana in the company of Their girlfriends when Candravali’s close friend Padma happened by.

Padma thought to get Radharani in trouble, so she went to Yavata to tell Jatila what she had seen. Anxious Jatila made her way to the appointed spot and indeed found Radha and Krsna together.

Caught off guard, the divine couple were frozen in fear. They stared speechlessly at Jatila who, horror-struck, stood a short distance away. Just then, Radha’s close friend Syama-sakhi happened to pass by.

Jatila thought that she had finally caught her daughter-in-law redhanded, and so she decided, with Syama-sakhi as her witness, to report Krsna to Kamsa and to lock up Srimati Radharani forever.

But Syama-sakhi was clever. Taking in the scene, she came to her friend’s rescue by making up a story. When Jatila asked, “Syama! I have faith in you. What do you see?” Syama replied innocently:

“See? Krsna is up to His tricks as usual. He has dressed Subala up as a girl, and the two jokers are pretending that they are the Yaksas and Yaksis who regularly come here to bathe and enjoy this forest.”

Knowing her eyesight to be bad and Padma to be always antagonistic to Radharani, Jatila replied, “Yes, yes. That’s what I thought. Subala and Krsna!” And with that the angry old woman hobbled home.

Bhandiravana’s natural beauty and its suitability as both a playground for the *gopas* and a pleasure garden for the *gopis* endear it to Radha and Krsna, who even have names associated with it.

Krsna is called Bhandiresa, the master of Bhandiravana, and Bhandira-tata-tandavi, He who dances in Bhandiravana. Radharani is called Bhandira-tata-mandana, She who decorates Bhandiravana.

At the edge of a large meadow in the northeastern corner of Bhandiravana is a shady *(chaya)* forest called Chaheri, where the cowherd boys sometimes rest while the cows graze nearby.

The most famous pastime to take place in Bhandiravana was the marriage of the divine couple, an event portrayed elaborately in both the *Garga-samhita* and the *Brahma-vaivarta Purana.*

In Vraja, Radha and Krsna always enjoy the taste of love by acting as paramours, but as a pastime They marry at Bhandiravana so that small-minded men cannot fault Them for being illicitly connected.

Once, Nanda Maharaja was herding cows in Bhandiravana with baby Krsna in his arms when a strong wind filled the sky with clouds and blocked out the sun. The dense darkness frightened Krsna.

Being so far from Gokula and having no other recourse, Nandaraja prayed to Lord Narayana for shelter. At once a beautiful cowherd damsel appeared and lit up the forest with Her radiant beauty.

Though She had not yet taken birth on earth, this *gopi* was Radha, just descended from Goloka. Earlier, Garga Muni had revealed Radha’s and Krsna’s identities to Nanda, so he recognised Her.

Radha’s complexion was golden, Her garments blue. Her movements resembled the ebb and flow of ocean waves, and the jingling of Her anklets and other jewellery resounded like the warbling of swans.

Nanda Maharaja bowed before Radha and placed baby Krsna in Her arms, saying, “O Radha! Here is my son, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. I know You are His first beloved, the Supreme Goddess.

“Because I am controlled by the modes of nature, I think that Krsna is my son and that He — who is feared by fear personified —is afraid. Still, I request that You take Him back to His mother in Gokula.”

Srimati Radharani, who was very pleased by King Nanda, said, “O noble one! This divine form of Mine is very difficult to see, but for one who has seen it, nothing is out of reach. Ask Me for a boon!”

Bowing his head, Nanda Maharaja humbly replied,

*yadi prasannasi tada bhaven me bhaktir drdha kau yuvayoh padabje*  
*satam ca bhaktis tava bhakti-bhajam sangah sada me ’tha yuge yuge ca*

**“Millennium after millennium, may I have firm devotion to You and Krsna. May I always live in the company of Your pure devotees, and may my devotion to them equal my devotion to both of You.”**

Saying, “So be it!” Srimati Radharani held baby Krsna to Her breast and carried Him deep into the forest, leaving Nanda Maharaja to first offer his obeisances to Sri Radha and then look after his cows.

Within Bhandiravana is Bhandiraka, a hidden grove of trees and vines with a *kunda* at its centre. This grove is inaccessible to everyone except the residents of the upper and lower heavenly planets.

Radha brought Krsna there, and when She did, Narada Muni says, the opulence of Goloka Vrndavana descended upon the forest and transformed the soil to *cintamani* and the trees into *kalpa-vrksas*.

The grassy banks of the Yamuna transformed into jewelled steps that led to golden palaces. Swaying in a sweet spring breeze, the grove revealed its true form with glistening pavilions and lapis courtyards.

As Radha watched Vrndavana cast off its material disguise to lay bare its eternal form of sweetness and opulence, the baby in Her arms also assumed His eternal feature as a handsome teenage youth.

Radharani beheld the sight of the original Cupid, who was as splendid as a dark cloud, draped in golden garments, ornamented with the Kaustubha jewel, and holding a bamboo flute in His hand.

Krsna greeted Radha with a sweet smile, gentle words, and a tender embrace. The divine couple then sat upon a magnificent throne and talked, all the while drinking in the joy of each other’s company.

After some time Lord Brahma appeared from his abode, as if called for, and with Radha’s permission he came before the divine couple and bowed down low, his four heads touching Their lotus feet.

Befitting such a rare occasion, and such an exalted person, Brahma recited beautiful prayers to glorify Radha’s and Krsna’s many incarnations, features, and pastimes and then bowed again to Radha.

Receiving a glance of consent from Krsna, Brahma washed Radha’s feet with water from his *kamandalu* and then dried them with his own hair, all the while shedding tears of ecstasy from his eight eyes.

Radha was visibly taken aback by Brahma’s boldness, and so the creator said to Her, “O mother! I once performed penance at Puskara for sixty thousand years, after which Your Lord appeared before me.

“He asked me to accept a boon, and I requested to see the lotus feet of Radhika. Your Krsna then told me that at a fitting time and place, what is impossible for others would become possible for me.”

After bowing down, Brahma again offered prayers that disclosed the esoteric truths of Srimati Radharani. Like Nanda Maharaja, Brahma begged for unalloyed devotion to Radha’s and Krsna’s lotus feet.

Brahma then requested,

**“My master and mistress! You are one soul in two bodies, inseparable as the complete energetic and the complete energy; still, in deference to the ways of men, You should marry.**

**“Your pastimes as paramours are understood by transcendentalists, but conditioned souls should be reassured that although You sometimes appear to contravene** ***dharma,*** **You still conform to it.**

**“If it is widely known that You were married in childhood, then Radharani’s later marriage to another will appear like a drama, and Your apparent transgressions of morality will seem insignificant.**

**“Faith in You is the cornerstone of liberation. But anyone who finds fault in You will thus he undermining their impetus to follow Your teachings and their own hopes for perfection, without a doubt.**

**“For this reason I request You to embrace the ways of the world for the benefit of others. Please allow me to perform Your marriage ceremony and proclaim You husband and wife. That is my plea.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Radha and Krsna at once accepted Lord Brahma’s proposal. Overjoyed, the creator respectfully seated the prospective bride and groom before the sacrificial arena and invoked the sacred fire.

Brahma performed the wedding ceremony beneath a banyan tree called Bhandira-vata, not to be confused with the Bhandira-vata on the opposite side of the Yamuna where Pralambasura was killed.

The creator chanted the appropriate mantras and performed the rituals involved in a fire sacrifice. Then, playing the role of Sri Radha’s father, he asked Her to bow to Krsna, which She happily did.

After directing the divine couple to circumambulate and then bow before the fire, Brahma engaged Radha and Krsna in the different parts of a Vedic wedding, which They completed with graceful dignity.

Krsna held Radha’s hand in His and recited seven Vedic hymns. Brahma then placed Radha’s hand on Krsna’s chest and Krsna’s hand on Radha’s back as She recited the bride’s seven Vedic vows.

Afterwards Brahma handed Radha a knee-length garland of *parijata* flowers swarming with humming bees. As Krsna reverentially bowed to receive Her token of love, Radha placed the garland on His neck.

In turn, as Radha’s bashful, doe-like glance met Krsna’s sparkling eyes, Krsna placed a beautiful garland upon Her neck. Radha then gracefully sat at Krsna’s left side and recited His names in Her mind.

The two youths sat upon separate thrones as Brahma joined his palms and had Radha and Krsna repeat five Vedic hymns after him. As a father gives away his daughter, Brahma, crying, gave away Sri Radha.

Radha and Krsna again circled and offered Their obeisances to the fire. They then gave audience to those who could see Them. As the demigods showered flowers, Gandharvas sang and Apsaras danced.

The pious residents of the higher planetary systems, the liberated sages of the universe, and the birds and animals of the forest came in pairs before the newlyweds to offer blessings and gifts of love.

Krsna turned to Brahma and said, “Since you presided over this auspicious occasion, My heartfelt desire is to offer you *daksina.* This is the tradition of the *Vedas,* and of Vraja. Please ask for something.”

His palms joined, his voice trembling slightly, Lord Brahma replied, pr*abho me dehi tvad-anghryor nija-bhakti-daksinam:* “O Lord! As *dak sina,* please give me pure devotion to Your lotus feet.”

Krsna happily fulfilled Brahma’s request and then gave him this order: “O son! Now you may return to your own abode and with devotion conscientiously perform the duties I have entrusted to you.”

Bowing, Brahma left, and as he did, the opulences of Goloka were covered by the natural sweetness of Bhandiravana, leaving only the birds and other forest creatures to keep Radha and Krsna company.

As befitting newlyweds, Radha and Krsna delighted in the treasures of Their love as They played games, walked through forest groves, relished different foods, and talked on the bank of the Yamuna.

With a laugh Krsna disappeared into a grove of flowering vines and hid from Radha, only to be caught by Her from behind. She then hid from Him in a garden, and Krsna, informed by a monkey, found Her.

The divine couple then returned to the courtyard of Bhandiraka where They performed a type of *rasa* dance suited for a single couple, amazing each other with Their skills, movements, and affection.

Years later, Krsna would call the *gopis* to this spot with His flute-song and enjoy *rasa* dancing with them, and so Bhandiraka is also known by the familiar names Vamsivata and Rasa-sthali.

While playing water sports after Their wedding, Krsna stole Radha’s play lotus and She in turn stole His flute. When He said, “Give Me back My flute!” She mocked Him, saying, “Give Me back My lotus.”

After making peace and returning each other’s property, Radha and Krsna entered a grove where Krsna dressed, ornamented, and decorated Srimati Radharani to His heart’s full satisfaction.

Just when Radha was about to dress Krsna, He changed into an infant crawling on the ground, crying after His mother, looking here and there in fear, just as He had been when Nanda had given Him to Her.

At first Radha was disappointed that Their loving pastimes had been interrupted, but then Krsna’s voice came from the sky and reassured Her that They would continue Their pastimes in the future.

Radha again embraced baby Krsna, holding Him tightly in Her arms, and left Bhandiravana, carrying Him along the shore of the Yamuna until She reached Gokula and the palace of Nanda Maharaja.

Mother Yasoda was overjoyed to see a goddess holding her infant son. She took her child, covered Him with kisses, and breastfed Him while Radha explained to Yasoda how She had come to carry Krsna.

Srimati Radharani said, “A storm appeared, and your baby became fearful of the wind and darkness. His father, considering the child’s welfare, asked Me to bring Him back to the shelter of your arms.

“My clothes are soaked, and I am tired from carrying this plump, hungry baby over the muddy pathways. I left My own home long ago. Please allow Me to leave now. May everything be auspicious!”

Saying this, Radha graciously accepted Mother Yasoda’s words of praise and offerings of food and then, carrying a box of gifts from the queen of Vraja, she left Gokula for Her original abode in Goloka.

It is said that whoever hears, reads, or recites a narration of the divine couple’s auspicious wedding beneath the banyan tree in Bhandiravana will never be touched by the effects of their past sins.

Near the wedding arena is Venu-kupa, also known as Dauji-kupa, a well *(kupa)* that Krsna created with His flute *(venu)* to purify Himself from the sin of killing Vatsasura, who had assumed the form of a calf.

Of course, no sin is involved in anything Krsna does. And Vatsasura was a wicked demon inimical to the Lord. Nonetheless, he looked like a calf, and killing a calf is just as sinful as killing a human being.

Consequently, when Krsna met the *gopis* here, they refused to talk to Him since He had been defiled by the greatest of sins. Krsna tried to reason with the girls, but they were in no mood for compromise.

“We are cowherds,” they said. “Our livelihood depends on our mother the cow and our father the bull. Thus a calf is like our own brother or sister. Do You think that words alone will expiate such a sin?”

Krsna had no idea how to win over the *gopis.* Explaining to them that He was the supreme pure and that Vatsasura’s soul had been liberated would hardly pacify the *gopis.* It would only start an argument.

Finally He surrendered. “What do you suggest?” He asked the girls. The *gopis* replied with one voice, “If You bathe in all the holy places of the universe, then, and only then, will You be free from Your sin.”

Krsna shrugged His shoulders as if to say “Is that all?” Playing His flute, He began to coax streams of water from the ground. Shortly those streams took on personified forms and introduced themselves.

The *gopis* were wide-eyed in amazement. After the personified holy places had disappeared, Krsna stuck His flute in the ground at the spot where the sacred waters were seeping out and created a well.

As the *gopis* looked on, Krsna cheerfully bathed with well water, singing cowherd songs and feeling pleased with Himself. After bathing and dressing, He again presented Himself before the *gopis.*

“Have I now been cleansed of sin?” Krsna asked. The *gopis* gave up their contrariness, clapped, cheered, and praised Krsna and His flute for the mystic power by which they performed such wonderful deeds.

Word quickly spread amongst the cowherd boys that Venu-kupa was equal to the holy places of the universe. Whenever they were in Bhandiravana, they would go there to bathe and drink the water.

One day Balarama came here to bathe, carefully placing His clothes and turban on a boulder nearby. He felt so much ecstasy as He bathed that the stones around Him, including the boulder, softened.

Balarama’s turban made an imprint in the boulder that can still be seen today beside the nearby temple where His Deity is worshipped. For this reason the well is also named after Him, Dauji-kupa.

Many other wonders are connected with this well, which draws pilgrims throughout the year. For example, if the new moon falls on a Monday, the well water is said to turn to milk on that day.

The same phenomenon happens on every appearance day of the twenty-four incarnations of Visnu. And on the appearance day of Dhruva, the ten incarnations of Visnu are said to appear there.

**\* \* \* \***

Just beyond Venu-kupa on the *parikrama* path is a temple of Sridama, which marks the place where Krsna’s dear friend once sat in sorrow. Two pastimes explain why this was a place of unhappiness for him.

On one particular day the *gopas* were playing in Bhandiravana in two teams. As usual, the losers had to carry the winners on their backs. Krsna’s side lost that day, so Krsna had to carry Sridama.

But cowherd boys from both teams objected to Krsna having to carry anyone on His back. One boy said, “Krsna is too weak to carry you, Sridama.” “Besides,” another said, “He is the son of the king.”

A third boy said, “And Garga Muni said that Krsna is as good as Narayana. Would you have Narayana carry you?” Finally the boys said in unison, “It is an offence for which you will surely be sorry.”

In the heat of childish play Sridama could not accept these arguments as being anything but excuses for Krsna to avoid His duty. “Krsna should abide by the rules like everyone else,” he protested.

“Although weak, a king’s son, and equal to Narayana, He tends cows, milks them, and carries pails of milk on His head. What is the difference between that and carrying a milkman on His shoulders?”

A few *gopas* took Sridama's side, but most chided him, saying, “If you make Krsna carry you, we will not let you play with us.” But Sridama was obstinate: “What makes you think I will want to play with you?”

After much argument, Sridama made Krsna, who had been silent on the issue, carry him to the Bhandiravata and back. As he got down from Krsna’s shoulders, Sridama raised his arms in a sign of victory.

But the other *gopas* did not share Sridama’s joy, and when he came to join them, they told Sridama, “We warned you, and now you can reap the bitter harvest of your offence and play by yourself.”

The boys neglected Sridama. No matter how much he tried, he could not convince the *gopas* to let him join them, and so while they played together, he sat in exile on the far side of Venu-kupa.

Sridama sat in sorrow with his head in his hands, not because he could not play, but because he could not play with Krsna. Suddenly he felt someone gently caress his shoulder and heard a soft voice say:

“Friend! I am your property.” It was Krsna, smiling at Sridama and speaking the sweetest words to him. “No matter what the others may say about you, I am always yours to do with as you please.”

Sridama looked at Krsna, who continued, “Even if you were as heavy as mount Meru, even if My father was the emperor of the world, or even if I was Narayana, I would consider it a privilege to carry you.”

Sridama's eyes filled with tears as he asked, “Am I not a burden for You like the others say?” Krsna took his hand, “Friend! It is not by the strength of muscles that I carry you, but by the strength of love.

“My love for you is such that when you are on My shoulders, I feel that a flower is resting there.” These sweet words wiped away Sridama's sorrow, and the two boys embraced and cried in bliss.

The other boys, who were watching this exchange from a distance, felt that they had been too harsh with Sridama. They welcomed him back into their group, and once again Sridama’s cries filled the air.

The other pastime involving Sridama’s lamentation relates to Krsna’s departure from Vrndavana. Like the Vraja-vasi men, Sridama had accompanied Krsna to Mathura and to the wrestling match.

Then, after Kamsa’s death, Sridama also returned with the Vraja- vasis to their homes and tried to continue life without Krsna. But it was not possible. How does a body continue to live without its soul?

Unable to bear the suffering of others and unwilling to increase the others’ suffering with his own, Sridama came to Bhandiravana, where he remembered the wonderful games he had played with Krsna.

Sridama lived in solitude beneath the trees of Bhandiravana and sustained his life by chanting Krsna’s names. Day after day, Sridama waited for Krsna to return because Krsna had said he would.

When they parted ways in Mathura, Sridama had asked Krsna, “How long before You return to us?” and Krsna answered, “It will take Me a few days to kill some demons. Then I will come back.”

Sridama had looked straight into Krsna’s eyes, but his friend could not meet his glance — he knew it would be more than a few days. “Brother!” Sridama said. “Until You return, I will not eat or drink.”

These words made signs of alarm flash on Krsna’s face. The last thing He wanted His friends to do was to add self-imposed austerities to the pain of being separated from Him. That He could not bear.

Krsna grabbed Sridama’s hand and said, “Don’t make Me suffer.” But His stubborn friend said, “Since You will only be gone a few days, a little fasting will do me good. We will feast when You return.”

As the caravan of Vraja-vasis slowly moved to the horizon, Sridama turned to follow it. After taking a few paces he turned back to look at Krsna, who had not taken His eyes off His beloved companion.

“Friend!” he called back to Krsna, “I will be waiting for You in Bhandiravana. When You return to Vraja, do not forget me. I won’t eat until I see Your lotus face. Don’t forget.” Then he walked away.

Whether Krsna would be gone from Vraja for a few days or for a few years didn’t matter much to Sridama. Every moment for him was like an eternity. He couldn’t tell the difference between days and years.

But Krsna came back. And when He did, He went to find Sridama in Bhandiravana at once. Crossing the Yamuna in His chariot, Krsna drove as far as Chaheri, from where He continued on foot.

Krsna searched the *gopas’* favourite stomping grounds until He found Sridama sitting beneath a tree, eyes closed in meditation like a great yogi, quietly chanting Krsna’s names, tears flowing down his cheeks.

Chanting Krsna’s names and living in the forest of Vrndavana had kept Sridama youthful looking, but his body was lean from fasting, his hair dishevelled and unkempt, his clothes faded and threadbare.

Krsna almost fainted to see His friend’s austere appearance — as the son of King Vrsabhanu, Sridama was no less a prince than He. Walking up to Sridama, Krsna softly said, “Friend! I have returned.”

Deep in meditation, Sridama heard Krsna’s voice but thought it was a part of his internal vision. He just went on chanting until he had heard several times, “Friend Sridama! Open your eyes. I am here.”

Gradually Sridama opened his lotus eyes and saw Krsna standing before him, dressed not as a *gopa* but as a king. Still, it was Krsna, who said, “See! I told you I would come back in just a few days.”

Again, whether it was a few days or a few years did not matter to Sridama. What mattered was that Krsna was back. Sridama rose to his feet, examined his friend closely, and then warmly embraced Him.

Yes, Krsna was hack! Sridama repeatedly caressed Krsna’s arms, hack, and shoulders to reassure himself that he was not just seeing things, that Krsna had physically returned. He felt his own life returning.

Yes, Krsna was hack! And as Sridama held his friend to his chest, the satisfaction of tightly holding onto the condensed form of bliss drove the vast emptiness from his heart and he wept aloud in happiness.

Krsna was hack! It had been more than a few days that the trees and vines of Bhandiravana had been standing barren in Krsna’s absence, hut now they showered the two friends with newly blossomed flowers.

Krsna would leave again, and again He would return. Sridama’s sitting place is the perfect spot for meditating on how separation from and meeting with Krsna eternally alternate like the changing seasons.
