This cycle of separation and meeting enriches the love between Krsna and His companions. By cultivating this mood, our own attachment to Krsna will increase until it becomes like Sridama's.

In fact, such perfection will come through surrendering to Sridama. Dasa Gosvami thus prays,

*krsnasyoccaih pranaya-vasatih sampravinah sakhinam syamangas tat-sama-gunam vayo-vesa-saundarya-darpah*  
*Snehad andhah ksanam akalanaj jayate yo ’vadhutah sridamanam hari-sahacaram sarvada tam prapadye*

**“Sridama-sakha is the most expert and clever of the cowherd boys of Vraja.**

**“He is the abode of the most intense love for Krsna. His complexion is dark, and he is proud that his qualities, age, clothing, and handsome features closely resemble that of his beloved friend.**

**“If for a single moment Sridama cannot see Krsna, whom he considers more dear than his own life, he trembles with anxiety. I completely take shelter of Sridama, the constant companion of the Lord.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Bhandiravana, especially at the Yamuna’s shore, is one of the most scenic and solitary parts of New Vraja-dhama. It is so conducive for remembering Krsna that I was reluctant to leave it behind.

But one special feature of *parikrama,* when approached in the proper mood, is that we are reluctant to leave every pastime place we visit. Only the lure of the next place gives us the inspiration to move on.

Heading north, I arrived at Matha, or Mathavana, a small forest where Krsna and Balarama played with Their friends as the cows grazed contentedly on the sweet grasses of its assorted pastures.

Varying accounts tell us the origin of Mathavana’s name. One account contends that the name is derived from the clay-like soil *(matha)* from which villagers manufacture cups, pots, plates, and so on.

More specifically, it is named after the large churning pots *(matha)* that were made here during Krsna’s time and the buttermilk that the villagers sold after churning their butter out of cream.

Others say this area is named after the pot of buttermilk *(matha)* that Krsna once knocked over while He and His friends were busy stealing milk products from the homes of the villagers in this area.

Still others contend that because the woodlands, fruit orchards, and gardens here are replete with pastures *(matha),* the entire area became known as Mathavana, the “forest of pastures.”

When Siva was bewildered by Lord Krsna’s Mohini-murti incarnation and was chasing after Her, he discharged semen. It is also said that a drop of Mahadevas semen fell at Mathavana.

Sri Suka says,

**“Following Mohini, Lord Siva went everywhere — near the shores of the rivers and lakes, near the mountains, near the forests, near the gardens, and wherever great sages lived.”**

Visvanatha comments that Mohini-murti dragged Lord Siva through hermitages to show the sages that even a self-controlled person like Siva can become bewildered in the company of beautiful women.

Scriptures repeatedly warn that everyone, even liberated souls, should avoid mingling or dallying with any member of the opposite sex other than one’s own spouse, especially in a solitary place.

From Mathavana I walked along the path to where it makes a sharp right. There I stopped to see the southern and southwestern petals of New Vraja-dhama on the western side of the Yamuna.

Opposite to Tapovana on this side of the Yamuna is the forest of Bhusanavana. The *gopas* ornamented *(bhusana)* Krsna there with fresh sprouts, leaves, and flowers, all beautified by His touch.

The cowherd boys, wondering how this was possible, immersed themselves in discussing Krsna’s transcendental form. They concluded that Krsna was the ornament of all ornaments.

Krsna appears in many wonderful forms in countless incarnations, but His original form as a cowherd boy in the full bloom of youth is most suited to His transcendental pastimes as a human being.

Krsna is especially adept at the arts of dancing and flute playing, skills that enhance the sweetness of His transcendental form, which attracts everyone and submerges the pious in love for Him.

One cowherd boy asked, “What is Krsna’s butter-soft body made of?” Another boy answered, “It is pure transcendence, pure goodness in its original form. What else could be so sweet and attractive?”

A third *gopa* said, “Whatever it is made of, it is our secret treasure.” But another boy argued, “Sri Radha and Her friends would not agree with you. They think that Krsna’s beauty is their treasure.”

And still another boy added, “Krsna’s bodily beauty is so sublime that it even attracts Him. Upon seeing His own reflection, Krsna thinks of becoming a *gopi* just to know what Radha tastes by seeing Him.”

In this way, as some *gopas* served Krsna fruits and sweets, others discussed His beauty and how His other opulences — knowledge, wealth, strength, fame, and renunciation — all serve that one.

The reason Krsna’s beauty is so unique is that—unlike His other opulences, which can also be found in Vaikuntha — the sweetness and intimacy He displays in Vrndavana cannot be found anywhere else.

Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu spoke of Krsna’s beauty to Sanatana Gosvami:

**“Ornaments caress that body, but the transcendental body of Krsna is so beautiful that it beautifies the ornaments He wears.**

**“Therefore Krsna’s body is said to be the ornament of ornaments. Enhancing the wonderful beauty of Krsna is His three-curved style of standing, and above all these beautiful features —**

**“Krsna’s eyes dance and move obliquely, acting like arrows to pierce the minds of Srimati Radharani and the** ***gopis.*** **When the arrow succeeds in hitting its target, their minds become agitated.”**

The *gopis’* attraction to Krsna cannot be compared to the infatuation ordinary young girls have for a handsome boy. The transcendental influence of Krsna’s bodily beauty is seen in its universal effect.

Krsna is attractive not only to demigods and other residents of this universe but also to the presiding Deities of the Vaikuntha planets, and even to Their chaste wives, the goddesses of fortune.

Still, the intensity of Krsna’s appeal varies according to the devotion of the beholder. Amongst all devotees, the *gopis* are supreme; thus, they see Him in His full beauty as the transcendental Cupid.

Krsna’s five arrow-like weapons — form, taste, smell, sound, and touch — conquer the obstinate minds of the beautiful gopis and impel them to enjoy the *rasa* dance and other transcendental pastimes.

In that festival of dancing, music, and loving embraces, the *gopis* taste the sweetness of Krsna’s beauty that others merely talk about, and thus the *gopis* become objects of worship for all lovers of the Lord.

The topic of Krsna’s beauty is endless, but the *gopas* had to return home, and so their discussion ended. Surrounding the ornament of ornaments, they walked with Him back to Nandagrama.

It was in New Vraja-dhama’s Bhusanavana in 1994 that the Hungarian *yatra* first began to observe summer festivals in a makeshift temple that was later replaced by a large tent.

Those were extraordinary days. In exchange for chanting Hare Krsna in the company of senior devotees, everyone welcomed the excitement of austerity: tent living, bucket showers, and simple fare.

The Gosvamis and their immediate successors gave up opulent lives to reside as mendicants in Vrndavana. And for the pioneers of New Vraja-dhama, austerity was the hallmark of those first few years.

As in Bhauma Vrndavana, things in New Vraja-dhama have developed: devotees now live in comfortable homes with running water, electricity is provided by solar panels, and pathways are paved.

After the completion of the Krsna-Balarama temple in Ramana-reti, Srila Prabhupada also lived in a house with all amenities to show us how to maintain the spirit of Vraja in comfortable surroundings.

The essence of Vrndavana is to keep Krsna at the centre of our lives by talking about Him and chanting His names in the company of pure devotees. That Vrndavana spirit is available under any circumstances.

And yet as I looked out over the meadows between Bhandiravana and Bhusanavana, I could not help but feel nostalgic for a time when youthful enthusiasm enhanced the Vraja spirit of New Vraja-dhama.

Then again, the fruit orchard that covers the hillside overlooking that stretch of land reminded me that with each successive year those trees bear sweet fruit that we offer to Radha and Syama.

Similarly, with the passing of time, Krsna Valley sees the birth of devotee children, our “hope for the future,” who with their youthful enthusiasm for Krsna will keep fresh the spirit of the *dhama.*

One way to keep that spirit fresh is to observe festivals associated with Vraja and with our Vaisnava tradition, such as those described in the appendix “The Yearly Festivals of New Vraja-dhama.”

**\* \* \* \***

From Bhusanavana I turned my attention to a remote area of New Vraja-dhama, its southwestern petal, the farthest part of which is not yet the legal property of Radha and Syamasundara.

At the very tip of the petal is Bhajana. Like Kosikala in Vraja during Krsna’s time, Bhajana was a sleepy market town where the *gopas* would buy and sell cows, even though the market in Kosi was better.

In a forest not far from Bhajana the cowherd girls and some of the cowherd boys once came together to worship *(bhajana)* the divine couple with songs *(bhajana*s) about Their qualities and pastimes.

After a day of playing Holi, Radha and Krsna retired to the dense blossoming forest gardens that abounded in this remote perimeter of the *dhama* rarely visited by anyone. Their privacy was assured.

Settling down in one such garden beneath a cluster of trees heavily laden with fruit and flowers, Radha and Krsna rested and accepted the loving service of Their intimate *gopi* and *gopa* friends.

Most cowherd boys have no access to Krsna’s amorous dealings with Radha and the *gopis;* only a rare few have such privilege, such as His dearest friends (*priya-narma-sakhas*) Subala, Arjuna, and Ujjvala.

As mentioned earlier, the groves around Syama-kunda belong to these intimate *gopa* friends of Krsna, who serve the divine couple under the guidance of the most confidential gopis *(asta-sakhis).*

Like those *gopis,* these *gopas* have firm confidence (*visrambha*) that they are equal to Krsna, which results in very intimate dealings with Him and makes these *gopas’* love quite appealing to the Lord.

Increasing degrees of intimacy distinguish friendship from servitude, parental love from friendship, and amorous from parental love. In intimacy, the love of the *priya-narma-sakhas* resembles amorous love.

In Bhauma Vrndavana three categories of these *gopas* have access to serving Krsna in His amorous dealings with the *gopis:* the eternally perfect, perfected practitioners, and those who were once demigods.

These *gopas* help decorate Radha and Krsna, entertain Them, fan Them, and care for Them in various ways. In Bhajana they were engaged in singing delightful songs to glorify the divine couple.

As usual, these boys were each under the tutelage of a different *gopi,* and together the boys and girls created a wonderful atmosphere that intensified the divine couple’s yearning for each other.

To accompany the boys’ singing, the *gopis* danced and played out dramas with the movements of their hands and eyes. With these arts they evoked shouts of praise from both Radha and Krsna.

The domain of amorous love is ruled by the *gopis,* and it should always he understood in that way. If any cowherd boys are present in such exchanges, it is only by the invitation and supervision of the *gopis.*

Jiva Gosvami, in his elaborate analysis of the amorous mellow, implies this in his mention of the *gopas:*

**“The cowherd boys are only briefly mentioned here. Although many cowherd boys —**

**“Such as the** ***priya-sakhas*** **and** ***narma-sakhas*** **are very close friends of Lord Krsna, because they are males, an elaborate description of them here in the midst of a discussion of the** ***gopis*** **is inappropriate.”**

Here again we should note Jiva Gosvami’s instruction that certain pastimes are not to be heard or repeated by devotees, even though these pastimes are certainly part of Krsna’s Vrndavana life.

One example is Krsna's display of amorous attraction even as a child of three or five. Srila Prabhupada says that learned scholars do not discuss this topic because the age is inappropriate for such activities.

We must therefore practise caution and use discrimination in studying Krsna’s pastimes and in sharing them with others, being careful to always take guidance from learned senior Vaisnavas.

North of Bhajana is Parasauli, where the Vraja-vasis worshipped a deity of goddess Katyayani, the deity to whom the *gopis* turned to for shelter in the days that followed Krsna’s departure from Vrndavana.

After Radha and Visakha had entered the sun planet through the waters of the Yamuna, another 16,100 gopis worshipped Katyayani on the riverbank, praying that Krsna might return to Vrndavana.

But the demon Bhaumasura kidnapped the *gopis* and held them captive in Pragyotisa-pura. After having moved to Dvaraka, Krsna killed the demon, rescued the girls, and accepted them as His wives.

In describing the pastime of Krsna’s conquest over Bhaumasura, the *Visnu Purana* states, “Within the maidens’ quarters, O wise one, that Lord of unequalled prowess found 16,100 princesses.”

Just as the Krsna of Vrndavana appeared in His plenary portion as the Lord of Dvaraka, the young Vraja *gopis* appeared in expansions as Krsna’s queens, living with His children in luxurious palaces.

In summary, as Katyayani-devi once fulfilled the desires of the *kanya kumaris* to have Krsna as their husband, she also fulfilled the Vraja *gopis’* desires to be reunited with Him in Dvaraka.

One aspect of this pastime clears the doubts of those who think that the contamination of past sins disqualifies one from going back to Godhead: Krsna accepted kidnapped women as His own wives.

Vedic culture enjoins that an unmarried woman who spends the night in the house of a man — for whatever reason — is tainted by sin and thus ineligible for marriage and unable to reside anywhere else.

Yet, despite their misfortune, the captured *gopis* harboured only one desire, *bhuyat patir ayam mahyam dhata tad anumodatam:* “May providence grant that this man become my husband.”

Impressed with their sincerity, Krsna overlooked whatever external considerations there may have been and accepted these women as His wives, embracing them to His heart without reservation.

If we remain similarly fixed in our determination to attain Krsna, despite past disqualifications and the contamination of unfortunate circumstances, Krsna will accept us as He did the imprisoned girls.

Rupa Gosvami quotes an unknown Vaisnava saint who glorifies the fact that Krsna appreciates whatever sentiment of surrender *(bhava' grahi)* we may have, disregarding our external inadequacies:

**“Because He is very affectionate, Krsna promises to give fearlessness to His devotees by removing their sufferings and their sins, and in return generously bestowing upon them limitless auspiciousness.**

**“Prahlada, Vibhisana, Gajendra, Draupadi, Ahalya, and Dhruva testify to the virtue of the Lord’s affection to devotees; thus, O world, serve the husband of the goddess of fortune and no one else.”**

Nohajhila lies at the centre of the southwestern petal and just outside New Vraja-dhama’s border. In Bhauma Vrndavana it is surrounded by a marsh *(jhila*) that is not connected to the Yamuna but fed by rain.

The land was swampy even in Krsna’s time, so the *gopas* would avoid the area. But while their cows grazed in nearby pastures, from a distance they would watch the flocks of waterfowl nesting there.

Some parts of Vraja are not as well known as others. They are not connected to specific pastimes of the Lord; still, they lie within the precincts of His eternal abode, so they are also worthy of our respect.

The various parts of our bodies may be of greater or lesser importance in relation to one another, but because they are all integral to our physical existence and well-being, they all require care and attention.

Just inside the road that marks the boundary of New Vraja-dhama’s current property is Baghari, which gets its name from a large tiger *(vyaghra)* that once threatened the *gopas* but was driven away.

Though fear personified is afraid of Krsna, in His human-like pastimes *(nara-lila)* He sometimes exhibits fear to increase His devotees’ love for Him and to taste the pleasure of taking shelter in others.

During Krsna’s time the area from Mathavana to Nohajhila was a dense jungle with hardly any arable land. Humans avoided the area, but wild animals like black deer, boar, and tigers lived there happily.

On their way to Marava, Bhajana, or Raya, the cowherd boys would usually skirt this jungle on one side or the other. But at times, while the cows rested, they would venture boldly within its borders.

Sometimes the boys would track wild animals, at other times they would enact the pastimes of Rama, hunting demons who had assumed the guise of animals, like Marici, who had become the golden deer.

Once, while walking along the forest path on such an escapade, the boys came face to face with a tiger. And it was no ordinary tiger, but a beast so large that its shoulders towered over the frightened boys.

Like an ordinary child, Krsna at once yelled, “*Vyaghra! Vyaghra!*” and turning on His heels He ran in the direction from which He had come, followed by His terrified friends, screaming as they ran.

That same infallible boy of boundless strength who had, all by Himself, fearlessly combated powerful demons like Baka, Vatsa, and Agha, now ran for dear life from a relatively insignificant tiger.

Balarama, Subala, and some of the braver boys guarded Krsna from behind with sticks, but they too were influenced by Krsna’s unusual lack of courage and didn’t stand their ground in the face of danger.

As for the tiger, he was a resident of Vraja. Having regularly heard the sound of Krsna’s flute, he may have looked fierce, but his heart was full of devotion, so he bounded after the boys like a playful dog.

This was the tiger’s first sight of Krsna. Enchanted by the wielder of the flute, the gigantic cat was understandably curious. Krsna and the *gopas* turned and ran, but this *vyaghra* wanted to get a closer look.

Yogamaya surely must have enjoyed watching the comedy she had staged as she saw the boys repeatedly looking fearfully over their shoulders, shouting, “It’s coming after us! Run faster! Faster!”

To get the attention of someone, anyone, farmers or villagers nearby, the boys filled the jungle with screams of “Tiger! Tiger!” When they finally reached the village, they ran through shouting, “Tiger!”

Hearing the cries of “Tiger!”, many village men grabbed sticks and machetes. As soon as the creature came into view they charged it en masse, making loud noises by screaming and beating pots.

When the tiger saw these armed men charging at him, he quickly jumped off the forest path into the thick bushes and disappeared, happy to have seen Krsna, but sad that he could not see more of Him.

Because the cowherd boys called out *vyaghra* (“tiger”) as they ran through the village, that forest hamlet was renamed Vyaghari. Today it is known as Baghari, the place where Krsna ran in fear of a tiger.

Sukadeva Gosvami confirms that during play Krsna would sometimes imitate bird calls, or sometimes He would “...run away \[along\] with the smaller animals in mock fear of lions and tigers.”

**\* \* \* \***

To the west of Baghari is Raya, one of Nanda Maharaja’s many storehouses in Vraja. To the north of that is Venuya, where Krsna spoke to the *gopis* with His flute and pacified their minds.

Before Krsna and the *gopis* first met, the young girls of Vraja would spend their days wistfully thinking of Him. Sometimes they gathered together in small groups to talk about Him in hushed tones.

Each *gopi* felt the type of separation a girl feels when she is in love but has not yet had a rendezvous with her lover *(purva-raga).* In this state the flute plays a major role in requiting the *gopis*’ loving feelings.

The *gopis* saw the flute as their primary rival, but they also recognized it as a friend, just as amongst themselves they sometimes vied for Krsna’s attention but also felt a common bond as objects of His love.

The flute had already attained the nectar of Krsna’s lips — a treasure the *gopis* could as of yet only dream about — but even while envi- ously criticising the flute, they also felt themselves in its debt. Why?

The sound of the flute put the *gopis’* minds at rest — it let them know that Krsna was happy and free from danger. And His happiness was their ultimate goal, despite their own sadness at not being with Him.

The transcendental nature of the flute is such that, with the same tune, it can communicate a variety of messages to suit the devotional moods of a variety of listeners. This was the case at Venuya.

From atop a small hill, Krsna played a captivating melody on His flute, a melody that told the cows not to stray too far. To those that had strayed, it called them by name and told them to quickly return.

Meanwhile, some cowherd boys had gone in search of fruits for a snack. To them the flute said, “I am starving! How long will I have to wait?” Filling their baskets, the boys hurried back to Venuya.

In Vrndavana, Mother Yasoda was always in anxiety for Her son. As she instructed tailors and jewellers in creating a new wardrobe for Krsna, she heard the flute say, “Mother! I am all right. Don’t worry!”

And as the *gopis* went about their household chores or gossiped in back lanes, they heard the flute say, “Sometime soon, fate will arrange for us to meet.” The flute made them blush and cover their faces.

Because Krsna’s flute conveyed messages individually suited to Vraja- vasis of all description throughout Vrndavana, especially to the *gopis,* the hill where Krsna played the flute is known as Venura.

Not far from where I stood are two pastime places: Harasali, where Krsna and the *gopis* enjoyed *rasa* dancing, and Varahara, where Krsna, at play with His friends, took the form of a boar a second time.

In the *rasa* dance, Krsna, who is also called Hari, captures the minds of all the *gopis* but one — Sri Radha; indeed, She captures His mind. For this feat She is called Hara, and this village is known as Harasali.

Harasali-vasis proclaim that the *rasa* dance, though described in general terms as Krsna’s dance with the cowherd girls of Vraja, is more precisely Radha’s and Krsna’s dance in the company of many girls.

Radha and Krsna are two halves of the indivisible Absolute Truth. *Acaryas* such as Rupa Gosvami have therefore disclosed some of Krsna’s names that proclaim Their mutual interdependence.

Srimati Radharani’s pivotal stature in the *rasa* dance dawns on the horizon of the thoughtful Vaisnava’s heart as he sings and contemplates these names at pastime places such as Harasali.

Krsna is *radhika-hrdayonmadi vamsi-kvana-madhu-cchatah* and *radha*-p*arimalodgara garimaksipta-manasah,* He whose honeyed flute music maddens Radha’s mind, and whose heart is stirred by Her fragrance.

He is also called *kamra-radha-mano-mina-badisi-krta-vibhramah,* the fisherman prince of Vrndavana whose charming pastimes are the hooks He casts to catch the fish of beautiful Radharani’s heart.

He is *prema-garvandha-gandharva-kilakincita-ranjitah,* He who is attracted by Radha’s ingenious amorous devices, who is as blinded by love for Him as She is by Her own contrary feminine pride.

Krsna is also known as la*litavsya-dhi-radha-manabhasa-vasi-krtah, t*he supreme independent person who is controlled by the slightest shadow of unsubmissive Radha’s jealous loving anger.

He is also known as *radha-vakrokti-piyusa-madhurya-bhara-lampatah,* the one who is always greedy to taste the sweet nectar of Srimati Radharani’s expertly phrased and ingeniously crooked words.

Krsna is called *mukhendu-candrikodghurna-radhika-raga-sagarah,* the soothing rays from whose full-moon face cause great tidal waves to swell and crash in the bottomless ocean of Srimati Radharani’s love.

He is also known as *vrsabhanu-suta-kantha-hari-hara-harinmanih,* the handsome sapphire necklace that decorates the graceful neck of King Vrsabhanu’s delightful daughter, Srimati Radharani.

Krsna is also called *phulla-radhika-mallini-mukhambuja-madhuvratah,* a restless and resolute bumblebee that constantly hovers over the dark red blossoming lotus flower of Srimati Radharani’s mouth.

And finally He is called *radhika-kuca-kasturi-patra-sphurad-urah- sthalah,* He whose chest is attractively decorated with the musk that was once the ointment smeared upon Srimati Radharani’s breasts.

Rupa Gosvami says that just by reading these ten names, devotees become dearer to Sri Krsna. Then they will be able to understand the mysteries of the Lord’s special attachment to Srimati Radharani.

At Varahara, Krsna again revealed the opulence and majesty of His boar incarnation to His wonderstruck friends, as He had done for them at Apsara-kunda and for the *gopis* at Varaha-ghata.

The *gopas* had already seen Krsna display this form, but His friends were just as amazed to see it as they had been before. It was as if they had never seen it. Such is the inconceivable nature of divine love.

In a pure devotee’s heart, love for Lord Krsna induces astonishment with everything related to Him — form, qualities, and activities. The greater the love, the greater the sense of astonishment.

Moreover, since the cowherd boys’ love for Krsna is always increasing, their astonishment at seeing Him as a gigantic boar blossomed, enhancing their already heightened feelings of love even further.

And the boys saw not only the towering form of a boar in front of them but also the entire pastime of Lord Varaha’s lifting the earth from the bottom of the ocean and His fighting with Hiranyaksa.

The cowherd boys saw the universal ocean and, within it, two great combatants with their unlimited strength wielding divine weapons and locked in fierce battle for the future of the earth planet.

Awestruck, the boys heard the thunderous roars of the two adversaries, saw the sparks of their clashing weapons become stars, and felt the spray from the agitated waves of the Garbhodaka Ocean.

Finally they saw Lord Varaha rob the life of the golden-haired demon Hiranyaksa with a casual slap to the head and heard the *devas* praise the Lord as they celebrated His victory with *kirtana* and *puspanjali.*

In Nanda Maharaja’s court, the *gopas* had heard bards recite the narrative Krsna had just brought to life. And their mothers had many times told them the same tale in soft voices to put them to sleep.

Once Krsna had closed the curtain on the pastime of His second incarnation, the *gopas* stood and wondered whether what they saw had been real, or just another one of Krsna’s magic tricks.

Whatever they had seen was further evidence of how extraordinary Krsna is, be He God or a magician. The *gopas* took turns repeatedly embracing Him as they drove their cows towards Mathavana.

That night the *gopas,* even as they were being bathed and dressed for bed, excitedly demanded that each member of their households listen to how Krsna had conjured up the form and pastimes of Lord Varaha.

The love and wonder flowing from the mouths and eyes of the boys was so contagious that the elder Vraja-vasis, who loved Krsna with all their hearts, were swept away on the waves of their sons’ narrations.

Long after both children and adults had gone to sleep, the vessels of their minds continued to ply the ocean of Krsna’s pastimes in their dreams, rising and falling in the waves of astonishing love.

**\* \* \* \***

I continued to walk west, which meant climbing uphill. All- auspicious Bhadravana, the favourite forest of Balabhadra, Lord Balarama, was to my right as I began what would be the last phase of my *parikrama.*

Krsna’s elder brother is called Rama because He pleases the residents of Vrndavana, especially Krsna. He is also called Balabhadra, because His extensive strength is the cause of auspiciousness (*bhadra*).

By using His strength to subdue demons, Balarama makes Vraja auspicious. By empowering devotees with spiritual strength, He makes their lives auspicious — they are destined for all-auspicious Goloka.

Just as Lord Krsna’s favourite forest, Vrndavana, is named after Vrnda-devi, Lord Balarama’s favourite forest, Bhadravana — the forest of auspiciousness — is named after Him, Balabhadra.

Even a casual visit to Bhadravana assures one residence in either Nagaloka or the heavenly planets. What, then, can be said of the destination of one who actually resides there, as did Rupa Gosvami?

While residing on the bank of Bhadra-sarovara, Rupa Gosvami completed his enchanting drama *Lalita-madhava,* which he began many years earlier under the direction of Queen Satyabhama.

On his first visit to Vraja, Rupa Gosvami, inspired to write a book about Krsna’s pastimes, made an outline of the drama, which he continued to develop in Puri during his visit with Lord Caitanya.

On his way to Puri, in a village called Satyabhama-pura in Orissa, Queen Satyabhama came to Rupa in a dream and said, “Write a separate drama about Me. By My mercy it will be especially beautiful.”

Upon waking, Rupa Gosvami thought, “Satyabhama-devi has ordered me to write a drama about Her; thus the pastimes I have collected should be divided into two: one set about Vraja, the other Dvaraka.”

Once he had arrived in Jagannatha Puri, Rupa Gosvami took up residence with Haridasa Thakura. Sri Rupa soon met Lord Caitanya, who had been anticipating the arrival of His dear servant.

The day after Rupa Gosvami arrived, the Lord paid him another visit. As the Lord was leaving, He casually said, “Do not try to take Krsna out of Vrndavana, for He does not go anywhere else at any time.”

Caitanya Mahaprabhu also recited this well-known verse from the *Yamala-tantra*,

*krsno ’nyo yadu-sambhuto yah purnah so ’sty atah parah*  
*vrndavanam pantyajya sa kvacin naiva gacchati*

**“The Krsna known as Yadu-kumara is Vasudeva Krsna \[of the first** ***catur-vyuha*****\]. He is different from the Krsna who is the son of Nanda Maharaja \[the original Personality of Godhead,** ***svayam-bhagavan*****\].**

**“Yadu-kumara Krsna manifests His pastimes in the cities of Mathura and Dvaraka, but Krsna the son of Nanda Maharaja never at any time leaves Vrndavana.”**

After saying this, the Lord left.

Sri Rupa could at once understand that Lord Caitanya had confirmed Satyabhama’s order to divide his one book into two separate dramas: one about Syamasundara, and one about Vasudeva Krsna.

Rupa Gosvami divided his drama, giving each its own invocation and introduction. The first, about Krsna’s Vraja pastimes, he called *Vidagdha-madhava,* the second, His life in Dvaraka, *Lalita-madhava.*

Rupa Gosvami began the task of dividing the work into two parts in Puri in Sakabda 1437. *Vidagdha-madhava* was finished in Gokula in Sakabda 1454, and *Lalita-madhava,* in Bhadravana in Sakabda 1459.

Srila Prabhupada has often advised us to learn about Vrndavana and Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes there by reading the books our *acaryas* have written, not by prematurely trying to reside in the *dhama.*

It is in just that context that His Divine Grace refers to *Lalita*-m*adhava:*

**“Actually going to Vrndavana involves taking shelter of the Six Gosvamis by reading the** ***Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu*** **—**

**“*****Vidagdha-madhava, Lalita-madhava,*** **and the other books that they have given. In this way one can understand the transcendental loving affairs between Radha and Krsna.”**

It behoves us to take this advice.

More than any other book I have read — aside from Srila Prabhupada’s own books, of course — *Lalita-madhava* has awakened my desire to understand the pastimes of the divine couple.

Although *Vidagdha-madhava* is full of Krsna’s Vraja pastimes, *Lalita-madhava* is richer in the moods of separation, which increase the reader’s hankering to see Radha and Krsna united in Vrndavana.

Bhadravana is an exceptional place to read, to remember, or to hear this wonderful book, because Srila Rupa Gosvami completed it there. He writes,

**“In the Sakabda year 1459, in the month of Sukra —**

**“On Sunday, the fourteenth day of the moon, after offering my respectful obeisances to Lord Sri Krsna, I completed this book** ***\[Lalita-madhava\]*** **in the forest of Bhadravana. Standing on the shore —**

**“Of the deep river of transcendental mellows, I have freely sprinkled its nectarean waters in all directions \[in the form of the words contained in my book\]. I pray the exalted devotees will forgive me.”**

The name Bhadravana generally refers to the single forest, but the name is also used to indicate all five forests of Balabhadra, just as Krsnavana indicates Krsna’s seven forests in Vraja-mandala.

In New Vraja-dhama, the row of trees that runs through the centre of the *dhama's* western petal delimits the upper portion of the individual forest named Bhadravana, most of which is a fertile agricultural field.

The crops grown in that field include wheat, mustard, and oats. Every year the residents of New Vraja-dhama gratefully take part in the joyous midsummer harvest festival celebrated there.

On a sunny summer morning, to the musical accompaniment of a resounding *kirtana,* devotees carry Govardhana Lala to the tree-line holder of Bhadravana and celebrate their most important festival.

We can neither chant Hare Krsna nor worship Radha and Syamasundara without eating, and so we consider the harvest festival essential to both our physical well-being and our spiritual lives.

Cowherds, *pujaris, sannyasis, grhasthas,* adults, children — everyone tries their hand at cutting wheat with a scythe and turning over the soil with a plough pulled by a team of oxen. It’s great fun for all.

*Kirtana* fills this attractive corner of the *dhama* as the devotees cook fresh grain and vegetables on a cow-dung fire. We also thresh some of the freshly cut wheat and then stone-grind and sift it on the spot.

When the wheat flour is ready, the cooks make Vraja-vasi-style *capatis,* and while all this is going on we sit in the shade to hear about the importance of depending on the land, the cows, and the oxen.

Finally, the lunch is offered to Govardhana Lala, and after He has eaten His remnants are served to the devotees. The taste of this feast, being the taste of simple living and high thinking, is second to none.

Bhadravana is truly auspicious, for it is not only the place favoured by Lord Balabhadra’s pastimes but also the source of our grains, which Krsna personally declares to be the very means of subsistence.

On His *parikrama* of Vraja, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu visited Bhadravana. From there the Lord continued on towards Gokula, passing through forest-like Mahavana along the way.

**\* \* \* \***

Vaikuntha-pura is situated in the southeastern corner of Bhadravana. It was there in Bhauma Vrndavana, at the repeated insistence of His friends, that Krsna revealed the unlimited expanse of Vaikuntha.

The cowherd boys were reminded of Krsna’s divine powers as they passed by Varahara on the way to Bhadravana. Their chatter gradually led them to request Krsna to again display His god hood.

“Friend,” the boys said, “if you truly are Narayana, then You should show us Your eternal abode, the spiritual sky, and Your eternal companions like Garuda and Laksmi-devi. This is our request.”

Krsna replied, “My dear friends! Why do you want to sec a place inferior to your own and a form of Mine that cannot satisfy your hearts? Instead, let us play in nearby Bhadravana and enjoy.”

But the boys thought Krsna was merely trying to avoid their request. One boy said, “How can you say that Vrndavana is better than Vaikuntha, or that seeing Narayana would not be pleasing to us?”

Another boy added, “These are just excuses. Either fulfil our desire, or admit Your inability to do so. But if You keep bluffing, as You arc no doubt doing now, we will not allow You to play with us today.”

Krsna was not at all happy that their fun was being interrupted by this request, but His friends were adamant, and so He reasoned that the fastest way to get back to playing was to submit.

Raising His arms and speaking loudly enough to silence His babbling friends, Krsna said, “Join your palms in front of you, close your eyes, and say this prayer to the Supreme Lord: *om namo narayanaya”*

The cowherd boys did just that. When they opened their eyes they saw the vast expanse of the spiritual sky with its unlimited Vaikuntha planets floating by them like bubbles rising to the top of a pond.

The planets glowed with radiant opulence that filled the vast space in between them, and although both planets and space were limitless, their entirety was inconceivably visible in the limited sky of Vraja.

Whichever expansion of Krsna a gopa was curious to see, the respective planet, the form of the Lord, and the corresponding residents appeared before him in an unending spiritual landscape.

The predominant feature of the Vaikuntha planets was their overwhelming spiritual opulence, which manifested in various ways to match the unique devotional moods of each planet’s residents.

Each of these Vaikuntha-vasis is endowed with nearly unlimited powers to facilitate the awe-inspiring ways in which they serve the Supreme Lord; still, they always feel like paupers who possess nothing.

The residents of Vaikuntha often dress and ornament themselves like the Lord Himself, their bodily features are sometimes identical to His, and their mystic powers are only slightly less powerful than His own.

In all places and at all times they joyfully sing Vedic hymns and prayers that describe the Lord’s features and prowess and His mission in re-establishing religious principles in the material world.

Some Vaikuntha-vasis even sing of His earthly pastimes as a *gopa,* although they never cease to worship Him with reverence. Nor do they ever call Him by name, but rather address Him always as “Lord.”

These visions left the *gopas* awestruck, but the boys missed the sweet sports of Vraja. The Vaikuntha planets did not accommodate the casual friendship they had with Krsna. How could they be attracted?

It was just as Krsna had predicted: the vision of Vaikuntha and the forms of Lord Narayana could not satisfy the *gopas'* hearts. Then, just to reinforce this truth, Krsna performed another miracle.

Suddenly the Lord’s Vaikuntha forms took on the appearance of Krsna, and Narayana’s associates transformed into Vraja-vasis. Laksmi and Her maidens became *gopis,* the Lord’s servants were gopas.

The gardens of Vaikuntha instantly became Vrndavana, where cows wandered about just as they do in Gokula. For a moment it appeared to the cowherd boys that Vaikuntha was exactly like Vrndavana.

But that conviction was only momentary because, despite their seeing everything as Vraja, it didn’t feel like Vraja. Where there should have been intimacy and sweetness there was formality and reverence.

Even as they observed the Lord of Vaikuntha moving about just like Krsna, the boys could sense that Vaikuntha’s so-called Vraja-vasis could not bring themselves to exchange intimately with their Lord.

Moreover, this knowledge — that the Vraja they were seeing was actually Vaikuntha, and that the Krsna there was really Narayana — invoked feelings of reverence within the *gopas’* own hearts.

Such feelings strongly conflicted with the *gopas’* spontaneous loving mood, and this conflict of mellows increasingly disturbed their minds, causing them to feel dissatisfied and eventually morose.

Beset with sadness, the *gopas* thought, “In Vaikuntha there is no prince of cowherds with whom we can share friendly embraces and humorous talks. This place is not for us. We don’t like it here.”

As soon as the *gopas* had come to this conclusion, Krsna removed the vision of Vaikuntha and its Lord and residents, and allowed the boys to once again perceive the sights and sounds of Bhadravana.

In a joking voice Krsna said, “O friends! You have seen the highest abode, the ultimate goal, the place where there is no anxiety. Why then do your faces show such pronounced signs of dissatisfaction?”

Overjoyed to see their friend, the cowherd boys crowded around Krsna, embraced Him, and congratulated Him for showing them Vaikuntha. Then they disclosed the root cause of their unease.

The *gopas* said, “Neither the opulent abode of Vaikuntha nor its master, the husband of the goddess of fortune, please our hearts as much as sporting intimately with You in Vrndavana.

“Whatever Garga Muni or the other sages or the scriptures may say about You, we only want to follow Your earlier advice and play by that lake in Bhadravana. Let’s not waste another moment. Let’s go!”

Rejoicing in the intimate spirit of His friends, Krsna pointed to a tree in the distance and cried, “Let’s race to that tree!” At once He ran through the field, His friends running close behind Him.

Further along in a leafy forest is Sarakoriya, where Krsna conjured up so much milk at His friends’ request that the cream (*sara*) the *gopas* skimmed off and ate forced them into blissful immobility.

It was one of those rare days when the boys’ lunch packs failed to arrive on time. Seeing no immediate solution to their hunger, the *gopas* turned to Krsna in desperation, calling out, “Gopala!

“You must be as hungry as we are! Until our lunches arrive, please find a little milk for us to drink.” Krsna at once responded to His friends’ discomfort and thought, “Why should they just have a little!”

Having resolved to alleviate their hunger, and without another thought, Krsna clapped His hands and pots of milk suddenly appeared beside each boy, filling the *gopas*’ hearts with wonderment and joy.

Every boy had two large pitchers of milk — more than he could possibly drink by himself. They all sat down at once and joyfully drank to their hearts’ content, praising Krsna all the while.

After finishing his first pitcher, each hoy skimmed the cream from his second pitcher and, with gusto, ate the cream as dessert, saving the skimmed milk to drink with his lunch when it finally arrived.

Eventually the servants appeared, carrying the *gopas'* lunches on their shoulders. They found all the boys asleep amidst milk pitchers scattered here and there. It was a surprising but amusing sight.

**\* \* \* \***

Bhadravana is bordered by fragrant Lohavana. Simply *seeing* Lohavana frees one from sin. Krsna and His friends enjoy herding cows in this forest, once the residence of the demon Lohajangha.

The first pastime place in Lohavana is Krsna-kunda. Here, near the Krsna-kupa well, the demon Lohajanghasura lived in a hillside cave and greedily dominated the entire forest area as if it belonged to him.

Amongst oral traditions there is a difference of opinion over who killed Lohajangha, Krsna or Satrughna. The *Varaha Purana* simply says, “The demon Lohajanghasura was killed at this place.”

One version contends that Krsna killed a demon near this well, a demon with skin *(jangha)* like iron *(loha).* However, authoritative sources such as *Srimad-Bhagavatam* give no such account.

A second account attests that it was Satrughna who killed Lohajangha, a feat he perfomed when Lord Ramacandra sent Him to Madhuvana to kill Lavana, son of the demon Madhu.

Nonetheless, all sources agree that Lohajangha was killed in the forest that now bears his name. In Bhauma Vrndavana, by the side of Lohavana’s Krsna-kunda, stands what is left of his iron form.

Lohavana, the eleventh forest of Vraja, served as the battlefield upon which Krsna defeated Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, and the enormous armies he brought with him to destroy Mathura.

After Krsna killed Kamsa, Kamsa’s two wives — who were the daughters of Jarasandha— returned to their father and tearfully recounted to him how Krsna had made them widows.

Having heard this news, Jarasandha vowed to rid the earth of the Yadavas. He marched on Mathura with an army, set up camp in Lohavana, and from there proceeded to surround Mathura.

Krsna was determined in His mission to rid the world of impious fools like Jarasandha, whose intentions He was fully aware of. The Lord devised a strategy to lure Jarasandha into unwittingly helping Him.

Krsna’s plan was to kill Jarasandha’s armies but to spare Jarasandha, who would then foolishly bring legion after legion to Mathura, making it easier for Krsna to rid the world of its unnecessary burden.

While Krsna and Balarama were making plans for Their conquest to come to Them, Their armoury descended from Vaikuntha: two war chariots with drivers, equipment, and the Lords’ personal weapons.

Without wasting time, Krsna and Balarama mounted Their chariots. Commanding a relatively small force of soldiers, They met and destroyed Jarasandha’s army, leaving only the king with his breath.

Humiliated but still full of false hope, Jarasandha returned to his capital and raised another army, only to be defeated a second time. Again Jarasandha’s soldiers were killed and the shamed king released.

Blinded by anger, Jarasandha raised seventeen armies, one after another, marched upon Mathura, lost each battle at Lohavana, and was sent back to his city alone and humiliated in defeat.

Adhering to brahminical culture, Jarasandha always had *brahmanas* perform sacrifices to assure his victory. But following his seventeenth defeat, he threatened to kill the *brahmanas* if he lost again.

As Jarasandha set out for Mathura on his eighteenth campaign, those *brahmanas* sent a message to Krsna informing Him of the fate they would surely suffer if Jarasandha were to be defeated another time.

Meanwhile, Providence sent King Kalayavana to lay siege on Mathura from another direction, just as Jarasandha approached. It appeared that Krsna would have to face two opponents at once.

To avoid putting His family in harm’s way, Krsna had the demigods construct the city of Dvaraka in the western ocean. He then transported the people of Mathura to the safety of their new home.

Once Krsna was satisfied that His subjects were safe, He faced Kalayavana unarmed. But instead of fighting with the Yavana, Krsna lured him into a cave where Mucukunda burnt the king to ashes.

Sri Krsna then returned to Mathura, destroyed the barbarian army of Kalayavana, and set off to join His family in Dvaraka, just as Jarasandha arrived with his eighteenth battalion.

Krsna wanted to protect the *brahmanas* of Magadha from danger. On the pretext of rescuing Rukmini from Her impending marriage to Sisupala, Krsna left Jarasandha, feigning fear for the second time.

In this way Krsna and Balarama led Jarasandha away from Mathura. After tricking the king of Magadha, the two brothers travelled to Dvaraka. Later, Jarasandha finally met his end at Bhima’s hands.

Lohavana was just on the other side of the Yamuna from Mathura; it therefore served as a convenient battlefield for Krsna to fulfil His promise of annihilating the miscreants *(vinasaya ca duskrtam).*

There is a boat landing in Lohavana with a less violent history than the battlefield. Krsna moored a boat there, hoping to ferry the *gopis* to Mathura and submerge them in the blissful waters of His pastimes.

We may wonder what the *gopis* were doing in Lohavana or why they were carrying butter from Gokula to Mathura, but we do know that this pastime must have occured after they had moved from Raval.

Amorous exchanges are out of place in childhood. And parents, especially Mother Yasoda, would not permit their children to row across the Yamuna on their own. The *gopis* must have been older.

Indeed, according to *Bhakti-ratnakara*, Krsna and the *gopis* arc adolescents, which means they must have been living in Vrndavana and been on some kind of mission to Mathura through Mahavana.

If Sri Radha and the *gopis* had been taking their milk products to market in Mathura, why would they have gone through Mahavana, taking the trouble to unnecessarily cross the Yamuna twice?

Moreover, why would Princess Radha, dressed in silks and ornamented with diamonds, have to sell butter in the first place? Would selling a few pots of butter change Her family’s fortunes?

And even if Radha and the *gopis* were trying to teach us the importance of maintaining our livelihood by depending on the cows, why go to Mathura when there was a market in their own village?

There can be only one answer to all these questions: Krsna. The *gopis’* crossing the river Yamuna, travelling to Mahavana, and selling butter is all for one purpose: to enjoy pastimes with their beloved.

**\* \* \* \***

The adventure of crossing from Lohavana to Mathura is similar to that of the crossing from Raja-ghata to Bilvavana. Narahari Cakravarti narrates the escapade, citing verses from *Padyavali.*

He says that once when Radha and the *gopis* came through Lohavana carrying pots of milk, Krsna was waiting for them in an old leaky boat. Radha took advantage of this opportunity to enlist His services.

Upon arriving at the boat landing, the *gopis* repeatedly called out to Krsna, who appeared to be napping in His boat: “Take us to the other side of the Yamuna!” All glories to doubly indolent Lord Krsna!

But Krsna was only pretending to sleep, so the *gopis* found it difficult to wake Him. Only after a great effort on the part of the cowherd girls did Krsna finally sit up and talk to His prospective clients.

At first, Srimati Radharani and Her beloved spoke in riddles. Sri Krsna began, “My dear young girl! Please step into My *tari.” Tan* means boat, and Krsna used the locative case *tarau.*

But Radha interpreted *tarau* as the locative case of *taru* (tree) and replied, “Why should I climb trees?” Krsna said, “O bewildered girl. I didn’t mean tree, I meant *tarani!” Tarani* is another word for boat.

Srimati Radharani then took *tarani* to mean the sun and answered, “Why would I want to go to the sun?” Smiling, Sri Krsna said, “I have used all these words to mean nau!” *Nau* also means boat.

Taking *nau* to mean “us,” smiling Radha said, “All these words are meant to bring Us together.” I worship unconquerable Krsna, who happily smiled as Radha defeated Him in this playful duel of words.

Once they had agreed on the fare, Krsna repeatedly assured the cowherd girls that His seaworthy vessel would ensure a calm crossing to the other side. The *gopis* giggled to hear Srimati Radharani retort:

“What You say is true. There are no big waves on the Yamuna, and this is a sturdy new boat. Yet I still have a reason to be afraid because You, O Madhava, are the reckless captain of the boat.”

Krsna feigned offence at Radha’s lack of faith in His navigational skills. He told the *gopis* to either walk across or take another boat. Radha then said, “The river is very deep, this is an old boat—

“And we are simply helpless girls. The situation is very dangerous for us. Still, O Madhava, just now Yours is the only boat, and You are the only captain who can take us slender girls across the Yamuna.”

Certainly, the *gopis* did not desire to go in any boat besides Krsna’s. They negotiated a fair price for crossing and then entered the vessel, filling Krsna’s heart with divine bliss simply by their presence.

The river was calm as they departed from the landing, but suddenly the sky was overcast and winds stirred the surface of the Yamuna. Soon, waves spilled into the boat, threatening to fill it with water.

All of a sudden Krsna stopped the boat in the middle of the Yamuna and demanded immediate payment of the fare. He smiled as He gazed at the frightened face of Radha, who had no money to give.

A large wave nearly capsized the boat and interrupted this exchange, which scared the *gopis* into accepting Krsna’s demand: “Either throw your possessions overboard, or drown in the river.”

Anxious Radha said, “O Yadunandana! By Your order I have cast My milk products, necklace, and even My bodice into the water; still, the shore of the Yamuna River has not come any closer.”

To increase His own pleasure, Krsna requested the girls to bail the water out with their hands. As they did, He casually embraced Radha, who complained, “The boat is being violently tossed by the wind.

"Filling with water, it is now sinking into the Yamuna. Alas! Destiny has become My enemy. Even in this calamity, lusty-hearted Krsna, son of a respectable king, repeatedly puts His hands on Me!”

Despite doing their best to bail the water out of the boat, the *gopis* could not keep pace with the rain or the waves. And when they turned to Krsna for help, He merely laughed and egged them on.

Radha anxiously exclaimed, “My hands are exhausted. They can no longer push the water out. Meanwhile, You just make jokes. O Krsna! If I live through this, never again will I place My feet in Your boat.”

Since Krsna was too busy entertaining Himself to be of any help, Srimati Radharani turned to Her friends and begged them to fervently pray for divine intervention in their time of need.

*“O gopi* friends! Please bow down before your chosen deity and pray that either the Yamuna River will only be knee deep when we fall in, or that we will be blessed with a boat captain other than Krsna.”

But no divinity arrived to intervene; rather, the wind increased and the waves got higher. The only thing calm in Vraja was Krsna. Turning to Lalita, Radha cried, “The boat rocks to and fro.

“The river is deep. The reckless son of Maharaja Nanda is the captain. I am a helpless girl. The sun is setting in the west, and the village of Vraja is still far away. O friend, what will I do now?”

Then, laughing in ecstasy, mischievous Krsna started to rock the boat. Radha tugged at Lalita-devi’s arm and pleaded, “He pays no attention to My prayers, He does not hear My begging in a broken voice.

“He does not consider My repeatedly bowing down before Him. O friend! What will I do now? In the middle of this wave-filled river, the reckless son of Maharaja Nanda violently shakes the boat.”

Finally, Radha Herself pleaded to the skies with raised hands, “The Yamuna is filled with huge waves, and the boat is filling with water. Still, Krsna is not afraid.” Krsna replied, “O beautiful Radha!

“Don’t be so harsh. By Your mercy, We will live through this. All You need to do is pay the boat fare of a promise to enjoy with Me a festival of amorous pastimes in the caves of Govardhana Hill.”

Rupa Gosvami does not cite any verses to confirm whether or not Radha gave, or fulfilled, such a promise. But we do know that the *gopis* reached the shore at Mathura and arrived home safely that day.

Sri Rupa does, however, add a final verse to this section of his anthol ogy, a verse in which, some time later, Krsna seems to think that Srimati Radharani does owe Him some form of payment.

While walking beside Govardhana Hill, Sri Radha felt a pebble hit Her back. She turned around and saw Krsna standing behind a tall pile of cow-dung patties, motioning for Her to join Him.

But Radha refused to respond to Krsna’s call, and so He gestured as if He had something for Her. Not one to be so easily tricked, She said, “O Krsna! Cheater hiding behind a heap of dried cow-dung!

“Why do You uselessly beg Me in this way? Go away! Can’t You think of any better tricks? You used to be so expert at tricking the *gopis* by frightening them in an old boat. Where is that expertise now?”

May the vision of Srimati Radharani falling at the feet of the Krsna- boatman as He rocks His old boat in the Yamuna during a summer storm, and the sound of Her crying out, “Oh, save Me!” protect us all.

**\* \* \* \***

A yore and Gauravai are two important places on the perimeter of Lohavana. Both are connected to Krsna’s return to Vrndavana. Hearing of the events in these two towns frees one from all miseries.

On the occasion of a solar eclipse the Yadavas and the kings of Bharata-varsa met at Kuruksetra. Hearing that Krsna and Balarama would be there, Nandaraja and the Vraja-vasis also attended.

Krsna extended His stay at Kuruksetra to give pleasure to the Vraja-vasis, and upon their request He even agreed to return to Vrndavana, a loving exchange celebrated by the Ratha-yatra festival.

Just at that time, the demon Salva laid siege to Dvaraka from his aerial city, obliging Krsna to return to His capital and assist Pradyumna, Satyaki, and other Yadu heroes in the battle.

Just after Krsna killed Salva with His *cakra,* Narada Muni delivered a challenge to the Lord from Dantavakra, a friend of Salva who was waiting to fight with Krsna just outside of Mathura City.

Krsna at once hurried to Mathura and clashed with the demon in the clearing in which His grandson Vajranabha would later establish the town Datiha, named after the killer of Dantavakra *(dantavakra-ha).*

As expected, Krsna triumphed over Dantavakra and his supporters. Now that the Lord was in such close proximity to His relatives, He seized the moment to fulfil His promise and return to Vraja.

But first He went to Visrama-ghata to cleanse Himself from the blood of Dantavakra. There the locals told Him that His father, mother, and friends were not in Nandagrama but in Lohavana.

Upon returning from Kuruksetra, Nanda Maharaja could not bear the thought of facing the residents of his city without Krsna by his side, and so he accepted the invitation of his friend Dhana.

Dhana was the leader of a town in Lohavana. He received Krsna’s divine father with so much honour *(gaurava)* that when Nandaraja entered the town, it was renamed Gauravai, now known as Gaurai.

While living at Gauravai, the Vraja-vasis heard that the Yadu’s had suffered at Salva’s hands. Thinking that Krsna had been imprisoned by the demon, they thought to burn themselves alive.

Only the persuasive powers of a *brahmana* reassured the Vraja-vasis to continue living. He argued that, whatever might be going on in Dvaraka, Krsna’s promise could never prove false.

And didn’t Nanda Maharaja have a letter from Krsna that said, “O father! I live neither in Indraprastha nor Dvaraka but in this letter. Please keep it in your pocket so that I can live there always.”?

After bathing at Visrama-ghata, Krsna drove His chariot across the Yamuna. His mind reeling from the ecstasy of returning home, He blew on His conch so that everyone would know of His arrival.

The sound of the Pancajanya directly entered the hearts of the Vraja-vasis, who immediately began to shout “Jaya! Jaya!” in astonishment. Men and women, young and old, ran in the direction of the sound.

The call of the conch and the rattling of chariot wheels could be heard everywhere. As the Vraja-vasis neared the source of these sounds, their ecstasy increased step by step until they were stunned.

Unable to move any further, the Vraja-vasis stood on the road, and at the the first glimpse of Krsna’s chariot they all made a great tumult *(rava)* by calling out, “Welcome! Welcome!” *(aya, aya).*

Thus the place where the Vraja-vasis greeted Krsna is called Ayara or Ayore. That place is still covered with the many flowers and flower petals that the demigods showered upon Krsna and His kin.

Krsna’s return to Vrndavana and His subsequent visit was as much a source of bliss for Him as it was for the Vraja-vasis. Once again He was united with His parents, friends, cows, and forest animals.

Mother Yasoda sat Krsna on her lap and inspected His limbs, just as she had done when He was a child. She cried pitifully to see the scars from His violent encounters with enemies on the battlefield.

During the day, Krsna and His friends would take the cows to the pasturing grounds, and the boys would absorb themselves in play without fearing demons, for Krsna had now killed them all.

But the most wonderful event was Krsna’s marriage to Radha and the *gopis,* a festival Paurnamasi made possible by revealing the truth about the *gopis:* there had been real *gopis* and replicas.

Many years before, when the *gopis* were to be married, Yogamaya created replicas of them. Those replicas lived with and served their husbands while the original *gopis* met and danced with Krsna.

Whenever it suited the circumstances, Yogamaya made the two types of *gopi* forms appear and disappear, a secret of which not even the *gopis* themselves were aware. Only Krsna knew the truth.

To convince the people of Vrndavana of this fact, Paurnamasi made both sets *of gopis* simultaneously visible to everyone; thus they all saw two Radhas, two Visakhas, two Lalitas, two Candravalis, and so on.

Seeing this, the village elders, and even the gopis’ husbands, gave their blessings for Krsna to marry His beloveds. But then, surprisingly, the gopis themselves became obstacles to that divine union.

They said, “During those times Mother Paurnamasi merged us with our replicas, we lived with our husbands. Thus we are contaminated by the sin of living in the homes of men other than Krsna.

“The only way we can be purified is through a trial by fire. Actually, this has long been our vow.” Having said this, the *gopis* produced a letter they had written long ago. The letter read:

“If we ever break our vows to Krsna in body, mind, or words, while awake or even while dreaming, let our bodies burn in a trial by fire.” Hearing this terrible vow, the Vraja-vasis were filled with sorrow.

In response, Yogamaya summoned Durvasa Muni, who attested to the gopis’ purity by saying, “Previously, the *gopis* asked me, ‘Who is Krsna to us?’ I replied to them, ‘He is your husband.’”

Then he said, “To pacify these women’s minds, I shall manifest a fire from my austerities and they may walk through it one by one. Thus their unwavering chastity to Krsna will be known to the world.”

The people of Vraja gathered in a field at the edge of town. There, Durvasa created a raging fire through which the *gopis* walked, emerging unscathed, fresh, as if they had just been in a spring shower.

Thereafter, an elaborate wedding celebration took place, fulfilling the long-cherished desire of the *gopis*’ parents that their daughters marry Krsna. In this way Radha and Krsna were finally united.

Jiva Gosvami felt obliged to elaborately describe the wedding of Krsna in his *Gopala-campu* because during his time many people could not accept the perfection of Radha’s and Krsna’s paramour love.

After hearing *Gopala-campu,* we may be left with the impression that the earlier, unwedded relationship between Krsna and the *gopis* matured in marriage, which is their perfect, eternal relationship.

A number of devotees during Sri Jiva’s time reasoned like that; in fact, such logic continues to this day amongst those who think that paramour love is but a means to superior wedded *(svakiya)* love.

True, Krsna and the *gopis* relish both Unwedded and wedded love in Goloka Vrndavana; still, paramour *(parakiya)* love is the superior mellow. Thus, of the two, Krsna relishes paramour love the most.

This truth is confirmed in other writings by Srila Jiva Gosvami, but it was Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura who conclusively addressed the wedded-versus-unwedded controversy in detail.

In his dissertation, Cakravarti Thakura shows how Jiva Gosvami’s teachings actually confirm the superiority of paramour love, which is consistent with the mature deliberation of all previous *acaryas.*

The essence of Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s argument, which is the Gaudiya Vaisnava conclusion on the topic, is described in the appendix entitled, “The Svakiya-Parakiya Controversy.”

Krsna’s pastimes as the husband of the *gopis* take place in a different portion of Goloka Vrndavana than do His pastimes as the paramour of Radharani and other young girls. Kaviraja Gosvami confirms:

**“Increasing love is experienced in various tastes, one above another. But that love which has the highest taste in the gradual succession of desire manifests itself in the form of conjugal love.”**

**“Thus I call it** ***madhura-rasa.*** **It has two further divisions: wedded and Unwedded love. There is a great increase of mellow in the Unwedded conjugal mood. Such love is found nowhere but in Vraja.”**

After two months in Lohavana, Krsna approached His father and mother with a request: He wanted to return with Srimati Radharani and the *gopis* to Vrndavana, the sacred playground of their youth.

Nanda Maharaja blessed his son but requested Him never to leave Vrndavana again. Krsna readily agreed. Nanda then begged Krsna to make another promise, though he was not sure how Krsna would fulfil it.

Nandaraja said, “Since Vasudeva and I are like one soul in two bodies, I cannot tolerate seeing him in the pain of separation from You. Please stay in Vrndavana, but please also return to Dvaraka.”

Smiling at His father, Krsna again readily agreed. He would be eternally in two places at once: Vraja and Dvaraka. Actually, He is always in both places, though at times visible, at other times invisible.

Krsna then revealed to His father that He would perform a third miracle and take the partial expansions of the Vraja-vasis — like Drona in Nandaraja and Dhara in Yasoda — back to Godhead.

Krsna then expanded Himself and His chariot and — to the topmost spiritual planet, Goloka Vrndavana — He brought those Vraja-vasis whom He had, at Akrura-ghata, promised a Vaikuntha destination.

In a second form He simultaneously returned to Dvaraka, and in His original form, now invisible to everyone but fully liberated souls, Krsna remained with His eternal associates in Bhauma Vrndavana.

In other words, at Gauravai, Krsna concluded His Vraja pastimes. The eternal features of Goloka that had manifested themselves on earth disappeared from view, obscured by a layer of material energy.

Thus Bhauma Vrndavana displayed its covered form, as Raghava Pandita confirms:

**“All the places where Krsna performed His pas- times can be seen in ecstasy by people who are fortunate.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Continuing to walk along the tree line that marks the centre of the western petal of New Vraja-dhama, I came to Kheriya, said to be the place where the *gopas* fearfully called out, "*Khayare! Khayare!*”

The word *khaya* means “to eat” and *Khayare* means “he will eat us.” Lohajanghasura is said to be the cause of the *gopas’* cries. But exactly which *gopas* cried out and at what time in history is not clear.

If, as already mentioned, Satrughna killed Lohajanghasura during the former's reign over Mathura, then the cowherds of that time were clamouring due to their having caught sight of the demon.

If the *gopas* were Krsna’s associates, and Lohajanga was long dead, then the calls of *Khayare* were merely play. But if it was Krsna who killed the demon, then His friends were calling out in fear.

Most of Krsna’s pastime places are clearly linked to the pastimes they played host to, hut in some places, such as Kheriya, there is ambiguity and even complete ignorance about the pastimes themselves.

And then there are certain pastime places that have been covered or completely lost — due to neglect or urban development — and are no longer part of the *parikrama* of Vraja or of pilgrims’ meditations.

Such is the influence of material time! It covers knowledge of the *dhama* and even of Lord Krsna Himself, who declares that the time factor severs connection with Him *(sa kalaneha...yogo nastah*).

A little further past Kheriya is Vandi, which in contrast to the obscurity of Kheriya is well known as the place where the ancestors of Nanda Maharaja worshipped two forms of Durga: Vandi and Anandi.

Because Vandi was Nanda Maharaja’s ancestral place of worship, oral tradition has it that Krsna’s hair-cutting ceremony took place here in the presence of the deities. But the story does not end there.

After that ceremony, the two deities of goddess Durga, eager to continue seeing the beauty of Nanda Maharaja’s young son, took human forms and performed menial service in the king’s palace.

Vandi and Anandi made cow-dung patties in the pastures around Gokula. When they delivered the dry patties to the palace as fuel for cooking, they were able to see baby Krsna and play with Him.

It is common knowledge that demigods and goddesses do not touch the ground when they come to earth. These two *devis,* however, not only walked the earth but also collected and pressed cow dung.

Vandi and Anandi, intensely eager to see the Supreme Lord, gave up all sense of pride in their high birth as heavenly goddesses and assumed the position of common serving maids (*sudranis*).

And because they were willing to accept any menial work in the service of the Lord, Vandi and Anandi were blessed with the vision of Krsna playing as a baby in the courtyard of Nanda Maharaja.

In Bhauma Vrndavana, Vandi is a black deity with four arms; Anandi is a red deity who uses her eight arms to fight the Mahisa demon. Two lakes, one behind each temple, bear Vandi’s and Anandi’s names.

Just past Vandi in New Vraja-dhama is a place highly revered by the residents of the *dhama:* the cemetery where the deceased cows and oxen of Syamasundara’s herd are ceremonially buried.

This narrow strip of land is like a ribbon hanging from the tip of the western petal of the *dhama,* a ribbon that broadcasts the glories of the dearest among the lifelong servants of the Divine Couple.

It is here that we bury deceased cows like Sarasvati and Rati, and oxen like Balarama and Radha-Syama, and from where they then ascend to the final destination attained by all offenseless servants. Glories to them!

From here the *parikrama* path makes a sharp right towards Baladeva where I stopped to look at the clearing to the west, known as Saukara-tirtha, where Lord Varaha first appeared to deliver the earth.

This is the outer perimeter of the *dhama.* It is said that fasting while residing here purifies one of all offences. In Navadvipa, the place of Lord Varaha’s appearance is also where offences are forgiven.

In New Vraja-dhama, the area between the Yamuna and Lohavana, from Saukara-tirtha to Nanda-baithaka in Mahavana, is now a reed- bed filtration system that serves the needs of the *dhama.*

From here pilgrims may cross the Yamuna by bridge at Saukara-tirtha, follow the *parikrama* path through Mathura, cross back over the Yamuna to the guest house, and on to Gokula.

Or they may walk within the line of trees above the filtration plant and go first to Baladeva, then Nanda-baithaka, and on through Mahavana to Gokula, thus completing their *parikrama.*

I chose the second path, staying well within the woods known in Bhauma Vrndavana as Vidrumavana because of the coral *(vidruma)* that paves the ground and the coral-coloured leaves on the trees.

Baladeva, the first place I came to, is the pastime place of Krsna’s elder brother. Thus it is also called Dauji (“elder brother”), and it boasts a rich tradition of worshipping Lord Balarama’s Deity form.

Just as Khambi marks the northern boundary of Bhauma Vrndavana, Baladeva marks its southern boundary. Lord Balarama identified this border with a single stone pillar, as He did in Khambi.

Whenever the *gopas* trek all the way out to Lohavana or Mahavana, Lord Balarama likes to graze the cows in the open meadows there while He and His friends rest together in the shade of the trees.

The Lord is very much at home in Baladeva, which locals assert is the birthplace of His wife Revati, even though *Srimad-Bhagavatam* states that she was raised in Kusasthali and married Him in Dvaraka.

It is not impossible that Revati was born here, though I have yet to see scriptural evidence that supports this claim. If she did, it must have been in an age prior to the one in which Balarama appeared.

In fact, Sukadeva Gosvami tells King Pariksit that twenty-seven cycles of four ages passed while Maharaja Kakudmi visited Lord Brahma to enquire about who his daughter Revati should marry.

When Revati, who was thus from a previous *yuga,* met her future husband, Balarama, she was so much taller than the Lord that He pulled her down to His size with the flat end of His plough.

In any case, revati-devi is present there in Baladeva. When Vajra dedicated this petal of Vraja to Lord Balarama, he commissioned a carver to fashion a deity of Revati to face the Deity of the Lord.

The Deity of Balarama there is said to be Vraja’s largest and one of its four presiding Deities. He has a dark complexion and lotus-petal eyes. His right hand is raised, and in His left He holds a cup of *varuni.*

It is said that the Deity is made not of black stone but of red sandstone, but from repeated massages with aromatic oils and exposure to lamp and incense smoke, Balarama is now blackish.

Revati is not a Vraja-vasi but the Lord’s consort in Dvaraka, and so she stands on an altar facing Balarama, an altar not visible from the temple room door. She must be seen from a special side door.

Baladeva is one of the few Deities that never left Vraja for Jaipur, although at different times He had to leave His temple and hide to avoid attacks by the soldiers of Muslim kings like Aurangzeb.

On one such occasion, soldiers came to raze the temple. The priests were in such a rush that they threw Dauji upside down into a lake known as Sankarsana-kunda, Dugdha-kunda, and Ksira-sagara.

The Deity remained in Sankarsana-kunda for many years, until some cowherd men noticed that two of their cows would go to the lakeside every day and pour their milk onto a protruding rock.

At that time Gokulanatha, the fourth son of Viththalesvara, was in the area. He heard about the cows’ behaviour and had some men extract the rock, which proved to be the base of the Dauji Deity.

Once retrieved from the lake, Gokulanatha made plans to move the Deity to Gokula, but Balarama refused to budge. Thus the Lord was reinstalled at His original place, which was then known as Ridha.

The Deity of Lord Balarama is offered *bhanga,* butter, and sugar. He receives special worship on full-moon days. There are also special festivals held here during Holi and on Balarama’s appearance day.

It is said that long ago, villagers dug Sankarsana-kunda and filled it with the milk of 100,000 cows as an offering to Lord Balarama. Because the lake was indeed an ocean of milk, it is called Ksira-sagara.

This is reminiscent of the pastime wherein Narada Muni visits Lord Balarama in Svetadvipa, another ocean of milk. This place Ksira-sagara seems the ideal place to hear this wonderful pastime.

**\* \* \* \***

Overcome with ecstasy due to Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s imminent appearance and His mission to distribute love of God, Narada Muni once travelled to the abode of Lord Balarama in Svetadvipa.

Within the ocean of milk, Narada Muni saw a wonderful city served by gentle breezes fragrant with the scent of divine flowers and shining with the soft soothing glow of a million moons.

The inhabitants of that city were all fixed in pure goodness. Free from the fourfold miseries, they were friendly to one another. They constantly sung the praises of their milk-white-complexioned Lord.

Narada thought, “Fortunate am I, for soon I will sec the master of the three worlds. Millennium after millennium He descends to earth along with Lord Krsna to kill demons and give joy to His devotees.

“Lord Balarama serves Krsna in three abodes: in Patalaloka as the support of the entire universe, in Svetadvipa as Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s associate, and in Goloka as Lord Krsna’s elder brother.

“When Lord Krsna walks, Balarama is His umbrella; when the Lord sits, Balarama is His throne; when annihilation arrives, Balarama is the banyan leaf upon which the Supreme Lord lies down.”

Filled with such thoughts, Narada entered the city. Directed to a glistening palace, he found the master of the three worlds, Lord Balarama, seated upon a crystal-white throne studded with pearls.

The Lord’s smile was nectar sweet and His eyes, red like lotus flowers, looked drowsy. His speech was slurred from drinking honey-wine, but He was fully cognisant of every detail of creation.

His left hand rested on His thigh and His right held His wife Revati’s hand as He listened to Her loving words and accepted the tasty betel leaves she gracefully placed into His lotus mouth.

All around, thousands of smiling maidservants dutifully rendered services like fanning Him or playing musical instruments, their bracelets and ornaments sprinkling drops of nectar in the milk ocean.

As Narada entered, the Lord received him with a glance, and as Narada prostrated himself, Balarama lifted His servant up, embraced him, and spoke pleasant words of welcome filled with love.

The Lord asked, “O Narada! Dear Muni, please tell Me from where you have come. What have you been doing? And what secret do you keep hidden in your heart that waves of bliss now stir within Me?”

Clasping the Lord’s feet, Narada replied, “What can I say that You, the Supersoul, don’t already know, have not made me think, or will not prompt me to say? Still, I will follow Your order and tell You.

“My bliss arises from knowing that Your Divine Grace and Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu will appear on earth to inaugurate the *sankirtana* movement and stem the flow of Kali’s fearful influence.

“The sinful nature of the people of Kali-yuga leaves them devoid of hope for deliverance unless You intercede for them. You will thus descend to earth to reclaim Your devotees and establish true religion.

“Tasting varieties of loving devotion through *nama-sankirtana* in the company of Your eternal associates, You will intoxicate everyone with the special love that the Vraja-vasis feel for You and Krsna.

“O Lord! You will take birth on earth as Lord Nityananda. Your absorption in *nama-sankirtana* will show others how to cultivate pure devotion to Krsna and reap its ultimate fruit, love of God *(prema).”*

At these prophetic words, Lord Balarama joyfully rolled His head and, forgetting Himself in divine ecstasy, let out peals of laughter that echoed through the palace like rolling thunder.

The Lord then said, “Narada! You and your followers must join Us on earth. What has so far remained unknown to the people of the world, I will now reveal to them by appearing alongside My Gauranga.”

Having received this order from his Lord, Narada did not waste any time but informed other great souls, like Lord Siva, of the descent of Gaura and Nitai. Then Narada took birth for our deliverance.

The appearance and pastimes of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu and Lord Nityananda are recorded in the immaculate writings of great souls like Vrndavana Dasa Thakura and Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami.

Another great poet, Narahari Cakravarti, tells how Suryadasa Sarakhela gave his daughters Vasudha and Jahnavi in marriage to Lord Nityananda. One night the *brahmana* had a dream.

He saw himself offering the hands of his two daughters in marriage to Lord Nityananda as *brahmanas* chanted wedding hymns and the demigods overhead showered flowers on the proceedings.

As Suryadasa gazed at his new son-in-law, he saw Lord Nityananda transform into milky-complexioned Lord Balarama, and his two beautiful daughters became golden-complexioned Varuni and Revati.

Overwhelmed by such divine beauty, Suryadasa wept, and his tears roused him from slumber. He got out of bed enriched with a complete understanding of his duty to his daughters in service to the Lord.

As I recalled the pastimes Lord Balarama performed in His forests, a prayer came into my mind,
