*revati-ramana tvam vai baladevacyutagraja*  
*halayudha pralamba-ghna pahi mam Purusottama*

**“O husband of Revati! O Lord Balarama! O elder brother of Lord Krsna! O Lord who holds a plough! O killer of Pralambasura! O Supreme Personality of Godhead! Please protect me!”**

Following the *parikrama* path from Baladeva towards Gokula, I arrived on the edge of Mahavana at a resting place of Nanda Maharaja aptly called Nanda-baithaka (“the sitting place of Nanda”).

The king of the *gopas* rests there while herding his cows. And to obtain a son, he once worshipped a deity of Lord Siva in this forest. After Krsna’s birth that deity was called Gopala-lala Mahadeva.

This area is also known as Devanagara because Nanda Maharaja would often come here in the company of his friend Devaspati. The Govardhana-sila that belonged to Devaspati is still worshipped here.

I passed the “Elephant Guest House” in the shadow of Mahavana, offering respects to the divine forest Krsna chose as His birthplace in Bhauma Vrndavana and which lies at the centre of Goloka.

My thoughts and emotions were enriched by devotion to the Lord, because I knew that this would be the last leg of my *parikrama.* After passing through Mahavana I would reach the end of my pilgrimage.

Impending separation from the objects of our love — like separation itself— invariably elevates our attachment for them. It was thus with great anticipation that I entered the forest of Krsna’s childhood.

## Chapter 30 - Syama-mandira to Ramana-reti

Rupa Gosvami tells us that Krsna’s grandfather Parjanya Maharaja lived with his cowherd subjects in the area of Nandagrama, where like a rain cloud he showered his opulence upon everyone.

It is said that Maharaja Parjanya resembled Dhruva in wisdom, Prthu in glory, Bhisma in strength, Lord Siva in friendship, Lord Brahma in honesty, and in power he resembled the Supreme Lord Visnu.

King Ugrasena had bestowed upon Parjanya all the land in the area, but when Kamsa came to power, demons like Kesi so harassed the Vraja-vasis that Nandagrama lost its charm for Parjanya and his kin.

Maharaja Parjanya then moved his dependents to Mahavana, where the tranquility of the ancient forest promised safety for the Vraja-vasis and its green pastures provided grass in abundance for the cows.

As the twelfth forest of Vraja, Mahavana is also known as Maharanya and Brhadvana. Inaccessible to ordinary souls, Mahavana is the object of meditation for those devotees who aspire for love of God.

If one is fortunate enough to enter Mahavana, the denizens of Indraloka praise that blessed soul. By fasting, bathing, and worshipping there, one is freed of sin and attains all perfections.

Upananda was the eldest of Parjanya Maharaja’s five sons. When the time came for the king to retire to a solitary place and worship the Lord, he handed over responsibility for the kingdom to Upananda.

Upananda, however, considered his younger brother Nanda the most qualified to lead, so Upananda proposed that he act as an adviser and that Nanda be king, a proposal the Vraja-vasis heartily accepted.

Nanda’s means of protecting his dependents was based on following the rules of *dharma.* It was therefore not astonishing that the Vraja- vasis attained the four goals of life as well as devotion to the Lord.

Located at the edge of Mahavana, Nanda’s opulent capital, Gokula, was full of beautiful palaces, regal gates, and floral gardens, whose combined beauty and grandeur eclipsed the kingdom of heaven.

Scriptures tell us about a host of places where Krsna enjoyed pastimes in Gokula and the surrounding area of Mahavana. Some prominent places whose locations have not been lost to antiquity are as follows:

The palace of Nanda Maharaja, where the cart was kicked over, as well as those places where Trnavarta fell to earth, Putana was killed, Krsna toppled the twin *arjuna* trees, and Mother Yasoda gave birth.

When Caitanya Mahaprabhu visited Mahavana He saw these pastime places, and His ecstasy increased from one to the next. Sometimes He felt Himself to be a devotee, sometimes He felt Himself to be Krsna.

As the *brahmana* Krsna Dasa took Caitanya Mahaprabhu from place to place, describing Krsna’s playful childhood antics at each spot, he would observe Lord Caitanya’s complete absorption in divine trance.

Finally, after having heard about the mellows and transcendental glories of Sri Krsna’s childhood pastimes, Caitanya Mahaprabhu lovingly embraced Krsna Dasa, infusing His guide with *krsna-prema.*

The convention on *parikrama* is to discuss the Lord’s pastimes in the sequence in which we come to the places where He performed them, rather than in the chronological sequence the pastimes occurred.

Up to this point in my *parikrama* I had followed this convention, but I thought a change might be in order when I came to Gokula, where Krsna displayed so many famous pastimes in a relatively small area.

In Gokula, to narrate Krsna’s childhood pastimes in chronological order might be more transcendentally pleasing to readers, and would at the same time not interfere with the *parikrama* of serious pilgrims.

Consequently, I decided not to follow the sequence shown on the *parikrama* map of Mahavana. I pray that my readers may have a more rewarding experience by hearing about Krsna’s childhood in this way.

Gokula’s most prominent feature is the palace of Nanda Maharaja. It is quite similar to Nandaraja’s palace in Kaman called Caurasi- stambh, which is named after the eighty pillars that support it.

In New Vraja-dhama, Nanda-bhavana is represented by a pavilion on the crest of a hill that overlooks the Yamuna and grazing pastures beyond, all the way to Nandagrama. The view is breathtaking.

In Bhauma Vrndavana, archeological evidence and historical records both show that the present Nanda-bhavana, also called Assi-stambh (“eighty pillars”), is neither in its original place nor its original form.

The Muslim ruler Aurangzeb had the original palace dismantled and relocated some hundred metres to the southeast, where the pillars were rearranged so that it would resemble a conventional mosque.

Such are the ravages that time and man inflict upon the holy *dhama.* One of those eighty pillars shows marks Krsna made by wiping stolen butter from His hands — evidence of His regular childhood pranks.

On the altar of Nanda-bhavana are deities of Krsna, Balarama, Nanda Maharaja, and Mother Yasoda. Nearby is the balcony on which Yasoda-devi churned butter on the day Krsna felled the *arjuna* trees.

Krsna lived in this house for three years and four months, so every bit of space inside it and in the area surrounding it is a holy place where childhood pastimes marked by unimaginable sweetness took place.

**\* \* \* \***

In this chapter and the next we shall hear about Krsna’s appearance and His pastimes in Gokula, up to the toppling of the *yamala-arjuna* trees, which prompted the Vraja-vasis’ move to Vrndavana.

For the people of Gokula, the palace of Nanda Maharaja was a beacon of auspiciousness. Nonetheless, they felt troubled — as did Nanda and Yasoda themselves — because the king and queen had no children.

The *brahmanas’* mantras and sacrificial offerings had not borne fruit, intensifying Yasoda-devi’s anxiety that not only would her maternal desires remain unfulfilled but her family line would end as well.

In private, Maharaja Nanda once reassured his wife: “Do not be discouraged that others’ piety do not afford us a son. The son I am praying for cannot be attained by karma — He is the cause of karma.

“I do not desire the sort of offspring that can be invoked by means of fruitive sacrifices. My desire is to have all-merciful Lord Narayana — and no one else — as my son. He is the child upon whom I meditate.”

Yasoda-devi asked, “Tell me, what does this child look like in your meditation?” “He is all-attractive,” Nanda said, “with a dark complex- ion and lotus eyes. He plays on your lap as He drinks from your breast.

“I cannot say whether I am dreaming or awake. What do you think?” Yasoda smiled, “Who am I to say? But still, I suggest we detach ourselves from the impossible desire to have the Lord as our own son.”

But Nanda Maharaja was adamant: “Even when I try to control my mind I see within me the form of Lord Narayana. He has fulfilled our desires in the past, and He can fulfil our present desire as well.”

Convinced by her husband’s devotion, Yasoda suggested, “Then let us serve the Lord by following the Dvadasi vow for one full year.” Nanda eagerly agreed, and from that very day they practised penance.

At the completion of that year, both Yasoda and Nanda had the same dream, in which Lord Narayana appeared to them and said in a kind voice, “Do not lament! Your devotion to Me will soon bear fruit.

“That boy of bluish complexion upon whom you always meditate will take birth as your son and please you in every way. He will also awaken pure devotion to Himself in the hearts of pious souls.”

Full of astonishment, Nandaraja and Yasoda-devi awoke and revealed their dreams to each other. Their already intense desire to have the Lord as a son swelled like the ocean tide on a full-moon night.

What greater joy could come to the foremost embodiments of parental love? Yet, miraculously, another promising omen appeared to Nanda and Yasoda: Paurnamasi and Madhumangala arrived in Vraja.

After the Vraja-vasis had welcomed Yogamaya, they asked what she could tell them of Vraja’s future. The *brahmani* revealed to them that Nanda and Yasoda would soon give birth to the embodiment of bliss.

On that same evening, Rohini-devi secretly arrived in Mahavana. Riding a horse all the way from Mathura, she had been consigned to Nanda’s care by her husband, who feared King Kamsa’s wild anger.

The blissful reunion of Yasoda and Rohini was like the meeting of the Ganges and the Yamuna at Prayaga, and in the same way that the two rivers conjoin further downstream, the two women were inseparable.

Rohini-devi was three months pregnant when she arrived. Maharaja Nanda, whose friendship with Vasudeva was like the bond between brothers, sheltered Rohini in his palace as if she were his sister.

Four months after her arrival in Vrndavana, Yogamaya mysticall exchanged Rohini’s embryo for Devaki’s, making it appear that, under the duress of Kamsa’s tyranny, Devaki had suffered a miscarriage.

Rohini's pregnancy continued for another seven months. It was therefore after fourteen months that she blissfully gave birth to a beautiful hoy who shone with the whiteness and purity of a full moon.

The newborn’s eyes were as restless as lightning, His hair as black as night, His complexion as soothing as a white cloud, and His effulgence as brilliant as the sun. The sight of Him brought pure bliss.

The astrologers were amazed at the baby’s chart. Calling Him Balarama, they found Him to be the source of both endless bliss and divine strength, with which He would protect cows and kill demons.

The most profound prediction, however, was that of Balarama’s protective fondness for His younger brother, with whom He would reestablish the religious principles demons like Kamsa had undermined.

Some time later, one night in the month of Magha to be more precise, Yasoda-devi had a vision that seemed to verify Lord Narayana’s promise, Paurnamasi’s prophesy, and the astrologers’ readings.

She saw a boy, the vision of whom was obscured by the form of a celestial girl. The boy entered from Nanda’s heart into her own, just as the girl entered her womb. Yasoda-devi was completely astonished.

Nanda also saw the children transferred from himself into his wife, but he was a simple-hearted cowherd and so could not explain what had happened, other than to say it filled him with ineffable love.

The paleness in her face and the swelling of her belly, however, soon made it clear that Yasoda was pregnant. Hearing this, all the eminent women of Gokula brought Yasoda precious gifts to make her happy.

Just as the flame in a lamp illuminates both the lamp itself and everything that surrounds it, Lord Krsna’s personal effulgence illuminated both Yasoda-devi and the entire material creation.

The Vraja-vasis were elated that their king would finally have an heir. Even little Balarama would climb up on Mother Yasoda’s lap to feel the bliss of being close to His transcendental brother.

Like all women, Yasoda — although naturally grave and self-controlled— would ask for palatable foods such as rice covered with ghee, made fragrant with camphor, and topped with *tulasi* leaves.

In the eighth month of Yasoda-devi’s pregnancy, when it was clear that she was about to give birth, accompanied by the experienced mothers of Gokula, she entered the maternity room Nanda had built.

This building was situated on a hill near the Yamuna River and is presently called Syama-mandira. At the foot of the hill was a lion’s gate called Nanda-haveli with many columns. It resembled a mansion.

At the time of Krsna’s birth in Gokula—just as the demigods had come to Devaki during the time of her pregnancy — the *devas* also came to Mother Yasoda, but disguised as *gopas* and *gopis* bearing gifts.

The auspiciousness of Krsna’s appearance was evident in the change in Vraja’s atmosphere. Gokula became peaceful, for the Vraja-vasis’ hearts were at last immune from fear of King Kamsa and his cohorts.

Auspicious stars and planets filled the sky, the air was aromatic, the breeze was pleasing to the touch, bodies of water were clear and crowded with lotus flowers, and trees and creepers were in full bloom.

Birds and bees that by nature would usually sleep in the evening awoke to sing together as if in praise of the Lord, and rain clouds gathered in the sky, heralding Krsna’s birth with deep rumbling.

Krsna’s appearance is one of His most mysterious pastimes. He personally encourages us to understand it in truth *(tattvatah)* and thus qualify ourselves to return to His own abode, Goloka Vrndavana.

After describing the reasons for His appearance in this world, the Supreme Lord Krsna tells Arjuna,

*janma karma ca me divyam evam yo vetti tattvatah*  
*tyaktva deham punar janma naiti mam eti so ’rjuna*

**“One who knows the transcendental nature of My appearance and activities does not, upon leaving the body, take his birth again in this material world, but attains My eternal abode, O Arjuna.”**

Scriptures like *Harivamsa* and *acaryas* like Sri Jiva tell us that Krsna took birth from Devaki and Yasoda simultaneously. Those two forms merged together to become the celebrated cowherd of Vrndavana.

**\* \* \* \***

Vasudeva’s and Devaki's devotion was mixed with knowledge of and awe at Krsna’s divinity. *Srimad-Bhagavatam* therefore says that it was actually Lord Visnu who took birth as their son in Kamsa’s prison.

This is confirmed by the description of Vasudeva’s newborn child: His four hands held the symbols of Visnu, His chest bore the mark of Srivatsa, and His neck showcased the unique Kaustubha gem.

After Vasudeva and Devaki had offered prayers to the Lord, Devaki voiced anxiety at her son being seen by others in a transcendental four-armed form that contained the entire creation within it.

She thought that people would not believe such a birth was possible and would therefore ridicule her. More importantly, in that distinctive form she would not be able to hide her son from Kamsa.

She said, “O Madhusudana! Because of Your appearance, I am becoming increasingly fearful of Kamsa. Therefore, please arrange that the demon not understand Your appearance from my womb.”

Within Mother Yasoda’s womb were twins, Krsna and Yogamaya. But when Devaki requested Vasudeva Krsna to assume the form of a normal child, Yogamaya transported Krsna to Mathura unseen.

Sri Suka says, “...by His internal energy, He then transformed Himself into a small human child.” Jiva Gosvami explains that the two-armed form of Krsna merged the four-armed form into Himself.

While Krsna was still in Yasoda-devi's womb, in a subtle form invisible to everyone including Vasudeva and Devaki, Yogamaya Paurnamasi carried Krsna to Mathura as the wind carries a blue lotus.

In Kamsa’s prison, the son of Yasoda then absorbed the four-armed baby into His original form. To Vasudeva and Devaki it looked as if their son had cast aside His divine symbols and His two extra arms.

Srila Prabhupada indirectly corroborates this account in commenting on Sukadeva Gosvami’s explanation:

**“In other words, He transformed Himself into His original form,** ***krsnas tu bhagavan svayam.”***

Since Vasudeva Krsna cannot directly become Syamasundara Krsna, Srila Prabhupada’s words imply that Syamasundara Krsna must have appeared to give the sense that Vasudeva had transformed Himself.

Meanwhile, at the exact moment Vasudeva was about to take the baby from Kamsa’s prison, Yogamaya took birth from Yasoda, who did not know the gender of her newborn, having fainted in childbirth.

The same Yogamaya who had transferred Balarama from Devaki's womb to Rohini's, and Krsna from Yasoda’s womb to the prison cell in Mathura, appeared as a baby girl on the bed beside Mother Yasoda.

Vasudeva and Devaki were desperate to hide their newborn son, even though He had already concealed the signs of His divinity. But they were still shackled in chains. How could they hide Him from Kamsa?

The Lord’s parents were frightened that Kamsa would kill the new-born as he had their other sons, but Yogamaya would soon open an unexpected chapter in Krsna’s transcendental pastimes.

By the influence of her inconceivable mystic power, Yogamaya made the guards in King Kamsa’s palace in Mathura, as well as the cowherd women attending Queen Yasoda in Gokula, fall fast asleep.

Mysteriously, the chains fell from Vasudeva’s body and the doors of the prison swung open. Baby Krsna then told His father to take Him to the home of Nanda and exchange Him for Yasoda’s newborn girl.

Encouraged by Devaki, Vasudeva cautiously left the cell carrying Krsna in his arms and saw that the guards, like all the guards in Kamsa’s palace, were fast asleep, and the doors were all eerily ajar.

Devaki had given birth to the Supreme Lord. But sadly He was taken away before she barely had a chance to embrace Him, to say nothing of breastfeeding Him or relishing the other joys of motherhood.

Mother Yasoda, in stark contrast, was personally able to bathe, ornament, and feed Krsna to her heart’s content. From the transcendental point of view, she was more fortunate than Devaki.

The doors of the prison were quite thick, fixed to the walls with large bolts and chained shut, but they opened by themselves, making way for Vasudeva as he walked along the familiar prison corridors.

When Vasudeva reached the main gate of the palace he first saw Kamsa’s personal guards fast asleep. Then he beheld the gigantic form of Ananta, waiting to shield him and baby Krsna from the rain.

Startled by Ananta’s towering hoods, Vasudeva was reluctant to enter beneath the divine serpent, until Krsna gently kicked his father’s arm and inspired him from within by saying, “Take Me to Vraja!”

Effulgent Krsna, who like a blazing sapphire lamp lit the way, rested peacefully in Vasudeva’s arms as His father easily navigated through the dense darkness of the city alleyways and the forest pathways.

We have already heard about Vasudeva’s journey through Mathura and Ambikavana in chapter two. He arrived at the shore of the Yamuna at what is now Koila. From there he could go no further.

Vasudeva gazed at the frothing river and wondered how he would cross over to Gokula. There were no boats there at night, and even if there were, no boatman would have dared take him across the river.

Vasudeva glanced at Ananta as if to say, “Now what?” And in reply, the river stopped flowing and gradually parted for Vasudeva, creating a dry path on the riverbed from one bank to the other.

Prompted by Ananta, Vasudeva climbed down the riverbank and walked along the riverbed, unsteadily at first, with water towering on both sides and Krsna joyfully wiggling His little feet and hands.

But halfway across, water started to cover Vasudeva’s path, first up to his knees and then to his chest. He was forced to lift Krsna over his head and frantically call out, “Someone, take Him!” *(koi le \[h\]u).*

From this exclamation comes Koila, the name for where Vasudeva first entered the water. Just as he cried “Someone, take Him!” a high wave washed Krsna out of his hands and into the current of the river.

Vasudeva panicked. As he desperately searched the water all around him, his hot tears fell into the frothing waves. Ananta also searched, frantically swimming in circles, hoping for some sign of infant Krsna.

Just when it seemed that Vasudeva would go mad from anxiety, or that Ananta would dry up the river with the flames from His mouths, Yamuna-devi rose out of the water with baby Krsna in her arms.

Shyly approaching Vasudeva and looking warily at Ananta, the goddess carefully handed the baby to its father and apologised, saying, “Forgive me sir! I just wanted to play with Him awhile.”

As Vasudeva took the baby, the goddess disappeared. The path to the far side was again free from water, allowing Vasudeva to easily reach shore and continue on to Yasoda’s maternity house, Syama-mandira.

Nanda Maharaja had posted guards around Syama-mandira, but, like Kamsa’s guards and the senior women of Vrndavana attending Mother Yasoda, they were all fast asleep under Yogamaya’s spell.

Walking carefully amongst the sleeping women, cradling baby Krsna close to his heart, Vasudeva finally entered the room in which Mother Yasoda was sleeping with her newborn daughter.

In the dim light of fading ghee lamps, Vasudeva gazed lovingly at baby Krsna, pressing his beautiful son close to his chest for a long time. Perhaps he would never get to hold Krsna like this again.

A flash of lightning and a thunderclap suddenly broke his paternal reverie. Vasudeva reluctantly placed Krsna beside Yasoda, lifted the infant girl in his arms, and left, glancing at baby Krsna one last time.

Krsna lay playfully by Yasoda’s side, moving His hands and feet and filling the dark room with the soft effulgence of His transcendental body. Gradually, the warmth of Yasoda’s body lulled Him to sleep.

Retracing the route he had taken to bring Krsna to Gokula, Vasudeva now carried Yogamaya to Mathura. Entering the prison, he placed Yogamaya in Devaki's loving hands and swore his wife to secrecy.

One by one the doors swung closed and locked behind Vasudeva. Once he had replaced the chains on his limbs, it looked as if he had never left his cell. Finally, as small babies do, Yogamaya began to cry.

We may wonder how it was possible for Vasudeva to even think of sacrificing Yasoda-devi’s daughter to protect his own son. But Vasudeva was faultless because Yogamaya directed him from within.

In any case, Kamsa could not kill Yogamaya. When he tried to do so, she slipped from the demon’s grasp, rose into the sky, and proclaimed that the boy who would kill Kamsa had already been born elsewhere.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura says that Krsna’s birth to Yasoda is not common knowledge. Most people think that He was born to Devaki, who has since become famous as the mother of God.

Devaki's fame, however, is Yasoda’s mercy; in fact, the name Yasoda means, means, “the giver” *(da)* of “fame” *(yasah)* Because of their friendship, Yasoda allowed Devaki to become famous as Krsna’s mother.

**\* \* \* \***

Once Vasudeva had left the Syama-mandira to make his way back to Mathura, Krsna started to cry, as do all new-born babies. But unlike other babies, His crying resembled *brahmanas* chanting *omkara.*

Krsna’s transcendental sobs first woke Mother Yasoda’s attendants, who rushed into the maternity room, showered the beautiful baby with feminine affection, and gently roused the queen of Gokula.

Her eyes transfixed on the child by her side, who by the gentle movement of His hands and feet bewildered the mind of every woman present, Yasoda-devi was stunned with maternal ecstasy.

Mother Yasoda’s intense love clouded her discrimination. As she gazed upon Krsna she wondered whether He was indeed her son or a sapphire doll, a garland of blue lotuses, or a cloud descended to earth.

With the coaxing of her friends, Yasoda was finally able to recognise her son. She was overwhelmed by the sweetness of His limbs, the gracefulness of His movements, and the softness of His complexion.

Due to the effects of ecstatic love, a constant stream of milk flowed from Yasoda-devi's breasts. As she breastfed Krsna for the first time, the women rejoiced at this sight of the eternal mother and her son.

It is nccessary that the umbilical cord be cut immediately after birth. But because Krsna had been brought from Mathura, one may wonder whether or not the ceremony to cut the umbilical cord took place.

Srila Prabhupada gives credence to two possibilities: either the *gopis* were in such ecstasy that they overlooked the ceremony altogether, or Yogamaya arranged that the cord be reconnected to Yasoda.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura insists that there must have been an umbilical cord and that it was cut. Local tradition also refers to a location near Syama-mandira where the umbilical cord was buried.

And Jiva Gosvami describes a ceremony in which the cord was cut, although he says that the nurse who performed the task declared that rather than a normal cord, a lotus was connected to Krsna’s navel.

Srila Prabhupada concludes:

**“Even though there may be doubts about the cutting of the umbilical cord, and even though it is possible that this was not done,...such events are regarded as factual.”**

Just as an expert magician easily hypnotises his audience, baby Krsna effortlessly cast a spell upon the women of Vrndavana, as a result of which they all wished that He had been born as their own son.

While Krsna was being bathed and anointed with auspicious items, a *brahmani* went to inform Nanda Maharaja that his son had been born, and the town crier spread the news throughout all of Gokula.

Nanda Maharaja was in the barn with his herd when the *brahmani* finally found him and respectfully said, “O King! Your queen has given birth to a son. Will you not come and see the joy of Gokula?”

This news made Maharaja Nanda’s hair stand on end; indeed, for several moments he stood motionless as his *gopa* friends excitedly shouted, “Jaya! Jaya!” and lovingly congratulated their great king.

Nanda Maharaja then called his brothers, dressed himself in his best clothes, and accompanied by *brahmanas* and village elders went to the maternity room to perform the birth ceremony *(jdta-karma).*

Nanda Maharaja was not the only one who was eager to see Krsna. A noisy crowd of women, *gopas, brahmanas,* and even children, all dressed in their finest and carrying gifts for the baby, went with him.

Although he was eager to see his son, Nanda Maharaja deferred to the seniority of the *brahmanas,* who chanted mantras, offered blessings, and placed auspicious items on the child’s head.

Thereafter, Rohini-devi brought Krsna into the outer chamber, where Nanda Maharaja finally saw, with his own eyes, the same child his meditations had enabled him to see within his heart for so long.

Only Mother Yasoda could surpass Maharaja Nanda’s love for the newborn. These two great souls possessed the purest love for Krsna. Any attempt to depict what they felt must fall short of the full truth.

At the sight of beautiful baby Krsna with a full head of black curly hair, Nanda Maharaja thought, “Visvakarma himself must have carved this beautiful child from a block of blue *cintamani* stone.”

Upon discovering auspicious signs such as the conch, disc, and lotus upon the palms of Krsna’s hands and the soles of His feet, Nandaraja remembered Lord Narayana and thought himself most fortunate.

To increase Nanda Maharaja’s bliss, Upananda’s wife took Krsna from Rohini and placed Him in Nanda’s lap. And when Yasoda heard about it, she shared her husband’s ecstasy. They were both stunned.

Again pure *brahmanas* performed rituals, chanted mantras, and offered blessings in abundance, after which — according to Srila Jiva Gosvami — it was time to cut the umbilical cord.

Once the umbilical cord had been cut — if there was one there to cut — Nanda Maharaja went outside the Syama-mandira. Near a sacrificial arena, he generously gave charity to the *brahmanas.*

The extent of the king’s generosity was boundless. He distributed cows, grains, gold, and ornaments to the *brahmanas* in such profusion that they could not take away all the gifts they had received.

It is said that the twice-born who had accepted the king’s invitation received in total two million well-decorated cows, plus seven hills of grain covered with jewels and embroidered cloth.

Once the *brahmanas* were pleased, Nandaraja went on to give charity to the rest of the citizens. Much to the amazement of his treasurers, as soon as Nanda’s coffers had been emptied, they would fill up again.

Whoever came to Nanda Maharaja left praising the king’s generosity and bestowing their blessings upon newborn Krsna, a treasure of greater value to the king of Vraja than even the wealth of the *devas.*

Nanda Maharaja gave gifts in proportion to the recipients’ learning and devotion, all the while thinking, “May Lord Visnu be pleased by this act of charity, and by His pleasure may my son be blessed.”

The *gopas’* wives and daughters who entered the maternity room blessed Krsna with the words: “May You live long and, as the future king of Vraja, may You give protection to its residents and cows.”

Krsna’s appearance in Gokula invoked such spontaneous joy and piety in its residents that they showered gifts upon Him. Those gifts exceeded in value the wealth Nanda Maharaja had distributed.

Nandaraja had accumulated such vast wealth as a result of his piety, but he knew that opulence, like all things, must be purified; that could only be done by giving his wealth in charity to the *brahmanas.*

About this purificatory process, Sukadeva Gosvami says,

*kalena snana-saucabhyam samskarais tapasejyaya*  
*sudhyanti danaih santustya dravyany atmatma-vidyaya*

**“O King! By the passing of time —**

**“Land and other material possessions are purified; by bathing, the body is purified; and by being cleansed, unclean things are purified. By purificatory ceremonies, birth is purified —**

**“By austerity, the senses are purified; and by charity offered to the** ***brahmanas*****, material possessions are purified. By satisfaction, the mind is purified; and by Krsna consciousness, the soul is purified.”**

After the initial exchange of gifts, Nanda Maharaja and his subjects commenced a festival of bliss in which the *gopas* and *gopis,* accom- panied by joyful music, sang the glories of Krsna’s birth.

The spirit of *sankirtana* permeated the Vraja-vasis, so much so that even sober seniors like Upananda danced like carefree youths and took part in a festival of sprinkling one another with yogurt and milk.

Sometimes the men would dance and sing as the *gopis* watched, clapping and urging their spouses on. Sometimes the *gopis* would dance, and their husbands would encourage them in the same way.

Covered in milk products and tired from dancing, everyone then entered the waters of the Yamuna, where along with Nanda they splashed water on one another as if they were all young children.

After applying valuable oil to their bodies, bathing, and dressing, the Vraja-vasis all converged on Paurnamasi’s hut to receive her blessings. And finally they all went to the king’s palace.

Nanda Maharaja seated his guests in the grand hall and inner courtyard and personally supervised the serving of *prasada,* again and again begging his guests to eat as much of the feast as they desired.

The Vraja-vasis were finally satisfied, so they bade farewell to their joyful king and returned to their homes. In a state of bliss unlike any they had felt before, they stayed up all night chanting Krsna’s glories.

His guests having departed, only Nanda’s family remained. The king, who felt that by Krsna’s birth he had attained a wealth more valuable than millions of universes, then enjoyed his own *sankirtana* festival.

Unable to restrain his voice from singing the glories of his son, or his feet from dancing in bliss, the king of Gokula set aside all gravity and composure, and ecstatically performed *kirtana* in his palace court.

Swept up by the waves of Nanda Maharaja's bliss, Upananda, Abhinanda, Sannanda, Nandana, and their wives and servants, as well as Rohini-devi, and even the palace guards chanted and danced.

The sound of their kirt?na blended with the sankirtana in the other houses of Gokula. The thunderous concert woke the residents of Vaikuntha from their sleep and induced them to praise Krsna's birth.

Beautiful songs, such as echoed through the streets, pastures, and forests of Gokula and into the Syama-mandira where Yasoda and Krsna slept.

As soon as the sound of nama-sunkirtana drifted into baby Krsna's ears, His eyes opened wide. Lying on His back, He smiled joyfully and moved His little hands and feet in time with the music.

Many centuries later, Caitanya Mahaprabhu would visit the place of Krsna's birth festival, where there stood a temple of Madana-gopala, whom Sanatana Gosvami would later rename Madana-mohana.

At that time Lord Caitanya was overwhelmed with ecstatic love. His singing and dancing so captivated the residents of Cokula that they were inspired to sing Krsna's name a way they never had before.

The sight of Madana-gopala completely agitated the Lord's heart with symptoms of ecstasy, farcing the people to conclude that He could not he an ordinary person hut Krsna Himself disguised as a sannyasi.

In this way, while remembering the events surrounding the celebration of Krsna's birth, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu completely enchanted the residents of Gokula and then continued on His way.

**\* \* \* \***

On the evening of Krsna's birth celebration, a messenger sent by Vasudeva arrived in Cokula with the news that Devaki's daughter had escaped Kamsa's wrath and suitably chastised the demonic king.

Nanda Maharaja and the gopas rejoiced to hear this, but they were not so happy to hear about Kamsa's plan to kill every child — particularly boys — born in the kingdom within the last ten days.

Reflecting on what they had just heard, Maharaja Nanda and his brothers decided that the best way to divert Kamsa's attention from Gokula would be to pay their annual tax and offer him special gifts.

But Nanda did not want to go to Mathura right away. He would wait until the sixth day after Krsna's birth, when Yasoda would leave the maternity room and return to the palace, the festival of sasthi-puja.

He therefore sent the courier back to Vasudeva with a message: he would be in Mathura in five days. After fulfilling his obligation to Kamsa, Nanda Maharaja would then meet privately with Vasudeva.

Every day Nanda Maharaja held a great festival for his people. When he was not attending to his guests, he was feasting his eyes upon the beauty of his little son and lovingly embracing the boy to his chest.

In spite of the tremendous risk posed by King Kamsa's infanticidal decree, Nanda Maharaja continued to invite trustworthy people to visit Gokula and behold the splendid glory of his newborn son.

In fact, just as the scent of a blossoming lotus naturally attracts greedy bees from far and wide, Krsna's presence spontaneously attracted pious souls not only from Vraja but from the entire universe.

As was the custom, six days after Krsna's birth, Yasoda left the maternity room with her son. Accompanied by other women, she was welcomed at the palace and worshipped by her husband, Nanda.

Now settled back into her home, Yasoda felt at peace, despite the commotion her subjects caused by constantly coming to see Krsna. To satisfy the Cokula-vasis, Yasoda eagerly gave them darsana of her son.

The effect of seeing Krsna was extraordinary; both adults and children felt ecstatic symptoms like shivering or crying. And, after seeing Krsna, the image of Him stayed within their minds for days.

Just before he was about to depart for Mathura, Nanda Maharaja repeatedly kissed Krsna's face and body and then held the child at arm's length to gaze at Him. The king almost forgot his mission.

But a wise nurse addressed Krsna, "O Syama! Your father is asking for Your permission to visit the king of Mathura." At this, Krsna sweetly smiled at His father as if to say, "Please, go perform your duty!"

As planned, Nanda Maharaja left senior gopas in charge of Gokula and travelled to Mathura hoping to appease Kamsa with the yearly tax, consisting of cartloads of valuable cloth, gold coins, and jewels.

Thereafter, Nandaraja went to his ancestral home in Mathura and secretly met with Vasudeva. The two cousin-brothers lovingly embraced and enquired about the welfare of each other's families.

Vasudeva and Nanda were both grandsons of Devamidha, a Yadu king. But Vasudeva's father Sura had married a ksatria's daughter, while Nanda's father Parjanya had married the daughter of a

As a ksatriya, Vasudeva was therefore superior; still, because Nanda Maharaja was older, he did not how to Vasudeva, rather he embraced him. This is an example of the intricacies of Vaisnava etiquette.

Vasudeva congratulated Maharaja Nanda on his newborn, hut because Vasudeva was not sure whether Nanda knew that the two babies had been exchanged, he did not specify the child's gender.

After some time Vasudeva said, "O brother! Although you are comfortable in this house, do not stay here for long. Return to Gokula soon, for I expect that there may he some disturbances there."

Heeding the sage advice of Vasudeva and feeling some premonition himself, Nanda Maharaja had his companions yoke their bulls, and at once they set out for Gokula, conversing about Krsna along the way.

In the meantime, as Kamsa requested, Putana, the Raksasi sister of the demons Baka and Agha, had been wandering through the villages around Mathura, eating newborn children or drinking their blood.

In her previous life, Putana had been Ratnamala, the daughter of Bali Maharaja. When Vamanadeva appeared in her father's sacrificial arena, Ratnamala felt great maternal affection for the Lord.

At first sight of the brahmana boy, she thought, "Oh, how I would love to embrace and feed that little brahmana as my son!" But once the Lord had cheated Bali of his empire, Ratnamala's heart changed.

She thought, "Since this Visnu is such a great cheater, if He were my son I would cheat Him and offer Him poison from my breast." Reading Ratnamala's thoughts, Vamanadeva said, "So be it!"

Ratnamala was thus reborn as the hideous witch Putana, whom divine providence directed to Gokula so that she could fulfil her own perverted maternal desire to try and poison Lord Visnu, Krsna.

Disguised as a female mendicant with matted locks, Putana arrived in Gokula on the night Nanda Maharaja was in Mathura, but she knew better than to attack the Vraja-vasis in her customary way.

Putana could sense that the soldiers of Nanda Maharaja were powerful enough to invoke the Narayana weapon and kill her, so she decided to wait until morning, when she would try another approach.

When the sun rose, Putana again transformed herself, this time into a beautiful woman, shapely, well dressed, and carefully ornamented. She entered Nanda's compound as if she were the goddess of fortune.

Jiva Gosvami says that usually Putana could neither go in any place Narayana was worshipped, nor harm the children of devotees, but in Gokula she was allowed to do so by Yogamaya's special arrangement.

Due to her extraordinarily beautiful appearance, neither the palace guards nor Krsna's nurses thought to stop Putana from coming into the inner residence of the palace where Krsna was lying in His crib.

Putana entered the bedroom and, with her beauty and gracefulness, as well as the false tears rolling down her checks and the milk steadily flowing from her breasts, won the trust of both Yasoda and Rohini.

To further mystify the two women, the horrible demoness said, in a voice choked with emotion, "O Yasoda! You must be very tired from executing the many duties involved in caring for your newborn son.

"As soon as I heard the news of that glorious child's birth, I wanted to let Him drink the auspicious nectar of my breasts. My breast milk will grant Him a perfect body, a long span of life, and true happiness."

Yasoda and Rohini were mesmerised. They thought, "Perhaps this beautiful woman is Ambika, Indrani, or Laksmi, compelled by love for Krsna to come from the celestial regions and feed Him personally."

For that reason they did not object when Putana sat beside the crib, placed Krsna upon her lap, and pushed the nipple of her breast into His mouth, just as a loving nurse would do to a young ward.

Holding Krsna in her lap, Putana could understand that this baby was not ordinary. His power was so awesome that He could end her life as quickly and as effortlessly as a hurricane could blow out a candle.

And yet, despite Putana's suspicion that she was holding death personified, the illusory potency of Yogamaya forced her to continue breastfeeding Krsna, who peacefully drank her milk with closed eyes.

Srila Prabhupada tells us that our venerable acaryas give a variety of reasons for Krsna's closing His eyes:

**"Some say that Krsna closed His eyes because He did not like to see the face of Putana, who had —**

**"Killed so many children and who had now come to kill Him. Others say that Putana hesitated to take the baby on her lap because something extraordinary was being dictated to her from within —**

**"And that in order to give her assurance Krsna closed His eyes so that she would not be frightened. And yet others interpret in this way... According to Vedic rules, the killing of a woman, a brahmana —**

**"Cows, or a child is strictly forbidden. Krsna was obliged to kill the demon Putana, and because the killing of a woman is forbidden according to Vedic sastra, He could not help but close His eyes.**

**"Another interpretation is that Krsna closed His eyes because He simply took Putana to be His nurse. Putana came to Krsna just to offer her breast for the Lord...and He accepted her as a nurse.**

There are also varying opinions on the poison Putana used. Sukadeva Gosvami and others say that she smeared her breast with poison, while Jiva Gosvami says that her breast milk itself was poisonous.

Everyone agrees, however, on what happened next. Krsna placed His small hands firmly on Putana's breast, held tightly to the demoness, and angrily sucked out her life force along with her milk.

**\* \* \* \***

Putana felt an unbearable burning pain in every part of her body. Trying to free herself from Krsna, she repeatedly cried out, "Please leave me!" But, determined in His mission, Krsna would not let go.

Jiva Gosvami says that Putana flew out of the window and into the sky like a bird, with Krsna still hanging on to her breast. Yasoda and Rohini, eyewitnesses to this kidnapping, fainted on the spot.

But Putana could neither fly very far, nor sustain her form as a beautiful woman for long. She resumed her original form, struggled with the baby on her breast, and finally fell to the ground.

Cakravarti Thakura offers another version. He says that Putana, with Krsna grasping her breast, ran from the house, out of Gokula, and in her huge form collapsed on a forest on the village outskirts.

To avoid harming any Vraja-vasis or cows, Yogamaya arranged that Putana fall forwards onto the riverside, not backwards onto Gokula; thus, only trees were crushed when her gigantic body fell.

The spot where Putana fell is called Putana-khadda, because of a gulley (khadda) Krsna created by dragging the horrible demoncis's enormous dead body some distance along the river Yamuna's shore.

When the mountainous creature suddenly fell from the sky, the Vraja-vasis felt the earth tremble under their feet and heard trees crash to the ground as if struck by King Indra's thunderbolts.

The nurses in Nanda-bhavana took note of where Putana fell to the ground, and so while some women tried to revive the two mothers, others ran to where the monster lay sprawled across the ground.

The nurses climbed up Putana's arms and found Krsna fearlessly playing on the demoness's chest. Overjoyed to see the child unscathed, they quickly brought Him hack to the palace.

Yasoda and Rohini were still unconscious, however, and no effort could revive them, until one intelligent gopi placed Krsna in their laps. The two mothers then gradually returned to consciousness.

Even though Krsna was now safely under their protection, when Yasoda and Rohini remembered how Putana had kidnapped Krsna, or heard the story of her death, they trembled and cried in anxiety.

Only after Krsna peacefully drank milk from their breasts did the minds of both mothers become steady. Repeatedly kissing Krsna and smelling His head, they called for an arati to be performed for His protection.

Just then Mother Yasoda remembered Balarama. Anxious for His safety as well, she stood up to get Him, but was restrained by Rohini, who had a nurse bring baby Balarama from an adjoining room.

Satisfied that Balarama was unharmed, Mother Yasoda again turned her attention to Krsna, bathing Him in cow urine and the dust raised by the cows to remove the impurity of wicked Putana's touch.

Then, to protect Krsna's tiny body, Mother Yasoda recited a mantra that Garbhodasayi Visnu had originally spoken to Lord Brahma, hearing which the brahmanas exchanged glances of amazement.

Brahma had passed the mantra on to Lord Siva, who in turn had given it to Durvasa, who finally transmitted the mantra to Mother Yasoda as a means by which she could give protection to her son.

Looking at the many saintlly women of the village who had crowded into the palace, Yasoda-devi thought that the ultimate protection for Krsna would be the good wishes of the Vaisnavis, and thus she said:

"My husband and 1 had no great desire for children, hut because all of you desired Him, this child has appeared, and since you have so mercifully given Krsna to us, in return, I now offer Him to you."

Holding Krsna, Mother Yasoda touched Him to the feet of the women of Gokula, one by one. They in turn blessed the child with their touch and these words: "O Yasoda! Beautiful wife of our king!

"Please listen to what we have to say. Whatever pious acts we have inherited from the paternal and maternal branches of our families we offer for the safety and happiness of your wonderful child, Krsna."

After this exchange, Krsna was again offered arati The women then discussed Putana's attempt to kill Krsna, continuously consoling one another. While this was going on, Maharaja Nanda entered Vraja.

Putana's horrible body was so large that the closer Nanda Maharaja came to it, the harder it was for him to determine what it was; thus the excited Vraja-vasis had to tell him that it was a dead Raksasi.

But when Nanda Maharaja heard that this terrible demoness had tried to poison his son, he fainted on the spot, only to be revived with great difficulty by his patient and stout-hearted brothers.

After Nanda's brothers had reassured him that Krsna had not been harmed, Upananda ordered some men of lower caste to chop Putana's body into pieces, pile the pieces in one place, and set them on fire.

Because Krsna had sucked Putana's breast, she was purified of all sinful reactions and bodily impurities. It was for this reason that as her body burned it gave off a sweet fragrance like aguru incense.

That fragrance pervaded the whole of Vraja; in fact, people came to Gokula curious to find the source of this celestial aroma, only to be told the smell was coming from the burning body of a dead Raksasi.

Hearing that Krsna had sucked the life air from the demoness, the Vraja-vasis offered the child their blessings and exclaimed that Lord Narayana must have given baby Krsna special protection.

The smoke and ash from Putana's burning body settled on the other side of the river at Koila, blackening the bank where Vasudeva had entered the river a week earlier to bring Krsna to Gokula.

After Nanda Maharaja had composed himself, he said to his companions, "Vasudeva was right! He warned me that some disaster would befall Gokula. He must be the mystic in our family."

Then Nanda Maharaja, his body soaked in tears, hurried up the hill to his palace, where he was greeted by Mother Yasoda and the other women in the courtyard before taking his seat upon the throne.

Tungi-devi handed Krsna to Mother Yasoda, who placed Him in Nanda Maharaja's lap. Not only was the torment in the king's heart checked, it was replaced by indescribable transcendental bliss.

With his eyes the king hungrily tasted the beauty of Krsna's form and the nectar radiating from His lotus face. Then Nandaraja smelled the fragrance of his son's head and the aroma of His body.

With his other senses Nanda Maharaja relished the touch, sound, and taste of Krsna's limhs, voice, and lips, and loudly praised Lord Narayana, who had protected his son from a ghastly calamity.

The king then distributed charity to the brahmanas and implored the members of that saintly class, especially goddess Paurnamasi, to bless his young son with a long life and freedom from future danger.

Putana had offered her breast to poison Krsna, but Krsna overlooked her evil motive, accepted her gesture as motherly, and bestowed upon her the perfection of life after she had left that horrible body.

In this regard, Uddhava speaks of Krsna's memorable kindness,

*aho baki yam stana-kala-kutam jighamsayapayayad apy asadhvi*  
*lebhe gatim dhatry-ucitam tato nyam kam va dayalum saranam vrajema*

**"Alas! How shall 1 take shelter of one more merciful than He who granted the position of mother to Putana although she was unfaithful and she prepared deadly poison to be sucked from her breast?"**

Sukadeva Gosvami also confirms that Putana attained the position of a mother in Vaikuntha. And Brahma adds that Putana's family members also shared in her perfection.

Since the gopis who offered their breast-milk to Krsna with love also returned to Goloka as His mothers, one may wonder if Krsna lacks discrimination, treating His devotees and His enemies equally.

The answer is that Putana and the gopis did not attain the same destination. Cakravarti Thakura confirms that Putana did not attain the form of a nurse, but rather a form like that of a nurse.

Putana was admitted to that part of Goloka Vrndavana where Krsna is worshipped in a mood of reverential love. In contrast, by their spontaneous love the gopis attained Krsna in all-attractive Vraja.

In this way, Krsna holds true to His promise: "As all surrender unto Me, I reward them accordingly." He may have bestowed His mercy on Putana, but the mercy He offered to the gopis is still unmatched.

Similar good fortune awaits those practising devotees who always remember Krsna in His form as a baby and lovingly offer Him seasoned sweet milk, the finest fruits, and His favourite milk sweets.

People who hear this pastime of Krsna's killing Putana — or any of His childhood pastimes — with faith and devotion will attain attraction to Him and everything related to Him (govinde labhate ratim).

Bhaktivinoda Thakura proffers that discussing the killing of Putana will free us from the influence of two kinds of unauthorised gurus: the pseudo spiritual master and our own contaminated intelligence.

A person who is not on the transcendental platform and yet accepts his own intelligence as the ultimate authority is said to have surrendered to a fallible, imperfect guru — surely he will be misled.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda confirms this by saying that the sastic statement, "sometimes one acts as one's own instructing spiritual master," refers to a person in samadhi, not a conditioned soul.

Furthermore, one may accept another person who is incapable of acting as spiritual master, one who cannot guide one to Krsna — a karmi, jnani, or a neophyte devotee unable to give proper guidance.

A neophyte, for example, may know nothing of the goal of pure devotional service yet profess to know, or a devotee may know the goal but be unable to teach disciples according to their qualifications.

Athese so-called spiritual masters will be exposed as inadequate and unauthorised to those devotees who faithfully hear about and discuss the Supreme Lord Krsna's pastime of killing the demoness Putana.

**\* \* \* \***

In days and weeks that followed Putana's death, Krsna's beauty and childish sweetness increased without limit. He attracted crowds of Vraja-vasis to visit Him at Nanda Maharaja's palace in Gokula.

They would stand around Krsna's crib and gaze without blinking at His dark restless eyes, charming smile, and cloud-blue complexion. They would play with Him until He laughed, and then laugh as well.

Sometimes Krsna would move His legs, making a soft tinkling sound with His anklets to signal that He wanted to be held. If no one picked Him up He would cry, and when they did He would laugh with glee.

Whenever He was hungry He would cry. Then after drinking His mother's milk He would peacefully fall asleep. And when He awoke, the sunbeams of His smile would thrill whoever was present.

At three months, Krsna turned over in His crib. A soon as one of the nurses noticed this, she told Mother Yasoda, who, overjoyed, immediately made arrangements for the uttana ceremony.

In the Vedic culture a baby's first attempt to rise and turn over is a special event celebrated by the festival called utthana. At that time the child is taken outside of the house for the first time.

This festival took place in the courtyard of Maharaja Nanda's palace. Yasoda-devi invited village women to sing and dance and brahmanas to chant Vedic mantras, thus creating an auspicious atmosphere.

A large ornate cart stood in the courtyard. A family heirloom, it was always piled high with assorted valuable pots, pans, and vessels used for special occasions like bathing ceremonies or sacrifices.

The cart and its contents represented Nanda Maharaja's resources, and were seen by the people as a clear symbol of the goddess of fortune's grace upon their king and indeed the whole of Gokula.

First Krsna was bathed. Then He was dressed in yellow cloth, beautifully adorned with ornaments, and finally covered by the brahmanas' mantras for protection and tucked into a new bed.

This bed had been crafted for the occasion. Its frame was fashioned from a combination of semi-valuable stones and it was fitted with a new mattress covered by fine sheets and a small perfumed pillow.

The ceremony and subsequent offering of gifts took four and a half hours to complete. During that time Krsna fell asleep. Still lying in His new bed, He was then placed in the shade under the cart.

Mother Yasoda lay beside Krsna on a mattress until she was satisfied that He was indeed sleeping soundly. She then entrusted a small group of five-year-old boys to keep an eye on Him.

At that time, unseen by anyone, a demon friend of King Kamsa named Utkaca entered into the framework of the cart with the intention to make it collapse on baby Krsna and crush Him to death.

News had reached Mathura that a mysterious infant had killed Putana, so Utkaca was careful not to simply adopt a disguise; rather, he used his ability to become invisible to achieve Kamsa's aim.

Utkaca had previously been a son of Hiranyakasipu who once caused a disturbance in the asrama of Lomasa Muni. The muni cursed Utkaca to live without a gross body until Krsna gave him liberation.

When Utkaca, who possessed only a ghostly form, entered the cart, his weight bent the axle, pressing the wheels into the earth and lowering the heavy wagon closer and closer to baby Krsna beneath it.

As the cart bore down on Krsna, He awoke and began to cry, not due to the danger but because He was hungry. But the noisy ceremonies drowned out the sound of His crying, so no one came to feed Him.

Angry at being neglected and well aware of Utkaca's wicked scheme, Krsna casually kicked the cart, lifting it into the air and breaking it to pieces, its axle, wheels, frame, and contents scattering everywhere.

The agonising groans of Utkaca blended with the noise of the breaking cart and the falling utensils. He was spread throughout the cart, so he was broken into just as many pieces as the cart itself.

The Vraja-vasis panicked when they saw pieces of the cart fly in all directions and heard the heart-stopping moans of the dying demon. They feared that a ghost had come to attack their darling Krsna.

Ignoring everything else, Mother Yasoda shot forward and grabbed Krsna in a flash, trying desperately to cover her infant son with her own body, just as a cow would shelter her calf in a heavy storm.

The commotion that the falling cart and the wailing spectators had caused in the courtyard drew the attention of Vraja's leaders, including Nanda Maharaja, who had been overseeing the ceremonies.

Nanda quickly surveyed the scene before him and heard his subjects' testimonies, then he carefully inspected baby Krsna's limbs. Once he felt satisfied that his son had not been harmed, he became peaceful.

Meanwhile, Mother Yasoda excitedly interrogated the young boys who had been looking after Krsna. At first reluctant, the leader of the boys finally blurted out, "O mother! I tell you the truth.

"Your son Krsna lifted His foot and kicked the cart. It then flew into the air as gracefully as if it were a bird." The other children confirmed the boy's assertion, imitating Krsna and laughing.

The elders dismissed the boys' story as childish prattle. But some Vraja-vasis who had been reminded of Putana's death harboured doubts. They thought, "Maybe the child did it. Maybe He did!"

Thinking it to be likely that the cart's collapse was the work of a demon or a malefic planet, Nanda Maharaja requested the brahmanas to chant hymns and perform auspicious rites for his son's protection.

Meanwhile, the men reassembled the cart and replaced the utensils and paraphernalia that were scattered everywhere. As a symbol of the wealth of Nanda Maharaja and his clan, the cart was worshipable.

Finally, as Krsna was being bathed in auspicious substances, the brahmanas performed a sacrifice and Nanda Maharaja distributed charity to ensure Krsna's security, well-being, and good fortune.

Later, with the ceremonies complete and the guests departed, Maharaja Nanda brought his family members together and revealed his mind: "These two boys are difficult to care for separately.

"Their mothers love Them equally but arc often distracted by their various household duties. Let us select an auspicious day and hold a festival to fix the idea in Their minds that They must stay together."

According to the king's order, on a day marked by music and prayers, Krsna and Balarama were ceremonially bound together. From that day on, whether eating, sleeping, or playing, They were inseparable.

This festival took place in the palace of Nanda Maharaja, in the same courtyard where Krsna had toppled the cart and killed Utkaca, who is also known as Sakatasura, the cart demon.”

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura says that the pastimes of Krsna's childhood display the power and majesty of the Lord. By sucking out Putana's life, Krsna showed the immeasurable power of His lips.

In killing the cart demon at the age of three months, Krsna showed the power of His feet. And in His next pastime, the killing of the whirlwind Trnavarta, He showed the power of His hands.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda makes an interesting point about Krsna's killing the cart demon, a point that both regulated practitioners and those aspiring for spontaneous devotion would do well to consider.

He likens regulated devotion devoid of knowledge of its goal — the attainment of spontaneous attachment—and unfit devotees' attempts at spontaneous devotion to be no more than cart-like burdens.

The acarya further warns that premature attempts to inspire vraja- bhakti in the hearts of sakata-like regulated devotees will prove to be destructive burdens for both spiritual master and disciple.

Burdened by the offence of preaching the glories of Krsna and His holy name to faithless souls, such a guru will fall away from the path of pure devotional service in the company of his misled disciples.

The bona fide spiritual master discusses spontaneous devotional service only with qualified disciples, and then only in proportion to their eligibility. To neophyte disciples, he awakens it gradually.

Unfortunately, there will always he unauthorised gurus who instruct sakata-like disciples to perform service in the mood of the Vraja-vasis without considering whether those practitioners are truly qualified.

Such gurus and their disciples can be saved from disaster by hearing from and associating with realised Vaisnavas, whose instructions and example give proper guidance on the path leading to vraja-bhakti.

Just as Krsna liberated Sakatasura, devotees who sincerely hear this pastime will be liberated from being weighed down by the burdens of aimless devotion, artificial practices, and premature instructions.

Srila Rupa Gosvami cites an unnamed Vaisnava who prays

*ati-lohita-kara-caranam manjula-gorocana-tilakam*  
*hatha-parivartita-sakatam mura-ripum uttama-sayinam vande*

**"Lying on His back**

**"His hands and feet charmingly reddish, and His forehead gracefully decorated with yellow gorocana tilaka... Lord Murari violently overturned the cart. I offer my respectful obeisances unto Him."**

**\* \* \* \***

Next, Srimad-Bhagavatam records the killing of Trnavarta, then Mother Yasoda's first vision of the universe in Krsna's mouth, followed by the name-giving ceremony for Krsna and Balarama.

Jiva Gosvami, however, first presents Krsna's and Balarama's name-giving ceremony, pointing out that the sequence in the ?hagavatam is not chronological but reflects Sukadeva Gosvami's ecstatic feelings.

As days turned into weeks, the two brothers began to recognise the people around them. Their mothers would point to a guest and joke, "Is he part of our family?" and the boys would laugh in reply.

Meanwhile, King Kamsa, constantly anxious to know where the son of Vasudeva might be hiding, was sending his supporters to search high and low for the child who had been prophesised to kill him.

Vasudeva was well aware of Kamsa's evil intentions, and yet to properly perform Krsna's and Balarama's name-giving ceremony, he secretly sent Garga Muni, the priest of his dynasty, to Gokula.

Nanda Maharaja received Garga Muni in a manner befitting a sage of his stature by bathing the Muni's feet and offering him worship. Nanda then asked how Vasudeva was faring under Kamsa's scrutiny.

In response, Garga Muni brought great joy to Nanda Maharaja by disclosing the purpose of his visit. After further talks, they decided that the name-giving ceremony should be performed in secret.

The sage said, "Goddess Durga told King Kamsa that Vasudeva's son had been born somewhere in the kingdom. Since then the demon has been enquiring from everyone about the boy's whereabouts."

"O saint!" Nanda Maharaja replied. "Please conduct this ceremony in the barn with only my intimate family members present. Except for the chanting of your sacred mantras, we can forgo the formal rituals."

To avoid attracting the attention of anyone, Nanda Maharaja and Garga Muni went together to the barn, which was empty at that time because Nanda's men were all out herding the cows and calves.

Nandaraja sent a servant to call Mother Yasoda and Rohini-devi from the palace. They soon appeared, with their sons in their arms, curious to know why they had been asked to come alone to the empty barn.

As soon as Garga Muni saw Krsna and Balarama, he recognised Them as the ultimate cause and substance of all existence, who had appeared in the village of Gokula as the sons of Their pure devotees.

Gazing upon Krsna, the sage felt ecstatic symptoms, like bewilderment and trembling, stir within him. He wondered how he would be able to conduct the name-giving ceremony in such a state.

Garga Muni thought, "If I hold on to the babies' feet, their parents will think I have gone mad. If I embrace Them to my chest, they will think I am frivolous. But if I do nothing, I will be the loser."

Finally, the sage gathered his wits and thought, "Never mind! I shall play the role of the impartial sage, knowing all the while that today my studies, my senses, and my very life have all come to perfection."

Garga Muni signalled to the two mothers, who humbly came forward with their sons and offered respects to the sage. The muni pronounced blessings for the boys and asked everyone to he seated.

Mother Yasoda and Rohini-devi tried to hold on to their spirited boys, who were enthusiastically trying to wiggle off Their mothers' laps and crawl around this new place that They had never seen.

Garga Muni watched the boys' movements as he worshipped various deities, headed by Ganesa. After carefully appeasing planetary deities, he pronounced the children's names and explained their significance.

First he spoke about Mother Rohini's son: "Yogis find happiness (ramante) in Him, He is the supreme enjoyer (ramati), and His qualities delight (ramayati) all devotees; thus He will he called Rama.

"Because He was pulled (sankarsana) from Devaki's womb, He unites the families of Nanda and Vasudeva. And because He attracts all people and removes their sins, He will be called Sankarsana.

"Because after annihilation He alone remains (avasesa), He is called Sesa, because He is as powerful (bala) as the Supreme Lord, He is called Bala, and because He enjoys wrestling, He is called Baladeva.

"Because He enjoys (rama) the mellow of humour when His friends tease Him after defeating Him in games of riddles, saying, 'O Deva! What use is Your strength (bala) now?' He will be called Balarama."

Rohini's son has countless names, all as eternal as He Himself. Chanting those names gave Garga Muni untold bliss, but the sage was obliged to stop, for names even more relishable were yet to come.

After a moment's pause the sage went on, "Now, ? King, please hear the names of your son." Attracted by Krsna's appearance in different ages, however, Garga Muni first sang these glories of the Lord:

"Your son Krsna appears as an incarnation in every millennium. In the past, He assumed three different cotours — white, red, and yellow — and now He has appeared in a blackish colour.

"In another Dvapara-yuga, He appeared as Lord Ramacandra in the cotour of suka, a parrot. Att such incarnations have now assembled in Krsna.” After saying this, the sage paused for a few more moments.

He wanted to see if Nandaraja and the mothers had understood what he had just said. Srila Prabhupada writes that the muni's words partially explained Krsna's position and partially covered the facts.

The parents had been attentive, but the awe-inspiring wonders they heard about Krsna were like mountains submerged in the fathomless ocean of their parental love, lost from sight in the waters of affection.

Sri Garga said,

**"Appearing in ages one after another in white-, red-, and yellow-coloured forms, at the end of this Dvapara-yuga He has a dark (krsna) complexion. Therefore, your son is called Krsna.**

**"Great sages explain the meaning of the name Krsna in uncountable ways. They say that krsi means 'material existence' and that na represents bliss (ananda), or that na means 'one who stops.'**

**"He is the personification of bliss, who by His attractive qualities steals the hearts of His companions and cleanses the sins of devotees, bringing their materia! existence to an end. Thus He is called Krsna.**

**"The letter ? in His name stands for kamala-kanta, the husband of the goddess of fortune, r stands for Rama, the supreme enjoyer, and s stand for sad-guna-pati, the master of six opulences.**

**"Alternatively, the letter s stands for svetadvipa-nivasa-krt, 'He who resides in Svetadvipa,' n for Lord Nrsimha, and a for aksara, 'the immortal,' and agni-bhuk, 'He who enjoys sacrificial offerings.'**

**"These letters combine to form the name of the Supreme Person, Krsna, who is the master of countless universes, the presiding Deity of the Vaikuntha planets, and who resides in His own abode of Goloka.**

**"Another name for your son is Vasudeva," Garga Muni continued, "because He previously appeared as the son of Vasudeva, and because He pervades the senses (vasu) and heart (deva) of all living entities.**

**"O King! I have mentioned but two names of your transcendental son — Krsna and Vasudeva. In truth, His names are as innumerable as His pastimes. Thus both names remain secret even from the Vedas.**

**"Dear Nanda Maharaja! Hear me well! Do not he surprised at the extraordinary deeds of your son, who has appeared to protect His devotees and to remove the earth's burden by killing the demons.**

**"Your fortune knows no bounds, for the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is greater than the greatest, has appeared in your home as a small child and will accept your occupation as a cowherd."**

Hearing all these wonderful things, Nanda Maharaja looked at the two boys, their mothers, and then at the sage and said, "I accept everything you say, hut such things cannot stay fixed in my mind."

Within his heart, Garga Muni bowed to the spontaneous love of Nanda Maharaja, then he revised his statements, speaking in words that the king of the gopas would be able to understand and remember.

Garga Muni said,

*tasman nandatmajo yam te narayana-samo gunaih*  
*sriya kirtyanubhavena gopayasva samahitah*

**"In conclusion, therefore, ? Nanda Maharaja, this child of yours is as good as Narayana.**

**"In transcendental qualities, opulence, name, fame, and influence, He is exactly like the Supreme Personality of Godhead Narayana. You should all raise this child very carefully and cautiously."**

Nanda Maharaja's eyes filled with tears of love as Garga Muni elaborated on this statement:

**"Because you have pleased your worshipable Deity, Narayana, He has given you a son like Himself.**

**"Even the purest activities are fraught with obstacles, so protect your son carefully by constantly chanting His names in the company of the Vraja-vasis. In turn, He will protect you as only Narayana can."**

It is interesting to note that, even though Garga Muni declared Krsna to be Lord Narayana's equal, the sage's words imply that Narayana is actually inferior to Krsna in many significant ways:

Krsna grants liberation to the demons He personally kills. He bestows great ecstasy upon His devotees. And He enacts the rasa dance, a pastime so unique that it is inaccessible even to Laksmi-devi.

Next Nandaraja requested the sage to give an astrological reading of Krsna's birth. Garga said,

**"Since your son was born in the year called Vibhavasu, Vasu and the whole universe will be pleased with Him.**

**"Since He was born under the Rohini constellation, He will be the master of many herds of cows, and because His ascendant is Taurus, He will doubtlessly be the protector of innumerable bulls.**

**"His dignified planets indicate a transcendental majesty upon which sages will fix their minds. They will likewise meditate upon His words, which are themselves the substance and conclusion of all scriptures.**

**"Your son's chart says that He will destroy the demons and will be the cause of auspiciousness not only for you, not only for His devotees, not only for the creation, but also for the creator, Lord Siva himself.**

**"As Sambu, Lord Siva is originally responsible for injecting the living beings into the material energy. He is thus also known as the creator, but that creative potency finds its source in your son, Krsna.**

**"As I have already told you, because your son is like Narayana, He will be the source of bliss for humans and demigods alike and the cause of affliction for arrogant demons like Kamsa and his ilk.**

**"O King! Those who love Him — as you and your people surely do — will never again see repeated birth and death, but will live with Him eternally in His abode of cows. That is the essence of His chart."**

Having said this much, Garga Muni then swore the king to secrecy, saying, "Do not reveal these confidential truths to anyone." He then placed Krsna on Nanda's lap and for some time was lost in bliss.

Then Garga placed Balarama in Nanda's lap as well. The sage relished having physically embraced the Absolute Truth and marvelled at the fortune of the Vraja-vasis, who could live and play with Them.

Garga Muni got to his feet and walked as far as the barn door. Raising his hand in a gesture of blessing, he turned and said, "May you remain prosperous with your cows and sons." And with that he left.

As his guest departed, Nanda thought, "The words of this great soul confirm the dreams I had of this boy. They were not illusion. After such a long time, I finally have a son who is equal to Narayana.

"It may be that the Lord has fulfilled my desire in return for my pious deeds of protecting cows and giving charity to the brahmanas. In any case, my heart overflows with bliss, and I desire nothing more."

**\* \* \* \***

Nanda Maharaja then returned to his palace and secretly arranged for Garga Muni to receive a wealth of gold and cows in return for risking his life to perform the name-giving ceremony for the two boys.

It was imperative Kamsa not find out that Garga Muni had conducted the actual name-giving ceremony for Nanda's sons. And yet, despite the danger, a public name-giving ceremony would also be necessary.

If such an event did not take place, the residents of Gokula would think it odd. Surely such talk would eventually reach Kamsa, who would grow suspicious and perhaps come to uncover the truth.

Nanda Maharaja therefore asked the pure brahmanas of Gokula to conduct a large public ceremony, an event that brought great joy to Nanda's people and at which he freely gave charity to everyone.

Krsna's ear-piercing ceremony is said to have taken place at Krsna-kupa, halfway between Nanda Maharaja's palace and the cow barn. Jiva Gosvami, however, offers a different version of this event.

He suggests that no such ritual was necessary because Krsna and Balarama had holes in Their ears from birth. He therefore concludes that Garga Muni did not perform the car-piercing ceremony.

But in order to avoid suspicion from Kamsa's spies, who were constant roaming about Vraja, it is possible that at this place Nanda Maharaja also had the brahmanas feign an ear-piercing ceremony.

After the name-giving ceremony, Krsna's and Balarama's parents and the rest of the Vraja-vasis began calling Them by name, but because They were always together, the boys were sometimes confused.

Someone would call out Krsna's name, and Balarama would make a sound. Or someone else would call out Balarama's name, and Krsna would kick His legs, His anklets tinkling in such a pleasing way.

Mother Yasoda's and Maharaja Nanda's repeated calls for Krsna were like constant sankirtana, pouring nectar all over Gokula and into the ears of the Vraja-vasis and of the two transcendental brothers.

In a short time, Krsna and Balarama learned to crawl. And soon They were quite agile, quickly crawling to Their mothers as They tried to repeat Their own names in sweet broken words, "Rna!" and "Bam!"

Once, as Krsna was crawling very quickly, the tinkling of His anklets and waist bells startled Him. He then sat down and looked around to see where the noise was coming from, making Yasoda laugh in bliss.

It was not long before the brothers could not be kept within the con- fines of the house; instead, They would crawl around in the palace courtyard, and the village children would come to play with Them.

Sometimes Yasoda-devi would come out of the house and catch Krsna exploring the recesses of the courtyard. Lifting Him to her breast, she would cover His face with kisses and wipe the dirt from His limbs.

On most days Nandaraja would return from the pastures in time to see Krsna playing in the courtyard. Holding the boy on his shoulders, the king would gallop like a horse, making Krsna laugh with glee.

When Krsna first saw the reflections of birds in the polished marble floor or in a sparkling gem, He would try to touch the creatures with His soft reddish fingers, amusing the nurses that took care of Him.

On one occasion, Krsna ventured beyond the courtyard through the main gates, which were guarded by a statue of a lion on either side. Frightened by the sight of the ferocious beasts, He began to cry aloud.

Some elderly gopis picked Him up, cuddled Him to stop His crying, and took Him back inside, gently scolding Yasoda, "O beautiful one! Take care! This restless boy should not go past the courtyard."

Srila Jiva Gosvami composed a song to praise these pastimes. It begins,

*valayita-balya-vilasa jaya bala-valita hare*

**"O Hari! AH glories to Your childhood pastimes, which You enjoy with Balarama."**

*Ringana-keli-kule janani-sukha-kari*  
*vraja-drsi sukrta-sphurad-avatari*

**"You give happiness to Mother Yasoda with Your crawling. And the sight of You blesses the eyes of every last person in Vrndavana."**

*Kinkini-gana-ranane hrdi ruci-dhari*  
*pada-yuga-calana-kutuka-vihari*

**"O child! The eager movements of Your feet stir Your anklets to make tinkling sounds that delight the hearts of all."**

*Gorasa-kirni-bhave panke laghu-cari*  
*varana-karana-vag-aticari*

**"Entering fearlessly into the courtyards of others, You are indifferent to the dirt, muddy with milk, that smears Your body as You play."**

*Akalita-jana-milane tasmad apasari*  
*jananim prati gati-capala-bhari*

**"O Krsna! Even when You meet strangers, You share Your bliss with them and then quickly crawl hack to the safety of Your mother's lap."**

*Janani-stana-vasane bhaya-bhag anuhari*  
*tatra payorasa-visarahari*

**"You hide beneath the cloth that covers Mother Yasoda's breast. Holding her breast with Your hands, You drink its nectarean milk."**

*Vapusi mrda-maline mrdutapahari*  
*janani-kara-krta-mrjaydhari*

**"Like a lion cub You smear Your body with fresh dirt. And Your mother, like a lioness, lovingly cleanses Your limbs with her own hands."**

*Api tandra-valane stana-pam anukari*  
*janani-smita-patad-amrtasari*

**"While drinking from one breast You hold the other and fall asleep with mother's milk on Your face, Yasoda's radiant smile Your shelter."**

On one occasion, Krsna crawled into Nanda Maharaja's treasury, abundant with jewels and shiny walls. Seeing His own image reflected everywhere, He was afraid of the many unfamiliar boys His own age.

Unable to startle those children, or to wipe their image from the walls with His hands, Krsna quickly crawled back to His mother's lap, held His body against hers, and hid His lotus face under her veil.

It was only another short time before Krsna tried to stand. But after taking a few steps, He would fall back onto His bottom and cry until His mother took His hand, raised Him up, and walked beside Him.

Gaining confidence with every step, Krsna's lotus face would beam with smiles — until Mother Yasoda let go of His hand. Krsna would again fall down and pound the ground with His palms in frustration.

Calling out, "O poor boy! Poor boy!" Yasoda-devi would take Krsna onto her lap, rock Him back and forth, and kiss His face over and over until He took courage and tried to walk once more.
