With time Krsna gained strength and learned to balance Himself. He would walk slowly from His mother's arms to an object some distance away, touch it, then turn and toddle back quickly to her open arms.

One day, after Krsna had gained proficiency in walking, elderly Mukhara played a joke on the toddler. She asked Him to fetch heavy objects like a large clay pot, a wooden seat, and a metal drinking cup.

Krsna followed Mukhara's orders. Carefully concentrating, He picked up each object and tried to carry them all at once, but when He could not, He dropped the heavier items and just brought the lighter ones.

Just as quickly as Krsna learned to walk, He also learned to talk, though Balarama was the first to started pronouncing words. A nurse full of affection for Krsna gave the infant His first lessons in speech.

She made Him repeat But, when finally in front of His parents, Krsna combined the two words and proudly said, "Mata."

As Krsna's vocabulary grew, His mother would test Him: "Son! Are You ready for the forest?" Krsna answered, "Yes!" Smiling, she added, "And will You be able to protect Your friends?" "Yes!" He replied.

His nurses would point to an object and say its name. Krsna would then reproduce the sound and remember it from that time on, never to forget it. The elderly women were stunned by His intelligence.

Mother Yasoda and Rohini-devi taught their young sons each other's names. From that time on Balarama would call Krsna by His name, and Krsna would call Balarama Dauji ("elder brother").

One of Krsna's grandmothers once asked Him to name the limbs of His body. Unable to do so, He promptly toddled off to His mother and requested her to teach Him, which she happily did.

Later, Krsna returned to the company of the elders and waited until they again asked Him, "Where are Your eyes? Your ears? Your nose?" Krsna responded by confidently pointing to each limb one by one.

And when they asked, "Where arc Your teeth? Show us Your teeth!" Krsna amazed everyone by pointing a delicate finger to His mouth and replying sweetly, "My teeth have not come out yet."

One day, as Yasoda was breastfeeding Krsna, she thought that she could feel His teeth coming in. When He had finished eating, she said, "Open Your mouth and let me see if any teeth have come yet."

Just as she had suspected, Mother Yasoda saw Krsna's baby teeth, which looked just like tiny drops of milk in His little mouth. On another day, Mother Yasoda was again breastfeeding her darling son.

Just as Krsna was finished, He yawned. Within the mouth of her child, Yasoda could see the entire creation — the upper and lower planets, the earth, luminaries, mountains, rivers, forests, and oceans.

As Mother Yasoda observed this display of Krsna's majesty, her love did not bow in the least to His divinity; instead, she prayed to Narayana, "O Lord! Please protect my son from this disturbance."

Thakura Bhaktivinoda says that Yasoda-devi's indifference to Lord Krsna's opulence is not material; rather, it is the symptom of a great transcendentalist, caused by the influence of Krsna's sweetness.

Cakravarti Thakura says that Krsna sometimes tests whether His devotees' love will wane in the face of such awesomeness, hut the Lord's majesty simply causes the love of pure devotees to increase.

The acarya also quotes Brahma, who says that Yasoda-devi saw the universe in Krsna's abdomen, not in His mouth, "O Lord! You exhibited the universe within Your abdomen before Your mother!"

Wherever Yasoda saw the universe in her son's body, the event was quickly obscured by her deep absorption in the sweetness of His enchanting acts, by which He also captured the Vraja-vasis' hearts.

Nanda had thought it would be easier to look after Krsna and Balarama if They stayed together, but now that the two brothers were inseparable conspirators, it was nearly impossible to control Them.

Krsna would suggest, "Let Us go outside to play!" Looking here and there, Balarama would reply, "Mother will be angry with Us." But Krsna would insist, arguing with confidence, "No she won't."

The boys were attracted to whatever was dangerous: the jaws of wild beasts, the fangs of hooded snakes, the horns of cows, the flames of cooking fires, and the sharp edges of knives. They were fearless.

Yasoda and Rohini were in such anxiety over their sons that they could not properly attend to household duties; indeed, in addition to being daring, the boys also found various ways to trick Their mothers.

The boys ventured into the forbidden areas outside the courtyard, only to be caught by Their nurses and brought back into the house. But the boys again disappeared and returned to Their playground.

Yasoda sent her servants to bring the boys back, but again and again They would slip from the grasp of Their caretakers and run out the gate. Finally, Yasoda and Rohini had to take up the task themselves.

The two mothers carried their wiggling and laughing sons into the house, where they rubbed Them with oil, bathed, dressed, and fed Them, and lovingly put Them to sleep by telling Them fantastic tales.

About these childhood pastimes, Sri Kaviratna says,

*aho ahobhir na kaler viduyate sudha-su-dhara-madhur am pada pade*  
*dine dine candana- candra-sitalam yaso yasoda-tanayasya giyate*

**"One who daily sings the glories of Yasoda's son, glories as cooling as sandalwood and camphor, is never troubled by Kali-yuga; rather, at every step he finds a torrential flood of the sweetest nectar."**

**\* \* \* \***

One evening, as Yasoda-devi was putting Him to sleep, Krsna asked, "Mata! Will you tell Me an adventure story?" Mother Yasoda stroked her son's head and began, "There was once a king named Rama!"

A smile appeared on Krsna's lips as He nodded and said, "And then?" Mother Yasoda continued, "He had a beautiful wife whose name was Sita." Krsna's eyelids were getting heavy. Sleepily, He said, "And?"

Gently stroking her son's face, Yasoda went on, "On the order of His father, Rama went into exile with Sita and lived happily in the Pancavati forest until a demon called Ravana kidnapped Sita."

Hearing the narration of His own pastimes from ancient times, Krsna startled His mother by suddenly sitting up and calling out "Laksmana! Where is My bow? Hurry! Where is My bow? We must rescue her!"

On another night, before going to steep herself, Yasoda-devi looked in on Krsna and found Him sitting in bed playing with His toys, ignoring the goddess of sleep, who stood waiting beside His bed.

Yasoda-devi entered the room, sat on Krsna's bed, and embraced Him. Then she said, "O my child! ? my rising dark moon! AH of Cokula is deep in sleep and dreaming of You. Are You not feeling tired?"

"No, mother!" Krsna replied, still absorbed in play. "Somehow sleep has forgotten about Me tonight." Putting His toys in their box and making Him lie down with His head in her lap, Mother Yasoda said:

"Listen, my little son! I will tell You a bedtime story that will make You fall asleep." Krsna settled comfortably into His mother's lap and sighed, "What is this story I have never heard? Please tell Me."

Mother Yasoda then told the story of little Prahlada and how he remained faithful to Lord Narayana even though his demonic father Hiranyakasipu tortured him and tried to kill him in so many ways.

But the boy remained unharmed despite his father's numerous attempts to kill him. Finally the great demon challenged his son to invoke Lord Visnu, who was supposed to be Prahlada's protector.

When Mother Yasoda said to her little son, "Then Lord Nrsimha appeared from the pillar! Lord Nrsimha was very eager to rip the demon to shreds!" a smile suddenly appeared on Krsna's beautiful lips.

Let us pray that the smiles and exclamations that dance upon Krsna's lips as He hears His mother tell the pastimes of His own incarnations to Him as bedtime stories protect us and fill our hearts with bliss.

In what seemed like a very short time, Krsna's first birthday arrived. Nandaraja decided to hold an unforgettable festival to honour Lord Narayana, to please the and to bring joy to his subjects.

He celebrated Krsna's first birthday with mantras, song and dance, a bathing ceremony, fire sacrifices, distribution of charity, and Vedic and traditional rituals like releasing a fish, which brings long life.

To this day, Krsna Janmastami is the main festival of Gaudiya Vaisnavas and is observed by all Hindus. My humble request is that the residents of New Vraja-dhama continue to diligently celebrate it.

The appendix entitled "How To Observe the Janmastami Festival," largely adapted from Sri Hari-bhakti-vilasa, gives guidelines by which this annual celebration can be continued and expanded.

News of Krsna's birthday celebration reached King Kamsa's ears, fuelling his suspicion that this child might be the hoy whose birth would turn out to be his death knell, as Durga-devi had predicted.

Since both evil fiends Putana and Sakata had met their ends in Gokula, Kamsa called upon a more powerful demon, Trnavarta, and ordered him to find one-year-old Krsna and kill Him without delay.

In his previous life, Trnavarta had been a powerful and religious king by the name Sahasraksa, who was famous not only as a performer of sacrifices and a giver of charity but also as a devotee of the Lord.

Once, on the bank of the river Reva (Narmada), intoxicated by Cupid's influence, the king was enjoying himself with a bevy of women in a garden filled with pleasure groves and flowering vines.

Durvasa Muni happened to be passing by just at that time. Though Sahasraksa saw the sage, he was so distracted by his companions that he neglected to show even a semblance of respect to Durvasa.

Seeing that wealth and fame had corrupted Sahasraksa's devotion, the sage cursed the king, saying, "Because wanton sensuality has made you behave like a demon, ? foolish one, become a demon!

As do most souls who are cursed, be they devotees or demons, King Sahasraksa begged for mercy. In response, Durvasa said, "Don't worry! In the future, the touch of Krsna's lotus hand will liberate you."

The king took birth as Trnavarta and later joined Narakasura. Like Arista, Kesi, and others, he eventually united with Kamsa to subdue all pious kings and enjoy the pleasures and opulence of Mathura.

In only a few moments Trnavarta reached Gokula. From high in the sky above Nandaraja's palace he observed Mother Yasoda playing with Krsna in the courtyard, repeatedty lifting the child up in the air.

Trnavarta thought, "I will assume the form of a whirlwind, lift both the child and His mother into the air, and dash them to the ground from a great height. In this way my mission will be a success."

But, with His perfect intelligence, all-cognisant Krsna could understand that danger was about to befall Gokula and that the demon was targeting not only Him but also His beloved mother.

To remove His mother from harm's way, Krsna became so heavy in her arms that she could neither hold Him up nor even keep Him in her lap. She was at once forced to place Him on the ground.

Krsna's sudden heaviness made no sense to Mother Yasoda. She thought, "No one can bear this weight." And how correct she was! Krsna weighed as much as the sum total weight of all existence.

Alarmed that her son had become as heavy as a mountain, Mother Yasoda also sensed some disturbance and immediately took shelter of Narayana. Looking up towards Vaikuntha, she prayed, "O Lord!

"You have given me this son, therefore You must now protect Him." Thinking that some demon had entered her son, Yasoda left Him on the ground and called for brahmanas to chant protective mantras.

While Krsna was sitting there, apparently enjoying Himself like an ordinary child, Trnavarta manifested his full strength in the form of a whirlwind, covering all of Gokula in fearsome darkness.

Suddenly, threatening winds carrying dust and leaves and black clouds showering hailstones and rain converged upon Gokula, blinding residents, tearing branches from trees, even shaking houses.

The roaring wind made it impossible for the Vraja-vasis to communicate, and the stones and broken pots flying here and there made it impossible for them to move about outside the buildings.

While the Vraja-vasis' homes and hearts were thus afflicted, Trnavarta snatched up little Krsna and carried Him high into the air, leaving Nanda Maharaja's subjects and family members in turmoil.

As soon as the storm struck, Yasoda ran back to Krsna. But when she entered the courtyard, her son was nowhere to be found. She groped around in the storm like a drowning person searching for a buoy.

Unable to find her son anywhere in the courtyard, Mother Yasoda went mad with worry, thinking that Krsna had been blown away in the wind. In the ecstasy of love she fell unconscious to the ground.

Meanwhile, Krsna rode high into the air in Trnavarta's arms. Many times while Yasoda-devi was playing with Him, He had thought, "Mother can only lift me a little, but I want to play in the sky."

Therefore, to fulfil His own desire to fly, as well as the celestial damsels' long-standing desires to have a closer look at Him, Krsna bewildered Trnavarta into lifting Him high into the sky above Vraja.

**\* \* \* \***

The wind Trnavarta created was strong enough to diffuse Krsna's bodily fragrance throughout the heavenly planets, which brought pleasure to the demigods, in stark contrast to the Vraja-vasis' sorrow.

As the storm abated, Mother Yasoda returned to consciousness. She searched for Krsna everywhere, hut to no avail. Heartbroken, she lamented more pitifully than a cow laments for her lost calf.

Rohini and other friends heard Yasoda-devi crying and quickly arrived on the spot. Unable to see Krsna, they too lamented, attracting the other women of the village with their loud wailing.

The waves of sorrow this lamentation generated spread from Nanda Maharaja's palace throughout Cokula and the surrounding woodlands and pastures, attracting the gopas who were out herding the cows.

As Rohini-devi comforted her, Mother Yasoda said, "O friend! Since you are preventing me from dying, please tel! me what I should do in my child's absence and before my husband's imminent arrival?"

Fully aware that below Him the Vraja-vasis were sinking rapidly into the quicksand of separation, child Krsna decided to end His sightseeing tour and fulfil Durvasa Muni's curse on Trnavarta.

Clutching the demon's neck as if He were afraid of falling, Krsna assumed a steadily increasing weight until Trnavarta could no longer by upwards and instead was forced to hurtle helplessly to earth.

Trnavarta felt as if an iron mountain were hanging from his neck. Unable to free himself from Krsna's grasp, or the unbearable weight, he was both amazed and dismayed by the child's incredible prowess.

Trnavarta fell from the sky like a meteor, and Krsna, not satisfied to simply weigh the demon down, strangled him, making his eyes pop out of their sockets and his arms and legs go stiff like stone.

The gopis were still running here and there in search of Krsna when Trnavarta came crashing down onto a large stone slab just outside the village, halfway between the palace and where Putana had fallen.

The demon hit the ground with a roar so deafening that it frightened all of Cokula. Some women warily approached Trnavarta's corpse, asking one another, "What is it? From where did it fall?"

The women timidly inspected Trnavarta's body and were wonder- struck to find Krsna crawling on the demon's chest. The baby acted as if He were playing in the courtyard of His house.

The gopis snatched Krsna from the demon's body, quickly carried Him to the palace, and placed Him in Mother Yasoda's arms. Nanda Maharaja had just arrived after running home from the pastures.

Yasoda-devi placed Krsna on her lap and gazed with unblinking eyes at His soft blue body. Still in a state of shock, she was at first unable to fully grasp the value of the treasure she had tost and then regained.

But as the scent and touch of Krsna's limbs awakened Yasoda's senses, she came to full consciousness and allowed Krsna to suck her breast. She said, "O darling! You make so much trouble for Your mother.

"Of course, I am to blame for leaving You outside and unprotected. Such carelessness shows that I am a mother in name alone; still, You are so forgiving that You accept my service nevertheless."

Yasoda handed Krsna to Nanda Maharaja, who smelled his son's head and embraced Him. Meanwhile, the other gopis inspected the child's limbs for bruises. Nearby, some elder gopas boldly declared, "Just see!

"Because this cruel, envious demon kidnapped an innocent child, Lord Narayana, the protector of His devotees, struck down the Raksasa, putting an end to a lifetime or more of sinful acts."

Looking up from his son's face, Nandaraja added, "In previous lives we must have performed many austerities and pious acts and carefully worshipped the Supreme Lord for Him to have returned this hoy."

The elder gopis added, "If anything had happened to Krsna, who is our very life, we would all have died. But now that He is safe, we should invite the brahmanas and hold a festival to celebrate."

Following this good suggestion, Nanda Maharaja organised a grand festival in which the brahmanas chanted mantras, the Vraja-vasis sang Krsna's glories, and finally everyone enjoyed a lavish feast.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda says that Trnavarta represents the false arguments raised by Mayavadis, logicians, and Buddhists, arguments that obstruct loving devotion from dawning in our hearts.

Just as Krsna mercifully freed the Vraja-vasis from the blinding whirlwind of Trnavarta, His mercy also dispels the effects of false arguments from the hearts of sincere seekers of the Absolute Truth.

According to the Garga-samhita, when Trnavarta died his soul merged into Krsna's body. Brahma-vaivarta Purana, however, says that by Krsna's touch the demon returned to Goloka Vrndavana.

These two statements may appear mutually exclusive, but that is not necessarily the case. First Trnavarta's soul merged into Krsna, and from there he attained a spiritual form and the Lord's eternal abode.

Considering Trnavarta's previous devotional activities, his return to Goloka should not come as a surprise. Moreover, precedent for his atypical path to Godhead can be found in the demise of Sisupala.

Sukadeva Gosvami said,

**"\[After Krsna killed Sisupala\] an effulgent light rose from Sisupala's body and, as everyone watched, entered Lord Krsna just like a meteor falling from the sky to the earth.**

Although it appeared that He achieved impersonal liberation, the also says that Sisupala was an eternal associate of the Lord, thus he actually went back to Godhead to resume his service.

After the festival celebrating Trnavarta's death, some gopas privately advised Nandaraja, "It appears that demons are attracted to Gokula. You should keep your boys in the house. Don't let Them go outside."

Nanda Maharaja took this warning seriously. While the cowherd men cleared away Trnavarta's body, Nanda told Yasoda and Rohini that they were no longer to allow the two boys out of the house.

Filled with anxiety to protect Krsna and Balarama, the two mothers struggled to keep their restless sons inside, distracting Them with toys and inviting the local women and other children to play with Them.

Krsna and Balarama played together. Sometimes They made each other laugh, sometimes They quarrelled. While quarrelling, each one often threatened the other by boasting of His superior strength.

Balarama would say, "I am older than You and bigger as well. Be careful!" Krsna would reply, "I have killed three demons. You haven't killed any. So what's the use of Your age and size? I'm stronger."

To display His strength, Krsna would parade around the room with His arms in the air, laughing and showing off His muscles. But sometimes He would trip, fall, and cry, making His mother laugh.

In Their infancy Krsna and Balarama were clothed only by the ten directions, waist bells and anklets Their only ornaments, but as They grew older Their mothers wanted to dress Them like princes.

Mother Yasoda would tie a soft golden dhoti around Krsna's waist, hang costly necklaces on His chest, and place earrings in His cars, but as soon as she finished, Krsna would undo all her hard work.

He would forcefully remove His ornaments, sometimes crying when a ring or bangle would not come off. Finally He would pull off His dhoti, retaining only the peacock feather that crowned His full head of hair.

But Yasoda was just as persistent. She would say, "The son of a king cannot be seen parading around naked forever." And so she would dress and ornament Him again. And again He would shed everything.

Gradually Yasoda's perseverance triumphed, however, and Krsna submitted to her will. When the elder women flattered Krsna, praising His handsome looks, He would strut around like a peacock.

Child Krsna was very possessive of His toys and belongings. If anyone, desiring to tease Him, took away even the most insignificant toy, Krsna would fly into a tantrum until it was returned.

But whenever He took one of His brother's toys, Krsna would simply laugh and refuse to return it. And if it were taken back from Him, He would pout for some time and then scheme how to steal it again.

To distract His roving eyes from the world outside, the cowherd women would say, "O son of Nanda! Let's perform arati. Now, to keep time to our singing, accompany us by dancing. Now dance! Dance!"

At this Krsna would clap His small hands and recite mantras like thi, cleverly moving His feet and body in time to the women's singing. Pastimes like this one left everyone enchanted.

Once the Vraja-vasis wondered, "How does this little child know dance steps that are a mystery to even Lord Siva?" And someone answered, "He learned by watching us dance during our festivals."

Everyone admitted that this was the most logical explanation, but they also wondered whether it could be true. After all, He danced with such spontaneity and expertise. Could He just be imitating?

Just as His audience was thinking like this, Krsna stumbled and fell. He then got up, shyly ran to the safety of His mother's lap, hid Himself under her veil, and drank her breast milk contentedly.

But seeing Krsna at the centre of attention made Balarama angry. In frustration, He too went to the shelter of His mother's arms and drank her breast milk. In this way, the two brothers fell asleep.

An unknown author sings of child Krsna on Yasoda's lap,

*utphulla-tapincha-manorama-srir matuh stana-nyasta-mukharavindah*  
*sancalayan pada-saroruhagram krsnah kada yasyati drk-patham me*

**"When will infant Krsna, charmingly decorated with a great peacock feather on His head, wriggling His lotus toes, His lotus mouth placed on His mother's breast, enter the pathway of my eyes?"**

**\* \* \* \***

Many days after Mother Yasoda saw the universe in Krsna's mouth, bewilderment caused her to let down her guard. Taking advantage, the two boys quickly found Their way into the courtyard to play.

Just then Maharaja Nanda returned home and saw the boys outside and unsupervised. "I told you to keep the children inside," he gently scolded his wife, "but I see that They are now playing outside."

Still dazed from her divine vision, Mother Yasoda replied, "I have tried my best, but nothing seems to work." Nanda Maharaja enquired, "Why is that?" Gathering her thoughts, Krsna's mother replied:

"I have repeatedly forbidden Them to leave the house. But ever since the day Krsna yawned and I saw the universe inside His mouth, I have lost all perspective of what is 'inside' and what is 'outside.'"

Nanda Maharaja was a wise king and a great devotee. Remembering Garga Muni's words, he said, "Your vision and the fact that it has bewildered you must he the work of Lord Narayana, our only shelter."

Nandaraja accepted the incident as a sign from the Supreme Lord. "Lord Narayana must want us to depend on Him to protect Krsna." From then on Nanda's children were allowed to roam freely outdoors.

Krsna's and Balarama's friends, such as Vasudama, Sridama, and Sudama, would go with the brothers on Their outings. But sometimes Krsna would leave the others to wander in the forest alone.

Hearing of this, Nandaraja thereafter sent two armed servants to protect Krsna. Now the group of boys looked like the retinue of a king (Krsna), with His ministers (friends), and soldiers (the bodyguards).

In the open fields of the village, Krsna would throw dirt all around, covering Himself and His friends with the dust of Vraja. Sometimes He and His friends would make houses or castles out of mud.

Krsna would then break His friends' mud houses. In retaliation, they would break His. Biting His lips in anger, false tears in His eyes, Krsna would then rebuild His own house while ignoring His friends.

The demigods who were fortunate enough to witness Krsna playing were amazed: "He who by His glance creates millions of universes now plays in the dirt, making houses out of mud with His small hands."

As always, Krsna's beauty enchanted the mothers of Gokula. They all tried to lure Him into their homes, saying, "O darling! Come play in my courtyard. I have some nice food for You and Your friends."

Krsna, the beloved of every mother's heart, sweetly replied, "Thank you! But I cannot come to your house, because I have no time." Still, the women would bring out butter or yogurt and feed it to Him.

In Krsna's and Balarama's intense play, They would sometimes catch the tails of calves and hold on as the calves dragged Them here and there across the ground, through mud puddles and cow dung patties.

When Gokula's women heard the brothers' shrieks of joy, they would abandon their housework and leave their homes to enjoy the children's antics, which were always the talk of Vrndavana.

One day Krsna and His friends were playing on the bank of the Yamuna at Ramana-reti, some distance from Gokula. Krsna decided to expand the glories of Vrndavana's dust by eating some.

Seeing this, Krsna's friends ran hack to Maharaja Nanda's palace. Balarama told Yasoda, "Mother! Krsna is out of control. He ate clay even though we tried to stop Him. Even now He's eating more."

Her face flushed with anger, Mother Yasoda grabbed a stick and quickly ran out of the house followed by the children, who directed her to where Krsna, covered in mud, was sitting by the riverbank.

Yasoda came up from behind Krsna, grabbed His muddy hand, and said, "Capricious boy! Your brother and Your friends have told me that You are eating dirt. Why are You doing such a naughty thing?"

Lowering His face, Krsna murmured, "Mother! I did not do anything wrong." "You ate some of this dirt," Yasoda snapped back in a fiery mood. "Your friends are witnesses to Your mischief."

But Krsna still denied any wrongdoing, "Mother! These boys stole sweets from their homes and ate them here, but because I did not want to eat stolen food, they made up a story to conspire against Me."

But Mother Yasoda was not so easily fooled. "That can't be true!" she exclaimed. "Why would Your brother conspire against You?" Krsna had an answer for that as well, "The other day My brother ate dirt.

"I was going to tell You about His nonsense, so He turned the tables on Me and made up this story to discredit Me." This amused Yasoda to no end, but she kept her composure and continued to frown.

Yasoda lifted Krsna's face and wiped some dirt from His mouth. Holding it in front of Him, she said, "And what is this, little rascal?" "They smeared dirt on My mouth," Krsna said, "but I wouldn't cat it."

Mother Yasoda looked into Krsna's face, "And how am I to know that You're telling the truth?" Krsna just shrugged, "Mother! If you don't believe Me, then you can look in My mouth and see for yourself."

Trying to suppress her smile and retain a tone of anger in her voice, Yasoda-devi said, "Then open Your mouth and let me see!" This was the moment of truth that Krsna feared and had hoped to avoid.

He had eaten dirt, and there were traces of it in His mouth. If Yasoda saw dirt in His mouth, she would surely punish Him. And if He didn't open His mouth, that would expose His guilt all the same.

Absorbed in the identity of a little boy, Krsna was afraid that He would be punished, not only for eating dirt hut also for telling a string of lies. It seemed that, this time at least, late had Him cornered.

Krsna decided that it would be better to obey His mother's order. As He fearfully opened His mouth, Yogamaya exerted her influence over Yasoda-devi and showed her the universe within her son's mouth.

And just as before, Mother Yasoda saw the unlimited cosmic manifestation in every detail, all within the mouth of her little boy. Then she saw herself and Krsna seated by the bank of the Yamuna.

Her mind and body overwhelmed with astonishment, Mother Yasoda forgot all about Krsna's having eaten dirt. She wondered whether she was dreaming or bewildered by some sort of illusion.

Arguing within herself, Yasoda thought, "I cannot he dreaming, because my eyes are open. Neither can this he an illusion of the demigods, because i am too insignificant for them to bother with.

"Am I insane? No, my mind has been stable since my birth. Perhaps this vision is due to my son's mystic power. Didn't Garga say that He would have qualities like the Supreme Lord Narayana?"

Reflecting on this final thought, she recalled Krsna's hunger, thirst, disobedience, and innocence — all symptoms of an ordinary child — and rejected the idea that He was the cause of what she had seen.

Finding no explanation for her vision, and having no other shelter, Yasoda-devi surrendered to the Supreme Personality of Godhead Narayana and began to think in a more detached, philosophical way.

She thought, "By the same illusion that made me see the universe in the mouth of my son, I think that I am Nanda's wife, the queen of Vraja, the possessor of great wealth and cows, and Krsna's mother.

"These are all misconceptions, for everything belongs to the Supreme Lord. Only He can protect my son from demons and other dangers. How can I? I should give up the delusion that I am Krsna's mother."

Krsna could detect that His mother was abandoning her feelings of possessiveness over Him and He became alarmed. "If mother stops thinking I am her son," He thought, "who will feed and cuddle Me?"

Yogamaya responded to Krsna's will, this time by blinding Yasoda-devi with love in such a way that she would abandon her philosophical attitude and forget the universal form she had just seen.

Sukadeva Gosvami tells how Yasoda-devi again embraced the wonder of her son:

**"Mother Yasoda took her son on her lap as before, feeling increased affection in her heart for her transcendental child.**

The place where Krsna revealed to Yasoda-devi the universe (brahmanda) within His lotus mouth is called Brahmanda-ghata. Because He ate mud (mrttika) here, He is known as Mrttikabihari.

Kavi-karnapura reveals another reason why Krsna ate dirt: to glorify the dust of Vraja, which is fully transcendental, like cintamani, and worshipable for all, especially the devotees, just like Him.

Even as a baby the Lord could eat the dust of Vrndavana without ill effect, but we cannot imitate Him, for we will fall sick. We can, however, as a sign of respect, consume a speck or two of vraja-rajah.

In this regard, Caitanya Mahaprabhu also ate dirt when He was a child, which He did to reveal the defects of Mayavada philosophy and the reasons why we should not feast on the dust of the holy dhama.

**\* \* \* \***

One day, little Nimai was playing with His childhood friends. After some time, Mother Saci brought a plate of rice and 'sweets and requested her son to stop playing and sit down to eat His meal.

At first, unknown to Saci-devi, Lord Caitanya began to eat the dirt on the ground around Him instead of the delicacies His mother had brought. When she saw this she exclaimed, "What arc You doing?"

Saci hastily took the dirt from the Lord's mouth and wiped His hands clean while repeatedly enquiring why He had done such a thing. Crying crocodile tears, He implored, "Why are you angry with Me?

"You give Me dirt to eat every day, so what am I doing wrong now? Rice, sweets, indeed every kind of food is nothing but a transformation of dirt, as is this material body. So why blame Me?"

The Lord's mother was astonished to hear her son espousing Mayavada philosophy, hut patiently she enquired, "Who has taught You this philosophical speculation that justifies eating dirt?

"Listen as I explain the proper understanding of things. Earth transformed into grain nourishes the body and makes it strong. But raw dirt, if eaten, makes the body diseased, and the body dies.

"In a similar way, a pitcher made of earth can carry water for our use, hut a raw lump of earth just soaks up whatever water is poured onto it and is of no value for holding or carrying water. Do You understand?"

Little Nimai happily said, "Why didn't you teach Me this practical process of self-realisation before? Now that I understand it, I will not eat dirt when I am hungry; instead, I will drink your breast milk."

Following the example of the Lord, who played the role of the perfect devotee, we should not eat the dust of Vraja hut show it respect by walking in hare feet, rubbing it on our body, or tasting a speck of it.

When Caitanya Mahaprabhu visited Mahavana, He sat on the steps of Brahmanda-ghata and in ecstasy recalled the loving exchanges that took place there between Krsna and His mother, Yasoda-devi.

In 1971, Srila Prabhupada took a group of his disciples on parikrama of Vrndavana. Stopping at Brahmanda-ghata, Srila Prabhupada at first only sprinkled water on his head, thinking it too cold for a hath.

His Divine Grace directed the women to bathe at one location and the men at another. As he watched the men bathing, suddenly he put on a gamcha, walked to the river, and sprinkled water on his head.

Then Srila Prabhupada waded out into the Yamuna and repeatedly submerged himself, splashing a little with the devotees. Finally he came out and dressed again, decorating his body with fresh tilaka.

My first visit to Brahmanda-ghata was quite significant for me. When I first became a devotee I had heard about the pastime that occurred there. Even at that time the story had seemed so familiar.

I felt that somehow I had heard it before. In the same way as when I first read about Mother Yasoda's binding Krsna, when I heard how she saw the universe in His mouth I knew what would happen next.

Near Brahmanda-ghata is Cintaharana-ghata, named after the anxiety (cinta) Mother Yasoda felt seeing the universal form in the mouth of her tiny son. A deity of Lord Siva is worshipped there.

Yasoda petitioned this deity of Lord Siva to free (harana) Krsna from the dangerous situation that had caused her vision. Because Lord Siva freed Yasoda from her anxiety, he is called Cintaharana Mahadeva.

As in Bhauma Vrudavana, Brahmanda-ghata in New Vraja-dhama is surrounded by peaceful Ramana-reti, also known as Ramaka, where Krsna and His cowherd boyfriends enjoyed their childhood play.

While the gopas were playing here, Krsna once revealed that the entire universe was contained within His body. He showed this vision to Durvasa Muni, but not in the same way He had done to Yasoda.

The sage Durvasa, having heard that the Supreme Lord Krsna had appeared on earth, came to the Yamuna River and took up residence near Raval, on the opposite side of Mahavana from Cokula.

One day, while walking along the sandy shore of the Yamuna, Durvasa Muni saw a group of young boys playing. He could recognise Krsna amongst them by noting the Lord's unique bodily features.

The sage was incredulous to see the Supreme Lord Krsna rolling on the ground while fighting with His friends, or running on the beach, naked like them, laughing, shouting, and sometimes crying.

Durvasa thought, "Why would the supremely opulent Lord roll on the ground with children? This must he some other boy named Krsna, the son of someone named Nanda, not the Krsna who is the Lord of all."

As Durvasa was thinking in this way, Krsna approached the sage of His own accord and sat in his lap. Krsna then rose again, laughed sweetly, and, as He did, inhaled the sage through His lotus mouth.

Suddenly Durvasa found himself in a mysterious, unpopulated land. For some time he wandered through forest after forest asking, "Where am I?" As if in reply, he saw before him all the planets of the universe.

Durvasa came to earth and wandered from continent to continent. Finally he sat on a mountain and performed austerities for a billion years until the endless waters of devastation covered everything.

A thousand ages passed as the sage tossed back and forth in the waters of dissolution. Then he saw another universe, in which he ascended to the heavenly planets and lived for a lifetime of Brahma.

From his position in the heavens tie saw an opening in the universal shell. Meditating on the Lord, he passed through the opening to find a great ocean in which millions of universes floated like bubbles.

Crossing that ocean to its far shore, the sage then entered Goloka, where he saw Vrndavana forest, Covardhana, and the Yamuna River, and felt happy at finally having attained the shelter of the dhama.

Divine fate guided Durvasa into a forest grove full of gopas, gopis, and cows. In the centre of that grove, on a lotus throne by Sri Radha's side, sat Krsna, master of Goloka, Vaikuntha, and countless universes.

The sage looked on in amazement as Krsna laughed. Again he felt himself inhaled into Krsna's mouth and then exhaled. And there he was, sitting on the Yamuna's bank, Nanda's laughing son before him.

Durvasa then understood that the son of Nanda, Krsna, who was playing with the boys on the sandy banks of Mahavana, was the same Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna, Lord of Goloka Vrndavana.

Repeatedly bowing before Krsna, the sage offered the following prayers, which when recited early in the morning make Maharaja Nanda's happy son appear within the vision of His devotee.

Durvasa prayed,

*balam navina-sata-patra-visala-netram bimbadharam sajala-megha-rucim manojnam*  
*manda-smitam madhura-sundara-manda-yanam sri-nanda-nandanam aham manasa namami*

**"I bow before Nanda's gently smiling, sweetly graceful, handsome son, whose large eyes are hundred-petal lotuses, whose lips are bimba fruits, and whose complexion is ns splendid as a monsoon cloud.”**

With tearful eyes, Durvasa continued,

*manjira-nupura-ranan-nava-ratna-kanci-sri-hara-kesari-nakha pratiyantra-sangham*  
*drstyarti-hari-masi-bindu-virajamanam vande kalinda-tanuja-tata-bala-kelim*

**"My respects unto He who, decorated with jingling anklets, a belt of nine jewels, a beautiful necklace, a string of lion's claws, dots of musk, and glances that remove all suffering, plays on the Yamuna's shore.**

Concluding his prayer, Durvasa said,

*purnendu-sundara-mukhopari kuncitagrah kesa navina-ghana-nila-nibhah sphuranti*  
*rajanta anata-sirah-kumudasya yasya nandatmajaya sa-balaya namo namas te*

**"Obeisances to You, who are Balarama's companion and Nanda's son, whose bowed head is a lotus flower, and above whose full-moon face curly locks of hair glisten like new dark monsoon clouds.”**

Having finished his prayers, Durvasa again bowed before the Lord. He then fixed Krsna's childlike form within his heart and repeated the prayers he had composed as he headed north to Badarikasrama.

When Raghava Acarya brought Srinivasa and Narottama to Ramana-reti, he told the two young saints about how Sanatana Gosvami would daily visit Mahavana just to see the Deity of Madana-gopala.

One day, as Sanatana walked along the sands of Ramana-reti, he caught sight of an extraordinary hoy playing with His friends. The Gosvami watched the boys for a while and then followed them home.

Sanatana followed the boys into Madana-gopala's temple and found that all the boys, including the extraordinarily beautiful one, had disappeared. The only person he could see was Madana-gopala.

The Gosvami offered his obeisances to the Deity. He would not tell anyone of this incident. After some time he returned to his own residence, absorbed in thoughts of Madana-gopala's beauty.

One night Madana-gopala appeared to Sanatana Gosvami in a dream and said, "I do not like living in Mahavana. I want to stay with you instead." Then the Lord disappeared, and Sanatana awoke.

The saint felt great ecstasy but, again, did not reveal the wonder of what he had seen to anyone. He simply continued his devotional practices and his services to Caitanya Mahaprabhu's mission in Vraja.

The Lord's and Sanatana's mutual desire to he together was soon fulfilled, however, when Purusottama Chauhe, the custodian of Madana-gopala, entrusted the Deity to Sanatana Gosvami.

Madana-gopala was relocated to Sanatana's residence at Dvadasaditya-tila, where He became known as Madana-mohana. Eventually, He was installed in the first major temple of Vrndavana.

A glories to Sanatana Gosvami, who completely controlled Madana- gopala with his devotion! A glories to Madana-gopala, who came under the loving control of His pure devotee Sanatana Gosvami!

**\* \* \* \***

A woman of the Pulinda tribe, the lowest class of Vraja-vasis, once stopped outside Nandaraja's palace to sell fruit. "O Vraja-vasis!" she called out. "If you desire fruits, come purchase them from me."

Eager to bestow causeless mercy on the fruit vendor — and to eat fresh fruit — Krsna picked up a handful of grains from the ground and went to exchange the grains for fruit, following the barter system.

But by the time Krsna reached the fruit vendor, all the grains had slipped through His fingers. Still, He extended I lis empty palms, and with an enchanting smile said, "Give Me some fruit for these grains!"

The elderly Pulindi was beside herself with bliss at seeing Krsna's beauty. In that state of mind she filled Krsna's hands with pilu fruit, oblivious to the fact that she was receiving nothing in return.

By His mystic potency, Krsna's little hands could hold the entire contents of the fruit vendor's basket, but she didn't mind. She thought the sight of child Krsna to be worth many millions of fruits.

Having emptied the fruit vendor's basket, Krsna returned to His father's house. Meanwhile, by His omnipotent desire He filled her basket with gold and jewels and her heart with pure love for Him.

The fruit vendor was so overwhelmed by ecstasy that she failed to notice the priceless, though weighty, new contents of her basket. Her only thought was to collect more fruit to bring to Krsna's family.

Only after she reached home did the Pulindi realise what she had been carrying. But still, rather than joy, she felt sorrow for being deprived of the real treasure of Krsna's incomparable beauty.

Krsna skipped through His father's house in happiness, for He knew that He had rewarded a person who, though born into poverty and strife, properly treasured the true wealth of devotion to the Lord.

Proudly, Krsna laid out His bounty of fresh fruit before His mother. "From where did You get these fruits?" she asked. And Krsna replied, "Ipurchased them from an old woman. I gave her some grains."

But Mother Yasoda was not pleased "O son! You should not trust strangers the way you trust the people of this house." In a voice tinged with mystery, Krsna said, "Mother! I know nothing about mistrust."

As the father of all living entities, Krsna is equally disposed to everyone; indeed, He is more eager to give conditioned souls devotion to Him than they are willing to accept it—He trusts everyone.

As mother and son were talking, the fruit vendor returned with more fruit. Hearing her call, Krsna ran out of the house with Mother Yasoda following behind, eager to see her son's new acquaintance.

The Pulindi filled her eyes with the sight of Krsna's form, her ears with the sweetness of His voice, and respectfully offered Yasoda-devi a basket of fruit that mother and son then carried into the house.

Then another astonishing thing happened. In the days that followed the fruit vendor's visit, whenever Krsna saw a family member or guest, He would tell His mother, "Give him fruit!" or "Give her fruit!"

And no matter how many fruits she gave out, the basket always stayed full. Mother Yasoda was astonished! Moreover, the taste of the fruit was so nectarean that those who ate it could not stop praising it.

They would say, "I have never eaten such tasty pilu fruit before." And how right they were! The fruit from the Pulindi's basket was the condensed form of Krsna's compassionate love for the unfortunate.

Dear readers! Of Krsna's many childhood pastimes, the most well known and well liked arc His pastimes of stealing milk products and sharing the spoils with His friends and the monkeys of Vrndavana.

I can only narrate a few of the unlimited pastimes Krsna enacted as a child, hut I do so with confidence that reading and hearing them will inspire feelings of bliss in all devotees, both young and old.

But before I do, let me confess an early motive lor my joining ISKCON. When this butter addict first read about Krsna's penchant for consuming quantities of butter, I thought, "This God is for me!"

Hopefully my devotional motivations have diversified since that time, but I will always remember that first thrill 1 felt discovering that God and I had something in common — we both love butter!

Krsna's affection for butter, yogurt, and so on is further enhanced by the taste these foods acquire by being stolen. Dear readers, please note that stealing was not also a trait I shared with the Lord!

Krsna's fondness for stealing butter persisted for as long as He lived in Vraja, and so Srila Prabhupada writes,

**"He is very famous amongst His pure devotees as the Makhana-cora \[butter thief\].”**

Amongst the many factors that contribute to Krsna's habit of raiding His mother's store of butter, two stand out: His speed at running, and His taste for foods other than His mother's breast milk.

"But why did He steal at all?" one might well wonder. Because, Srila Prabhupada explains, He is the source of the wholesome, all-perfect stealing propensity we sec in this world in its perverted form.

The awakening of Krsna's propensity to steal coincided with His increased appetite, and His omnipotence led Him into the dark storeroom but concealed the fact that Yasoda was following behind.

As He reached into an open container full of butter, Krsna saw His own reflection in a shiny marble column and thought it to he another hoy who had happened upon the scene of His misdemeanour.

Startled and shivering in fear, Gopala said, "Dear brother! If you don't tell My mother, I will share some of this butter with you and we can enjoy together. But you must be quiet, lest she catch us."

Overhearing Krsna's broken whispers from her hiding place, Yasoda could barely keep from laughing out loud. Then, as if she were ignorant of what was going on, she innocently came before her son.

Caught red-handed, Krsna's propensity to lie tried to rescue His propensity to steal. Pointing to His own reflection, He said, "Mother! You're just in time. This greedy boy came here to steal your butter.”

"I forbade Him, but He ignored Me. When I got angry with him, he also got angry with Me." Shaking His head mischievously, a sly smile on His lips, Krsna went on, "But I am not at all greedy for butter.

On another day, Mother Yasoda was in the courtyard doing housework. Having neither seen nor heard her son for quite some time, she became suspicious, so she called into the palace, "O Krsna!

"Where are You, darling? What are You doing?" Krsna had taken advantage of Mother Yasoda's absence to scamper into the storeroom and scoop out a handful of butter. In response, He yelled, "Mother!

"My hand was burning from the heat caused by the ruby bangles you placed on My wrist, so I stuck it into a pot of butter to relieve the burning pain. Don't worry, though, the pain is not too bad."

Yasoda, Rohini, and their servants exchanged smiles and knowing looks, and Yasoda replied, "Oh dear! That sounds terrible. My son! Come sit on my lap at once and show me the burns on Your hand."

Krsna swallowed as much butter as He could, cleverly wiped His mouth clean, and left the house to sit on Yasoda-devi's lap, holding His right hand before His chest as if it were paining Him.

Mother Yasoda looked at Krsna's wrist and indulged Him by kissing it. "Oh! Just see how Your wrist is burned!" she said. "My poor baby! I will remove these bangles so they will no longer give You pain."

Generally when Mother Yasoda caught Krsna in the act of stealing she would reprimand Him, not for the loss of butter, but to fulfil her parental duty of training Him to be honest and law-abiding.

On one such occasion Krsna responded to her scolding by crying, rubbing His eyes, and babbling on and on, until Mother Yasoda started to feel guilty for perhaps having been too severe with Him.

She rocked Him back and forth, wiped the tears from His chubby face with the end of her veil, and, as she caressed His buttery limbs, said, "O son! Our entire stock of butter, ghee, and yogurt arc for You."

At this, Krsna stopped crying. Hidden by Yasoda's veil, He opened His eyes wide and broke into a broad smile. Seizing the moment, He sobbed, "Is it all Mine?" Yasoda replied, "Yes, dear! All of it."

May we always hear, speak about, and remember Krsna's stealing,

*dura-drsta-navanita-bhajanam janu-cankramana-jata-sambhramam*  
*matr-bhiti-parivartitananam kaisavam kim api saisavam bhaje*

**"Seeing a pot of butter in the distance, baby Kesava quickly crawled there, anxiously turning His face in all directions out of fear of His mother. I worship these childhood pastimes of the Lord."**

**\* \* \* \***

Just as pouring ghee on a fire merely feeds its flames, Krsna's stealing only intensified His desire for butter until He thought that anything that was white, like the moon for instance, was made of butter.

One full-moon night Mother Yasoda sat outside in the courtyard chatting with some elderly gopis. Meanwhile, Krsna played nearby, every so often glancing with longing eyes at the silvery moon.

After a time He came up behind His mother. To get her attention, He pulled the veil from her head, loosened her braid, and patted her on the back as He whispered something no one else could hear.

Yasoda's heart was always full of motherly affection, hut at that moment she didn't want to interrupt her conversation with her friends. She asked two servants to look alter Krsna, which they eagerly did.

Taking Krsna to the other side of the courtyard, the women fondled Him and said, "What do You want, dear Krsna? Do You want some condensed milk?" Krsna looked at them and firmly replied, "No!"

One nurse said, "Would You like some nice creamy yogurt?" Again Krsna shook His head and said no. "How about some curd?" the other nurse then offered, hut still Krsna's answer was no.

Thinking that Krsna was pouting because Yasoda had not given Him attention, the women consoled the child, saying, "Don't be angry with Your mother. Tell us what You want. We will get it for You."

"I want freshly churned butter," Krsna replied eagerly. One of the women rose to her feet, saying, "I will go into the house right now and bring You a whole tray of Your mother's most delicious butter."

But Krsna stopped her with another emphatic no. Confused, the servant asked, "Whose butter do You want?" "No one's!" Krsna replied. Pointing to the moon, He added, "I want that butter."

The two servants laughed and said, "Little boy! That is not churned butter. That is a royal white swan gliding across the lake of the sky." But whatever it was, butter or not, Krsna wanted the moon.

"Then give Me that royal swan so I can play with it," He answered. "Catch it quickly before it swims away!" Working Himself up into a frenzy, Krsna kicked His feet and shouted, "Get it! Get it now!"

Hearing Krsna's tantrum, some other gopis tried to pacify Him, "O child! Do not cry! These nurses have told You a lie. That is not a royal swan but the moon in the sky. It is called Candra."

Undaunted, Krsna replied, "Then give Me that Candra so I can play with it. I want it right now. Get it!" Krsna's antics had become too much for the gopis to handle, so they brought Him to Mother Yasoda.

Holding her sobbing son on her lap, Mother Yasoda comforted Him with her hand and spoke sweetly into His ear, "Dear! What You said at first was correct. That Candra is actually freshly churned butter.

"But Providence has arranged that I cannot give it to You, no matter how much I may want to. The moon looks very tasty, I admit, but it actually has deadly poison spots on it. No one can eat it!"

Mother Yasoda's words calmed Krsna, who then asked, "Mother! Why are there poison spots on the moon?" Pleased that her son had calmed down, Yasoda rocked little Krsna back and forth and replied:

"Listen, my dear son! In this universe there is an Ocean of Milk — " "Mother!" Krsna interrupted. "How many cows did it take to get enough milk for an ocean?" This made the gopi audience giggle.

Mother Yasoda, who was also laughing, said, "The Milk Ocean was not made by cows!" Krsna leaned back to look in His mother's eyes and said, "How can that be? How can there be milk without cows?"

Stroking Krsna's face, Yasoda answered, "The one who gave cows the ability to transform grass into milk can also make milk without cows." Krsna seemed satisfied, but He was still curious, "Who is that?"

Lowering her head in respect to the Lord, Yasoda replied, "He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Although all-pervading, He is invisible to material eyes and therefore You and I cannot see Him."

Krsna again looked at His mother, this time with a slight smile curling up His lips, and said, "Mother! Is everything you're telling Me true?" Rather than defend herself, Yasoda-devi cited scripture.

"Listen!" she said. "Long, long ago the demigods and the demons churned the ocean of milk. Mount Mandara was the churning rod, and the king of serpents, Vasuki, was the churning rope.

"The demons and demigods pulled on the opposite ends of Vasuki." Krsna asked, "Did they churn like you and the other ladies do?" Yasoda nodded, "Yes! But their churning produced a deadly poison."

Krsna interrupted again, "Mother! How can churning milk produce poison? I thought poison came from snakes." "Yes," Yasoda replied, "poison does come from snakes. But it came from milk first.

"Mahadeva drank that poison to save the universe. When some drops of the poison seeped through his fingers, the snakes drank it. That is why they are now poisonous." Little Krsna shook His head in wonder.

Mother Yasoda continued, "The moon was also horn from the churning of the Milk Ocean, but it too was touched by drops of poison, which we now see as marks on the moon. Can You see them?"

Yasoda-devi turned Krsna so He could examine the moon. "I see them!" He shouted. She then concluded, "That is why we cannot eat butter from the moon. It is poisonous. But we can eat Gokula butter."

Turning Krsna so that they were again face to face, Yasoda said, "Now please take my freshly churned butter instead of the moon." Krsna nodded in agreement and yawned to show that He was sleepy.

As Mother Yasoda carried her son into the palace, even before she could lay Him down on the feather-soft bed in His room, He had fallen fast asleep in her arms, dreaming about an ocean of milk.

The next morning Mother Yasoda woke Krsna up with a tray full of butter, yogurt, and other treats. After He had rinsed His mouth and washed His face, she gave Him the tray, saying, "Take what You like."

Krsna impishly crossed His arms, looked at His mother, and said, "I will not eat anything. Last night I was hungry. But, instead of feeding Me, you put Me to sleep with a story about poison on the moon.

"I was tormented by hunger all night. So why should I eat your food now?" Mother Yasoda put the tray down and replied with a smile, "If You were hungry all night, who stole the butter from the storeroom?"

Understanding that His theft had been discovered and that His false accusation had been exposed, Krsna looked away, unable to meet Yasoda's gaze. Then He suddenly threw His arms around Her neck.

Laughing all the while, Krsna embraced His mother as she lovingly held His butter-soft body of condensed bliss. And she laughed as He whispered in her car, "I never steal butter, especially not yours."

O Gopala! AH Your pastimes are sweet, but Your Makhana-cora pastimes are especially relishable due to the buttery fingerprints You leave on them after stealing Your mother's freshly churned butter.

May that divine form of Yours that thrills at the sound of the churning rod and stealthily enters Mother Yasoda's kitchen to steal a handful of fresh butter protect us at all times. We are Yours!

**\* \* \* \***

Through His pastimes of stealing Mother Yasoda's butter and yogurt, Krsna's desire to taste the butter of the other women of Gokula awoke in His heart, a desire He felt duty-bound to honour.

Word of Krsna's antics soon spread all over the village, and the women of Vraja, who loved Krsna more than their own sons, longed for Him to play in their own homes and to steal their own butter.

As the gopis milked their cows and churned butter, they thought, "This milk is for Gopala. This butter is for Syama." Lying awake at night, they imagined they were feeding Krsna with their own hands.

Day and night Krsna's transcendental form played in the gopis' minds. As they tended to their household duties, they thought of bathing, dressing, nursing, and feeding Him as if He were their child.

Just as the young gopis would later meditate on Krsna as their paramour or husband, the older gopis meditated upon Him as their son. They lamented, "Why did fate not make Krsna my child?"

But divine fate had blessed Yasoda-devi to he Krsna's mother. It was this unparalleled good fortune — more than her position as queen— that won her the heartfelt allegiance of every woman in Vraja.

The elder gopis would talk amongst themselves: "The woman who gave birth to Krsna is worshipable by the wife of Narayana and by the wives of the demigods, not to mention ordinary women like us."

And Krsna did not neglect the pure love of these elder gopis. While playing in Mother Yasoda's courtyard in His original form, He played in the minds of Vrndavana's mothers in His sphurti expansion.

The gopis saw child Krsna (Krsna-kumara) with a face like a blue lotus, dispelling both darkness and sorrow by the rays beaming from His various smiles, be they shy, broad, eager, or laughing.

Krsna's eyes sparkled with innocence and excitement, spreading wide like the petals of a lotus feeding honey to the bee-like locks of hair that constantly dangled around the petals' reddish outer corners.

If one were to compare Krsna's face to a dark moon spreading radiant nectar throughout the night, then His body would be compared to blazing sapphires dispelling the inauspiciousness of the universe.

Krsna's form — enhanced by His clothes and ornaments — charmed the minds of animate beings and transformed the nature of inanimate things by making water turn solid and solid things liquid.

Just as the sound of Krsna's flute stayed in the ears of the young gopis like birds nesting there, the sound of His broken words and childish laughter resonated in the ears of the elder gopis like a perpetual echo.

Just as desire trees daily bear ripened fruits, Krsna's childhood pastimes continuously displayed ever fresh features, like turning over, crawling, talking, standing up, walking, and stealing butter.

The women of Cokula on earth, by mentally sharing in the motherhood of Yasoda, tasted a sweetness they could not taste in Goloka, where Krsna does not age but is an eternally fresh youth.

The elder gopis submerged their minds in thinking of Krsna, such as how He duelled with His friends using the twigs of trees. In this way they were absorbed in a peerless standard of Krsna consciousness.

Yet the nature of loving devotion is that it always wants to serve, taste, and love Krsna more and more, and so the gopis wanted not only to think about but also to serve Krsna directly by feeding Him.

Fully aware of the elder gopis' desires, Krsna contemplated how He could satisfy them. In other words, the gopis' desires became Krsna's desires. It is in this sense that the Lord and His devotees are one.

Krsna had to eat His meals at His mother's house, so He decided to go to the other gopis' homes at unscheduled times, between meals, and secretly eat their butter, yogurt, and other milk products.

The gopis would constantly complain to Yasoda about Krsna's misconduct, but within themselves they cherished His stealing their butter as the highlight of their lives and the main source of their bliss.

The gopis' complaints reinforced Yasoda-devi's special and direct relationship with Krsna as His eternal mother, but within their hearts they always thought that they too were Krsna's mothers.

In this way Krsna accepted the elderly gopis' maternal sentiments and service by stealing their butter and simultaneously proclaimed to the entire world that Mother Yasoda is unmatched as His only mother.

We should note that Krsna's dealings with the householders of Cokula were not based entirely on stealing and distributing their milk products, nor on the havoc He created in achieving those ends.

Krsna and Balarama would sit with other cowherd boys in the courtyard of a friend, playing or just talking. In this way They would enchant the adults with Their beautiful forms, gestures, and speech.

At such times the gopis would be pleased to offer Krsna and Balarama fruit juice to drink and sweetmeats to eat. Sometimes they would bring jewellery from their own treasuries and decorate the brothers.

The Vraja-vasis considered Krsna to be a walking good-luck charm whose presence brought all auspiciousness to their hearts and homes. That fact alone more than made up for His frivolous antics.

And yet, Krsna's ability to roam free was a cause of concern for His mothers and nurses, who had difficulty keeping an eye on Him to ensure that He was out of harm's way and not disturbing others.

One minute Krsna and Balarama were in the palace courtyard with Their friends, the next minute They were gone, having intentionally tricked Their caretakers. One time They disappeared down the street.

Full of anxiety, Yasoda and Rohini went with the nurses on a house- to-house search lor the two brothers, enquiring from the elder gopis, "Have you seen our sons?" or "Have our naughty boys passed by?"

Krsna's attendants loved Him with all of their hearts; still, they could be heard cursing the boys under their breath as they followed the brothers' distinctive footprints, saying, "They went this way."

Meanwhile, knowing that Their mothers were searching for Them, the brothers were playing a sort of hide-and-seek with the adults, fleeing from one hiding place to another when Their seekers got near.

Only with great difficulty did Mother Yasoda's gopi posse track down and catch Krsna and His brother. When they finally caught up with Them, the queen of Vraja held Krsna's ear firmly as she scolded Him.

Then, tightly holding Their arms, sometimes dragging and sometimes pushing Krsna and Balarama, the two mothers lovingly escorted the boys home to bathe, dress, and feed Them and then tuck Them in.

Krsna's attraction to playing with His friends was so strong, however, that instead of resting, He and His brother Balarama would sneak out of Their beds and out of the palace to begin Their play anew.

One day Krsna and His friends escaped to where the lower animals like buffalo and goats were kept. They decided that they would be cowherds and pretend the goats were cows by trying to milk them.

Eventually, Krsna asked Balarama, "Why don't We herd the calves the way We see our elders do with the cows?" "Good idea!" replied Balarama, who was just as naughty as His younger brother.

Excitedly They ran to the corral where the milk-white calves were kept. Krsna opened the gate and the boys led the animals out into the yard, herding them with little sticks, as They had seen Their fathers do.

But when the frisky calves refused to do what the boys wanted, Krsna and Balarama tried to control the animals by holding on to their tails. Their friends then followed suit, creating an hilarious scene.

Sukadeva Gosvami narrates these pastimes:

**"Within Nandaraja's house, the cowherd ladies enjoyed seeing the pastimes of Rama and Krsna. The babies would catch the ends of the calves' tails —**

**"And the calves would drag Them here and there. When the women of the village saw these pastimes, they certainly stopped their household activities and laughed and enjoyed the incidents."**

As always, the supreme method of relishing pastimes like these is to speak or sing of them (sankirtana) in the company of others. And that's exactly what the residents of Cokula did, day and night.

Through praise or complaint, within their homes or in public, to outsiders or amongst themselves, the Vraja-vasis spoke only about Krsna and His antics. One could say that Cokula was abuzz.

Indeed, the elder gopis were so intoxicated by the bliss of krsna-sankirtana that they seized every opportunity to relish its nectarean taste and to share that taste with Yasoda, their sankirtana leader.

The gopis knew that the best gift to offer their queen — better than butter, silks, or gold — was to submerge her in talks of her son. And so, on the pretext of complaining about Krsna, they did just that.

**\* \* \* \***

After gathering up their list of complaints, a delegation of Gokula's women walked up the hill to Nanda Maharaja's palace and stood at the main gate, from where they were led inside to a reception hall.

At the news that the elder women of the village had arrived, Mother Yasoda set aside her housework and seated her guests on rows of ornamental seats facing the golden throne reserved for her.

Pretending to be in an angry mood, the women warned Yasoda-devi, "O Queen! If you do not find a way to control your unruly son, we will all surely suffer the consequences when He grows up.

"Krsna creates so much mischief now. We expect Him to destroy our village by the time He is just a few years older. Your duty is to protect us from danger, and now is the time to begin fulfilling that duty."

Mother Yasoda's heart surged with pride at Krsna's daring; still, with a frown she replied to her accusers, "O noble women of Vraja! What has my son done to make you speak such disparaging words?"

One gopi said, "O devi! Are you really so unaware of what goes on in your kingdom? Where are you when at dawn your restless son sneaks around the neighborhood in search of butter? Are you asleep?

"Surely you know that He releases our calves from their pens." Queen Yasoda replied, "Why are you so angry? He is just trying to help." Another gopi interrupted, "But He is doing so at the wrong time.

"The calves run everywhere and drink the cows' milk, causing us so many problems." "But His intention is good," Yasoda countered. "He wants to help." A third gopi objected, "He wants to help Himself!”

"While we run around trying to catch the calves and keep them away from their mothers, Your son sneaks into our houses, cats our yogurt and butter, and then runs away. What kind of help is that?"

Yasoda tried to calm the women, "Why are you so merciless? Just give Him good instruction." A grey-haired gopi replied, "Giving good instruction to your son is like pouring water on stone to grow crops."

Another woman added, "We give Him good advice, hut He simply ridicules us in return." Another gopi said, "Having grown tired of counselling Him, we once threatened to tie Him up and heat Him."

Mother Yasoda leaned forward with alarm, "How cruel of you! What happened then?" "I'm not sure what happened!" the gopi replied. "He smiled at us so sweetly that we forgot everything and couldn't move.

"It was quite mysterious! As we stood there hypnotised by His beauty, Your son sat calmly in front of us, ate our butter, drank our milk, and then calmly walked out the door, flashing us a departing smile."

Yasoda could hardly restrain her laughter or suppress the love welling up in her heart. "Krsna is so wonderful!" she thought. In Krsna's defence, she answered, "It sounds to me that you happily fed my son."

"No!" another gopi testified. "When I tried to explain that He should not steal, He angrily shouted hack at me, 'It is you who are the thief. Your house and everything in it, cows included, belongs to Me."'

Yet another housewife added, "It is not an exaggeration to say that your son is the acarya of thieves." Yasoda was not happy to hear Krsna called a thief. "Surely, you're making these stones up," she said.

"Krsna is just a child. How much butter can He eat? When you see Him coming, give Him a little of what you have in your storehouses, and He will go away satisfied. That will he the end of that!"

"O Queen!" the women replied in unison. "You don't understand! You feed Him so much that He is never hungry. We offer Him food, hut He refuses it. His joy comes from stealing, not from eating.

"Sometimes He doesn't even touch the food, but feeds it to the monkeys. And when they can't eat any more, He says, 'How can I eat alone without My monkey friends!' Then He breaks all our pots."

"Impossible!" exclaimed Yasoda. "Not impossible!" one gopi retorted. "It is a fact." Mother Yasoda insisted, "Then hide your stock so He cannot find it." A gopi replied, "We tried that, with mixed results."

"What does that mean?" Yasoda-devi asked, do which one gopi said, "We keep our butter in a dark place, but He finds it by the natural effulgence of His body. He is like a lamp walking in the darkness.

"And if He cannot find the hiding place, He says, 'just watch! If you don't give Me yogurt, I will come tomorrow with a flarning torch to hum down your house with all your relatives and children still in it.'"

Another gopi added, "Or in anger He takes revenge by pinching and teasing our babies until they cry. Who can tolerate such things?" Undaunted, Yasoda advised, "Hang your butter out of His reach."

"We do!" some gopis blurted out. "But Krsna and His friends create makeshift steps from crates and churns to steal our goods. Or, if they can't reach, they break the jars from below and spoil everything."

Laughing, Yasoda said, "How can He know if a pot holds milk or butter without seeing inside of it?" The gopis said, "Somehow He has a sixth sense when it comes to milk products. It's uncanny, but true.

"The other day He snuck into one of our storehouses and with a kind of spear poked holes in a hanging pot. His friends stood around drinking the cascading stream of milk as if drinking from a fountain."

The gopis added, "If some obstacle prevents Him from stealing, then He and His friends gleefully pass stool and urine in our homes." Yasoda-devi protested, "That's just some powder mixed with oil."

"No it's not!" the women countered. "He actually desecrates our homes. And during Sanjhi, when we decorate our walls and courtyards, He comes and throws dirt all over our colourful designs.

"He pulls our braids and saris and even kicks us! And sometimes He proposes marriage to our daughters. ? Queen, beware! He steals our butter now, but soon it will be our gold or, worse, our daughters."

As the gopis were speaking, Nanda Maharaja entered the assembly with Krsna. Sitting apart from the women, with his son on his lap, the king politely listened to the many complaints of his subjects.

Krsna could tell that He was the topic of their discussion. Feeling embarrassed, He blushed and pretended to look here and there — everywhere but at the gopis, whose adoring eyes were for Him alone.

Mother Yasoda noticed Krsna's guilty looks and laughed, and the gopis laughed along with her, saying, "Even if He will not listen to us, at least you should teach Him how to act properly here at home."

This last statement may sound like a reprimand, but it was actually the elder gopis' indirect invitation for Krsna to continue His mischief in the houses of Cokula. How could it be taken otherwise?

Finally, Mother Yasoda concluded, "I have heard your wise counsel, every word, and I will take it to heart." But, looking at Krsna's guilty face, she could not control her smile. The meeting was about to end.

Then, suddenly Krsna spoke up, "Mother! I know that these women are lodging complaints against Me. But their words are false. I go to their houses at sunrise to visit their sons, who are My friends.

"But if My presence causes these ladies so much trouble, then I will no longer visit My friends. I will live a life of seclusion here with you." As Krsna spoke these clever words, He shed a river of crocodile tears.

Mother Yasoda took little Krsna on her lap. Not inclined to scold Him, she tried to lift His spirits by taking His side. "O gopis!" she said. "You are all telling lies. My darling son Krsna is telling the truth.

"He is just a small boy. How could He possibly do the things you accuse Him of? Anyway, you have scolded Him. Is there anything left for me to tell Him?" Saying this, Yasoda kissed her son's teary face.

After Queen Yasoda's final words, Rohini-devi, in a gesture of friendship, applied tilaka to the foreheads of the women of Cokula and then escorted them out the gate and into the village below.

When the women had left, Mother Yasoda looked Krsna in the eyes and said, "My son! Your greed has caused much trouble to our friends. Such behaviour may be tolerated here, but not in others' homes.

"Therefore, from now on You must stay here and play — either alone or with Your friends." But Nanda Maharaja felt compelled to speak up in defence of His precious son. "Come. Sit on my lap," he said.

Krsna jumped off His mother's lap and climbed onto His father's. Wagging a finger at His wife, Nanda said, "This hoy is faultless. He always behaves Himself. Why do you side with these envious ladies?

"I think that you should he punished, not Him." Nanda Maharaja then stroked Krsna's head and cooed softly in His ear, "My dear hoy! Just stay here with Your father and do not go to anyone else."

At this, ever contrary and unpredictable, naughty Krsna squirmed out of Maharaja Nanda's grasp, ran across the room, and climbed onto Mother Yasoda's lap instead, giving both parents a hearty laugh.

Holding Krsna to her breast, Yasoda-devi thought, "Let the ladies of Cokula drown in the bliss of my son's mischief-making. And when they complain to me, let these stories drown me in bliss as well."

**\* \* \* \***

The women of Vrndavana would regularly complain about Krsna's misbehaviour, but because He knew that it gave them transcendental pleasure, He never stopped raiding their homes and storehouses.

One day Upananda's wife, Prabhavati, came alone to lodge a complaint with Yasoda. She said, "O Devi! We are so close to each other that we see no difference between each other's possessions.

"My stock of butter, ghee, milk, and yogurt is yours, and I take it that yours is mine. Nevertheless, your son, to learn right from wrong, must also learn how to discriminate between His house and that of others.

'In one way or another this boy has become a thief. When I try to correct Him, He talks back to me and then runs away. As His mother, it is your duty to teach Him to respect others people's property.

"He is, after all, the son of Vraja's king. If He steals, all the boys His age will follow His bad example. Even now they accompany Him wherever He goes and join in His mischief. Please do something."

Prabhavati's words made Yasoda feel annoyed with Her absent son. Nonetheless, she spoke gently to her senior cousin. Yasoda-devi said, "I just cannot understand! My warehouse is overflowing with butter.

"Still, my son rarely eats butter or yogurt here. Now I understand why. He is eating at the homes of others, and uninvited no less. ? honourable one! Next time Krsna steals from your home, catch Him.

"Bring Him to me with butter still on His chubby face, and I will teach Him a lesson He won't forget. In the meantime, please forgive His offences and let there be no ill will between us and our families."

Prabhavati-devi, delighted to hear Mother Yasoda's words of reassurance, went home in a happy mood, where she eagerly waited for Krsna to again set foot in her house so that she could catch Him.

It wasn't long before Krsna had finished His rounds of Gokula's storehouses. Upananda's home was next in line to serve as the arena for the cowherd boys' daily sacrifice to the Supreme Lord.

In that sacrifice, fortunate Prabhavati's butter would be the oblations, Krsna the head priest, the cowherd boys' mouths the sacrificial fire, and the village monkeys the beneficiaries of the gopas' charity.

Stealthily making their way out of a grove, Krsna and His friends scaled the outer wall of Upananda's house, quietly dropped into the inner courtyard, and scurried into the storeroom.

But the boys were surprised and disappointed when they saw all the milk, butter, and yogurt suspended from the ceiling, out of their reach. Some gopas even turned to leave. But Krsna whispered, "Stay!"

He deftly constructed a makeshift platform by piling together a crate, footstool, and grinding mortar, hut when He climbed on top of it with the help of His friends, the milky bounty was still too far away.

Just as Krsna was about to give up and climb down, Subala handed Him a stick. Krsna used the stick to poke the clay pot until it broke, spilling freshly churned butter all over Krsna and onto the floor.

Scooping up the soft delight, the boys and their monkey friends greedily stuffed it into their mouths, softly giggling to themselves and complimenting Krsna for His cleverness. Then Prabhavati arrived.

Seeing her in the doorway, stick in hand, one boy shouted, "Quick! Run! We're caught!" The gopas ran around the storeroom in a panic. Some even ran right past Prabhavati and her menacing stick.

But Krsna couldn't get past His aunt. By Yogamaya's design, eager Prabhavati was allowed to catch Krsna despite His superior agility, and hold on to His wrist despite His wriggling and cries for help.

Abandoned by His friends and held captive by His determined aunt, Krsna shed false tears that filled the trough He made by dragging His feet as Prabhavati pushed and pulled Him back to Nandaraja's palace.

By the time the two arrived in the courtyard, Krsna was truly scared. He thought, "Mother will be angry and hit Me with a stick," so He used the edge of Prabhavati's sari to cover His head in shame.

But as soon as clever Krsna heard His mother's voice, He manifested a portion of His mystic potency and transformed Himself into Prabhavati's son, still keeping His head covered with her garment.

Mother Yasoda quickly assessed the scene before her as she listened to Prabhavati explain, "This rascal son of yours broke into my house, shattered a pot of butter, and ate the contents with His cohorts."

Ashamed of her incorrigible, wayward son, Yasoda-devi impatiently replied, "O mother! Remove your garment from His face. I have every intention to banish this mischievous hoy from my house forever."

When Prabhavati removed the cloth from Krsna's face, she was amazed to see her own son standing by her side, and Yasoda laughed with relieved surprise, wondering what this drama could be all about.
