But Prabhavati had no explanation. For a moment she was speechless as Yasoda said, "Devi! This is not my son, but yours. It is Kandava. Why have you unjustly accused my boy and played this trick on me?"

Prabhavati tried to hide her embarrassment with anger. Pulling on her son's arms and shaking him, she said, "How did you change places with the son of Vraja's queen! Tell me now, or I will punish you."

But Kandava just looked silently at the ground as if humiliated by his mother's conduct. Having no other recourse, Prabhavati left Nanda Maharaja's palace bewildered, her head hung low in shame.

After mother and son had departed, Yasoda, Rohini, Nanda Maharaja, and Balarama all laughed heartily, saying, "This attempt to besmear the good name of Krsna was foiled by His own purity."

Meanwhile, on the way back to Upananda's house, Krsna regained His confidence and abandoned His disguise as Kandava. Seeing Krsna in His original form, Prabhavati let go of His hand in amazement.

Krsna wagged His forefinger at His aunt and said, "Auntie! If you try to take Me to My mother again, I will take on the form of your good husband, and you will be discredited as the madwoman of Gokula."

Wide-eyed and speechless, Prabhavati wondered what kind of mystic power this little hoy had, and from where it had come. Fearing that He would make good on His threat, she stopped trying to catch Him.

Gradually word spread from Prabhavati's courtyard: if Krsna were caught stealing butter, He would use magic to escape punishment by embarrassing anyone who tried to bring Him to justice.

The elderly gopis had no doubt that Krsna had special powers. It was already well known that He had killed powerful demons. Thus, out of fear of being humiliated, they also stopped trying to catch Him.

Having instilled this fear into the hearts of the elder gopis, Krsna and His cowherd friends stole butter, milk, and yogurt with impunity. In this way, Krsna spent His childhood in Gokula in great happiness.

An unknown Vaisnava prays,

*dadhi-mathana-ninadais tyakta-nidrah prabhate nibhrta-padam agaram ballavinam pravistah*  
*mukha-kamala- samirair asu nirvapya dipan kavalita-navanitah patu mam bala-krsnah*

**"Awakened at dawn by the sound of yogurt-churning, Krsna stealthily entered a gopi's home, blew out the lamps, and stole a handful of butter. I pray that child Krsna may protect me."**

## Chapter 31 - Yamalarjuna-tirtha to Raval

Krsna's pastimes of stenting butter are as coundess as the waves on the Ocean of Milk. Thus far we have hardlyet us relish one final and most glorious pastime.

By binding Krsna's belly (udara) with a rope (daman), Mother Yasoda made Him famous as Damodara. I hope to praise this pastime in detail in a separate book, but for now let us hear the damodara-lila in brief.

The poet Sri Kavisekhara enjoins us to visit the place where this pastime took place and to also hear Vrndavana's residents personally describe how Krsna immortalised Mother Yasoda's love for Him:

**"When will I become so fortunate as to visit sacred Mathura Puri and there shed tears of bliss as I drink from the stream of nectar words flowing from the mouths of the old guides there who say —**

**"'Here was Nanda Maharaja's home. Here the cart was broken. Here Lord Damodara, who breaks the bonds of birth and death for His devotees was Himself tied up with ropes by Mother Yasoda'?"**

Just two years after Krsna's birth, early on Dipavali day, Mother Yasoda was personally churning butter and cooking milk for Krsna, duties she had taken up after her servants repeatedty burnt the milk.

The milk she was churning butter from was special. It came from eight cows selected from Nanda's herd. They grazed only on the most fragrant grass, and each was as rare as a horse with one black ear.

From this extraordinary milk Mother Yasoda would churn butter that was even more extraordinary due to her touch, which was saturated with the transcendental maternal love emanating from her heart.

Mother Yasoda reasoned that the exceptional taste of this butter would cure Krsna of the attraction He had to the butter in the other houses of Cokula and thus bring His days of stealing to an end.

Balarama and Rohini-devi had gone to Upananda's house for a visit, and the queen's servants had not yet arrived to assume their duties, so Mother Yasoda was alone with Krsna and the household chores.

Meanwhile, Krsna was sleeping peacefully. Mother Yasoda gently kissed His forehead on her way to the spacious veranda, which was accessible from her kitchen, Krsna's bedroom, and the storeroom.

The veranda looked out upon the stunning landscape of Cokula village and Mahavana forest in the distance, which was flooded with the sublime sights, sounds, and scents unique to morning in Vraja.

While fresh milk was simmering in the kitchen, Mother Yasoda continued churning butter, glancing from time to time at little Krsna sleeping in His bed or at the large pot of milk heating up on the stove.

Mother Yasoda could not restrain the love for Krsna welling up in her heart. It soon appeared upon her lips as a song about His childhood activities, composed by her or one of the other women of Gokula.

In a voice as sweet as that of the queen of cuckoos, Yasoda-devi joyously sang a song with the following refrain,

*gokula-pati-kula-tilaka tvam asiha*  
*krta-sukrta-vraja-racita-sukha-vraja nayananandi-samiha*

**"O Krsna! ? tilaka decoration in the family of Gokula's king! You bring such great happiness to the pious people of Vraja by delighting their eyes with the soothing vision of Your divine form."**

Sukadeva Gosvami beautifully describes the picturesque scene, in which the eternal embodiment of transcendental maternal love, Yasoda-devi, is fully absorbed in loving service to her divine son:

**"Dressed in a saffron-yellow sari, with a belt tied about her full hips, Mother Yasoda pulled on the churning rope, labouring considerably, her bangles and earrings moving and her whole body shaking.**

**"Because of her intense love for her child, her breasts were wet with milk. Her face, with its very beautiful eyebrows, was wet with perspiration, and malati dowers were falling from her hair."**

Srila Prabhupada comments on Sukadeva Gosvami's words as follows:

**"One should take advantage of the full description provided here by thinking of Mother Yasoda in maternal affection for Krsna.”**

Every kind of devotee will benefit from thinking of Mother Yasoda as she pulls the churning rod with her soft, elegant hands, but those devotees aspiring for parental affection will be especially inspired.

As if keeping time to her singing, Krsna's mother rhythmically pulled the ropes back and forth, making the emerald-studded bangles on her lithe, delicate arms jingle and chime like musical instruments.

Her hard endeavour gradually caused drops of perspiration to moisten the locks of hair that danced upon her forehead and spread the end of her black braid across her back like the tail feathers of a peacock.

Jewels, flowers, and peacock-feather decorations fell to the ground from Mother Yasoda's loosened wavy hair, as if demigods in the sky above were offering oblations of respect to her lotus feet.

Mother Yasoda's body — particularly her shoulders, breasts, and hips — swayed hack and forth, causing her necklaces, earrings, and other ornaments to sparkle in the rays of the early morning sun.

The glinting light from her ornaments reflected off her beautiful, blackish face, just as lightning dances within a dark rain cloud, and perspiration dropped from her glistening forehead like a light drizzle.

From a distance, one could not tell whether it was the movements of the orange sari covering Yasoda-devi's form or the autumn sun rising on the horizon that was was driving away the darkness of night.

Was it the blessings of the demigods that allowed Yasoda's delicate, refined form to sustain the stress of constant labour, which was especially visible in her beautiful arched neck and swaying shoulders?

No! It was the irrepressible volcanic power of her transcendental love for Krsna that fuelled Mother Yasoda's movements, making her willing and able to serve Him through any menial or laborious task.

The loud churning sounds rising from the mouth of the butter pot and the butter splashing at her feet both testified to the source of her empowered dedication to her little child — her intense maternal love.

As she sang about Krsna, Yasoda would sometimes stop to remember the naughty look in His eyes when she caught Him stealing, or His bold defence, "Mother! Why not be proud of My expertise as a thief?"

While Mother Yasoda was deeply absorbed in such thoughts, Krsna awoke. Out of hunger, He began to cry, "Mother! Mother!" But Yasoda didn't respond. Rubbing His eyes, Krsna climbed out of bed.

He sleepily waddled out of His room and followed the sound of churning to the veranda, where He found His mother, put His hand on the churning rod, and said, "Mother! You must feed Me now."

Yasoda-devi stopped her work, picked up her son, sat down on a settee with Him on her lap, and allowed Krsna to drink the milk that had already been flowing from her breast out of maternal affection.

As is the habit of every mother, Yasoda-devi watched her son suck her breast and gazed at the beauty of His face, His black curly locks, and His soft chubby limbs. Suddenly, a sound disturbed her reverie.

The milk in the kitchen was starting to foam up. Although Krsna had not finished eating, Mother Yasoda put Him down on the daybed and quickly ran into the kitchen to stop the milk from boiling over.

How could Yasoda-devi, the peerless exemplar of motherly love, abandon her hungry son? In that moment she considered one service to Krsna more important — and more urgent—than another.

Mother Yasoda's conduct was completely suited to one under the influence of divine love. But Krsna, in His role as a hungry baby, did not appreciate her gesture. Just like the milk, His anger boiled over.

Biting His lip and shedding false tears, Krsna picked up a stone and struck the pot without making a sound. Though the pot cracked open, He did not take any of the churned butter that flowed onto the floor.

Considering how He could teach His mother a lesson, Krsna playfully stomped His feet in the spilled butter and then wandered around the veranda and His bedroom, leaving buttery footprints everywhere.

Entering the storeroom and locking it behind Him, Krsna showed His cleverness by using a servant's bed as a ladder and tasting the contents of every hanging pot. Finally He left, taking a pot with Him.

But, as an afterthought, Krsna took a broom that was leaning in a corner and used its handle to break some of the pots hanging from the rafters, causing buttermilk, yogurt, and ghee to spill onto the door.

Then, looking here and there to see if anyone was watching, Krsna left the storeroom through the door that opened onto the courtyard, holding the pot of butter against His chest with His two little arms.

He climbed upon a wooden mortar for grinding spices, called the monkeys, and fed them handfuls of butter. When some of His gopa friends arrived, He also shared His ill-gotten gains with them.

**\* \* \* \***

Meanwhile, wanting to embrace Krsna and to continue feeding Him, Mother Yasoda returned from the kitchen, only to be startled by the chaotic scene she found there. "It must have been Him!" she thought.

Seeing the broken pot, pools of butter, and sticky footprints here and there, Mother Yasoda was at first worried about the welfare of her darling, albeit naughty, son. Then she heard a celestial voice say:

"The thirsty baby bee was not satisfied with honey. It has broken the lotus bud, only to see the contents flow out without honey, and has flown away to another lotus flower to drink the nectar there.

"O mother! You have shown dexterity in taking the milk off the fire, but now you will have to show that you can extinguish the raging fire of your son's wrath. After all, He is not an ordinary boy."

Hearing this, Mother Yasoda was relieved, douching her forefinger to her nose, she laughed as she waded through the debris Krsna had left in His wake, following His buttery footprints to search Him out.

As she passed through the storeroom, she could hear Krsna's voice in the courtyard. She craned her neck around the door and saw Him up to no good, looking here and there in fear of her inevitable approach.

Mother Yasoda paused for a moment to relish the sight of her mischievous son, who was anxiously looking all around, planning for the escape He would have to make whenever His mother arrived.

"Such a rascal!" she thought. "I have patiently tried to teach Him right from wrong, but He goes on acting like a common criminal, deriving happiness from His thievery. This time I'll teach Him!"

Looking around the dimly lit storeroom, Mother Yasoda found a stick used for scaring monkeys. She kept it hidden from view as she stealthily came up behind Krsna, hoping to grab Him before He ran.

It is said that a thief has a hundred eyes, but the owner of wealth has only two. Something — perhaps His friends, the monkeys, or His own talent for lawlessness — warned Krsna that His mother was nearby.

Krsna saw Yasoda-devi, jumped down from the mortar, and ran away in fear as His mother angrily called after Him, "Stop! Stop, You king of thieves! Where do You think You're going? Come back here!"

Frightened by Yasoda's anger, and even more so by her stick, Krsna ran around the courtyard, finding places where she could not easily follow, repeatedly looking back to see if she was still chasing Him.

Whenever Krsna saw His mother behind Him in hot pursuit, He would let out fearful squeals that attracted the neighbours to the main gate. From there they watched the divine chase with amusement.

"Stop! Stop!" Mother Yasoda called out. "I will, if you drop your stick," Krsna answered. He then stopped at a distance from Yasoda, who said, "If You fear punishment so, why did You make that mess?"

"Please drop your stick," Krsna pleaded, but seeing that she held on to both the stick and her anger, He started running again. Though not as agile as her son, Mother Yasoda continued to chase after Him.

But repeatedly turning His head to look behind Him was definitely slowing Krsna down. As Yasoda gained on Him, He called out, "Mother! Don't punish Me! If you drop your stick, I will surrender."

Mother Yasoda was in no mood for compromise. Although by their austerities yogis and jnanis fail to attain the Supreme Lord, by her resolute determination born of love for Him, Yasoda captured Him.

Once in His mother's grasp, Krsna showed even greater signs of fear than He had before. Rubbing His tear filled eyes with His palms, He loudly sobbed, "Mother! Mother! Please don't beat Me. Please don't."

To see the Supreme Lord Krsna, out of fear of whom the wind blows, smearing the black ointment around His teary eyes and showing such trepidation at His mother's hands, the demigods were bewildered.

Her forehead covered with beads of perspiration, still breathing heavily, Yasoda-devi lifted the stick and mildly rebuked her trembling son, "Remember this stick the next time You want to steal butter."

Krsna tried to hide His body behind hers as He shouted, "Mother! Don't beat me!" Uneasy that Krsna might be unduly afraid, Yasoda tossed the stick away, and replied, "But You are a bad boy! A thief!"

"If You want to save Yourself from punishment," she continued, "tell me how the mortar and pots were broken. And don't lie!" His eyes fixed on the stick now lying nearby, Krsna answered, "I didn't do it!

"You ran so quickly to the kitchen that your ankle bells must have struck a hole in the churn. Seeing butter flowing everywhere, the monkeys came inside. They pulled down this pot, and I caught it.

"Can't you see? I am faultless! But you came after Me with that stick, chasing Me as if I were a thief. Where is the justice in that?" Yasoda stood with mouth agape listening to Krsna's elaborate network of lies.

Waving her forefinger wildly, she fumed, "Not only are You a clever thief, hut a clever liar as well. You arc a king's son, and yet You make friends with monkeys. I think You must he a monkey Yourself."

Sensing that He was not going to get a heating, Krsna became indignant at being called a monkey. "If I am a monkey," He threatened, "then let Me go to the forest and live amongst My kind."

Krsna's words had the desired effect. They frightened Mother Yasoda, who thought, "This hoy is so proud that just to spite me He might actually run off into the forest. To stop Him, I must tie Him up."

Looking sternly at her son, Mother Yasoda said, "You are a liar and a thief whose restless eyes bewilder everyone. To curb Your restlessness, so that I can resume my household duties in peace, I will tie You up."

With that Yasoda took a silk ribbon from her hair and began to tie it around Krsna's waist. Now boiling with indignation, Krsna shouted, "Rohini! Balarama! You arc not here, so My mother is torturing Me."

Although Balarama was too far away to hear, Krsna's calls drew more neighbours into the courtyard. To have some fun, they jokingly mocked Yasoda-devi by repeating words she once spoke to them.

The gopis said, "O Queen! This hoy is innocent. Innocent! He was just trying to help you. Feed Him a little butter and hang your goods out of His reach. You arc blaming Him for your own negligence."

Ignoring her neighbours, Yasoda-devi dragged Krsna to the mortar He had been sitting upon, and to teach Him a lesson and to ensure that He could do no more nonsense that day she tried to tie Him to it.

Awed by the power of Yasoda's love, Sri Suka says,

**"The Supreme Personality of Godhead has no beginning and no end, no exterior and no interior, no front and no rear. In other words, He is all-pervading.**

**"Because He is not under the influence of the clement of time, for Him there is no difference between past, present, and future; He exists in His own transcendental form at all times.**

**"Being absolute, beyond relativity, He is free from distinctions between cause and effect, although He is the cause and effect of everything. That unmanifested person \[avyaktam\] —**

**"Who is beyond the perception of the senses, had now appeared as a human child, and Mother Yasoda, considering Him tier own ordinary child, bound Him to the wooden mortar with a rope".**

Because Krsna pervades all space and time, He is unlimited and can cover, or bind, all limited things. How then can a limited string bind Him? Sri Suka answers,

**"By the power of a love like Yasoda-devi's."**

But achieving the feat of binding Krsna would take time and effort. The ribbon from Mother Yasoda's hair was long enough, but when she wrapped it around Krsna's waist, it was two fingers too short.

Perplexed, Mother Yasoda took a second silken string from her hair and tied it to the first. But this longer ribbon was still two fingers short. Amazed, the eider gopis and their sons pressed in closer to see.

Understanding that His mother wanted to tie Him up, Krsna resisted, thinking, "How can I let My mother bind Me before I've finished My daily rounds of stealing butter and playing with My friends?"

Cakravarti Thakura says that as Krsna thought in this way the potency to reveal opulence (*vibhuti-sakti*) pervaded His body, inspired by the potency to fulfil His desires (*satya-sankalpa-sakti*).

For that reason, until Yogamaya ordered that the influence of these two potencies should be withdrawn, no matter how much rope Mother Yasoda tied together she was unable to bind Her son.

**\* \* \* \***

The gopis observing this spectacle laughed and said, "O Queen! We tried to tell you that your son has the power to bewilder others in order to fulfil His own purposes. Now you can see that for yourself."

Yasoda looked up from her labour and replied, "I think you are under His spell, not me." And she thought to herself, "These are not Krsna's powers. As Garga said, my son is protected by the Supreme Lord."

Then she called out to her servants, "Kurangavati! Lavangavati! Bring some soft twine from the house." But as much rope as there was in the palace, even tied end to end, it was still two fingers short.

Unable to conceal her amazement, Yasoda said, "This gap, though just two-fingers wide, seems to be as vast as the breadth of the universe. Lord Narayana must be enacting a pastime to show us His power."

"Some time ago you placed a golden chain around His waist," the elder gopis observed, "but now all the rope in your house cannot bind Him. You mustn't provoke whatever mysterious forces are at work."

But, desiring to teach Krsna a lesson, her face and body wet with perspiration, Yasoda looked up at the women and replied, "Even if I have to tie together all the ropes in Gokula, I will bind this thief."

Yasoda then exercised her authority as queen and ordered all the women in Gokula to bring churning ropes from their houses, which she tied together one at a time. Still, the rope was two fingers short!

"Two things amaze me," Mother Yasoda thought to herself. "First, this rope measures one hundred hastas, and it still cannot encircle the waist of my tiny child Krsna, even though His girth hasn't changed.

"Second, no matter how much rope is added, the shortage always remains the same size: two fingers wide, never one, three, or four. I must be suffering under the influence of some malefic planet today."

Fearing Yasoda's anger, the gopis kept quiet as they watched their queen attempt to tame her naughty son. At the same time they relished a special joy due to their own maternal love for the thief.

In the tug of war between Yasoda's persistence and Krsna's obstinance, Mother Yasoda prevailed. In the competition between a devotee and Krsna, by Krsna's grace, the devotee is always victorious.

Krsna's mercy (krsna-krpa) is the king of all His potencies. Upon seeing His mother's fatigue in trying to discipline Him, this krsna-krpa exerted its supremacy by melting the Lord's heart.

The appearance of Krsna's mercy caused the satya-sankalpa-sakti and the vibhuti-sakti that had been pervading Krsna's body to retreat, and the two fingers' gap between the ends of rope then disappeared.

These two fingers represent the two factors that make any endeavour in devotional service successful: the devotee's faithful effort to serve the Lord, and the Lord's mercy upon His determined servitor.

Krsna destroyed many demons that represent the various obstacles to devotional life, but His damodara-lila is superior to all of those feats because it declares to the world that He is bound by love alone.

Krsna's submission to love is His natural disposition, it is not merely a drama. Indeed, the very essence of His internal potency is love, and by surrendering to it He tastes the highest bliss, His ultimate goal.

At this point in his description of the damodara-lila, Sukadeva Gosvami kindly tells us how to attain the sort of loving devotion that brings Krsna under control: follow devotees like Mother Yasoda.

The sage's words urge us to abandon all other spiritual disciplines in favour of loving devotion,

*nayam sukhapo bhagavan dehinam gopika-sutah*  
*jnaninam catma-bhutanam yatha bhaktimatam iha*

**"The Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Sri Krsna, the son of Mother Yasoda and Nanda Maharaja, is accessible to devotees engaged in spontaneous loving service, but —**

**"He is not as easily accessible to mental spectators, to those striving for self-realisation by severe austerities and penances, or to those who consider the body the same as the self."**

As Yasoda struggled to bind Krsna, He cried and cried until His eyes were red from constant rubbing and His breath was short from repeated sobbing. This scene filled His friends with sorrow.

Krsna was aware that His mother's relentless efforts were the result of her desire to do what she considered best for Him, and He also recognised the fatigue she endured in loving devotion to Him.

Her breathing was heavy, her hair scattered, her skin was wet with perspiration, and her limbs ached with exhaustion. She repeatedly stopped to rest, but she always resumed her effort to bind Him.

Thus, He who embodies eternal bliss and knowledge, who has no inside or outside, no beginning or end, who is both inside and outside of everything, and is the sum total of all, took pity on His mother.

To spare Mother Yasoda from further exhaustion and anguish, Krsna submitted to her desire out of compassion and allowed her to tie the rope around His waist, binding Him to the mortar nearby.

Having finally succeeded, Yasoda-devi profusely scolded her son. Then, after instructing the other boys to stand guard over Krsna, she returned to the palace, and her duties, accompanied by the gopis.

The moment His mother was out of sight, Krsna stopped crying, became peaceful, and began contemplating the next chapter of His adventures. That day's excitement had not yet come to an end.

Tugging on the rope, Krsna quickly discovered that He could move the mortar that was fixed to His waist. He felt joy at the prospect of dragging it around the courtyard and then down the hill.

Still tied up, Krsna played with His friends, making them laugh by moving the mortar here and there. Then, true to His impish nature, He incited the boys to steal butter from the empty homes of the gopis.

Once all the boys, with the exception of a few toddlers, had gone off to raid the storerooms of Gokula, Krsna recalled Narada Muni's curse upon the two sons of Kuvera — Manigriva and Nalakuvara.

These two youths had become proud of their status as Lord Siva's associates. In the company of young women, they would wander through the gardens of Mount Kailasa, intoxicated on Varum wine.

Once, as Manigriva and Nalakuvara were enjoying themselves with the celestial damsels in the waters of the Mandakini Canges, divine fate arranged that Narada Muni pass by the site of their revelry.

The two demigods were naked, hut they were too intoxicated to cover themselves in the presence of the saint. And Narada Muni, seeing that they had lost all decency, cursed them to become trees.

Sobered by Narada's curse, the sons of Kuvera begged that he show leniency. The great sage then assured them that after a hundred celestial years they would he liberated by the Supreme Lord Himself.

Nalakuvara and Manigriva then appeared as two arjuna trees growing side by side near the bank of the Yamuna. During the whole of their long lifespans, they retained full remembrance of their identities.

Remembering Narada Muni's words, the two trees waited for the time when Krsna would come and deliver them. That time came on the morning of Dipavali, after Yasoda had bound Krsna to the mortar.

As Krsna crawled to the centre of the courtyard, He dragged the mortar behind Him. Looking out the palace gate and down the hill towards the Yamuna, in the distance He could see the two trees.

The Vraja-vasis called these two trees yamala-arjuna trees because they shared the same root system and thus appeared like twins (yamala). They were leafy, old, expansive, and extremely tall.

The demigods residing within the trees had been purified by suffering at the mercy of men, animals, and the elements. Recalling Narada's prophesy, they eagerly anticipated the day the Lord would free them.

Knowing that it was time to make Narada's words come true, Krsna slowly moved towards the trees, followed by a small group of children, who said, "Krsna must want some shade from the scorching sun."

As He crawled towards the trees, Krsna thought, "Because Narada Muni is My dear devotee, I will fulfil his words by giving these two demigods whatever that great soul promised them."

**\* \* \* \***

Krsna passed between the two trees, but the mortar dragging behind Him got stuck sideways. As He pulled on the rope, the trees slowly bent in His direction, creaking loudly as if from discomfort.

Pulling the mortar behind Him, His curly hair brushing against His shoulders, His eyes alive with excitement at the unfolding adventure, Krsna tugged on the rope and effortlessly uprooted the trees.

We may wonder how the ribbon from Mother Yasoda's hair, or even the ropes meant for churning butter, could be strong enough to uproot two enormous trees. One would expect that they might break.

But Krsna's potency of untimited strength (virya-sakti) empowered those relatively flimsy cords and made them as sturdy and strong as Vasuki when he was used as the churning rope for Mandara Hill.

The trees fell away from Krsna, creating a fearful crashing sound that caused the residents of Gokula to lose consciousness for an entire muhurta. Only His companions remained conscious at that time.

During that brief interval, as the young children looked on and listened in amazement, Nalakuvara and Manigriva offered prayers to the Lord, received His blessings, and then returned to heaven.

Released from their confinement, the two grateful celestials illuminated the ten directions with their bodily effulgence as they appeared before Krsna and offered the Lord suitable prayers.

Nalakuvara and Manigriva praised Krsna’s divinity, a truth only His devotees understand, though it is clearly manifest in the pastimes of His innumerable incarnations, such as the fish and the boar.

Two of the celestials’ statements were especially significant: the brothers identified themselves as followers of Narada Muni and asked that they be always engaged in speaking of Krsna’s glorious pastimes.

Krsna smiled to hear His devotees offer these prayers, yet His mind was still absorbed in the loving altercation He just had with Yasoda. He could not help but think, “They are praising Me for freeing them.

“But mother doesn’t praise Me. She scolds Me and then ties Me up. The words of chastisement I receive from the Vraja-vasis are much more appealing to Me than the prayers of these two demigods.”

Remembering His devotee Narada Muni, Krsna spoke to the two celestials in His soft childish voice. He told them that their seeing Him and receiving love for Him were both results of Narada’s grace.

Krsna said,

*sadhunam sama-cittanam sutaram mat-krtatmanam*  
*darsanan no bhaved bandhah pumso ’ksnoh savitur yatha*

**“When one is face-to-face with the sun, there is no longer darkness for one’s eyes.**

**“Similarly, when one is face-to-face with a** ***sadhu,*** **a devotee, who is fully determined and surrendered to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, one will no longer be subject to material bondage.”**

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura cites another reading of this verse, which says that until one is face-to-face with a *sadhu,* liberation remains out of reach and one’s material bondage must continue.

This raises a question: After seeing a pure devotee like Srila Prabhupada, why aren’t all souls liberated/ Visvanatha tells us that the rising of the sun docs not dispel the darkness for a blind man.

And Srila Prabhupada himself observes that “persons who arc too much offensive, who commit *vaisnava-aparadhas,* or offences to a *sadhu,* will have to take some time before being rectified.’’

Cakravarti Thakura gives another reason that the effects of *sadhu*-*sanga* may be delayed: As long as one commits offences to the holy name, he or she cannot be liberated even by seeing Narada Muni.

The privilege of directly seeing great souls like Narada Muni or Srila Prabhupada will only liberate us from material bondage when we no longer act offensively towards such souls or the Lord’s holy name.

During the period in which we continue to commit offences in our devotional lives, our hope for progress lies in our efforts to rectify our misconduct and purify ourselves through constant *nama-sankirtana.*

After Nalakuvara and Manigriva had departed for heaven, the boys with Krsna — who had stood still like painted pictures, yet witnessed everything that had happened — talked excitedly amongst themselves.

When the villagers finally regained consciousness, the crashing sound of the felled trees was still ringing in their ears. Seeing the two uprooted trees in the distance, they wondered what had happened.

Heading in the direction of the disaster, they spoke to each other along the way: “How could trees fall without any wind?” “There was no rain, wind, or lightning.” “And there are no elephants in sight.”

As the men and women of Vrndavana arrived at the site of the fallen trees, they saw Krsna playing nearby, dragging the mortar around. Surrounding the child, they enquired, “How did this happen?”

Just then Nanda Maharaja arrived. Upon seeing His father, Krsna began to cry. Nandaraja spoke soothing words to the child as he untied Him. He then embraced Krsna, pacifying Him in many ways.

Repeatedly kissing Krsna’s face, Nanda Maharaja asked his son a question, even though he already knew the answer, “Who has tied You up like this? Where is that rascal who tied You to this mortar?”

Pacified by His father’s affection, Krsna quietly sobbed into Nanda Maharaja’s ear, “Father! It was mother who tied Me up.” Meanwhile, the cowherd men were excitedly discussing what had happened.

The elder *gopas* said, “For these trees to have fallen over with no wind, their roots must have been rotten. But it’s clear that the roots and branches — every part of these trees — are sound and healthy.

“Whatever the reason, it is a miracle that Krsna was not harmed, even though He was playing beneath the trees when they fell. This is yet more evidence that He is personally protected by Lord Narayana.”

Nanda Maharaja enquired from the boys that were there, “How did this happen?” They told him, “Krsna pulled the mortar between the trees, and when it got stuck He kept pulling, and the trees fell down.

“Then two effulgent beings came out of the trees. They praised Krsna for some time and then disappeared.” At this, the assembly of Gokula’s cowherd men and women broke out in amused laughter.

The *gopas* and *gopis* who had parental love for Krsna dismissed this account as childish prattle, but other members of the community thought to themselves, “Maybe Krsna could have done it. Maybe!”

**\* \* \* \***

Then Nanda Maharaja took Krsna to the Yamuna. After they had both bathed, Nandaraja requested the *brahmanas* to chant protective mantras and perform rituals to remove negative influences.

He then rewarded the *brahmanas* with gifts and reassured his subjects with sweet words. Finally Nanda and Krsna returned to the palace accompanied by the sounds of drums, *karatalas,* and singing.

Mother Rohini and Balarama had also returned, so Nanda Maharaja sat down with his sons, playing with Them and telling Them stories for an hour or so until he could see that They were well occupied.

Satisfied that his sons were now peaceful, Nanda Maharaja went to the barns to supervise the evening milking. Meanwhile, Mother Yasoda sat locked in her own room in self-imposed exile.

Ashamed for having bound Krsna and devastated at having put His life in danger, Yasoda-devi would neither leave her room nor talk to the other women of the house. She just stayed by herself and cried.

After having served Nanda his supper, Rohini went to console Yasoda with sweet words and convince her to eat. But Yasoda-devi — eyes red from crying, bed soaked with tears — was inconsolable.

Concerned that Krsna have sufficient milk and aware that Mother Yasoda was not nursing Him, Nanda Maharaja brought fresh milk from the barn, mixed it with sugar, and fed Krsna and His friends.

As the king sat and watched Krsna eat, Rohini and some of the senior women came to present Yasoda’s case. They pleaded, “O King! Your wife has not eaten all day. Neither will she speak to anyone.”

Nodding his head pensively, Nanda Maharaja replied, “What can I do? She is undergoing the proper atonement for one needlessly overcome by anger. For such mistakes, one should show remorse.”

“Oh! Your soft-hearted wife will be devastated by such words,” Rohini replied with tears in her eyes. Nanda Maharaja spoke to Krsna, who was playing nearby with Balarama, “Will You go to Your mother?”

Krsna shook His head forcefully and said, “No! I will stay with you.” Disappointed, Mother Yasoda’s attendants coaxed Krsna: “Dear child! Then whose milk will You drink when You become hungry?”

With finality, Krsna responded, “I will drink cow’s milk mixed with sugar.” “And who will You play with?” the women asked. Krsna answered, “With My father and My brother Balarama.”

Now it was Nanda Maharaja’s turn to test His son. He asked, “What about your brother’s mother, Rohini? Will You go to her?” Krsna turned away and said, “No! She went away and left Me to be tied up.”

Taking a few steps forward, tears flowing from her eyes, Rohini-devi said softly, “My son! Why are You being so merciless.Your mother is suffering.” But Krsna, starting to cry, only looked at His father.

At a signal from Rohini, Balarama went to take Krsna’s hand in order to go with Him to His mother, hut Krsna pulled away from His brother’s touch and climbed into His father’s lap with tear-filled eyes.

Looking for a way to invoke Krsna’s eternal love for His mother, Nanda Maharaja raised his fist and said, “Son! If You agree, then I will go to Your mother right now and beat her for her misdeeds.”

Hearing this, Krsna at once grabbed His father’s fist with His soft hands, tears rolling down His cheeks. “Son, You are right,” the king replied, “I needn’t punish her now, for she is dying of sorrow anyway.”

Krsna was at once full of anxiety to hear that His mother was dying. Crying for her, He called out piteously, “Where is My mother! I must see her right now. Mother! Mother! Where arc youMother!”

Struck by worry, Krsna ran to Rohini. She embraced the child and carried Him into Yasoda’s room, where He ran to His mother, who was lying in bed. Now crying in happiness, He hugged and kissed her.

As she held Krsna in her arms, Mother Yasoda’s aching heart melted. Her sobbing could be heard throughout the palace, the sound of which made her husband, and everyone else present, weep in bliss.

By Krsna’s magical touch, Mother Yasoda regained her natural effulgence and beauty. She reassured her friends that she was all right, happily breastfed her son, and again tasted transcendental bliss.

Krsna and His mother were happily reunited on the evening of Dipavali, the same day Krsna was bound, but for the next two days, out of fear, Yasoda would not come into the presence of her husband.

On the evening of the third day, however, Nanda Maharaja asked Krsna to find His mother. Following Nanda’s order, Krsna enticed His mother to come before the king by pulling on the edge of her sari.

With that, the pastime of binding Krsna came to an end, a pastime in which Krsna showed such extraordinary mercy to Mother Yasoda that not only demigods but also the goddess of fortune was amazed.

Thus Sukadeva Gosvami says,

*nemam virinco na bhavo na srir apy angu-samsraya prasdaam lebhire gopi yat tat prapa vimuktidat*

**“Neither Lord Brahma, nor Lord Siva, nor even the goddess of fortune —**

**“Who is always the better half of the Supreme Lord, can obtain from the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the deliverer from this material world, such mercy as received by Mother Yasoda.**

Ever since the time Yasoda-devi playfully bound Krsna with the silk ribbon in her hair, the men and women of Vrndavana, and even Krsna’s own friends, would often jokingly call Him Damodara.

The veranda of Maharaja Nanda’s palace, where Mother Yasoda first churned (*manthana)* yogurt (*dadhi*) and Krsna angrily broke the butter churn, is now immortalised as Dadhi-manthana-sthala.

Mother Yasoda caught and tied Krsna in the courtyard of Nanda’s palace below, and Krsna uprooted the twin *arjuna* trees near the Yamuna River at a place called Yamalarjuna-bhanjana-tirtha.

To these places of Lord Damodara’s pastimes, to Lord Damodara Himself, and to the memory of this enchanting pastime, in which He was bound by His mother, let us offer our obeisances again and again.

With a straw in my mouth I offer respectful obeisances again and again to my worshipable deity, Mother Yasoda, who binds with unbreakable ropes of love that Lord whom fear personified fears.

**\* \* \* \***

Let us now conclude this narration of Krsna’s childhood activities in Gokula by recounting a few pastimes that happened mostly in the area of Nanda Maharaja’s royal residence on the hilltop.

First let us hear about the birth of Lord Balarama, which is generally said to have taken place in Nanda Maharaja’s house, a little more than a year prior to Lord Krsna’s own appearance in Gokula.

As already mentioned, Rohini-devi was three months pregnant when her husband Vasudeva sent her to the safety of Gokula with a request that his dear friend Nanda Maharaja personally take care of her.

Rohini-devi happily lived in Nanda Maharaja’s palace as if she were a part of the immediate family. She and Mother Yasoda were extremely close friends; in fact, they were practically inseparable.

When Devaki was pregnant with her seventh child, Balarama, Krsna ordered Yogamaya to transfer Him to Rohini’s womb. To the people of Mathura it appeared that Devaki had suffered a miscarriage.

This took place at midnight during the seventh month of Rohini’s pregnancy, which, according to Sri Jiva, continued for another seven months, keeping the household of Nandaraja always in suspense.

At that time it was customary for women to give birth in a maternity room, separate from the residential quarters, just as Mother Yasoda gave birth to Yogamaya in the Syama-mandira near the Yamuna.

But because Lord Balarama took birth at an unexpected time, He was born inside Nanda Maharaja’s home. The next morning Rohini-devi proudly displayed her newborn son. He was radiant as the moon.

The *Garga-samhita,* however, gives another account of Lord Balarama’s appearance, in which He takes birth after staying only five days within Rohini’s womb. Such a birth is also unexpected.

This alternate version also says that Balarama appeared at midday rather than midnight, but because Srila Prabhupada says Balarama appeared at midnight, that is the account his followers accept.

Upon the birth of Lord Balarama, in Vasudeva’s absence Nandaraja performed the child’s birth ceremony, sponsored a joyful festival, and profusely distributed charity as if he were doing so for his own son.

Even the great Vyasadeva came to the ceremony. He asked to see the newborn and disclosed to Nanda that the child was Ananta Sesa and that He had been transferred from Devaki’s womb to Rohini’s.

Upon seeing the child, Vedavyasa offered many prayers, such as***,***

*jaya jayacyuta deva parat para svayam ananta dig-anta-gatam yasah*  
*sura-munindra-phanindra-varaya te musaline baline haline namah*

**“O infallible Lord! O Supreme one! O Lord Ananta of universal fame! Glory unto You! Obeisances to You, holding a plough and club, master of demigods, great sages, and regal serpents!”**

Srila Vyasadeva then departed, leaving Nanda Maharaja to wonder how he had become so fortunate as to have Lord Balarama take birth in his kingdom, not to mention within the walls of his own house.

Nearby, to the south of Maharaja Nanda’s palace, is a small hill *(tila)* where the king would brush *(dhavana)* his teeth *(danta)* every morning. The entire hill is therefore named Danta-dhavana-tila.

Another pastime place is the makeshift wrestling arena in the palace courtyard, not far from where Krsna overturned the cart and killed Sakatasura. In this arena Krsna and Balarama wrestled each other.

Sometimes, when the boys were there playing, elderly *gopis* would visit. The *gopis* would entice the brothers by saying, “Let us see You boys wrestle. The winner gets the parcel of sweets that we brought.”

Induced by Their greed for butter and the ebullient energy of child' hood, Krsna and Balarama would lock arms as Their friends cheered and the elder *gopis* watched, amused and fully satisfied.

The place where Krsna honed His wrestler’s (*malla*) skills with Balarama and His friends is called Malla-tirtha. Gopisvara Mahadeva, the elder *gopis’* worshipable deity, mercifully presides over this area.

Nearby is another Deity, this one known as Maha-malla-raya (“the king of great wrestlers”), sometimes mistakenly thought to he Krsna the killer of Kamsa’s wrestlers, not the child wrestler of Gokula.

Downhill from Nandaraja’s palace is Sanatana Gosvami’s Mahavana residence, a deep, cave-like hollow in the ground, the entrance of which lies in the direction of a well known as Sapta-samudrika-kupa.

When Sanatana Gosvami stayed here the local villagers were so impressed by his wisdom and purity that they tried to serve him in various ways, even though he humbly refused their offerings.

Jagadananda Pandita once came on pilgrimage from Jagannatha Puri to Mathura and was very pleased to meet Sanatana Gosvami. The senior Vaisnava took Jagadananda Pandita on *parikrama* of Vraja.

They finished their circumambulation in Mahavana, and so the two saints stayed in Sanatana Gosvami’s cave in Gokula, from where Jagadananda would daily go to a nearby temple to cook his meals.

Sanatana Gosvami, on the other hand, would beg alms from the homes of *brahmanas* and from the temples in Madhuvana, and whatever he received, he accepted as his meal for the day.

Sanatana would also beg for the ingredients Jagadananda Pandita needed to prepare his own meals, and the elder saint would occasionally share whatever Jagadananda had prepared.

In this way the two lived happily together. As Jagadananda was leaving for Puri, he gave Sanatana a message from Lord Caitanya: “I am also coming to Vraja. Please arrange a place for Me to stay.”

The Gosvami was delighted to receive this order. After some thought he decided that the plateau on Dvadasaditya-tila would be the most fitting place to receive and to serve Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

Sanatana Gosvami had collected some valuable items that would help to remind the Lord of Vrndavana. After carefully packing them, He sent those items with Jagadananda Pandita as gifts for Lord Caitanya.

Regarding this, Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami says, “The gifts consisted of some sand from the site of the *rasa-lila,* a stone from Govardhana Hill, dry ripened *pilu* fruits, and a garland of \[gunja berries\].”

After Jagadananda Pandita had left for Jagannatha Puri, Sanatana Gosvami, aggrieved with ecstatic love in separation from his friend, felt as if he had lost the company of Caitanya Mahaprabhu Himself.

But, with Caitanya Mahaprabhu's request in mind, Sanatana Gosvami prepared to return to Vrndavana, arrange a suitable place for the Lord to stay there, and eagerly wait for His arrival.

Further east of Sanatana Gosvami's cave is the place where Krsna’s ear-piercing ceremony took place beside a well known by three names: Krsna-kupa, Nanda-kupa, and Sapta-samudrika-kupa.

Scripture also tells us the forefathers used to visit a dear-water lake called Sapta-samudrika-kunda that once existed there. It is possible that the Sapta-samudrika well might have been a lake in the past.

It is said that if one offers oblations to one’s ancestors (*pinda*) at Sapta-samudrika-kunda on Monday after the new moon, the act is equivalent to performing the same ritual at holy Gaya.

Regarding the well, oral tradition says that the demigods created it for Krsna, blessing its water to be warm in winter and cool in summer. Nandaraja is said to have regularly drawn water from it for his bath.

Within the precincts of Bhauma Vrndavana there is another village known as Gokula. It is a few kilometres west of the Gokula in Mahavana where Krsna took birth and enjoyed childhood pastimes.

This second Gokula is also known as New Gokula because it was founded relatively recently by Vallabhacarya, who established it as the Vrndavana headquarters for his followers, the Pusti-marga sect.

The followers of Vallabhacarya say that this is the original Gokula. They have even erected memorials there to commemorate Krsna’s pastimes. But locals and Gaudiya Vaisnavas both reject this claim.

When Srila Prabhupada took his disciples on *parikrama* of Vraja, their visit to Mahavana brought them near to New Gokula, hut His Divine Grace declined to visit, directing devotees to “old” Gokula.

Although the name Mahavana refers to the forest spread over a large portion of this shore of the Yamuna, the name is also linked with the village of Gokula; thus the village is also known as Gokula-mahavana.

Most of the village established by Vajra — which survived four thousand years of deterioration and neglect — was finally destroyed when Mahmud of Ghazni sacked Mathura and Gokula.

Our Gaudlya predecessors visited Gokula often hut did not construct temples there. Neither did they put as much energy into developing the places of Krsna’s childhood as they did in developing Vrndavana.

Still, the forest of Mahavana, the village of Gokula, and the places where Krsna revealed in His childhood pastimes and gave bliss to the Vraja-vasis, are places we pray to, meditate upon, and worship.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami provides one such prayer to Mahavana, which especially emphasises Krsna’s divine appearance with these words,

*avirbhava-mahotsave muraripoh svarnoru-mukta-phala—*  
*Sreni-vibhrama-mandite nava-gavi-lakse dadau dve muda*  
*divyalanikrti-ratna-parvata-tila-prasthadikam cadarad viprebhyah kila yatra sa vraja-patir vande brihat-kananam*

**“During the great festival of Lord Krsna’s birth, the king of Vraja respectfully gave to the** ***brahmanas*** **a mountain of glittering jewel ornaments, an even greater mountain of grains —**

**“And two hundred thousand young cows, all beautifully decorated with gold and pearl necklaces. I offer my respectful obeisances to Mahavana, the place where the king gave charity so generously.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Having narrated Krsna’s childhood pastimes in chronological order and named some of the innumerable places of His pastimes in Gokula, I now describe the last leg of my *parikrama*— the holy town of Raval.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami says that because Raval is the birthplace of Sri Radha it is the chief *(mukhya) of* all other towns. He therefore refers to it as Mukhycravali in the following prayer.

*Gandharvaya jani-marur abhud yatra sankirtitayam anandotkaih sura-muni-naraih kirtida-garbha-khanyam*  
*gopi-gopaih surabhi-mkaraih samparite 'tra mukhye ravalyakhye vrsaravi-pure priti-puro mamastam*

**“In the city of Mukhyeravah the precious jewel known as Srimati Radharani took birth in the mine of Kirtida-devi’s womb, which is glorified by jubilant demigods, sages, and human beings.**

**“I pray that when I enter King Vrsabhanu’s capital city of Mukhyera- vali, populated with many** ***gopas*** **and** ***gopis,*** **and** ***surablu*** **cows, I may drown in a great flood of transcendental bliss and love.”**

In Bhauma Vrndavana, Raval is to this day a remote, undeveloped cowherd village; indeed, the temple that commemorates King Vrsahhanu’s home is modest and rarely visited by pilgrims.

Ordinary vision does not reveal Raval as Dasa Gosvami describes it; still, its spiritual atmosphere invites one to chant Hare Krsna and eventually, through purified vision, glimpse the true Mukhyeravali.

I recall once sitting on top of the temple at Raval and chanting Hare Krsna with a few devotees. Although I was unable to see the original form of Sri Radha’s birthplace, its presence could be felt.

Srila Prabhupada writes that even beginners can feel the presence of the *dhama:* “...still, if you go to Vrndavana without knowing about Krsna, you will at once feel Krsna consciousness.”

The end of my *parikrama* was drawing near. Thoughts crowded my mind and emotions rose in my heart, all of which were appeased by chanting the holy names and remembering Srimati Radharani.

In New Vraja-dhama, Raval is also secluded, peaceful, and spiritually uplifting. As I sat upon a log there, I let my mind flow with the currents of remembrance and listened to the sound of the Yamuna.

From Gokula, Lord Caitanya visited Raval and exhibited symptoms of ecstasy so uniquely wonderful that the villagers there concluded, as they did wherever He went, that He was Krsna Himself.

By seeing the Lord’s beautiful features and by hearing Him chant Krsna’s names, people were overwhelmed with spiritual emotions. Following His lead, they would also dance and sing in ecstasy.

What was Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s divine absorption while in Raval? Was He absorbed in the mood of Krsna visiting Radha’s birthplace, of Radha returning home, or of a perfected devotee on pilgrimage?

Only the Lord knows the contents of His own heart, though at that time they produced symptoms of ecstasy visible in His behaviour and form for many hours. Finally, He left for Mathura, His heart at peace.

When Raghava Acarya brought his young wards to Raval, they remained there throughout the night, discussing Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s visit and the childhood pastimes of Radha and Krsna.

In the early nineteenth century, the Yamuna’s shifting current swept away the temple Lord Caitanya and His followers once visited. Since that time a new temple was built, dedicated to Radha asLariliji.

Srimati Radharani appeared in this world to assist Krsna in His mission to reveal the loving exchanges that go on in Goloka and, in that way, to entice conditioned souls to return back to Godhead.

In Her desire to be close to Krsna wherever He goes, Radha made Her appearance, accompanied by *gopas* and *gopis,* in Raval, the ancestral home of Maharaja Vrsabhanu and his beautiful wife Kirtida-devi.

Scripture and oral tradition give three reports of Srimati Radharani’s appearance, saying that She took birth from the ground, a lotus, and the womb. It is also said that She appeared in Raval and Varsana.

In a Radhastami lecture, Srila Prabhupada once described how King Vrsabhanu was surprised to find Sri Radha buried in the earth, and how the king proudly presented the beautiful baby to hiswife.

The king was ploughing his fields with a golden plough to conclude a sacrifice the *Vedas* prescribe for kings with no issue, at the end of which the earth was supposed to bring forth a child.

In much the same way, Sukadeva Gosvami describes that Sita-devi also appeared to Janaka Maharaja from the furrows he was making with a plough *(sira),* for which the king is known as Siradhvaja.

Srila Prabhupada does not explicitly state that Radharani’s father was performing a sacrifice; he may have been simply cultivating his fields. In any case, this is how His Divine Grace says baby Radha appeared.

The second version of Srimati Radharani’s appearance is well established in the oral tradition of Vraja and it is the one most often narrated on *parikrama* parties visiting both Raval and Varsana.

In this version, King Vrsabhanu, while bathing in the river Yamuna early one morning, saw a thousand-petalled lotus flower floating towards him. In the centre of that lotus was an effulgent baby girl.

As the king lifted the smiling baby out of the lotus and embraced Her, he felt waves of transcendental bliss course through his body. Lost in the throes of that intense ecstasy, he could neither move nor speak.

After some time Maharaja Vrsabhanu finally regained his composure. Bubbling with joy, he returned to his palace and placed the child in the arms of his queen, who was also consumed by parental bliss.

The third version of Srimati Radharani’s appearance, one often repeated in scriptures, is that She was born from the womb of Kirtida- devi, without Kirtida’s having been impregnated by her husband.

Thus, as clouds floated peacefully in the sky, Radharani made Her appearance at midday, on the Monday of the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the moon in the month of Bhadra (August-September).

As did Krsna’s appearance one year earlier, Radha’s appearance made the rivers clear, purified the directions, and invoked gentle, cooling breezes laden with the sweet aroma of blossoming flowers.

Electrified by their good fortune, and by the celestial beauty of their newborn child, Kirtida and Vrsabhanu distributed unlimited charity as the demigods showered flowers upon Vrsabhanu’s kingdom.

Day by day the child’s beauty and qualities unfurled like lotus petals opening in the heat of the sun, but the sun that made Radha blossom was Nanda’s boy, who was then playing in the dust of nearby Gokula.

The beauty and influence of the newborn girl astonished the Vraja *gopis* who came to see Her. They would excitedly praise Kirtida’s good fortune as they rocked the child in Her golden, gem encrusted cradle.

Even great demigods and sages cannot hope to see Srimati Radharani, the supreme goddess of fortune, but the *gopis* of Vrsabhanu’s kingdom constantly and affectionately cuddled, caressed, and played with Her.

**\* \* \* \***

Unlike Krsna’s childhood pastimes, which are amply recorded in the writings of Vyasadeva and Gaudiya *acaryas,* most of the following pastimes are part of oral tradition, as told on *parikrama* to Raval.

The scriptures record Radharani’s pastimes only when they are integral to Krsna’s. This shows that Srimati Radharani is to be heard of and meditated upon in relation to Sri Krsna, not alone.

One day, Narada Muni visited baby Krsna in Gokula. Assuming that the Lord’s pleasure potency, Sri Radha, must also have taken birth nearby, the sage visited all the homes in Mahavana one by one.

Although the great sage saw many young boys and girls and many beautiful newborns, he did not see a single child whose glance or presence made him feel irrepressible and incomparable bliss.

Finally, after having searched through most of Raval, Narada Muni came to the palace of Maharaja Vrsabhanu. Narada was cordially greeted by the king’s attendants and at once brought into his court.

After respectfully worshipping the sage, King Vrsabhanu enquired about the purpose of Narada’s visit. But Narada answered with a question of his own, “Has a girl recently taken birth in your house?”

“Yes! By the grace of the Lord I have been blessed with a daughter of divine countenance,” Maharaja Vrsabhanu proudly replied. Thinking he had at last come to the right place, Narada asked to see the girl.

However, the king had more to say. “Unfortunately this child has not yet opened Her eyes. We do not know whether She is blind or a celestial who is unwilling to look at the imperfections of this world.”

But, at Narada’s request, the baby was brought before him. With deep spiritual insight he at once recognised Her to be Srimati Radharani, and with great difficulty he restrained his ecstatic emotions and said:

“O King! Providence has surely blessed you. Quickly, bring me items for a purificatory rite. I will perform a ceremony to ensure that in time this child blesses the world with the glance of Her doe-like eyes.”

Seizing this golden opportunity, Vrsabhanu Maharaja left Narada alone with Radharani and went about collecting the paraphernalia for blessing the newborn. Meanwhile, Narada knelt before Sri Radha.

He offered prayers to Lord Krsna’s eternal pleasure potency, who had appeared on earth to serve the Lord’s pastimes and display the pinnacle of spontaneous love for Krsna and the symptoms it invokes.

As Narada Muni offered prayers, the little baby playfully wiggled Her hands and feet. But, knowing that Narada was eager to behold Her original form, Radharani finally appeared to him as a fresh youth.

Srimati Radharani’s incomparably beautiful adolescent form, flanked by Lalita and Visakha, rendered Narada speechless. He took in the wonder of the moment with transcendentally enlivened senses.

Narada’s bliss was short lived, however, because just before King Vrsabhanu returned, Sri Radha resumed Her form as a baby. Narada hid his ecstasies and, as promised, performed the ritual tor the child.

Narada’s vision of Radha’s youthful form was short, too short for him to render any service to Her. And Krsna was missing. Though elated by what he had seen, Narada left the palace hankering for more.

The sage then went to Naradavana. There, after long enduring austerities under Vrnda-devi’s direction, he was able to enter Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes in the form of a *gopi* some call Naradiya.

Narada Muni continues to travel throughout the universe, glorifying the Lord wherever he goes. He is a fitting exemplar for all *sanyasis* and travelling preachers, as shown by his thoughts, words, and deeds.

One of Narada’s prayers is perfectly suited for preachers,

*sri-rasa-rangasya vikasa-candrika dipavalir ya vrsabhanu-mandire*  
*goloka-cuda-mani-kantha-bhusanam dhyatva param tam bhuvi paryatamy aham*

**“I wander this earth meditating on Her, who is a moon shining in the arena of the** ***rasa*** **dance, who is a host of bright lamps in Vrsabhanu’s palace, and who is the central jewel in the necklace of Goloka.”**

Although Radha did not open Her eyes during or immediately after Narada’s ceremony, King Vrsabhanu had great faith that whatever the sage had said would come to pass. It was simply a matter of time.

Indeed, the next day, Paurnamasi-devi arrived to see the newborn. When she was shown little Radha, the *brahmani* at once recognised Her as the original Laksmi-devi, the Supreme Lord’s eternal consort.

Taking Vrsabhanu and Kirtida aside, Paurnamasi confidentially instructed the fortunate parents in the transcendental truths of their daughter, just as Garga Muni had instructed Krsna’s parents in His.

Paurnamasi said, “This girl is not ordinary. Great personalities like Brahma, Siva, and Narada worship Her, knowing that She can fulfil all their desires — material and spiritual. So please take care of Her.”

They were joyful to hear their daughter’s glories, but the king and queen also expressed concern for Sri Radha’s blindness. “Not to worry,” Paurnamasi reassured them. “This is just Radha’s pastime.”

Later that day, Nanda Maharaja and Yasoda arrived. They were close friends of King Vrsabhanu; indeed, they had arranged his marriage to Kirtida. They brought with them their own little son, Krsna.

The anxious parents of Radharani confided in their elder well- wishers. They were deeply troubled by their daughter’s blindness. Was it an ill omen? How could such a remarkable child he handicapped?

While this conversation was going on, Krsna climbed down from His mother’s lap and went into the bedroom where Radharani was sleeping. Climbing up on Her bed, He gently touched Radha’s eyes.

As soon as Radha felt Krsna’s touch, She became aware that the person for whom Her eyes were created was there with Her. Casting off Her blindness, She opened Her cloud-blue eyes and smiled.

Soon the parents came into the bedroom and saw the two children sitting on the bed and playing. Both couples were equally overjoyed that Radha had mysteriously opened Her eyes and regained Her sight.

Both sets of parents marked this event as a sign that Radha and Krsna were eternally paired, that They knew no one else but each other, and that in this life They should again be united in marriage.

Her vision restored, Radharani began to move, crawl, and in time to play with young girls Her own age. The elder gopis marveled at the small baby’s lady-like gestures, which were evident even in Her play.

When Radha turned seven months old, Mother Kirtida decided it was time to celebrate her daughter’s first-grain ceremony ***(****anna-prasana*). Elaborate arrangements were made, and many guests were invited.

Mother Kirtida sat near the fire with Radharani on her lap as the *Brahmanas* performed a sacrifice and chanted auspicious mantras. Beside Kirtida sat her friend Yasoda with her son Krsna on her lap.

Mother Yasoda held a bowl of sweet rice, from which she would feed Krsna whenever He felt hungry. At one point, Radha unexpectedly reached over, took a morsel from Krsna’s bowl, and ate it.

Thus Srimati Radharani’s first grains were Sri Krsna’s remnants. This spontaneous event strengthened the two mothers’ conviction that Divine Providence had chosen their children for each other.

Though Srimati Radharani’s pastimes are unlimited, I shall corn elude by narrating how Durvasa Muni once blessed Radharani that whatever She cooked would have the taste and the effect of nectar.

**\* \* \* \***

One day, when Radha was a few years old and accustomed to imitating Her mother’s domestic duties such as cooking and cleaning, Durvasa Muni appeared outside the entrance to Vrsabhanu’s palace.

The sage had already confirmed for himself that Krsna was indeed the Supreme Lord, now he also wanted to verify what he had heard from the celestials: that the goddess of fortune had appeared in Raval.

Little Radha and Her young girlfriends were happily playing in the courtyard when Durvasa Muni arrived. The awesome features of the sage scared away all the girls, except for Srimati Radharani.

Radha had often seen Her parents greet saints and yogis. In imitation of them, She fearlessly touched Durvasa’s feet then joined Her small soft palms together and sweetly said, “*Svagatam!* Welcome!”

Amazed by the delicate beauty and aristocratic bearing of this tiny girl, Durvasa bent over and gently asked Radha, “Who are You, little girl? And what games have You been playing with Your friends?”

In a steady voice, Radha answered, “My name is Radha, the daughter of Queen Kirtida. My friends and I have been pretending to cook for Maharaja Nanda’s son, the killer of Putana and Trnavarta.”

As She finished speaking, Sri Radha pointed to the courtyard and a small makeshift temple fashioned from mud. There sat a likeness of child Krsna decorated with flowers, leaves, and bits of colourful cloth.

Because the residents of Vraja were always speaking about Krsna, He had become the centre of little Radha’s life. At Radha’s insistence, Her mother had given Her a doll of Krsna to play with.

Thus the activities of Radha and Her friends would generally centre around dressing and decorating Krsna’s image, cooking for Him, offering Him *arati,* and then tucking Him in as they sang for Him.

Radharani’s attraction to serving Krsna was not just the result of hearing about Him. She was His eternal consort. Her spontaneous inclination to serve and worship Him increased with every day.

Just as young girls play with dolls, Radharani and Her friends played with a doll of Krsna. Seeing this, Durvasa raised his thick eyebrows in wonder and asked the tiny girl, “Are You an attentive house wife?”

“I am not married,” little Radha replied. “But because Krsna is well known to be very demanding and capricious, My friends and I try to serve this doll of Him in a way that He will be satisfied with us.”

Durvasa Muni was taken aback by Radharani’s reply. No ordinary girl her age could think such thoughts, let alone find words for them. Desiring to test Radha further, the sage said, “Little Radha!

“Yesterday was Ekadasi and today I must break my fast. Won’t You cook sweet rice for Your Krsna and feed me the remnants? In this way, I will complete my vow and also test Your skill as a cook.”

Though She appeared to be a tiny child, Sri Radha at once accepted the sage’s request. She offered him a seat on a bench beneath a tree and ran into the palace to tell Mother Kirtida of Her new service.

Just to hear the news that Durvasa Muni had arrived was enough to strike fear in the hearts of the palace residents, who knew Durvasa was easily angered, thus they warily offered their respects from afar.

But when the *gopas* and *gopis* saw how fatherly the sage was behaving towards little Radha, they felt somewhat reassured and at once sprang into action to fulfil his request, making preparations for sweet rice.

Mother Kirtida personally collected the ingredients. As she began to stoke the fire, Sri Radha came into the kitchen and announced, “I must cook! The great yogi has asked Me to make sweet rice for him.”

But the queen was not willing to make child’s play out of Durvasa’s meal at the risk of provoking him in a way that could bring a curse upon their household. Sweetly stroking her daughter’s face, she said:

“Darling! I will cook, and You watch.” But Radha would not have it. “Mother! You don’t understand. The saint wants to test My cooking.” Kirtida poured milk in a pot and then turned to face her daughter.

The queen could see the determined look on little Radharani’s face, and she knew that when her daughter wanted something, She would persist until She finally got Her way. It was Her contrary nature.

Durvasa would have to break his fast soon, so they had no time to waste arguing. The queen nodded her head and said, “All right. Let me bring the ingredients. Then You can mix them and stir the pot.”

A servant set up a bench for Radha to stand on, and Kirtida, after bringing the rice, sugar, camphor, and bay leaves, measured out the proportions. Then she and Radha together placed them in the milk.

Radha took the large wooden spoon from Her mother’s hand and insisted that She be the one to stir the mixture until the rice had cooked. She also helped pour the sweet rice into clay pots for cooling.

With plenty of time for Durvasa to break his fast, the clay pots were brought outside and placed before the image of Krsna. Little Radha made the offering in Her own way and with Her own words.

The offering complete, Radha helped Her mother seat the sage comfortably in the courtyard. When Kirtida brought a pot of sweet rice, Radha spooned its contents into a clay bowl before Durvasa.

Durvasa Muni took note of the little girl’s refined manners and listened to Her eloquent words. After he had intoned mantras over the food in front of him, he smiled at Radha and said softly:

“Now I will see how well You cook, and how much Your hero Krsna savours Your cooking.” But even before Durvasa put the sweet rice to his lips, its aroma had already captivated his mind. It was celestial.

As he ate the sweet rice, the sage could discern two things: materially, it was perfect in appearance, taste, and texture, and spiritually, it was mixed with *prema,* from both Radha the cook and Krsna the enjoyer.

Without looking up, the sage ate every last drop of sweet rice, his bliss increasing with each mouthful. There could be no doubt about it! A child with such sublime touch must be the Supreme Lord’s consort.

Under the influence of spiritual ecstasy, Durvasa Muni foresaw both how Radha’s and Krsna’s loving pastimes would unfold on the petals of the lotus of Vraja as well as his service to the divine couple.

Durvasa understood that he would come to be known throughout Vraja as the initiator of one of Krsna’s important daily pastimes, for Yasoda-devi would soon ask Radha to cook for Krsna every morning.

After washing his hands, feet, and mouth, the Muni scanned the courtyard, looking first at the Vraja-vasis who had crowded around and then at the little girl patiently standing there before him.

Trying to wrest control over his ecstasy, Durvasa spoke to little Radha, “O child! You have served me with devotion and given me a taste of Your unmatched culinary skill. I must reward You.

“In the form of the following blessing, I shall share with You half of what my austerities have brought to me.” Hearing this, the Vraja-vasis whispered to one another. Radha joined Her palms in respect.

The *muni's* eyes clouded with tears as he said, “I declare that whatever You cook will taste like nectar. In addition, whoever tastes it will never see disease, defeat from enemies, or bad fortune.

“O Radha! For as long as this world turns, You will be famous as the empress of cooks, and because everything You touch will turn to nectar, You will be known by names like Amrta-pani. *Om!* *Tat! Sat!”*

After hearing this wonderful blessing, Vrsabhanu, Kirtida, and little Radharani bowed down together to offer their respectful obeisances at the feet of the sage, and the villagers buzzed with excitement.

His mission complete, Durvasa Muni suddenly disappeared, leaving the assembly of *gopas* and *gopis* wondering how he had departed. Overjoyed for her daughter, Kirtida kissed and embraced Radharani.

As she tightly held her effulgent child in her arms, Kirtida exclaimed, “O Radha! How fortunate we are! By the sage’s blessing even the Supreme Lord will insist on eating from Your hands. Just imagine!”

Mother Kirtida was right. Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, was extremely eager to savour the tastes of amorous love with which Srimati Radharani would spice every dish She cooked.

And, as a result of Durvasa’s public blessing, all of Vrndavana soon resounded with the news that Radharani’s cooking surpassed that of Laksmi-devi and was the cause of all good fortune for whoever ate it.

When Mother Yasoda came to hear that whatever Radha cooked acted like the armour of Lord Narayana, she at once thought of her son, Krsna, who was a constant target for ferocious demons.

Yasoda and Kirtida were such close friends that Yasoda had no qualms about asking Radha to cook for Krsna every day, knowing that, through Radha’s hands, He would get Durvasa’s potent blessings.

It is doubtful that as a small child Radharani would have travelled to Gokula every day to cook for Krsna, but it is certain that She made daily trips to Nandagrama after Her family had moved to Varsana.

Our Vaisnava *acaryas,* however, mostly describe Her treks to Nandagrama from Yavata — not from Varsana — and Her preparing Krsna’s breakfast there after She had married the *gopa* Abhimanyu.

In addition to cooking Krsna’s breakfast daily, She also prepared sweets for Him every afternoon. Yasoda would feed Krsna the sweets at supper. Radha also helped to cook Krsna’s annual birthday feast.

The conservative culture of Vraja would hardly approve of a young girl cooking for a boy to whom She was not betrothed, not to mention a young bride cooking for an unmarried man known to be a libertine.

But Durvasa Muni’s blessings on Radharani justified such an exceptional situation, though the blessing did nothing to prevent rumour- mongers from asserting that the underlying cause was illicit.

Still, all of Vraja knew the benefits of Radha’s cooking. And since Krsna was the one protecting them from demons, the Vraja-vasis almost unanimously agreed that She be allowed to cook for Him.

**\* \* \* \***

Sitting in the meadow that marks the remote hamlet of Raval, I looked around New Vraja-dhama. My *parikrama,* like all *parikramas* of Vraja, had come to an end at the birthplace of Srimati Radharani.

In Bhauma Vrndavana, the *pandas* of Varsana are keen to point out that Radha was born there. They fail to point out, however, that She took birth in Varsana in a previous day of Brahma, not in this one.

Both Raval and Varsana are places of Sri Radha’s birth, hut in the present day of Brahma She appeared at Raval and manifested Her childhood pastimes for as long as Her family lived in Mahavana.

When Nanda Maharaja moved his subjects to Vrndavana forest, his good friend King Vrsabhanu decided to follow suit. In this way, Mahavana ceased to be the Vraja-vasis’ primary place of residence.

Seated on a tree stump, I listened to the sounds of New Vraja-dhama. Were these the sounds of Mahavana without the voices of Krsna and Balarama happily playing with Their friends by the Yamuna’s shore?

Or was it the epilogue of the many footsteps I had taken to walk around the *dhama* eagerly remembering Krsna’s pastimes with His associates, wondering to myself when I too would see those pastimes?

From Raval I would make my way to Visrama-ghata, offer my obeisances to the *dhama* and its residents, return to Radha and Syamasundara, and reveal the contents of my heart to Them.

That would complete my circumambulation of New Vraja-dhama. The success of my *parikrama* would depend upon whether or not my efforts and my consciousness had been pleasing to the divine couple.

By Srila Prabhupada’s grace, Radha and Syamasundara have appeared in Hungary, and by Their grace, Vrndavana is manifesting itself in New Vraja-dhama— this peaceful valley has become a holy place.

By circumambulating the entire *dhama,* carefully chanting Krsna’s holy names, and remembering His pastimes, we serve both the divine couple and New Vraja-dhama, purifying our hearts with every step.

Bowing down in the dust of the *dhama* and offering a humble prayer at even one of Krsna’s pastime places qualifies us for the mercy of the Lord’s abode, by which we may eventually become Vraja-vasis.

Like the waters of the Yamuna flowing near my feet, thoughts of the *dhama* flowed through my mind. I absorbed myself in the serenity of the woods and pastures all around me and then knelt to offer prayers.

Although a full *parikrama* of the *dhama* begins and ends with a bath and prayers at Visrama-ghata, I made my prayers here in secluded Raval instead, lest my paltry devotion be overestimated.

Visrama-ghata is beside New Vraja-dhama’s main road, frequented by cars and pedestrians. Rather than make a show of my devotion, I chose to pray in private instead of in public by the roadside.

There in the tall grass I prayed, “O Srila Prabhupada! New Vraja-dhama is our attempt to fulfil your desire that ISKCONestablish places of pilgrimage to glorify Krsna’s pastimes. May you be pleased!

“O Radha and Syama! Carrying the burdens of an impure heart and impending old age, I beg for the blessing of love for You so that I may stay free of temptation and absorbed in Your service till the end.

“By remembering Your transcendental forms, names, and pastimes, even one as stone-hearted as I cannot fail to be moved, thus I bow down before Your abode and the souls who reside there. Hare Krsna!

“O Syama! In the hearts of those who visit Your land with the faith that You eternally engage in blissful pastimes there with Your companions, a special sweetness awakens. May that taste he mine!

“In the eternal city of Mathura, You brought Kamsa’s reign to an end by killing him. You freed Your parents from the shackles of separation by wiping away their happy tears with Your own hands.

“Although the forest of Madhuvana is known for the honey dripping from its abundant beehives, Your radiant smile surpasses that honey in sweetness and with its taste intoxicates the bee-like *gopis.*

“O You who killed Dhenuka’s cohorts in order to give the *gopas* access to the fruits of Talavana, will You also remove my stubborn ass-like attachments and let me taste the juicy fruit of serving You?

“Because Kumudavana is full of blossoming lotuses, the *gopis* go there to collect flowers for worshipping the sun god, but they themselves end up being offered to that youth of countless lotus like qualities.

“In Khadiravana, in a grove of *campaka* trees, Campakalata collects flowers with which to string garlands for You and Radha. I pray that in some distant future I may assist in that sort of service.

“The transcendental forest of Kamyavana fulfils Your every desire for enjoyment. Since that all-cognisant forest knows the innermost aspirations of my heart, will it kindly bestow its mercy upon me?

“O supremely merciful Lord who gives full protection to those who faithfully serve the supreme *dharma,* in the way the cow Bahula was true to her word in Bahulavana, I offer You my respectful obeisances.

“Had I a hundred mouths I would be unable to properly glorify the forest where *tulasi* plants grow in abundance, Vrndavana, the best of all twelve forests of Vraja and the place of Your eternal *rasa-lila.*
