**Festivals for New Vraja-dhama**

ISCKON already has a schedule of festivals and observances based on the Gaudiya Vaisnava calendar *(panjika).* It includes Ekadasis, Krsna’s major pastimes, the appearance days of His incarnations and eternal associates, and the appearance and disappearance days of great devotees. To these I have added select festivals celebrated in Bhauma Vrndavana. My intention is to increase our opportunities to be absorbed in Krsna consciousness. Vaisnava culture should be so fully absorbing to devotees— especially to children — that they will shun those cultural norms and practices of the host society that are destructive to the development of Krsna consciousness.

Some devotees may question why I am adding festivals that Srila Prabhupada did not have us observe during his manifest presence. His Divine Grace personally replies, “Best way to maintain enthusiasm is by regular chanting with the devotees together in the temple and by having festivals. So you should immediately have one festival then everyone will be busily engaged. There are so many festivals that I can give you, one for every day.”

I cannot overstate the importance that such festivals hold for children, as such festival days form a foundation that makes the children’s participation in Krsna consciousness fun, exciting, and memorable. New Vraja-dhama’s and the Hungarian *yatra’s* challenge is to present Krsna consciousness in a way that will satisfy the younger generation and inspire them to make Krsna consciousness not just their religion but also their way of life, their own culture. By expanding our present list of festivals I hope to help meet that challenge. To that end, the children should not only be observers but also participants. They can even help to organise some festivals. In this way they will develop a sense of ownership in their spiritual culture.

Of course, listing the festival days on the calendar and actually observing them are two different things. With the exception of major festivals like Janmastami or Ratha-yatra, ISKCON is currently quite lax in observing all the holy days on its calendar. This neglect is especially evident in respecting our previous a*caryas’* appearance and disappearance days, which seldom get much more than a mention in the announcements following *mangala-arati.* As a result, we not only disrespect our worshipable superiors but also lose the opportunity to remember them and accrue the blessings that accompany such remembrance. Leaders must therefore dedicate themselves to helping devotees properly celebrate these festivals without disturbing their other services. It is my humble suggestion that this may be achieved by incorporating the festivals into morning and evening programs, entrusting their organisation to counselling groups or *gurukula* classes, and seeing that their expenses are sponsored by individual families or other small groups of devotees.

In the calendar on page 832 of this volume, I have marked each festival with an asterisk or asterisks to indicate relative importance. A single asterisk (\*) means that the festival is compulsory, two asterisks (\*\*) means that it is important, and three asterisks (\*\*\*) means that it is optional. I have kept the descriptions of the festivals short, as time and space do not permit me to do otherwise. I therefore request that the managers of New Vraja-dhama use this appendix as the basis for a lengthier manual that some qualified devotee may compile in the future.

An integral purpose in establishing these festivals is to encourage devotees to perform them at those places in New Vraja-dhama that are most directly related to the pastimes that the festivals are meant to commemorate. That will highlight the importance of both the festivals and the holy places, and it will give devotees the opportunity to visit parts of the *dhama* that they do not regularly see.

I have tried to be as faithful as possible to the actual dates of Vrndavana’s many festivals when inserting them into our existing calendar. In some cases, however, I have rescheduled festivals that either coincide with major festivals we already observe or take place during times of the year when it would be too austere to observe them outside.

It is my firm hope that by observing these festivals the residents of New Vraja-dhama and the surrounding community of Krsna Valley will bond together as a family and better serve Radha-Syamasundara and Their abode.

**\* \* \* \***

There are many aspects common to all Vaisnava festivals, while other aspects arc unique to only certain festivals and serve to distinguish them from others. These unique aspects include who is being honoured, the place where the festival is observed, the relevant pastime, and other unique details. Both common and unique aspects will now be described.

**Aspects Common to All Festivals**

The following aspects should be common to all festivals: Accompanied by *kirtana,* take the festival Deities — little Radha-Syama, and Govardhana Lala when appropriate — to the festival site. At the site, offer them *bhoga* and a*rati,* glorify the pastime or persons the festival is meant to commemorate, perform *nama-sankirtana,* and distribute *prasada* to the devotees.

Pictures of the pastime or of the person or persons being honoured can also be included in the procession and may also receive worship similar to what the Deities receive. At the conclusion of such worship, these pictures may be circumambulated three times.

The pastimes honoured by these festivals should be represented by a diorama or a picture, either of which can be placed before the altar in the temple room. This will provide everyone — devotees and visitors alike — with the opportunity to remember the pastime throughout the day. A brief written explanation can also be placed before the picture or diorama. Whenever possible, devotees can also perform dramas to re-enact or commemorate the pastimes.

The main emphasis of any festival should always be *sankirtana.* This will compensate for any shortcomings in the festival’s observance. The mood involved in observing a festival is also important. We must bear in mind that these are religious festivals; appropriate respect should be shown in the devotees’ speech, conduct, and consciousness. While these festivals are meant in part to serve the societal needs of the devotee community, they should never be seen, nor treated, as mere social functions.

**Aspects Unique to Individual Festivals**

The remainder of this appendix is dedicated to brief descriptions of New Vraja-dhama’s yearly festivals, giving details unique to each. The leaders of New Vraja-dhama may note that — aside from those Gaudiya Vaisnava festivals traditionally observed within ISKCON — the timing of these festivals can be changed if the time for their observance is inconvenient due to the cold climate of Hungary.

**Appearance and Disappearance Days of Acaryas:** The proper observance of these festivals is described in the appendix entitled “The Worship of Vaisnava Samadhis,” found in volume five. In addition, a short description of these saints’ lives and holy activities should be included at the beginning of *Srimad-Bhagavatam* class.

**Appearance of the Lord and His Expansions:** As these festivals already have their own well-established traditions, I have not described them here. Specific details related to the celebration of Janmastami are described in the appendix entitled “How to Observe the Janmastami Festival” on page 873 in this volume. Details related to other such festivals should be outlined by those in charge of Deity worship.

**Ekadasi:** Each Ekadasi has a corresponding pastime that may be briefly described at the beginning of *Srimad-Bhagavatam* class. It is obligatory that devotees fast from beans and grains on every Ekadasi. Other forms of observance are optional.

**Holi and Holika-dahan:** Although generally a game for children, adults may also play Holi amongst themselves. The game is played at various locations in Vraja on different days. Coloured powder or coloured water—either sprayed with syringes (*pickari*) or thrown in balloons— may both be used. Players are allowed to team up in a number of ways, including boys against girls — as the young *gopas a*nd *gopis* of Vraja sometimes play — or in various small groups of girls against girls or boys against boys. The boys may identify themselves with Krsna’s cowherd boyfriends and dress accordingly, and the girls may similarly identify with Radha’s *gopi* companions. Players may even organise the Holi festival so that it commemorates the specific Holi pastimes of the Lord and His associates and in so doing enhance the fun with dialogue between the players. In any case, *kirtana* must always accompany the game. The duration for games of Holi may vary, but thirty minutes is certainly sufficient, especially if the game is played multiple times on several consecutive days. At the end of playing Holi, participants and observers should receive light *prasada,* including sweets at the very least.

In the morning on the days that Holi is played, all the necessary supplies should be offered to Radha-Syamasundara, and then later removed from the altar when it is time to play. Devotees may also play Holi with the Deities by taking a small portion of coloured power in their hands, offering it to the Deities like they would a flower, and then placing that *prasada* on another plate. The *prasada* can then he used for smearing on the faces of the devotees. If not enjoyed as a friendly battle between rival groups, Holi can very nicely be enjoyed with the participants smearing a little coloured power on one another’s cheeks or forehead while saying, *“Holi he."*

Holika-dahan, the burning of Holika, traditionally falls on Gaura-purnima, but it should not be celebrated on that day as it detracts from the worship of Lord Caitanya. Devotees may therefore choose another date either before or after Gaura-purnima that will be more suitable for enacting the burning of Holika. Alternately, it can be included as part of the Nrsimha-caturdasi celebrations.

**Carkula:** This game is for females, both young and old, and is meant to display the participants’ skill in carrying pots of water on their heads. Each woman balances a pot of water on her head. A lit ghee lamp floats on the water. Without touching or holding the pots with their hands, they try to sing and dance in a circle along with the sound of a *kirtana.* Those who spill water or drop the pots must leave the circle of dancers. After the circle makes three complete revolutions, the remaining contestants place a second pot on top of the first, and then a third pot is added after another three rounds. Anyone who is able to dance with three pots on her head is a winner and will receive Radha-Syamasundara’s *maha-prasada.* This festival is performed at Mukharai, and the participants are encouraged to dress colourfully in the manner of the *gopis.* The festival need not last longer than twenty or thirty minutes.

**Baladeva-darsana:** Devotees carry the festival Deity of Lord Balarama to Baladeva, where they describe the pastimes of the Lord. This festival may be accompanied by offering *arati* and *bhoga* to the Lord.

**Yamuna-chath:** This festival celebrates Yamuna-devi’s appearance in this world. It is observed by carrying a picture of goddess Yamuna in a procession to Visranti accompanied by *kirtana. Arati* is offered to the river with a fifty-four-wick ghee lamp, followed by an offering of food, and concluding with narrations of her appearance and the pastimes that take place on her shores.

**Gvala-mandali:** After taking a picture of Sridama in *kirtana* procession to Bhandiravana, devotees worship both the picture they have brought and the Mukuta-sila found there by offering them *arati* and *bhoga* and narrating pastimes that involve Sridama. Since the pastime of the Mukuta-sila takes place on Rama-navami, this celebration can he completed in one hour, preceding the evening program in the temple.

**Hanuman-jayanti:** The deity of Siddha-Hanuman may be taken in procession from Naimisaranya in Khonha to Chata (Chatravana), where *arati* and *bhoga* may be offered to Lord Rama’s foremost devotee, and narrations or dramatisations of his pastimes can take place. He should then be taken back to Khonha.

**Ganga-saptami:** On this day, Ganga-devi descended to earth, landing first in the matted locks of Lord Siva. The festival is observed at Manasa-ganga on Govardhana Hill with offerings of *bhoga* and *arati,* accompanied by *kirtana,* and enriched by descriptions of the glories of Ganga-devi.

**Circumambulation:** On various days of the year, devotees circumambulate Vrndavana town or Vrndavana and Mathura to show respect to the holy *dhamas.* That circumambulation can be accompanied by *kirtana,* or devotees may chant *japa,* walking alone or in groups. As an act of worship and a sign of respect, devotees may carry incense with them. Sometimes it is recommended that circumambulation be performed in the evening, at which time devotees may carry torches.

**Jala-yatra:** As this is the beginning of monsoon season, the temple can he decorated accordingly, with an emphasis on fountains.

Children may enjoy playing with water pistols or Holi syringes filled with water at Aghavana and Parasauli. Before the fun, Sukadeva Gosvami’s description of the rainy season may be read from *Srimad*-*Bhagavatam* (Canto 10, chapter 20). The play should be accompanied by *kirtana,* and refreshments should be served at the end.

**Ganga-dasahara:** On this day Maharaja Bhagiratha induced the Ganges to flow. This pastime may be told at Ramana-reti, and then children may fly kites while *kirtana* is taking place. Devotees should sprinkle themselves with Ganges water and offer prayers to Ganga-devi. A picture of Mother Ganga may be worshipped with *kirtana* and offerings of *bhoga* and *arati.*

**Ratha-yatra:** The children of New Vraja-dhama already observe the Ratha-yatra festival by pulling their cart from the *gosala* to the temple, but the extra distance to Jnana-gudari may be included in their route and the procession can stop there. Before or after the procession, it is recommended that someone narrate the conversation between Uddhava and Vidura *(Srimad-Bhagavatam,* Canto 3, chapter 2) and explain its relevance to Ratha-yatra.

**Guru-purnima:** On this day it is suitable for men to shave their heads. The festival may start with the devotees carrying a picture of Sanatana Gosvami in procession to Manasa-ganga, where the Gosvamis passing should be described. From there, the procession may continue to Madana-mohana temple, where offerings of *bhoga* and *arati* should be made to the picture of Sanatana Gosvami and further pastimes of the Gosvami may be narrated. Similar worship may also he offered to a picture of Vyasadeva. All of this should be accompanied by *kirtana.* Following these observances, devotees should circumambulate Vrndavana and Mathura while performing *kirtana* and then respect *prasada* to conclude the ceremony.

**Birthday of Garuda:** This festival may be observed at Garuda- Govinda with offerings of *bhoga* and *arati,* performance of *kirtana,* and discussion of the appearance of the deity in Bhauma Vrndavana and the pastime related to this place. Any other pastimes related to Garuda may he described or enacted, and all devotees may offer ghee lamps to Garuda-Govinda.

**Gajendra-moksana:** On this day, the elephant Gajendra’s liberation may be described and the Raksa-bandhana festival may be celebrated. To celebrate Raksa-bandhana, sisters tie sacred threads around their brothers’ wrists. Traditionally, it is on this day each year that wives who have been visiting their parents return to their husbands’ homes.

**Lattha-mela:** Although this festival has little spiritual significance, it is nonetheless entertaining. Comprised essentially of a feat of skill, it is enjoyed in various forms, either by individual participants or teams. The objective is to climb up a slippery pole, ten metres tall, in order to knock a pot from the top of the pole and win a plate of *maha-prasada.* Beside the pole, participants may also erect a scaffold from which to pour water onto the contestants to make the climb more difficult.

**Rasa-lila Observances:** There are many times and places at which the *rasa-lila* occurs throughout the year, such as Karhela, where that sublime dance festival takes place on the seventh day of the waning moon of Hrsikesa. Given a particular place and time, devotees may go to hear a narration of the pastime. If a particular place is not given, the festival can be observed before the Deities or at any one of the *dhama’s* many *rasa-mandalas.*

**Varsana and** Raval **Procession:** On Radhastami, devotees may have a *kirtana* procession to these two places, stopping for some time at each place to hear narrations of Srimati Radharani’s pastimes. Offerings of *bhoga* and *arati* may be made to the festival Deities, and the festival should conclude with *carana-darsana* in the afternoon.

**Mora-kutira:** For this celebration two devotees may dress as Radha and Krsna and enact the divine couple’s pastime at Mora-kutira. When the drama is finished, the ladies may reward “peacock Krsna” with sweets that he should then distribute to the rest of the devotees. Once again, the festival Deities should preside over this event, wearing peacock feathers and one of Their peacock outfits.

**Vilasa-garh:** On this day the festival Deities enjoy being swung by Their devotees. They also accept offerings of *bhoga* and *arati.* The devotees should perform *kirtana* and discuss appropriate pastimes of the divine couple.

**Sankari-khor:** This festival includes a retelling and a re-enactment of the pastimes at Sarikari-khor. Devotees are encouraged to assume appropriate roles and perform the drama in the presence of the festival Deities, after which Their Lordships should be taken to Prema-sarovara for boating pastimes and a discourse on the divine couple’s activities related to that place.

**Bathing at Specified Ghatas:** Although devotees may bathe in the sacred waters of New Vraja-dhama at any time, to bathe on specified days is particularly auspicious. For example, one such occasion is Parsva-ekadasi, on which it is recommended to bathe at Visrama'ghata. Before bathing, devotees should at least offer *arati* to the sacred *tirtha,* but it is better to make an offering of sweets as well. Needless to say, relevant pastimes can be retold.

**Brahma-vimohana-lila at Caumuha:** Accompanied by *sankirtana,* devotees may process to Caumuha, where the entire pastime of Brahma’s bewilderment may he narrated or enacted along with offerings of *bhoga* and *arati.* At this time some calves may also be brought to Caumuha for the devotees to feed.

**Sanjhi:** The tradition of Sanjhi is one that the senior members of New Vraja-dhama may learn and then teach to the community’s children. It includes decorations inside and outside of the temple. Those outside of the temple may be done on the ground or on the exterior walls of buildings. Because Sanjhi is a Vrndavana tradition worthy of devotees’ time and attention, I recommend that they study the art sufficiently before inaugurating its public display in the two weeks of the year during which it is actively observed. The book “Evening Blossoms” by Asimakrishna Dasa may be used as reference.

**Celebration of Bahula and Bati at Bahulavana:** As with other festivals, a *kirtana* party may process to Bahulavana, where offerings of *bhoga* and *arati* and continued *kirtana* should accompany a narration of Bahula’s deliverance. Devotees, either adults or children, may also enact this pastime, and a cow and a calf from the *gosala* may stand in as representatives for Bahula and her calf.

**Reunion of Rama and Bharata:** After circumambulating Vrndavana, devotees should gather in the temple to hear about the relationship between Rama and Bharata and how the divine brothers were reunited following Ramacandra’s successful conquest of Lanka. Other pastimes from the Ramayana may also be retold or reenacted.

**Kamai Rasa-lila:** Because this nocturnal *rasa* dance occurs on the *purnima,* when Radha and Krsna meet They are dressed in white in order to remain hidden from view. To celebrate this special occasion, the temple, the curtains on the altar, and the Deities should all be decorated in white. In the evening, a procession may go to Kamai, where devotees may offer *bhoga* and *arati* to the festival Deities and discuss *rasa-lila* pastimes before a small bonfire.

**Killing** **of Trnavarta in Gokula:** Devotees process with the festival Deities to Gokula, where they narrate and re-enact the death of Trnavarta at Nanda-bhavana, accompanied by *sankirtana* and offerings of *bhoga* and *arati.*

**Dipavali:** At present, the festival deities of Sita-Rama, Laksmana, and Hanuman are accompanied by *kirtana* on procession through Vrndavana village to the temple. Since the procession begins at the temple, before joining the deities in Vrndavana village, it can go first to Manasa-ganga. At that place, lamps should be put all around and devotees should narrate the pastime of Krsna’s invoking Ganga-devi in Bhauma Vrndavana and the other pastimes that took place there. Then *parikrarna* of Govardhana should continue to Vrndavana village and back to the temple.

**Govardhana-pula:** In addition to the presently established arrangements for observing Govardhana-puja, a separate Annakuta food offering may be performed at Aniyora as weather permits, accompanied by offerings of *arati* and/or *abhiseka* to Govardhana Hill. Devotees may also re-enact selected portions of the pastime at Aniyora. In any case, devotees must circumambulate Govardhana Hill. This aspect of the festival is essential, not optional.

**Yama-dvitiya:** Procession accompanies the festival Deities to the Yamuna, where everyone bathes. On this occasion, sisters offer sweets to their brothers, and brothers give gifts to their sisters. In so doing, brothers vow to protect their sisters. Devotees should describe how Radha and Krsna follow this same tradition with Their respective siblings. The Yama-dvitiya exchange that took place between Yama and Yami should also be described. Those places on the Yamuna that are appropriate for observing this festival are varied, including Visrama-ghata, Kaliya-gbata, and other *tirthas.*

**Putana’s Death in Gokula:** This celebration commemorates the death of Putana with a procession to Gokula, where the festival Deities are offered *bhoga* and *arati*, and the pastime is retold or reenacted at Nanda-bhavana. Thereafter devotees may continue on to Putana-khadda, where they may burn an effigy of the demoness and perform *kirtana.*

**Dhobi-marana at Mathura:** This festival commemorates Krsna’s killing the washerman in Mathura. If weather permits, the morning program may be held at the appropriate place in Mathura, where this pastime should be retold and regular service should be offered to the festival Deities.

**Gopastami:** In addition to dressing Srimati Radharani as a *gopa,* the morning program may be held in the *gosala,* where Krsna’s first outing with the calves may be commemorated. Krsna’s other pastimes with the cows may also be retold, and devotees dressed as *gopas* and *gopis* may feed the cows and herd them in the area surrounding the *gosala.*

**Circumambulation of Mathura:** A procession may accompany the festival Deities to Mathura, where the devotees should visit all of the main pastime places in the area until reaching Janmasthana. Once there, *bhoga* and *arati* should be offered to the Deities, and Krsna’s adventures in Mathura — not including His birth — should be narrated.

**Kamsa’s Death:** On the day following the circumambulation of Mathura, Krsna’s killing of Kamsa can be retold or re-enacted at Ranga-ksetra. From there, an effigy of Kamsa should be dragged all the way to Visrama-ghata while the devotees mock and verbally deride the demon. Once at Visrama-ghata, devotees may bathe and perform *kirtana.* The effigy of Karhsa may be burned, though a little further upstream.

**Davanala-kunda:** On this day the festival Deities may be taken in procession to Davanala-kunda, where they should be offered *bhoga* and *arati* followed by a narration of Krsna’s swallowing the forest fire. Devotees may also wish to commemorate the pastime with a bonfire and a re-enactment. This festival is best observed in the evening.

**Kesi-ghata:** A *kirtana* procession may accompany the festival Deities to the Yamuna at Kesi-ghata, where the devotees should offer *bhoga* and *arati* to the Deities. *Arati* should also be offered to the Yamuna, followed by a narration and re-enactment of Krsna’s slaying Kesi. It is suggested that — at this and all of the festivals commemorating Krsna’s killing demons — one devotee describe the particular obstacle on the path of devotional service that the demon represents.

**Kaliya-daha:** Observance of the chastisement of Kaliya may be performed in a way similar to the festival commemorating the killing of Kesi. It may also be observed during the evening. A small diorama or at least a picture and a short written description depicting this pastime may also be placed near the altar. If the weather at this time of year is too cold, it may be necessary to celebrate in the temple room.

**Imli-tala** **and Bhatrola:** On this day Caitanya Mahaprabhu arrived in Vrndavana. Devotees may take the festival Deities on procession to Imli-tala, where a picture of Lord Caitanya may be worshipped alongside the Deities, followed by a narration of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s pastimes in Vrndavana. From there devotees may continue to Bhatrola. After worshipping Their Lordships again, devotees should narrate or re-enact Krsna’s pastime with the wives of the *brahmanas.*

**Gopi-ghata:** To commemorate the first day that the young *gopis* worshipped Katyayani, devotees may lead a procession to Gopi-ghata and, after worshipping the festival Deities, narrate the pastime of Krsna’s stealing the *gopis’* clothes. The Katyayani-vrata can alternately be commemorated at the end of the month, but it will likely be very cold at that time.

## Appendix 33

***The Svakiya-Parakiya Controversy***

*(This appendix follows from Jiva Gosvami’s description of Krsna’s marriage to the gopis following His return to Vrndavana from Kuruksetra as described in chapter twenty nine.)*

In the detailed study of any subject, controversies arise by necessity. Differences in human nature give rise to different perceptions of the varieties inherent within Krsna’s creation. This variety allows even liberated souls to describe aspects of the Absolute Truth in different ways. And yet, because Krsna is the all-pervading cause of all causes, seers of the truth resolve those differences and synthesise them into one unified *siddhanta.* Srila Prabhupada called this concept “unity in diversity.”

At the time of its composition, Srila Jiva Gosvami’s *Gopala-campu* was at the heart of one such controversy within the Vaisnava community. In that hook, Jiva Gosvami describes how Krsna’s paramour relationship with the *gopis* concludes in marriage, and how that married state is the eternal status of the *gopis* in Goloka. This thesis implies that *parakiya-bhava* is but a means to a greater end, *svakiya- bhava.* Some learned Vaisnavas in Sri Jiva’s time argued that, in light of the Gosvami’s thesis, Vaisnava *siddhanta* on *sadhana* (“spiritual practice”) and *sadhya* (“spiritual perfection”) would apparently have to be redefined.

Up to the time of this controversy, the common understanding of the followers of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu had been that *parakiya-bhava* was the most complete expression of amorous love, hut that both *svakiya-bhava* and *parakiya-bhava* were eternally manifest in Goloka. It was further understood that either eternal relationship with the Lord could be attained by practising devotional service in its respective mood.

Narottama Dasa Thakura, one of the foremost students of Jiva Gosvami, expresses this understanding in his *Prema-bhakti-candrika, sadhane bhabiba jaha siddha-dehe paba taha raga pathera ei sei upaya:* “Whatever I contemplate during the practice of devotional service, I will certainly achieve upon perfection in a spiritual body.”

Why, then, did Sri Jiva write that only *svakiya-bhava* was to be had at the stage of perfection in *madhurya-rasa?*

The correct answer to this question is of great importance to Gaudiya Vaisnavas for two reasons. First, it clarifies the proper *siddhanta* of the *sampradaya* on the practice and perfection of *madhurya-rasa,* and second, it removes any doubt about Jiva Gosvami’s fidelity to the teachings of his guru, Srila Rupa Gosvami.

To this day, *rupanuga* Vaisnavas hold that the teachings of Caitanya Mahaprabhu exalt the *parakiya-bhava* of the damsels of Vraja as the highest expression of love for Krsna.

For example, Krsnadasa Kaviraja quotes Srila Rupa Gosvami as saying, “Increasing love is experienced in various tastes, one above another. But that love which has the highest taste in the gradual succession of desire manifests itself in the form of conjugal love.”To this, Kaviraja Gosvami adds, indicating the supremacy of loving exchange in unwedded love:

*ataeva madhura rasa kahi tara nama*  
*svakiy a-parakiya-bhave dvi-vidha samsthana*

**“Therefore, I call it** ***madhura-rasa.*** **It has two further divisions, namely wedded and unwedded love.”**

*parakiya-bhave ati rasera ullasa*  
*vraja vind ihara anyatra nahi vasa*

**“There is a great increase of mellow in the unwedded conjugal mood. Such love is found nowhere but in Vraja.”**

Srila Prabhupada elaborates on this conclusion, in light of Bhaktivinoda Thakura’s own commentary on these verses from the *Caitanya-caritamrta:*

**“Of the four kinds of reciprocation of loving service —** ***dasya, sakhya, vatsalya*****, and** ***madhurya*** **—** ***madhurya*** **is com sidered the fullest. But the conjugal relationship is further divided into two varieties, namely** ***svakiya*** **and** ***parakiya.*** **...Expert analysts have decided that the transcendental ecstasy of the** ***parakiya*** **mellow is better because it is more enthusiastic… The risks involved in such love of Godhead make this emotion superior to the relationship in which such risk is not involved. The validity of such risk, however, is possible only in the transcendental realm.** ***Svakiya*** **and** ***parakiya*** **conjugal love of Godhead have no existence in the material world, and** ***parakiya*** **is not exhibited anywhere in Vaikuntha, but only in the portion of Goloka Vrndavana known as Vraja.”**

The arguments of the *acaryas* confirming the superiority of the *parakiya-rasa* over the *svakiya-rasa* and the eternality of *parakiya-rasa* in *aprakata* Vrndavana are voluminous. Therefore, I shall not review those arguments in detail. I shall simply present their essence.

One can find that essence in the analysis of the difference in the moods of married and unmarried lovers.

The intense love a wife has for her husband, called *samanjasa* love, occasionally displays a desire for personal enjoyment. It is this desire that keeps the wife under the husband’s — in this case Krsna’s — domination. However, the love a girl has for her paramour, called *samartha* love, is more intense and it is completely free from the desire for personal enjoyment. *Samartha* love only desires the enjoyment of the beloved, Krsna. And this desire keeps Krsna under the control of such lovers, the *gopis* of Vraja.

The *svakrya-gopi’s* desire for personal enjoyment checks the development of her *prema* and limits it to the stage of *anuraga.* But the selfless love of the *parakiya-gopi,* free from limitation, reaches *prema’s* highest stage, *maha-bhava.*

In other words, because the *parakiya-gopi* can rise to the topmost stage of *maha-bhava* and the *svakiya-gopi* cannot, the conclusion reached by advanced transcendentalists is that *parakiya-bhava,* not *svakiya-bhava,* is the fullest and final expression of amorous love. And one can find that love in its full glory only in the Vraja portion of Goloka.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura presents a lengthy analysis of this topic, hut in essence his conclusion is that

**“The** ***rasa*** **of paramourship is certainly the extracted essence of all the** ***rasas.*** **If it he said that it does not exist in Goloka, it would be highly deprecatory to Goloka.”**

Having clarified the supremacy of *parakiya-bhava,* I return to the original question: Why did Srila Jiva Gosvami stress *svakiya-bhava* as supreme?

To this question, Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura gives a comprehensive answer, in which he explains that Srila Jlva Gosvami was convinced of the superiority of *parakiya-rasa*, and was himself a follower of that mood. But the Thakura also points out that because mundane moralists and some of Jiva Gosvami's followers could not comprehend the purity of *parakiya-bhava,* and because that ignorance was an obstacle to their spiritual development, Jiva emphasised *svakiya-bhava* over *parakiya-bhava.*

The exact words of Bhaktivinoda Thakura are as follows:

**“Not one of the true followers of Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu rejected the pure** ***parakiya-rasa.*** **Who can he a better teacher of this** ***rasa*** **than Srila Svarupa Damodara Gosvami? He taught the truth of the pure** ***parakiya-rasa*** **and Srila Jiva Gosvami, Srila Rupa Gosvami, and Srila Sanatana Gosvami all accepted his teachings in this matter.**

**“In his own personal devotional service, Srila Jiva Gosvami did not accept** ***svakiya-rasa.*** **However, he did explain that even in Vraja some devotees manifest a scent of** ***svakiya-rasa.*** **When** ***samartha-rati*** **carries a scent of** ***samanjasa-rati,*** **then** ***svakiya-rasa*** **is present in Vraja. Therefore when a slight sense of** ***svakiya-rasa*** **is present, the devotee may be called a worshipper in** ***svakiya-rasa.***

**“Srila Jiva Gosvami had two kinds of disciples. One was situated in pure** ***parakiya-rasa*** **and the other in** ***parakiya-rasa*** **mixed with** ***svakiya-rasa.*** **According to the different inclinations of his disciples, he gave different appropriate instructions. This he clearly explained in his** ***Locana-rocani tika*** **on** ***Ujjvala-nilamani, svecchaya likhitam kincit:*** **‘I have written what is suitable for devotees who are inclined in a certain way.”**

The followers of Thakura Bhaktivinoda should consider these words to be the ultimate conclusion regarding *svakiya-rasa.* I thus end further discussion on this subject and request the reader to bear these words in mind whenever Krsna’s marriage to the *gopis is* mentioned.

## Appendix 34

***How to Observe the Janmastami Festival***

*(This appendix follows from Nanda Maharaja's preparations for the first Janmastami festival as they are described in chapter thirty.)*

In his Hari-bhakti-vilasa, Srila Sanatana Gosvami says, “The vow of Janmastami is compulsory for everyone. It is a regular observance that frees one from all sin and grants all kinds of transcendental benefits.”

In 1966, just months after he had established ISKCON, Srila Prabhupada showed his followers how to observe Janmastami: he instructed them to alternate every half-hour — from morning until midnight — between chanting japa and speaking about Krsna. At midnight there was a special arati and then a feast was served to the devotees.In the years since that first Janmastami, both during Srila Prabhupada’s physical presence and now in his absence, Janmastami continues to be celebrated throughout ISKCON with increasing pageantry and solemnity.

Although the essence of Janmastami is to chant Krsna’s names and hear about His glories, there are detailed scriptural injunctions regarding the observance of Janmastami that, if known and followed, can help devotees to better please Krsna. Sanatana Gosvami, for example, spends more than three hundred verses detailing ways to praise the Lord through celebrating Janmastami, thus encouraging us to worship the Lord in the best possible way and, in doing so, derive the greatest possible benefit.

The acarya says that Vaisnavas should make a great celebration of Janmastami, during which they should fulfil their own vows and worship Krsna in opulence. Srila Prabhupada also writes, '‘This Janmastami day is the most opulent festival day for the devotees, and it is still observed with great pomp in every Hindu house in India.”

And of course Krsna Himself teaches us about the importance of knowing the truths of His birth — which must include the celebration of His birth — as the means for opening to us the gates to His own abode:

*janma karma ca me divyam evam yo vetti tattvatah*  
*tyaktva deham punar janma naiti mam eti so ’rjuna*

**“One who knows the transcendental nature of My appearance and activities does not, upon leaving the body, take his birth again in this material world, but attains My eternal abode, O Arjuna.”**

This appendix presents Sanatana Gosvami’s teachings in a summarised form, which the devotees of New Vraja-dhama may strive to perfect in observing the annual festival that commemorates Krsna’s appearance.

**The Origin of Janmastami**

In conversation with Krsna, Yudhisthira Maharaja once asked to describe the origin of the Janmastami vow, the details of its execution, and the benefits that one derives from it. As pure devotees, the Pandavas would observe Krsna s birthday every year, but Yudhisthira wanted to hear from Krsna Himself how this celebration came to be and whether or not they were observing it correctly.

Krsna happily replied, “O Emperor! After I had killed Kamsa, and the wrestlers lay dead in the sports arena, Devaki and Vasudeva stood up in the grandstand crying tears of bliss. Accompanied by their kinsmen, My parents ran to where I was. Devaki embraced Me and placed Me on her lap, crying uncontrollably. After embracing Balarama, Vasudeva also embraced Me, saying, ‘Today all my suffering has borne its auspicious fruit, for today I have found my sons.’”

Remembering that day with fondness, Krsna continued, “Seeing My parents’ happiness, some other family members said, Today rays of happiness, not the rays of the sun, are shining upon the people of Mathura.’

“After much embracing and conversing someone said, ‘O Lord! Your victory over the demon Kamsa is like a new birth for us and for You. We shall celebrate it in a grand way. However, we also desire to celebrate the actual day on which You took birth from Devaki and request that You personally reveal the appropriate time and describe the process to us.’

“When My father Vasudeva heard this request, the hairs of his body stood erect. Glancing at Balarama, he turned to Me and said, ‘Son! You must fulfil the desires of the people. Please disclose the truth of Your birth to them.’”

On His father’s order, Krsna revealed the vow of Janmastami to the people of Mathura along with this prophesy: “This festival will first be celebrated in Mathura, but later it will become famous throughout the world.”

There is no restriction as to who can observe the festival of Krsna’s appearance. Devoted men and women of every varna and asrama can follow the full vow of Janmastami from the age of eight. If one is younger, he or she may be excused from fasting or observe a modified fast as is appropriate to the circumstances.

Krsna appeared in this world during the monsoon season, at midnight on the eighth day (astami) of the dark fortnight (krsna- paksa) of the month of Bhadra (August-September), when the sun was in Leo and the moon and the star Rohini were both in Taurus. Because His sister, Durga, also appeared on that day, Janmastami is a celebration of her appearance as well.

Because it is the most praiseworthy (jaya) day of all and because it brings victory (jaya) in every sense of the word, Janmastami is also called Jayanti. Although the people of Mathura began to observe it after Krsna described it to them, great devotees like Prahlada Maharaja had followed it since antiquity. Indeed, people who desire health, happiness, and peace must observe Janmastami annually, for neglecting to do so will only bring ruin.

**The Vow of Janmastami**

In addition to the formal ceremonies that comprise Janmastami, scriptures prescribe that to follow the “vow of Janmastami” is to observe a dry fast, abstaining completely from food and water. When Srila Prabhupada first introduced Janmastami he encouraged his early disciples to follow such a vow, but when they could not, he gave them a concession to eat some rock candy, or a little fruit. However, he preferred that devotees fully embrace the vow of abstaining from all food and drink.

Brahma once told Narada that eating on Janmastami is a sin equivalent to eating from the hand of a corpse. Other scriptural statements equate eating on Janmastami with eating human flesh or with committing every sin in the world, including killing a brahmana or a cow.

Hearing such statements we may wonder, “Why then did Srila Prabhupada make concessions for his followers?” The answer is that the essence and purpose of Janmastami is service to Krsna and absorption in Krsna consciousness. If fasting seriously inhibits us from serving Krsna and instead makes us conscious of our hunger, then it is better that we eat a little food and use the energy it gives us to fully participate in the Janmastami festival.

If, however, we eat not out of devotional need but to gratify our senses, or because we are unwilling to undergo an austerity we are capable of performing, then we should consider ourselves culpable for that offence.

It is said that those who fill their bellies on Janmastami will be sent to a hell where the Yamadutas feed them only one sesame seed each. Such persons, even if they strictly follow other vows, like the Dvadasi vow, will also take a hundred and one generations of their families to a similar hellish destination.

After having been reprimanded by the representatives of Yamaraja, one can expect to be born as a ferocious jungle beast, or as a raksasa (man eater). Scripture warns that the reaction that comes from neglecting the vow of Janmastami cannot be counteracted by other vows, austerities, or spiritual practices.

Although scripture calls fasting and keeping an all-night vigil the “vow of Janmastami,” it is implicit that this is done to minimise our bodily needs, while other acts of worship, like nama-sankirtana and reading Bhagavad-Gita or Srimad-Bhagavatam, are the primary acts we should perform to celebrate Krsna’s appearance.

Moreover, scripture says, the acts of worship a Vaisnava grhastha performs to celebrate Janmastami must be proportionate to his means, otherwise he resides in hell for the duration of a day of Brahma. This is equally true of his ability to sponsor acts of worship.

**The Glories of Janmastami**

Although scriptures often describe the dire consequences of neglecting to follow dharma, they also list the benefits of doing so. This type of carrot-and-stick technique is intended for the many classes of followers who need to be motivated to serve Krsna either by threat of punishment, promise of reward, or both. Pure devotees extract the essence of these scriptural statements as being “follow dharma to please the Lord.” They therefore celebrate Janmastami for that reason — to please Krsna.

The following section describes some of the material and spiritual benefits of observing Janmastami and its celebrations. Pure devotees consider these benefits of secondary importance to the actual privilege of being able to serve the Lord.

Krsna Himself tells Yudhisthira Maharaja, “O delight of the Kurus! By once fasting during Janmastami a person becomes free from the sins of seven births. Of this there is no doubt.

“Such a person gives birth to righteous progeny, attains health and peerless good fortune, and having been purified at heart he is spontaneously drawn to truth and religion.

“If he so desires, the person who observes the day of My birth can travel on an airplane for a hundred thousand years to see and enjoy the many pleasures of the universe, and after that he can return to this earth to enjoy the remains of his pious credits.

“On this earth he becomes the ruler of a great kingdom, a kingdom filled with all desirable things, all pious deeds, and many cows, but free of any suffering, where he lives for a long time enjoying whatever his heart desires. Then, at the end of life he goes to the spiritual world, Vaikuntha, where there is no repetition of birth and death.”

After describing the benefit an individual enjoys for fasting on Janmastami, Krsna also describes the benefits that a home, and finally that a country receives by regularly observing Janmastami.

Krsna told King Yudhisthira, “All opulences comes to a home where the pastime of My birth from Devaki is worshipped. Fearful diseases and other calamities can never enter there, and that home need have no fear of snakes, tigers, disease, sins, thieves, or the king.

“In addition, a home that simply houses a book describing the vow of Janmastami will never see a miscarriage, a stillborn child, a resident becoming a widow, or—amongst family members — any misfortune, deception, or quarrel.

“In the country where pictures of My birthday are visible and worshipped with sandal paste, and where My birth is always written of in many books and studied with care, the citizens are beautified by all the ornaments of spiritual life. Moreover, such a country need have no fear of enemies, plagues, or other calamities, and will be blessed with as much rainfall as desired.”

Since Janmastami is the celebration of the appearance of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, it is no surprise that its observance gives liberation and that the benefits it offers surpass those of other religious activities. It is said that even accidental observance of the Janmastami vow leads to the spiritual world of Lord Visnu.

We all experience the spiritual joy that Janmastami affords the senses, and indeed the heart, of those who honour it. But those persons also unknowingly attain the result of performing many kinds of fire sacrifices, chanting mantras, and distribution of charity, all multiplied a hundredfold. Moreover, Krsna Himself—who forgives the sins of a child, youth, or adult who carefully worships Him on this day — also multiplies the benefit of any devotional or religious activity performed, like japa, sacrifice, bathing, and so on, a hundredfold.

The observance of Janmastami insulates one from the influence of Kali-yuga. It equals many millions of sacrifices, pilgrimages, gifts of cows, charitable acts, and pious deeds. It surpasses serving parents, ritualistic or family gurus, giving up one’s life for a religious cause, helping others, and never speaking a lie. It brings piety, wealth, sense gratification, and liberation. In short, it fulfils all desires. But best of all, devotees who observe Janmastami can expect to he favoured by the supreme goddess of fortune, Srimati Radharani. Brahma there' fore tells Narada, “O great sage! I have not seen anything in the Vedas or the Puranas equal to or better than the vow of Sri Krsna Janmastami.”

**The Method of Observing Janmastami**

Aside from performing a dry fast and keeping an all-night vigil, the aspects of observing Janmastami that the acarya places emphasis on are as follows:

(1) Rising early and bathing

(2) Physically announcing to the Lord one’s determination to follow the vow of fasting and keeping a vigil (sankalpa)

(3) Hearing, chanting, and remembering Krsna’s names and childhood pastimes (sankirtcma) throughout the entire day of Janmastami, continuing into the following day (Navami) until breaking one’s fast

(4) Bathing the Deities on the altar and offering Them a new dress (srngara)

(5) Bathing at midday in a holy river or other body of water (snana)

(6) Performing abhiseka of the Deities (along with a deity of Devaki)

(7) Constructing a maternity room (sutika-grha) including deities of Krsna and His parents as well as others

(8) Installing (prana-pratistha) and worshipping (puja) the maternity room

(9) Worshipping the moon with arghya at moonrise

(10) Describing the events of Krsna’s birth and childhood pastimes, performing dramas that depict the same, and reading Bhagavad-gita (lila-kirtana)

(11) Performing a birth ceremony prior to midnight, including bathing Krsna, cutting the umbilical cord, worshipping goddess Sasthi, and having a name-giving ceremony for Krsna in the maternity room (jata-karma)

(12) Decorating the Deity room before midnight

(13) At midnight, making offerings and performing arati

(14) Honouring a feast of ekadasi-prasada at midnight.

(15) Hearing narrations of Krsna’s pastimes as well as singing and dancing throughout the night

(16) At dawn, performing one’s morning duties and offering prayers to the Lord

(17) Performing worship of Durga-devi

(18) Distributing charity and feeding the brahmanas

(19) Completing the vow by breaking one’s fast

Let us now hear a brief description of the different aspects of the Janmastami observance as listed above, which in their entirety truly constitute a grand festival.

**(1) Rising early and bathing**

In the way that devotees are austere and self-controlled during Ekadasi and Dvadasi, they should he similarly controlled on Janmastami and the following Navami. After rising, a devotee should brush his teeth, bathe, decorate his body with tilaka, and dress in fine clothes for the pleasure of the Lord.

**(2) Pronouncing one’s determination (sankalpa)**

Srila Prabhupada says, “...even if one is hungry, if on a particular day he is determined to observe fasting, he can naturally conquer the disturbances of hunger and thirst.” Krsna suggests that on the morning of Janmastami we make a verbal commitment to our vow. If that solemn vow is accompanied by the sort of determination to which Srila Prabhupada refers, we will be helped in our commitment to fast and remain awake throughout the night.

The Lord gives us the following sankalpa-mantra:

*atha tatra mantrah*  
*adya sthitva nirdharah sarva-bhoga-vivarjitah*  
*bhoksye ‘ham pundarikaksa saranam me bhavacyuta*

**“The \[sankalpa\] mantra is, ‘Today I stand before You. I am fasting. I have not eaten anything. Only tomorrow will I eat. O infallible, lotus-eyed Lord, please become my shelter \[to observe the vow of Janmastami\].”’**

**(3) Hearing, chanting, and remembering Krsna’s names and pastimes (sankirtana)**

As already mentioned, the purpose of the Janmastami festival is to please Krsna, and the best way to please Krsna is to glorify Him (sankirtana) by singing His names and discussing His pastimes and instructions. Sanatana Gosvami makes specific reference to the Bhagavad-gita as being part of this Janmastami sankirtana. This sankirtana should begin with mangala-arati on the Astami day and can continue until the time of breaking fast on the Navami.

In ISKCON, Srila Prabhupada’s appearance day (Vyasa-puja) falls on the Navami day. By celebrating the appearance of His Divine Grace we are more than adequately fulfilling the sankirtana requirement just mentioned. In this case, the performance of sankirtana concludes with Srila Prabhupada’s Vyasa-puja feast, the time for breaking one’s fast.

But considering that Srila Prabhupada inaugurated the practice of honouring a Janmastami feast after the midnight arati — after which most devotees take rest for some time — it is recommended that a few devotees stay awake and continue performing sankirtana in the presence of the Deities until the Vyasa-puja celebrations resume. Thus the sankirtana observance for Janmastami will remain unbroken.

Singing the Lord’s names, with or without dancing and instrumental accompaniment, reciting prayers to the Lord, and reciting His childhood pastimes arc all recommended ways to please Him. These activities may be performed by all devotees together in one group, or by separate, smaller groups. For example, while some devotees chant the maha-mantra, others may discuss Krsna’s pastimes. Details of this sort are left up to the discretion of festival organisers.

**(4) Bathing and dressing the Deities (srngara)**

This practice is well known and well practised in New Vraja-dhama, as it is throughout ISKCON. Sanatana Gosvami reminds us that we should not fail to bathe the Deities with aromatic oils and dress them in new garments. Of all annual festivals, the festival of Janmastami is the most prominent, and thus the Deities as well as the altar should be very opulently decorated with festoons, flags, Power vases, garlands, and other items in order to beautify the Lord and His surroundings.

**(5) Bathing at midday**

At midday one should take a bath in sacred waters, such as the waters of the Yamuna, and thereafter recite the diksa-mantras. It possible, one may change into fresh clothes and then touch an amalaki fruit to his or her head. The amalaki fruit is dear to Krsna and its touch inspires devotion to the Lord.

**(6) Public bathing of the Deities (abhiseka)**

After the devotees have bathed, they may then participate in the bathing of the Lord, called abhiseka. The standard practice of Gaudiya Vaisnavas, including ISKCON devotees, is to perform an elaborate bathing of the temple Deities on Janmastami. Srila Prabhupada writes, “This bathing ceremony is technically called abhiseka, and even today this is observed in all the temples of Vmdavana on Janmastami Day, or the birthday anniversary of Lord Krsna.” This abhiseka ceremony is reminiscent of the first bath Krsna received to celebrate His appearance on this planet. It is accompanied by nama-sankirtana, the blowing of conch shells, and the recitation of auspicious mantras.

Sanatana Gosvami adds an additional feature to the abhiseka: bathing and worshipping small deities of Devaki and Krsna. He briefly describes a large pot filled with water, which serves as a stand, decorated with aguru- and camphor-scented leaves and flower garlands. On top of the pot are placed golden deities of Devaki as she breastfeeds Krsna.

These deities should be bathed in the standard way, with milk and other substances, and then anointed, dressed, and decorated just like the temple deities, and finally offered fresh fruits and foods cooked in ghee. Throughout the rest of the Janmastami festival the deities of Devaki-Krsna should he served in the same way as the deities on the altar. When the festival is over, Devaki-Krsna can be put to rest until next year. These deities are the Janmastami festival deities (utsava-murti).

The worship of Devaki-Krsna as just described may be taken in two ways: some devotees may wish to worship Devaki as the wife of Vasudeva, others as Yasoda-devi, the wife of Nanda Maharaja. After all, both women are Krsna’s mothers and both are known by the name Devaki:

*dve namni nanda-bharyaya yasoda devakiti ca*  
*atah sakhyam abhut tasya devakya sauri-jayaya*

**“The wife of Nanda had two names, Yasoda and also Devaki. Therefore it was natural that she \[the wife of Nanda\] develop friend' ship with Devaki, the wife of Sauri \[Vasudeva\]."**

**(7) Constructing the maternity room (sutika-grha)**

Sanatana Gosvami and various scriptures emphasise the importance of constructing an elaborate maternity room to serve as an object of meditation for devotees throughout the Janmastami festival. Preparation of the maternity room can certainly be done before the festival. However, if well organised, it can be assembled in the morning hours of the Astami and then placed in a prominent part of the temple after the abhiseka. In either case, devotees may consider it an important aspect of the Janmastami observance, providing a focus for their meditation throughout the day.

It is recommended that the maternity room be opulently decorated with jewels, silks, and garlands. Sanatana Gosvami’s descriptions of the room include aspects of both Kamsa’s jail and Gokula; logic dictates that these two portions of the maternity scene should appear side by side, not as one composite picture. The items that comprise the maternity room may be either three dimensional or painted, as is most practical. While size is not specified, it too may vary according to available space, up to life-size proportions.

Some of the items that may be included in the two parts of the maternity room are as follows:

In the prison are shackles, an iron sword, a lamp, water, and a fire. A club lies by the prison door, outside of which are guards and within which is the deity of Devaki, lying down on a bed. Beside her is sleeping baby Krsna, His chest marked with Srivatsa, His neck bedecked with garlands, and holding the symbols of Visnu in His four hands. Vasudeva should be seen armed with a sword and shield, Kamsa shown resting not far away, and demon guards like Arista, Dhenuka, and Kesi are also asleep nearby, weapons in hand.

In Gokula, Yasoda should he seen reclining with her newborn daughter, surrounded by a churning rod and other items characteristic of a cowherd’s home. Nanda Maharaja, many gopas and gopis, Balarama, and also Garga Muni should stand around Yasoda. At a distance, Kaliya can be seen swimming in the waters of the Yamuna.

Above the two adjacent scenes, demigods, Nagas, demons, and other celestials should be flying in the sky, offering respects and bearing gifts.

**(8) Installation (prana-pratistha) and worship (puja) of the maternity room**

Formal installation of the deities of Devaki and Krsna appears to he optional, as in one instance in Hari-bhakti-vilasa Sanatana Gosvami does not mention it, but in another he docs. Whether installed or uninstalled, what is really important is one’s meditation on the Lord and His mother while they are being worshipped.

That worship is focused on Devaki, who is offered incense, flowers, food, and prayers, such as the following:

“All glories to beautiful-faced Devaki, the mother of the demigods. You are the happy-faced mother of a newborn son served by many celestials with songs, instruments, and gifts.

“O girl with the beautiful face! You were pleased when the demigods worshipped you. Now as I worship you with devotion please he merciful to me. Having given birth to the Supreme Lord, you are the abode of spiritual bliss, please make me the object of a similar divine joy.”

Thereafter, devotees may worship Krsna with either five or sixteen ingredients, as appropriate, offering the Lord payers like the following: “O Lord Krsna, who descends to this world in many thousands of incarnations and has appeared today in His original form, inconceivable to even Brahma and Siva! O Lord who lays in His mother’s lap, I offer my respectful obeisances unto You.”

Throughout the day, Devaki and Krsna should be given offerings comparable to those given to the temple deities.

**(9) Worshipping the moon**

Because Krsna appeared in the dynasty of the moon, and because the moon — conjoint with the Rohini star in Taurus — is influential in defining Krsna’s astrological chart, Sanatana Gosvami offers brahmanas, and brahmanas only, the opportunity to offer arghya to the moon god at moonrise.

This offering should be accompanied by meditation on Lord Krsna and recitation of the following mantra:

*dadhi-puspaksatair misram tato ’rghyam sasme muda*  
*ksirodamava-sambhuta atri-netra-samudbhava*  
*arghyam indo grhana tvam rohinya sahito mama*

**“O moon god born from the milk-ocean and from Atri’s eye! O moon god now associating with Rohini, please accept this arghya mixed with yogurt, flowers, and unbroken rice.”**

Hari-bhakti-vilasa mentions a second bathing of the deities after moonrise. Considering that Srila Prabhupada did not insist on this second bathing, we can take it as optional, depending on our resources.

**(10) Describing Krsna’s birth and childhood pastimes, perform dramas depicting the same, and read Bhagavad-gita (lila-kirtana)**

This item re-emphasises the importance of sankirtana, in the sense that it reminds festival organisers and participants that sankirtana should he performed continually throughout the festival.

Because guests tend to congregate in the temple in the hours leading up to midnight, this time may be considered ideal for the presentation of dramas that depict Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes, starting with His birth and ending with the killing of Kamsa. Sanatana Gosvami specifically mentions dramas of this sort, and Srila Prabhupada also considered them an excellent way to absorb both actors and spectators in remembrance of the Lord.

According to Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu and His followers celebrated the Janmastami festival dressed as cowherd boys. Thus devotees are also encouraged to dress as Vraja-vasis to better enter the mood of the festival.

In addition to the recitation of scriptures like Srimad-Bhagavatam, Sanatana Gosvami specifically advises devotees to discuss Bhagavad-gita (gita-sastra-kathalapaih). This kind of continual sankirtana is certainly pleasing to the heart and inspires spiritual bliss. As already mentioned, dramas and scriptural recitation can be interspersed with nama-sankirtana and even japa in order to provide variety. This sort of variety makes it that much easier for everyone, even guests and new devotees, to concentrate on the central focus of the festival — the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna.

Another type of sankirtana Srila Prabhupada encouraged on Janmastami was asking individual devotees to share their own realisations, their experiences in Krsna consciousness, or their own narrations of Krsna’s pastimes. This certainly increases devotee participation and interest.

**(11) Birth ceremony (jata-karma)**

In the half-hour leading up to midnight, devotees can perform rituals at the maternity room that would have taken place for Krsna’s birth. These include the actual birth ceremony, cutting of the umbilical cord, bathing, worship of goddess Sasthii, and the name-giving ceremony.

These ceremonies may be enacted with brahmanas chanting traditional mantras while the other devotees perform nama-sankirtana. The devotees should be able to observe the proceedings. At the completion of each individual ritual, devotees may call out, “Jaya!” At the completion of the name-giving ceremony devotees may rise and observe the midnight arati.

**(12) (13) Decorating the Deity room and midnight arati**

Prior to arati the altar Deities are again freshly dressed and, if possible, the altar is decorated again, or some decorations are added to embellish Krsna’s new oufit. This evening dressing and the subsequent arati are both well-established iskcon traditions and require little in the way of further elaboration, other than to briefly discuss the ghee lamp being offered.

Special festivals are often marked by offering not the regular 5-wick lamp, but a 54- or 108-wick lamp, which certainly require more care, but are pleasing to the Lord and to the congregation of devotees.

**(14) Midnight feast**

The scriptural tradition is to break fast either at the end of the tithi at around midnight, or at the end of the time when the Rohi.nl star is conjoined with the moon, iskcon tradition, however, has been to break fast immediately after arati. Since that was Srila Prabhupada’s standard, it is followed to the present day. What has changed since that time is what we eat to break our fast.

In ISKCON’s formative years, devotees ate grains in Srila Prabhupada’s presence. But scriptural references and Srila Prabhupada’s own statements on breaking fast for Gaura-purnima make it clear that Vaisnava tradition is to serve an Ekadasi meal — not a feast, but something light.

The main feast comes later on the Navami day, after Srila Prabhupada’s Vyasa-puja, which coincides with Nanda Maharaja’s festival for the birth of his son. This feast is referred to as Nandotsava.

**(15) Continued sankirtana**

The period between midnight arati and mangala-arati of the Navami tends to be a quiet time in ISKCON’s temple rooms. However, because Krsna’s birth took place at midnight, this is the time that Nanda Maharaja and his family were most joyful. For that reason, some devotees should continue to dance, chant, and discuss Krsna’s pastimes until Srila Prabhupada’s Vyasa-puja celebration begins in earnest.

**(16) Morning duties and prayers (pratah-krtya)**

Devotees are meant to bathe at dawn on the Navami day, which obviously requires that they rise before dawn, perform their morning duties — including dressing in clean clothes — and participate in the Vyasa-puja celebrations to complete their Janmastami vow.

For 1SKCON devotees, the main festival on the Navami is Srila Prabhupada’s Vyasa-puja. Nonetheless, devotees may perform the following activities recommended by scriptures without disturbing the glorification of His Divine Grace.

Upon entering the temple room, devotees may offer prayers to Lord Krsna, both in the maternity room and on the altar. Sanatana Gosvami suggests the following prayer:

**“I offer my respectful obeisances to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who, in order to give protection to Brahma and all other living entities in this world, was born as the son of Vasudeva and Devaki. Obeisances to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is the son of Vasudeva and the auspiciousness of the cows and brahmanas. May there be peace. May there be auspiciousness.”**

**(17) Durga-puja**

Since Yogamaya also appeared at the same time as Krsna, Hari-bhakti-vilasa recommends that we offer a flower or incense to her representation in the maternity room. Alternately, devotees in New Vraja-dhama can also worship Yogamaya in her temple. Keeping in mind that Srila Prabhupada was wary of demigod worship, such veneration should be modest and should in no way detract from the worship of the Deities or Srila Prabhupada.

**(18) Distributing charity and feeding the brahmanas**

Following the example of Nanda Maharaja, devotees should distribute charity according to their means. The Deities and Vaisnava brahmanas are the first object of devotees’ charity. When distributing charity, a donor’s motivation is to please the Lord, and thus at the time of giving he says, krsno me priyatam iti: “May Lord Krsna be pleased with me.”

Their Lordships may he offered gold or currency, silk cloth, jewellery, and other items needed for Their decoration or maintenance. These items are best acquired according to the advice of the head pujari.

The most common, and most favoured, form of charity to Vaisnavas and to brahmanas is the distribution of krsna-prasada. Thus devotees may sponsor—in part or in full — the post-midnight Ekadasi meal or the feast on Srila Prabhupada’s Vyasa-puja day.

In this regard, all devotees should consider that as with EkadasI, breaking fast for Janmastami—-and all other festivals — is best done by respecting Lord Jagannatha’s maha-prasada. The Vayu Parana says, “If one desires to destroy all his sins, without a single sin remaining alive, one should, at the festival’s end, break his fast by eating the prasada remnants from Lord Jagannatha.”

**(19) Breaking fast**

The last item of the Janmastami vow, by which the vow is completed, is the feast. While respecting Krsna’s remnants is a natural source of enjoyment for the devotees, it should be done — as should all other parts of the vow — to please Krsna. Thus while honouring prasada devotees are encouraged to recall the moments of the festival that were most meaningful to them or to discuss Krsna’s birth and the pastimes connected to it. Conversations of this sort are all-auspicious and will give the devotees spiritual joy.

Having eaten to their full satisfaction, devotees can then go before the Lord and offer Him their obeisances and the prayers that effortlessly pour from their hearts — hearts overflowing with the satisfaction of having fully observed Janmastami and pleased Radha-Syamasundara.

**Conclusion**

This appendix — based on Sanatana Gosvami’s own lengthy description — elaborates on the basic Janmastami festival given to us by Srila Prabhupada. While Srila Prabhupada obviously simplified the observance of Janmastami in comparison to what had been given by bis predecessor, he kept intact the essence of Janmastami, which is to fast and do nothing else but glorify Krsna until the actual time of His appearance.

Srila Prabhupada made concessions for his disciples by instructing them to follow Ekadasi only by fasting from grains and beans. At the same time, he had no objection to their following Ekadasi as it was recommended by Lord Caitanya — namely fasting completely from food and water and staying awake the entire night — as long as such a practice did not interfere with their service. Thus, for Krsna’s pleasure devotees are free to follow other versions of the Ekadasi vow, guided by these two extremes.’

The same principle applies to Janmastami. Devotees may either follow the basic Janmastami vow given to us by Srila Prabhupada, or add to it other aspects given by Sanatana Gosvami, up to and including the full observance described in this appendix.

Whichever authorised version of the Janmastami vow a devotee follows, he or she can rest assured that they have pleased the Supreme Lord and His associates. Sanatana Gosvami says:

*evam janmastamim krtva kartavyam navasisyatc*  
*sarvam punya-phalam prapya anta yati padam hareh*

**“When one observes Janmastami in this way, nothing else remains that he need do. He has already attained all pious benefits. At the end of this lifetime he will go to the abode of Lord Krsna.”**

## About the Author

Sivarama Swami was born in Budapest, Hungary in 1949, and his family emigrated to Canada during the failed 1956 Hungarian revolution. He became a disciple of A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, the founder-acarya of ISKCON, in 1973 and entered the renounced order of life (sannyasa) in 1979. Sivarama Swami is well known for his deep knowledge of Vaisnava literature and has written many books about Gaudiya Vaisnavism, including the “Krsna in Vrndavanai series. He is a member of ISKCON’s Governing Body Commission and is responsible for projects in Hungary, Turkey, and Romania. Although he travels and speaks internationally, he spends as much time as possible at New Vraja-dhama (Krishna Valley), a replica of Vrndavana and self-sufficient farming project in Hungary’s countryside.
